Remaining decisions to resolve

The following outstanding decisions should be recorded in a decision register, with an accountable owner, evidence required, due date and status. They should be treated as proposals for further review, not as decisions already authorised or implemented.

  • Group structure and jurisdiction. Confirm the intended role of each proposed entity and the country in which it would operate, hold assets, employ people or conduct business. Compare feasible structures against commercial purpose, tax residence, reporting obligations, substance requirements, control and cost. Do not incorporate or transfer assets until qualified advisers in each relevant jurisdiction have checked the design and its cross-border consequences.
  • Ownership and family governance. Agree who may own, lead and work in each part of the group; how family and non-family decision-makers are appointed; and which matters require board, family council or shareholder approval. Set out conflict-of-interest, confidentiality, dispute-resolution and related-party transaction procedures. A clear separation between family discussion, ownership decisions and business management is consistent with established family-business governance guidance (International Finance Corporation [IFC], 2011; IFC, n.d.).
  • Succession and continuity. Decide the intended process—not merely the preferred successor—for leadership transition, incapacity, retirement, death or disagreement. Confirm how the horological succession proposals relate to wider family, business and estate arrangements. Any succession charter should be coordinated with valid wills, ownership documents and applicable law by qualified current advisers.
  • Funding and financial controls. Approve a realistic capital plan for each proposed activity, including staged funding, contingency reserves and criteria for stopping or scaling a project. Identify who may commit funds, borrow, invest or provide guarantees, and establish reporting and independent review. Any fundraising, investment offer or financial promotion must be checked for applicable regulation before use.
  • Business priorities and pilots. Rank proposed activities by readiness, capability, capital required, risk and measurable benefit. Select a limited number of pilots, each with a named lead, budget, customer or user evidence, milestones and a go/no-go review. In particular, define what success would mean for the apprenticeship model and secure-hotspot device before committing to wider deployment.
  • Education, training and mobility. Clarify the objective, intended participants, costs and outcomes of the São Paulo course map and other learning plans. Check admissions, safeguarding, visas, insurance, accommodation and recognition of qualifications with current providers and qualified advisers. Family-business education is more effective when it develops the whole person and connects learning with practical experience, rather than treating training as a stand-alone activity (Barbera et al., 2015).
  • Technology, information and intellectual property. Decide who owns, administers and can access family and business systems, code, records and intellectual property. Set rules for account recovery, permissions, backups, incident response and handover when a person leaves a role. The technology-independence proposals should be tested for security and maintainability before being relied upon for critical operations.
  • Product readiness and responsibility. Before any device or other product is sold, distributed or used in a consequential setting, identify the applicable safety, radio, electrical, consumer, labelling and import requirements in every target market. Establish a testing, quality-control, warranty, support and product-liability plan. Technical feasibility alone is not evidence of legal market readiness.
  • Data and privacy. Identify what personal or sensitive information each proposed service collects, where it is stored, who can access it and how long it is retained. Decide who is responsible for privacy governance, security incidents and responding to individuals’ requests. Obtain jurisdiction-specific advice before collecting or transferring data, particularly across Nigeria, Mauritius and Brazil.
  • Review and accountability. Adopt a regular review cycle for the group plan, with a concise dashboard covering finances, risks, delivery milestones, training outcomes and unresolved approvals. Record decisions and assumptions, including reasons for deferring a project. Family-business research is evolving; governance and strategy should therefore be reviewed as the family, enterprises and external conditions change (McLarty et al., 2026).

18. Professional advisers

The plans raise issues that cannot safely be resolved from a strategy document alone. Legal, tax, trust, investment, immigration, product certification, data protection and succession issues need qualified current advice. Advice should be obtained from professionals authorised and experienced in the relevant jurisdiction and subject matter; a general adviser in one country should not be assumed to cover the others. A practical advisory team would include:

  • Nigerian counsel and accountant: to review Nigerian entities and operations, employment and commercial arrangements, tax and reporting, any local fundraising, and the legal and regulatory position of proposed products or services.
  • Mauritian counsel and tax adviser: if Mauritius is being considered for a holding, investment or other role, to test whether the proposed purpose, governance, substance, ownership and reporting arrangements are lawful and commercially appropriate. Obtain coordinated cross-border tax advice rather than relying on a single-country view.
  • Brazilian counsel and accountant: where the São Paulo education or any business activity could involve residence, study, employment, contracting, payments, tax, consumer obligations or data processing. Confirm current immigration and education requirements before making commitments.
  • Trust, private-client and succession specialists: to review any proposed trust or family-wealth arrangements, wills, incapacity planning, beneficial ownership, inheritance consequences and the interaction between family charters and enforceable legal instruments.
  • Regulated investment and fundraising advisers: to review investment governance, risk appetite, due diligence and any proposal to solicit capital, make investment recommendations or offer financial products.
  • Product compliance and technical specialists: to determine the certifications, testing, import approvals, safety documentation and post-market obligations applicable to the secure-hotspot device or other products in each intended market.
  • Data-protection and cybersecurity advisers: to map data flows, assess applicable privacy requirements, prepare appropriate notices and agreements, and test security, access control, backup and incident-response arrangements.
  • Independent accounting and governance support: to help establish budgets, management accounts, internal controls, audit or assurance requirements, decision records and board or family-council processes.

The advisers should receive the relevant source documents, a clear statement of intended activities and a list of decisions sought. Their written advice should identify assumptions, jurisdiction, date, limitations and required actions. The family should retain responsibility for decisions; professional advice does not replace suitable governance or ongoing compliance.

19. Conclusion

The House of Ezeme materials describe an interconnected ambition spanning family governance, business and ownership structures, succession, learning, technology and enterprise development. Their value will depend on turning that ambition into a sequence of evidenced, affordable and accountable decisions. The immediate priority is not to implement every proposal at once, but to confirm purpose, ownership, capability, cost and risk, then proceed through controlled stages. A useful first stage is to establish the governance and financial foundations: agree decision rights, record the intended roles of entities, create a reliable financial baseline and appoint accountable leads. The family can then select a small number of viable pilots and define their success measures, safeguards and stopping conditions. The education and apprenticeship proposals should be linked to demonstrated learning and employment outcomes; the technology and product proposals should pass security, certification and market-readiness checks before wider use. The family should distinguish aspirations, working assumptions, approved decisions and completed actions in all planning documents. It should also revisit those documents as circumstances, regulations and family priorities change. Sound family-business governance supports continuity and accountability, but it cannot substitute for professional advice on the legal and financial consequences of implementation (IFC, 2011; IFC, n.d.; Lagos Business School, n.d.). Next steps: upload the local reference file for review; verify the current state of each proposal and the family’s finances; then ask Nigerian, Mauritian and Brazilian counsel and an accountant to review the plans before any legal implementation. The preliminary load estimates are about 213 kWh/day for Building 1 and 212 kWh/day for Building 2. A 250 kWh battery at 85% provides 212.5 kWh nominally usable, approximately the estimated daily load before inverter losses, reserve, ageing and temperature effects. Appendix C. Akuzo Dual-Server Specification — Summary, Risks and Implementation Conditions

A. Status and scope

This appendix summarizes the proposed Ezeme Family Server and Akuzo Building Management Server (BMS) programme for the Akuzo compound, Nkpor, Anambra State. The equipment, capacities, room locations, services, growth assumptions and rollout months below are proposals in the supplied specification, not verified site conditions, approved engineering designs, confirmed prices or demonstrated service levels. They require validation before procurement or construction. The proposal envisages two separately managed facilities within the compound. The Family Server would serve the Ezeme household; the BMS would support building operations and a capped, view-only Jellyfin service for residents. The BMS is proposed to expand as buildings are added. Its larger scale, revenue role and broader user base also make it a higher-impact operational and privacy risk.

B. Architecture, tiers and separation

The proposed Family Server has five trust tiers: Tier 0 networking and security edge; Tier 1 household applications and media; Tier 2 AI and compute; Tier 3 identity, credentials and governance; and Tier 4 local backup and recovery. The BMS has corresponding C0 networking, C1 virtualized business and building services, C2 media and storage, and C3 backup and continuity tiers. Separate VLANs and firewall rules are proposed within each facility. VLANs are logical controls, not physical security boundaries. Each tier needs documented addressing, routing, default-deny rules, permitted service flows, administration paths, logging and recovery procedures. The specification should resolve conflicting descriptions of the Family Server edge: it assigns gateway and VLAN roles to both OPNsense on Protectli hardware and a UniFi Dream Machine SE. It should identify one authoritative routing and policy-enforcement design and define the role of every switch, controller and firewall. The proposed “no shared cable, switch, VLAN or credential” rule conflicts with the proposed family dashboard feed from the BMS. A feed cannot cross a complete network disconnection without a defined interface. Design it as an explicitly approved, one-way transfer, preferably through a BMS-controlled export or tightly constrained intermediary in a screened network zone. Permit only specified status fields, use authenticated and encrypted transport, and test that the Family Server cannot initiate control or administration traffic to the BMS. Do not treat a read-only application screen alone as proof of one-way network access. The Family Server also requires clarification: Vaultwarden’s application, database and keys cannot be operationally independent of one another. Authentik must be reachable by services that use it. Define which components hold secrets, how services obtain them, how access is logged, and how service outages are handled. A separate VLAN does not by itself make a credential store unreachable or safe.

C. Proposed hardware, rooms and services

The proposed Family Server includes enterprise compute for household files, photos, identity, automation, cameras and Jellyfin; a GPU server for local AI and media transcoding; a small restricted vault host; and a 60-bay backup chassis. The BMS proposal includes a three-node Proxmox cluster, two 60-bay media/storage chassis, transcode nodes, a separate backup chassis, redundant firewalls, tenant networking and business services. Listed software includes Nextcloud, Immich, Vaultwarden, Authentik, Home Assistant, Frigate, Jellyfin, Odoo, Prometheus and Grafana. These are proposed selections, not evidence that the specified configurations are compatible, licensed, supportable or sized for actual workloads. The Family Server is proposed beneath Building 1; the BMS is proposed in a dedicated ground-level room between Buildings 1 and 2. The underground location is not endorsed by this appendix. Before committing to it, qualified structural, geotechnical, civil, mechanical, electrical and fire professionals should assess groundwater and seasonal flooding, surface runoff, tanking and penetrations, drainage, sump redundancy, safe egress, fire compartmentation, floor loading, equipment access and replacement routes. A sump pump with battery backup is not proof against flooding, and a room below grade may be difficult to inspect, evacuate or recover after water ingress. Compare an above-ground, flood-protected location before design freeze. Both rooms need engineered heat-load and airflow calculations, not cooling capacity inferred from equipment lists. The proposed 2.5-ton Family Server cooling and 5-ton BMS cooling must be checked against measured or manufacturer-rated IT load, local ambient conditions, redundancy, heat rejection, condensate management, filtration and maintenance access. Specify alarms and an out-of-hours response. Fresh-air exchange, if required, must be designed for the room and equipment; it is not a substitute for cooling. Review humidity control, dust, corrosion, acoustic exposure and hot-aisle/cold-aisle arrangements. Top-loading storage chassis need service clearance above them, which may conflict with rack layout. Electrical design must establish actual continuous and peak loads, phase and circuit allocation, earthing, bonding, surge protection, transfer switching, generator capacity, fuel autonomy and safe shutdown. The proposed 10–15 kVA shared generator has not been shown to support the BMS servers, cooling, pumps and building loads simultaneously. UPS VA ratings do not establish runtime or compatibility with GPU transients. Provide load-bank testing, monitored circuits, battery replacement plans and an orderly shutdown strategy. Coordinate smoke detection, suppression and any power-cutoff relay with fire and electrical professionals; indiscriminate power cutoff can increase data loss or life-safety risk. Specify appropriate detection, extinguishing method, emergency procedures and fire-rated separation. The listed storage totals are planning estimates, not guaranteed usable capacity. Raw disk capacity, RAID/ZFS or Ceph layout, parity, replication, spares, formatting, snapshots and growth headroom materially change usable capacity. Two storage chassis, ZFS replication and Ceph should not be described as a single replicated pool without a validated design. Confirm drive interface and server compatibility, storage failure domains, network throughput, software support and recovery time. A three-node Proxmox cluster does not automatically guarantee service continuity “within seconds”; quorum, fencing, storage availability, application dependencies and tested failover are required. Likewise, caching does not establish capacity for 100 or more concurrent streams. Measure expected concurrency, bitrates, internet/Wi-Fi capacity and transcode demand in a pilot. Validate the GPU, power, cooling and driver choices against actual workloads.

D. Backup, off-site design and access

Local snapshots and replication help recover from some failures but do not protect against a site-wide event, theft, destructive error or ransomware that reaches the backup system. The Family proposal sends only Tier 3 vault backups off-site; that leaves household files and photos without an off-site copy. The BMS proposal sends billing and tenant records off-site but excludes the media library. These are deliberate cost and data-priority choices, not complete disaster recovery. Adopt a documented, encrypted backup policy that identifies priority data, retention, recovery-point and recovery-time objectives, access controls, immutable or offline copies, and restoration owners. Keep at least one recoverable copy off-site for critical household and business records, application configuration and encryption-key recovery material, subject to privacy and cost review. Test restores regularly, including a full rebuild exercise. Document how keys are recovered if the primary vault or site is unavailable. A backup chassis in the same room is not an off-site copy. The intended boundary is that family services are restricted to the household and BMS services to authorized residents and staff. Implement separate identity realms, credentials, administrative accounts, remote-access keys, logging and incident procedures. Do not extend the family Tailscale mesh to BMS users. Require MFA for administrators, managed devices where practicable, prompt patching, secure out-of-band management and restricted vendor access. Tenant Wi-Fi, cameras, building controls, servers and staff administration need separate policies. Building controls should remain safe and operable locally if the BMS or network fails.

E. Costs, staffing and principal risks

The supplied specification does not provide a costed bill of materials or project total. Missing costs include current equipment and disk quotations, shipping, import duties and taxes, installation, structured cabling and fibre, racks and civil works, waterproofing, drainage, electrical upgrades, generator and fuel, cooling and energy consumption, UPS battery replacement, internet circuits, off-site storage, software or support contracts, spares, insurance and ongoing maintenance. Obtain local, landed-cost quotations and a whole-life operating-cost estimate. Confirm that proposed products are available, supported and serviceable in Nigeria before standardizing on them. The BMS is described as a business asset but has no defined staffing plan or service commitment. Name accountable owners for infrastructure, applications, billing, facilities controls, security and data protection. Set coverage hours, escalation, backup checks, patching, access approval, incident response, vendor support and resident communications. Facilities staff should receive documented procedures and role-based training; a runbook does not remove the need for competent technical support. Budget for planned maintenance and replacement, not just initial deployment. Key risks include flooding, fire, overheating, unstable power, cooling failure, equipment theft, accidental damage, delayed spares, misconfiguration, exposed management interfaces, compromised remote credentials, insider misuse, ransomware and dependence on one operator. CCTV, tenant identity, billing and occupancy-linked service controls create privacy and misuse risks. Define camera purpose, placement, signage, access, retention and disclosure rules; exclude private interiors as proposed. Review handling of children’s and tenant data, consent and lawful basis, retention, breach response and cross-border encrypted backups under applicable Nigerian data-protection requirements. Confirm rights and licensing for any paid or shared Jellyfin content. Do not automatically suspend essential building services when a payment is overdue; separate billing enforcement from safety-critical controls.

F. Recommended implementation gates

  • Design gate: Confirm user counts, service levels, data volumes, concurrency, privacy requirements and recovery objectives. Commission site, flood, structural, electrical, fire and cooling reviews. Resolve the gateway design and specify the one-way status-feed boundary before construction.
  • Cost and procurement gate: Produce a compatible, vendor-verified bill of materials, landed capital cost, operating budget, support plan, spare-parts strategy and staged procurement decision. Recalculate usable storage and power from a validated configuration.
  • Build and commissioning gate: Approve room drawings, drainage, power, cooling, fire protection, access control, cabling and monitoring. Test generator/UPS operation, cooling alarms, leak detection, failover, access logs and emergency shutdown before loading production data.
  • Pilot gate: Bring up isolated networks and a small set of non-critical services first. Test tenant Wi-Fi isolation, family/BMS separation, service limits, camera access, workload capacity and the status-feed direction. Do not promise availability based only on cluster or firewall redundancy.
  • Data and recovery gate: Before migration or paid launch, verify encrypted backups, off-site access controls, restore procedures, key recovery, ransomware protections and a witnessed recovery drill. Record evidence and remediate failures.
  • Operational launch and growth gate: Assign trained owners, approve runbooks and privacy notices, establish monitoring and incident escalation, and set a review period. Add storage, compute or buildings only when measured demand, support capacity, power, cooling and updated cost justify expansion.

The programme should proceed as a professionally reviewed, staged proposal. Neither the underground siting nor the stated capacities, security properties, uptime expectations or growth economics should be treated as established until the relevant design, commissioning and recovery gates have been passed.

Appendix D. Ozi Ikoro Master Business Plan Summary

Purpose and status of the plan

Ozi Ikoro is proposed as a hybrid museum, contemporary art gallery and anthropological research hub in Awka, Anambra State. Its plan centres on converting a warehouse into a flexible cultural venue that combines heritage interpretation, scholarship, conservation, digital media and commercial activity. The source document is a business-plan proposal, not evidence that the site has been secured, the institution established, collections acquired, partnerships agreed or funding raised. All facilities, prices, staffing, income targets and milestones below should therefore be treated as proposed assumptions until verified through feasibility work and implementation.

Mission, identity and visitor offer

The proposed mission is to document, preserve and commercialise the material and oral history of the East through anthropology and modern curation. “Ozi Ikoro,” translated in the plan as “Message of the Drum,” expresses an institution intended to communicate history, culture and identity through objects, images and scholarship. Its stated values are integrity in acquisition and provenance, accessibility, scholarship, preservation, interpretive innovation and commercial viability. The proposed visitor sequence moves from an entrance courtyard and reception through three museum zones, a digital theatre, a visible conservation area, a library, and a store or café. The warehouse’s exposed structure is intended as part of the institution’s identity. Suspended textiles, mobile partitions, shelving, lighting and changes in floor treatment would define flexible spaces without requiring permanent walls. The plan anticipates a mural, an entrance sculpture and night lighting, subject to design, permissions, cost and accessibility review. The three museum zones are: “Footprints in Red Earth,” for historical artefacts; “The Future of Form,” for contemporary Nigerian art; and “Drawing and Object,” pairing artworks with related objects to explore visual histories. The artefacts zone would display approximately 30–40 objects at a time and rotate them quarterly. The commercial gallery would mount quarterly solo exhibitions of around 20–30 works and an annual thematic group exhibition. A drawing table and community wall would invite visitor participation. The proposed anthropology library and archive would hold reference and rare books, digitised records and photographs, oral histories, maps and research materials relating to Igbo and Southeast Nigerian studies. In-library access is proposed to be free, with registered researcher borrowing and appointment access for rare books. The plan does not yet specify collection-development priorities, rights management, cataloguing standards, opening hours or a fully costed climate-control strategy. The digital theatre is proposed as an 8m by 10m space with acoustic treatment, modular seating, a 12-screen “decoder wall” and three to five individual viewing stations with headphones. Scheduled screenings and self-directed browsing would draw on historic film, television, missionary, community and contemporary footage, including sensitively contextualised material relating to the Biafra War. Use of these materials depends on identifying rights holders, securing permissions and providing appropriate historical context. A glass-enclosed conservation corner, approximately 6m by 8m, would make selected preservation work visible to visitors. The proposed facilities include dry-work and wet-preservation areas, specimen storage, task lighting, a fume hood, personal protective equipment and an eyewash station. A small collection of animal specimens is proposed for research and education, sourced only through documented natural deaths, permitted roadkill collection or donations, with no endangered species without permits. The detailed handling, licensing, occupational safety, hazardous-waste and specialist staffing requirements remain to be established before this activity proceeds.

Audiences and public engagement

The plan identifies local residents and schools, Awka and Onitsha business communities, Nigerian and diaspora art collectors, researchers, universities, tourists, corporate clients and the wider public as audiences. It proposes school visits, free local admission days, elder-led oral-history work, travelling exhibitions, community identification of photographs and consultation with elders, cultural groups and Ozo title holders. These are proposed programmes; community consent procedures, participant compensation, safeguarding arrangements and data-use protocols are not yet specified.

Revenue model and financial assumptions

Proposed income sources include admissions, memberships, art sales, store and café sales, events and rentals, consultancy, grants and donations. The stated admission prices are ₦1,500 for adults, ₦500 for students, free for children under 12, ₦3,500 for a family ticket and ₦1,200 per person for adult groups of ten or more. Proposed annual memberships range from ₦15,000 for Friends to ₦250,000 for Benefactors, with a ₦200,000 corporate tier. The gallery proposes a 40% commission on art sales, with 60% paid to the artist, as well as art advisory and rental services. The plan gives indicative price bands from ₦50,000–₦500,000 for emerging artists, ₦500,000–₦3,000,000 for mid-career artists and ₦3,000,000 and above for established artists. A separate “Mantlepiece, Statement and Monument” schedule gives overlapping ranges, so a single transparent pricing framework should be confirmed. Other proposed income includes store and café sales, consultancy, facility hire and an annual gala with tickets of ₦50,000–₦100,000, corporate tables of ₦500,000–₦1,000,000 and an asserted annual net target of ₦10–20 million. That gala target is not supported by a cost model in the source. The proposed Year 3 revenue mix is 40% art commission, 15% admissions, 10% memberships, 15% store and café, 10% events and rentals, 5% consultancy, and 5% grants and donations. These percentages add to 100%, but the plan provides no total revenue forecast, capital budget, operating-cost schedule, cash-flow plan, tax treatment, break-even analysis, sensitivity analysis or evidence that the proposed prices match local demand. They should be treated as planning assumptions, not forecasts.

Operations, governance and ethical stewardship

The proposed warehouse-scale team comprises a full-time Director/Curator, Assistant Curator/Registrar, Gallery Manager and Conservation Assistant; part-time Librarian/Archivist and Marketing/Admin staff; two to three part-time docents; and contracted facilities and security staff. Volunteers could include students, retired professionals, community elders and artists. Recruitment, salary levels, staff training, workload, volunteer supervision and succession arrangements require further planning. The plan proposes university relationships for exhibitions, student prizes, internships, residencies and research, and names institutions including Paul University, Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University, Godfrey Okoye University, Madonna University and Enugu State University of Science and Technology. These are prospective partners, not confirmed agreements. The plan also identifies possible collaboration with state cultural ministries, the National Commission for Museums and Monuments, community groups and international archival programmes. Collection ethics are central to the stated values. Historical acquisitions are proposed only where legally and ethically obtainable, with full provenance; family heirlooms, reputable dealers, reproductions and contemporary artist submissions are identified as possible sources. The plan recognises that Igbo-Ukwu originals cannot be assumed available for display and proposes high-fidelity replicas. Before acquiring or exhibiting material, Ozi Ikoro should adopt written policies for provenance research, title and export/import checks, culturally restricted material, consultation and consent, repatriation claims, loans, deaccessioning, conflicts of interest and documentation. Digitised colonial records, photographs and films also require rights review and culturally informed access terms. QR-linked interpretation, English and Igbo content, audio description, virtual tours and digital educational resources are proposed. The target of digitising five objects weekly, or 260 annually, is an operational ambition rather than a funded capacity estimate. The proposed “Certificate of Authenticity” records artwork details and an Ozi Ikoro inventory code, but should be supported by registrar procedures and clear artist agreements; it must not imply independent authentication beyond the evidence held by the institution. The source anticipates eventual foundation status in Year 3, but does not define the current or future legal entity, board composition, fiduciary duties, appointment process, financial controls or reporting obligations. The Ezeme master plan should require a governing board or equivalent oversight body, approved policies, annual budgets, independent accounts and clear authority over acquisitions, sales and restricted funds before launch.

Relationship to Ozikoro, Ozituma and the family group

The source plan does not define the mandates, ownership or legal relationship of Ozi Ikoro, Ozikoro, Ozituma or the family group. Their relationship must therefore be set by the Ezeme master plan, rather than inferred from similar names. A suitable proposal is for the entities to share a family-level vision and, where agreed, coordinate referrals, communications, procurement or selected services. Ozi Ikoro should nevertheless operate as a distinct institution with its own legal and administrative identity, governing authority, bank accounts, budget, contracts, staff responsibilities, collection register, donor restrictions and performance reporting. Any shared services, premises, staff, branding or financial support should be documented through written agreements, with costs and decision rights disclosed. This arrangement would permit portfolio coordination without treating the entities’ assets, income, liabilities or cultural mandates as interchangeable.

Phased launch and key gaps

The plan proposes Year 1 for warehouse conversion, systems installation, an initial collection, a digital archive, university approaches and a soft opening. Year 2 would establish market presence through six exhibitions, a first gala, a catalogue and a target of 100 members. Year 3 would pursue foundation status, a regional conference, international grants and more than 200 members. These milestones depend on secured premises, approvals, capital, staffing and operating funds, none of which is verified in the source. A gate-based launch should first confirm feasibility, legal status, building condition, accessibility, fire and life safety, security, insurance, climate control, collection policies and rights clearances. Public opening should follow only when essential systems and competent staff are in place. Key missing plans include a site survey and conversion cost plan; a detailed three-year budget and funding strategy; a demand and visitor study; a collections and storage capacity plan; a conservation risk assessment; emergency and business-continuity procedures; a digital preservation and cybersecurity plan; and measurable outcomes for community benefit, research, access and financial sustainability. These matters are prerequisites for converting the promising concept into a deliverable and accountable component of the Ezeme master plan.

Appendix E. Programme-by-programme source coverage audit

This audit was added after a second, targeted search of Google Drive by file name and by distinctive project phrases. It separates standalone documents from sections contained inside broader documents, so the family does not mistake a programme heading for a separately saved file.

1. Nkpor Furniture & Soft Furnishings Cluster — the engine

Sources:Ezeme Group Master Plan;Nkpor Ezeme Furniture and Soft Furnishings Apprenticeship Model. The Group Master Plan identifies soft furnishings/upholstery, furniture and agriculture as the three cash engines. The apprenticeship model sets out the combined workshop, institutional fit-outs, supply chain, partner-settlement/equity concept and proposed growth cycles. Both are dedicated source documents.

2. Akuzo Residence and Akuzo Court — the two costed buildings

Sources:Akuzo Development Programme;Akuzo Urban Transformation Plan v3. The Development Programme describes the two building proposals, unit mixes, construction-company model, power and utility assumptions, and budget claims. The Urban Transformation Plan sets out the wider 30-year residential district and production-township vision. Both are dedicated source documents.

3. Akuzo Dual Server Programme — two independent facilities

Source:Akuzo Dual Server Specification. Describes separate Ezeme Family Server and Akuzo Building Management Server facilities, trust tiers, network boundaries, applications, backup design and operating assumptions. Dedicated source document found.

4. Ezeme Jewellery Bank — pledge, never sell

Source:Ezeme-Horological-Succession-Charter. Contains a section titled “On the Ezeme Jewellery Bank and the Permitted Loan”. It sets out a proposed collateral-loan arrangement for registered charter watches while prohibiting sale of the watches. The Jewellery Bank is a substantive section in the watch charter; no separate file named “Ezeme Jewellery Bank” was found in the searchable account.

5. Secure Personal Hotspot Programme — 20 units from Shenzhen

Source:Ezeme Family Secure Hotspot Device. The document itself is titled “Ezeme Family Secure Personal Hotspot Program — Revised Specification, Family Allocation & China ODM Sourcing Plan”. It specifies 20 units, 14 personalised units and six spares, proposed hardware/firmware, and Shenzhen-area ODM sourcing. Dedicated source document found.

6. Ezeme Hardware Platform — five generations, beginning with a ten-unit pilot

Source:Ezeme Family Tech Independence Guide. Section 6 includes “The Ezeme Hardware Platform”, the Media Frame, manufacturing philosophy and a hardware roadmap. The roadmap explicitly lists Generation One — Foundation; Generation Two — Smart Home; Generation Three — Family Productivity; Generation Four — Infrastructure; and Generation Five — Future Innovation. The Media Frame manufacturing section specifies a ten-unit pilot before later production batches. The platform, five-generation roadmap and ten-unit pilot are contained in the Tech Independence Guide; no separate file named “Ezeme Hardware Platform” was found in the searchable account.

7. Ezeme Agriculture — the third cash engine

Sources:Ezeme Group Master Plan; supporting references inHouse of Ezeme Corporate Architecture,Ezeme Family Holding Structure, andHouse of Ezeme Raising Plan. The Group Master Plan expressly names agriculture as the third cash engine, with production in the Idemmili belt and processing in Nkpor. It links agriculture to agro-manufacturing and the land-acquisition/development fund. Other documents connect agriculture to the proposed child-domain, education and ownership structure. Found in the Group Master Plan and supporting family documents; no separate file titled “Ezeme Agriculture” was found in the searchable account.

8. São Paulo — separate company / Brazil venture

Sources:Ezeme 11-Year Plan;Ezeme São Paulo Course Map. The 11-Year Plan details the Brazil-to-global smart-interiors venture: São Paulo salon mirror/vanity pilots, embedded Ezeme OS, skills and supplier learning, customer acquisition and staged market expansion. The Course Map supplies a learning pathway. The plan does not use the exact phrase “separate company” in the searchable text reviewed, so the legal separation instruction should be confirmed and written explicitly into the final corporate structure. Two dedicated source documents found; separate-company wording needs explicit governance/legal confirmation.

What the second search established

  • The eight programme areas are not all eight separate files. Several are named sections inside the Group Master Plan, Tech Independence Guide or Horological Succession Charter.
  • The primary connected Drive account contains the dedicated documents listed above and was searched by title and by multiple exact or paired content terms.
  • A Drive item titled My House Plan was also identified as a possible additional residential source, but downloading its contents returned a permission error. It is therefore not counted as reviewed.Open My House Plan.
  • A second connected Google Drive account could not be searched because its connection returned an authentication-scope error. The search is therefore comprehensive for the accessible primary account, but cannot honestly be described as exhaustive across that second account until it is re-authorised.
  • The next revision of the family plan should use this source map as a traceability register: every major programme should have one canonical document, an owner, a version date, a budget, an implementation status and links to supporting documents.

documents/HOUSE_OF_EZEME.html.html:
THE HOUSE OF EZEME — ARCHITECTURE OF RECORD

Companion to the website at site/. Every structural claim below is sourced from the family's own library at ~/Projects/Ezeme/.research/gdocs/ — the plan files are cited inline. Nothing here is invented, and where the library and reality differ, this document says so.

1. The three layers, and why they are separate

plans/00_Family_Business.md §1 states the cardinal rule: the family business is not a company. It is three things stacked, and they must never be confused with each other.

Layer What it is What it must never do
FamilyThe House of Ezeme — Charter, Assembly, Council, CourtManage companies
OwnershipThe Trust → the PTC → Family HoldingsTrade or operate
EnterpriseEzeme Group → five branches → operating companiesDecide family questions

Each layer is forbidden from doing the others' work. This is what makes the enterprise investable and the family survivable at the same time — the failure mode of most family wealth is a single generation treating the company as a personal estate, or the company treating the family as staff.

2. The ownership chain

plans/README.md states it, and it is the form that appears on every licence application:

Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius, Trusts Act 2001)
   → Ezeme Family Holdings PTC Ltd          (trustee)
   → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd  (GBC — the ownership layer)
   → Ezeme Group Nigeria Ltd                (the mother company)
   → Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu (the five branches)
   → 54 operating companies

Naming is settled at v5.0. Companies take a child's name plus a plain function — the Dangote pattern. Akunnia's companies take the short form Aku. The library records a naming correction of record: the Mauritius layer is Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd, and plans that write "GBC" there are defective on a licence application that must name a shareholder correctly (LICENCE_OWNERSHIP_AUDIT.md §4.4 item 62).

3. The five institutions and two support bodies

EZEME_FAMILY_KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md §2, drawn from the Ezeme Family Governance Charter — itself explicitly modelled on Ụmụnna (Igbo kindred deliberation) but scoped to this household and bloodline rather than the wider kindred.

THE EZEME FAMILY
   ↓
FAMILY ASSEMBLY          all members — monthly; larger Annual Assembly each December
   ↓
FAMILY COUNCIL           the cabinet — weekly, Saturday evening
   ↓                    ↓
FAMILY COURT         FAMILY BUSINESS BOARD
(justice)            (business and wealth)
   ↓
FAMILY TREASURY      FAMILY SECRETARIAT & ARCHIVE

The Firewall is the principle that makes the whole thing work: the Court does not decide business questions; the Board does not adjudicate personal grievances. A disagreement between siblings who also work together is a family matter unless the Business Board formally determines it has business consequences. No person may be judge, prosecutor and accused in the same matter.

Membership follows Igbo kindred custom — once admitted to sit in the meeting, a member's voice carries equal weight regardless of age or seniority. A member either has not yet been admitted, or is admitted and equal. There is no graduated vote.

Stage Age Rights
Observer8–12Present; may speak when invited; no vote
Participant13–17May raise matters; account recorded and weighed; no vote
Member18+, on Council admissionFull and equal voting rights in Assembly, Council, Court and Board

Family Officers: Family Head · Chairperson · Judge/Justice Chair · Secretary · Treasurer · Business Board Chair · Archivist · Children's Representative (formal voice for the younger generation before voting membership).

Rhythm: Saturday morning — Court, only when a matter requires it; Saturday evening — Council, then informal family time. First Saturday monthly — Business Board. A separate Saturday — Assembly. December/January — Annual Assembly.

4. Reserved matters

plans/00_Family_Business.md §2 — acts requiring Family Holdings' consent, not any individual's:

  • change of name, or brand disassociation from "Ezeme"
  • disposal or encumbrance of material assets above an annually fixed threshold
  • issuance of shares, dilution, or admission of any external investor
  • any pledge or charge over shares
  • change of control, merger or listing
  • winding up
  • appointment or removal of external auditors

Standing rights sit with Family Holdings rather than any person, so they survive succession automatically: a permanent non-removable Family Director on every subsidiary board; quarterly management accounts and annual audited statements; right of first refusal on share transfers; drag/tag-along restricted to intra-family or approved transfers.

Two rules with long consequences:

  1. Cap-table hygiene. No entity anywhere issues equity to employees, operators or partners at

Group or holdco level. Employee ownership exists only inside operating subsidiaries, capped, and never touching the Mauritius layer. *The library calls this "the price of institutional capital."

  1. Beneficial ownership is unconditional; operational control is not. An heir does not lose

their stake by stepping back — but operational control is granted, not inherited, and a non-engagement trigger refers control to the Group Board, which appoints a steward. Nothing is confiscated. Control, not ownership, is what moves.

5. What the public site may carry, and what it may not

This is a design decision with a legal and reputational edge, so it is written down rather than left to whoever edits the site next.

Public (ezeme.org) Family only (/family/)
The House, its motto, its five branchesThe constitution and its amendments
Each branch's remit and its companies by nameCouncil and Court minutes
That the programme exists, and its horizonReserved matters, cap table, the cap-table rules
The Record — dated, verified, and nothing elseCapital requirements and the reconciliations
Live ventures (Ozikoro, OmaPolo)The 60-plan library in full
The per-child roadmaps
Anything naming a family member's private affairs

No capital figure, valuation, or funding number appears on the public site. The library states a programme capital requirement in the trillions of naira; publishing that beside a family that today holds two domain names and one live platform invites exactly the wrong attention and makes every future claim suspect. The Record states what exists. The family area holds what is intended.

6. The honest gap

The architecture above is complete and coherent. Almost none of it exists yet.

Library Reality, 9 October 2026
ConstitutionWritten, with five institutions and a Court procedureNot adopted
Ownership chainSpecified to the entity nameNo entity incorporated
Group and branches60 plans, 54 companiesNone trading
Domains—ezeme.org held and empty (HTTP 522); ozikoro.com and omapolo.com live
CapitalProgramme requirement stated in the plansNo capital raised

This is not a criticism of the plans — it is the sequencing fact that should drive the next year. The library was written as a destination. The work now is the first mile: incorporate the two live ventures properly, adopt the constitution, secure the Tier 1 domains, and let the website describe an institution at the beginning rather than an empire that does not exist.

The next ninety days, in order:

  1. Secure the domains — Tier 1 of DOMAINS.md. Cheap, and every one is a door you do not want

someone else holding. akunnia.com especially: the only branch name still free.

  1. Adopt the constitution — the Charter exists as a document; give it a date, a signature and a

first Assembly. A constitution that has never been used is not yet a constitution.

  1. Incorporate correctly, once — the two live ventures (Ozikoro, OmaPolo) are the only real

assets. Their ownership is the first test of the chain and the first place a mistake compounds.

  1. Publish this site — site/ on ezeme.org, with the family area closed until it can be

genuinely gated at the edge (site/FAMILY-ACCESS.md is not yet written; the source layout is site/).

  1. Fix the birth anchor — the per-child roadmaps are keyed to each child's age. One date —

the first child's birth year — resolves every band in docs/ROADMAPS.md to a calendar.

FOUNDING AND MATURITY — what is being built now, and every business in the library

Two corpora, one document. The first section is the programme being founded now, from the family's own earlier documents. The rest is every business in the 60-plan library, read at its founding year and at maturity.

What this is. For each of the 54 companies, the plan's own milestone table read at two points: the founding year — what the business does when it starts — and maturity, the last year its plan states. Every line is extracted verbatim from section 9 of the plan of record. Nothing is authored.

How it is keyed to a child. The library anchors its horizon at Year 1 = 2027 (plans/16_Aku_Bank.md labels its columns Y1 (2027) … Y15 (2041)), so:

calendar year  =  2026 + plan year
child's age    =  plan year - (birth year - 2027)

If the first child arrives in the programme's first year, then plan Year 1 is that child's age 0–1 and the whole table below resolves to ages. One date — the birth year — sets every row. Until then the rows are dated in plan years, which is how the plans state them.

Every business, and what it depends on

Read this before the year columns below. The library does not state a start year for each company. Each plan's milestone table begins at its own Year 1 because that is the year the plan assumes it is funded — which is why the year columns below are identical across all 54 businesses and cannot be used to sequence them.

What the library does state is the dependency graph: section 11 of every plan names the other businesses it buys from, supplies, or cannot operate without, and cites them by plan file. A business cannot begin before its prerequisites exist, so that graph — not the year columns — is what sequences this programme.

The third input is the group plans' thematic year rows (Land, Farms, Processing, Storage, Trading, Manufacturing), which mark a dash where a theme has not started. Those are thematic rather than one-row-per-company, so they set the shape of a branch's early years without naming each company.

What this means for the roadmaps. The founding-year content and the maturity targets below are extracted and real. The calendar assignment requires three things this workspace does not have: the first child's birth year, the board's sequencing decision, and the capital in hand. Until then the order is determined by the prerequisite column, and it should be read as a graph rather than a schedule.

THE FOUNDING PROGRAMME — what is being built now

Read this first. The 60 plans that follow are the destination: a conglomerate at a 15-year horizon, Year 1 set at 2027. The businesses actually being founded now are not in the library at all. They are in the family's own earlier documents, and they are nearer and more concrete than anything below. This section states them, what each requires, and what must happen before what.

One mechanism has been scrapped. The Igba Odibo apprenticeship equity model — settling apprentices into 50% ownership of new branches — is no longer the plan. The furniture and soft furnishings business stands; how it grows in place of Igba Odibo is not written down anywhere, and is the first item below.

1. Nkpor Furniture & Soft Furnishings

The first operating business. One workshop, two crafts — furniture builds the frame, soft furnishings finish it — so an institution can order a complete fit-out from one contract.

What founding it requires

  • Workshop space in Nkpor with room for a woodworking floor and a soft furnishings floor side by side
  • Both equipment sets: woodworking machines, and sewing and upholstery machines

The honest ceiling. Africa's entire capital stock is roughly $2 trillion. A $15–25bn platform is therefore a meaningful share of African alternatives flows — and reaching it requires international LP capital, not African. The hub is not optional; it is the precondition.

First ninety days

  1. Decide the hub: London or New York. This gates everything — authorisation, tax structure and talent pool. London is likely simpler for an Africa-facing manager; New York carries more prestige and deeper capital.
  2. Commission the licence-by-licence ownership audit before incorporating the hub. A London or NY manager above Nigerian operating companies may disqualify the Group from NBC, NACOC and other licences. Resolve this first, not after.
  3. Instruct counsel in four jurisdictions simultaneously — UK or US (manager), Cayman or Delaware (funds), Mauritius (holding), Nigeria (operations and assets). They must draft in coordination, not sequentially.
  4. Design the carry scheme — pool size, vesting, hurdle, clawback, and the firewall keeping carry out of Group equity. This document determines whether the Group can hire deal talent.
  5. Identify the microfinance bank acquisition target and open the CBN change-of-control conversation early. MFB acquisitions take time, and CBN approval is the critical path. In parallel, identify a licensed finance company for Aku Credit and a licensed private guard company for Aku Security — all three are acquisitions, all three sit on the same critical path, and none of them should wait on the hub being authorised.
  6. Map the first consolidation sector. Furniture and soft furnishings is the natural first — the Group already knows the trade, has the workshops and the apprenticeship model, and the sector is exactly the fragmented shape the strategy targets.
  7. Hire the Managing Partner before anything else. In this model the first senior hire is the strategy. Without a credible deal originator the funds cannot be raised and the hub is an empty office.
  8. Set the self-limiting rules as board resolutions — no fund above 25% Group-originated assets, stepping to 15% by Year 6; related-party transactions approved by independents sitting alone; and Group disputes above a stated value to independent arbitration institutions, never to Aku Arbitration.
  9. Stand up the governance half first, because it is the only part that earns in Year 1. Secure the private guard company and the finance company, recruit the legal team, and put Aku Legal to work on title perfection for land the Group is already buying. The finance half needs five years and outside capital; this half needs a licence, a team and a first client — all three of which the Group already has.
  10. Size the market before committing capital to it, because §2 could not. §2.4 names five figures that do not exist in reliable published form, and this action replaces each estimate with a measurement: the avoided-fee baseline audit (Aku Legal), the consolidated security vendor schedule (Aku Security) and the Group contract universe (Aku Arbitration), the current books of the three acquisition targets in item 5, one named research house engaged on Nigerian mid-market credit, and the AVCA and PenCom dataset subscriptions the library already cites. One budget line, five measurements, and a named-company pipeline on Aku Technology from Year 1 — which is what an investment committee can act on and an LP can audit.

Second child's domain plan. Domain corrected to Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security, with real estate removed to Okodu Group where the Master Plan places it (§6.5). Engine model is Blackstone — control, credit and carried interest — not BlackRock.   1. Decide the hub: London (FCA) or New York (SEC). This gates authorisation, tax structure, talent pool and fundraising. London is likely simpler for an Africa-facing manager; New York carries deeper capital pools and more prestige.
  2. Commission the licence-by-licence ownership audit before incorporating the hub. A London or New York manager above Nigerian operating companies may disqualify the Group from NBC, NACOC and other licences. Resolve this first — it is the one decision that can invalidate the structure.
  3. Appoint the three independent Group directors and seat an independent on the Investment Committee. Nothing else in this plan completes without them, and no LP, DFI or regulator engages before it is done. Publish the independence criteria and the IC's terms of reference.
  4. Adopt the capital allocation framework as a board resolution — the §4.1 split, the hurdle rates, the passion-asset list, the rule that the sponsor case is never the base case, and the 25%→15% Group-originated cap. This is the document that prevents risk #1.
  5. Design the carry scheme before hiring anyone senior — pool size, hurdle (8%), catch-up, vesting, whole-of-fund waterfall, clawback, and the firewall keeping carry out of Group equity. This document determines whether the Group can hire deal talent at all.
  6. Instruct counsel in four jurisdictions simultaneously — UK or US (the manager), Cayman or Delaware (the funds), Mauritius (the holding layer), Nigeria (operations and assets). They must draft in coordination, not sequentially, before the hub is incorporated.
  7. Hire the Managing Partner, then the CFO. The Managing Partner writes the sector strategy; the CFO builds the GP commitment reserve, the valuation policy and the LP reporting standard. Two hires before any technology spend and before any deal is signed.
  8. Close one partner buyout and one bolt-on inside a sector the Group already operates. The cheapest, fastest, least contestable control transactions available, and the first two data points of the only track record the Group will have for five years. Both are related-party matters if any Group company is involved: independent directors sitting alone, external benchmark pricing, independent valuation on file.
  9. Identify the Nigerian fund-manager acquisition target under the 30 June 2027 deadline and open the SEC conversation early. The recapitalisation deadline means sub-scale managers must raise ₦500m–₦2bn or sell, and buying a registered manager is usually faster than a de novo application. In parallel, open the FCA or SEC-US conversation — authorisation takes 9–15 months and sits on the critical path to Fund I.
  10. Map the first consolidation sector. Furniture, soft furnishings and building materials are the natural first: the Group already knows the trade, has the workshops and the apprenticeship model, and the sector has exactly the fragmented shape a control strategy targets. Name the three acquisition candidates and the exit route for each before any approach is made.

  2. Establish the two legal boundaries before a single approach is made, because they decide whether the strategy is possible at all. First, Rule 5.2: the proprietary interest in the licence remains with the Exchange, and on liquidation or receivership the licence reverts to it — so only a solvent share purchase works. Second, Rule 6.5: six months of inactivity revokes the licence — so a dormant target must be recapitalised and trading inside that window. A registered product, or a licensed site, is cheaper than the 240-day clock and the ₦21bn plant it would otherwise justify — and this register is what tests that trade before T1 is released.

The day-90 gate. Proceed to T1 only if all four hold: (i) written NAFDAC confirmation of the licence and registration pathway; (ii) at least four Wave 1 molecules confirmed biowaiver-eligible, or their BE costed and accepted; (iii) competitive capex proposals within ±20% of the US$12.6m T1 budget; and (iv) the Managing Director and Head of Quality Assurance identified and reachable. First ninety days

The two regulator questions to NACOC — submitted in writing through Ghanaian counsel, and answered before any cannabis-related spend beyond legal and licensing work:

  1. Is eligibility for a medicinal cannabis licence limited to Ghanaian citizens, or does it extend to permanent residents — and specifically, does Ghanaian Indefinite Residence granted by the Ministry of the Interior satisfy the test? If it is citizens only, the residence route fails entirely and the strategy changes.
  2. Does the ownership test bind the licensee's shareholding, its directors, or both — and if shareholding, what minimum percentage must be citizen or permanent-resident held? This sets the cap table.

Legal work, commissioned in parallel:

  • Ghana counsel — the NACOC licensing instrument and 11-licence regime; applications, fees, timelines; eligibility and ownership tests read from the primary instrument, not the press.
  • Ghana immigration counsel — Indefinite Residence eligibility, the continuous-residence period, application, and how the status is maintained and lost (Ministry of the Interior).
  • South African counsel — SAHPRA GACP and GMP licence conditions; whether change of control requires consent and whether licences survive the transaction; conditions precedent; export authorisation procedure.
  • Nigerian counsel — the NAFDAC NCS pathway; Controlled Medicines Regulations 2019; whether a foreign GMP certification is accepted; import permit requirements; NDLEA's role alongside NAFDAC.
  • A written anti-front opinion covering the whole structure, confirming every licence is held by the entity that actually conducts and controls the licensed activity and that no nominee arrangement exists anywhere in the chain.
  • Corporate and governance — incorporate the ring-fenced vehicle with its own constitution, board (two independents) and bank accounts; adopt the licence register, controlled-substances register and anti-bribery policies; appoint the qualifying family member(s) by Business Board resolution with a defined mandate and real remuneration.

Budget ₦95m (Nigerian and Ghanaian counsel). §5's conclusion — that this set is earned rather than bought — rests on this opinion, so it must be commissioned now, not assumed.

The freeze stands until both NACOC answers are in writing and NAFDAC has confirmed whether SAHPRA GMP certification will support a narcotics import permit. No cultivation, facilities, procurement or product claims anywhere until the licences exist to support them.

  2. Commission an agronomic soil and water survey of the acquired land, and a yield-potential assessment by crop. Do not plant before this is done.

  4. Tender the Nkpor processing line to at least three equipment vendors on fixed-price contracts with performance guarantees. Do not accept a single quotation.
  5. Sign the first institutional offtake letters with the Group's own entities — Idenze University, the teaching hospital, the staff estates — to establish base load before the line is built.
  6. Recruit the Head of Agriculture and the Head of Storage & Offtake. These two roles determine whether the group makes money in years 1–3.
  7. Design the contracted-farmer programme — input supply, agronomy support, guaranteed offtake price, and a written contract in the farmer's language and the local dialect. This programme is Isiome's real competitive moat: once a farmer is supplied and bought from, they do not switch.

Budget ₦200m across the domain — roughly ₦5–6m a target for legal, financial and regulatory-file diligence across some thirty candidates, plus valuations, one written view per regulator on change-of-control mechanics, and a single consolidated report to the Group board. The deliverable is a priced buy-list, and its purpose is the rule itself: no licence in this domain is ever a reason to defer a business.

The sourcing thesis is dated and published: licensees facing a four- to ten-fold recapitalisation inside eighteen months must raise, merge, sell or be suspended, so 2026–2027 is the window in which this licence is genuinely available. The de novo application in action 2 proceeds regardless; the two run together and neither delays the other.

Export revenue — re-derived from one basis, and the resolution is §3's own revenue shares. (Corrected — see ../NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md.) The row previously read 2.1 / 16.0 / 44.0 / 150.0 / 330.0 and was impossible: export revenue cannot exceed total revenue, and at ₦1,600/USD it did so in four of five years — Year 5 US$44.0m was ₦70.4bn against ₦52.0bn of revenue (135% of the whole company), Year 10 US$150m was ₦240bn against ₦150bn (160%), Year 15 US$330m was ₦528bn against ₦290bn (182%).

The plan held two internally consistent but mutually incompatible architectures. This table now uses one, and it is the revenue row — for three independent reasons:

  1. §3 states the only authoritative share. The two export legs are "Export of raw commodity — Yr 5: 24% of revenue" and "Regional export of processed and branded food — Yr 5: 9%", so export is 33% of revenue by the plan's own arithmetic. 33% of ₦52.0bn = ₦17.16bn ≈ US$10.7m — which is what the table now shows.
  2. The tonnage reconciles the same way. Year 5's book is 90,000 t (T3). At the plan's own FOB of ~US$1,340/t ≈ ₦2.14m/t, ₦17.16bn of export is ~8,000 t — about 9% of tonnage but 33% of revenue, which is exactly the shape the plan describes: "the highest-value leg per tonne." The old US$44.0m would have required ~32,800 t of export, over a third of the entire book in the highest-value product, alongside a ₦52bn revenue line it could not fit inside.
  3. The revenue row is corroborated and the export row was not. Revenue agrees with §3's shares, with §7's working-capital intensity (₦12bn on 90,000 t implies ~₦46bn of annual purchases and an ~11% blended gross margin, inside §7's spread table), and with §7's Year-5 arithmetic (₦2.4bn fixed cost + ₦2.6bn EBITDA ⇒ ~₦5.0bn of contribution). The export row agreed with nothing except itself.

The row is now monotonic (0.9 → 4.5 → 10.7 → 30.9 → 59.8) and below revenue in every year. (An earlier note recorded that Year 1 "cleared" at US$2.1m — but ₦3.4bn against ₦4.2bn is 80% of revenue, which is no more consistent with a 33% export share than the Year-5 figure was with 135%. Both ends of the old row departed from §3's stated share, in opposite directions, which is the evidence that the row was never derived on one basis at all.)

[verify] — one residual question for the plan owner, and it is narrow. The corrected row holds export at 33% of revenue in every year, because 33% is the only share the plan states — it gives shares for Year 5 only. If the export share is meant to rise over time (the plan's T4–T5 tranches add "own port-side consolidation", "origination offices in two non-Nigerian markets" and "West African distribution footprint", which would argue for an increasing share), the row should be restated on that basis and the Year-5 anchor kept. The mechanism is now explicit: export revenue = stated export share × the revenue row ÷ the plan's FX rate — so the plan owner changes one number, the share, and the row follows. Everything downstream that used the old export figure must be re-checked — the NEXIM 50% export-orientation eligibility test at §5 item 9 is the material one, since at a 33% export share the company does not meet it in any year and must qualify on another limb or re-plan the facility.

Reconciliation. Tonnage is sourced through Isiome Storage and Isiome Foods at transfer prices benched to Onitsha; where those plans quote their own tonnage, their figures govern. The ₦650,000/t maize placeholder in 05_Isiome_Storage.md conflicts with the 2026 grain trough and with this plan's ₦350,000–470,000/t range; Isiome Group must adopt one measured price book before either plan is used for capital.

First ninety days

  1. Commission the commodity and corridor price survey first — three seasons of Onitsha and Nkpor prices, farm-gate-to-FOB spreads for sesame, cashew and ginger, actual levies at Seme, Idiroko and Jibiya, ocean freight by destination, certificate fees. This gates every later tranche.
  2. Incorporate at CAC and register as an exporter with NEPC, then instruct counsel on ETLS and AfCFTA origin documentation for each corridor.
  3. Recruit the Trade Compliance Manager and the Credit Control Manager first, both reporting to the board — before the first order, not after the first loss.
  4. Open the banking structure — naira-first accounts, an export domiciliary account, and a letter of intent with a NEXIM participating bank for RRF rediscounting.
  5. Meet the Onitsha wholesale associations and twenty verified buyers on written credit terms, and sign the first ten institutional contracts with Group schools, hospitals and estates.
  6. Sign the first three confirmed-order export contracts on LC or advance terms — two processed-food regional orders, one raw-commodity order — and refuse everything else.
  7. Lock the document chain: pre-shipment testing, fumigation, NAQS inspection scheduling, and a NAFDAC export e-licence application for the priority Foods products.
  8. Sign the Uli Freight corridor tariff and the Aku Capital trade-finance mandate, with credit cover through Aku Insurance, effective before the first cargo moves.
  9. Set board policy: naira at ₦1,600/USD; gearing ≤40%; no unhedged USD debt; position limits (35% commodity, 25% counterparty, 60 days); no export tonne without a matched sale; 90-day repatriation; working capital only against confirmed orders or receipts.
  10. Publish the Storage and Foods transfer-price schedule on day one and correct the maize price book across Isiome Group, so all three companies plan against one measured series.
  11. Open the exporter and customs-agent acquisition file — the acquisition action for this plan. Instruct counsel to identify existing export trading companies and licensed customs agents trading this plan's corridors and price them: NEPC, CAC and NAFDAC file search per target, a written opinion on whether NEPC registration and customs agency transfer on a change of control, a repatriation and customs-compliance record check on each, and a valuation of the buyer book. Budget ₦30m — ₦5m a target across up to five candidates, plus the opinion. The sequencing is deliberate: rent a licensed agent for the first consignments (action 7), acquire only when a target's buyer book is worth more than its licence, and treat direct licensing as the last resort rather than the first. The proposed twenty-fold customs-agent fee rise makes the incumbent materially more valuable, and that window is the reason to move in Year 1 — [verify] the fee in force before budgeting it.

Discipline: acquisition capital is released only against a completed diligence file, an independent valuation and evidence that the trailing income was actually collected. No catalogue is bought on projected royalties. Growth that outruns diligence capacity is how catalogue buyers destroy capital, and the diligence queue — not the balance sheet — sets the acquisition pace.

First ninety days

Days 1–30 — build the standard before buying anything. (1) Appoint the Managing Director / Head of Rights and the Head of Legal & Business Affairs; the lawyer's first deliverable is the ten-point title template. (2) Commission counsel opinions on the CMO position after the July 2026 Court of Appeal ruling, the CBN repatriation route for dollar royalties, and NDPA 2023 duties. Days 31–60 — diligence, price discovery and the factory. (6) Audit the Group's own catalogue: sample 500 titles, measure metadata completeness, quantify the collection gap — the first real test of the §7 collection-uplift assumption, free of charge. (7) Hold at least ten seller conversations across legacy labels, estates, producer back catalogues and film producers, to test whether 5–8× is real in Nigeria given that no disclosed comparable exists. (8) Commission an independent valuation of the Group catalogue to fix the arms-length transfer price. (9) Scope and cost the metadata remediation factory before Tranche 1 is drawn. (10) Retain an international sub-publishing partner for UK and US collection, with audit rights.

Days 61–90 — first capital, first asset. (11) Recruit the Heads of Royalty Accounting, Metadata & Registrations and Collections. (12) Complete diligence on the first two Tier-2 targets and put a written offer on one, with escrow, a 12-month title warranty and an earn-out on verified income. (13) Present the fund eligibility pack to the Uli Group board and the Akunnia investment committee — diligence standard, valuation methodology, the 14–18% discount-rate rationale, the collection-uplift gate — so the Year 3 vehicle is designed now, not improvised. (14) Establish the related-party register and annual independent-director review. (15) Day-90 board decision: release Tranche 1 capital only if the Group audit has quantified a collection gap, one external acquisition has cleared diligence, and step 7 supports an entry multiple at or below 8×. If not, run Year 1 as a rights-administration and documentation-services business on the Group catalogue, re-test in twelve months, and buy nothing.

Market, catalogue-multiple, securitisation and copyright-regulatory figures are sourced, including IFPI Global Music Report 2026, the Astor catalogue-multiple report via Music Ally, Hipgnosis Songs Fund's FY2022 valuation disclosures, Canon Music's KBRA pre-sale report, and Nigeria's NCAC/RegalStone music market report. Two limitations are important: no disclosed price or multiple exists for any African catalogue transaction, so every African entry multiple in this plan is an assumption requiring local verification; and no African catalogue has ever been rated or securitised, so the pooled-vehicle advance rate and discount rate are conservative planning judgments rather than comparables. Operating, capital and unit-economics figures are planning estimates at ₦1,600/USD requiring verification — particularly Nigerian catalogue pricing, DSP minimum guarantees and naira cost of funds — before any capital is committed. documents/ROADMAPS.html.html:
EZEME — PER-CHILD BUSINESS ROADMAPS

How these are keyed. The family begins with the first child, and each branch belongs to one child. So these roadmaps are anchored to that child's age, not to a calendar year: a business is founded when the child reaches the band that calls for it. Once a birth year is fixed, every band resolves to a date, and the plan library's own horizon (Year 1 = 2027) can be mapped onto it.

Where the content comes from. Every milestone and every first-ninety-days action below is extracted verbatim from the plan of record in the family's library — sixty plans at ~/Projects/Ezeme/.research/gdocs/plans/. Nothing in those sections is authored here. What is authored is the framing and the proposed phase assignment, and the proposals are labelled as such.

What is not yet done, stated plainly. Assigning each business to an age band requires two things this round did not have: the first child's birth year, and the board's sequencing decision. The framework and the extracted content are complete; the per-business assignment is the next step.

The age bands

Child's age What the family is doing
Birth – 2Incorporate nothing in the child's name. The parents build the two live ventures and write the constitution. The child's branch exists only as a plan of record.
3 – 6The land position and the first licence application in the branch. Assets are bought in the Group's name, never the child's.
7 – 12The first operating company of the branch trades. Education and apprenticeship begin deliberately, not by accident.
13 – 17The child learns the branch from inside it — school holidays in the business, not beside it. Cap table and reserved matters are settled in writing.
18 – 22Formal training, and the first independent mandate inside the branch. The transfer of responsibility is scheduled, not left to succession events.
23 – 30The child chairs the branch. The parents move to the family layer: the Council, the constitution, the office.
30 +The generation that inherits holds an institution, not a portfolio. The work of the roadmaps is to make that true.
