(b) The root cause — and it means this is a real gap, not a citation error. ASERC's Clause 6 is near-verbatim boilerplate from NERC Regulation No. NERC-R-0110A, Regulation for the Application for Licence (2010), which cross-refers to "Regulations for Licence and Operating Fees 2010". ASERC's Clauses 13(d), 14(b) and 15(c) are word-for-word NERC's with "2010" changed to "2026" — and Clause 15(b)'s "within the first five (5) years of the initial term of the licence" is copied from NERC too. The same architecture appears in the EMRC "Licensing Regulation Template" (v2-0, 2025-08-08), which requires "Proof of payment of the non-refundable license fee, in line with the Commission's Schedule of Licence and Operating Fees" and itself contains no figures.

ASERC inherited a template whose fee figures live in a sibling instrument it has not yet made. The dangling cross-reference in Clause 6 is the template's, with the year swapped. §4.1's finding is therefore not a defect in the library's research and not a defect in ASERC's drafting — it is an artefact of a new regulator standing up on a borrowed template.

This closes U-06, and it means 42_Okodu_Power.md should say the figures do not yet exist publicly, rather than that they are hard to find.

"How long is a license valid? License validity depends on the category and terms set by ASERC under Section 42(10)." — ASERC FAQ Q9

Two independent analogues agree on the effect: Electricity Act 2023 s.72(10) — "The tenure or duration of a license may be open or shall be valid for such duration as stipulated in such license granted by the Commission…"; and EMRC Model State Electricity Law Template s.67(5) — "the tenure or duration of a license may be open or shall be valid for such duration as may be prescribed in the license granted by the Commission." ⚠️ Caveat on the EMRC template, now established (§6g): it is a model for states to adopt, and its numbering does not map to Anambra's — its s.13 is "Appointment of Commissioners" and its s.78 is "Restriction on licenses". So template s.67(5) is usable as evidence of what a law of this family provides, but must never be cited as Anambra's s.42(10), nor used to fill any Anambra numbering gap. So the plan's assumption is directionally supported — the term is optional rather than fixed — but "25-year tenor" remains an assumption, not a fact: the only real ASERC data point is the interim distribution licence to First Power Electricity Distribution Company Ltd (FPEDC), granted 27 November 2025 and reported as lasting one year; and no ASERC licence template is published. NERC benchmark: 10 years (grid), up to 10 years (embedded), 5 years (captive permits).

(f) Background facts worth carrying into the plan, including one that makes the gap commercial rather than academic.

  • ⚠️ Electricity Act 2023 s.230(7) provides that a successor company incorporated and licensed by a State regulator "shall have no further obligation to pay any form of license fees to the Commission." So FPEDC's — and Okodu Power's — licence fees now run only to ASERC. The missing ASERC fee schedule is therefore a live commercial unknown in the plan's own cost base, not a housekeeping gap. This is the strongest reason to make the enquiry to ASERC promptly.
  • The NERC→ASERC transfer was by Order dated 16 October 2025, effective 17 October 2025, with EEDC required to incorporate a subsidiary within 60 days — which became First Power Electricity Distribution Company Ltd (FPEDC) (Templars).
  • Although ASERC signed four instruments in June 2026, its site publishes only three — the Business Rules is not on /regulations/ (§4.9(a)).
  • Currency caveat on the benchmark: NERC-R-0210A was made under s.96(2)(h) of the Electricity Power Sector Reform Act 2005 — a repealed statute — and sits on nerc.gov.ng in a 2019 directory.   • No Nigerian law-firm alert or news report located publishes a single ASERC fee figure — consistent with §4.9(a).

It did, however, surface three points that are material risks to the library and are more urgent than a missing citation, each resting on secondary reporting only:

L-1 · The NBC Code provisions the broadcast plan is built on may have been nullified — ENFORCEABILITY IN ISSUE.

L-7 · The change-of-control gate may be the wrong regulator entirely — and this one is checkable. 32_Uli_Broadcast.md:120 asserts that "NBC's prior written approval of the transfer or assignment of a licence" is a condition of every broadcast licence, and 28_Uli_Group.md:164 makes "NBC approval of change of control" the critical path. A codified prior-approval regime for ownership changes was located — but at the Nigerian Communications Commission, not the NBC: an NCC licence condition reading "this Licence is personal to the Licensee and shall not without the prior express consent of the…", and an NCC + CAC prior-approval requirement for 10% shareholding changes in communications companies (NCC press release — the regulator's own communication; Olaniwun Ajayi client alert). Closing action: cite the NBC provision that imposes prior consent, or re-express the plan's critical path against the NCC/CAC regime with the correct regulator named. L-8 · Two of the Plan B claims fail on characterisation, not on wording — a distinction the library has not made. 54_Aku_Security.md:68 converts a revocation power into a pre-clearance duty: "revocable where ownership or control passes to a company unsuitable to hold it (s.4(4))" → "Change of control is a regulatory event — pre-cleared, not notified afterwards". The Anambra State Electricity Law 2025 could not be obtained from any source — not from ASERC's site, not from anambrastate.gov.ng (whose laws index lists nothing past the Homeland Security Law 2025, uploaded 17 January 2025), not from the NGF repository, and not from gazettes.africa (HTTP 403), placng.org, nigerialii.org, lawglobalhub or lawpadi. So every Anambra finding below rests on ASERC's own statements and its sealed 2026 Regulations — the regulator's representations about its enabling Law, which are strong but are not the Law's text.

⚠️ And the document most likely to be mistaken for the Law must not be used as it. The NGF-repository PDF whose cover reads "(Insert state name here) State Electricity Law, 2025" is the EMRC MODEL/TEMPLATE (v2-0, 2025-08-08) — a template for states to adopt. Its numbering does not map to Anambra's: template s.13 = "Appointment of Commissioners" and template s.78 = "Restriction on licenses". So it must never be used to confirm what Anambra's ss.13 or 78 say — and by the same logic, template s.67(5) is usable in §4.9(e) only as evidence of what a state electricity law of this family provides, not as Anambra's s.42(10). W-19 · Captive power is a permit or licence, not a "registration" — and the plan's framing is wrong. ← new wrong substance

The plan treats captive power as "captive power registration" with a fee. Two corrections, both now sourced:

  • Below 1 MW for own use it is EXEMPT. ASERC's FAQ, on "activities that do not require a full license": "Under Section 33(3), certain small-scale operations may operate without a license … Captive power plants generating electricity solely for own use, or renewable/off-grid developers serving specific communities provided the generation capacity is below 1MW."
  • Above the threshold it requires a captive generation PERMIT or LICENCE. The Investment in Electricity Market Regulations 2026, clause 9.5: "Captive generation facilities shall require a captive generation permit or licence issued by the Commission, where the installed capacity exceeds the threshold determined by the Commission." Clause 9.8 permits surplus power to be sold to a licensed distribution company, eligible customers, licensed traders, or injected into the network subject to approval, and clause 9.9 makes the sale of surplus subject to separate Commission authorisation — which materially widens the plan's captive option.
  • No fee figure is citable — none appears in any readable instrument, and the schedule it points to is unpublished (§4.9(a)). Patch P-22.

⚠️ Caveat on the Investment Regulations, and it matters. That instrument's own title page reads "DRAFT INVESTMENT IN ELECTRICITY MARKET REGULATIONS, 2026", its clause 1.1 self-cites a different title ("Anambra State Electricity Investment and Market Development Regulations, 2026"), and clause 1.4 makes commencement conditional on publication in the Anambra State Official Gazette — which could not be confirmed. So the instrument publishing the captive-power permit requirement may itself be a draft. The library should cite it as the 2026 Investment Regulations as published by ASERC on 17 September 2026, flagged as unconfirmed-commenced. This also qualifies U-08: the two dependent plans in 43_Okodu_Solar.md and 44_Okodu_Grid.md are resting on a possibly-draft instrument.

✅ Four Anambra citations confirmed in substance (not verbatim — the Law is unread):

  • s.33(3) is the licensing-exemption provision ✓ — and s.33 is also the source section for the generation, distribution and trading licences.
  • s.40 governs licence transactions ✓ — ASERC: "No license may be transferred, assigned, franchised, or merged without ASERC's prior written consent under Section 40." The library's 42_Okodu_Power.md:104 states this correctly.
  • s.41(2) requires publication of the application notice in at least two newspapers ✓ — implemented by clause 10 of the Application for Licences Regulations (within 14 days of acknowledgement, one local and one national newspaper).
  • s.42(10) delegates validity to the terms set ✓ — ASERC FAQ Q9. And no fixed licence term was found in the Law or in any of the three 2026 Regulations (152 pages, fully OCR'd). The term evidence is: a Provisional Licence is 12 months; clause 13(b) allows an amendment application "at least nine months before the expiration of the licence"; clause 15(b) requires a tenure-extension application "within the first five (5) years of the initial term of the licence"; the Schedule notes that "Renewal cannot be for more than the initial term of the licence being renewed"; and FPEDC's interim licence ran 27 November 2025 to 26 November 2026 — a 12-month term. So the plan must not assert any fixed statutory term (10/15/25 years) for any Anambra licence class.

⚠️ s.13 and s.78 — the recital is verified; their content is not. The regulation's recital is verbatim correct: "In exercise of the Powers to make Regulations conferred by Section 13 & 78 of the Anambra State Electricity Law, 2025 (the Law)…" — and it is independently corroborated, because the Customer Protection Regulations 2026 recite "sections 12, 13, 28 and 78", and ASERC's FAQ treats s.78(3)–(4) as the consultation precondition for making regulations. NGX: Rule 7.1 quoted from deleted text; Rule 5.4 drops "or any part of the undertakings". COREN: s.11(2) paraphrases repealed text. Anambra: s.4 cited for licensing when it establishes ASERC; captive power called a "registration" when below 1 MW it is exempt and above it is a permit or licence
Wrong instrument cited as authority1The library's isa2025.pdf is the 2024 Bill, byte-identical to the billdownload/11160.pdf URL three plans cite as "ISA 2025". See also §6g: COREN's own link to its "amendment" is a 2017 draft bill
Could not verify3ISA s.240(4) and s.244(1) penalties; all ASERC and NERC fee figures; whether the NMMR 2011 carries the controlling-interest rule. Plus, from §6g: whether ss.13 and 78 of the Anambra Law are its regulation-making powers; whether the Investment Regulations have commenced; and whether a gazetted COREN firm-registration regulation exists at all

Corrections applied in place: 0. Four patches (P-1 … P-4) and two recommended additions (P-5, P-6) are specified verbatim in §3; application was blocked by the sandbox boundary, not by any doubt about the finding (§0.2). One further correction — re-sourcing the ISA 2025 link — is specified as U-01a.

A caution about the delegated passes and about the brief, learned the hard way. Four headline calls reversed once the plans — or the instruments — were actually read. The causes differ, and that is the lesson:

  1. NAICOM ₦25.1bn was called "unsupported… probably wrong", the tier structure "possibly invented" — but 14_Aku_Insurance.md:89 cites the same NAICOM circular and states the tiers correctly. Real defect: a ₦15bn / ₦20bn / ₦25.1bn inconsistency within the plan (§6b L-4). Cause: the pass worked from the brief, not the library text — its grep/glob were dead, so it never opened a plan.
  2. MDPO was called a "conflation of two instruments" — but 58_Okodu_Fuel.md:83 splits licensing from fees correctly and explicitly (§6b L-6). Same cause.
  3. "₦400m for a Broker-Dealer" was reported wrong substance, "the operative figure is ₦2.00 billion" — but ₦400m is the fidelity bond, 20% × ₦2bn ✓, and the library states the capital separately as ₦2.00bn, matching the circular exactly (§6d). Cause: the brief misdescribed the claim.
  4. The COREN worked example in the brief — "It is annual (s.11(1)) … and s.11(3) states the Council 'shall not be involved in the registration of contractors'" — asserts two section numbers that are both wrong. Registration is biennial under s.6(5), and s.11(3) was deleted by the 2018 Amendment Act, the bar surviving in the s.21(c) proviso (§6f). The library reproduced the brief's error verbatim. Cause: the brief itself.

All four point the same way, and 3 and 4 sharpen it: the library's law is more reliable than a brief-based or summary-based reading of it. Its failures are of consistency, attribution and numbering provenance — three capital figures in one plan, two validity rules in one plan, four requirements credited to a circular that contains none of them, six rule numbers parsed from an amendment instrument's markup — not of knowing the instrument. Where the delegated passes read the actual documents (§6d, §6e, §6f), they confirmed the library on eight separate instruments. That is the diagnosis the correction effort should be aimed at: re-attribute, reconcile and renumber; do not re-research.

One more methodological note for the record: the passes that recovered their shell and read primary instruments produced findings of a completely different quality from those that could not. The environment, not the task, was the limiting factor — and the same failure would have caused the same gap in any agent working this library.

Two headlines within my own verification, and the second matters more than the first.

  1. The library's own copy of "ISA 2025" is a Bill. md5 proves isa2025.pdf is https://www.nass.gov.ng/documents/billdownload/11160.pdf — the Investments and Securities Bill, 2024, 351 sections, warehouse division ss.230–257, whose operative text says "pursuant to this Bill". The enacted Act isa_act.pdf has 358 sections and the division at ss.240–266. Three plans cite the Bill as their authority. Every agent that opens the library's own file reads Bill numbering, and the offset is not uniform (+6 to +10) — so it cannot even be corrected by arithmetic. This is the mechanism, not just the symptom.
  1. The paragraph that was written to document the Bill/Act problem regressed on the Bill/Act problem. The errors cluster in one block of one file — 05_Isiome_Storage.md, lines 36–55, the very passage whose own note reads "the Bill is not the law". Ten lines above that warning, rows 39 and 40 still carry Bill numbers (s.237, s.232). The correction was performed; the source fix was not. Everything else the library says about warehouse receipts — s.245(1), s.246(1), s.249(1), s.357 — and its entire Aku Markets conduct block (ss.62, 121, 122, 126, 127, 129, 137, 349) is correct, several of them verbatim to the word. The library's law is right; its filing is wrong.

8. Task B — bottom line

The ASERC fee figures are not in the Application for Licences Regulations, and they are not published anywhere else either — and the reason is now known. Clause 6 and its three siblings in Clauses 13, 14 and 15 each say the fee is "as provided in the Regulations for Licence and Operating Fees 2026" — a separate instrument. That instrument does not exist in published form: ASERC's entire media library was enumerated through its REST API (41 items, 8 PDFs), a sweep for naira figures across every page returned zero matches, and the Commission's own site says its instruments are "still being developed". The cross-reference is inherited boilerplate — Clause 6 is near-verbatim NERC Regulation NERC-R-0110A (2010), which points to "Regulations for Licence and Operating Fees 2010"; ASERC's 13(d), 14(b) and 15(c) are NERC's word-for-word with the year changed. A new regulator standing up on a borrowed template has left a dangling reference, and the figures it points to have not yet been made.

So the correct entry for the library is neither a figure nor an enquiry into the wrong document: it is a statement that the fees are unpublished, with the enquiry re-aimed at ASERC itself. Full detail in §4.9.

(a) Replacement text for 42_Okodu_Power.md:115 — the block that misdirects the reader

The existing block tells the reader to "start at the back — pages 50–59", which are application forms, and says the scan also holds the Customer Protection and Investment Regulations, which it does not. Suggested replacement:

📄 Where the ASERC licence fees actually are — and it is not in this document. The ASERC licence fees are not published in the Application for Licences (Generation, Distribution & Trading) Regulations 2026 (Reg. No. ASERC/R/LLE/002-2026). Read in full — all 59 pages — that instrument contains no fee figures at all. Clause 6 provides that the applicant "shall upon submission of the Application Form, pay a non-refundable processing fee as provided in the Regulations for Licence and Operating Fees 2026, as amended", and Clauses 13(d), 14(b) and 15(c) repeat the same cross-reference for amendment, renewal and tenure extension; Clause 12(c) provides that the licence fee is notified in writing and paid before grant. Its nine schedules (1A–1E, 2, 3, 4, 5) are submission requirements and application forms — there is no Schedule of Fees. ⚠️ An earlier note here directed the reader to pages 50–59; those are forms, and reading them resolves nothing. The instrument to obtain is the "Regulations for Licence and Operating Fees 2026" — named five times in the Licensing Regulation, not among the four regulations ASERC signed in June 2026, and therefore to be requested from ASERC directly. Licence terms and whether captive registration carries a fee are separate questions this instrument does not answer either: Chapter IV governs extension of tenure and fixes only that an extension application must be made "within the first five (5) years of the initial term", and the Customer Protection and Investment Regulations are separate ASERC instruments, not part of this scan. Fee amounts stay [verify] throughout this section. (Full analysis: CITATION_AUDIT.md §4.)

(b) What each open ASERC question needs

*Audit prepared 25 September 2026. All quotations transcribed from the documents named in §1. Where a claim could not be checked against the operative instrument, it is recorded as could not verify with the specific enquiry that would settle it — no figure or section number in this document has been inferred, interpolated or guessed. The Bill/Act comparison in §1.1 rests on md5 hashes and on both documents' own Arrangements of Sections.**

CONSOLIDATED_CAPITAL_PLANS.md  ·  19,338 words

CONSOLIDATED CAPITAL PLANS — Ezeme Group

One defensible capital requirement per group, net of known double-counts — for the first time in this library.

Prepared for the Ezeme Group Board and the Family Council. Naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD and not comparable across plans (the library carries six rates — see §7.6).

0. Basis, placement, and method

0.1 Placement note — read first

The plan library this document reconciles is no longer at the path given in the brief. It now lives at:

```

/Users/nzeora/Projects/Ezeme/.research/frozen_v1/plans/ (61 plans, SHA-256 frozen)

/Users/nzeora/Projects/Ezeme/.research/gdocs/ (companions + NUMBER_RECONCILIATION_V2.md)

```

The brief's path, /Users/nzeora/Documents/Ezeme/.research/gdocs/, is where this file has been written, because that is the only tree this session can write to. It should be mirrored to /Users/nzeora/Projects/Ezeme/.research/gdocs/CONSOLIDATED_CAPITAL_PLANS.md, alongside NUMBER_RECONCILIATION_V2.md, which was written the same way and to the same place.

0.2 Revision audited — and why this matters

Every figure below is taken from frozen_v1/, the immutable SHA-256-frozen snapshot of the plan library frozen at 2026-09-25 04:20 WAT. Integrity was re-verified for this document:

```

$ cd .research/frozen_v1 && shasum -a 256 -c PLANS.sha256

... 61 lines ... plans/61_Isiome_Manufacturing.md: OK → 61 of 61 OK

```

This is the third numerical pass over this library, and each has used a different base. The v1 audit (NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md) was run against a moving tree and its own §0.1 warns that ten files changed while it audited. The v2 pass (NUMBER_RECONCILIATION_V2.md) was the first run against the freeze. Congruence between the three bases is partial, and where it is not, I say so rather than averaging.

⚠️ A material trap for any reader coming from v1. Four of the numbers v1 built conclusions on are superseded in the frozen revision, and this document uses the frozen figures:

PlanWhat v1 readWhat frozen_v1 saysLine

Where v1 and frozen disagree, frozen governs. Where the frozen revision is itself internally inconsistent, that is reported and not resolved (§2, §6).

0.3 What this document is, and what it is not

It is a reconciliation: the company plans' own stated capital requirements, grouped, with the known double-counts netted as explicit adjustment lines, and one net figure per group.

It is not a replacement for a tender, a valuation or a regulator's answer. plans/50_Akuzo_Development.md:23 already makes reconciliation the board's first duty; this document is its arithmetic, not its evidence.

No plan file was edited. This is the corrected basis; a human folds it in. §5 states exactly what each group plan's capital table should be replaced with.

0.4 The method, and its four honest limits

Method. For each company: fixed/capex, working capital (revolving), and locked regulatory capital, summing to the plan's own stated total. Where a plan quantifies working capital, its figure is used. Where it does not, I estimate from that plan's own stated revenue, inventory days, debtor days and cost structure and mark it [verify]. Where a plan states a rule rather than a number — 42's "working capital is 8–10% of tranche value", 43's "10–12%", 58's "60 days of inventory and receivables" — the rule is applied to the plan's own base and marked as derived.

Four limits, stated before any table so they are not discovered later:

  1. The working-capital column mixes two different bases. Nine plans state working capital as a cumulative programme tranche (02's ₦44.4bn, 61's ₦6.80bn, 19's ₦3–6bn, 23's ₦0.9–1.4bn); three state it as a point-in-time requirement at a named year (05's Year-5 ₦22–26bn of stock, 06's "₦3.1bn at Year-3 volumes", 56's ₦0.93bn of receivables); one states it as a residual (07's ₦76.1bn = ₦83.1bn − ₦7bn fixed). These are not additive on one basis. The column is given because the brief requires it and because omitting it is worse, but the total in it is a financing requirement across the programme, not a single-year peak. No plan in this library restates its working capital to a common basis — that is the missing convention.
  2. "Regulatory capital" is the library's least-priced column. Only three Uli plans put a licence figure inside §6; eight Uli plans state none. 44_Okodu_Grid.md and 50_Akuzo_Development.md state none. The largest single item, the ASERC generation and distribution licence fee, is genuinely unavailable: the 59-page ASERC instrument the plans point to contains no fee amounts at all — every fee cross-refers to a different instrument, the "Regulations for Licence and Operating Fees 2026", which is not in the library.
  3. Where a plan states no revenue, working capital cannot be estimated from it. That is true of 28, 30, 40, 41, 01, 08, 17, 25 and 24 (whose only stated figures are ₦250m and ₦1.5bn+₦800m fragments). For those the estimate rests on a physical driver — capacity, positions, mandates — and is the weakest class of number in this document.
  4. Two of the five groups are not fully determinable, and §4 says so per group rather than manufacturing precision.

PART 1 — One consolidated capital plan per group

Twenty-five companies in Isiome, Akunnia, Idenze and Okodu; thirteen in Uli. Columns are as briefed: Fixed/capex · Working capital (revolving) · Regulatory capital (locked) · Total · Basis/note.

Totals are the plan's own stated total where it has one. Where a plan has no total row, the sum is computed and shown.

That is the sum of 16's four cumulative tranche columns (16:117) — a total programme figure including systems, branches, banking talent and an operating reserve. 7. Standing conclusions

  1. The Group's consolidated capital requirement is ₦4.63–4.77trn, or US$2.89–2.98bn indicative at ₦1,600/USD, net of ₦306.3bn of demonstrated double-counts — deployed over ~15 years, of which roughly ₦2.9trn falls after Year 5 [verify] — my own reading of five separate phasing tables, since no Group-level cash-flow statement exists to test it against.
  2. Equity ₦3.24–3.68trn (69–78%); debt ₦1.01–1.48trn (22–31%); and ₦431–501bn of the debt is revolving working capital that must be a self-liquidating facility, not equity — 31–46% of all the Group's debt. Locked regulatory capital of ₦241.6bn must be equity, and ₦200bn of it is Aku Bank alone.
  3. The largest single netting is ₦128.4bn — Okodu Grid's distribution network duplicated inside Okodu Power, which turns on an ASERC franchise question that has not been answered.
  4. Three of the four "known Isiome double-counts" net to zero, because they are between the group plan and its own companies — and the group plan is excluded from the sum entirely. One of the four — the 8,000 t gate silo — nets to zero because 04 excludes the silo by construction. The library was more careful here than its own audit credited.
  5. Two groups' requirements are not fully determinable, and this document does not manufacture a number for either. Uli turns on what "Cumulative" means — ₦171.2bn at both ends. Okodu is a floor pending the Akuzo tender and pending 43 stating how much of its 260 MWp it owns — against which up to ₦257bn is potentially duplicated.
  6. The highest-value single action is still not an arithmetic one. It is one measured cost book (59:182 budgets ₦12m at day 60; 50:23 calls it the board's first duty), ASERC's written answer on the transfer order and franchise boundary (41:208), and a board decision on what each Uli terminal row means. Until those three exist, this document is the best available reconciliation — and it is a reconciliation, not a valuation.
  7. Seven-tenths of the Group requirement sits in a plan that quantifies its own working capital; three-tenths does not — measured by company capital (70–71%). Measured by money, only 9–16% of the ₦432.2–500.0bn working-capital column is my estimate; the rest is a plan's own figure. The gap is concentrated in Idenze (35–38% stated) and Okodu (58.8%), and in both groups the missing working capital sits inside an unnamed tranche rather than being absent.

EZEME GROUP — EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

A board-grade summary of the Ezeme Group business plan library. Prepared for a bank credit committee and prospective co-investors.

Sources. plans/README.md (authoritative index), plans/00_Family_Business.md, the five group plans (plans/01_Isiome_Group.md, plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md, plans/17_Idenze_Group.md, plans/28_Uli_Group.md, plans/41_Okodu_Group.md), the company plans, EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md, EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, EZEME_FAMILY_KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md and the concurrent NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md audit.

FX. Naira is primary in every plan; dollars are indicative at the library rate of ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026). Dollars are not comparable across plans — six rates are in circulation (₦1,600 / 1,500 / 1,400 / 1,360 / 1,350 / 1,328).

Revision warning. The library was renumbered and rewritten while this summary was prepared; filenames are as at 25 September 2026. Three plans (plans/61_Isiome_Manufacturing.md, plans/59_Okodu_Housing.md, plans/60_Okodu_Estate_Services.md) post-date the audit's snapshot. 1. The proposition

Ezeme Group is a Nigerian family holding company, incorporated in 2025 and headquartered at Nkpor, Idemili North LGA, Anambra State, building ten industry sectors under one ownership, one board and one set of accounts. It is organised into five sector groups named for the founder's five children in birth order — Isiome, Akunnia, Idenze, Uli, Okodu — in the Dangote pattern. Its ultimate shareholder is a Mauritius discretionary trust (Trusts Act 2001) whose trustee is a family private trust company. Operating companies, employment, tax residency, land title and day-to-day governance stay in Nigeria; only the trust, the trustee company and the holding GBC sit offshore (plans/00_Family_Business.md §3).

Two features distinguish the plan and both are checkable in the documents. First, the five domains are designed to trade with each other, and several of the largest customer relationships are internal and contracted before the first asset is ordered. Second, the finance arm is designed as a control investor and third-party fund manager earning management fees and carried interest, explicitly on the Blackstone model rather than the BlackRock model the library was first built toward (plans/README.md).

Register this first. No Group-level profit and loss account, balance sheet or cash-flow statement exists anywhere in the library (plans/README.md open item 2). No group plan states group revenue or EBITDA; four of five cannot be reconciled on the P&L because they do not attempt one. Every group plan understates its own group by 7–10×, because group tables are first-phase build programmes read as totals. The company-level plans are detailed and internally disciplined; the aggregation above them has not been done. That is the central qualification on everything that follows.

Where this summary's brief named a fact the library does not contain, the library has been followed: the brief refers to buying an existing NGX dealing member, and no plan in the library proposes that (§8).

The reason is stated bluntly: the Charter "governs a household of seven. It cannot govern a conglomerate. Standing rights sit with Family Holdings, not with any individual, so they survive succession: a permanent non-removable Family Director on every subsidiary board; quarterly management accounts and annual audited statements; right of first refusal on share transfers (plans/00_Family_Business.md §3).

The Capital-Source Ownership Rule makes any business funded by Group capital a controlled subsidiary unless the Family Holdings board resolves otherwise in writing at the time capital is committed. Cap-table hygiene is hard: no entity anywhere may issue equity to employees, apprentices, operators or partners at Group or holdco level; employee ownership exists only inside operating subsidiaries and never touches the Mauritius layer. This is stated as the precondition for every institutional mandate.

One rule protects the licences specifically: regulated functions report to the board, not to the operating executive — pharma quality assurance to the board, the finance CRO to the Audit & Risk Committee rather than the CIO (plans/00_Family_Business.md §6). Honoured at company level in plans/06_Isiome_Foods.md, plans/18_Idenze_Pharma.md and plans/02_Isiome_Seed.md.

2.4 Carried interest — the rule that must not be blurred

The Group's rule is that no equity is issued above subsidiary level, protecting family ownership. Carry is deliberately not equity:

"Carry sits at fund level and shares in fund profits. It never touches ownership of Ezeme Group, the five groups, or any operating company." The family retains 100% of the operating conglomerate; partners share in the returns their own funds generate. (plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md §7)

Mechanically, the licensed manager earns the management fee; the GP entities — owned by Aku Capital — own the carried interest (plans/10_Aku_Asset_Management.md §2).

That rule has a second consequence which is unresolved. Because Ezeme Group, Akunnia Group and Aku Capital cannot issue shares to a seller, listed equity cannot be used as acquisition currency at holdco level. Consideration must be cash, hedged debt, or rollover equity inside the target. Acquisition pace is capped by Aku Capital's own cash generation and borrowing capacity rather than by a share price — which makes Aku Bank's deposit base strategically important rather than merely convenient — and sector holdco IPOs do not solve it unless the family accepts outside shareholders at holdco level, which the current rule forbids. plans/README.md: "This should be decided deliberately rather than discovered in a negotiation."

3. The five domains, in birth order

Each group plan carries the same twelve sections and is the parent brief for the companies beneath it. Only the mother company carries the Ezeme name; "Aku" is the established short form of Akunnia, not a separate name.

3.1 Isiome — Agriculture & Food Systems + Manufacturing & Industrial Production

Mandate, in the family's own words: "Isiome grows it, builds the machines that work the land, and then processes what comes off it. His edge is owning the equipment layer that every farm and factory in the empire depends on" (plans/01_Isiome_Group.md §1). Master Plan §6.1: "Isiome's domain spans the entire value chain from field to finished product… The factory floor converts agricultural raw materials and imported industrial inputs into packaged, export-ready goods."

Companies (7). Isiome Seed · Machinery · Farms · Storage · Foods · Trading · Manufacturing.

Strategic case. Own the value chain, not the farmland — Africa's production is ~60% smallholder, so land ownership is neither available nor the source of margin. Inputs, mechanisation, offtake, storage, processing and trading are. The library's most important commercial judgement sits here: storage and offtake are the profit engine, not primary production. "Isiome Farms is the 200-hectare laboratory and tonnage reserve that makes the silo and the processing plant financeable — and if it is ever the most profitable agricultural entity in Isiome Group, then Storage or Foods has failed" (plans/04_Isiome_Farms.md §1).

Three corrections the company plans made to the group plan. Warehouse receipts gained statutory force under the Investments and Securities Act 2025 (s.246(1) — "first proof of the holder having proprietary rights in the commodities", with transferability by endorsement under s.249(1)) 2025 (Part XV; s.246(1)), making SEC registration of warehouse operators and collateral managers mandatory — Year-1 work, not Year-5. Toll storage alone does not carry the hub: Year-5 break-even needs 82% utilisation on the tariff alone, failing the Group's own 75% ceiling, so the plan splits the business into Isiome Storage Ltd and a separate SEC-registered collateral-management company with its own board, independent director, audit and insurer. Note also that the 2026 tariff regime removed the import-substitution protection — machinery went to 0% import duty on 1 July 2026 — so Manufacturing's case rests on proximity, logistics and Group captive demand, not a tariff wall (plans/61_Isiome_Manufacturing.md).

Manufacturing was the missing half of the domain: Master Plan §6.1 names the sector as "Agriculture & Food Systems + Manufacturing & Industrial Production," and six of seven plans addressed only agriculture.

3.2 Akunnia — Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security

Mandate, in the family's own words: "orchestrating the structural, private development of African industry from a global hub — like London or New York… I want to buy entire companies, reshape industries, and make an astronomical amount of money doing it" (plans/README.md). plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md §1: "the structural, private development of African industry. Not passively financing it — buying the fragmented companies, consolidating them, professionalising them, and owning the result." The governance half is spelled out in Master Plan §6.2: "The legal and compliance function handles all land title conveyancing, Group contract law, and arbitration. Security coordination for all Nkpor zones is also under her domain" — which the plan calls "not administrative overhead — it is a business," and the only part of the domain that earns revenue in Year 1.

Companies — 13 named, 12 plans exist. Finance: Aku Capital · Bank · Credit · Private Equity · Asset Management · Insurance · Treasury · Advisory · Markets · Technology. Governance, law, security: Aku Legal · Aku Security (no plan exists) · Arbitration.

Strategic case, and the correction that produced it. Four plans were rewritten because the library was first built toward the wrong peer: "BlackRock gathers passive money at 3–15 basis points; Blackstone buys control at 1.5–2.0% plus 20% carried interest." Rewritten: plans/09_Aku_Capital.md, plans/10_Aku_Asset_Management.md, plans/11_Aku_Technology.md (internal infrastructure, not a product) and plans/12_Aku_Markets.md (securities dealing — though plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md §1 says it is "reduced or closed"). The last two still carry banners admitting they predate the restructure.

The structural argument is that the Group already builds and owns what a control investor wants to buy. A financial buyer from New York must hire people to learn a sector; the Group already employs them — and a buyout model rewards operational improvement, which a conglomerate can supply and a pure financial sponsor cannot.

Aku Bank is the funding engine — the one piece Blackstone does not have. The plan quantifies the advantage at deposits 5–9% against wholesale 22–30%, worth ₦1.8bn a year on ₦10bn of loans. It then negates it: the same plan states the bank "never lends to another Aku financial entity," cites the CBN's Draft Ring-Fencing Guidelines for Closely Linked Entities (June 2026) as barring linked financial entities from lending to one another, and prohibits linked lending in its first-ninety-days list. plans/51_Aku_Credit.md prices the same deposits at 12–18%, roughly halving the claimed spread.

Where real estate is not. Master Plan §6.5 places property under Okodu; an earlier revision's "Aku Real Estate" has been deleted twice over. Aku lends against property, invests in it through funds, perfects title to it and insures it. It does not own or operate it — the distinction decides which balance sheet carries the asset, which regulator has jurisdiction, and whether the return is rent or fees.

3.3 Idenze — Education & Human Capital + Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals

Mandate, in the family's own words: "Education builds people; healthcare keeps them alive and capable. A healthy, educated workforce is the foundation of every other division." And the frame for the whole enterprise: "education — and childhood itself — is the first investment. Before any expansion, the education and the wellbeing of all five children are funded and protected" (plans/17_Idenze_Group.md §1).

Companies (11). Pharma · Therapeutics · Consumer Health · Sterile Injectables · Distribution · Research · Healthcare · University · Polytechnic · Schools · Learning.

Strategic case rests on one structural claim: the Group's university and teaching hospital can run the pain, arthritis and cannabinoid trials in-house. No Nigerian competitor owns both a pharmaceutical manufacturer and an accredited medical school. The library is honest that this cuts both ways — "when the sponsor owns the trial site, regulators and reviewers question the evidence" — and requires visibly independent research governance: a separate ethics committee, a documented conflict-of-interest policy, and publication rights sitting with the investigators. "Get this wrong and the evidence is not accepted, which destroys the entire advantage."

The market case is the strongest import-substitution argument in the library, and it is sourced. Africa carries 25% of global disease burden and 18% of global population but produces ~3% of global medicine; over 70% of medicines and over 95% of APIs are imported; only ~15% of Nigerian manufacturers hold GMP certification and capacity utilisation is 40–50%. Policy has turned in the industry's favour (October 2024 Executive Order; Nigeria Tax Act 2025 making pharmaceuticals VAT zero-rated from 1 January 2026). The counter-risk is on the record: 88 pharmaceutical plants were under construction as of March 2026 under the 5+5 policy, arriving exactly when the Group would be building.

Two corrections added plans that did not exist. Healthcare was the missing pillar: Master Plan §6.3 names a clinic, a University Teaching Hospital and a pharmaceutical unit; the clinic and hospital had no plan and are now covered by plans/56_Idenze_Healthcare.md. Without the teaching hospital the university's health sciences programmes cannot be accredited. And the polytechnic is the more immediately valuable education asset: cost per student place is ₦6.5m (~US$4,040) against ₦21.2m (~US$15,700) at the university. The sharpest ratio in the domain is Idenze Learning's — licensing the accredited model reaches a student for ₦0.28m (~US$178), roughly 1/74th of an owned university place — the argument for the pan-African ambition, subject to the plan's rule that curriculum licensing cannot precede proof.

The cannabinoid programme is the domain's most carefully structured and least certain piece. No cultivation in Nigeria; South Africa holds the first licence of record (SAHPRA GACP + GMP), acquired rather than built; Ghana is the destination licence via a qualified family member's Indefinite Residence; Nigeria manufactures the finished dose under NAFDAC NCS import permits; CBD-dominant first; ring-fenced in its own vehicle with its own board. A de novo site is $8–15m over 24–36+ months with no guarantee of award against $2.5–7m over 6–12 months for a distressed licensed entity. Two blocking unknowns gate spend: Ghanaian eligibility, and whether NAFDAC NCS accepts SAHPRA GMP (§11).

3.4 Uli — Media & Information Systems + Transport & Logistics

Mandate, in the family's own words: "Uli moves ideas and things. In the modern economy, narrative infrastructure and physical logistics are both distribution systems. Controlling what people hear and how goods reach them gives her enormous combined influence" (plans/28_Uli_Group.md §1). Her pillar in the source documents is "Culture, Press, Broadcasting & Supply Chain"; her final degree is Marketing, Distribution & Exhibition at the National Film and Television School; her bachelor's is Global Communication Science (UvA).

Companies (13). Film · Music · Animation · Broadcast · Rights · Distribution · Cinemas · Publishing · Brand · Freight · Warehousing · Fleet · Special Logistics.

A misreading corrected, and why it matters commercially. The domain was first framed as "media," which understated it and overstated its risk. This is the creative industries — film, television, music and their distribution and exhibition — paired with physical supply chain. "A film studio and a record label make the Group loved, not feared. The media-risk warning applies to news and press — the 'Press' in her pillar — not to film and music" (EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md §4.3).

Strategic case turns on three things. (1) The catalogue is a financial asset class — the clearest case in the Group of one domain producing an asset class another domain sells. (2) Licensed controlled-substance logistics is a moat almost nobody can replicate, subject to a qualification the company plan itself raised (§8). (3) The under-monetisation is measured, not asserted: Nigeria's 2025 box office was ₦15.6bn, up 34.72%, with Nollywood at 49.4% against Hollywood's 48.8% — but the NFVCB classified 1,185 Nigerian films in 2025 and only 81 reached a cinema screen, under 7%. That ratio proves the post-theatrical tail is unmonetised. In music, Nigeria generated ₦901bn (~US$600m) in 2024 but publishing, brand and sync were only 3% of artist income against 65.7% live and 30.1% streaming. The constraint: no disclosed price or multiple exists for any African catalogue transaction, and no Africa-focused royalty securitisation vehicle exists.

Three findings the company plans imposed on the group plan. Uli Cinemas — occupancy governs: the industry-average Nigerian screen runs at ~2.7% seat occupancy; cash break-even is 3.6%; full-cost break-even needs ~16.6%, "which no Nigerian cinema has sustained." That sets the structure — Tranche 1 is a leased site (₦1.4bn, no land risk) and the ₦3.6bn flagship is held in Aku Infrastructure Fund I, not on the operating balance sheet. Uli Warehousing — 40% gearing is a ceiling, not a plan: at a ~13% unlevered yield and naira lending above 30%, debt at 40% consumes essentially the entire net operating income in interest, pushing required occupancy from 44% to 79%; practical gearing is 15–25%. Its break-even series is the clearest statement of the Group's financing constraint anywhere: 29% cash, 44% full-cost, 64% at 20% debt, 79% at 40% debt. Uli Brand — the internal advantage must be a documented discount, not an unpriceable favour: an agency inside a media group buys placement at cost from its own inventory, worth roughly ₦820m a year retained in Group margin — but only because Uli Brand buys from Uli Broadcast at a published, board-approved rate card, the same card offered to external agencies, and Broadcast remains free to sell to Brand's clients' competitors. The ₦820m is "a ceiling on what Uli Brand may charge internally, not a guaranteed revenue line."

Freight economics are corridors, not wheels. Cost ₦48/tonne-km against ₦93 revenue; break-even 5.8 loaded legs a month owned versus 8.6 leased, against 10 available — and the capital-allocation test is explicit: does this spend increase control of the corridor, or merely the count of wheels?

3.5 Okodu — Energy & Utilities + Construction & Real Estate

Mandate, in the family's own words: "You cannot build without power, and power is useless without structures to serve. Okodu is the empire's engineer" (plans/41_Okodu_Group.md §1). Master Plan §6.5: "His real estate arm manages all staff apartments, student housing, commercial letting, and the Akuzo storey building portfolio," and "As the Group's largest landowner by Year Twenty-Five, the real estate portfolio generates more annual revenue than any single production cluster."

Companies (10). Power · Solar · Grid · Fuel · Construction · Materials · Real Estate · Housing · Estate Services · Akuzo Development.

Strategic case: this is the Group's asset factory, and therefore the source of the assets Akunnia's funds will warehouse and syndicate. "Energy and construction are upstream of finance in the value chain, not parallel to it." Okodu produces long-lived, inflation-linked cash flows — the profile African pension funds are structurally under-allocated to. The evidence cited is the regulator's own: PenCom's Q1 2026 data shows Nigerian pension assets at ₦29.52tn with 58.07% in FGN securities and only 3.95% in alternatives, and PenCom's own risk register lists R1 as real returns below inflation and R3 as FGN concentration, prescribing the mitigant as a shift into "alternatives, infrastructure, and inflation-linked instruments."

Three corrections of substance. The regulator is ASERC, not NERC: the Anambra State Electricity Law 2025 created ASERC, with ASEMA for technical standards, and ASERC must decide an IEDN application within a statutory three months — but the transfer order's scope and legacy-instrument novation are unresolved, and both plans say: do not commit Tranche 2 capital before ASERC answers in writing. Price against diesel, not the grid: Band A is ₦225/kWh and Bands B–E ₦40–63, with ₦358.32bn of subsidy in Q1 2026 alone — no sensible reference. The customer's real alternative is a generator: ₦1,800/litre ÷ ~2.6 kWh/litre + ₦70/kWh O&M ≈ ₦780/kWh, so a tariff around ₦230/kWh is a 40–50% saving on what they actually pay today. And the MW target was corrected downward, honestly: "500 MW+ by Year 6" is unreachable on the Nkpor campus — Nkpor delivers ~31 MW by Year 5 — so reaching 500 MW requires acquiring operating portfolios.

The avoided-cost case is the strongest number in the library, and it is internal. At diesel of ₦1,800/litre, the Group's own Year-3 energy spend falls from ₦11.16bn to ₦3.17bn a year — ₦7.99bn avoided — against ₦52bn of Tranches 1+2 capital: a 6.5-year unlevered payback and ~3.5-year equity payback, holding down to ₦1,200/litre diesel. "The first customer is the Group itself, which removes the demand risk entirely." The plan adds the metric that governs the platform — collection efficiency, break-even at ~72%, below which the asset destroys cash at any tariff — and adopts a 1.00 meter-to-customer ratio enforced on Group facilities too.

And it produced the library's most consequential cost finding. The Akuzo Urban Transformation Plan costs a storey building at ₦35m–₦50m; the Akuzo Development Programme — an itemised bill of quantities for the same buildings — totals US$967,000 and US$999,000 ≈ ₦1.55–1.60bn each. That is a factor of 31–44×. plans/41_Okodu_Group.md §4 states the BoQ is credible and itemises why (structural frame US$150,000; elevator US$25,000; 60 kW solar US$68,000; 250 kWh battery US$38,000; biodigester and generator US$55,000; LPG grid US$18,000; cistern US$55,000; fit-out US$110,000 plus US$50,000 for two penthouses) — "₦35m — roughly US$22,000 — cannot build any of that." The ₦1.23bn line appears to be the land figure from the land budget carried across by mistake. plans/45_Okodu_Construction.md, working separately, derived ₦750,000/m² and reached ₦1.48bn per five-storey building, within 5% of the BoQ. Consequences the plan states: the real-estate programme is roughly thirty times more capital-hungry than the Master Plan implies (₦1.23bn for 27 buildings becomes of the order of ₦40bn+); Year-8 self-financing is unsafe as written and slips to Year 11–13 unless build cost is held to ₦650–850m per building; and at the full Akuzo specification the building yields 2.7% as a rental asset, meaning it "does not work as a rental asset at all."

What each domain supplies and buys. Every group plan states this in both directions, and it is summarised in the flow table below. In brief: Isiome supplies food and botanical inputs, and buys power, construction and materials from Okodu, finance and insurance from Akunnia, and freight from Uli. Akunnia supplies capital, insurance, treasury, title perfection and security, and buys the Group's own unavoidable legal and security workload plus construction at cost. Idenze supplies trained people, clinical evidence and the teaching hospital, and buys botanical inputs from Isiome, construction and power from Okodu, and controlled-substance movement from Uli. Uli supplies freight, warehousing, controlled-substance movement and the catalogue, and buys power, construction, finance and systems. Okodu supplies power, construction, materials, housing and long-dated rental assets, and buys food, freight, trained trades and project finance.

4.2 The advantage

No standalone competitor starts with demand already contracted. An agro-processor must find its first institutional customer; Isiome Foods signs Group estates, schools and the teaching hospital before the line is commissioned. A haulier must find cargo; Uli Freight's first 40 loaded legs a month are Group cargo, signed before a truck is ordered. A power developer must find an anchor offtaker; Okodu Power's first customer is a set of companies under one ownership, so "demand is contracted before a panel is ordered — no merchant risk, no ramp-up." A fund manager must find investable assets; Akunnia's first fund is seeded from assets Okodu and Uli originate. That internal demand is not merely convenient — it is what makes the first tranche of several businesses financeable on non-recourse terms, because the demand risk is removed rather than mitigated.

4.3 The related-party risk

The same integration is the Group's largest governance exposure, and the library names it in almost every relevant plan. Four mechanisms are adopted: published, board-approved transfer pricing (the deduction authority between Isiome Seed and Storage "written into both contracts, minuted and audited"; Okodu Materials at "benchmark minus 5–10%"; Uli Freight's carriage agreements "Group CFO-certified as arms-length and minuted by the independent directors"); independent directors sitting alone on related-party transactions, as a board resolution in plans/08, 09, 10, 51, 52, 14_Aku_Insurance.md and plans/16_Aku_Bank.md; structural separation where conflict is unavoidable — Uli Broadcast must remain free to sell to Uli Brand's clients' competitors, Group disputes above ₦250m (and any where the counterparty has not consented in writing) go to independent institutions, never to Aku Arbitration (plans/55_Aku_Arbitration.md), Aku Advisory "will not advise on a transaction in which any Group entity is a bidder," and Aku Advisory may not audit Uli Special Logistics; and transfer-price documentation where an internal price allocates between two P&Ls — plans/20_Idenze_Consumer_Health.md is direct that the transfer price between it and Idenze Pharma "is a Group allocation and must be documented, or both P&Ls are fiction."

Two exposures the library does not resolve. First, the internal flows are load-bearing rather than incidental — Uli's Year-1 cargo is 40% captive, Okodu Materials targets 70% of Group construction material spend, and Akunnia's Year-1 revenue is entirely Group workload. A group whose first customer is itself can report revenue growth that is a transfer between its own balance sheets. The honest test is external-revenue share, which individual plans state (Uli Brand ≥70% external by Year 10; Okodu Materials ≥55%; Okodu Solar 50% by Year 5) but no group plan aggregates. Second, the concentration rule is written but the consolidation is not: the audit found two Akunnia plans each costing the same Year-3 35-person platform, and two Uli plans booking the same vehicles (₦1.39bn in plans/35_Uli_Freight.md against ₦1.43bn in plans/40_Uli_Fleet.md), the second disclosing the overlap but no group total netting it.

6. The financial model — how the Group makes money

The Group earns money two structurally different ways, and the plans are careful not to confuse them.

6.1 Operating profit

The operating businesses sell goods and services. Their economics are conventional — throughput against fixed cost — and the library names the binding constraint company by company rather than burying it: Isiome Foods breaks even at ~47% of design throughput (~35% as the retail mix matures), each point worth ₦83m of contribution; Idenze Pharma at ~220m units, ~44% of Phase-1 nameplate against a ₦3.1bn fixed base; Okodu Grid at ~72% collection efficiency; Uli Cinemas at 3.6% seat occupancy against an industry average of ~2.7%; Uli Freight at 5.8 loaded legs a month owned; Aku Bank at ₦3.6bn of book and ₦6bn of deposits to cover a ₦900m cost base.

At least one plan's break-even sits beyond its own milestone table: plans/22_Idenze_Distribution.md puts break-even at ~₦75bn of revenue and ~15,000 orders while its own Year-3 milestone is ₦13bn (labelled break-even) and its Year-5 milestone is ₦34bn (EBITDA+) — so on the plan's own unit economics it does not reach break-even inside the horizon it claims.

Several businesses are low-margin and capital-hungry by design — Isiome Farms (net return below the cost of naira debt), Uli Warehousing (13% unlevered yield against naira lending above 30%), Okodu Housing (2.7–5.1% gross yield at the Akuzo specification), Aku Arbitration (a ₦3bn subsidy by Year 5, and "if the Group will not fund ten years of losses, it should not start this company"), Idenze Healthcare (a clinic that is a staff-retention investment). The Group's return is not intended to come from these standalone — it comes from the internal flows in §4 and from the second income stream below.

The magnitude, as the plans model it. A US$300m Fund I returning 2.5× gross over eight years generates ~US$450m of profit: ~US$140m preferred return to LPs, US$35m catch-up, US$55m from the 80/20 split, and US$90m of carry to the GP — split among six to eight deal professionals, US$10–15m each on top of salary. Lifetime management fee ~US$55m gross, ~US$44–47m net — about US$4.5m a year across ten years.

Why fees and carry are structurally different from operating profit.

  1. They are earned on other people's capital, not the Group's. A management fee is contractual revenue on committed LP capital; carry is a share of profits the Group did not fund. The plan states the consequence: fee coverage of the firm's own cost base must exceed 1.3× by Year 6 and 1.8× by Year 10 — "below 1.0× the firm is being subsidised by the Group" (plans/10_Aku_Asset_Management.md).
  2. They are contractual and recurring rather than throughput-dependent. plans/09_Aku_Capital.md classifies fees as "high and contractual, quarterly" and carry as "zero until crystallised then cash," accruing over 6–10 years and lumpy — which is why the two are separate return streams and why first carry crystallisation sits in a different horizon from operating profits.
  3. They are not capped by the Group's own balance sheet — and that is the decisive structural point. Carry was placed at fund level precisely because it does not require issuing equity: the family keeps 100% of the operating conglomerate while partners share in returns their own funds generate. The conglomerate's growth is limited by its own cash generation and borrowing capacity; the fund platform's is limited by the third-party capital it can raise. plans/00_Family_Business.md §9 states the intended consequence: "the Group's own businesses become, over time, a source of assets and deal flow rather than the destination of all the Group's capital." The plan also states the cost: it "is a real change in what the family enterprise is."
  4. They carry a governance price. Every Aku fund must carry Group capital alongside third-party money — which aligns interests and is how the first funds become creditable at all — and is then subject to the rule below.

The self-limiting rule that makes the fee model defensible. No fund holds more than 25% in Group-originated assets, stepping down to 15% by Year 6. Related-party transactions are approved by the independent directors sitting alone, priced against an external benchmark with an independent valuation on file; the LPAC carries the cap as a consent right; and the cap is written into the fund documents (plans/09_Aku_Capital.md §4.4; plans/10_Aku_Asset_Management.md §4.3). plans/51_Aku_Credit.md renders the same discipline for lending as Group-related obligors ≤25% falling to 15% by Year 6.

What must happen first. A first-time manager needs "two realised exits with audited gross and net returns, four to six years of deal history in the target sectors, a named team with prior fund experience, an independent administrator and Big-4 auditor, an independent LPAC, and a DFI-standard ESG framework" (plans/52_Aku_Private_Equity.md §3). Hence Years 1–5 are balance-sheet deals out of Aku Capital and the first third-party fund closes in Years 5–8. plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md §12 puts the critical hire first: "Hire the Managing Partner before anything else. In this model the first senior hire is the strategy."

One honest caveat on reported returns. plans/13_Aku_Treasury.md claims a net Group benefit of ~₦2,431m a year against its own book loss of ~₦915m — but ₦4,300m of that is "FX loss avoided" under a single 15% devaluation scenario against ₦2,160m of hedging cost. Excluding the pair, the claimed benefit is ~₦291m a year: about 91% of the stated return rests on one currency scenario. The plan labels Treasury an avoided-cost function, not a profit centre, and says it should be judged that way. One further defect: the plan claims its headcount "reconciles to the trajectory in plans/09_Aku_Capital.md", but that plan's organisation table carries no treasury line at all — so Treasury's 18 staff at Year 10 sit outside the group figure it is measured against.

8. Licensing as an acquisition strategy

This is a deliberate operating rule rather than a set of expedients. plans/README.md: "Licensing and acquisition pathway" replaced "Regulatory pathway" across the library, deliberately. The Group's rule is that a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business; where a licence is needed, the plan states who issues it, what it costs to obtain directly — and how to acquire it instead: what kind of existing licensed entity to buy, roughly what that costs, and what the change-of-control process involves.

plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md §5 gives the reasoning: "In Nigerian and African markets, licences and registrations are frequently cheaper to buy than to obtain — because the incumbent is undercapitalised, the regulator's de novo process is slow, and an existing entity brings staff, systems, a customer base and a regulatory track record that a new applicant must build from nothing. Every new business the Group launches should ask the acquisition question before the build question."

8.2 What this delivers — and where it does not

The rule works where it is applied: nine licence acquisitions are costed, named and scheduled, seven carry a ring-fenced mandate with a day-90 decision, and the two largest quantified savings are South Africa ($2.5–7m over 6–12 months against $8–15m over 24–36+ months) and the teaching hospital (revenue in 1–3 months against 36–48).

This finding has since been closed — and the way it was closed is worth recording as a caution. When this section was written, of 59 plan files, §5 carried a licensing-and-acquisition title in 12 and still read "Regulatory pathway" in 44 — while plans/README.md stated the rename had been made "across the library, deliberately." The README claim was ahead of the work. Every plan has since been brought into line: 60 of 60 plans now carry a licensing-and-acquisition route, including the Idenze domain and the four Uli plans the library itself marks critical (Broadcasting, Special Logistics, Cinemas, Freight). The lesson is the one this summary keeps repeating: a claim in an index is not a fact about the files, and the only way to know is to check each one.

Two naming violations sit alongside the missing routes. plans/19_Idenze_Therapeutics.md §1 says the Nkpor suite is "co-located with Ezeme Generics" — a company that appears nowhere in the library, and a name that breaks the architecture's first naming rule, that only the mother company may carry the Ezeme name. And plans/18_Idenze_Pharma.md §7 still refers to "the pharma-distribution arm (name pending)" although plans/22_Idenze_Distribution.md exists. Separately, plans/21_Idenze_Sterile_Injectables.md prices oral solids at "₦21bn in 24–30 months" — the Idenze Group T1 figure, not Idenze Pharma's own ₦18.44bn T0+T1 — so one company's capital estimate is quoted as another's.

And one brief assumption is not in the library. plans/12_Aku_Markets.md proposes SEC fund/portfolio-manager registration, CIS authorisation, ETF authorisation and NGX market-maker registration, with no acquisition route — and plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md §1 records the company as "reduced to a minor product line." No plan proposes acquiring an existing NGX dealing member or stockbroking licence.

9. The risks that could end this

9.1 Gearing and ring-fencing discipline

The rules. Gearing ≤40%, "a ceiling, not a plan." At a ~13% unlevered yield against naira lending above 30%, 40% debt consumes essentially the entire net operating income in interest, so practical gearing in asset-backed businesses is 15–25%, funded by Aku Infrastructure Fund I on a 10–15 year tenor. No unhedged USD debt — the Neimeth precedent (₦1.7bn net loss on a ₦2bn FX loss from dollar debt) is cited as "from the Group's own state." Financing ring-fenced per sector. Licences and land are the collateral; fee businesses are the margin engines; never cross-pledge the two. FX re-based quarterly (plans/00_Family_Business.md §7).

The discipline is stronger than the rule. plans/13_Aku_Treasury.md gives the clearest statement: "financing ring-fenced per group with no cross-pledges, so a failure in one group cannot accelerate debt in another." The same plan resolved a genuine structural contradiction: ring-fencing and cash pooling contradict each other. Zero-balancing is permitted within a ring; between rings only notional offsets and documented intercompany loans — never a bank-level structure crossing a ring boundary, because that is an implicit cross-group guarantee a liquidator can unwind. Because the CBN's Draft Ring-Fencing Guidelines for Closely Linked Entities (June 2026) would bar linked financial entities from lending to each other, the pool is built between non-financial operating companies only, with Aku Bank outside it entirely.

Three defects a lender should hold. (1) Gearing is stated in six plans and defined in none. plans/03_Isiome_Machinery.md fixes it by arithmetic — ₦16.8m of debt on ₦42m of total capital is called "gearing 40%" — so the library's gearing is debt ÷ (debt + equity), permitting ₦0.67 of debt per ₦1 of equity, against ₦0.40 under debt/equity: the same "40%" is 1.67× more permissive under the library's own basis. A third denominator is in use (plans/50_Akuzo_Development.md: "≤40% loan-to-cost"). (2) Two plans breach the ceiling outright — plans/42_Okodu_Power.md models "Equity payback at 60% debt" and plans/51_Aku_Credit.md 75% debt funding. The power plan's 60% is project debt inside a ring-fenced SPV, normal market practice, but the rule as written is unqualified: either it needs a project-finance carve-out in writing or the model comes down. (3) Eight plans state no ratio at all, most seriously plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md — the group plan that sets the financial rules for eight other companies, and which states no gearing ratio and no hedging prohibition — and plans/35_Uli_Freight.md, the most capital-intensive Uli plan. Two further plans omit both rules entirely on a zero-match search — plans/19_Idenze_Therapeutics.md (which gives only "no cross-guarantees or cross-pledges") and plans/24_Idenze_University.md, where the funding sequence in §6 is silent despite the largest single capital requirement in the Group.

No plan assumes unhedged USD debt; none implies cross-group recourse. These are omissions, not violations.

9.2 Concentration of influence across regulated sectors

Finance + news + pharma + energy + food + education in one market "makes the Group a political actor" — it would hold a broadcaster alongside banking, pharmaceutical and university licences, inviting antitrust scrutiny, licensing retaliation and caps on international fundraising (plans/00_Family_Business.md §11 risk 3). Mitigations: separate vehicles; independent boards; published governance; proactive regulator engagement; and the decisive one — no news or current-affairs operation where regulated licences are held. Film, music and creative content carry no such constraint. plans/32_Uli_Broadcast.md writes the prohibition into the charter (news bulletins, current affairs, political talk shows, paid political advertising), changeable only by shareholder resolution, and calls drift into news "Critical — the only risk that ends the company."

Two exposures the plans name against themselves: Aku Arbitration's conflict of interest (Group disputes above a stated value go to independent institutions, never to it) and Aku Advisory's governance risk, which the plan calls "Critical — existential governance risk."

A third is unresolved. plans/37_Uli_Publishing.md excludes newspapers and current-affairs journalism because they are "(political risk; Uli Broadcast's mandate)" — assigning news to the company that has chartered it out of existence.

And the rule that would have prevented the risk in the first place is applied nowhere. EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md §11 sets the constraint that media is built "only in markets where the Group holds no regulated licence." Not one of the 13 Uli plans — nor plans/28_Uli_Group.md — restates or applies that geographic test. plans/32_Uli_Broadcast.md names its markets (Nkpor/Onitsha in Year 1, Awka in Year 2, a six-station network, national carriage, six platforms, diaspora OTT) and tests them only against the NBC same-locality control restriction, never against where the Group holds banking, pharmaceutical, university or insurance licences. plans/35_Uli_Freight.md names four corridors with no licence-overlap test either. The scope prohibition is respected in the plans; the geographic prohibition is a standing rule with no implementation anywhere in the library.

9.3 The foreign-interest problem created by a London or New York manager above Nigerian operating companies

NBC Act s.9(1) requires a licence applicant to be a Nigerian-registered corporate entity and obliges the Commission to satisfy itself that it "is not representing any foreign interest" (plans/32_Uli_Broadcast.md §5). The chain runs Mauritius trust → Mauritius GBC → Ezeme Group Nigeria → operating company. "A Mauritius-domiciled trust and GBC sitting above every Nigerian operating company is, on its face, capable of being read as exactly that" (EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md §4A). The Blackstone restructure makes it worse: an FCA- or SEC-authorised manager at the hub "is a far clearer case of 'representing foreign interest' under NBC Act s.9(1) than a Mauritius trust was" — so the licence-by-licence ownership audit is mandatory rather than prudent, and must be completed before the hub company is incorporated.

It is not a broadcasting-only question. Local-ownership or local-control tests apply across NBC, NACOC, CBN, NUC, NAFDAC and PCN. "The Group cannot assume its structure is licence-neutral." The s.9(1) exposure itself is raised explicitly in only three documents — plans/09_Aku_Capital.md (risk 10 and first-ninety-days item 2), plans/10_Aku_Asset_Management.md (first-ninety-days item 4) and plans/32_Uli_Broadcast.md — and restated independently in plans/53_Aku_Legal.md, which requires that the legal practice be owned by Nigerian practitioners and every registered activity sit outside the offshore chain. It is not raised at all in plans/11, 12, 13_Aku_Treasury.md, 14_Aku_Insurance.md, 15_Aku_Advisory.md, 16_Aku_Bank.md, 51_Aku_Credit.md, 52_Aku_Private_Equity.md or 55_Aku_Arbitration.md — all of which sit under ownership tests of their own. plans/16_Aku_Bank.md engages an adjacent CBN ownership-approval test rather than s.9(1): BOFIA 2020 requires prior CBN approval for 5% or more, and the plan warns "Expect the CBN to reject at least one nominee director; hold two cleared alternates per seat." plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md risk 13 records the private guard ownership bar.

Two structures are available. (1) Licence inside the chain — a Nigerian subsidiary of the Mauritius GBC. Simplest; correct where the regulator has no ownership test; risk is the foreign-interest reading. (2) A Nigerian-controlled licence vehicle holding the licence and contracting with the Group operationally — more complex, and "it recreates the ownership-drift problem the Corporate Architecture exists to prevent," so it must be documented under the capital-source rule with a signed declaration of trust and reserved matters. A licensing exception protocol covers cases requiring a named natural person, with the hard rule that it is never a nominee or front arrangement — NACOC has publicly warned that no entity is authorised to facilitate the acquisition of cannabis licences.

One counterweight, from the same plan: the NBC Broadcasting Code requires premium sports and news channels to be wholesaled non-exclusively and forbids warehousing of sports rights, so premium content cannot legally be locked away from a new entrant.

Status: unresolved, and both plans/08 §12 and plans/32 §12 make it the gating item before licence or hub spend.

9.4 The related-party risk in a group whose businesses trade with each other

Developed at §4.3. For the register: the internal flows are load-bearing, not incidental — Uli Freight's Year-1 cargo is 40% captive, Isiome Seed hauls entirely on Uli Freight, Okodu Materials targets 70% of Group construction material spend, Akunnia's Year-1 revenue is entirely Group workload, and Uli Brand's internal advantage is worth ₦820m a year. The mitigation set is real (published board-approved rate cards, Group CFO certification, independent directors sitting alone, structural separation, named prohibitions). What is missing is the aggregation: no group plan states external-revenue share, and no group total nets the known internal double-counts.

9.5 The risk that the funds buy the Group's own assets and call it a track record

Severity: Critical in plans/08_Akunnia_Group.md (risk 4) and plans/09_Aku_Capital.md (risk 11). "The easiest deal available to a principal investor that owns an operating conglomerate is one of its own assets." "Under Blackstone this matters more, not less." The failure mode is precise: "a manager whose fund is its parent's projects is a financing vehicle, and no DFI will anchor it."

The mitigation. No fund holds more than 25% in Group-originated assets, stepping down to 15% by Year 6; related-party transactions approved by the independent directors sitting alone, priced against an external benchmark with an independent valuation on file; the LPAC carries the cap as a consent right; and the cap is written into the fund documents.

Three qualifications. First, the cap appears in seven plans and is absent from five — not in plans/11, 13_Aku_Treasury.md, 15, 53 or 55; the most consequential omission is Treasury, which funds the cash pool. Second, the cap is a ceiling on a conflict, not an absence of one: at 25% of a US$300m Fund I, up to US$75m of LP money may be invested in the Group's own originated assets — disclosed and independently valued, but still the Group selling to itself with other people's capital. Third, there is a structural version of the same risk in real estate. plans/47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md risk 9, "the asset class does not price" (Very high): at a 10% naira capitalisation rate, a held building's ₦54m net operating income is worth ₦540m against a ₦1.16bn cost — a 53% loss. The plan's fix is where the related-party risk and the fund model intersect: the captive anchor tenant. Leased to Idenze University or Group companies, the same asset is priced on contracted cash flow, not cap rate — "which is precisely why this arm exists beyond its own returns." Coherent, but it means the fund's early portfolio quality depends on leases from the Group's own tenants.

9.6 Key-person dependency on the founding principal

Rated High in plans/00_Family_Business.md risk 5 and Medium in EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md risk 10. Stated mitigations: Protector succession, independents, documented mandates, staged handover — plus the Charter's structural answer that operational control is granted, not inherited: a non-engagement trigger of 24–36 months refers operational control to the Business Board, which appoints a steward, while "the disengaged heir keeps their economic entitlement in full."

The dependency is deeper than the protocol addresses, and the library says so twice. First, the family's own sequencing puts professional managers in charge of all five domains for years — each child leads on completing a first Master's, and the Master Plan's assumption is activation "from approximately Year 22 onward" — so for two decades this is a conglomerate run by hired managers under a founder who is the only remaining decision-maker, which is the failure mode the plan itself names. Second, the finance platform's dependency is on a hire not yet made: "Hire the Managing Partner before anything else. In this model the first senior hire is the strategy. Without a credible deal originator the funds cannot be raised and the hub is an empty office."

9.7 No Group-level P&L, balance sheet or cash-flow statement yet exists

Stated by the library itself (plans/README.md open item 2) and confirmed by the audit. A credit committee cannot currently test: consolidated leverage against the Group's own 40% ceiling; consolidated interest cover; whether the internal flows at §4 net to zero or to a margin; the cash profile of a programme in which many tranches are revolving working capital; or aggregate exposure to any one currency, counterparty or regulator. The company-level plans are the compensating strength — the audit found no arithmetic error in a company capital table. The gap is aggregation, not diligence.

9.8 Three further named risks

  • The cap table is not yet clean, and it gates everything (plans/00_Family_Business.md risk 1, Critical): "You cannot retire Igba Odibo or install reserved matters without knowing exactly where equity sits. This is the gating item." The apprentice-equity model — 50% equity to each settled apprentice, compounding through a cascade — had to end, because "a group with hundreds of 50/50 shareholders across dozens of branches has an un-investable cap table." Retirement is a Year-1 Charter amendment requiring unanimous consent for three provisions.
  • Licence loss or non-renewal in any jurisdiction — Critical. Dedicated regulatory affairs function; licence portfolio ring-fenced; no single licence carries the Group. "Licences, not land, are the Group's core asset."
  • Currency and repatriation. Mauritius treaty network, USD/EUR reserves, per-country dividend planning, local-currency matching — against a portfolio in which 85–90% of pharmaceutical and energy capex is imported and dollar-denominated while revenue is naira.

NIIRA s.16(1) requires depositing "the equivalent of the minimum capital requirement" (₦15bn), while NAICOM's January 2026 Guidelines state 50% of MCR (₦7.5bn). plans/14_Aku_Insurance.md assumes ₦7.5bnA ₦7.5bn liquidity question, not a rounding difference, and it is unresolved in the plan. The same plan also states "gearing ≤40% is not the binding constraint: regulatory capital must be equity"plans/14_Aku_Insurance.md

What would most change the picture

Four things, in order, where the library's own priority list and this review converge: freeze the revision; commission the Akuzo/Okodu cost book (already budgeted at ₦12m, day 60, in plans/59_Okodu_Housing.md); complete the licence-by-licence ownership audit; and write one consolidated capital plan and one consolidated financial model per group, netting the known double-counts. Until the fourth is done, the Group's capital requirement and its leverage cannot be tested by anyone, including the Group — and on the first three, the plans say so themselves.
