The scope prohibition (no news) is respected; the geographic prohibition is a rule with zero implementationHighBefore any broadcast licence application: map every proposed Uli market against every market where the Group holds a regulated licence, and publish the exclusion list as a board-approved schedule. A rule that exists only in this document is not a control
12A Year-1 insurance gap that no plan owns. 40_Uli_Fleet.md records that Aku's motor line is scheduled Year 5–6, so Fleet must use external underwriters for Years 1–4 — while 35_Uli_Freight.md requires goods-in-transit, liability and marine open cover bound "before the first load" in Year 1, naming Akunnia as the supplierHighBind the Year-1 cover with external underwriters, budgeted explicitly, and stop describing Aku Insurance as the supplier of coverage it cannot write until Year 5. Better an externally placed policy than an uninsured first load
13Fleet ownership is unresolved, not merely double-counted. 38_Uli_Special_Logistics.md states it "owns its licences, vehicles, crew and custody record" and "shares no vehicle pool"; 40_Uli_Fleet.md states "Fleet owns these units" and flags the point as an open board itemMediumA single board decision on whether the controlled-specification units sit inside the ring-fenced licence holder or on Fleet's balance sheet. The ring-fence argument should win — a controlled-substance licence whose vehicles are shared across a group is a licence risk, not an efficiency

14. Immediate next actions — the first ninety days

  1. Commission the two NACOC questions (§12.1–2). Nothing else in the cannabinoid programme proceeds until answered.
  2. Convene the Family Business Board to appoint the qualifying family member for the Ghana residence process and commence it. The clock on this is measured in years — every month of delay is a month of delay on the licence.
  3. Commission counsel opinions in parallel: Nigeria (CAMA transfer, NAFDAC NCS pathway, Charter amendments), Mauritius (trust, PTC, GBC), South Africa (GACP+GMP acquisition targets), Ghana (residence + licensing), Kenya/Rwanda (anchor market entry).
  4. Commission an audit of every existing entity to map the current cap table before restructuring — you cannot retire Igba Odibo without knowing exactly where equity sits.
  5. Draft the Group Board charter and the independence criteria, and shortlist independent directors.
  6. Appoint the Group Regulatory Affairs lead — the single most under-rated hire in the plan, and the function that will hold the Group's most valuable assets.
  7. Open the NAFDAC NCS relationship formally and begin the import-permit documentation pathway, so that it is routine by the time the first API shipment is ready.
  8. Freeze all cannabis-related spend except licensing and legal work. No cultivation, no facilities, no procurement until the eligibility question is answered.

15. What this architecture commits the family to

Stated plainly, because the documents show this family responds to clarity:

  1. The cap table comes before ambition. No institutional capital, no listing, no pension mandate, and no partner of consequence will engage until Igba Odibo is retired and the structure is audited.
  2. Licences, not land, are the Group's core asset. Regulatory affairs is therefore a first-class function, and licence hygiene outranks growth every time they conflict.
  3. Family governance and corporate governance must be separated before the Group outgrows the Council's weekly rhythm — which it already has.
  4. Creative content is the Group's safest power and its best export. Film, television and music build brand rather than political exposure, earn hard currency, and produce a catalogue that is a genuine financial asset class feeding Akunnia's funds. Only the news part of Uli's pillar carries concentration risk, and it should be separated or deferred.
  5. Finance is a consequence, not a cause. The African champion asset manager is built out of assets the other four domains create. Anything else is a family office with a grander name.
  6. Blackstone scale requires deals, carried interest and a global hub — not passive scale. Returns come from buying control, improving operations and selling, not from AUM accumulating at basis points. The carry scheme and the hub are the two structural preconditions; without them the Group cannot hire the talent that sources and executes transactions, and the strategy fails at the first step.
  7. The cannabinoid line is legal, licensable and strategically sound — but only offshore-cultivated, Nigeria-manufactured, ring-fenced, and never concealed. Concealment was never what made this valuable; the licence is.

EZEME GROUP — NAMING ARCHITECTURE

The children's names. Nothing else.

Version: 5.0 — final. Supersedes v1.0–v4.0, all withdrawn.

Decision (user): "I love the use of my kids name for each company, and that is enough. The rest of the words and name can be ignored."

Every Igbo word register is dropped. No dictionary words, no dialect sourcing, no coined vocabulary. The naming is settled.

The scheme

Ezeme Group is the mother company. Every other company is named for one of the five children, plus a plain English descriptor — the Dangote pattern (Dangote Group → Dangote Cement, Dangote Sugar, Dangote Flour).

```

EZEME GROUP (mother company)

│

├── ISIOME GROUP — 1st child · First Son · Patriarch

│ Agriculture & Food Systems + Manufacturing & Industrial Production

├── AKUNNIA GROUP — 2nd child · First Daughter · Matriarch · Chief Investment Officer

│ Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security

├── IDENZE GROUP — 3rd child · Second Son · Senior Male Heir

│ Education & Human Capital + Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals

├── ULI GROUP — 4th child · Second Daughter · Senior Female Heir

│ Media & Information Systems + Transport & Logistics

└── OKODU GROUP — 5th child · Third Son

Energy & Utilities + Construction & Real Estate

```

Sector wording above is taken verbatim from Group Master Plan §6.1–6.5. Birth order and titles are taken from the family's own records.

Companies are [Child] + function

GroupCompanies
Isiome GroupIsiome Seed · Isiome Machinery · Isiome Farms · Isiome Storage · Isiome Foods · Isiome Trading · Isiome Manufacturing

Group-level and family entities: Ezeme Group · Ezeme Family Office · Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd (the GBC holding company) · Ezeme Family Holdings PTC Ltd (the Mauritius private trust company that acts as trustee) · Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius, Trusts Act 2001)

Ownership chain, exactly as the family's own Corporate Architecture sets it out:

```

Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius, Trusts Act 2001)

└── trustee: Ezeme Family Holdings PTC Ltd

└── Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd — Global Business Company

```

Naming correction of record. Earlier revisions of the plan library abbreviated the Mauritius holding layer as "Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) GBC." The family's Corporate Architecture names it Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd — the word Family is part of the legal name, and it distinguishes the holding company from the PTC trustee. Corrected across all documents.

Two naming rules the library follows. (1) Only the mother company carries the Ezeme name — no subsidiary is ever "Ezeme X"; the child's name sits at the group level and repeats down the operating companies. (2) "Aku" is not a separate name — it is the established short form of Akunnia, and Akunnia's companies use it because Akunnia is her own name shortened, exactly as the family writes it.

Why this is the right answer

  1. It is how the family already thinks. The Charter binds offices to names — Isiome is Patriarch, Akunnia is Matriarch. The Corporate Architecture already names the five child groups Isiome Group, Akunnia Group, Idenze Group, Uli Group and Okodu Group. This scheme makes the naming consistent with the family's own governance instead of layering invented vocabulary on top of it.
  2. It is institutionally clean. A company named for what it does can be sold, merged, listed or inherited without carrying a person's identity into a transaction. The child's name belongs at the group level, where it marks ownership and mandate.
  3. It survives. Names that depend on a dialect decision can be re-litigated forever — as the last four versions of this document demonstrate. Names that are the family's own cannot.
  4. It is legible. A partner, regulator or lender in any jurisdiction can say "Idenze Pharma" on the first attempt.

The three-name rule — retained

A regulated business may still need three names: the legal name the regulator approves, the trading name the market sees, and the product name registered for each medicine. So:

  • Idenze University is the trading name on an NUC-approvable legal name.
  • Idenze Therapeutics products take neutral brand names — medicines regulators restrict brand names that imply efficacy or promise a cure.

Registration rule — retained

Before anything is registered, run: CAC availability, NAFDAC register, trademark databases (Nigeria and the offshore jurisdictions), and a cross-language check in the markets the entity trades in (French, Hausa, Arabic, Portuguese, Swahili).

LICENCE_OWNERSHIP_AUDIT.md  ·  41,307 words

EZEME GROUP — LICENCE-BY-LICENCE OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL AUDIT

Status: decision document for the board — not a summary.

Prepared: September 2026.

Currency: naira primary. Dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Dollar figures appear only where a plan itself states them.

Sources: the 60-plan library at .research/gdocs/plans/ (index plans/README.md), read section 5 of every licence-bearing plan and swept every plan for every regulator name in sections 4, 9, 10, 11 and 12; EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md (§4A and §8); EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md.

Primary sources obtained and read directly for this audit: National Broadcasting Commission Act (Cap N11 LFN 2004, including the Second and Third Schedules); Private Guard Companies Act (Cap P30 LFN 2004, full text); Anambra State Homeland Security Law 2025 (s.7 read in the gazetted text); the NBC Broadcasting Code (6th edition, amended addendum). Practitioner/industry summaries are labelled as secondary wherever relied on.

File-location note. The Ezeme library was relocated during the preparation of this audit. The live library — the 60 plans and the five companion documents — is now at /Users/nzeora/Projects/Ezeme/.research/gdocs/. This file was written to /Users/nzeora/Documents/Ezeme/.research/gdocs/, because the writing session's sandbox was scoped to the Documents workspace and could not write to Projects. Before relying on this document, copy it to the live library at /Users/nzeora/Projects/Ezeme/.research/gdocs/LICENCE_OWNERSHIP_AUDIT.md. The document is self-contained and requires no other file to be read first.

0. THE ANSWER, BEFORE THE DETAIL

Three facts decide this audit, and none of them is the fact the library has been arguing about.

  1. The foreign-interest problem is broader than the library thinks, and narrower in one place. The library treats "representing any foreign interest" as an interpretation question about the word representing. It is not. The NBC Act itself directs the Commission, in determining the grant of a licence, to consider "the structure of shareholding in the broadcasting organisation" (§9(4)(a)) and makes it a Commission function to ensure adherence to the rules on "the participation of foreign capital in relation to local capital in broadcasting" (§2(1)(r)). On the statute as written, a licensee ultimately owned by a Mauritius discretionary trust is not a close call. Conversely, the same statute is silent on change of control — the Third Schedule, paragraph 5 says flatly that "A licence shall not be transferable" — so the acquisition route the Uli Broadcast plan builds its whole strategy on has no statutory consent process at all. Both halves of that finding are load-bearing, and both point the same way: buy the company, never assume a consent.
  1. One licence cannot be cured by any ownership structure the library has considered, and the same statute contains an exemption the library has not noticed. The Private Guard Companies Act's long title describes it as "An Act to regulate and provide for the licensing of private guard companies which must be wholly owned by Nigerians". The library's remedy for Aku Security — "a Nigerian-controlled vehicle ... the Group's economic interest delivered by ... dividends to the Nigerian holder" — satisfies the operative s.13(1)(e) director test but may not satisfy the long title, because the remedy contemplates the Group holding economic equity in the licence vehicle. If "wholly owned by Nigerians" is read as the Act's object (and s.4(4)'s revocation trigger is drafted around ownership or control, not directors), then the vehicle must be 100% Nigerian-owned, with the Group earning only fees, and the Group's equity must sit outside. This is not settled law and must be put to counsel — but the audit must not assume the favourable reading, which is what every plan currently does. The counterweight is s.36(3)(b): the Act does not require a licence of "any inspector, guard, watchman, or other person employed to do inspecting, guarding, watching or inquiry work for one employer only". A Group company guarding only its own premises with its own directly-employed staff falls outside the Act entirely — so a material part of what the Group wants from Aku Security may not need the licence at all, and the board should establish that before it spends money on owning a licensee.
  1. The hub is not a licence problem. It is a value-extraction problem. On the statute, no licence in this library requires the Group to own the licensed entity. What they require is that the controlled activity be conducted by a properly constituted, compliant licensee. A London or New York manager above Nigerian operating companies does not need to hold any Nigerian licence to earn management fees, carry and systems royalties. So the sequencing answer is not "resolve the licences, then incorporate the hub." It is: incorporate the hub, but never let the hub own a licence-gated Nigerian company — and never let the hub appear in a licence application. The distinction between owning and earning is the whole architecture.

On the regulator's published and reported eligibility test the Group can satisfy it by structure — a Ghanaian company with approximately 50% Ghanaian shareholding or a majority Ghanaian board — which is not the structural impossibility the library assumes. See the NACOC row in §F and the corrected exposure ranking below.

69 doubtful rows. The audit does not attempt a second aggregated number for these, because the interesting fact is which they are. The pattern in the doubtful list is the audit's most useful single observation. Only eleven of the 69 are doubtful because of the Group's ownership chain — the financial-services, insurance and education registrations listed above, plus NACOC. The other 58 are doubtful because a Nigerian regulator has not published a position — on whether a certificate follows the entity, the premises or the product; on whether a change of control continues a registration or restarts it; or on what an unpublished fee actually is. That is a much more tractable problem than a structural one, and it is solved by the regulator letter in §3.4 rather than by restructuring the Group.

The top five exposures, in order — see §3 for the reasoning:

#ExposureWhy it ranks here
1NBC broadcast licence (all classes) — Uli BroadcastThe only licence in the Group whose refusal is not a business setback but a structural verdict on the ownership chain. Statutory shareholding test, statutory foreign-capital function, no transfer mechanism, and a post-grant revocation hook. It also gates the media domain's whole acquisition strategy and, because the hub sits above everything, it is the licence most worsened by the Blackstone restructure.
2Private Guard Companies Act licence — Aku SecurityStatutory object is wholly Nigerian ownership; a citizenship bar on every director (s.13(1)(e)); automatic revocation trigger on change of ownership or control (s.4(4)); licence cannot be sold or let (s.26); per-employee ministerial approval (s.7); and a 2025 state-layer registration on top. The Group's own plan already concedes the chain "cannot sit above this licence" — the audit's addition is that the concession is insufficient.
3NACOC Ghana medicinal-cannabis licence — Idenze TherapeuticsRanked third on consequence, but the audit found it is less impossible than the library assumes — and the library's stated plan for it may not work. The eligibility test binds shareholders and directors, not the licence, so it cannot be bought or transferred. But NACOC's own statements show a company route — about 50% Ghanaian shareholding or a majority Ghanaian board — that the Group can satisfy by structure. The serious risk is different: the architecture document's decided route depends on a family member's Ghanaian Indefinite Residence, and residence is not citizenship.
4NAFDAC NCS / NDLEA / INCB controlled-substances set — Idenze Therapeutics, Idenze Distribution, Uli Special LogisticsThe one licence family the library already concedes is not acquirable. Per-shipment, named licensee, no standing permit, quantities matched to a national estimates line that is not assignable. A share purchase likely triggers re-vetting rather than continuation.
5CBN banking authorisation through to national commercial — Aku BankNot a nationality problem but a continuous-approval problem: BOFIA 2020 requires prior CBN approval for 5% or more, a fit-and-proper assessment of every significant shareholder, and CBN approval for later changes to shareholding, board, management, products, capital and branches. Every layer of the Mauritius chain, including the trust and its beneficiaries, becomes a disclosed controller. [verify] — the primary text of BOFIA 2020 was not reachable in this session.

0.2 What the library gets right, and what it gets wrong

The library is unusually honest about licensing. Seven of its positions survive this audit intact and should not be relitigated:

PositionWhereVerdict
A share purchase does not avoid the Minister's consent on a mineral title46_Okodu_Materials.md §5⚠️ CORRECTED IN PART — the conclusion may hold in practice, but the statutory basis the library cites does not exist. The library attributes to s.147 NMMA 2007 the proposition that the consent is unavoidable on either structure, quoting practice language about "disposal of controlling interest in entities holding exploration or mining rights". The audit obtained the Act and read s.147 in full. Its heading is "Transfer of mineral title". The words "controlling interest", "change of control", "shares", "shareholding" and "transfer of shares" appear nowhere in the Act except in s.53. s.147 therefore does not reach a share transfer at all. The library's quoted sentence is a practice position — most likely a Mining Cadastre or Ministry guideline — and the library cites it without a source. Two provisions the library misses, and both matter. (i) s.147(6): "The approval of the Mining Cadastre Office shall not be required for an assignment to an affiliate, where the obligations of the affiliate are guaranteed by the assignor or by a parent company." That is an express exemption for intra-Group transfers, and no plan in the library mentions it. (ii) s.147(8): the transferor remains liable for pre-transfer obligations including environmental ones — which matters to the Group as a seller, not only as a buyer. And s.147 is internally ambiguous about who approves: s.147(1) requires "the approval of the transfer by the Minister", while s.147(5) provides that "the Mining Cadastre Office shall approve a transfer". The board must not treat "Ministerial consent is unavoidable" as settled law. It is a practice risk requiring a written MCO position, not a statutory certainty.
COREN firm registration is annual and conditional on named engineers, not an entity asset45_Okodu_Construction.md §5Right, and the most useful counter-intuitive finding in the library. A share purchase does not carry it; a change of ownership that removes or dilutes the qualifying engineers destroys the basis for it. Buy the firm and tie the engineers, or buy the plant and hire the engineers.
The controlled-substances set cannot realistically be bought19_Idenze_Therapeutics.md, 38_Uli_Special_Logistics.mdRight, and the plans say so plainly rather than inventing a market.
NUC's position on change of control is unpublished24_Idenze_University.mdRight. The transaction is the purchase of the company that is the licensee; the licence does not move. Resting a ₦bn acquisition on an unpublished position is correctly identified as the risk.
NBTE's position on change of control is equally unpublished25_Idenze_Polytechnic.mdRight, and the file's cross-reference to plan 24 is correct.
SEC warehousing/collateral-manager separation is compelled by statute, not preference05_Isiome_Storage.md, 36_Uli_Warehousing.mdRight. ISA 2025 s.250(3) bars a receipt issuer from trading the commodities it is registered to store.
Licences granted to a named licensee are non-transferable, so acquisition must be a share purchase19, 35, 36, 39, 40, 54Right in substance, but see §0.3 — "share purchase" is not a universal solvent.

Four things the library gets wrong or understates. These are the corrections this audit adds:

#What the library saysWhat the sources sayConsequence
1NBC "prior written approval of the transfer or assignment of a licence is a condition of every broadcast licence, and a change of control of the licensee is treated as a transfer" (32_Uli_Broadcast.md §5)Third Schedule, para 5: "A licence shall not be transferable and the licensed station shall not be changed without notifying the Commission of the intention and the reasons for such change." There is no statutory consent power and no change-of-control provision.The ₦58m ninety-day action budgets ₦10m for an NBC opinion on a consent process that does not exist in the statute. Reframe the question: will the Commission treat a share purchase as outside para 5, and what does it require of the new controlling shareholder? Nothing may be spent on the acquisition assumption until answered.
2The s.9(1) test is a question of whether the Commission reads "foreign interest" as reaching ultimate beneficial ownership; it is "the gating question" (32_Uli_Broadcast.md §5; EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md §4A)s.9(4)(a) requires the Commission to consider "the structure of shareholding in the broadcasting organisation". s.2(1)(r) makes foreign-capital participation a standing Commission function.This is no longer a reading question. The statute instructs the Commission to look at the shareholding structure. The base case for planning must be that a Mauritius-trust-owned chain fails, and the licence must sit in a Nigerian-controlled vehicle. The plans' "no tranche assumes the favourable answer" discipline is correct and must now be enforced as a hard gate, not a caution.
3Aku Security's remedy is "a Nigerian-controlled vehicle outside the offshore chain", with the Group's economic interest delivered by management, secondment and systems contracts and by dividends to the Nigerian holder (54_Aku_Security.md §5)The Act's long title: "companies which must be wholly owned by Nigerians." s.4(4) permits revocation where "the ownership or control of, or any controlling interest in the company to which the licence relates has passed to any other company or organisation which is generally unsuitable to be considered for the grant of such licence.""Nigerian-controlled" and "wholly owned by Nigerians" are different tests. If the long title governs, a partly foreign-owned vehicle fails even with an all-citizen board, and dividends to a Nigerian holder who is not the Group are not the Group's economics. This must go to counsel as a discrete question, and the fallback structure must be modelled now: 100% Nigerian-owned licensee, Group earns fees only.
5The library cites "Rule 5.2(b) reversion, Rule 6.8(7) and Rule 6.15(14) change notifications" as the NGX rules governing a dealing membership (00_Family_Business.md instructs "buy an existing NGX dealing member"; the rules are named in the library's own audit brief)Read against the Rulebook of The Exchange 2015 and its SEC-approved amendments: Rule 6.8(7) does not exist (Rule 6.8 is "Dual Board Membership Prohibited", a single sentence with no sub-paragraphs); Rule 6.15(14) is a renumbering artefact of a 2016 amendment markup in which "6.1514" means new 6.15 = old 6.14 — the rule intended is Rule 6.14; and Rule 5.2(b) is an insolvency provision (the licence reverts to the Exchange on expulsion, winding up, liquidation or receivership), not a change-of-control rule. The rules that do govern a change of control are Rules 5.1, 5.4, 6.6, 6.9, 6.12 and 6.14, and none of them is cited anywhere in the library.The Group would have modelled a dealing-member acquisition against two rules that do not say what it thinks and missed the three that do. Rule 6.9 requires prior written Exchange approval for any change in control or shareholding structure; Rule 5.1 requires the acquirer to qualify as a dealing member in its own right and imposes a 6% transfer fee on the consideration; and Rule 6.4(b) revokes the licence if the Dealing Member is inactive for six consecutive months — which is the constraint that actually threatens an acquired licence the Group does not immediately activate.
4The Group's licences are each, in effect, either inside or outside the chain, and the test is assessed once at application (32, 54, 53, 38)Several regimes impose obligations on every officer, every employee, and every movement, and re-test on change of control and renewal: PGCA s.7 (every employee approved), s.4(1) (two-year term), s.11(2) (lapse on non-renewal), s.14(1)(b)(ii) (annual return naming every employee); NBC Third Schedule para 10(f) (post-grant revocation on facts that would have precluded grant); NAFDAC/NDLEA per-shipment authorisation.Licence ownership is not a one-off filing. It is a standing disclosure regime, and the Group must be structurally able to satisfy it every year, at every renewal, after every board change. That is an argument for the licence vehicle to be genuinely, permanently Nigerian — not a nominee arrangement that has to be re-papered.

0.3 The one rule the plans state but do not apply

41_Okodu_Group.md §5 states the correct general rule — "every acquisition is structured as a share purchase where the instrument is entity-attached; and every offer carries the licence or title as a condition precedent rather than an assumption." The library then applies it unevenly. Three counter-examples the audit found:

  • COREN firm registration (45_Okodu_Construction.md): the instrument is not entity-attached. It attaches to named engineers and lapses annually. A share purchase does not carry it.
  • NMMA s.147 Ministerial consent (46_Okodu_Materials.md): the consent is required either way. A share purchase does not avoid it, and s.147(10) makes the buyer's own qualifications part of the filing.
  • NFVCB film classification (34_Uli_Distribution.md): not transferable at all, per title. A library purchased by share purchase still cannot be booked until each title is re-classified.

The correct formulation, which this audit uses throughout, has three limbs and not two:

For every licence: (i) does an ownership, control or citizenship test apply? (ii) is the instrument attached to the entity, the premises, the product, or the person? (iii) who must consent to the change, and is that consent statutory or discretionary?

The library answers (ii) well and (iii) poorly.

One further point in the library's favour, and it is worth recording because the library never joined it up. The Group's own Akunnia plan, at 08_Akunnia_Group.md:492, already concedes the general principle: under risk 7, "Political risk on control transactions — High — Some African jurisdictions restrict foreign control of strategic sectors; local partners where required." The library therefore knew that foreign-control restrictions exist as a category; what it never did was test its own portfolio against them licence by licence. That is precisely what §4A of the operating architecture asked for and what this audit supplies. The second Akunnia-level statement is more concrete still, at 08_Akunnia_Group.md:497, under risk 12 (concentration of influence): "Separate vehicles; no news operation where regulated licences are held." That is a structural answer to the NBC problem adopted at group level — separate vehicles and no news — and it is stronger than anything in plan 32, because plan 32's own version of it is a content-scope decision (entertainment, sport, film and lifestyle) while plan 08's is an ownership decision. The two should be read together, and the audit adopts both: the licence vehicle is separate, and it carries no newsroom.

The Act expressly legislates about a shareholder holding a controlling share when it wants to — in s.53 — and it says nothing about share transfers in s.147. Ministerial / MCO consent on transfer of a mineral title — s.147 NMMA 2007The Minister for the approval limb and the Mining Cadastre Office for the registration and (on the face of s.147(5)) the approval limb; recorded by the MCOOkodu Materials Ltd (as buyer)The primary text of s.147 was obtained and read for this audit, and it does not say what the library says it says. s.147 is headed "Transfer of mineral title". s.147(1): "Subject to subsections (2), (5) and (6) of this section, a mineral title is transferable under this Act subject to the approval of the transfer by the Minister and registration of the transfer with the Mining Cadastre Office." s.147(3)–(4): the holder applies to the MCO in the prescribed form with such details as it requires. s.147(5): "The Mining Cadastre Office shall approve a transfer of a mineral title under subsection (1) of this section if the transferee is a qualified applicant, provided that the application for transfer shall be deemed automatically approved if not acted upon by the Mining Cadastre Office within thirty days from official receipt thereof." s.147(6): "The approval of the Mining Cadastre Office shall not be required for an assignment to an affiliate, where the obligations of the affiliate are guaranteed by the assignor or by a parent company." s.147(8): "The transferor of a mineral title shall remain liable for the performance of any obligations arising out of acts or contracts made in respect of the Mineral Title Area, including environmental obligations, incurred prior to the date of the transfer." s.147(10): "No mineral title or rights therein may be assigned to a person to whom that mineral title could not have been granted under this Act." The words "controlling interest", "change of control", "shares", "shareholding" and "transfer of shares" appear nowhere in the Act except in s.53.⚠️ DOUBTFUL — and the library's certainty is not supported. The library asserts that "disposal of controlling interest in entities holding exploration or mining rights is another way of transferring the exploration and mining right and as such will require the consent of the Minister" and attributes it to s.147. That sentence is not in s.147 or anywhere else in the Act. It is a practice position the library cites without a source. What s.147(10) does confirm is the transferee test — no assignment to a person to whom the title could not have been granted — and on ss.47–51 a "body corporate duly incorporated under the Companies and Allied Matters Act" is a qualified applicant for every mineral title class. So the statute imposes no ownership, citizenship or foreign-interest test on a corporate title holder, and s.147 does not on its face reach a share transfer.[CHAIN] — confirmed from primary text: no ownership test attaches to a mineral title[B] The instruction to counsel must be rewritten, and this is one of the audit's most consequential corrections. Ask three things in writing: (1) Does the MCO or the Ministry treat a change of control of a corporate title holder as a "transfer of a mineral title" requiring approval under s.147(1), or as outside s.147? Please identify the instrument or guideline on which that position rests, if any. (2) Does the s.147(6) affiliate exemption apply to a transfer between two companies under common ultimate ownership, and what evidence of the parent guarantee is required? — this is the exemption no plan mentions, and it may remove the approval step from intra-Group reorganisations entirely. (3) Where the approval limb falls under s.147(1) on the Minister but s.147(5) says the Mining Cadastre Office "shall approve", which body in fact issues the approval, and does the 30-day deemed-approval clock in s.147(5) apply to the Minister's limb as well? The counter-intuitive answer the brief asked for therefore cuts the other way from the library's version: the share-purchase "trap" is a practice risk, not a statutory rule — and the same section contains an affiliate exemption that makes intra-Group mineral-title transfers cheaper than the library assumes.

PART 2 — THE THREE STRUCTURAL ANSWERS

Every licence that fails or is doubtful falls into one of three answers. The answer is determined by what the instrument attaches to, not by how exposed the business feels. The three tests are applied in this order:

  1. Is there an ownership, control or citizenship test at all? If not — [CHAIN].
  2. Does the test reach ownership, or only directors and officers? If ownership, the vehicle must be Nigerian-owned, not merely Nigerian-controlled.
  3. Does the instrument attach to the entity, the premises, the product, or a named person? If a named person, no structure solves it.

2.1 Answer 1 — the licence can sit in the existing chain ([CHAIN])

The test: the regime imposes no ownership, control, citizenship or foreign-capital test, and the instrument is entity-attached so that a share purchase carries it.

What makes it acceptable, stated precisely. A Nigerian-incorporated subsidiary of a Mauritius holdco is an ordinary Nigerian company. It is registered under CAMA; it is a body corporate registered under the Companies and Allied Matters Act in the exact words of NBC Act s.9(1)(a); it is a "company incorporated in Nigeria" in the exact words of Private Guard Companies Act s.36(1). Nothing in Nigerian company law disqualifies a foreign-owned Nigerian company from holding a licence. The disqualification, where it exists, comes from the sectoral statute — and it exists in far fewer places than the library fears.

The eighty-odd licences where the chain is acceptable fall into five families, and the reason is the same in each: the regulator regulates the activity, the premises or the product, not the shareholder.

Trade-offs of Answer 1. It is the cheapest, fastest and cleanest. Its only cost is a disclosure cost: the chain becomes visible in every application, and every regulator that has a discretionary power — the NBC, the CBN, the NUC, the NSCDC — will see it. Answer 1 is therefore correct only where the discretion is bounded by a published rule. Where the regulator's power is discretionary and unpublished, Answer 1 is not safe even if it is lawful, because the Group cannot predict the outcome. That distinction — bounded rule versus unbounded discretion — is the real dividing line in this audit, and it is not the distinction the library has been using.

Trade-offs of Answer 2, stated honestly.

  1. It recreates the ownership-drift problem the Corporate Architecture exists to prevent. EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md §4A says so. A licence vehicle owned by Nigerian individuals who are not the Group is, over a generation, a genuine third-party company. The declared trust and the reserved matters are the mitigation, and they must be signed at formation — not later.
  2. It reduces the Group's economic return on the licensed business. Fee-only extraction captures a margin, not a residual. On a security business at scale that is materially less than 100% ownership — and the board should price that in before buying the company rather than after.
  3. It reduces the value of the licensed entity in a future transaction. A buyer of the Group cannot buy the licence vehicle; it can only buy the service contracts, which are terminable.
  4. It makes the consolidated accounts harder to explain. The licence vehicle is either consolidated (making the Group the owner, which contradicts the structure) or not consolidated (making it a related party, which the auditors will test).
  5. It is nonetheless correct, because the alternative — losing the licence, or holding it under a structure the regulator has not approved — is worse, and because the licences affected are flagships.

Class 3 — a person must be appointed or approved, but no continuing qualification is required. The PGCA per-employee approval is the archetype: s.7 requires an approval for every person employed, and s.30 makes it an offence to employ a person whose approval was refused or cancelled. This is a process cost, not a key-person risk.

The implications, stated plainly:

  1. The person is a hard constraint on hiring, and it is a constraint on timing, not just on qualification. In an acquisition, the person must be identified and contractually committed before completion, or the licence lapses at completion. The audit endorses this as a general rule for all seven Class-1 acquisitions.
  2. Their departure strands or suspends the licence, and the loss is detected at renewal — which is at most twelve months away, and for COREN exactly twelve months. There is no structure that fixes this.

PART 3 — THE SEQUENCING DECISION

3.1 The sequencing answer, corrected

The board asked which licences must be resolved before the hub company is incorporated. The audit's answer is that the question has been mis-framed, and the correct framing changes the plan:

The hub's incorporation is not gated by the licences. The hub's ownership of anything licence-gated is.

The reason is that no licence in this library requires the Group to own the licensed entity. They require the licensed activity to be conducted by a properly constituted licensee. A London or New York manager can be incorporated and authorised tomorrow without holding a single Nigerian licence, provided that:

  1. the hub does not appear as a shareholder, director, officer, controller or "foreign interest" in any Nigerian licence application or filing;
  2. the hub holds no equity in any Nigerian licence-gated company — it holds the fund vehicles, the GP and the fee streams; and
  3. every economic flow from a Nigerian licence vehicle to the hub is a documented, arm's-length fee, secondment recharge, systems licence or IP royalty, not a dividend or an equity return — except where the statue permits dividends.

This is a materially better answer than "wait", for three reasons. First, it preserves the Group's capital-formation timetable: the hub is the precondition for international LP capital (EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md §8: "The hub is not optional; it is the precondition"). Second, it removes an artificial dependency: the NBC and NACOC questions take months and cannot be accelerated, and nothing about them requires the hub to exist. Third, it makes the licences easier: a Group that has already decided its licence vehicles are Nigerian-owned has a much simpler conversation with the NBC than one that asks permission to be foreign-owned.

What must nonetheless be settled before incorporation, because incorporation creates the thing that is hard to unwind. Four items, and only four:

3.4 The questions to put in writing to each regulator

Send these as one consolidated engagement, from Nigerian counsel, on Group letterhead, in the first thirty days. Each is drafted to elicit a yes-or-no answer, not an opinion. NBC — the highest priority, issue first

  1. Does the Commission read the s.9(1)(b) test — that the applicant "is not applying on behalf of any foreign interest" — as reaching the ultimate beneficial ownership of the applicant through a Mauritius discretionary trust and a Mauritius global business company, or as confined to the identity and residence of the Nigerian licensee's directors and officers?
  2. In applying s.9(4)(a) — that the Commission "shall consider ... the structure of shareholding in the broadcasting organisation" — what information does the Commission require about shareholders above the immediate Nigerian applicant, and at what threshold is a shareholder treated as a foreign interest?
  3. Does the Commission's function under s.2(1)(r), relating to "the participation of foreign capital in relation to local capital in broadcasting", impose a numerical limit on foreign equity in a licensee? If so, what is it, and where is it published?
  4. Third Schedule, paragraph 5 provides that "A licence shall not be transferable". Does the Commission treat a purchase of 100% of the shares of a licensed company as a transfer requiring approval, as a change of station requiring notification, or as neither?
  5. If a Nigerian-owned licensee is managed under an arm's-length services contract by a company that is itself owned offshore, does that arrangement engage s.9(1)(b) or Broadcasting Code s.3.15.1(e) ("foreign ownership or arbitrary interference")?

The word "Nigerians" does not appear anywhere in the Act, so those rules must sit in COREN's regulations made under s.11(3) — or in no instrument at all.Obtain COREN's registration regulations and firm-registration rules made under s.11(3) and quote the qualifying-personnel provisions. Direct request to COREN. The 90% Nigerian-practitioner figure must not be relied on until sourced — it is the only workforce-level citizenship test in the library, it sits inside a licence the construction business depends on, and on the primary text it is not statutory. Second question in the same letter: does a building and civil contractor fall within s.11(2) at all, given the s.11(3) proviso?

What remains open: whether the MCO or the Ministry nevertheless applies a practice under which a change of control of a corporate title holder requires approval. The library asserts that practice and cites no source for itWritten request to the Mining Cadastre Office for the instrument or guideline on which the practice position rests, if any — and for the s.147(6) affiliate-exemption mechanics
14NMMA 2007 — foreign participation in mineral titlesClosed from primary text during the audit. ss.47–51 were read. A "body corporate duly incorporated under the Companies and Allied Matters Act" is a qualified applicant for the Reconnaissance Permit (s.47), the Exploration Licence (s.48), the Small-scale Mining Lease (s.49) and the Mining Lease (s.50); the Quarry Lease (s.51) admits an individual Nigerian citizen or a body corporate. No ownership, citizenship or foreign-interest test attaches to a corporate title holder, whatever its ultimate ownership. The only shareholder-level provision in the entire Act is s.53, which disqualifies an applicant where "within a period of five years before the date of the application a shareholder holding a controlling share of the applicant has been convicted of an offence under this Act" — a criminal-conviction test, not a nationality test. s.54 requires proof of working capital and technical competence, and s.45 bars officers of the MCO and Ministry from holding or acquiring titlesNone required. The audit also obtained NACOC's reported statement of the eligibility test (Head of the Cannabis Regulations Department, 19 February 2026, following NACOC's press release of 11 February 2026 and Parliament's approval of the framework): individuals — Ghanaian, aged 18+, no criminal record, documented access to land; companies — "about 50 per cent of shareholders or the majority of directors must be Ghanaians." What remains open: that test is sourced to a press release and a radio interview, not to L.I. 2475.Obtain the text of L.I. 2475 and read the shareholder and director provisions off the instrument. Direct request to NACOC for the Regulations and for written confirmation of the percentages. This is still the highest-priority unwritten source in the audit, though no longer the highest-priority unknown — the direction of the answer is now clear and it favours the Group

The library says none exists; the audit could not confirm or refute the existence of an unpublished internal positionDirect written request to the NUC. The library's ₦150m opinion with three approaches is the correct response and should be commissioned

These are not gaps in the audit's research; they are gaps in the regulators' published position. Each is a genuine unanswered question of Nigerian regulatory practice, and each is a condition precedent the board should impose.

4.4 Internal contradictions in the library that the audit found and did not resolve

These are not licence questions, but they affect licence decisions and the board should see them together.

#ContradictionWhereWhy it matters to a licence decision

4.5 What this audit did not do

The board should know the boundaries of what it holds.

  1. No Nigerian, Mauritian, South African, Ghanaian or United Kingdom counsel has been instructed. Every legal statement in this document is a research finding, not advice. The register's [verify] items are the instruction list.
  2. The audit did not value any licence. It states what each licence costs to obtain and what the library says it costs to acquire. No transaction price in the library is sourced, and the library says so itself in eight places (plans 29, 31, 32, 34, 36, 39, 41, 44).
  3. The audit did not test the underlying commercial case for any business. A licence that can lawfully be held is not a licence worth holding.
  4. The audit did not examine Mauritian trust law, exchange control, or the tax consequences of the structure. The Mauritius Trusts Act 2001, the GBC regime and the Group's treaty position are outside its scope. They are not outside the board's, because a structure that satisfies every Nigerian licence test and fails Mauritian substance requirements has not solved anything: 00_Family_Business.md §5 already requires real Port Louis substance — "Substance is mandatory, not decorative."
  5. The audit did not verify the six largest remaining [verify] items — BOFIA 2020, the SEC regime, the NGX Rulebook, NUC, NBTE and NDPA 2023 — because the primary texts were not reachable from this session. NMMA 2007 was reached and read, and the result corrected the library. They are the first instructions in §3.4 and items 1–20 of §4.1. Two adjacent items were partly closed during the audit and are recorded as such: Engineers (Registration, etc.) Act Cap E11 s.11 was obtained and read (§M), and the NACOC regime was established from the regulator's own press statements (§F).
  6. The audit did not obtain the NGX Rulebook. Three rules the library cites (5.2(b), 6.8(7), 6.15(14)) remain unquoted.
  7. The audit did not confirm the existence of the CBN Ring-Fencing Guidelines for Closely Linked Entities. The library cites it as a constraint on the Group's structure. If it does not exist, a citation to it should be removed from the archive.
  8. A finding about the library's own sourcing, which the board should weigh when it reads Part 4. For the financial-services domain the gap is not only in this audit's access — it is in the library. A file-level sweep of 08_Akunnia_Group.md, the Akunnia group plan, returns zero matches for every one of the following: BOFIA, ISA 2025, NGX Rules 5.2(b), 6.8(7) and 6.15(14), SCUML, NFIU, EFCC, FCCPC, NDPA, NDPC, Bureau de Change, IMTO, payment service provider, FMDQ, CSCS, NASD, Agusto, GCR and Datapro. NGX appears once in the entire plan — as "increasingly IPO on the NGX or abroad" (08_Akunnia_Group.md:141), an exit route, not a licence. The consequence is that the Akunnia group plan does not name the statutes or the rulebook that govern its own licences. The company plans do better — 16_Aku_Bank.md names BOFIA and the 5% approval, and 05_Isiome_Storage.md names ISA 2025 and quotes its sections — but the group plan that is supposed to be the parent brief for all of them names none of it. That is why twelve of the twenty ownership-test gaps in §4.1 sit in the financial-services domain: the library never cited a source for them, so there was none to check.

CLOSING — THE DECISION THE BOARD IS ACTUALLY MAKING

Three decisions, in order, and they are separable.

Decision 1 — accept the ownership principle. That no licence-gated Nigerian company will be owned by the hub or by any non-Nigerian person, and that the Group's return from those companies is fee-based. Cost: nil. Time: one board meeting. Consequence of deferring it: every later restructuring triggers the change-of-control events the licences fear. This is the only one of the three that must precede the hub's incorporation.

Decision 2 — accept that two licences will be held in Nigerian-owned vehicles and that the Group will not own them outright. The NBC broadcast licence and the Private Guard Companies Act licence. Cost: ₦110–182m to form, ₦14–28m a year per vehicle, and the residual return on two businesses. Consequence of deferring it: the media domain and the security domain cannot be underwritten, because neither business exists without its licence, and neither licence can be acquired lawfully inside the chain. For the PGCA licence the audit adds a question the library has not asked: whether the Group needs the licence at all for its own estate requirement, given s.36(3)(b). If it does not, Decision 2 reduces to one vehicle, not two.

Decision 3 — commission the thirty-eight written questions, and hold every licence-dependent capital commitment until the six that gate structure are answered. Those six are: NBC questions 1–6, the NSCDC question 7 (the PGCA long title), NACOC questions 12–14, the NAFDAC NCS/NDLEA question 14, the NUC question 24, and the CBN question 22 (the ring-fencing instrument's existence). Cost: ₦180–260m. Time: 2–6 months for the fastest, 6–12 for the slowest. Consequence of deferring it: the Group commits capital against unpublished regulatory practice in four regimes at once — which is precisely the discipline that 19_Idenze_Therapeutics.md and 32_Uli_Broadcast.md already apply, and which the audit's only substantive criticism of the library is that it applies that discipline in two domains and not in the other twelve.

The audit's summary judgment. The library is right about the existence of the foreign-interest problem and wrong about its shape. It is not one question about the meaning of the word representing in one statute. It is a set of attachment questions — entity, premises, product or person — answered by thirteen different statutes, and in only two of them does the answer reach the Group's ownership chain in a way that no structure can cure. 21 register rows fail, 70 are doubtful, and of those 70 only twelve are doubtful because of the Group's ownership chain. The other 58 are doubtful because a regulator has not published a position — not because the Group's structure is wrong. That is a much better position than the library's own framing suggests, and it is only visible once the register is built licence by licence.

End of audit. 251 register rows across 13 domains: 136 pass, 69 doubtful, 21 fail, 22 person-held, 3 recorded for completeness. 62 [verify] items in Part 4, of which 20 are ownership tests. Four of those 20 were closed or partly closed during the audit from primary text or the regulator's own statements: the NMMA 2007 title-qualification and s.147 questions (closed, and the library corrected), COREN Cap E11 s.11 (closed on the Act, open on COREN's regulations), and the NACOC regime (closed on the statutory basis and the direction of the eligibility test, open on L.I. 2475). Primary text was obtained for the NBC Act, the Private Guard Companies Act, the Engineers (Registration, etc.) Act Cap E11, the Anambra Homeland Security Law 2025 and the NBC Broadcasting Code; NACOC's regime was established from the regulator's own statements; the remaining ownership tests rest on the library's own citations and are flagged individually in §4.1.

NUMBER RECONCILIATION — Ezeme Group plan library

Numerical audit of the 48-plan business plan library.

Auditor: numerical reconciliation pass. No plan was restructured. Three figures were corrected in place (§7); everything else is reported.

0. Scope, revision audited, and a material warning

0.1 The library was being rewritten during this audit

This is the single most important caveat in the document, and it changes how the findings should be used.

When I began, the directory held the 48 plans the brief described. While I was reading them, a concurrent renumbering and rewriting pass completed. Between the first and last read:

Consequences a reader must hold onto:

  1. The numbering in the audit brief is now superseded. The brief's "ignore 16, 48, 49, 51+" instruction was right when issued and is now out of date — the plans it told me to ignore have been renumbered into the ranges I was told to audit. My findings cite the filename current at the time of reading; where a plan was renamed I give both.
  2. The Akunnia findings are the least stable. 09_Aku_Capital.md and 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md were replaced mid-audit. 10 now carries an appendix ("what the previous version of this plan asserted, and why it is withdrawn") and its own headcount note says the Year-10 figure fell from 277 to 155. Any Akunnia total must be recomputed on the frozen revision.
  3. A frozen snapshot is preserved at .research/tmp/snap_0147/ with MD5SUMS.txt and MANIFEST.txt, so every figure below can be traced to a specific revision.
  4. This reconciliation should be re-run on the final revision. A partial re-base of a moving library creates new inconsistencies faster than it removes them — which is itself the reason several corrections are recommended but not applied (§8).

0.2 What I verified independently, and how

Market prices were checked against primary and named sources, not against the plans. Where I could not verify a figure I say so rather than supplying a number.

1. Summary of findings

40 distinct numerical contradictions, plus 7 structural gaps that make part of the library unreconcilable as written.

The five findings that matter most

1. The construction-cost error is real, is a factor of ~31–43, and is confirmed against independent market rates.

50_Akuzo_Development.md:138–144 costs a five-storey, 2,000 m² Akuzo building at ₦35–50m, totalling ₦1,230.0m for 27 buildings. A detailed, itemised bill of quantities for the same two buildings totals US$967,000 and US$999,000 ≈ ₦1.55–1.60bn each (50:156; 41_Okodu_Group.md:132). ₦35m ÷ 2,000 m² = ₦17,500/m² — which is below even the cheapest independently published Nigerian rate (₦150,000/m²), let alone the verified band for quality work. 2. Every group plan understates its own group by 7×–10×.

No group plan has a total row that equals the sum of its companies. The group tranche tables describe a first-phase build, not a group capital requirement — but they are read as totals. Four of the five also contradict a figure stated inside their own text.

3. The diesel anchor is stale and now understates the avoided-cost case.

Plans use ₦1,800/litre as the customer's alternative. Verified September 2026 depot prices are ₦1,830–₦2,120/litre (Lagos Ibachem ₦2,000, Ibeto ₦1,970, Matrix Warri ₦2,120), with up to ₦2,300/litre retail. So the plans are conservative — the power case is stronger than modelled, not weaker. But the derived ₦780/kWh does not follow from its own stated formula (see Table 1).

4. Gearing is the library's worst-specified rule.

Six plans state "≤40%". Not one defines it. One plan fixes it arithmetically as debt ÷ total capital (03_Isiome_Machinery.md:131 + :118: ₦16.8m debt on ₦42m capital = "gearing 40%"). Under that definition a 40% ceiling permits only ₦0.67 of debt per ₦1 of equity; under debt/equity it permits ₦0.40. A third plan uses loan-to-cost (50_Akuzo_Development.md:150). And two plans breach the 40% ceiling outright: Okodu Power assumes 60% debt (42:149), Aku Credit models 75% debt funding (51_Aku_Credit.md:160).

5. Two plans book the same 35-person platform, and two book the same trucks.

10_Aku_Asset_Management.md:405 and 51_Aku_Credit.md:201 both reach a Year-3 total of exactly 35 staff; Aku Credit additionally prices a "full platform (35–40 staff, full compliance)" at 51:172. Separately, 40_Uli_Fleet.md:67 and 35_Uli_Freight.md book the same vehicles (₦1.39bn vs ₦1.43bn) — Fleet states this explicitly, but no group total nets it.

5. Table 4 — Gearing and financing rule compliance

5.1 The definition question — resolved from the library's own arithmetic

No plan in the library defines gearing in words. But one plan fixes it arithmetically, and the answer is unambiguous:

03_Isiome_Machinery.md:118 — "a 75hp 4WD tractor at ₦30m plus a ₦12m implement set = ₦42m of capital per unit"

03_Isiome_Machinery.md:131 — "Interest — ₦16.8m debt at 28% (gearing 40%)"

₦16.8m ÷ ₦42m = 40.0% — where ₦42m is total capital (₦25.2m of it equity). So the library's gearing is debt ÷ (debt + equity) — debt-to-total-capital, not debt/equity.

This is the difference the brief anticipated: under debt/total-capital a 40% ceiling permits ₦0.67 of debt per ₦1 of equity. Under debt/equity it permits only ₦0.40. The same "40%" is 1.67× more permissive under the definition the library actually uses. (The check is also independently consistent: ₦16.8m × 28% = ₦4.7m, matching the ₦4.7m interest line at 03:131.)

And a third basis exists. 50_Akuzo_Development.md:150 says "≤40% loan-to-cost", which is debt ÷ project cost — a different denominator again.

⚠️ And the library uses two conventions whose names look alike but whose bases differ. This is the sharpest form of the problem:

ConventionWhereBasis (from the plan's own figures)
"Gearing 40%" — a percentage03_Isiome_Machinery.md:131₦16.8m debt ÷ ₦42m total capital = 40.0% → debt ÷ (debt + equity)
"Leverage 0.3×" — a multiple51_Aku_Credit.md:133S1 ₦2bn debt ÷ ₦6bn equity = 0.33× → debt ÷ equity; S2 50/20 = 2.5× ✓; S3 60/25 = 2.4× ✓

So the library's percentage gearing is debt-to-total-capital while its multiple leverage is debt-to-equity — the same relationship expressed on two different denominators, with neither stated anywhere. A reader who assumes "40%" and "3.0×" are comparable is comparing ₦0.67 of debt per ₦1 of equity against ₦3.00 per ₦1. Recommend adopting the percentage form on debt ÷ (debt + equity) library-wide and stating it inline, and where a multiple is used, labelling it "debt/equity ×".

Recommendation: adopt debt ÷ (debt + equity) = debt-to-total-capital as the library definition, state it once in 00_Family_Business.md and in plans/README.md, and add the formula inline at every plan's gearing line. Where a plan means loan-to-cost, say so explicitly.

7. Corrections applied

Three figures were corrected in place. Each is a case where the same input had two different values and one was unambiguously an arithmetic or transcription error — not a judgement call. Each carries the bracketed note required. No plan was restructured and no figure that is a genuine estimate or judgement was changed.

7.1 28_Uli_Group.md:160 — USD unit typo

  • Before: | T1 — Year 1 | … | ₦6.0bn | $3.8bn* |
  • After: | T1 — Year 1 | … | ₦6.0bn | $3.8m (corrected — see NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md)* |

Why this is unambiguous. ₦6.0bn ÷ 1,600 = $3.75m, which rounds to $3.8m — the plan's own rounding convention, proved by the rows beneath it: T2 ₦8.0bn → $5.0m, T3 ₦10.0bn → $6.3m, T4 ₦12.0bn → $7.5m, T5 ₦28–35bn → $17.5–22m. The bn for m is a pure unit typo: "$3.8bn" would imply ₦6.1 trillion. The stray is the existing "\indicative" footnote at 28:166 and was preserved.

7.2 17_Idenze_Group.md:283 — stated total ≠ sum of its own stated addends

  • Before: ~214 education staff at Year 5 (Schools 45 + Polytechnic 74 + Learning 90, alongside pharma)
  • After: ~209 education staff at Year 5 (Schools 45 + Polytechnic 74 + Learning 90, …) — with the note that 45 + 74 + 90 = 209.

Why this is unambiguous. The sentence states its own derivation and the derivation gives 209. All three components independently verify against their own company plans: Schools Year-5 = 45 (26_Idenze_Schools.md:211, whose own row 30 + 15 = 45 ✓); Polytechnic Year-5 = 74 (25_Idenze_Polytechnic.md:214); Learning Year-5 = 90 (27_Idenze_Learning.md:135, whose row 24 + 13 + 14 + 26 + 9 + 4 = 90 ✓). The components are correct; only the total was wrong. The "~" hedge does not rescue it, because the addends are enumerated explicitly.

7.3 27_Idenze_Learning.md:138 — the same arithmetic error, propagated

  • Before: adding Learning, Schools (45) and Polytechnic (74) gives 214 education staff at Year 5
  • After: … gives 209 education staff at Year 5 (corrected — the stated components 90 + 45 + 74 sum to 209, not 214; see NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md)

Why it is corrected too. A second plan states the same wrong number for the same sum — the classic propagated-error signature. Correcting only 17 would leave the two plans disagreeing again. Both now read 209.

7.4 What was deliberately NOT corrected

Everything in §8. The brief's rule is explicit — where the resolution requires judgement, change nothing and list it. In this library the majority of contradictions are judgement calls: which FX rate governs, whether Uli Cinemas is a captive or third-party customer, whether the group tranche tables are totals or first phases, and what a storey building actually costs. Substituting my own judgement for the family's on those would corrupt the record rather than reconcile it.

8. Corrections recommended but NOT applied

Each of these requires a decision only the family (or a tender, a valuer or a regulator) can make. Do not treat any of these as settled.

8.1 Maize / grain price — decide, then re-run

Decision required: which price book governs? 07_Isiome_Trading.md:228 already says "Isiome Group must adopt one measured price book before either plan is used for capital."

Recommendation: adopt ₦350,000–470,000/t on the verified FG guaranteed minimum price of ₦350,000/t and the AGRA parity figure of US$265/t ≈ ₦424,000/t; withdraw ₦650,000/t.

Why not applied: the change halves 05_Isiome_Storage.md's Year-5 working-capital requirement (₦22–26bn → ₦12–16bn), which is a financing ask, not a transcription fix. 05:9 already instructs the family not to commit capital either way.

8.2 The diesel→kWh arithmetic — re-derive from the audit 42:266 already requires

Issue: "₦1,800 ÷ 2.6 kWh/l + ₦70 = ₦780/kWh" actually gives ₦762; the stated "0.36–0.40 L/kWh" basis gives ₦718–790, not the "₦700–950" range quoted in two plans.

Recommendation: re-run the derivation from measured generator logbooks (litres/hour by load band) and publish one number.

Why not applied: ₦780/kWh is used consistently across 13 plans and anchors the ₦7.99bn/year avoided-cost case and the 6.5-year payback (41:70, 42:145, 43:17). Correcting it in one plan while leaving twelve would create an inconsistency; correcting it everywhere is a re-underwriting exercise, not a reconciliation. Also note the interaction with 58_Okodu_Fuel.md (§2.2): if the Group buys diesel wholesale, the captive avoided-cost case falls even if the external case does not.

8.3 Electricity tariff: captive ₦150 vs ₦160 vs ₦250/kWh — commercial decision

Decision required: is each Group site billed at the captive cost-plus PPA rate (~₦150/kWh) or the external C&I tariff (₦230–280/kWh)?

Recommendation: ₦150/kWh for genuinely captive Group facilities; ₦230–280/kWh for anything selling to third parties or not on a captive PPA. Fix 06_Isiome_Foods.md:180 (₦250/kWh) and 39_Uli_Cinemas.md:113 (₦160/kWh) to whichever applies.

Why not applied: at Uli Cinemas' 462,000 kWh the choice is worth ₦60–129m/year against ₦95.3m of EBITDA (39:122) — it decides whether the flagship site is profitable. That is the family's call, and 39:55 versus 39:113 shows the plan has not made it.

8.4 Construction cost and the Akuzo programme — the biggest item, and it needs a tender

Decision required: the family must commission one measured cost book to replace both the ₦40m figure and the ₦750,000/m² derivation. 59_Okodu_Housing.md:182 already budgets ₦12m · day 60 for exactly this, and 50_Akuzo_Development.md:23 makes it the board's first duty: "reconciling it before any building is committed is the board's first duty. The thesis is right; the cost basis has to be made true."

Recommendation: treat ₦750,000/m² as the planning rate for the full Akuzo specification (verified as defensible against Afrotools's ₦500,000–800,000/m² higher-spec band), giving ₦1.48–1.60bn per building and ≈₦40bn+ for 27 buildings — against the ₦1.23bn currently carried.

Why not applied: (a) the true figure is a range pending tender; (b) the change cascades into 41's T3/T4 tranches, 47's building economics, 45's revenue and 59's yield test — rewriting five capital stacks is restructuring, which the brief forbids; (c) 41:132 already carries the correction and the evidence, and 41:182 already says a consolidated plan is outstanding. The plan is flagged correctly; what is missing is the tender, not the note.

Also flagged: 59_Okodu_Housing.md:130 shows the Akuzo specification yields 2.7% at ₦750,000/m² — i.e. the full-spec building does not work as a rental asset at all. That is a strategy consequence the family must absorb.

Decision required: none — but it must be done once, everywhere.

Recommendation: re-base every dollar figure to ₦1,600/USD in one pass; correct 24_Idenze_University.md's USD column (computed at ₦1,350) and therefore 17_Idenze_Group.md:226 (~$188m → ~$158m) and the cross-reference in 27_Idenze_Learning.md:119.

9. Bottom line

The individual company plans are, by and large, internally disciplined. Every capital tranche table I tested sums correctly to its own stated total — I found no arithmetic error in a company capital table. Two cases are worth stating explicitly, because both look like errors and neither is:

  • 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md:308 appears to overstate its own detail by ₦10bn across four columns (T1 ₦8.0bn of items against a ₦7.5bn total, and so on). It does not. The Total row deliberately EXCLUDES the locked regulatory-capital row. Excluding it, every column reconciles to the decimal: T1 1.6+2.4+0.9+0.7+0.8+0.6+0.5 = ₦7.5bn; T2 = ₦38.0bn; T3 = ₦120.0bn; T4 = ₦360.0bn; grand total ₦525.5bn both ways. The exclusion is correct — the plan's own "three kinds of money" table classifies regulatory capital as "Deployable? No" — but it is easy to misread, and a careful reader did (a source extract for this audit recorded it as a ₦10bn error before I tested it). Recommend the locked row carry "excluded from Total" in its label.
  • 09_Aku_Capital.md:275 genuinely does carry a small one: the C-row detail reads "Fund I (USD 300m at 3%) ₦14.4bn" against a C-row column total of "₦14bn" — a ₦0.4bn (0.3%) gap, and 10 uses ₦14.4bn. Everything else in 09 reconciles exactly (A-row, B-row, C-row T3/T4, and all four column totals). Where plans are wrong, they are wrong in three consistent ways:
  1. Cross-plan, not within-plan. Inputs shared between plans (maize, diesel, tariffs, construction rates, FX, wages) were never put on one basis.
  2. Group-level aggregation was never done. Every group plan understates its own group by 7–10×, and two groups have no total at all.
  3. Rules were written but not defined. Gearing, in particular, is stated in six plans, met in most, defined in none, and breached in two.

The single highest-value action is not a correction — it is a freeze. Ten files changed while I was auditing them, two of them replaced outright. A reconciliation run against a moving library cannot be relied on, and it is the reason most of §8 is a decision list rather than a change list.

Priority order:

  1. Freeze the library and re-run this reconciliation on the frozen revision.
  2. Commission the Akuzo/Okodu cost book (§8.4, already budgeted at ₦12m · day 60 in 59_Okodu_Housing.md:182) — a factor-of-30 error on the Group's flagship programme, now confirmed against independent market rates.
  3. Define gearing once, in writing, as debt ÷ (debt + equity), and resolve the 60% and 75% assumptions (§8.5, Table 4).
  4. Adopt one measured grain price book and re-run Isiome Storage's working capital (§8.1).
  5. Re-run the diesel-to-kWh derivation from the generator audit 42:266 already requires, and separate the Group's own landed diesel cost from the customer's alternative now that 58_Okodu_Fuel.md exists (§8.2).
  6. Write one consolidated capital plan per group, netting the known double-counts (Akunnia's 35-person platform and the ₦120bn GP reserve; Okodu's solar/BESS across Power, Solar and Grid; Uli's fleet between Freight and Fleet).

Prepared for the Ezeme Group Board and the Family Council.

1.3 What this buys, and the limit — now measured rather than asserted

What it buys. Every figure below was read from bytes whose digest is pinned. A reader can re-run the two commands and obtain the same 66 OK lines.

The limit, and this run measured it. A hash check proves the snapshot has not changed since it was frozen; it does not prove the snapshot equals the current live tree. So the live tree was compared against the snapshot, file by file:

This is the freeze paying for itself, and the contrast with v1 is the point. v1 could not say how many files had moved, because it had no pinned reference. This run can, and did: one file, identified by name, in 61. The v1 objection cannot recur — and any future drift is detectable by the same three-line command rather than by re-auditing the library.

2. Method

2.1 The defect in v1 that this run exists to fix

v1 named its own weakness precisely: six of its findings were errors in v1's own report, and every one had the same cause — inferring "absent", "compliant" or "isolated" from files read closely, rather than sweeping that input across all 61. v1 flagged its remaining "absent from all N files" rows as provisional for exactly this reason.

The failure mode is specific and seductive: read four files, see no mention of an input, conclude the input is not in the library. That conclusion is evidence about four files, not the other 57. A sample cannot establish absence, compliance or isolation. Only a sweep can.

2.2 The method used instead

  1. Sweep mechanically over every one of the 61 files. Case-insensitive grep -n across frozen_v1/plans/*.md, so every hit carries a file and line number. No file skipped, none sampled.
  2. Report the complete hit list and the hit count, so a reader sees the sweep was exhaustive rather than being told it was. A hit count is the evidence; a bare conclusion is not.
  3. Conclude only after the hit list is complete. Where the list is long, the population is stated so no reader must trust a summary of unshown rows.

On "zero hits". A zero is reported only where the sweep genuinely returned zero, as "0 hits across 61 files". Where a pattern could be spelled another way (₦/NGN, m²/sqm, /tonne-km/per tonne-km), all spellings were swept before any zero was recorded.

Three false results this method produced, and how each was caught. These are recorded together because they are the same failure in three costumes, and because a method that hides them is not a method:

#The false resultWhat was actually trueHow it was caught
1cement = 192 hits across 50 files32 hits across 15 files — the unsigned pattern also matched "announcement" and "replacement"Re-run with \b word boundaries
2ring-fencing = 0 hits — a zero132 hits across 47 files — grep read the leading -? as an option flagA zero was implausible enough to re-test
3⚠️ FX "All 61 files carry one convention: ₦1,600/USD… No file states a different planning rate"Five files override it in their own headers (18 ₦1,400 · 19 ₦1,500 · 24 ₦1,350 · 35 ₦1,328–1,362 · 38 ₦1,500)Reviewer challenge, not self-caught

Result 3 is the most serious, and its cause is the one this section warns about. The pattern (₦\|N)1,?6(00)?/USD can only match ₦1,600 spellings. A file declaring "NGN 1,400 = USD 1.00" or "it uses ₦1,500/USD" is invisible to it — so the sweep returned a confident 109 hits and a false claim of uniformity, and this report briefly called it "the strongest result in Table 1." A too-narrow pattern does not produce a gap in the hit list that a reader can see. It produces a hit list that looks complete and isn't — which makes it more dangerous than the zero in row 2, not less. The correction is in §3.1 row 2, and the substantive consequence is now carried in §9: naira is the only library-wide comparable column.

The lesson, stated plainly: a hit count is evidence only when the pattern matches every spelling of the thing being counted — and the person who wrote the pattern is the last person likely to notice. Results 1 and 2 were caught by re-running the sweep; result 3 was caught only because someone re-read the claim and tested it. That is the argument for a reviewer, and it is why §3 shows hit counts rather than asserting exhaustiveness.

A document that corrected six of its own errors is a source of hypotheses, not of established fact. Every re-testable v1 finding was re-derived from the frozen files; where the two disagree, this report says so and shows the frozen line. Where v1 was right, it is confirmed and credited; where it was wrong, that is recorded rather than passed over.

2.5 Where this report could not be exhaustive — stated first

  1. Arithmetic coverage is 22 of 61 files — not 61. §5.1. This is the principal limitation and it is stated in the section, not hidden.

Recorded because an unread tail is an unread tail, and this report's whole argument is that absence must be swept for, not inferred.

4.6 Two hazards for anyone building a consolidated plan

Both surfaced in the Isiome detail and both would corrupt a roll-up done by file number or by "capital requirement" alone.

1. One company's "capital requirement" contains M&A consideration; its six siblings' do not. 61_Isiome_Manufacturing.md:139 bundles an explicit line — "acquisition of a certified regional factory or second plant 3.00" — inside its ₦38.20bn total. Build capex ex-acquisition = ₦35.20bn. So an Isiome sum mixes build capex with acquisition consideration in one of seven lines. It does not change the finding: Manufacturing still exceeds the whole group figure on the ex-acquisition basis too (₦35.20bn > ₦35.0bn). The same file also prints two thresholds in its own header (61:15): ₦6.7bn to first production and ₦38.2bn to Year 11 — T1-only and all-tranche, which must not be added.

2. The file numbers are a sequence, not an index — and the plans' own cross-references are frequently wrong. 01_Isiome_Group.md:308 (footer) reads "Next in birth order: 02 — Akunnia Group." But 02 is 02_Isiome_Seed.md; Akunnia Group is 08. 06:6 labels itself "third company of Isiome Group" while bearing number 06. 07:17 records a naming collision in another file: "09_Aku_Capital.md uses 'Isiome Trading' as shorthand for its index and ETF platform; that function belongs to Aku Markets." And three Okodu files disagree with the index about their own or their siblings' numbers: 44_Okodu_Grid.md:3 states its own number should be 46 — "the next free number in the 41–49 Okodu block: 46" — while its filename is 44; and 45_Okodu_Construction.md cross-references "Akuzo Development (#48)", "Okodu Materials (#44)" and "Okodu Power (#40)" for files now numbered 50, 46 and 42.

The pattern, across every pass: plans/README.md was consistently right and the plans' own cross-references were often stale. That is why the 50_Akuzo allocation and the 54_Aku_Security existence question were both resolved against the index rather than against the plans' prose — and it is the concrete reason §4.6's advice is resolve names against the index, not follow the plans' pointers.

The practical consequence, stated because it is a live trap for this very exercise: any roll-up keyed on file number, or on the phrase "capital requirement", will be wrong for at least one Isiome company and will mis-attribute at least one Aku line. The safe key is the company name resolved against the index in plans/README.md, and the safe field is a stated Total row — not the headline "capital" sentence. This is a mild vindication of v1's own instinct to cross-check against an index rather than the plans' prose.

And the honest frame for the Isiome number. All seven company Total rows reconcile exactly to their own tranche rows in both currencies — but the plans themselves mark nearly every figure as provisional: "every figure is a planning placeholder" (02:87, 05:125), "all to be replaced by firm quotations" (03:121, 04:165), "costs are planning estimates, not quotations" (61:7). The ₦318.5bn is a planning envelope, not a tender — and the same caveat applies to every company sum in this table.

3. ⚠️ One group tranche figure is doing duty as two different companies' plant costs. 21_Idenze_Sterile_Injectables.md:141 states "Oral solids reach first commercial batch on ₦21bn in 24–30 months", and 18_Idenze_Pharma.md repeats it four times (18:115, 18:124, 18:256, 18:258). But ₦21bn is 17_Idenze_Group.md's T1 row (17:243). Idenze Pharma's own T1 is ₦17.6bn (18:135) and its own total is ₦54.1bn (18:139). So a group-level tranche figure is being quoted as two different companies' plant costs — including by the company it purports to describe. This is the same failure mode as §4.1's 06:175 (a company quoting the group's ₦35bn tranche as the whole group's capital) and 05.7's 21:141. Three separate instances of a group number propagating downward into company plans and being restated as a company fact. For a consolidated plan, that means a figure found in a company plan cannot be assumed to describe that company — it must be traced to the file that owns it.

Related, and left unresolved rather than guessed: 21:99 claims sterile injectables cost "2.1× the oral solid plant's capital." Computed from the frozen totals: 85.0 ÷ 54.1 = 1.57×; 41.6 ÷ 17.6 = 2.36×; 85.0 ÷ 41.6 = 2.04×. The stated 2.1× implies a divisor of ₦40.5bn, which appears nowhere in either plan. Of 52 numeric exceptions found, 4 were unambiguous enough to correct. A correction pass that edited every mismatch would therefore have made the library less reliable, not more.

Fourteen of the escalations need one policy sentence each — "boarding is a supplement to tuition", "payback is unlevered and pre-interest", "the bond is a non-cash line", "tranche figures are programme budgets" — after which they can be applied mechanically. The plan's own break-even mix (₦981k) requires the supplement; the revenue table books the total. On the total reading the school does not break even at any occupancy its own claim states. This single answer restates §7 of that plan. (exc. 3)
  3. Okodu — is the energy programme ₦196bn or ₦684bn? 41 says ₦196bn (build on Nkpor); 42 says ₦684bn (including acquisition of operating portfolios). Both are arithmetically correct and they differ by ₦488bn. The answer determines whether the Group's largest capital commitment is 3× or 10× the rest of the portfolio. (exc. 21; §4.4)
