ISIOME MACHINERY — Mechanisation, Fleet Leasing and Equipment Assembly

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX: naira is primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM September 2026). Dollar figures are not comparable across plans.

Ezeme Group · Isiome Group (Agriculture & Manufacturing) · Entity: Isiome Machinery Ltd, plus a ring-fenced leasing SPV registered with the Equipment Leasing Registration Authority (ELRA). Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027. Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Isiome Group → Isiome Machinery.

Companions: 04_Isiome_Farms.md (the anchor customer), 02_Isiome_Seed.md, 05_Isiome_Storage.md, 06_Isiome_Foods.md, 01_Isiome_Group.md.

1. Thesis

Isiome Machinery owns the equipment layer every farm and factory in the empire depends on — and monetises it by the hour, not the sale. The Group's own words are a leasing thesis, not a dealership thesis: "His edge is owning the equipment layer that every farm and factory in the empire depends on."

Why leasing, as arithmetic. A new 75hp tractor costs ₦25–35m; a 60hp unit landed at about US$36,000, which is roughly 24 years of net farm income for a smallholder cultivating 1.5 hectares of maize (Agrimachinery Africa; ELRA–NADF; HTS Farms). Nigerian holdings average 0.7–2.2 hectares. A capital good priced at a generation of income will never be sold to those who need it — only rented to them. The Bank of Agriculture's MD says it plainly: "Farmers are not mechanisation service providers. A tractor is a business tool" (Agrocentric).

Utilisation is the entire economics. A parked tractor earns nothing and still depreciates, still pays insurance and still pays the operator. This is a scheduling and service business wearing a fleet's clothing. Its central risk metric is therefore one number: 1,280 engine hours per tractor per year (§7).

The honest caveat that shapes everything below. At September 2026 diesel prices, pure hire is thin, and this plan says so rather than hiding it. It works only because of four advantages a standalone operator lacks: the Group's own anchor demand, a two-season calendar, a spares-and-service margin on top of hire, and local fabrication of implements that cuts capital cost per unit.

2. Market

Nigeria's tractor density is 2.3 units per 1,000 hectares of arable land (Agrimachinery Africa), and NADF measures the gap in power terms — 0.3 horsepower per hectare against India's 2.6 (BusinessDay). Yet Nigeria took an estimated 38.6% of Africa's agricultural tractor sales in 2025. The market is real; only access is broken.

GapEvidenceResponse
Unaffordable machinesA 60hp tractor ≈ 24 years of a 1.5 ha smallholder's net incomeHourly service contracts, not sales
Utilisation, not machine countFarmers reverting to ox-ploughs as diesel passed ₦2,000/litre; an operator reports "tractors move around looking for work" (Daily Trust)Scheduling, telematics, a two-season calendar
No maintenance cultureAnambra's own hiring unit held 24 tractors yet saw equipment "abandoned as scraps" through skill gaps (UNIZIK)Own depots, spares stock, planned maintenance
Operator and mechanic shortageNADF is training 4,000 operators and mechanics, with John Deere's representatives and the ITF (Vanguard)Polytechnic pipeline and operator academy
Service and spares desertAfter-sales support is now the sector's weakest link, with duty no longer a differentiatorDepots across Idemili and the Onitsha–Awka–Nnewi triangle

The South-East is not the North, and this plan is built for the South-East. Holdings are small and fragmented, soils heavier, land dearer. The right machine is often a two-wheel tractor or a compact 50–75hp unit, not a 100hp row-crop tractor. Anambra is actively pushing estate-based and mechanised agriculture with private-sector participation (Anambra City) — a tailwind for permits, not a strategy.

Competitors: private hire operators (TOOAN, TOHFAN); federal and state schemes distributing tractors to service providers; pay-as-you-go platforms such as John Deere-backed Hello Tractor (Vanguard); dealers such as AGCOMS and TracTrac. Isiome's edge is not better iron — it is contracted demand, its own depots, its own operators, its own finance. No competitor starts with a 200-hectare farm on the books.

3. Product & service lines

Machine selection has one rule: buy only what named acreage can keep busy.

ClassSelectionRationale
Tractors50–75hp 4WD workhorse; a few 90–110hp units for heavy tillage and haulage75hp fits South-East plots and spares availability; bigger units raise capital cost per productive hour
Two-wheel tractors / power tillers8–18hp, ₦2.5–4mThe smallholder product: suits 0.5–2 ha, transportable, break-even at a fraction of a tractor's hours
HarvestersCombines for rice and maize; threshers and shellers for the restHighest revenue per hour in the fleet; bought only against aggregated acreage
IrrigationSolar pump sets, drip and sprinkler packagesThe dry-season revenue engine — turns one season into two
Planters and sprayersPrecision row planters, boom sprayers, fertiliser applicatorsLow-capital, high-utilisation implements that ride on tractors already owned

Four commercial lines:

  1. Service contracts (pay-per-hectare or per-hour). Isiome supplies machine, operator, fuel and maintenance; the farmer pays for the job. This is the only model that suits smallholders, and the only one keeping asset, operator and maintenance under Isiome's control. Indicative 2026 prices: ploughing ₦35,000–45,000/ha, harrowing ₦20,000–25,000/ha, ridging ₦20,000–28,000/ha (HTS Farms).
  2. Leasing to institutional lessees. Operating and finance leases to Isiome Farms, Okodu Group companies, estates and commercial farms — registered with ELRA, whose central registry of lease agreements is what lets lenders finance equipment without land collateral.
  3. Hire-purchase, used sparingly. Market terms are 30% down with the balance over two to three harvests, and the ELRA/NADF channel requires clusters with ≥10 hectares aggregated. Offer it only where Isiome Storage holds the offtake and nets instalments from produce proceeds. Cap the book at 15% of fleet value in the SPV — a machinery company that becomes an unsecured smallholder lender has changed industry and lost control of its asset.
  4. Depot services, spares and implements. Paid servicing, spares retail, operator hire, and from Year 3 locally fabricated implements sold and leased to third parties.

4. Operating model

The two-season calendar is the business model, not an optimisation. Break-even hours spread across one four-month tillage window are not achievable:

  • Season A (April–July): tillage, planting, fertiliser — the peak.
  • Season B (November–February): dry-season irrigation and second-cycle cropping, plus trailer haulage, threshing, and hire to construction and quarrying — where idle iron earns its keep. Okodu Group's own sites are a winter customer.
  • All year: maintenance, rebuilds and depot work scheduled into the trough, because a breakdown in peak season costs twice.

Scheduling. One dispatch desk owns every machine's calendar, booking against GPS-verified engine hours rather than promises. Smallholder demand is aggregated by Isiome Seed's farmer network into 10-hectare cluster blocks — a tractor working twenty adjacent one-hectare plots in a day is efficient; four scattered plots is not. The minimum block size is enforced commercially.

Depots and spares. Workshops at Nkpor, Idemmili and a third at Awka/Nnewi by Year 5 — bays, spares store, parts counter. Two rules: no machine operates more than 90 minutes from a depot it can be recovered to, and critical spares are held as stock, not ordered on failure. Imported spares carry FX and 60–90 day lead times; the answer is deeper local stock plus the locally fabricated part range.

Operator training. The sector's binding constraint is people. The Permanent Secretary's line at the policy launch is this plan's creed: "A tractor without an operator is an idle asset. A machine without maintenance is a depreciating investment" (FMNO). An Isiome Operator Academy runs a paid eight-week pathway — field operation, precision placement, daily checks, safety, machine care — with Idenze Polytechnic delivering technical modules. Operators are paid above the ₦70,000 statutory floor (TheCable) and bonused on hours, fuel efficiency and breakdown-free days — the last being the retention mechanism, since a good operator can always find work.

Telematics. Every machine above 8hp is instrumented: engine-hour logging for billing and service intervals, live location, geofencing, tamper and power-cut alarms, fuel monitoring. The standard loss is not a stolen tractor but "the hours a machine runs on someone else's land after dark, the fuel that goes missing between the store and the tank, and the service skipped because nobody logged the engine hours" (Fenix). Indicative cost: ₦200,000 per tractor in Year 1, ₦35,000 a year after; fuel monitoring ₦650,000/₦80,000; fleet dashboard ₦150,000/₦35,000 — vendor pricing, to be tendered. Data feeds a fleet platform (buildable with Aku Technology) producing the one board report that matters: hours per machine, revenue per hour, fuel per hour, unplanned downtime.

The local assembly case — and its limit. The case is import substitution, FX exposure, job creation and spares lead time. But the 2026 regime removed the tariff shield that made assembly viable, and a Nigerian tractor manufacturer with 6,000 units/year of capacity is publicly weighing relocation over exactly this (BusinessDay). Therefore: fabricate implements and light machinery — ploughs, harrows, ridgers, trailers, planters, threshers, frames — from steel sourced through Okodu Materials, and import engines, transmissions, gearboxes and disc blades as CKD. Do not attempt complete tractors. Implements fabricate 30–40% cheaper, carry far less FX, cut spares lead time from months to days, and employ 20–30 welders and fitters. All assembly ratios require firm quotation.

The licence is acquired, not waited for — and here the acquisition route is about certification, staff and an installed base, not about permission. Two facts set the posture. First, the 2026 regime removed the tariff shield (§5.3 above; 01_Isiome_Group.md carries the cross-cutting finding), so this business cannot be protected into viability and must be fast instead. Second, MANCAP and NACAM acceptance are what make a fabricated implement sellable to a stranger (§5.5) — and both attach to a product, a site and a testing history, which are slow to build and can be bought.

The honest part, and it cuts against paying up. Fees here are small and this plan does not pretend otherwise: the asset is certification, staff and an installed base — and no public price exists for a Nigerian certified workshop, implement fabricator or machinery assembler, so none is given. The one hard public anchor is that agricultural and manufacturing machinery now enters at 0% duty, which caps what any assembler's licence and goodwill can be worth: the Group must not pay a premium that assumes tariff protection that no longer exists. Where a certified workshop cannot be bought for less than building and certifying one, this plan builds.

Break-even utilisation — the central risk metric

Break-even is 1,280 engine hours per tractor per year — about 640 hours in each of two working seasons. Below that, capital is not serviced. The three thresholds are genuinely different businesses:

ThresholdHours/yrHours/seasonCovers
Cash break-even~475~240Operator, depot, insurance, fuel, maintenance
Full break-even~1,280~640Also depreciation and debt service — the plan's central test
Economic break-even~1,700~850Also a 20% naira equity return, above inflation

Reconciling 01_Isiome_Group.md, which states "break-even typically above 500 hours/season": that is cash break-even and is far too low for a leveraged fleet. 640 hours per season is the number that survives contact with a lender.

Sensitivity of returns to utilisation

Per tractor: ₦12,000 contribution per hour, ₦15.4m annual fixed cost, ₦42m capital.

Engine hours/yrContributionPre-tax resultReturn on capitalVerdict
400₦4.8m−₦10.6m−25%A parked tractor — the failure this plan exists to prevent

1,000₦12.0m−₦3.4m−8%Typical weak Nigerian utilisation. Still losing
1,280₦15.4m₦0.0m0%Break-even
1,600₦19.2m₦3.8m+9%A scheduled fleet with depots and an anchor customer
2,000₦24.0m₦8.6m+20%Two seasons, clustered, fully booked

Read that as a warning, not a forecast. Each extra 100 hours is worth ₦1.2m per tractor per year, so utilisation is worth more than price: a 10% tariff cut costs ₦2,800 × 1,280 = ₦3.6m a year, the same as losing 300 hours, while a 10% diesel rise lifts break-even by roughly 145 hours, because fuel is 43% of revenue. Levers, in order of value: fill the dry season; cluster the acreage; hold diesel cost (Okodu Power for depot load, fuel-monitoring telematics against siphoning); fabricate implements locally to cut capital cost per unit; shift the revenue mix toward harvesting and haulage, which earn several times a tillage hour.

Where the profit actually is. Hire alone returns roughly break-even at good utilisation, and this plan says so. The return comes from spares and depot service (high-margin, recurring, growing with every unit in the field), implement fabrication (30–40% cost advantage on a product with a captive internal buyer), and the harvest, haulage and irrigation hours of Season B. By Year 15 the target is ₦12–14bn revenue, 28–32% gross margin, 18–22% EBITDA, with roughly a third of gross profit from assembly and parts rather than hire. Unverified; replace with measured data.

First ten hires, in order: (1) Managing Director — has run a commercial hire or haulage fleet with a maintenance P&L, not a dealership; (2) Head of Fleet Operations — owns utilisation; (3) Head of Maintenance — the role that decides whether this business works; (4) Scheduling and Dispatch Lead; (5) Head of Fabrication; (6) Parts and Spares Manager; (7) Chief Operator / Training Lead; (8) Head of Lease Administration — ELRA registration, credit, offtake netting; (9) Fleet Data Analyst; (10) HSE and Compliance Officer reporting to the board, not the MD.

Leadership. Isiome's engineering training — industrial engineering at Tsinghua, smart manufacturing at NTU, biosystems and agro-technology at Wageningen — lands here more directly than on any other company in his domain. Until activation, professional management under Group oversight applies: activation is earned, not inherited.

Idenze Polytechnic's Agricultural Technology and Mechanical Engineering Technology departments are the supply line — target 50% of operators, mechanics and fitters from the polytechnic by Year 5, 100% by Year 10, with paid attachment on live machines from semester two, dual-appointment instructors drawn from Isiome's workshop, and certification of experienced operators who lack papers.

11. Integration

Sells and leases to.

  • Isiome Farms — the anchor utilisation, and the most important commercial fact in this plan. At 200 hectares a full open-field cycle runs roughly 6 tractor-hours per hectare across tillage, harrowing, ridging, planting, spraying and harvest haulage, so the farm alone is about 1,200 engine hours a year — close to one tractor's full break-even and double its cash break-even. The farm leases rather than owns, keeping capex off its balance sheet; the machinery company gets contracted base load and a demand forecast. Both plans work because of this trade.
  • Contracted smallholders through Isiome Seed — per-hectare service contracts, clustered into 10 ha blocks, priced so a one-hectare farmer can afford a ploughing he could never buy.
  • Isiome Storage and Isiome Foods — handling, haulage, mobile plant; and the offtake relationship that makes hire-purchase safe, because Storage can net instalments from produce proceeds.
  • Third-party farmers and institutions — the growth market and, by Year 10, most of the revenue.

Buys from.

  • Okodu Power — power for every depot, workshop and fabrication line, at cost-plus Group rates benchmarked to diesel. This matters more here than anywhere: welders, compressors and grinders on a diesel set at ₦700–950/kWh all-in against ₦1,850/litre fuel is a permanent disadvantage this Group can simply decline to carry.
  • Okodu Construction — depot buildings, workshops, hardstanding and access roads, competitively tendered against external bidders with a benchmarking file per package.
  • Okodu Materials — the steel, sections and fabrications the assembly line consumes, which is what converts the implement programme from aspiration into cost advantage.
  • Uli Freight — inbound machines and spares, exactly the project-cargo and abnormal-load capability Uli's plan carries, plus outbound implement exports into ECOWAS from Year 13.
  • Idenze Polytechnic — Agricultural Technology and Mechanical Engineering Technology graduates as operators, mechanics and fitters, with dual-appointment instructors and paid attachment on live machines.
  • Akunnia Capital — naira equipment finance, working capital, the ELRA-registered leasing SPV, treasury and FX policy; Aku Insurance for fleet, theft and third-party cover; Aku Technology for the fleet management and lease-administration platform.

Related-party discipline. Every flow above is intra-group, and intra-group flows are where family conglomerates lose institutional credibility. Competitive tender or an external benchmark on every material purchase; published arms-length tariffs for every service, benchmarked to market hire rates; independent-director approval on related-party contracts; disclosure to the Family Council. The point is not to route work to family companies — it is to build a machinery business whose largest customer holds it to institutional standards, so it can win third-party work on merit.

ISIOME FARMS — Primary Agricultural Production, Idemmili Belt

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary; dollars are indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Spot was ~₦1,328/USD (CBN NFEM, September 2026). Dollar figures are not comparable across plans. See plans/README.md.

Ezeme Group · Isiome Group (Agriculture & Manufacturing) · Entity: Isiome Farms Ltd (CAMA). Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027. Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Isiome Group → Isiome Farms.

Companions: 02_Isiome_Seed.md, 03_Isiome_Machinery.md, 05_Isiome_Storage.md (the profit engine), 06_Isiome_Foods.md. Isiome Farms supplies those companies; it does not compete with them.

1. Thesis

Isiome Farms is the Group's production base in the Idemmili belt — 100–200 hectares acquired progressively over fifteen years. It exists to guarantee tonnage into Isiome Storage and Isiome Foods, to prove yields and varieties the Group's contracted smallholders can copy, and to generate the agronomic data on which the whole Isiome chain is priced.

Stated plainly, because the Group responds to clarity: primary production is the lowest-margin step in the agricultural chain. It is the only step where output is fixed by weather and revenue by a farm-gate price the producer does not set. Its justification is supply certainty, demonstration and R&D — not profit. The margin is captured by Isiome Storage (buy at harvest, sell into scarcity) and Isiome Foods (process and package). This company is the input to both.

One sentence: Isiome Farms is the 200-hectare laboratory and tonnage reserve that makes the silo and the processing plant financeable — and if it is ever the most profitable agricultural entity in Isiome Group, then Storage or Foods has failed.

Why Idemmili, and why only production goes there. Idemmili land is the cheapest in the corridor (₦5–20m per plot against ₦25–70m in the Nkpor industrial zones), which is exactly why production belongs there and processing does not. Idemmili produces. Nkpor processes. That is the whole geographic design, and the reason this is a separate plan from 01_Isiome_Group.md.

2. Market

Demand is present, naira-denominated, and growing faster than supply. Headline inflation eased to 15.39% in August 2026, yet food inflation has repeatedly outpaced the headline rate — in May 2026 for the first time in eight months (NBS via Punch; TheCable; Nairametrics). That is the market: consumers paying more for food that is not being produced in greater volume.

GapEvidenceIsiome Farms' response
Post-harvest losses20–33% of produce lost between field and consumption, concentrated in perishables (FETiCON 2024; Vanguard)All output routes through Isiome Storage and the Nkpor cold chain; the farm never holds perishables
Unrealised irrigation3.14m ha of irrigable potential, largely undeveloped (JICA; Punch/NASENI)Own irrigation from Tranche 1; dry-season cropping is the highest-return use of the same land
Mechanisation deficitLow tractor density; the FG's flagship intervention is 2,000 tractors for 1.2m farmers (Punch; Guardian/BoA)Lease from Isiome Machinery; the farm validates the fleet's utilisation model
Input cost inflationFertiliser up 11% into the 2026 season (BusinessDay; AGRA)Group terms via Isiome Seed; forward purchase; organic matter to cut mineral dependence; own seed multiplication
Weak seed supplyCassava and maize seed systems remain largely informal and uncertified (IITA)On-farm seed bank and NASC-registered multiplication as a revenue line

Anambra already treats food security as a state priority (BusinessDay) — useful for permits, extension support and access to federal irrigation and mechanisation programmes, but a tailwind, not a strategy.

The farm's real market is internal. Customer of first resort is Isiome Storage and Isiome Foods, then the Group's own staff estates, Idenze University and the teaching hospital canteens; only the residual goes to Onitsha through Isiome Trading. No standalone farm in Anambra starts with its tonnage already contracted. That is the entire competitive advantage, and it depends on no external customer. Competitors, such as they are, are smallholders (Isiome's suppliers and customers, not rivals), a fragmented handful of large South-East farms, and importers.

3. Product & service lines

Enterprise selection follows a five-question screen: (1) does Isiome Storage or Isiome Foods have contracted demand? (2) is it mechanisable with the Isiome Machinery fleet? (3) can it be dried or stored rather than dumped at harvest? (4) does it carry a certified-seed advantage the Group controls? (5) does it survive without irrigation? Any line that fails (1) is not planted. The screen is what stops the farm becoming a collection of interesting crops.

Discipline rule. Lines 7–9 are infrastructure and belong on the farm's balance sheet. The silo itself does not. Bulk storage is Isiome Storage's mandate and capex; the farm is the anchor tenant at the farm gate, paying a published handling and storage tariff. Double-counting the silo would overstate Group capital and blur accountability for utilisation. Long-gestation cash crops — oil palm, cashew, plantain, timber — are planted only after Tranche 2 is profitable, because they lock land for three to five years while the Group is still buying title in the same belt.

4. Operating model

Land acquisition — the item that cannot be done informally

No verbal agreements. No informal purchases. Ever. Idemmili is a belt of family and kindred holdings where undocumented sales are normal practice, and land is the Group's most durable asset and its most litigable. The Group's policy that it "does not acquire land by displacing families" (../EZEME_FAMILY_KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md) is only credible if the paperwork is clean. Five steps, every block:

  1. Title investigation — Anambra State Land Registry search; root of title, correct vendor, competing claims, and confirmation that no Government acquisition or road reservation touches the parcel.
  2. Kindred consent documented — written consent from the family head and every recorded interest, witnessed, in English and Igbo. An unrecorded kindred interest is the commonest cause of Nigerian farmland litigation.
  3. Boundary survey and beacons — licensed surveyor's plan, beacons planted, coordinates into the farm GIS from day one.
  4. Deed of Assignment executed, then Governor's Consent obtained and perfected. Consent is not a formality: under the Land Use Act 1978 it is what makes the assignment valid against third parties, and an unconsented deed is the classic Nigerian title defect (UNIZIK J. Commercial & Property Law; NDIC).
  5. 5% of every land transaction budgeted to due diligence — legal, survey, search, valuation, stamp duty. A Group rule, not to be economised on.

Block structure. The 100–200 hectares are acquired as discrete blocks of 20–40 ha, each separately titled, irrigated, costed and audited. One failed block must not consume the programme, and block-level accounting is what makes yield data meaningful.

One pricing basis to reconcile before Tranche 1. The corridor price of ₦5–20m per plot is a development-land price. The Group's own land table separately carries ₦600m for "Agriculture (Idemmili, 100+ ha)", implying roughly ₦6m per hectare — one to two orders of magnitude below ₦5m for a single plot. Both can be true, because they price different things, but the knowledge base already flags this row as one that "mixes hectares with per-plot pricing." Counsel and a valuer must fix the agricultural per-hectare basis before the first tranche is committed; the capital plan below assumes ₦6–8m/ha and is exposed if that is wrong.

Soil and agronomy

A soil survey precedes planting on every block, without exception. The belt is a lowland and valley-bottom landscape where acidity, drainage and nutrient depletion vary over a few hundred metres — a blanket fertiliser programme wastes money on half the land and starves the other half. Programme: soil test per block every two years; lime to correct acidity; green manure and cover crops for organic matter; rotation in which cassava is never grown continuously; block-level nutrient budgeting, never district averages.

Irrigation and water

Rain-fed farming carries one reliable cycle in Anambra; irrigation carries two, and removes the plan's largest single risk. Nigeria's 3.14m hectares of irrigable potential is mostly undeveloped (JICA) and the Group should not wait for a public scheme. Design from Tranche 1: boreholes plus an on-farm reservoir for reliability, river abstraction only where rights are documented; drip for greenhouses and high-value vegetables, sprinkler for maize and vegetables. A water abstraction permit from the Anambra State water authority and the Nigeria Integrated Water Resources Management Commission is required for any material abstraction and must be secured before construction. Dry-season cropping is the highest-return use of irrigation capital, and the reason the second cycle pays for the system.

Yields per hectare — targets, all flagged

National averages are not a planning basis, and achievable yields on Idemmili soils are the single most important number the first ninety days must produce. Targets below are indicative, at 60–70% of well-managed irrigated potential.

Input costs

Seed, fertiliser, crop protection and feed are the largest variable cost and the largest inflation exposure — fertiliser rose 11% into 2026 (BusinessDay) and the trend is upward. Three defences: buy through Isiome Seed on Group terms and forward-purchase ahead of season; substitute organic matter, manure and rotation to cut mineral fertiliser per tonne of output; and multiply certified seed on-farm so the best genetics are produced, not bought. Per-crop input costs are flagged for local verification — they move every season and no figure here should enter a budget unverified.

Labour model

Two tiers, deliberately. Permanent staff for anything requiring judgement, continuity or a licence — agronomy, irrigation, livestock, engineering, records, security. Seasonal labour for land preparation, planting, weeding and harvest, engaged in documented gangs with the statutory ₦70,000 monthly minimum wage as the floor and above-market rates for skilled roles (TheCable).

Mechanisation is the labour strategy. Peak labour demand is the costliest and hardest constraint; leasing the Isiome Machinery fleet flattens peaks, and the farm's seasonal data becomes the fleet's demand forecast. On-site worker housing, built by Okodu Construction to the Group housing standard, stabilises the permanent cadre and reduces the seasonal scarcity premium.

Post-harvest handling into Isiome Storage

The farm does not sell at harvest. Every tonne follows a defined path: fast harvest into crates or bulk; moisture tested at intake; grain dried to safe moisture, then transferred to the Isiome Storage silo at the farm gate against a warehouse receipt; perishables into the Nkpor cold chain within hours; a weighbridge and signed intake note for every load; grades and rejects recorded per block. Price decisions belong to Isiome Storage. The farm is measured on tonnes, grade and cost per tonne — never on the price it happened to catch.

GPS, telematics and farm management systems

The farm is instrumented from Tranche 1, because the data is both the R&D asset and the evidence base for the extension programme. Block-level GIS with surveyed boundaries and crop history; telematics on every tractor, implement and vehicle via Isiome Machinery, giving hours, fuel, area worked and location; IoT soil-moisture and climate sensors per block; drone and satellite imagery for crop health, drainage and block measurement — the Group already treats its drone programme as "an aviation department, not a gadget purchase"; and a farm management system feeding the Group ERP, aligned to Isiome's own training in farm management systems, IoT sensors and satellite imagery. Two uses beyond operations: yield-per-block history is what makes the farm's cost of production defensible at a transfer-price review, and it is what the Group sells on, through extension, to contracted smallholders.

One boundary, stated explicitly. Primary production does not require NAFDAC registration; NAFDAC and SON attach to the packaged products Isiome Foods makes. The farm's obligation is traceability into that system — block records, input logs, harvest dates, batch identity — so Foods can register and defend every SKU. A second boundary, equally explicit: despite the Group's interest in botanical inputs for Idenze Pharma, there is no cannabis or controlled-substance cultivation in Nigeria by any Group company. "Botanical and herbal inputs" in 01_Isiome_Group.md means ordinary licensed medicinal and aromatic plant material grown under contract, and nothing else. Any proposal to read it otherwise must fail here rather than at a regulator.

Land is the licence here, and the Group's rule applies to it exactly as it does to a NAFDAC file: it is acquired, not waited for. Every other requirement in the table above is cheap, and — with the exception of the EIA — quick. Title is the exception, and title is the one the company cannot operate without. So the acquisition posture is inverted: buy the perfected title rather than create it.

Held outside this figure: the silo and dryer (Isiome Storage capex — the farm pays a tariff), tractors and implements (Isiome Machinery — leased), the processing plant (Isiome Foods), and site power and network (Okodu Group). Note that development is roughly twenty times land cost — the number the Group's own 30-year land table does not contain, since its ₦600m Idemmili line covers land acquisition only.

Cost basis (planning rates, all to be replaced by firm quotations): agricultural land ₦6–8m/ha; clearing, stumping and block layout ₦1.2–2.5m/ha; borehole, pump, tank and distribution ₦35–60m/scheme; drip installed ₦4–7m/ha; sprinkler ₦2.5–4m/ha; greenhouse installed ₦120–250m/ha; 1,000 m² earthen pond complete ₦6–10m; 20,000-bird poultry house complete ₦180–280m; worker housing unit ₦18–30m; farm office, store and workshop ₦120–200m; solar pumping and barn power ₦25–45m; FMS, telematics and IoT ₦40–70m; 10% contingency on all of the above.

Financing. Family equity for Tranches 1–2 while land is cheap and title is still being perfected; naira term debt against titled land and improvements from Tranche 3, arranged through Aku Capital, subject to gearing ≤40% and no unhedged USD debt. Imported equipment is priced naira-first at order; unavoidable dollar exposure is matched against Isiome Trading's dollar revenue, never left open on the farm's balance sheet. Working capital, not capex, is the binding constraint: one cassava cycle ties up input and labour cost for ten to twelve months before a naira arrives, and that must be funded without starving Tranche 2.

Where the tonne actually earns its money. The farm's share of the chain is the smallest slice and the only one exposed to weather. Indicative, per tonne of maize:

StepValueOwnerExposure
Farm gate, at harvest~₦650,000Isiome FarmsWeather, pests, farm-gate price

Of roughly ₦1.0–1.6m of margin in the chain, the farm captures the least and carries the most risk. That is not a flaw; it is the reason the plan is structured this way.

The structural constraint, as arithmetic. At Year 15 the farm carries 200 ha, ~340 permanent staff and ₦11.3bn of capital, producing roughly ₦7.5bn of revenue on a 25–35% gross margin. After fixed overhead — management, security, records, compliance — that is a net return on total capital employed in the low-to-mid single digits once land and worker housing are included at cost, below the cost of naira debt. Strip out land (which appreciates and is the Group's stated natural naira hedge) and worker housing (a staff-benefit asset) and the productive-capital return improves, but remains modest. As a standalone company this plan would not be written. It is written because the silo, the plant and the Group's food security are not financeable without it.

Transfer pricing is therefore a governance matter, not an accounting one. Every farm-to-Storage or farm-to-Foods sale is intra-group, and an unbenchmarked one lets the farm look profitable while the profit engine quietly loses money. Protocol: board-approved prices benchmarked to Onitsha market and published commodity reference rates, reviewed quarterly, disclosed to the Family Council, with independent-director approval required for any deviation above a fixed threshold. No year-end netting of intercompany balances.

Break-even. Cash operating break-even arrives at roughly 60–70 hectares under cultivation with irrigation on at least half — the point at which block gross margin covers fixed overhead. Fixed overhead, not gross margin per hectare, decides this plan, which is why Tranche 2 must reach 100 hectares rather than stall at 40. On sensitivity: a 20% yield shortfall removes roughly two-thirds of gross margin on an open-field line, and so does a 20% farm-gate price fall. Greenhouse and irrigated lines are the only ones where the downside is genuinely bounded — which is why they carry the protected-cropping capital despite the higher capex per hectare.

11. Integration

This is the company with the most connections in the Group, in both directions.

It supplies: Isiome Storage — the anchor tonnage that makes the silo and the offtake book financeable; a silo with no guaranteed intake is a warehouse, a silo with this crop behind it is a commodity position. Isiome Foods — raw material for garri, starch, flour, canned tomatoes and packaged goods at Nkpor, at known grade and known cost. Isiome Seed — certified seed from the registered seed bank. Isiome Trading — residual volumes to Onitsha and later ECOWAS through Uli Freight. The Group's own institutions — Idenze University and teaching hospital canteens, the staff estates, Uli's hospitality contracts; the captive demand that removes the farm's market risk in its early years, and the effect the Group's own plan records: "Agriculture income — steady parallel income; reduces staff estate costs." Idenze Pharma — ordinary licensed medicinal and aromatic plant material under contract, and nothing else.

It buys: Isiome Seed for inputs on Group terms; Isiome Machinery for mechanisation as a leased service, not an owned fleet, which keeps capex off the farm's balance sheet and gives the machinery company a guaranteed utilisation base; Okodu Power for site electricity at Group rates, with on-farm solar for pumping and barn load; Okodu Construction for housing, ponds, stores and access roads under competitive tender against external bidders, with a benchmarking file per package; Aku Capital for naira term debt against titled land, working capital and later commodity finance against warehouse receipts; Uli Freight for inbound inputs and outbound produce; and Idenze Polytechnic and Idenze University for agricultural technology graduates and a research field station.

Related-party discipline. Every flow above is intra-group, and intra-group flows are where family conglomerates lose institutional credibility. Rule: competitive tender or an external benchmark on every material purchase, published arms-length tariffs for every service, independent-director approval on related-party contracts, and disclosure to the Family Council. The point is not to route work to family companies; it is to build companies whose largest customer holds them to institutional standards, so they can win third-party business on merit.

The internal-customer advantage, stated once. No standalone farm in Anambra begins with its tonnage contracted, inputs sourced, mechanisation leased, power supplied, finance arranged and graduates recruited from inside one group. That is the whole advantage, and a competitor cannot replicate it.

plans/05_Isiome_Storage.md  ·  5,807 words

ISIOME STORAGE — Storage, Aggregation & Offtake

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD, not comparable across plans.

Ezeme Group · Isiome Group · Isiome Storage Ltd (CAMA), with collateral management in a separate licensed company (§5). Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027. Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Isiome Group → Isiome Storage. Geography: intake across the Idemmili belt, hub at Nkpor, outbound on Uli Freight.

⚠️ Unresolved price conflict, flagged by the Isiome Trading plan. This plan models maize at ₦650,000/t, but the trading plan's 2026 research puts the grain trough at ₦350,000–470,000/t. That is a factor of roughly 1.5 on the throughput this business is valued against — not a rounding difference. Because Isiome Storage's economics turn on cost of carry and trading spread, the error compounds: a lower buy price raises the storage-and-sell margin and changes break-even utilisation. Do not commit capital against either figure until Isiome Group produces one measured price book for the current season. The same applies to any other input cost shared between Isiome plans.

1. Thesis

Isiome Storage buys, conditions, holds and sells Nigerian agricultural commodities at the two moments they are mispriced — at harvest, when everyone must sell, and in the scarcity window, when everyone must buy — and sells the storage, drying, cold chain and warehouse-receipt capability that makes doing so possible.

One sentence: primary production is the only step where output is fixed by weather and price by someone else, so the reliable margin in Nigerian agriculture is not grown — it is bought at harvest and sold into scarcity, and the silo, the drier, the cold room and the receipt are the machines that let the Group do that on other people's money.

  1. The gap is forced selling. A smallholder who must sell to repay an input loan sells at the year's low; the holder collects the difference. Nigeria's food inflation hit 20.31% year-on-year in July 2026, a ten-month high, and food prices rose for seven straight months while headline inflation eased to 15.43% (Nairametrics; BusinessDay).
  2. The loss is vast. 20–33% of Nigerian produce is lost between field and consumption (FETiCON 2024; Vanguard); annual losses run to ₦3.5 trillion (NAN).
  3. Farmland is not available; chain control is. Production is overwhelmingly smallholder (~60%); the offtake layer above it is fragmented and informal.

04_Isiome_Farms.md puts the test in reverse — if the farm is ever Isiome Group's most profitable agricultural entity, Storage has failed. This company instead sells into captive demand: Isiome Farms' tonnage, smallholders supplied through Isiome Seed, and Isiome Foods, whose working-capital instrument is a receipt. Capital rule: every naira must increase tonnes under control or capacity earning a tariff, and the binding constraint is not capacity but working capital — financed by structured commodity finance against warehouse receipts.

2. Market

Nigeria's cold chain is short by roughly 50,000 tonnes of cold storage capacity (International Institute of Refrigeration, 2025) and needs the order of 5,000 cold trucks (EnviroNews). The Federal Government has launched a US$3.5bn post-harvest programme and is revamping grain-silo concessioning (Independent NG; Grain Journal). Public storage has a private failure mode: the strategic grain reserve is under-maintained, so the federal silo estate is now offered to private operators (AGRA; Guardian).

Warehouse receipts: the legal ground has just moved, and this matters more than any market fact here. For the first time Nigeria gives the receipt statutory force — under the Investments and Securities Act 2025 the SEC holds registration and oversight of commodity exchanges, collateral management companies and warehousing (Part XV, Division B — Warehouse Receipts, ss.230–257) (AO2 Law; Stren & Blan). The SEC has issued a circular on mandatory registration of collateral management companies, warehouse operators and warehouses (SEC Nigeria); the Warehouse Regulatory Agency Bill 2022 has not become law; and the World Bank already called the receipt collateral distinct from general goods in storage (World Bank). The instrument that funds Nigerian agriculture now has legal force and almost no private capacity behind it — AFEX is the exception (RVO). Registration is a Year-1 application, not a Year-5 ambition.

⚠️ The exact provisions — verified against the Bill text, because earlier revisions of this library cited this wrongly twice, and the precise wording matters to a lender. Read from the Act itself:

ProvisionWhat it actually saysWhy it matters here
s.245(1)"A warehouse receipt as defined in this Bill shall only be issued by an entity duly registered by the Commission"This is the registration mandate. The receipt cannot lawfully be issued by an unregistered operator — which is why the Year-1 filing is not optional
s.246(1)"A Warehouse Receipt drawn and issued shall be "first proof of the holder having proprietary rights in the commodities""The operative asset provision — and note what it does not say. It is evidentiary, not constitutive: the receipt is proof of proprietary rights, not a conveyance of them
s.249(1)"A warehouse receipt issued to the bearer or to the order of a named person shall be transferable by endorsement and delivery"Negotiability. This, not the proprietary-rights provision, is what makes the receipt transferable collateral a lender can take security over
s.237Form, standardisation and prescribed contentsThe Commission's rules bind the receipt's form — and therefore the lot ledger and system that issue it
s.232Insurance of warehouse and commoditiesConsistent with this plan's bailee's-liability and goods-in-store cover

Correction of record — and a warning about how the error was made, which matters more than the error. This library cited the receipt's proprietary effect variously as "s.357", "s.236(1)" and "s.246(1)". The correct citation in the enacted Act is s.246(1). Reading the Act itself settles it:

Provision (enacted ISA 2025)What it says
s.244Registration of collateral management company
s.245Issuance of a warehouse receipt — "shall only be issued by an entity duly registered by the Commission"
s.246(1)Warehouse receipt as evidence of proprietary rights — "A warehouse receipt drawn and issued shall be first proof of the holder having proprietary rights in the commodities"
s.247Form, standardisation and contents of warehouse receipts
s.249(1)Negotiable warehouse receipts — "transferable by endorsement and delivery"
s.357Interpretation — where "warehouse receipt", "warehouse" and "control" are defined

The trap: s.357 and s.246 are both correct, for different things. s.357 defines the receipt; s.246(1) gives it its proprietary effect. An earlier revision of this plan conflated the two, and then a later correction went further and wrongly declared s.357 non-existent — because the reviewer had checked a National Assembly Bill of the Act (351 sections, warehouse division at ss.230–257) rather than the enacted Act (358 sections, division at ss.240–266). Two different documents, two different numberings, and the Bill is not the law. The correction has been reversed and all citations now follow the enacted Act.

And the phrase the library has used — "a document of title" — is looser than the statute. A document of title in the strict sense transfers title by endorsement. s.246(1) makes the receipt "first proof" of proprietary rights — a statutory evidentiary presumption, not a conveyance — while s.249(1) supplies transferability. The practical effect is close, but a lender's counsel will read the distinction, so the plan states the statute's own words. Confirm the security-interest perfection route over a receipt with Nigerian counsel before relying on it as collateral.

Competitors leave the same opening. Informal aggregators hold no grading, weight discipline, receipt or financeable collateral, so they set the harvest low price this business buys against; and traders, the federal silo estate, AFEX and the cold chain operators are thin here.

The specific gap. No operator in the Idemmili belt and Nkpor corridor combines belt intake points, a graded and weighed hub, cold chain, a legally recognised receipt, and a trading book that can buy and hold. Isiome Storage sells the chain from farm gate to warehouse receipt — and sells the receipt to a lender, not only the storage to a farmer. No reliable figure exists for the region's storage deficit or unsold belt tonnage; the §12 survey produces them.

3. Product & service lines

  1. Storage as a service — conditioned, aerated, fumigated bulk and bagged storage; tariff, receipt and outturn guarantee; ₦/tonne/month. Yr 5: 12%.
  2. Aggregation and trading — buy at harvest, condition, hold, sell into scarcity; ₦/tonne spread. Yr 5: 78% — the engine.
  3. Offtake contracts — forward purchase at a guaranteed price and grade.
  4. Warehouse receipts and collateral management — receipt issuance, goods held to a lender's order, independent verification and release; fee on value under management. Yr 5: 3%.
  5. Cold chain — chilled and frozen storage and intra-belt movement, with temperature records. Yr 5: 5%.
  6. Drying and conditioning — moisture reduction, cleaning, grading, bagging; ₦/tonne. Yr 5: 2%.

Line 3 is the strategic product: an offtake contract at a published floor price, backed by input supply from Isiome Seed, makes a smallholder's season bankable. The contract is the intake; the silo only stores what the contract delivers. Line 4 is the licence — highest barrier, lowest capital, structurally conflicted (§5), so it sits in its own company.

4. Operating model

The design in one sentence: intake goes where the crop is; the hub goes where the power, roads, labour and buyers are. So belt intake points of 3,000–8,000 t, three to seven of them, because the first weighing and grading must happen near the field or the farmer sells to the trader who is there; and the Nkpor hub, expressway-facing, 30,000 t rising past 100,000 t, where power, roads, the Foods intake door and the haulage fleet already are.

Siting: above the 2022 Anambra flood line (verify before any foundation); wet-season articulated access; within reach of Okodu Power; never on land without Governor's Consent.

Specification. Steel silos with aeration and temperature sensing for anything held beyond a season, because flat stores cost less per tonne and lose more; driers sized to the intake peak; a 60-tonne weighbridge; a calibrated moisture meter per intake point; a hub laboratory; cold rooms with validated temperature mapping and alarms.

Intake and outturn. One route for every tonne: weigh in, the ticket issued by a clerk who does not handle goods; sample and test for moisture, foreign matter and aflatoxin risk before unloading; dry to safe moisture, recording wet and dry weights separately, because the moisture record is the price record; assign a lot number tying farmer, date, grade, moisture, truck and silo cell to one identity; outturn only against a written release authority; and reconcile weekly, escalating variances the day they appear. Custody separation is the control: those who handle goods must not count them — stock control reports to the board, with two-person cell access and CCTV. A 1% weight error is ₦6,500 a tonne, so the weighbridge, the lot record and the stock controller are the margin.

Insurance. Goods in store, bailee's and warehouseman's legal liability, business interruption and cover for goods held to a lender's order — no lender lends against an uninsured receipt. Placed through Aku Insurance, on Aku Technology's lot ledger.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

  1. Company registration — CAC. Isiome Storage Ltd, plus a separate collateral-management company.
  2. Land title — Anambra State Land Registry. Deed of Assignment + Governor's Consent on every site before construction; 5% due-diligence budget; no verbal agreements.
  3. Warehouse operator and collateral manager registration — SEC. Mandatory under the SEC circular; ISA 2025 Part XV gives the SEC licensing and oversight of warehousing. Year-1 application, and the licence that makes the business financeable.
  4. Receipt system compliance. Issuance, registration of possession and transfer, records, exchange listing, inspection. A written counsel opinion on enforceability before the first receipt is issued.
  5. Food premises, standards, fumigation — NAFDAC and SON. Registration of food-handling premises, aflatoxin control, licensed applicators, and Nigerian Industrial Standards for grade and moisture; a receipt's grade claim must match a published standard or a lender's valuation is unenforceable.
  6. Weights, fire, environment, export, insurance. Federal Weights and Measures calibration; Fire Service certificate per site; NESREA; NAQS phytosanitary certification; NAICOM-licensed cover for stock and bailee's liability. Watch item: the Warehouse Regulatory Agency Bill 2022 is not law.

The conflict that decides the corporate structure. Isiome Storage wants to trade its own book and to issue receipts on third-party goods held as loan collateral — in one entity an invitation to the oldest fraud in commodity finance: a receipt on goods already sold, pledged or moved. So Isiome Storage Ltd trades and stores, while a separate SEC-registered collateral-management company issues and administers receipts with its own register, board including an independent director, audit and insurer. The collateral manager is never the trade counterparty.

This is the most acquisition-friendly licence in the domain, and the reason is supply. Registration is mandatory for collateral management companies, warehouse operators and warehouses (SEC circular), and the receipt's legal effect is now statutory. The citation is not the one usually given, which is why it is set out precisely above: s.245 imposes the registration mandate, s.246(1) makes the receipt "first proof of the holder having proprietary rights in the commodities", and s.249(1) makes it transferable by endorsement and delivery. Read the earlier note in this section — s.357 defines the receipt, s.246(1) gives it its effect, and a previous correction that declared s.357 non-existent was itself the error, made by reading a Bill rather than the enacted Act.

Two provisions settle the corporate structure above from the statute rather than from prudence. s.250(3): a receipt issuer may not trade the commodities it is registered to store — which makes the separation of the collateral manager from the trade counterparty compulsory, not merely prudent. And s.240 makes operating an unregistered warehouse an offence (₦2m or five years), with s.244(1) doing the same for collateral management. The SEC's own rule is even more direct: "Electronic Warehouse Receipts shall only be issued by Collateral Management Companies" (SEC executed rules, 22 March 2021) — so the separate collateral-management company is not a structuring preference but the only lawful route to a receipt this plan can finance against.

The licence is buyable because a dated recapitalisation has manufactured sellers. SEC Circular No. 26-1 of 16 January 2026 raised minimum capital to ₦200m for a Tier 1 collateral management company, ₦500m for Tier 2, and ₦500m for a warehousing operator, with compliance required by 30 June 2027 and suspension or withdrawal of registration as the sanction (SEC Circular 26-1; PDF; Syntegral). SEC's own checklist pages still carry the superseded ₦50m figure — which indicates what existing licensees actually hold. That is a pool of registered operators required to raise capital four- to ten-fold inside eighteen months, or merge, sell or exit. The deadline manufactures willing sellers, and it is the strongest reason to move in 2026–2027 rather than later.

Why "almost no private capacity" is supportable rather than asserted. The most specific published evidence: "There are no comprehensive records of privately owned agricultural storage warehouses. Most of the existing warehouses are unregistered and unregulated" — and of public silos, 38% are fully operational, 8% partial and 54% not operational (AGRA/FSRD, Nigeria Storage Gap Report 2023). No published register or count of licensed collateral managers or warehouse operators could be found, so this plan states that formally licensed private capacity is very thin and cites the source rather than quoting a number it cannot support. The Group's rule therefore applies here in its strongest form: the licence is acquired, not waited for — and this is the one licence in the domain that carries a published deadline telling the Group exactly when the sellers will appear.

The licence price is not public — and the anchors below are asset values, not prices. No public price was found for an SEC-registered collateral manager or a Nigerian warehouse business: FCCPC merger notifications carry no price field, AMCON publishes no asking prices, and no NGX disclosure prices a storage business. What exists is indicative comparable value, and it is labelled as such: the Igbariam, Anambra silo was concessioned to Coscharis Farms at an ICRC-recorded value of ₦254,241,286; ICRC-recorded silo concessions total ₦15.1bn across 20 sites (median ₦442m); and the federal 19-silo concession to seven firms was struck at ₦1.3bn upfront plus ₦3bn a year plus a ₦6bn expected profit share — the closest thing to a market price for a silo business in Nigeria (ICRC; Independent). None of these is a licence price and none is used as one.

Recommendation for this plan: register, and run the acquisition scan in parallel. The replacement cost is now published — SEC fees plus ₦200m of capital the Group must inject on either route — while the purchase consideration is not. So the test is arithmetic rather than preference: acquire only if a registered licensee can be bought for less than the registration fees plus the capital the Group would inject regardless. The 30 June 2027 recapitalisation deadline is what makes that test likely to pass, and it is why the scan belongs in the first ninety days rather than after the silo is built.

The last two rows are the plan. Storage earns a modest repeatable return on a depreciating asset; trading earns far more on capital that is not the company's. Carry is the swing factor — a four-point move in the finance rate moves trading contribution by ~₦13,000 a tonne, about half the entire storage tariff — and at ~₦78,000/t it is larger than storage, drying, handling, insurance and shrinkage combined. If price does not rise by more than carry, holding loses money, so the position must be partly forward-sold to Isiome Foods and institutional buyers and partly hedged through Aku Treasury. Spoilage: cereals held six months, aerated and fumigated, 1.5% target loss and a 3.0% ceiling; perishables in cold chain 3.0%, against 20–33% without it.

Break-even utilisation. Year 5: 50,000 t silo × 1.6 turns = 80,000 tonne-seasons; contribution ₦24,500 per tonne-season; cash fixed cost ₦1.6bn. On the storage tariff alone break-even needs 65,300 tonne-seasons — 82% utilisation, which fails the Group's own 75% ceiling for adding capacity. Blended with the trading book (34,000 t at ₦85,000 net, ₦2.89bn) the fixed cost is covered and storage becomes upside; full cost arrives in Years 7–8, by growing the book rather than the silo.

(5) Stock Control and Inventory Manager — reports to the board, separate from operations; owns the variance register. (6) Warehouse Receipts and Collateral Manager — register, lender relationship, SEC interface; sits in the collateral company. (7) Cold Chain Manager. (8) Risk and Finance Controller. 11. Integration

Supplies to Isiome Foods — buffer stock and conditioned raw material, and above all the warehouse receipt behind Foods' cash gap (₦3.1bn at Year 3 per 06_Isiome_Foods.md); Isiome Trading — the domestic wholesale and ECOWAS export leg at a published transfer price; Isiome Farms — anchor tenant at the gate, measured on tonnes and grade, never on the price it caught; contracted smallholders via Isiome Seed — inputs, an offtake contract at a published floor price and a receipt per tonne, which is what makes contracted farming bankable; Uli Freight and Uli Warehousing — the outbound tonne and palletised space; Akunnia — Aku Capital structures the receipt-backed facility, Aku Insurance covers stock and bailee's liability, Aku Treasury hedges FX and price.

Buys from Okodu Power (power for aeration, drying and the cold chain at Group rates, with solar-plus-storage); Okodu Construction and Okodu Materials (silo civils, driers, cold rooms and belt points on fixed-price contracts); Isiome Machinery and Manufacturing (belt-to-hub movement and fabricated handling equipment); and Uli Freight and Aku Technology (movement including cold chain, and the lot ledger).

Boundaries. Cold storage is Isiome Storage's; refrigerated movement Uli Freight's; general warehousing Uli Warehousing's; the receipt Isiome Storage's; the sale Isiome Trading's. Every intercompany sale is priced to a published, board-approved tariff benched to Onitsha market, with no year-end netting — an unbenchmarked price lets the farm or the trader look profitable while the engine loses money.

12. First ninety days

  1. Commission the belt intake and price survey first — three seasons of Onitsha and Nkpor prices, Anambra's harvest-to-scarcity spread, storage tariffs, the receipt-backed lending rate and unsold belt tonnage. It gates every later tranche.
  2. File the SEC warehouse-operator and collateral-manager registration — no facility is credible without it.
  3. Instruct counsel for a written opinion on the ISA 2025 receipt — enforceability, SEC rules and fees, and the effect of the Agency Bill. Do not issue a receipt before it is in hand.
  4. Incorporate both companies and constitute both boards, with an independent director on the collateral company.
  5. Secure the first belt intake site with Deed of Assignment and Governor's Consent, above the 2022 flood line, and start the Nkpor hub land search. Land moves first.
  6. Tender silo, drier, weighbridge and cold room to three vendors on fixed-price contracts with performance guarantees.
  7. Sign the first offtake contracts — 100 Idemmili farmers, in their own dialect, at a published floor price with a grade and moisture schedule and delivery at a named point, alongside Isiome Seed.
  8. Recruit the Head of Trading, the Stock Controller and the QA Manager — two reporting to the board. Hire the stock controller before the first tonne.
  9. Set board policy: naira at ₦1,600/USD; gearing ≤40%; no unhedged USD debt; debt ring-fenced to Isiome Group; position limits; 1.5% shrinkage target; working capital drawn only against receipts.
  10. Execute the intercompany protocols on day one — transfer pricing benched to Onitsha market, carriage with Uli Freight, power with Okodu Power, and a commodity-finance mandate with Aku Capital. Arms-length and minuted.
  11. Run the licence-acquisition route in parallel with the SEC application — the acquisition action for this plan. Instruct counsel to identify the registered collateral managers and warehouse operators already in existence, and to rank them by the distance between their present capital and Circular 26-1's ₦200m (Tier 1 collateral manager) or ₦500m (warehousing operator) required by 30 June 2027 — because that gap, not goodwill, is what brings a seller to the table. Then price each: SEC-file and registry search, a written opinion on the change-of-control process, and a preliminary approach. Budget ₦30m — ₦5m a target across up to five candidates, plus the opinion. The sourcing thesis is dated and published: licensees facing a four- to ten-fold recapitalisation inside eighteen months must raise, merge, sell or be suspended, so 2026–2027 is the window in which this licence is genuinely available. The de novo application in action 2 proceeds regardless; the two run together and neither delays the other.

06 — ISIOME FOODS

Processing and packaging — Nkpor, Idemili North LGA

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary throughout; dollar figures are indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026). Do not compare dollars across plans.

Position in the programme: third company of Isiome Group. Follows 04_Isiome_Farms.md; the value step in the chain described in 01_Isiome_Group.md.
CompanyIsiome Foods — subsidiary of Isiome Group
OwnerEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Isiome Group → Isiome Foods
SectorFood processing and packaging (Agriculture & Manufacturing)
SiteNkpor, Idemili North LGA, Anambra State — approx. 4.5 ha, expandable
LinesCassava (garri, starch) · palm oil · canned and catering tomato · milled and composite flour · packaging · cold store
Horizon10–15 years, licensing and land front-loaded
Headline number~47% of design throughput is operating break-even on an institutional-heavy mix — falling to ~35% once retail-pack mix matures. The plant must sell before it must build

1. Thesis

Isiome Foods exists because processing is structurally the highest-margin step in the agricultural value chain, and because Idemmili should produce while Nkpor processes.

A tonne of cassava root leaves Idemmili worth roughly ₦140,000. The same tonne, washed, pressed, dried, milled and packed as 1 kg retail sachets of garri, is worth ₦1,350,000. The farm never sees that spread, and neither does the transporter. It is captured by whoever owns the press, the dryer, the mill, the seamer, the registration number and the shelf. The farm sells a commodity; the plant sells a product. The commodity price is set by weather and by the trader at the gate; the product price is set by the pack, the specification and the invoice — all of which the processor controls.

Two reinforcing reasons make Nkpor the right site:

  1. Land economics force the split. Idemmili plots run ₦5–20m; Nkpor plots are far too valuable to farm. Farming Nkpor destroys capital; processing Idemmili strands it. Processing, packaging, cold storage and selling are the highest use of the Nkpor site, and the only uses that pay for it.
  2. The Group is its own first customer. Idenze University, Idenze Polytechnic, Idenze Schools, the teaching hospital and the staff estates are demand that exists before a single line is commissioned. No standalone processor in Anambra can underwrite a plant against contracted institutional load; Isiome Foods can.

2. Market

The size and the shape

Nigeria's food economy is large, growing, naira-denominated and increasingly import-substitutable. Two numbers frame it. Nigeria spent roughly ₦1.72 trillion importing processed food products in H1 2026 alone, and the wider food import bill has been put at about ₦3.3 trillion (CSR Reporters; Tejcoms, H1 2026). Nigeria's packaged food market is tracked as a multi-billion-dollar category growing steadily on urbanisation and middle-class formation (Deep Market Insights; Euromonitor, Staple Foods in Nigeria).

Inflation has eased but remains the operating environment: headline inflation fell to 15.39% in August 2026 (Punch; TheCable) and food inflation overtook the headline rate in May 2026 (Nairametrics). Double-digit food inflation is simultaneously the problem and the margin: it widens the gap between farmgate and shelf, and the processor is the party standing in that gap.

Three specific deficits that are the actual opportunity

Cassava is short and getting shorter. Industry sources report that only about 5% of national cassava output is available for industrial application and that local production falls short of industrial demand (New Telegraph; BusinessDay). Anambra and the Idemmili belt sit inside the highest-yielding cassava corridor in the country. Isiome Foods' raw-material advantage is geographic, and a Lagos processor cannot replicate it.

Palm oil is structurally deficit. Nigeria, once the world's largest palm oil producer, now imports to fill the gap — the LCCI puts the annual loss at ~$550m, imports were reported as tripling quarter-on-quarter in 2026, and import value has been reported at ₦287bn (Punch/LCCI; CropGPT, Q2 2026; New Telegraph; Nairametrics). A domestic, NAFDAC-registered, traceable palm oil brand is direct import substitution, and the price umbrella is set by landed import cost.

Cold chain is the missing infrastructure. Post-harvest loss runs high across Nigerian perishables precisely because cold storage is absent, and cold chain has been repeatedly identified as the investment the country cannot keep ignoring (Vanguard; Guardian). This is the piece that makes the plant a logistics asset and not only a factory.

Competitors — and where they cannot follow

Competitor setPositionTheir weakness at Nkpor
Dangote, Flour Mills of Nigeria, Olam, BUANational scale, deep distribution, wheat- and import-grain-based portfoliosTheir cost base is dollar-denominated imported grain and Lagos-based logistics. They are not converting Anambra cassava and Idemmili palm fruit, and they have no reason to serve a university canteen in Nkpor
Dangote's tomato processingAfrica's largest tomato plant, ~$20m investedProduction was halted by smuggling and energy cost (BusinessDay, Aug 2026). The lesson is not that tomato is bad — it is that a retail tomato paste brand war is bad

The gap, stated precisely

Nobody in the South-East converts Nigerian cassava, Idemmili palm fruit and Nigerian tomato into NAFDAC-registered, spec-consistent, traceable packs at the scale, in the format, and with the documentation institutional buyers require. The artisanal mill has the product and no paperwork; the Lagos multinational has the paperwork and the wrong raw material. Onitsha main market — West Africa's largest distribution node — has no industrial food processor of scale within 20 km. Institutional demand is the most underserved segment in the country, because it is the only segment that will not buy loose product from an open sack. That is the entry wedge, and the Group's own institutions are the proof case.

3. Product & service lines

Cassava — garri and starch (the anchor line)

Garri (white and yellow, retail sachets through 50 kg institutional bags), high-quality cassava flour (HQCF), and native/industrial starch. This is the volume base, the fastest route to NAFDAC registration, and the line whose raw material Isiome Farms can guarantee. Garri is the flagship because it is Nigeria's highest-frequency staple and the most improvable: artisanal garri is inconsistent in sourness, moisture and grit, and a milled, graded, moisture-controlled product is a different product at the same price point.

Palm oil (the margin line)

Red palm oil, refined and fractionated palm olein as capability grows, and palm kernel oil. Front-loaded because the deficit is largest, the import price umbrella is highest, and the extraction is simple relative to the margin.

Canned and catering tomato (the seasonal line)

Not a retail brand war. A seasonal toll-processing and institutional-pack line: 70 g sachets and 2.5 kg catering tins for the Group's own kitchens, hospitals, schools and hotels, and bulk paste for food-service and industrial buyers. Retail-labelled tomato paste is deliberately deferred to Year 6+ and only entered with a cost position, not a hope.

Milled and composite flour (the volume line, entered late and sideways)

Isiome Foods will not compete in wheat flour. Wheat is an imported grain, so a wheat mill at Nkpor imports a dollar cost into a naira business and puts us head-to-head with four national millers who buy grain by the vessel. Instead: composite (cassava–wheat) flour, whole-maize and cassava flour, and speciality flours, sold to institutional bakeries and food manufacturers, positioned on Nigeria's long-standing cassava-inclusion policy and on the fact that our cassava is local and our competitors' wheat is not.

Packaging, cold storage and contract manufacturing (the services layer)

  • Retail versus institutional formats. The same tonne of garri sells as 1,000 × 1 kg printed sachets or as 20 × 50 kg plain bags. The pack is worth more than the product (§7).
  • White-label and institutional contract manufacturing. Third-party brands — supermarket own-label, hotel groups, ECOWAS importers, NGO and school-feeding programmes — manufactured under our NAFDAC registration and their brand. This monetises capacity without requiring us to build a consumer brand, and it fills the off-season.
  • Cold storage and warehousing as a service. Surplus cold-store capacity, warehouse-receipt storage and toll processing sold to third parties through Uli Warehousing.
  • Export formats. Institutional and export cartons (20 kg, palletised, EU/ECOWAS-label compliant) from Year 5.

4. Operating model

Plant design

One site, deliberately zoned, because the most common failure in Nigerian food plants is mixing wet and dry processes in one hall:

  • Wet hall — cassava washing, peeling, grating, pressing, fermentation, drying; palm fruit sterilising, digesting, pressing, clarification. SS304 contact surfaces, sloped floors, clean-in-place.
  • Dry hall — milling, sifting, blending, flour packing. Separated, humidity-controlled, dust-extracted. Flour and moisture do not coexist.
  • Tomato hall — seasonal, built for conversion to another duty in the off-season. Do not build a single-purpose seasonal hall.
  • Packaging unit — sachet, pouch, bottle and canning lines, with in-line metal detection and checkweighing on every retail line.
  • QC laboratory — adjacent to intake, so rejection happens before unloading, and to dispatch, so release happens at the dock.
  • Cold store and dry warehouse — separate buildings, separate power priority.
  • Dispatch and Uli Freight bay — dock-levelled, sized for 40-foot containers and articulated trucks.

Capacity and equipment

LineDesign intakeConversionFinished outputKey equipment
Cassava / garri60 t/day fresh root~24%14.4 t/day → ~3,600 t/yrWasher, peeler, grater, screw press, fermenters, flash dryer, sifter, packer
Cassava starch / HQCF40 t/day fresh root~22%8.8 t/day → ~2,200 t/yrRasper, extractor screens, hydrocyclones, disc separator, ring dryer
Palm oil200 t/day FFB~20% CPO40 t/day → ~10,000 t/yrSteriliser, digester, screw press, clarifier, vacuum dryer, kernel recovery

Design throughput is ~30,000 finished tonnes a year at Year 5 across the five lines, with room on the site for a second train.

Capacity utilisation is the discipline, not the aspiration

Every food plant in Nigeria is either running at 40–55% and complaining, or running at 80% and compounding cash. Three board-level rules:

  1. No new line until the existing line runs at ≥70% for two consecutive quarters. Growth is funded from demonstrated throughput, not optimism.
  2. The seasonal hall earns its keep in the off-season — toll milling, third-party packing, contract manufacturing — or it is not built.
  3. Utilisation is reported weekly, by line, to the board, with yield and rejection rate. A plant manager who cannot state today's utilisation cannot run the plant.

Intake and quality control

Every load is tested before it is accepted: moisture, foreign matter, insect damage, and aflatoxin in maize and groundnut-origin inputs — the single most consequential food-safety hazard in Nigerian staples — plus pesticide residue spot checks. Every lot is numbered back to the farm or aggregator that supplied it. Rejected loads are documented and the farmer is told why: rejection is a supplier-development tool, not a punishment. Retention samples are held for every batch for shelf life plus 90 days.

Packaging, warehousing and distribution

Retail formats: 500 g / 1 kg / 2 kg sachets for garri and flour; 500 ml / 1 L / 5 L for palm oil; 70 g sachet and 400 g can for tomato. Institutional: 25 kg and 50 kg woven bags, 25 L jerricans, 2.5 kg catering tins. Export: 20 kg poly-lined cartons, palletised and shrink-wrapped.

Distribution runs on three channels and no more: Uli Freight for Group entities, institutional contracts and ECOWAS corridors; own light vehicles for Onitsha main market and the Nkpor–Onitsha–Awka triangle; appointed distributors for Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt on written terms with credit limits. Group institutions are supplied direct, on standing order, with monthly consolidated invoicing — no distributor between the plant and the customer.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Food is regulated at product level, not company level: each SKU needs its own registration. That single fact drives the entire sequencing of this plan.

RequirementBodyNotes

Premises and production inspectionNAFDACFood premises are inspected and found GMP-compliant before products are registered. NAFDAC's production-inspection guidelines for food manufacturing facilities set out layout, flow and hygiene requirements (NAFDAC guidelines)

The licence is acquired, not waited for — and here the licence is the revenue date. The fact that drives this plan is stated above: food is regulated at product level, each SKU needs its own registration, and the clock stops on any compliance query — 9–15 months for the first SKU. That is a year of a built, depreciating plant with nothing lawful to sell. The Group's rule is to acquire rather than wait, and nowhere in the domain is the arithmetic sharper: NAFDAC's fees are small — the schedule is carried in full in 61_Isiome_Manufacturing.md — while a year of idle plant is not.

8. Organisation

The first ten hires, in order:

  1. Managing Director — a food manufacturer who has run a NAFDAC-inspected plant and taken a product through registration, not a group executive learning the category.
  2. Plant Manager — production scheduling, yield, OEE, and the person who owns utilisation as a number.
  3. Head of Quality Assurance & Food Safety — reports to the Isiome Foods board, not to the Managing Director.
  4. QA/QC Laboratory Manager — food technologist with microbiology and aflatoxin method experience.
  5. Head of Procurement & Outgrower Network — builds and holds the farmer base; the role that decides whether the plant eats.
  6. Head of Engineering & Maintenance — planned maintenance is what keeps a line at 80% instead of 55%.
  7. Head of Commercial & Institutional Sales — owns the Group contracts and the hospital, university and estate standing orders.
  8. Brand & Retail Trade Manager — pack design, price points, distributor management.
  9. Supply Chain & Distribution Manager — the Uli Freight interface, cold chain integrity, and Onitsha market logistics.
  10. Finance Controller — commodity working capital, batch costing, credit control, and an auditable intra-group settlement.

Then, before commissioning: Regulatory Affairs Officer (NAFDAC/SON dossiers, in post in week one), HSE & Environmental Officer, and HR/Admin Manager — the plant will not pass premises inspection without the first two.

The QA reporting line, stated plainly

The Head of QA reports to the board through a Quality & Food Safety Committee chaired by an independent director, with only a dotted line to the MD. QA holds three powers that the MD cannot override: batch release authority (no batch ships without QA sign-off), stop-line authority, and recall initiation authority. QA's budget, headcount and laboratory equipment are board-approved, not MD-approved. This is not bureaucracy — it is the structural answer to the risk that a plant under commercial pressure ships a batch it should not. A food business is one incident away from being a former food business, and the person who must say no cannot report to the person whose bonus depends on saying yes.
