11. Integration

This is the most connected company in the Group, because its inputs and its customers are both inside it.

Buys from:

  • Isiome Farms — cassava root, palm fruit, tomato, maize and vegetables from Idemmili. The plant's reliability anchor and the demonstration that the geographic split works.
  • Isiome Seed — inputs advanced to outgrowers, which is what makes the offtake contract enforceable and the farmer loyal.
  • Isiome Storage — buffer stock, warehouse receipts, and the collateral instrument behind commodity working capital.
  • Contracted farmers — 12,000 under offtake by Year 10, supplied with inputs and agronomy support, bought from at the farmgate.
  • Okodu Power — electricity for the plant, the cold store and the laboratory, at Group captive rates. This converts the plant's largest controllable cost from dollar-linked diesel into a naira intra-Group margin, and is the single biggest reason the cold store is viable.
  • Okodu Construction — the civils, halls, warehouse, cold-store envelope and effluent plant.
  • Okodu Materials — steelwork, roofing, pallets, racks and packaging structural materials.
  • Aku Capital — commodity working capital, warehouse-receipt finance, treasury and insurance through Aku Insurance.
  • Uli Freight — inbound raw materials and outbound finished goods, on the corridors that also carry the rest of Isiome's output.
  • Idenze Polytechnic — machine operators, QC technicians and engineering assistants, trained before they are needed.

Supplies to:

  • Every Group estate and staff residence — staple food at Group cost, which lowers the real cost of living for Group employees across all five domains and makes Group employment more competitive than any employer in the area.
  • Idenze University, Idenze Polytechnic and Idenze Schools — canteen and catering supply on standing order, plus student placement and food-science research access.
  • The teaching hospital — patient, staff and canteen catering supply; dietetically specified and documented, which is a requirement no artisanal supplier can meet.
  • Uli Group's hospitality and institutional contracts — food-service content, including catering and location services for productions.
  • Isiome Trading — the wholesale and export book; Isiome Foods makes the product, Isiome Trading sells the container.
  • Uli Warehousing — cold storage and warehousing services sold to third parties on surplus capacity.
  • The Onitsha market — direct supply through appointed distributors, positioning the plant within 20 km of West Africa's largest distribution node.

The internal-customer advantage, stated plainly: Isiome Foods does not need to find its first forty customers. The Group's own estates, schools, university, polytechnic, hospital and hotels are contracted base load before commissioning — which is precisely what takes the plant past its break-even threshold and removes the single greatest risk in Nigerian food manufacturing, which is a plant built before a market exists. No independent food processor in Anambra starts with demand already signed.

What Isiome Foods deliberately does not do: it does not farm at Nkpor, does not run its own long-haul fleet (Uli Freight does), does not generate its own power (Okodu Power does), does not build its own consumer brand in tomato paste, and does not compete in wheat flour.

12. First ninety days

  1. Commission a site and utilities survey at Nkpor — geotechnical, water borehole yield and quality, effluent disposal route, and a measured 30-day record of grid supply hours at the exact site. The power number decides the plant design.
  2. Open the Anambra land and title file — confirm the Nkpor plot with Deed of Assignment and Governor's Consent, plus Idemili North LGA planning approval. Do not build on an unperfected title.
  3. Appoint the Managing Director and the Head of QA. These two roles decide whether the plant is a food business or a liability. Appoint QA before the MD if the search requires it.
  4. Open the NAFDAC file in month one — pre-application meeting, premises inspection requirements, and the first eight SKU dossiers (garri white, garri yellow, palm oil 1 L, palm oil 5 L, palm oil institutional, cassava flour, composite flour, catering tomato). Registration is the critical path; every week of delay is a week of no revenue.
  5. Run a full local price survey before believing any number in §7 — Onitsha main market wholesale and retail for garri, palm oil, tomato and flour; farmgate cassava and FFB prices by LGA across a full season; sachet film, woven bag and tinplate prices landed at Onitsha. Re-underwrite §7 on the survey, not on the plan.
  6. Sign the first institutional offtake letters with Idenze University, Idenze Polytechnic, Idenze Schools, the teaching hospital and the staff estates — indicative monthly volumes, specifications and prices, expressed as a standing order with a notice period. This is the anchor load, and it must exist in writing before the line is ordered.
  7. Tender the garri and palm oil lines to at least three equipment vendors on fixed-price contracts with performance guarantees on yield, output and utility consumption. Commission a fourth, independent engineering review of the winning specification. Do not accept a single quotation.
  8. Design and open the outgrower programme — input supply through Isiome Seed, agronomy support through Isiome Farms, a written offtake contract in English and Igbo, cash-on-delivery payment terms, and farmgate collection by Uli Freight. Target 250 contracted farmers in Year 1.
  9. Commission the effluent and environmental design with Okodu Construction and lodge the NESREA and Anambra State applications. Wet cassava and palm processing produces the licence condition that most often delays a Nigerian food plant's opening.
  10. Set the financial policy as a board resolution — naira primary at ₦1,600/USD planning rate, gearing ≤40%, no unhedged USD debt, Isiome Foods debt ring-fenced from the other four groups, a 10% FX contingency on all imported equipment, 60 days of working capital funded by warehouse-receipt commodity finance, and commitment to the 70% utilisation rule before any second line is ordered.
  11. Open the certified-processor acquisition file — the acquisition action for this plan. Instruct counsel to identify small and mid-sized food processors in the South-East holding live NAFDAC registrations in garri, palm oil, tomato or flour, and MANCAP, and price them: NAFDAC and SON file search per target, a written opinion on whether each registration follows the entity, the product or the premises, and a valuation of the plant and the brand. Budget ₦40m — ₦5m a target across up to six candidates, plus the opinion and two valuations. The test is explicit: if an acquired range can be lawfully sold more than nine months before the first §5 registration would be granted, acquisition is the cheaper route to revenue. Action 4 continues in parallel regardless — the two are not alternatives, and neither delays the other.

A naming note. 09_Aku_Capital.md uses "Isiome Trading" as shorthand for its index and ETF platform; that function belongs to Aku Markets, and the Aku Capital plan should be corrected at next revision.

1. Thesis

Isiome Trading buys Nigerian agricultural commodity and processed food where it is cheapest, moves it to where it is dearest, and is paid partly in hard currency while its costs stay in naira — and it earns that living on the spread and the carry, never on the commodity itself.

One sentence: commodity trading is a thin-margin, high-turnover, working-capital-hungry business in which the trader never owns the price — only the spread between two markets and the cost of the money that carries the cargo between them.

  1. The margin is not in the commodity. Buy maize at ₦375,000 a tonne, sell at ₦425,000: ₦50,000 made. Fund that cargo for ninety days at 28%: ₦26,000 paid. The carry is more than half the gross spread — and it is decided by the finance desk, not the trading desk (§7).
  2. The domestic grain market is in a trough. Cereal prices fell below import parity through 2024–25, with maize as low as ₦180,000 a tonne before the Federal Government's ₦350,000/tonne guaranteed minimum price (Punch; AGRA Food Security Monitor 72 puts Nigerian maize at US$265/tonne). Compressed domestic spreads make export and processed lines the profit centre, not the residual one.
  3. The policy ground just moved in the trader's favour. Tinubu signed the Export (Prohibition) Act (Repeal) Bill 2025 in March 2026, repealing the 1989 law that restricted exports of beans, cassava, maize, rice and yam (New Telegraph). Non-oil exports reached US$12.8bn in 2025, up 21%, and agricultural exports ₦1.97trn in H1 2026 (Channels TV; TheCable/NBS).
  4. FX is structural, not opportunistic. A trader whose costs are naira and whose invoice is dollars holds a natural long-dollar position funded locally — the cheapest hedge the Group owns at 15.39% inflation and a 23% policy rate (Nairametrics). It must be repatriated within 90 days (§5).

Physical, not margin. Trading physical means owning title to a specific lot: custody, freight, storage, quality risk, and a cargo on the balance sheet until a named buyer pays. Trading on margin is a derivative position: no custody, no freight — instead mark-to-market variation margin, leverage and margin calls, with the underlying never delivered. Isiome Trading does the first, and touches the second only as a hedge against a physical position already owned, executed through Aku Treasury — never as a standalone book. If Year-5 EBITDA depends on the direction of maize prices rather than on tonnes moved and days funded, this company has failed.

2. Market

Onitsha is the base because the buyers are already there. Onitsha Main Market is the largest in West Africa, with an estimated annual trade volume above US$5bn across more than forty distinct markets in the metropolis (Pulse). It is a redistribution market as much as a retail one: goods bought there move onward across the South-East, the South-South and, informally, the north. The Group's second-largest advantage after its own value chain is a headquarters forty minutes from a market of continental scale.

That market carries a live political risk. Anambra's 2026 demolition of illegal structures there marked roughly 10,000 shops and drew a court restraint (BusinessDay; Guardian). So Isiome Trading takes space off the market, not in it — aggregation bays at Nkpor and Storage's silos, selling into Onitsha rather than renting inside it.

AfCFTA lowers the tariff and disappoints at the border. Nigeria adopted a schedule covering 80% of traded goods in April 2025 and plans to liberalise 90% of tariff lines in ten years, 7% in thirteen and hold 3% sensitive (World Bank; USDA GAIN NI2026-0010). Tariffs were never the binding constraint. WACTAF finds exporters spending ₦10.84m to move one truckload valued at ₦100m to Ghana — 10.8% of cargo value — dominated by a 7.23% "statistics levy" in Benin (Shipping Position; Guardian). Intra-African shipping remains the world's most expensive (Guardian), and LCCI notes Nigeria still lacks data showing AfCFTA tariff benefits (Leadership).

3. Product & service lines

  1. Domestic wholesale — grains, tubers, pulses and oils bought through Isiome Storage and sold into Onitsha, Nnewi, Awka and Aba; ₦/tonne spread. Yr 5: 46% of revenue, 22% of contribution.
  2. Institutional supply — contract supply of rice, garri, flour, beans, oils and packaged foods to schools, hospitals, barracks, hotels and the Group's institutions; cost-plus per tonne, the demand floor that keeps cash moving. Yr 5: 14% / 16%.
  3. Export of raw commodity — sesame, cashew, ginger, hibiscus and soya to Asian, Gulf and European buyers, and maize/sorghum within the region; FOB spread, USD. Yr 5: 24% / 34%.
  4. Regional export of processed and branded food — Isiome Foods' garri, starch, oils and packaged lines into Ghana, Benin, Togo, Cameroon and the diaspora trade; USD spread. The highest-value leg per tonne and the one that survives corridor charges. Yr 5: 9% / 18%.
  5. Trade agency and documentation services — running the export document chain for third-party processors and cooperatives; the desk is already built, so marginal cost is near zero. Yr 5: 4% / 6%.
  6. Offtake and pre-export finance support — buying on confirmed orders and structuring pre-shipment finance with Aku Capital and NEXIM. Yr 5: 3% / 4%.

Line 4 is the strategic product. Ad valorem border charges fall on cargo value, so a container of packaged garri carries a far better margin per naira of corridor cost than a truck of raw maize — and it is the only line that builds a brand rather than a relationship.

4. Operating model

The corridor rule, stated once: bulk raw commodity goes by sea; processed, branded and high-value goods go by road. Benin's charges are percentage-of-value, so the road corridor punishes exactly the low-value, high-volume export a bulk trader naturally makes. The design follows from that arithmetic.

Domestic book. Buy through Isiome Storage — which holds the silos, the weighbridge, the lot ledger and the harvest book — and sell into Onitsha through a small number of verified wholesalers and institutional buyers on written terms: named delivery point, grade, payment date. A trading business dies of receivables, not of stock.

Export book. Origination is confirmed order first, cargo second — no tonne is bought for export without a signed contract, an LC, a documentary collection with acceptance, or a cleared advance. Board-set limits: no commodity above 35% of the book, no counterparty above 25% of turnover, no open position beyond 60 days unmatched.

Documentation as a production line. Every shipment runs: NEPC registration → bank-issued NXP → NAQS phytosanitary certificate → fumigation → standards testing → NAFDAC export e-licence for processed goods → certificate of origin → customs declaration on B'Odogwu → CCI inspection → terminal and shipping. B'Odogwu is the live bottleneck: it cannot process multiple bills of lading concurrently and PAAR sharing takes hours to days (Shipping Position). So every delivery date carries fourteen days of slack.

Quality is bought at intake, not argued at the port. Specifications are contractual — moisture, foreign matter, admixture, aflatoxin and pesticide limits — and for the EU the increased official controls of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/194 on mycotoxin and contaminant risk (EUR-Lex). Practice: pre-shipment testing against the buyer's written specification, a retained sample per lot, and QA's right to refuse a load before it is bought — a rejection at destination costs a hundred times the inspection (§7).

Ports and partners. Lagos (Apapa/Tin Can) for containerised export, Onne as the eastern alternative; inland movement contracted to Uli Freight, with cold chain where the cargo is perishable.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

  1. Company registration — CAC. Isiome Trading Ltd, with a ring-fenced trade-compliance and documentation function; export liabilities never touch the Group's other balance sheets.
  2. Exporter registration — NEPC. The first statutory step of the export procedure, and the gateway to the certificate of origin and to incentives (NEPC ETLS guide).
  3. Customs — Nigeria Customs Service. Declaration on B'Odogwu, the NXP-linked process, and the Nigeria Export Supervision Scheme (NESS) charge of 0.5% of FOB on non-oil exports; zero export duty, VAT zero-rated (export cost framework 2026; NESS collecting banks). [verify] collection mechanism and bank panel.
  4. Phytosanitary — NAQS. A certificate per consignment after inspection and a token fee; cargo without one risks rejection or destruction at the importer's expense (NAQS).
  5. Processed food — NAFDAC. Product registration plus an export e-licence (Health Certificate, CCMFS, COPP, CFS or Export Certificate), applied through trade.gov.ng/nafdac with the company TIN. No e-licence is issued for goods that have already left the country (NAFDAC PID-GDL-011-00) — the licence is a production step, not a shipping step.
  6. Standards — SON. Nigerian Industrial Standards and MANCAP for manufactured products, plus testing against the destination market's requirements where stricter. [verify] which certificates a consignment needs, and their fees.
  7. Destination-market requirements. Ghana FDA and Standards Authority; food-safety registration in Benin, Togo and Côte d'Ivoire; Cameroon's CEMAC-era formalities; EU SPS controls. Build the file per destination before quoting.
  8. ECOWAS and AfCFTA origin. ETLS certificate of origin on the ECOWAS corridors; AfCFTA preferential origin where the destination is a state party — with the caveat that preference is only as good as the border's willingness to honour it (§2).
  9. Export finance — NEXIM. The Rediscounting and Refinancing Facility is available at a concessionary rate to trading as well as manufacturing companies with 50% export orientation, through a participating bank: pre- and post-shipment rediscounting at 60–180 days, refinancing to a year, the bank carrying 100% of credit risk (NEXIM). The Export Expansion Grant is real but slow — ₦330.08bn of claims being reconciled, 40% of monthly NESS collections ring-fenced for trade facilitation (ThisDay). Treat EEG as upside, never as a budget line. ⚠️ And check the eligibility test against the corrected export row: at the plan's own 33% export share (§9) the company is below the 50% export-orientation threshold in every year, so this facility must be qualified on another limb or re-planned. See §9's export-revenue note.
  10. FX repatriation — CBN. Proceeds must be repatriated within 90 days of shipment or the exporter is excluded from the official FX window, tracked against the TIN (CBN Forex Manual, via practitioner guidance). A dispute notice can pause that clock — the compliance officer's most valuable habit.

The licence is acquired, not waited for — and in export the acquisition route is the strongest in the domain after Storage's. Nothing in the list above is expensive in fees. What is expensive is what is expensive everywhere in this domain: time, relationships and a record. An exporter's real licence is not the NEPC certificate — it is a buyer who pays, a bank that discounts, a customs agent who answers the telephone, and a compliance history a lender will fund against. All four come attached to an existing export trading company.

12. First ninety days

  1. Commission the commodity and corridor price survey first — three seasons of Onitsha and Nkpor prices, farm-gate-to-FOB spreads for sesame, cashew and ginger, actual levies at Seme, Idiroko and Jibiya, ocean freight by destination, certificate fees. This gates every later tranche.
  2. Incorporate at CAC and register as an exporter with NEPC, then instruct counsel on ETLS and AfCFTA origin documentation for each corridor.
  3. Recruit the Trade Compliance Manager and the Credit Control Manager first, both reporting to the board — before the first order, not after the first loss.
  4. Open the banking structure — naira-first accounts, an export domiciliary account, and a letter of intent with a NEXIM participating bank for RRF rediscounting.
  5. Meet the Onitsha wholesale associations and twenty verified buyers on written credit terms, and sign the first ten institutional contracts with Group schools, hospitals and estates.
  6. Sign the first three confirmed-order export contracts on LC or advance terms — two processed-food regional orders, one raw-commodity order — and refuse everything else.
  7. Lock the document chain: pre-shipment testing, fumigation, NAQS inspection scheduling, and a NAFDAC export e-licence application for the priority Foods products.
  8. Sign the Uli Freight corridor tariff and the Aku Capital trade-finance mandate, with credit cover through Aku Insurance, effective before the first cargo moves.
  9. Set board policy: naira at ₦1,600/USD; gearing ≤40%; no unhedged USD debt; position limits (35% commodity, 25% counterparty, 60 days); no export tonne without a matched sale; 90-day repatriation; working capital only against confirmed orders or receipts.
  10. Publish the Storage and Foods transfer-price schedule on day one and correct the maize price book across Isiome Group, so all three companies plan against one measured series.
  11. Open the exporter and customs-agent acquisition file — the acquisition action for this plan. Instruct counsel to identify existing export trading companies and licensed customs agents trading this plan's corridors and price them: NEPC, CAC and NAFDAC file search per target, a written opinion on whether NEPC registration and customs agency transfer on a change of control, a repatriation and customs-compliance record check on each, and a valuation of the buyer book. Budget ₦30m — ₦5m a target across up to five candidates, plus the opinion. The sequencing is deliberate: rent a licensed agent for the first consignments (action 7), acquire only when a target's buyer book is worth more than its licence, and treat direct licensing as the last resort rather than the first. The proposed twenty-fold customs-agent fee rise makes the incumbent materially more valuable, and that window is the reason to move in Year 1 — [verify] the fee in force before budgeting it.

08 — AKUNNIA GROUP

Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security — the second child's domain

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is her group; her companies take the short form "Aku." See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary throughout; dollar figures are indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026).

Status: replaces the BlackRock-oriented version of this plan. The model below is Blackstone — control, alternatives, carried interest — not BlackRock's passive and index business. Title wording follows Group Master Plan §6.2 exactly.

Position in the programme: second child, second domain. Follows 00_Family_Business.md and 01_Isiome_Group.md.
GroupAkunnia Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group (the mother company)
HeirAkunnia — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer
SectorsFinance & Investment Systems · Governance, Law & Security
Companies — financeAku Capital · Aku Bank · Aku Credit · Aku Private Equity · Aku Insurance · Aku Treasury · Aku Advisory · Aku Asset Management
Companies — governance, law & securityAku Legal · Aku Security · Aku Arbitration
Companies — internal infrastructureAku Technology — consolidation, portfolio monitoring, fund accounting and the deal pipeline. Systems for the Group, not a product to sell.
Companies — execution, not productsAku Markets — securities dealing and secondary-market execution for the Group's own transactions and, over time, third parties. Not an index or ETF platform — passive products belong to the BlackRock model the Group has rejected
Global hubLondon or New York — the investment manager sits at the hub; the assets sit in Africa
MandateOrchestrate the structural, private development of African industry — buy entire companies, reshape them, and make extraordinary returns doing it
BoundaryFinance and institutional stability only. Real estate sits under Okodu Group ("his real estate arm manages all staff apartments, student housing, commercial letting, and the Akuzo storey building portfolio" — Group Master Plan §6.5). Aku does not develop, own or operate property.

1. Thesis

Blackstone is the correct model, and the previous plan was built toward the wrong one.

BlackRock manages passive money — index products, ETFs, and technology licensed at a few basis points. Blackstone manages control — it buys entire companies, replaces boards, engineers growth, and sells. The economics differ by an order of magnitude, and so does the skill:

BlackRock (wrong model)Blackstone (correct model)
What it sellsIndex exposure at 3–15 bpsControl and alternatives at 1.5–2% + 20% carry
How it growsAUM, passively, at near-zero marginal costDeals, actively, one transaction at a time
The skillDistribution and technologySourcing, underwriting, operating improvement
The brandScale and safetyWall Street prestige and aggressive returns
Talent modelSalaried, institutionalPartner economics — carry worth tens of millions
Flagship engineiSharesReal estate, private equity, private credit

The three things Blackstone actually is, in order of AUM:

  1. Real Estate — the largest owner of real estate in the world. This is the single biggest reason it became the largest alternative manager.
  2. Credit & Insurance — now the largest segment by AUM, and the fastest-growing. Private credit became the engine.
  3. Private Equity — the original business, and still the brand. Buying whole companies, fixing them, selling them.

Plus Tactical Opportunities and Hedge Fund Solutions.

Why this fits Ezeme Group better than the BlackRock model did. The Group already builds and owns real assets — Okodu Power's generation, Okodu Real Estate, Akuzo, Uli's corridors and warehouses, Isiome's processing. Blackstone's real estate and credit arms exist to buy exactly that kind of asset at scale. And the Group's five operating domains give it something a financial buyer from New York cannot buy: sector knowledge, proprietary deal flow, and the operational capability to actually fix what it buys.

The mandate, stated plainly: the structural, private development of African industry. Not passively financing it — buying the fragmented companies, consolidating them, professionalising them, and owning the result. Africa's industry is fragmented, informal and under-capitalised. That is not a problem; it is the opportunity, and it is the condition in which Blackstone-style control investing produces its best returns.

What changes — and what survives

Demoted or repurposed:

Previous planFate under BlackstoneWhy
Aku Markets (index & ETF platform)Closed or reduced to a minor product lineBlackstone has no index business. This was the iShares analogue, and iShares belongs to the wrong model entirely.
Aku Technology (portfolio & risk platform sold to institutions)Becomes internal infrastructure onlyBlackstone does not sell technology. It becomes the Group's own deal, portfolio and risk system — valuable, but not a business.
Aku Asset Management (pension & sovereign mandates)Becomes a distribution channel, not the coreInstitutional mandates matter for raising capital, but that is fundraising, not investing.

Corrected — the full company list, including the Governance, Law & Security half

The previous version of this plan omitted Akunnia's second sector entirely. The Group Master Plan §6.2 places under her "the legal and compliance function… handling all land title conveyancing, Igba Odibo equity documentation, Group contract law, and arbitration. Security coordination for all Nkpor zones is also under her domain." That is half her mandate, and it was missing. The corrected list, with each company's role and licence position, is in §3.

2. Market

This section did not exist in earlier revisions of this plan, and its absence was the document's largest analytical gap — because the two halves of Akunnia's domain sell into two entirely different markets. The finance half competes for capital and for deals; the governance half sells billable work to Nigerian landowners, developers, estates and institutions. They are sized in different units, bought by different people, and moved by different forces. The earlier version, which developed only the finance half, was in effect a finance plan with a legal annexe; this section treats both, and says so where they differ.

Two disciplines apply throughout, and both are deliberate. First: no market size below is invented — every figure is sourced or marked [verify]. Second: where the honest position is that no reliable figure exists, this section says so and names the first-ninety-days action that would establish it, in §2.4 and again in §12.

2.1 The benchmark: what Blackstone is, segment by segment

The reader needs the shape of the model before the African case, because this domain is being built to resemble it. From Blackstone's own quarterly reporting at 30 June 2026:

The library's earlier figure for the credit segment — roughly USD 443bn of a ~USD 1.35tn firm — is cited to the Blackstone 2026 10-K in 51_Aku_Credit.md §1; the Q2 2026 release now reports USD 469.3bn for the same segment.

Four things the table says, and each one decides something in this plan:

  1. Credit is the engine, not private equity. Credit & Insurance is the largest segment and took USD 143.0bn of the USD 262.5bn raised over the twelve months to June 2026 — more than half the firm's inflows. That is why Aku Credit is this domain's largest engine and Aku Private Equity is the brand (§3).
  2. Real estate is enormous — and Aku's relationship to it is deliberately not ownership. Real Estate is USD 314.2bn of assets, split into Opportunistic, Core+ and Debt Strategies. The analogue in this Group is not an Aku property business. Property is Okodu's (Master Plan §6.5): Aku may manage and invest in a real-asset fund, may lend against property, perfect title to it and insure it — and may not own or operate it. The full boundary and its consequences are in §7.
  3. The hedge-fund business now reports as Multi-Asset Investing, USD 108.6bn — the smallest of the four segments and the one with the least African analogue. Nothing in this plan proposes to build it.
  4. Perpetual capital is the strategic prize. USD 555.6bn of perpetual capital AUM, of which USD 463.0bn is fee-earning — 48% of all fee-earning AUM (Q2 2026 slides). In Africa, where assets are illiquid and holding periods long, the equivalent vehicle is worth more than it is to Blackstone (§7).

And the access problem, stated once, because it governs every fundraising assumption below. The LP base that funds a firm of this size — US and Canadian public pensions, sovereign funds, insurers and endowments — does not allocate to a first-time Nigerian family manager in Fund I, at any fee or in any structure (10_Aku_Asset_Management.md §1.3, §2.2). Blackstone is the benchmark for the business; it is not the benchmark for Fund I.

2.2 The finance half — the market it operates in

African private credit: why the gap exists

These figures are already in the library; they are cited here rather than re-derived. All are from 51_Aku_Credit.md §1–§2:

FactFigureSource
Private-sector credit~17% of GDPThe Sun / CPPE
Real-sector financing gap₦50trn (CPPE)Guardian
Policy rateMPR 23%, after a 350bp cutNairametrics, Sept 2026
Lending versus deposit rates~29% overdraft and 30–35% mid-market, against ~18% on deposits13_Aku_Treasury.md [verify]
Domestic private-debt demandARM ₦200bn private-debt programme; FCMB–TLG ₦20bn Series 2Nairametrics, Jan 2026

Why the gap exists, in the order that matters. Nigerian banks lend short and against collateral: deposits are shorter than a three-year amortising loan; security over chattels and receivables is slow to perfect and slower to enforce; single-obligor limits cap exposure to any one name; and workout capability is scarce. They largely do not lend to the mid-market on cash flow at all. Microfinance banks are too small; DFIs are concessional, slow and sized far above the middle. Nobody lends ₦200m–₦2bn for three to five years against a business's cash flow (51_Aku_Credit.md §1).

The customer the market is missing is a company with ₦500m–₦10bn of revenue, positive EBITDA, real assets and auditable accounts, needing ₦200m–₦2bn for three to five years — too large for microfinance, too small or too informal for a bank desk. And the price of that gap is the spread: mid-market borrowers pay 29–35% while deposits earn about 18%. That spread is the business. [verify] both rates at the date of commitment.

The LP market — and the regulator is instructing pension funds to buy what the Group builds

This is the most important paragraph in this section. PenCom — the regulator, not a broker — names R1 (real returns below inflation) and R3 (concentration in FGN securities) as two of the principal risks in Nigerian pension assets, and prescribes the remedy as a shift into "alternatives, infrastructure, and inflation-linked instruments." The regulator is instructing pension funds to buy what the Group builds: long-dated, inflation-linked, naira-denominated cash flows with a real asset behind them, originated across the other four domains (41_Okodu_Group.md §1 is the clearest statement of the asset profile). The binding constraint is not permission and not appetite — it is bankable pipeline, and pipeline is what a fund manager sells. Read with the rest of the table: a continent whose institutions hold over USD 600bn, told by their own regulator to buy alternatives they mostly cannot access, sitting on an industrial base that is majority informal, family-run and under-capitalised — which is to say, for sale (09_Aku_Capital.md §2).

Two consolidation events make the same point from the other side, and both are this domain's acquisition market. PenCom raised the PFA minimum capital to ₦20bn, rising to ₦25bn above ₦500bn AuM, by December 2026 — reported to have moved to June 2027, which delays exactly the flow of sellers this acquisition thesis depends on. Verify the operative date; a six-month extension pushes the PFA clock closer to the SEC's 30 June 2027 and defers the orphaned-mandate release (corrected — see CITATION_AUDIT.md) (Punch) — smaller managers will merge or sell, releasing experienced investment and compliance staff and orphaned mandates. And the SEC's revised manager minimum capital applies to existing operators by 30 June 2027, with new applicants complying from day one (SEC guidelines; Aluko & Oyebode) — a supply of registered managers that must sell or surrender, which is the acquisition route in §5.

And the honest ceiling, stated here rather than buried in a fundraising deck: Nigeria's entire pension pool is USD 18.5bn. At ₦1,600/USD, a USD 1bn fund is more than 5% of every Nigerian pension asset in existence, and the Year-10 target of USD 15–25bn (§9) exceeds the whole Nigerian pension industry several times over. The platform is therefore pan-African and DFI-funded long before it is Nigerian-pension-funded, and it is not reachable from African assets alone (10_Aku_Asset_Management.md §2.4). That is the constraint on the entire domain.

African private equity — deal sizes, sectors, and how illiquid the exits are

From 52_Aku_Private_Equity.md §2:

SectorsManufacturing, healthcare, food processing, logistics, financial services — each a Group domainThe Group already understands the sectors it would buy

The structural read: this is a buyers' market for control and a poor market for exits. African private capital is shifting to larger deals and fewer, more focused sectors, with exits rising but cash still trapped in older vintages (BusinessDay; AVCA). Africa's industry is fragmented, informal and under-capitalised — the condition in which consolidation produces its best returns (§3) — while the exit market is thin enough that the Group must identify the exit at entry and treat a trade sale as the base case (52_Aku_Private_Equity.md §4, risk 5). The two facts are one fact: the same illiquidity that gives the Group pricing power on the way in constrains it on the way out, which is why a perpetual vehicle matters more here than it does to Blackstone itself (§7).

The honest conclusion on competition: capital is not the scarce thing, and neither is process. Pan-African funds and DFI-backed managers have both. None of them has an operating conglomerate behind it — five domains that supply customers, executives who can be seconded as operating partners, construction at cost, and credit and insurance in-house. Deal flow and operating capability are the edge; the fee rate and the fund structure are not.

2.3 The governance half — a different market, and it must be said plainly

This half does not compete for capital. It competes for instructions. Its market is billable work — title files, contracts, licence compliance, guarding, arbitrations — sold to Nigerian landowners, developers, estates, institutions and corporates. It is sized in fees and cases, not in AUM, and its demand is created by exactly the conditions the finance half's borrowers complain about. It is also the only part of this domain that can earn revenue in Year 1 (§3).

Legal services in Nigeria

Structure: fragmented, and thin at exactly the volume end. Over 80% of Nigerian law firms are small partnerships or sole proprietorships (UNIZIK Journal of Human Rights Law, 2025); the capable top is Lagos-centric (Chambers Nigeria) and thin in the South-East for volume title work, which is precisely where the Group's land programme sits.

Fees are statutory floors, not a competitive market. The Legal Practitioners (Remuneration for Business, Legal Services and Representation) Order 2023 fixes minimum scales, and Scale 4 — property governs this domain's largest volume of work (Order text; overview):

Scale 4 — purchaser's lawyerMinimum fee
Value below ₦50m10% of value
₦50m–₦100m₦5m on the first ₦50m + 5% thereafter
Above ₦100m₦7.5m on the first ₦100m + 3% thereafter

Three consequences, and the first is why Aku Legal exists as a company rather than a cost line. A ₦300m acquisition carries a purchaser-side floor of about ₦13.5m — the same order of magnitude as the Group's own 5% due-diligence rule, which is why insourcing pays rather than merely appearing to. Fees may not be cut below scale, so this business cannot be won on price; and disbursements sit outside the scale — consent fees, searches, stamp duty — with interest at 10% a year. Anambra's own stack is published: a ₦50,000 application deposit, CGT from ₦50,000 to ₦5,000,000 by parcel band, stamp duty at 0.03% of premium, and a 60-working-day processing period (Anambra Ministry of Lands); confirm the consent fee percentage before modelling [verify].

Why land title is the highest-volume and highest-risk need in this market. Anambra land is largely held under family or communal title with no registered instrument, and is routinely sold twice, sold by a branch of a family without authority, or caught by outstanding probate (53_Aku_Legal.md §1; 59_Okodu_Housing.md §5). Title work is heavily intermediated by non-lawyers (African Journal of Legal Research, 2025), and compliance is permanent — every licence the Group holds needs a calendar, not a per-matter engagement. The market consequence is a demand-rich, supply-poor service: every landowner, developer, estate, cooperative and lender in the South-East faces the same problem — and an unperfected title is precisely what stops the pension and insurance capital described in §2.2 from reaching real assets.

The honest gap: no reliable, current published figure for the size of the Nigerian legal services market in naira was found. [verify] It is not estimated here. The first-ninety-days substitute is the avoided-fee baseline audit — the 90-day audit 53_Aku_Legal.md §7 already requires, which measures what the Group itself currently spends on external counsel, title perfection and compliance. That number is smaller than the market and far more useful, because it is the Group's Year-1 revenue floor and it can be measured rather than guessed.

Private security in Nigeria

Scale: large, licensed, and counted differently depending on who counts. Nigeria's private security industry runs over 250,000 personnel across more than 2,000 licensed companies (Nigeria Private Security Report 2026). Another count puts it at roughly 1,745 licensed private guard companies and over four million guards (New Telegraph), with 893 firms awaiting licences (Newsexpress) and only 50 licences issued in 2025 (NSCDC via The Cable). The two counts differ by roughly 2× on companies and far more on personnel — which is itself the market's defining feature: it is large because it is informal, and it is measured badly for the same reason.

Regulation: restrictive, enforced, and treated as a licence in §5. Private guarding is governed by the Private Guard Companies Act, Cap P30, LFN 2004 — a licence granted by the Minister of Interior through the NSCDC, valid two years, revocable where ownership or control passes to a company unsuitable to hold it (s.4(4)), with every employee requiring approval (s.7) and a bar on any director who is not a citizen of Nigeria (s.13(1)(e)) (Act text). Anambra adds a state registration requirement under the Homeland Security Law 2025, s.7(1), and regulates private outfits so they do not collide with Agunechemba (Law). That combination — a national licence with a citizenship test and a separate state regime — is why §5's acquisition route and its Nigerian-controlled vehicle are not optional.

Why the market is large and poorly professionalised. The sector is manpower-heavy and price-competitive, entered by small firms with no control room, no accreditation and no reporting standard; seven of the top ten ranked operators are Lagos-headquartered, and the South-East is served by small local firms (54_Aku_Security.md §2). The measuring report's own conclusion is that the moat has "moved from muscle to method" — technology, third-party validation and regulatory maturity, not headcount. And a demand shock has just widened that opening: in early 2026 the Nigeria Police Force began withdrawing personnel from private and VIP guard duties, moving thousands of contracts to licensed firms, so security is now simultaneously an operating cost and a compliance requirement (Nigeria Private Security Report 2026; BusinessDay).

The anchor customer is the Group itself — and this is a measured number rather than a market estimate: Nkpor zones A–D, the Idemmili belt, Akuzo, campuses, estates, depots, and a controlled-substance fleet whose diversion would end a licence. No third-party vendor is accountable for a narcotics diversion. Aku Security would be.

The honest gap: no reliable figure for the sector's annual revenue in naira. [verify] The counts above measure companies and guards, not spend. The first-ninety-days substitute is the consolidated vendor schedule — the Group's current security spend across every zone, site and contract, brought into one costed document, which is simultaneously the size of the internal market and the saving consolidation is meant to capture (§12 item 10; the governance half is stood up first under item 9).

Arbitration — a market Africa pays for elsewhere

The law was modernised in 2023; the market has not moved. The Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (26 May 2023) replaced the 1988 Act, adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law, and carries the New York Convention in its Second Schedule with no reservations (Keating Chambers; Legal 500). Four provisions matter commercially:

ProvisionEffect
s.16 — emergency arbitrator reliefA time-critical product the courts cannot match
s.61 — third-party funding permitted; maintenance and champerty abolished, disclosure requiredA funding market that needs administering
s.50 — costs include institutional and appointing-authority costsThe institution's fee is recoverable by statute
s.1(4); s.34(4) — a duty of expedition binding arbitrators, arbitral institutions, appointing authorities and the court; six years to enforce, excluding time in arbitrationA statutory service standard

Nigeria's institutions are few, and their rules are old. CIArb UK Nigeria Branch, LACIAC, the Lagos Court of Arbitration, NICArb and RCICAL — rules dated 2015, 2016, 2018, 2018 and 2019, none under amendment. There is no specialist arbitration court in Nigeria. RCICAL is an AALCO-established, non-profit regional centre, the only institution here with a treaty-derived mandate (Legal 500; AALCO).

And the honest point, which is simultaneously the loss and the opportunity: African commercial disputes are frequently arbitrated elsewhere, under foreign law. Africa hosts over 90 arbitral institutions, yet most African-related disputes are resolved outside the continent — investors and lenders insist on English law and a London seat, and FIDIC construction forms default to an ICC clause seated in Paris (SOAS survey, via Anjarwalla & Khanna). The same source records "a lack of trust in African arbitral institutions, many of which are newly established compared to seasoned entities like the ICC and LCIA." That sentence is this business's risk register in one line — and it is also why the market is contestable: every construction contract, land claim, offtake agreement, insurance claim and joint venture in this Group is a dispute that will be seated somewhere, and today the default answer is London or Paris. The price gap is real — the LCA runs to ₦100,000/hour and ₦800,000/day; RCICAL starts at US$3,000, rising to 7%; the ICC's filing fee is US$5,000, capped at US$180,000 above US$515m; the LCIA bills GBP 190–300/hour (55_Aku_Arbitration.md §7) — but price is not the constraint. Credibility is.

The demand case is the courts. A Nigerian commercial case sits 4 years 2 months in the High Court, 3 years 4 months on appeal and 6 years 6 months at the Supreme Court — nearly 13 years from filing to final judgment (Justice Research Institute, cited by Prof. Yemi Osinbajo, BusinessDay).

The honest gap: no reliable figure exists for the value of disputes that could be seated in Nigeria. [verify] There is no register of arbitrations that were not held. The first-ninety-days substitute is the Group's own contract universe — a counted list, not an estimate: every construction, offtake, supply, insurance and joint-venture contract the five domains have signed, with its dispute clause and its value. That count is the institution's first book of business, and it is the only sizing this market will yield.

2.4 What this section cannot size, and how the first ninety days establishes it

Five figures a reader would reasonably ask for do not exist in reliable, current, published form, and none is invented here:

  1. Nigeria's mid-market private-credit gap in naira. The CPPE's ₦50trn figure is the best available and is a real-sector financing-gap estimate, not a measurement of the credit market; the ~17% of GDP ratio is a banking-system statistic. Neither is a mid-market lending number. [verify]
  2. The value of the African mid-market buyout opportunity by sector. Deal sizes and flows are reported; sector-level pipeline value is not. [verify]
  3. The naira value of Nigeria's legal services market. No reliable published figure was found. [verify]
  4. The naira revenue of the private security industry. Company and guard counts are published; spend is not. [verify]
  5. The value of arbitrable disputes that could be seated in Nigeria. No register exists, by definition. [verify]

The first-ninety-days action that establishes each, and it is one action in four parts (§12 item 10):

  • Measure before estimating. Take the avoided-fee baseline audit (Aku Legal), the consolidated security vendor schedule (Aku Security) and the Group contract universe (Aku Arbitration). Three measured numbers where the market offers none — and all three are the first-year revenue floor rather than a forecast.
  • Read the targets' own books. Diligence on the licensed finance company, the microfinance bank and the licensed private guard company (§12 item 5) produces current, auditable loan-book, deposit and contract revenue for the exact market being entered — better evidence than any market report, and already on the critical path.
  • Buy the primary data once. Subscribe to the AVCA and PenCom datasets the library already cites, and commission one named research house for a Nigerian mid-market credit sizing note. One purchase, one budget line, one deliverable.
  • Start the pipeline record in Year 1. The deal-flow, portfolio and fund-accounting system on Aku Technology (11_Aku_Technology.md) converts the addressable market from an estimate into a list of named companies, with revenue and ownership — which is what an investment committee can act on and an LP can audit.

One boundary to close the section, because it governs what Aku may look at. Nothing in this market section is real estate. Property is Okodu's — Master Plan §6.5 — and Aku's involvement with property is financial and legal: it lends against it, invests in it through funds, perfects title to it and insures it. It does not own or operate it (§3, §7). Aku Markets is likewise not an index or ETF platform, and no part of the market case above depends on passive products.

3. Product & service lines

Akunnia's domain has two halves, and this plan previously developed only one of them. The Holding Structure gives her "Finance & Investment Systems" and "Governance, Law & Security", and the Master Plan §6.2 spells out what the second half means: "The legal and compliance function handles all land title conveyancing, Group contract law, and arbitration. Security coordination for all Nkpor zones is also under her domain, ensuring that the Group's legal framework and physical protection operate as a single integrated function."

The second half is not administrative overhead — it is a business. Title perfection, contract law, dispute resolution and security are all services the Group must buy — land title conveyancing, contract law and arbitration are fee-earning services the Group currently buys externally, and security is a cost it currently pays out — all of them are expensive and poorly supplied in Nigeria, and all of them can be sold to third parties once built. They are also, unlike the funds, capable of earning revenue in Year 1 — which matters enormously for a domain whose flagship businesses need five years before they can raise outside capital. Akunnia's mandate is that these operate as one integrated function, which is a genuine structural advantage: a group whose legal, security and financial functions are unified can move faster on transactions than one where three suppliers must coordinate.

The finance half

Aku Credit — the largest engine. Private credit to African mid-market companies. This is Blackstone's largest segment, and for Africa the case is stronger than anywhere else — bank credit is scarce, expensive and short-tenor. Aku Credit lends at 25–35%: the same rates the Group's own plans complained about as a borrower, now earned as a lender.

Group businesses are the proving ground before third-party lending. Aku Insurance's float and Aku Bank's deposits become the funding base — which is why the bank matters.

Aku Bank — the funding engine. The only part of this platform Blackstone does not have, and in African credit markets it is a structural advantage rather than a nice-to-have. The subsection below sets out the acquisition route.

Aku Private Equity — the mandate

Control buyouts of African companies. This is where "structural development of African industry" becomes operational. Africa's industry is fragmented: hundreds of small furniture workshops, food processors, logistics operators and manufacturers, mostly informal or family-run, with weak management and no access to capital.

The playbook, applied sector by sector:

  1. Consolidate — buy several small operators in one sector and merge them
  2. Professionalise — replace management, install systems, formalise financials
  3. Engineer growth — add capital, capacity and distribution; connect to Group demand
  4. Exit — sell to a strategic buyer, list, or hold in a perpetual vehicle

The Group's own domains are the map: furniture and soft furnishings (a trade the Group already knows), pharmaceutical distribution, food processing, logistics, building materials, media production. In each, the Group can buy the fragmented operators and become the consolidator — precisely what Isiome, Uli and Okodu were designed to do organically, now accelerated by acquisition.

Distressed and special situations are not a separate company. They are a sleeve inside Aku Private Equity and Aku Credit — in Africa, where currency crises and policy shocks regularly dislocate asset prices, the arm that buys when everyone else is selling is a genuine edge — and an earlier draft wrongly capitalised it as a standalone business ("Aku Tactical"). A sleeve needs a mandate and a capital allocation, not a company.

Aku Bank — from microfinance acquisition

The instruction is the right one: buy a licensed microfinance bank, then grow.

Why it works. Nigeria's MFB licence is achievable, the sector is large and fragmented, and many MFBs are under-capitalised and for sale. Buying one provides an existing licence, deposit-taking capability, a customer base, and a regulatory track record. Growing from there — to a state licence, then national — is a capital and compliance exercise with a defined path.

Why the bank matters strategically. A bank is the cheapest funding base in the structure. Deposits fund Aku Credit's loan book at a fraction of the Group's borrowing cost, which transforms the credit economics. Blackstone has no bank; the Group having one is a genuine structural advantage in African credit markets where wholesale funding is scarce and expensive.

2Grow the MFB — deposits, loan book, branch network, systemsYears 2–5

Constraints to respect: CBN capital requirements rise at each tier; the Draft Ring-Fencing Guidelines for Closely Linked Entities (June 2026) would bar linked financial entities from lending to one another, which constrains how the bank and Aku Credit interact; and related-party lending limits will restrict lending to Group companies. The bank must be independently governed, with its own board and a majority of independent directors. The governance half — where the revenue starts in Year 1

Aku Legal — the title and contract business. Land title conveyancing and perfection for every Group acquisition (Governor's Consent on every transaction, with 5% of every land budget held for due diligence — a hard Group rule), corporate and commercial law, contract drafting across all five domains, IP registration, and regulatory compliance advisory.

This is the Group's highest-volume legal need and its highest-risk. Nigerian land title is contested and documentation-poor. A legal capability that perfects title properly is simultaneously a cost saving and the thing that makes land bankable as collateral — which matters to a Group whose entire strategy rests on land acquisition. Once built, title perfection and compliance services are saleable to third-party landowners, developers and institutional investors, who face the same problem with no in-house solution.

Aku Security — the protection business. Manned guarding across the Group's clusters, estates, campuses and industrial sites; the community-integrated surveillance model the Group's own Akuzo plan specifies (a community gateway, a 16-camera CCTV network, solar streetlights with CCTV mounts, night patrols in two shifts, and a youth neighbourhood watch); control room and monitoring; asset-in-transit security; and the specialised handling the Group's controlled-substance logistics requires — two-lock systems, separate keyholders, dual GPS, two-person crews and pre-cleared routes.

The Group's own position is that security is achieved through community integration, not walls — "people protect what they own." Aku Security is the company that delivers that as one system rather than buying guards from three vendors. Private security in Nigeria is a licensed activity and the ownership rules are restrictive — see §5.

Aku Arbitration — dispute resolution. Administering arbitrations and mediations for third parties. The Group will generate disputes at scale — construction contracts, land claims, supply and offtake agreements, insurance claims, joint ventures — and Nigerian courts are slow enough that commercial disputes routinely run for years.

Honest framing, because this one is contestable. There is no licence to buy here; an arbitration institution has no credibility until parties choose it, and a new institution owned by a conglomerate carries an obvious conflict. So the rule is explicit and belongs in the Group's governance manual: Group disputes above a stated value go to independent institutions — never to Aku Arbitration. Aku Arbitration serves third parties, and it is built by recruiting practising arbitrators and retired judges, not by registering a company. It is the slowest of the three governance businesses and should be founded last.

4. Operating model

The global hub — London or New York

This is the structural heart of the restructure, and it inverts how the Group was built. Previously the Group was Nigerian with an offshore holding layer. Under Blackstone, the investment manager sits at a global hub and the assets sit in Africa.

```

EZEME FAMILY TRUST (Mauritius)

│

Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) — GBC

│

EZEME GROUP (Nigeria) — the operating conglomerate

│

▼

AKU MANAGEMENT COMPANY (London or New York) ← the hub

FCA-authorised (London) or SEC-registered (New York)

Employs the deal team; earns fees and carry

│

▼

AKU FUND VEHICLES (Cayman or Delaware LP)

Third-party LP capital + Group anchor capital

│

▼

AFRICAN ASSETS (companies, real estate, credit)

```

Why the manager must be at the hub:

  • Capital is raised there. The LPs who fund Blackstone-scale vehicles are in New York, London, the Gulf and Singapore — not Lagos.
  • Deal talent is there. The professionals who can underwrite a $200m buyout live and work in those markets and will not relocate to Lagos.
  • The prestige is there. "The pinnacle of Wall Street prestige" is a real recruiting asset, and it exists only in those two cities.
  • Financing is there. Leverage for large buyouts comes from global banks and credit funds.

Consequences:

  • FCA authorisation (London) or SEC registration (New York) for the manager. London is likely simpler for an Africa-facing manager; New York carries more prestige and deeper pools.
  • Funds are Cayman or Delaware LPs — standard for alternatives, and the market expects it.
  • The Mauritius GBC remains as the family's holding layer, but is no longer the centre of gravity.
  • Tax: the manager earns fees and carry at the hub; fund and asset-holding vehicles sit offshore; African assets pay local tax. This requires specialist counsel in four jurisdictions simultaneously — the single most complex element of the restructure.

⚠️ This materially worsens the foreign-interest problem already flagged. A London or New York investment manager above Nigerian operating companies is a far clearer case of "representing foreign interest" under NBC Act s.9(1) than a Mauritius trust was. The licence-by-licence ownership audit becomes mandatory rather than prudent, and it may mean licences must sit in Nigerian-controlled vehicles entirely separate from the Aku structure. Resolve this before incorporating the hub company.

The manager, the GP and the capital — three boundaries that make the hub work

The hub is a company, and what it owns matters as much as where it sits (10_Aku_Asset_Management.md §1.2):

  1. The manager manages; the GP owns the carry; Aku Capital owns both. The management company at the hub earns the fee; the GP entities earn the carried interest; Aku Capital holds the GP entities and the Group's own anchor positions.
  2. Aku Capital invests; the manager raises and manages. Group capital on the Group's own balance sheet is not AUM, and is never presented to an LP as third-party capital.
  3. The investment team sits inside the regulated manager, because that is where an FCA, SEC or Nigerian SEC regulator expects discretionary investment decisions to be made and supervised. Where 52_Aku_Private_Equity.md supplies personnel to the funds, the arrangement is a documented advisory or secondment agreement — delegating discretionary authority to an unlicensed group company is a registration event, not a staffing choice [verify the delegation rules with counsel in each jurisdiction].

Day-to-day, the finance half runs the standard sponsor sequence — origination, credit or investment committee, documentation, disbursement, monitoring, recovery — with the underwriting rules, funding sequence and exit routes set out company by company in 51_Aku_Credit.md §4 and 52_Aku_Private_Equity.md §4. The hub does not run the portfolio companies: deal professionals underwrite, negotiate, set strategy and sit on boards; the companies keep their own management and independent boards (52_Aku_Private_Equity.md §8).

The governance half runs on a different operating model

One standard, one file, one incident log. Aku Legal's product is the title file a lender can read — registry and probate searches, survey, vendor authority, kindred resolution, executed deed and registered consent, one file, one owner. Aku Security's product is a single security manual, approved post orders per site and one incident-reporting format across every zone, with guards vetted and paid above the minimum wage because guard complicity, not the perimeter, is how Nigerian sites lose goods. Aku Arbitration's product is a rulebook, a published fee schedule and published duration and cost statistics. None of the three is run as a department: each earns fees, each carries its own board discipline, and all three are bound by the Group's conflict rule — above a stated value, Group disputes go to independent institutions, never to Aku Arbitration (§3). Full operating models sit in 53_Aku_Legal.md §4, 54_Aku_Security.md §4 and 55_Aku_Arbitration.md §4.

A private credit book at 40% debt and 60% equity earns an ROE close to its asset yield, before the leverage that makes lending a business at all. Aku Credit therefore needs a deliberate, documented board carve-out with its own debt/equity cap — not a quiet breach of a Group rule — and the control that replaces the ceiling is a portfolio loss-rate gate, since a 2-point miss on losses costs roughly 30% of ROE, while leverage merely magnifies whatever the loss rate turns out to be. Every other company in this domain stays inside 40%. This is the same distinction drawn in plans/README.md open item 4: Okodu Power's 60% is a genuine breach and must be fixed; Aku Credit's is a category error in the rule.

7. Unit economics

Typical
Management fee1.5–2.0% of committed or invested capital
Carried interest20% of profits above an 8% preferred return

A single mid-size fund illustrates the magnitude. A $300m African buyout fund returning 2.5× over eight years generates ~$450m of profit. 20% carry is $90m, split among six to eight deal professionals — $10–15m each, on top of salary. That is why a talented principal takes an Aku offer over a larger base salary elsewhere.

The governance resolution — and it matters that this is stated precisely. The Group's rule is that no equity is issued above subsidiary level, protecting family ownership. Carry is not equity:

Carry sits at fund level and shares in fund profits. It never touches ownership of Ezeme Group, the five groups, or any operating company. The family retains 100% of the operating conglomerate; partners share in the returns their own funds generate. This gives Blackstone-grade incentives without diluting the dynasty.

The equity-as-currency problem, stated with the same rule. The rule that no equity is issued above subsidiary level has a second consequence that must be decided deliberately rather than discovered in a negotiation: Ezeme Group, Akunnia Group and Aku Capital cannot issue shares to a seller, so listed equity cannot be used as acquisition currency at holdco level. Consideration must be cash, hedged debt, or rollover equity inside the target — and acquisition pace is therefore capped by Aku Capital's own cash generation and borrowing capacity, which makes Aku Bank's deposit base strategically important rather than merely convenient (README.md, "The model: Blackstone, not BlackRock").

The Group as anchor LP. Every Aku fund should carry Group capital alongside third-party money — it aligns interests, proves conviction, and is how the first funds become creditable at all. But the self-limiting rule still applies: no fund above 25% Group-originated assets, stepping to 15% by Year 6. Under Blackstone this matters more, not less, because the temptation to buy the Group's own assets is greater.

Perpetual capital is the strategic prize. Blackstone's greatest innovation was open-ended vehicles — BREIT and BXPE — that raise capital continuously and never have to sell: USD 555.6bn of perpetual capital AUM at 30 June 2026, of which USD 463.0bn fee-earning, 48% of all fee-earning AUM (§2.1). In Africa, where assets are illiquid and holding periods long, a perpetual vehicle is more valuable than it is for Blackstone itself. Target: a perpetual African real-asset vehicle by Year 8–10.

One boundary to state precisely, because an earlier draft of this plan got it wrong. Aku may manage and invest in a real-asset fund. Aku may not own and operate property. The BREIT analogue, if the Group ever builds one, is a fund that holds assets on behalf of its investors and is managed by Aku for a fee and carry — it is not a division of Aku that buys buildings. Ownership and operation of the Group's own property stays with Okodu Group, whose plans cover land, development, housing, letting and estate management. The distinction matters because it decides which balance sheet carries the asset, which regulator has jurisdiction, and whether the Group's returns come from rent or from fees.

8. Organisation

The hub team — and it is a different team from before. Blackstone's model needs deal professionals, not asset managers. First ten hires:

  1. Managing Partner / Head of Aku — deal originator with a track record
  2. Chief Investment Officer
  3. Head of Private Equity — buyout experience
  4. Head of Governance, Law & Security — runs Aku Legal, Aku Security and Aku Arbitration; a senior Nigerian lawyer with regulatory standing
  5. Head of Credit — underwriting and portfolio
  6. Chief Financial Officer — fund finance, LP reporting, carry mechanics
  7. General Counsel — multi-jurisdiction structuring
  8. Chief Compliance Officer — FCA or SEC
  9. Head of Investor Relations — LP fundraising
  10. Head of Portfolio Operations — the operating partners who fix companies

The tenth hire is the one most often missed and most important. Blackstone's returns come from operating improvement, not financial engineering alone. The Group has an advantage here it should exploit: Okodu, Uli, Isiome and Idenze executives can serve as operating partners inside portfolio companies — in-house operational capability no financial sponsor in Africa can match.

Compensation. Base at 60–70% of global-bank equivalents, with carry making the difference. Partners expect carry. Without it the Group hires people who cannot source or execute deals, and the strategy fails at the first step.

The honest ceiling. Africa's entire capital stock is roughly $2 trillion. A $15–25bn platform is therefore a meaningful share of African alternatives flows — and reaching it requires international LP capital, not African. The hub is not optional; it is the precondition.

10. Risks

11. Integration

Under Blackstone the Group's role inverts: it stops being the asset and becomes the acquirer.

Supplies to the funds:

  • Deal flow — proprietary and sector-specific, from five operating domains. The Group's single biggest advantage over financial buyers.
  • Operating partners — Okodu, Uli, Isiome and Idenze executives who can fix what is bought.
  • Group demand — an acquired packaging company or logistics operator immediately has a Group customer, which de-risks the investment.
  • Okodu's construction and materials capability — a portfolio company that needs building or renovating gets it at cost, which no rival bidder can match. The asset stays on Okodu's books; Aku's exposure is financial, not proprietary.

Receives from the Group:

  • Anchor capital for fund one and beyond
  • Insurance float (Aku Insurance) and bank deposits (Aku Bank) as funding for Aku Credit
  • A captive legal, security and dispute-resolution workload — every Group land acquisition, contract and zone is billable work for Aku Legal and Aku Security from Year 1

The flywheel, restated for Blackstone: Okodu and Uli build and operate real assets → Aku Credit lends against African mid-market cash flows, funded by Aku Bank's deposits → Aku Private Equity consolidates fragmented sectors the Group already understands → operating partners from Isiome, Idenze, Uli and Okodu improve what is bought → Aku Legal perfects title and Aku Security protects the assets while they are held → exits return capital and carry → the track record raises the next, larger fund.

And the second flywheel, which costs nothing to start: Aku Legal, Aku Security and Aku Arbitration earn fees from the Group's own unavoidable workload, prove themselves against real disputes and real risk, and then sell the same service to third parties who face exactly the same Nigerian problem — contested land, weak contracts, unmanaged estates — with no in-house answer.

12. First ninety days

  1. Decide the hub: London or New York. This gates everything — authorisation, tax structure and talent pool. London is likely simpler for an Africa-facing manager; New York carries more prestige and deeper capital.
  2. Commission the licence-by-licence ownership audit before incorporating the hub. A London or NY manager above Nigerian operating companies may disqualify the Group from NBC, NACOC and other licences. Resolve this first, not after.
  3. Instruct counsel in four jurisdictions simultaneously — UK or US (manager), Cayman or Delaware (funds), Mauritius (holding), Nigeria (operations and assets). They must draft in coordination, not sequentially.
  4. Design the carry scheme — pool size, vesting, hurdle, clawback, and the firewall keeping carry out of Group equity. This document determines whether the Group can hire deal talent.
  5. Identify the microfinance bank acquisition target and open the CBN change-of-control conversation early. MFB acquisitions take time, and CBN approval is the critical path. In parallel, identify a licensed finance company for Aku Credit and a licensed private guard company for Aku Security — all three are acquisitions, all three sit on the same critical path, and none of them should wait on the hub being authorised.
  6. Map the first consolidation sector. Furniture and soft furnishings is the natural first — the Group already knows the trade, has the workshops and the apprenticeship model, and the sector is exactly the fragmented shape the strategy targets.
  7. Hire the Managing Partner before anything else. In this model the first senior hire is the strategy. Without a credible deal originator the funds cannot be raised and the hub is an empty office.
  8. Set the self-limiting rules as board resolutions — no fund above 25% Group-originated assets, stepping to 15% by Year 6; related-party transactions approved by independents sitting alone; and Group disputes above a stated value to independent arbitration institutions, never to Aku Arbitration.
  9. Stand up the governance half first, because it is the only part that earns in Year 1. Secure the private guard company and the finance company, recruit the legal team, and put Aku Legal to work on title perfection for land the Group is already buying. The finance half needs five years and outside capital; this half needs a licence, a team and a first client — all three of which the Group already has.
  10. Size the market before committing capital to it, because §2 could not. §2.4 names five figures that do not exist in reliable published form, and this action replaces each estimate with a measurement: the avoided-fee baseline audit (Aku Legal), the consolidated security vendor schedule (Aku Security) and the Group contract universe (Aku Arbitration), the current books of the three acquisition targets in item 5, one named research house engaged on Nigerian mid-market credit, and the AVCA and PenCom dataset subscriptions the library already cites. One budget line, five measurements, and a named-company pipeline on Aku Technology from Year 1 — which is what an investment committee can act on and an LP can audit.

Second child's domain plan. Domain corrected to Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security, with real estate removed to Okodu Group where the Master Plan places it (§6.5). Engine model is Blackstone — control, credit and carried interest — not BlackRock. Company plans in this domain: 09_Aku_Capital, 10_Aku_Asset_Management, 11_Aku_Technology, 12_Aku_Markets, 13_Aku_Treasury, 14_Aku_Insurance, 15_Aku_Advisory, 16_Aku_Bank, 51_Aku_Credit, 52_Aku_Private_Equity, 53_Aku_Legal, 54_Aku_Security, 55_Aku_Arbitration. 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md becomes the fund-distribution and LP-relationship arm; 11_Aku_Technology.md becomes internal infrastructure rather than an Aladdin analogue; 12_Aku_Markets.md is reduced or closed — index and ETF products belong to the BlackRock model the Group has rejected.

Plans added after the domain correction take the free slot 16 and then continue from 51; the README.md is the authoritative index and lists every plan in business order.
