09 — AKU CAPITAL

Principal investment and the GP holding company — where the money actually sits

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is the second child's domain — Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security — and her companies take the short form "Aku". See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX: naira is primary throughout; dollar figures are indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026).
GroupAkunnia Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group (the mother company)
HeirAkunnia — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer
EntityAku Capital Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Akunnia Group Ltd
What it isThe principal investment company, and the controlling entity of the finance half: the Group's own capital deployed into control positions, plus the holding company that owns the management company, the GP entities and the Group's stakes in the funds it sponsors
The analogueBlackstone Inc. itself — the corporate entity that owns the manager, holds the GP commitments, sponsors the funds, and consolidates the fee and carry streams
What it is notNot the fund manager (10_Aku_Asset_Management.md). Not a lender (51_Aku_Credit.md). Not an owner or operator of property (Okodu Group).
Horizon15 years, inside a multi-decade ambition. Year 1 = 2027

Status: rewritten. The previous version of this plan was built toward the BlackRock model — passive asset gathering, index products, risk technology licensed to institutions, fee compression as an opportunity, and a USD 14tn AUM target. All of it is withdrawn. The model is Blackstone: control investing, alternatives, private credit, real assets, carried interest. 08_Akunnia_Group.md defines the corrected model and this plan conforms to it. 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md holds the funds and the fundraising machine; this plan is where the money sits.

A planning instrument, not legal, tax or investment advice. Figures marked [verify] must be confirmed with the primary regulator or a named counterparty before money is committed.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Capital is where the money actually sits — the Group's own capital deployed into control positions, and the holding company that owns the management company, the GP entities and the Group's stakes in the funds.

The structure in one picture.

```

EZEME FAMILY TRUST (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → EZEME GROUP (Nigeria)

│

┌───────────────┴───────────────┐

▼ ▼

OPERATING CONGLOMERATE AKU CAPITAL

Isiome · Idenze · Uli · Okodu (principal investment + GP holdco)

(real assets, real customers) │ │ │

│ │ └── Stakes in funds (anchor LP)

│ └── GP entities (carry, skin in the game)

└── Aku Management Company (London / New York)

FCA-authorised or SEC-registered — fees

```

Aku Capital is the Blackstone Inc. analogue, not the Blackstone fund analogue. Blackstone Inc. is the listed corporate entity that owns the management company, holds the GP commitments that LPs demand, sponsors the funds, and consolidates management fees and carried interest into one balance sheet. Aku Capital does the same four things at the scale Africa allows:

  1. It invests the Group's own capital into control positions and bolt-on acquisitions — before any fund exists.
  2. It owns the management company at the hub (London, FCA · New York, SEC) that earns fees on fund capital.
  3. It owns the GP entities that hold the carried interest in the funds it sponsors.
  4. It holds the Group's own stakes in those funds as anchor LP and seed investor.

1.1 The twin balance sheets

This is the single most important distinction in the plan, and conflating the two is how family groups lose discipline.

Operating conglomerateInvestment balance sheet (Aku Capital)
What it holdsFive groups, plants, corridors, land, stock, customersEquity and control positions in companies, GP stakes, fund interests, cash awaiting deployment
Where it sitsEzeme Group (Nigeria) and its operating subsidiariesAku Capital Ltd and its investment subsidiaries
Return profileOperating margin, 8–20% on revenue; slow, cyclical, capital-hungryMultiple on invested capital; lumpy, illiquid, few but large outcomes
LiquidityWorking capital cycles; almost nothing is sellable quicklyEffectively zero liquidity for 3–7 years per position
ValuationDepreciated cost and earningsMarked, and marked conservatively — Level 3, quarterly, independently reviewed
GovernanceLine management, operating boards, a Group executiveAn Investment Committee with ≥1 independent voting member, a written investment policy, an annual allocation envelope
Failure modeA plant that cannot be sold at a profitA balance sheet that funds what the family wants rather than what returns
Who runs itDomain heads and their boardsAkunnia as Chief Investment Officer, with an independent-chaired IC

Why the distinction is load-bearing: the operating conglomerate is valued on what it earns; the investment balance sheet is valued on what it owns and can exit. A Group that treats a control position in a packaging company as "one of our businesses" will hold it forever, put family members in charge of it, and never realise the multiple that justified the purchase. Every Aku Capital position is a financial asset with a stated exit window and a stated return hurdle, even when it sits inside an operating sector the Group knows.

1.2 The benchmark, stated honestly

Blackstone's AUM reached about USD 1.27tn at Q4 2025 (Blackstone FY2025 supplemental, Jan 2026; Benzinga, Jan 2026). Its economic model is 1.5–2.0% management fee plus 20% carried interest above an 8% hurdle, over 10-year closed-end funds and perpetual vehicles, across private equity, real estate, private credit and insurance.

BlackRock (withdrawn)Blackstone (adopted)
What it sellsIndex exposure at 3–15bpsControl and alternatives at 1.5–2% + 20% carry
Flagship engineiSharesReal estate, private credit, private equity
How it growsAUM, passively, at near-zero marginal costDeals, actively, one transaction at a time
The skillDistribution and technologySourcing, underwriting, operating improvement, exits
AUM~USD 14tn~USD 1.27tn
Which one is relevantNoYes

Two calibrations that must be stated, because a careless reading of the benchmark misleads:

  • 1.5–2.0% + 20% is the private-equity-style rate, not Blackstone's blended rate. Blackstone's real-estate and credit vehicles price well below 2%, and its perpetual vehicles price closer to 1.25% on NAV. Assuming USD 1.27tn earns 2% overstates Blackstone's own economics. Aku Capital should plan on 2.0% on committed capital during the investment period for buyout funds, 1.5–1.75% for credit vehicles, and lower on anything perpetual.
  • Aku Capital will never reach USD 1.27tn, and should not plan as though it could. Africa's entire capital stock is roughly USD 2tn (AFC via Nairametrics, Apr 2026). Blackstone manages about two-thirds of the value of everything built on the continent. The honest Year-10 milestone — consistent with 08_Akunnia_Group.md — is USD 15–25bn of assets under management: roughly 1.5% of Blackstone, and a serious African platform. What Aku Capital copies is Blackstone's economics, not its AUM. Moving from 0% of returns coming from other people's capital to a majority coming from it is the entire strategic prize; the AUM number follows.

1.3 What this rewrite withdraws

WithdrawnWhy

The USD 14tn target and the four stages to global managerDeleted. Replaced by the USD 1.27tn Blackstone benchmark and an honest USD 15–25bn Year-10 platform target
Index, ETF and iShares analogues as growth enginesBelong to the rejected model; 12_Aku_Markets.md is reduced or closed
Fee compression as an opportunityIrrelevant to a business earning 2% + 20% on control capital. It is a risk to a passive manager, not to a sponsor
Licensing risk technology to competitorsDeleted. The Group's advantage is deal flow and operating capability, not software
"Scale without headcount"Deleted. Control investing is linear in talented people — every incremental dollar of carry requires underwriters, operating partners and a finance function. Headcount discipline is a cost target, not a strategy

2. Market

2.1 The opportunity is the condition of African industry

Africa's industry is fragmented, informal and under-capitalised. That is not a problem statement — in control investing it is the entry condition for the best returns available anywhere.

EvidenceFigureSource
African pension funds and collective investment schemesover USD 600bn, with under 10% in productive sectors in many marketsFSD Africa, Landscape Report on Africa's Institutional Capital Markets, Jan 2026
African state-owned assets under managementapproaching USD 1tnCNBC Africa
Africa's total capital stockroughly USD 2tnAFC via Nairametrics

— in FGN securities58.07%PenCom Q1 2026

Read together, those figures describe the trade. A continent with USD 2tn of capital stock, whose institutions hold USD 600bn+ and are told by their own regulator to buy alternatives they mostly cannot access, sitting on top of an industrial base that is majority informal, family-run, weakly capitalised and therefore for sale.

2.2 The competitive map for control investing in Africa

Competitor groupExamplesTheir constraintThe opening for Aku Capital
African mid-market PEDevelopment Partners International, Helios, African Capital Alliance, Adenia, Amethis, Metier, Ethos, KasadaPure financial sponsors: they buy, they borrow, they exit. The specific gap: nobody in Africa is simultaneously a control investor and an operating conglomerate. Every rival is a financial sponsor that must buy management capability; Aku Capital owns it already — Okodu's construction and materials capability, Isiome's agri-processing and trading, Uli's logistics and distribution, Idenze's regulated-facility operations. In control investing, the operating partner is the source of returns. The Group has four of them in-house.

2.3 The honest constraints

  • Nigeria's entire pension pool is USD 18.5bn. A USD 15–25bn Year-10 platform cannot be built from Nigerian institutional capital. It requires DFI anchors, pan-African pension capital (South Africa's PIC and GEPF alone are larger than every Nigerian pension fund combined), sovereign funds, and non-African LPs. That is a fundraising problem and it belongs to 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md — but Aku Capital's capital plan must assume it succeeds.
  • African exit markets are thin. Trade sales to strategics and secondary sales to other funds are the realistic exits; IPO exits are rare and getting rarer. Underwriting returns that require an IPO is the most common way African funds disappoint their LPs. Every deal paper must name two credible exit routes, at least one of which is a trade sale or a sale to another sponsor.
  • African acquisition finance is scarce. Leverage of the kind Blackstone uses (4–6× EBITDA from a syndicate of banks) is available in Africa only for the largest transactions and usually in hard currency, which collides with the Group's no unhedged USD debt rule. Assume lower leverage (1.5–3×) and more equity per deal than a US or European comparable, and therefore lower gross IRRs on the same asset quality.
  • The whole African private-capital market raises small numbers. African private-equity fundraising has recently run in the low single-digit billions of dollars a year, across the entire continent [verify against the current AVCA African Private Capital Activity Report]. Blackstone alone raises more in a single year than the African alternatives industry has raised cumulatively. This is the real reason Aku Capital's AUM ceiling is USD 15–25bn and not USD 1.27tn.

3. Product & service lines

Aku Capital has four sources of return and three product lines. They must not be mixed in reporting. The distinction matters because the last two are earned on other people's capital and are therefore not capped by the Group's own balance sheet — which is the entire reason for building the finance half.

3.1 The four sources of return

#SourceWho earns itPaid byCapped byTimingLiquidity

Why 3 and 4 are structurally different from 1 and 2. Sources 1 and 2 are bounded by how much equity the family owns. Sources 3 and 4 are bounded only by how much other people's capital the Group can attract and how well it performs on it. A USD 300m fund earns its manager roughly USD 55m of fees and USD 90m of carry over ten years on a GP commitment of roughly USD 9m — the arithmetic is in §7. To earn the same USD 145m from source 2 at a 3% dividend yield, the Group would need roughly USD 4.8bn of invested equity, which it will not have. That is the case for the fund business, and it is the only case that survives scrutiny.

Boundaries that must be stated, because the Group's rules depend on them:

  • Aku Capital does not lend. Balance-sheet lending is 51_Aku_Credit.md, which needs its own CBN finance-company licence and its own ring-fenced capital. Aku Capital may subscribe for credit-fund interests; it may not write loans.
  • Aku Capital does not own or develop property. Real estate sits under Okodu Group. Aku's exposure to property is financial and legal — it invests in it, lends against it (through Aku Credit), perfects title to it (through 53_Aku_Legal.md) and insures it (through 14_Aku_Insurance.md). It does not hold it. If the Group ever builds a BREIT analogue, it is a fund managed by Aku Asset Management for a fee and carry, holding assets on behalf of investors — not a division of Aku Capital that buys buildings.
  • Aku Capital does not manage third-party money. That requires the licences in 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md and belongs there. Aku Capital is the anchor LP, the GP and the owner of the manager — which is how a first-time manager avoids ever being described to an LP as an unlicensed discretionary adviser.

4. Operating model

4.1 Capital allocation discipline — the rules-based split

The risk that destroys family investment companies is not a bad deal. It is a balance sheet that funds the family's preferences. The control is a written allocation framework, adopted as a board resolution, with the numbers visible:

BucketPurposeIndicative share of the investment balance sheetRule

The five rules that make the framework bind:

  1. Every allocation clears a stated hurdle, in writing, before a term sheet is signed. The reference return is the naira FGN 10-year yield plus 700bps for naira deals, and 12% net in USD for dollar deals (both to be re-set annually by the Group Board against the then-current market) [verify the current FGN curve at each allocation].
  2. The sponsor case is never the base case. IC papers carry three cases; the decision is taken on the base case with no synergy credit, no Group-demand credit above contracted volume, and no exit multiple above the sector's traded comparables.
  3. Named passion assets are ruled out in advance. The board lists the categories the family may not be allowed to buy with Group capital (for example: media assets bought for influence, sports, aviation, anything bought so a family member can run it). Any proposal in a listed category requires the independent directors alone to approve it, and their reasons are minuted.
  4. No deal is approved to which a family member is emotionally attached without a documented dissenting opinion on file. A single independent director can force a second external valuation.
  5. Nothing is allocated that breaks the ring-fence. Funding is ring-fenced per group. Aku Capital does not cross-subsidise another group's capex, and no group's assets are pledged for another's debt. No cross-pledge, ever.
  6. No unhedged USD debt. Any hard-currency obligation is hedged or matched by hard-currency income before drawdown; a hedge that cannot be obtained at a defensible cost means the transaction does not proceed.

4.3 The GP commitment — the skin in the game

When funds are eventually raised, Aku Capital is both the anchor LP and the GP, through GP entities it owns.

  • What a GP commitment is: the GP's own money invested in its own fund, alongside LPs and on the same terms. LPs require it because it is the only structural answer to the question "will you behave like an owner or like a fee collector?" The standard range is 1–5% of total fund commitments: 1–2% for a large established manager, 2–5% for a first-time manager.
  • What it costs: on a USD 300m Fund I at 3%, the GP commitment is USD 9m (₦14.4bn) called over the five-year investment period, typically alongside the LPs' own calls. It is not a fee and not a sunk cost — it is at-risk capital that ranks pari passu with LPs and is returned with the fund's return. If the fund returns 2.5×, the USD 9m comes back as USD 22.5m plus its share of the preferred return.
  • How it is commonly funded, and the trap: many first-time managers fund the GP commitment by waiving part of their management fee (taking fees as invested capital rather than cash). LPs accept this, but insist that a meaningful portion be funded with cash, and that the arrangement be disclosed in the LPA. A GP commitment funded entirely out of fees is the GP investing other people's fee money — it is disclosed, it is accepted, and it is worth less as a signal.
  • What it does to Aku Capital's cash flow: the GP commitment is a pre-funded, drawn-over-time, illiquid obligation with a 10-year horizon. Aku Capital must hold a GP commitment reserve — a segregated liquidity bucket sized to the full uncalled GP commitment across every fund it is sponsoring — that can never be redeployed into a principal deal. A manager without this reserve is one capital call away from defaulting on its own fund, which is the single fastest way to end a franchise.
  • The governance rule, restated where it matters: carry sits at fund level only. It never confers, converts into, or votes any ownership of Ezeme Group, Akunnia Group, or any operating company. The family's rule is that no equity is issued above subsidiary level; carry is not equity, and that is the reconciliation. The family keeps 100% of the operating conglomerate; partners share in the profits of the funds they manage. A GP entity may be partly employee-owned — it is a fund-level vehicle, not a Group vehicle.

4.4 The self-limiting rules

No fund holds more than 25% in Group-originated assets, stepping down to 15% by Year 6. Related-party transactions are approved by the independent directors sitting alone, priced against an external benchmark with an independent valuation on file. Funding is ring-fenced per group. No unhedged USD debt.

Under the Blackstone model this matters more than it did under BlackRock, not less, because the temptation is greater: a principal investor that owns an operating conglomerate will always find that the easiest deal in the market is one of its own assets. The cap is what forces Aku Capital to become a sponsor rather than a family financing vehicle, and no LP, DFI trustee or regulator will engage without it.

4.5 Risk framework and reporting

  • The CRO reports to the Group Audit & Risk Committee, not the CIO, with unrestricted escalation to the Group Board.
  • Limits — single position, sector, country, currency, counterparty, fund-level concentration, GP commitment headroom — are monitored monthly and reported to the IC and the Audit & Risk Committee quarterly.
  • Positions are valued quarterly, and Level 3 and control positions annually by an independent valuer. Aku Capital's own financial statements are IFRS, Big-4 audited, and separately show the twin balance sheets.
  • Custody of fund interests and shares sits where it belongs — with the administrator, the registrar or a third-party custodian — never with a Group entity. Under the SEC's revised regime, a non-bank custodian needs ₦50bn plus 0.1% of assets under custody, so custody is bought, not built (SEC Guidelines on Revised Minimum Capital).

Three negotiating points hidden in that table, and a first-time manager will be asked for all of them:

  • Catch-up is worth USD 28m per fund. With no catch-up at all, the GP receives 20% of the excess over the preferred return only: 0.20 × USD 310m = USD 62m, or 13.8% of profit rather than 20%. A first-time manager will be asked to give up the catch-up, or to accept a 50% catch-up. Expect to concede it on Fund I and recover it on Fund III.
  • Whole-of-fund (European) versus deal-by-deal (American) waterfall. A whole-of-fund waterfall means the GP receives no carry at all until every LP has its capital and 8% preferred return back. It is what DFIs and public pension funds now demand as standard, and it is the cheapest concession a first-time manager can make: it costs the GP nothing if the fund performs, and it is the strongest possible signal that the GP is not harvesting early winners.

The family's rule is that no equity is issued above subsidiary level; carry is not equity. Employee equity, where it exists at all, exists inside operating subsidiaries — nowhere above them.

Under Blackstone the Group's role inverts: it stops being the asset and becomes the acquirer. Aku Capital is the hinge that turns the operating conglomerate's capabilities into investment returns.

Each turn is financed by the one before it; none requires raising outside money before the Group owns something worth financing.

12. First ninety days

  1. Decide the hub: London (FCA) or New York (SEC). This gates authorisation, tax structure, talent pool and fundraising. London is likely simpler for an Africa-facing manager; New York carries deeper capital pools and more prestige.
  2. Commission the licence-by-licence ownership audit before incorporating the hub. A London or New York manager above Nigerian operating companies may disqualify the Group from NBC, NACOC and other licences. Resolve this first — it is the one decision that can invalidate the structure.
  3. Appoint the three independent Group directors and seat an independent on the Investment Committee. Nothing else in this plan completes without them, and no LP, DFI or regulator engages before it is done. Publish the independence criteria and the IC's terms of reference.
  4. Adopt the capital allocation framework as a board resolution — the §4.1 split, the hurdle rates, the passion-asset list, the rule that the sponsor case is never the base case, and the 25%→15% Group-originated cap. This is the document that prevents risk #1.
  5. Design the carry scheme before hiring anyone senior — pool size, hurdle (8%), catch-up, vesting, whole-of-fund waterfall, clawback, and the firewall keeping carry out of Group equity. This document determines whether the Group can hire deal talent at all.
  6. Instruct counsel in four jurisdictions simultaneously — UK or US (the manager), Cayman or Delaware (the funds), Mauritius (the holding layer), Nigeria (operations and assets). They must draft in coordination, not sequentially, before the hub is incorporated.
  7. Hire the Managing Partner, then the CFO. The Managing Partner writes the sector strategy; the CFO builds the GP commitment reserve, the valuation policy and the LP reporting standard. Two hires before any technology spend and before any deal is signed.
  8. Close one partner buyout and one bolt-on inside a sector the Group already operates. The cheapest, fastest, least contestable control transactions available, and the first two data points of the only track record the Group will have for five years. Both are related-party matters if any Group company is involved: independent directors sitting alone, external benchmark pricing, independent valuation on file.
  9. Identify the Nigerian fund-manager acquisition target under the 30 June 2027 deadline and open the SEC conversation early. The recapitalisation deadline means sub-scale managers must raise ₦500m–₦2bn or sell, and buying a registered manager is usually faster than a de novo application. In parallel, open the FCA or SEC-US conversation — authorisation takes 9–15 months and sits on the critical path to Fund I.
  10. Map the first consolidation sector. Furniture, soft furnishings and building materials are the natural first: the Group already knows the trade, has the workshops and the apprenticeship model, and the sector has exactly the fragmented shape a control strategy targets. Name the three acquisition candidates and the exit route for each before any approach is made.

10 — AKU ASSET MANAGEMENT

Fund management and capital formation — the licensed manager and the fundraising machine

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is the second child's domain (Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security), and her companies take the short form of her name — Aku. This entity is Aku Asset Management Ltd (Nigeria) with a sister manager at the hub.

FX: naira is primary throughout; dollar figures are indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026).
GroupAkunnia Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group (the mother company)
HeirAkunnia — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer
EntityAku Asset Management Ltd (CAMA) — a licensed fund manager; plus Aku Asset Management (UK) Ltd or Aku Asset Management (US) LLC at the hub
What it isThe licensed manager of the Group's funds and, in time, third parties' funds — plus the capital-formation machine that raises them. It provides discretionary investment management to blind-pool and perpetual vehicles, and it runs the LP relationships that make those vehicles possible
The analogueBlackstone's fund-management and fundraising engine — the team that closes a USD 2bn African buyout fund and the LP relationships that get it closed
What it is notNot discretionary portfolio management for third parties — no listed-equity, fixed-income or multi-asset mandates. Not the principal investor (that is 09_Aku_Capital.md). Not the GP (the GP entities are owned by Aku Capital)
Horizon15 years inside a multi-decade ambition. Year 1 = 2027

Status: rewritten. The previous version of this plan was built toward the BlackRock model: competing with Nigerian and global asset managers for listed-equity and fixed-income mandates, "scale without headcount", index and ETF products, and licensed risk technology. All of it is withdrawn. The business is fund management — raising and deploying blind-pool and perpetual capital for control investments — and capital formation. 08_Akunnia_Group.md defines the corrected model; 09_Aku_Capital.md is the principal investor and the owner of this company.

A planning instrument, not legal, tax or investment advice. Items marked [verify] must be confirmed in writing with the regulator or with counsel: several figures below are read from press summaries and law-firm flashnotes, not from the instruments themselves.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Asset Management exists to raise blind-pool and perpetual capital for control investments in African industry, and to manage it under licence — because in a Blackstone-model business the ability to raise money is not support work, it is the binding constraint on everything.

1.1 What this company actually is

Two functions, one company:

FunctionWhat it doesWho it servesRevenue
Fund managementProvides discretionary investment management to the funds — sourcing, underwriting, execution, monitoring, exits — under an FCA, SEC or Nigerian SEC registrationThe funds sponsored by Aku Capital; in time, funds sponsored by third partiesManagement fee on committed/invested capital; carry accrues to the GP entities, not here
Capital formationRaises the capital: LP coverage, diligence responses, PPM and side letters, first close, final close, ongoing investor relations and reportingThe same fundsNothing directly — it is the precondition for the fee revenue

Fundraising is not support work. It is the primary constraint on growth — and this must be stated plainly, because it is the single most common error in African fund businesses. The Group's constraint is not deal flow: it owns an operating conglomerate that throws off proprietary transactions. The constraint is LP capital, and the LP market for a first-time African manager is close to closed. An African sponsor with excellent deals and no capital-formation capability has a hobby. An African sponsor with modest deals and a real fundraising machine has a business. The Group should staff this company accordingly — which means the Head of Capital Formation is the first senior hire, not the tenth.

Three boundaries that decide who does what, and the Group must hold them:

  1. The manager manages; the GP owns the carry; Aku Capital owns both. 09_Aku_Capital.md holds the GP entities and the Group's anchor LP stakes. This company earns the management fee; the GP entities earn the carried interest.
  2. Aku Capital invests; this company raises and manages. Group capital on the Group's own balance sheet is not AUM under management here, and is never presented to an LP as third-party capital.
  3. The investment team sits inside the regulated manager, because that is where an FCA, SEC or Nigerian SEC regulator expects discretionary investment decisions to be made and supervised. 52_Aku_Private_Equity.md is the Group's deal-origination and portfolio-operations company; where it supplies personnel to the funds, the arrangement must be a documented advisory or secondment agreement — delegating discretionary authority to an unlicensed group company is a registration event, not a staffing choice [verify the delegation rules with counsel in each jurisdiction].

1.3 The benchmark, stated honestly

Blackstone's AUM reached about USD 1.27tn at Q4 2025 (Blackstone FY2025 supplemental; Benzinga, Jan 2026), on 1.5–2.0% management fees plus 20% carried interest above an 8% hurdle, and it raises in a single year more than the entire African alternatives industry has raised cumulatively.

What that implies, without flattery: the Group's fundraising problem is not a product problem and not a pricing problem. It is an access problem. Blackstone's LPs — US and Canadian public pensions, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments — do not allocate to a first-time Nigerian family manager, at any fee, in any structure, in Fund I. The first funds are therefore raised from DFIs, African institutions and the Group itself, and the platform's USD 15–25bn Year-10 target (per 08_Akunnia_Group.md) is reached only if the Fund I record converts those LPs into repeat LPs and converts non-African LPs into first-time LPs by Fund III. That is a ten-year sales process. It starts in Year 1 and it is this company's job.

The constraint is bankable pipeline, not permission and not appetite. That is precisely the product this company sells: a fund that owns real, operating, cash-generating African companies.

⚠️ The honest sentence this plan owes the family: a first-time manager with no track record will be refused by most of the LP universe, and the refusals will be polite. The funding for Fund I comes from three places that a maiden fund can reach — the Group's own anchor capital, one or two DFIs with a mandate that permits a first-time GP, and a small number of African institutional or family-office commitments — and from nowhere else. Any Fund I plan showing a USD 300m target raised from global institutions is a plan that will not close.

2.3 The consolidation event, and why it is this company's opportunity

PenCom raised the PFA minimum capital to ₦20bn, rising to ₦25bn above ₦500bn AuM, by December 2026 (Punch). Smaller managers will merge or sell.

This creates three things this company can use: a supply of experienced investment and compliance professionals at the cheapest price Nigeria will see for a decade; a supply of orphaned mandates whose owners are being consolidated away; and a market in which the remaining PFAs are larger, under pressure to earn beyond FGN paper, and — critically — have almost no domestic origination capability to spend it on. That last point is the whole opportunity: they have the money, we have the assets.

And the mirror-image event on the manager side: the SEC's revised minimum capital applies to existing operators by 30 June 2027, and new applicants must comply from day one (SEC Guidelines on Revised Minimum Capital for Regulated Entities, 18 March 2026; Nairametrics, 16 Jan 2026; Aluko & Oyebode flashnote). Fund managers who cannot raise ₦500m–₦2bn by that date must sell or surrender. That is the acquisition market this plan is built to exploit — §5.

One honest constraint to close the section. Nigeria's entire pension pool is USD 18.5bn. At ₦1,600/USD, even a USD 1bn fund is larger than 5% of every Nigerian pension asset in existence, and the Year-10 target of USD 15–25bn exceeds the entire Nigerian pension industry several times over. The platform is therefore pan-African and DFI-funded long before it is Nigerian-pension-funded, and it is not reachable from African assets alone — the Year-10 number requires non-African LP capital entering by Fund III. That is the constraint on the entire domain, and it needs to be on the first page of the fundraising deck, not buried on slide forty.

3.2 Why closed-end comes first — and perpetual capital is the prize, but the last one

A perpetual vehicle raises capital continuously and never has to sell. BREIT and BXPE are Blackstone's greatest structural innovation: they convert lumpy, ten-year, fund-cycle revenue into a permanent fee base, and in Africa — where assets are illiquid and holding periods are structurally long — a perpetual vehicle is worth more than it is to Blackstone itself.

But it cannot come first, and the reason is mechanical, not strategic:

  • It needs redemption management — gates, a liquidity sleeve, a subscription/redemption queue, and a valuation process robust enough to survive an investor deciding to leave during a bad quarter. No first-time manager has the credibility to run that, and no investor will trust a new manager's NAV.
  • It needs an existing asset base, because a perpetual vehicle with no income-producing assets has nothing to pay redemptions from.
  • It needs a track record and an existing LP base — realistically, the investors who rolled over from Fund I and II.

Target: a perpetual African real-asset and credit vehicle by Year 10, funded from realised Fund I and II assets, with Group anchor capital and an existing LP base. Before then, closed-end only. A perpetual vehicle launched too early is a liquidity mismatch with a regulator's attention already on it.

4.3 Fund governance — because this is what LPs actually underwrite

  • A Limited Partner Advisory Committee (LPAC) on every fund, with defined consent rights: conflicts, valuation, extensions, related-party transactions, and — critically — the 25%→15% Group-originated cap.
  • An independent valuation policy, applied quarterly, with Level 3 and control positions valued annually by an independent valuer. NAV computation sits with an independent administrator, never the investment team.
  • A named auditor (Big-4 for dollar vehicles), custody with a third-party custodian under tripartite agreement — never a Group entity — and ILPA-template quarterly reporting.
  • A key-person clause naming the individuals whose departure suspends the investment period.
  • A conflicts policy that names the three conflicts this structure creates: (i) the manager's parent is the anchor LP; (ii) the manager's parent is also a potential seller of assets into the fund; (iii) the manager's affiliates are suppliers to portfolio companies. All three are manageable. None of them is manageable undisclosed.

The self-limiting rule, and it is a fund-document term, not an aspiration:

No fund holds more than 25% in Group-originated assets, stepping down to 15% by Year 6. Related-party transactions are approved by the independent directors sitting alone, priced against an external benchmark with an independent valuation on file. Funding is ring-fenced per group. No unhedged USD debt.

And the rule that makes carry acceptable to the family: carry sits at fund level only and never confers, converts into, or votes any ownership of Ezeme Group, Akunnia Group or any operating company. The Group's rule is that no equity is issued above subsidiary level. Carry is not equity — that is the reconciliation. The family retains 100% of the operating conglomerate; partners share in the profits of the funds they manage.

4.4 Distribution and placement — how a first-time African manager actually gets meetings

There is no shortcut and there is no cold-email channel that works. There are five routes, in ascending order of realism:

  1. DFIs, directly and early. IFC, BII, DFC, AFC, Proparco, DEG, FMO, Norfund. Brief them before the fund is marketed — ask what they would need in order to anchor, and build that. Attend the conference circuit where they are: AVCA's annual conference, SuperReturn Africa, the Africa Investment Forum, the IFC and BII LP days, the Africa CEO Forum. A DFI relationship takes 12–24 months and is the single highest-value activity in this company in Years 1–3.
  2. A placement agent. For a maiden African fund, expect 2–5% of commitments raised, and 5–7% for a genuinely first-time manager with no institutional anchor; many agents also require a retainer of USD 50–250k and a defined exclusivity period [verify current market terms — this varies widely by agent and by fund, and should be negotiated, not accepted]. An agent will refuse a mandate it believes it cannot sell, so most agents will decline a maiden African fund unless there is already a named anchor or a genuinely differentiated story. The honest use of an agent is to widen a fundraise that is already working, not to substitute for relationships the manager does not have.
  3. Anchor-first sequencing. Get one DFI anchor of USD 20–50m before marketing broadly. A USD 300m fund with a USD 125m first close (Group anchor capital plus one DFI) is a fund that can be marketed. A USD 300m fund with USD 40m committed is not. Every conversation before the anchor is a warm-up for the conversation after it.
  4. African institutions and family offices, tiered by realistic ticket size: PFAs and insurers for a naira debt vehicle; NSIA, Africa50 and the larger family offices for co-investment and later commitments; diaspora syndicates for co-investment at USD 1–5m tickets.
  5. The Group's own network — bankers, advisers, corporates, and the families the Group transacts with. Slow, personal, and often the source of the first non-DFI commitment.

The honest timeline: first-time fund closes commonly take 18–24 months from the first LP meeting to the final close. Budget:

  • Months 0–6: documents, track record pack, anchor DFI conversations, internal Group anchor commitment approved.
  • Months 6–15: anchor diligence (5–9 months of E&S, ABC, legal and investment diligence for a DFI), first close at USD 100–150m.
  • Months 15–24: marketing to core LPs against the anchor, second and final close at USD 300m.
  • Expect 30–50 qualified LP conversations for every commitment [verify], and expect the first six rejections to be about the absence of a track record, not about the fund.

5.2 The principle, and the two rules that govern it

In London and Lagos alike, an existing authorisation is usually faster to buy than to obtain, and occasionally cheaper — because the incumbent is sub-scale, the de novo queue is long and uncertain, and an existing firm brings staff, systems, an audit history and a regulatory record that a new applicant must build from nothing. Every licence in this domain asks the acquisition question first.

But two rules govern the acquisition route, and breaking either is worse than waiting:

  1. Never buy a regulated entity without full diligence on its legacy conduct. A manager with a past client-money issue, an unresolved complaint, an SEC or FCA enforcement history, or unauthorised business on its record is a liability with a licence attached. The regulator will make you own the history.
  2. Never assume the target's permissions cover the new business. Buying an authorised manager does not authorise a different activity — the variation of permission is the substantive application, and it can be refused.

And the deadline that shapes the Nigerian side: 30 June 2027. The recapitalisation requirement forces every sub-scale registered fund manager to raise ₦500m–₦2bn, merge or sell. That is a live acquisition market with a hard date on it, and the Group should be in it in Year 1 — not because the licence is the business, but because a registered manager with a fund book, a compliance history and a team is five years of standing the Group does not have to buy with time.

Two figures in the ladder above are now verified from the primary source. The SEC's Guidelines on Revised Minimum Capital (18 March 2026), Annex V state the tiers as Tier 3 PE Fund Manager ₦500m · Tier 2 limited scope ₦2bn · Tier 1 Level 1 ₦5bn · Tier 1 Level 2 ₦10bn, and §1.4 confirms the 30 June 2027 deadline for existing CMOs with new applicants complying from 16 January 2026 (SEC).

Two cost realities that first-time managers consistently get wrong:

  1. Fund formation costs are borne by the fund, not the manager — but only up to a cap.   2. Placement fees are paid by the manager, not the fund. Decision rule: do not launch a fund with a target below USD 250m. A sub-scale fund consumes the same compliance, legal, audit and LP-relations cost as a large one and produces a firm too thin to execute control transactions. If the market will not support USD 250m, the answer is a sector vehicle at USD 500m–1bn in a credit strategy where PFAs and insurers are natural buyers — not a small buyout fund.

7.3 Cost-income and why this is not a mandate business

Cost-income ratio is the wrong primary metric here, because there is no third-party AUM to scale against — there is committed capital. The metrics that matter:

And the comparison that justifies the whole structure. A USD 300m fund produces roughly USD 44–47m of fees and USD 90m of carry to the Group over ten years — about USD 135m — on a GP commitment of USD 9m and a firm cost base of roughly USD 40m. To earn the same USD 135m from the Group's own operating businesses at a 3% dividend yield would require roughly USD 4.5bn of invested equity the Group does not have. Fee and carry income is earned on other people's capital, is not capped by the Group's own balance sheet, and is limited only by how much capital this company can raise and how well the funds perform. That is the entire reason this company exists — and it is why fundraising is the binding constraint rather than a support function.

8. Organisation

The first ten hires, in order — and the first one is the one most often made tenth.

  1. Head of Capital Formation — the LP-facing leader. In a Blackstone-model business this is the highest-leverage hire in the company, and it should be made before the CIO. Recruit from a placement agent, a DFI's fund-investment team, or an established African GP's IR function — someone who already knows the DFI committees personally.
  2. Managing Partner / CEO — deal originator with a closed control-transaction record and the standing to sit across from a DFI investment committee.
  3. Chief Investment Officer — strategy, underwriting standards, investment committee discipline.
  4. CFO — fund finance, capital-call mechanics, carry and waterfall modelling, LP reporting, valuation policy.
  5. General Counsel — multi-jurisdiction fund documentation, side letters, LPA negotiation; the person who reads every word an anchor sends.
  6. Chief Compliance Officer — FCA, SEC and Nigerian SEC; marketing compliance; AML/CFT; the function whose failure ends the franchise.
  7. Chief Risk Officer — reports to the Audit & Risk Committee, not the CIO, with unrestricted escalation to the board.
  8. Head of Investor Relations & LP Reporting — ILPA reporting, quarterly packs, the LP meeting, and the discipline of never surprising an LP.
  9. Head of Portfolio Operations — value creation inside portfolio companies, using Group operating partners from Isiome, Idenze, Uli and Okodu.
  10. Head of Valuation & Fund Administration Oversight — the independent check on the deal team's marks and on the administrator.

The flywheel, restated for this company. Group capital buys and stabilises the first control positions → this company turns that audited record into a fundable track record → a DFI anchors Fund I → the anchor makes African institutional LPs and a second DFI possible → Fund I deploys into sectors the Group already understands, with Group operating partners improving them → exits return capital to LPs and carry to the GP → the record raises Fund II at double the size, with the first non-African LP → Fund III brings global institutional capital → a perpetual vehicle converts the whole thing into a permanent fee base. Each turn of the flywheel is financed by the one before it, and the constraint at every turn is the same: the ability to raise money.

12. First ninety days

  1. Hire the Head of Capital Formation before the CIO. This inverts the conventional order and it is correct: the constraint is LP capital, not deal capability, and the Group already owns deal flow. Recruit someone who has closed DFI and African institutional commitments personally.
  2. Build the LP coverage plan — every target LP named, tiered and owned. Anchors (DFIs), core (Nigerian PFAs and insurers, NSIA, Africa50), co-investors (family offices, diaspora). For each: what they can buy, what they need, who owns the relationship, next action, date. A live document reviewed monthly, starting now.
  3. Adopt the self-limiting rule and the carry firewall by board resolution — before any fund is documented. 25% → 15% Group-originated by Year 6; related-party transactions approved by independents sitting alone; carry at fund level only, never conferring ownership of Ezeme Group or any operating company; carry is not equity. Funding ring-fenced per group; no unhedged USD debt.
  4. Decide the hub and instruct counsel in every jurisdiction simultaneously. UK or US (the manager), Cayman or Delaware (the funds), Mauritius (the holding layer), Nigeria (the manager and the assets). They must draft in coordination, not sequentially. And commission the licence-by-licence ownership audit before incorporating the hub — a London or New York manager above Nigerian operating companies may disqualify the Group from NBC, NACOC and other licences.
  5. Open the DFI relationships early and honestly. Brief IFC, BII, DFC and AFC before anything is marketed. Ask what they would need in order to anchor, and build that rather than guessing. Note the honest distinction: InfraCredit provides guarantees, not LP capital — treat it as a credit-enhancement partner, not an anchor LP.
  6. Identify the Nigerian fund-manager acquisition target under the 30 June 2027 recapitalisation deadline, and in parallel identify a small FCA-authorised manager for the variation-of-permissions route. In London and Lagos, buying a registered or authorised manager is usually faster than de novo authorisation and occasionally cheaper. Both sit on the critical path to Fund I and neither should wait on the hub.
  7. Write the three documents a DFI reads before a track record: the valuation policy, the conflicts policy (naming all three structural conflicts in §4.3), and the E&S management system aligned to the IFC Performance Standards. Appoint the independent administrator and identify the custodian. Register for SCUML and write the AML/KYC and beneficial-ownership policy.
  8. Confirm the Group anchor commitment to Fund I in writing, and fund the GP commitment reserve. A fundraise cannot start without a named anchor; the Group is the anchor in Fund I, and the GP commitment reserve is the first thing a DFI diligence team will check exists.
  9. Model the waterfall, the J-curve and the fee base before a single LP meeting. Three cases — USD 250m, USD 300m and USD 500m — each with the concession case (no catch-up, anchor fee discount, 100% fee offset) modelled alongside the headline case. Do not go to market with a plan that only works on the optimistic terms.
  10. Inventory and independently value the Group's investable pipeline across all four domains, ranked by bankability, not ambition. Fund I is seeded from this list or not at all — and everything on it that originates inside the Group counts against the 25% cap.

11 — AKU TECHNOLOGY

Internal group technology: consolidation, portfolio monitoring and the mechanism of control

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is the second child's group (Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security); her companies take the short form "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Do not compare dollars across plans.

Status: replaces the BlackRock-oriented version of this plan. The previous version built Aku Technology as an "Aladdin analogue" — a risk and portfolio platform to be licensed to competitors, central banks and sovereign funds, on the argument that software revenue scales without headcount. That ambition is withdrawn in full. Blackstone does not sell risk software; it buys companies. There is no software product, no competitor licensing, no multi-tenant SaaS revenue line, and no market-sizing of "addressable African software spend."
GroupAkunnia Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group
HeirAkunnia — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer
EntityAku Technology Ltd (CAMA)
NatureInternal infrastructure, operated as a company — not a business with external customers
CustomersThe Group's own businesses — all five domains, every subsidiary, the funds, and the family office
PurposeTo make control investing possible at scale
HorizonYear 1 = 2027; fifteen years

Status of figures: a planning instrument, not legal, tax or investment advice. Items marked [verify] must be confirmed with the regulator or vendor before money is committed. Almost all enterprise software pricing in this document is not published by vendors — where that is so, the plan says so and gives the basis for the estimate rather than inventing a number.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Technology exists because a control investor buys companies and then has to govern, monitor and improve them — and none of that is possible without numbers the buyer can trust, in one place, on a fixed calendar.

The model correction, stated plainly. The previous version of this plan was the Aladdin analogue: a portfolio and risk platform built for the Group's own book and then licensed to the institutions the Group competes with, with the argument that "only two things in asset management scale without hiring in proportion to assets — index scale and licensed risk technology," and the evidence that Aladdin alone earns BlackRock roughly USD 1.7bn a year (Cinco Días, June 2026). That is a fact about BlackRock, and it belonged to the model the family has rejected. Blackstone's roughly USD 1.3trn of alternatives AUM is earned from 1.5–2.0% management fees and 20% carry above an 8% hurdle on capital it controls — not from licensing software at software margins. Blackstone does not sell technology. Neither does Aku Technology.

Why this matters more under Blackstone, not less. A passive manager can be indifferent to what its holdings do. A control investor cannot. The moment the Group owns a company outright, it inherits the obligation to run it — and the ability to run it is a function of what it can see:

What the Group must be able to do, on day one of every acquisitionWhat it requiresWhat breaks without it
Govern the company it just boughtConsolidated financial reporting across dozens of entities that keep books in different systems, on different calendars, in different currenciesThe board approves accounts it cannot verify
Monitor performanceA portfolio dashboard showing each company's revenue, margin, cash and covenant headroom, monthlyUnderperformance is discovered at the following year's audit
Improve what it boughtKPI visibility against the value-creation plan signed at closingThe operating thesis is a document, not a management system
Underwrite the next dealA deal pipeline and diligence repository with comparable-company and precedent-transaction evidenceEvery deal is priced on the seller's numbers
Report to LPs and compute carryFund accounting that produces NAV, IRR and the carry waterfall correctlyA fund whose waterfall is computed wrongly is in breach of its own agreement with its LPs
Answer to the family, the board and the auditorsConsolidated Group reporting that reconciles the Mauritius holding chain to Nigerian operationsThe family cannot see what it owns

Blackstone's real lesson here is not product — it is that operational data is the mechanism of control. Blackstone's returns come from buying well and then actually improving what it bought, and improvement is impossible without a monthly, comparable, credible view of every portfolio company. Technology is how a financial buyer becomes an operating owner. That is the thesis of this plan, and it is a cost-of-control thesis, not a revenue thesis.

What Aku Technology is, therefore. A company-owned internal technology function — incorporated, with its own board, budget and service obligations — whose only customers are the Group's own businesses. It runs the systems, owns the data architecture, and goes into every newly acquired company within days of completion to find out whether the numbers are true.

⚠️ The honesty problem this plan must confront first, because everything else depends on it. Nigerian mid-market companies — including the ones the Group intends to acquire — keep poor records. Books are often spreadsheets. Invoices and receipts are frequently unnumbered. Inventory is counted by eye. Bank reconciliations run months behind. And sometimes there are two sets of books: one for the tax authority and one for the owner. This is not a slur on Nigerian business; it is the normal condition of an informal, cash-heavy, credit-constrained economy in which formalisation is expensive and enforcement is uneven.

The consequence is the single most important operational sentence in this plan:

The first technology task after any acquisition is not installing software. It is making the numbers true.

An ERP installed over false numbers produces false numbers faster and more expensively. A dashboard built on un-reconciled ledgers is a confidence trick the Group plays on itself. So the sequence is: establish truth, then systematise. Never the reverse — and §4 sets out the 90-day process that does exactly that.

What Aku Technology is not. It is not a software vendor, it does not license anything to anyone, it does not serve external customers, it does not compete with Aladdin, and it is not valued on a multiple. It is judged on one thing: when the Group buys a company, how fast can it see that company's true numbers, and how reliably? A private equity firm that cannot see its portfolio's numbers cannot manage it — and everything in this plan is subordinated to fixing that.

2. Market

There is no external market, and the previous plan's market section is deleted because it measured one that does not exist. The withdrawn "$10–25m addressable African software spend" was a sizing of a software market the Group is not in. The relevant market is internal demand, and it is measurable.

Read that table twice, because it is the argument. The only line with no vendor is the last one — and it is the line the entire strategy depends on. Every acquired company arrives with untrustworthy numbers, and there is no product to buy that fixes them. That is the case for a permanent internal capability, and it is the strongest argument in this plan.

What is genuinely uncertain, and flagged. No verified figure exists for what a Nigerian private-equity or buyout firm spends on technology per professional, and this plan does not assert one. Establishing that benchmark — from comparable African fund managers, from the Group's own current spend across five domains, and from fixed quotes — is a first-ninety-days task, and the capital figures in §6 should be revised against it.

The three things that genuinely must be built — and no more

A build case is a claim on scarce engineering capacity. Three claims survive scrutiny:

  1. The Group reporting and consolidation layer above the bought engine. No vendor models Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Holdings (Mauritius) GBC → Ezeme Group Nigeria → five groups → operating companies, with a London or New York management company above Cayman or Delaware fund vehicles alongside it. The engine consolidates; the mapping, the intercompany elimination logic, the management-company-to-fund-to-asset relationships and the Group's own reporting pack are ours.
  2. The naira-first control and regulatory-reporting layer. Local chart of accounts, naira as the functional currency with dollar and other reporting views, IFRS accounts reconciled to Nigerian tax, and the SEC, PenCom and NAICOM reporting templates that the Group's own regulated companies must file. 08_Akunnia_Group.md §5 makes clear how many licences the Group will hold; each one files a return, and each return is a template someone must maintain.
  3. The management-accounts normalisation process and its tooling. The repeatable method that turns an acquired company's spreadsheets, dual books and un-reconciled ledgers into a standard monthly pack in under 90 days. This is a process asset with a small amount of software around it — a fixed chart-of-accounts mapping, a fixed data template, a reconciliation checklist and an exception log. It is the most valuable thing Aku Technology will ever build, because it is the thing no vendor sells.

The one calculation the Group must never get wrong

A fund's carried-interest waterfall is a contractual obligation, and the vendor's default model will not match the Group's LP agreement. Three facts decide whether the engine can be configured to the Group's terms or must be forced:

TermMarket practiceSource
Whole-fund (European) or deal-by-deal (American)85% of surveyed European funds use a whole-fund waterfall, with hybrid structures at 12%; 64% of surveyed North American funds use deal-by-deal, against 36% whole-fundProskauer, Under the Microscope, June 2026
Carry20% applies to 77% of surveyed North American fundsas above
Hurdle8% appears in 89% of the sample — but note that ILPA's Principles prescribe methodology, not a rate; 8% is market practice, not a standardas above; ILPA Principles 3.0, June 2019
Catch-up100% GP catch-up is common; 50/50 is more common in real estate. The arithmetic is fixed: with a 20% carry rate, the catch-up equals the preferred return ÷ 4 — so on a worked example of USD 80m of LP capital and USD 6.4m of 8% preference, the GP catch-up is USD 1.6m, after which profits split 80/20Alter Domus worked example; CMS
Escrow and clawback60% of surveyed European funds use no escrow; those that do most commonly escrow 50% of carry. ILPA's stated best practice is an "all capital back" waterfall, clawback disclosed every reporting period, gross of taxes paid, settled within two years of recognition, with joint and several liability and a NAV coverage test of at least 125%Proskauer; ILPA

The instruction to Aku Technology is therefore narrow and absolute: buy a fund-accounting engine with a configurable waterfall, map the LP agreement line by line against it before Fund I's first close, and have the mapping signed off by the Group CFO and outside counsel. Do not build a waterfall. Do not accept a vendor's "standard" waterfall without a written reconciliation to the LPA. A waterfall computed on the wrong convention is not an accounting error — it is a breach, and it is discovered by an LP, not by an auditor.

Everything else is purchased. Any proposal to build outside these three should be refused by default and required to argue why no vendor can be bought, configured, or hired to deliver it.

4. Operating model

4.1 A company with one customer group

Aku Technology is an incorporated company with its own board, its own budget and service-level obligations to every Group business. It runs on an internal charge-out model: each Group company is charged for the systems it uses and the support it receives, at cost plus a stated margin, so that consumption is visible and no Group business is subsidised by another without a decision.

Three service modes.

ModeTriggerWhat it does
RunAlwaysOperate the platforms; maintain the close calendar; produce the Group consolidation; keep the portfolio dashboard current; keep the systems secure and available
ChangeGroup or domain initiativeImplement a new system, migrate an entity onto the consolidation layer, extend a dashboard, integrate an acquisition
ResponseAn acquisition completesThe 90-day data truth process (§4.3), run by a standing team that does nothing else

4.2 Architecture principles

  • Buy commodity; integrate everything. Ledger, identity, storage, observability, consolidation and fund accounting are adopted. Nothing is written that a vendor already does well.
  • One entity model, one chart of accounts, one reporting calendar, one source of truth per data element. Every reconciliation problem in a conglomerate traces back to having two of something.
  • The Group owns the data. Contractual data ownership, portability and export in open formats in every vendor agreement, with escrow or export rights on termination.
  • Ninety-day absorber, not a twelve-month programme. An acquisition must be posting into the consolidation layer within one quarter.
  • Security by default. Least-privilege access, hardware-key multi-factor authentication, encryption at rest and in transit, segmented environments, and an append-only, tamper-evident audit trail — hash-chained to write-once storage so that not even an administrator can silently alter history, with four-eyes control on every material entry and retention of at least seven years [verify against SEC, PenCom and NDPC requirements].
  • No single-vendor dependency on the consolidation layer. The balance sheet of the Group must not be reconstructible only from one company's cloud.

4.3 The acquisition playbook — 90 days to true numbers

This is the operational heart of Aku Technology, and the reason it exists as a company rather than as an IT department. On completion of any acquisition, a standing team deploys. The sequence is fixed.

DaysObjectiveWhat actually happensFailure mode it prevents
0–7Control the perimeterTake custody of the accounting system, the bank mandates and the bank portals; dual authorisation on every payment; image every physical ledger, invoice file and contract; freeze the ERP or accounting software from unilateral changes; interview the finance staff separatelyThe seller keeps making payments after completion; records "go missing"
7–30Establish the cash truthBank reconciliation to the last statement for every account; physical cash count; confirm receivables directly with debtors and payables with creditors rather than trusting the ledger; reconcile loans and their covenant positions to the facility lettersCash is the one number that cannot be argued with. Everything else is reconciled to it
30–60Rebuild the ledgerMap the acquired chart of accounts to the Group's; rebuild the prior-year opening balances; identify and quantify the second set of books where one exists; quantify the tax exposure and take advice; restate inventory by physical count, not by ledger; reconcile fixed assets to sightA dual-books company carried into the Group's consolidation contaminates the Group's accounts and the audit
60–90Make the numbers recurringIssue the first monthly management pack the board can rely on; set the close calendar; load the company into portfolio monitoring with the value-creation KPIs and the covenant schedule; load the historic figures into the deal archive; go live on the consolidation layerThe company is consolidated but unmonitored; the operating thesis is never measured

Two rules make this work. First, the acquisitions team does not do this work — reporting to the deal team creates the incentive to find what the deal wanted to find. The team reports to the Group CFO and the Audit & Risk Committee. Second, a company that fails the 60-day reconciliation does not get a dashboard; it gets a remediation plan and a hold on Group funding. The dashboard is a privilege that truthful accounts earn.

4.4 Data residency and the Group's technology independence

The family's documents show a deliberate preference for controlling its own infrastructure, and that preference is not irrational: the Group's data is the map of what the family owns, what it is buying, and what it plans to sell. It is simultaneously the most valuable and the most sensitive dataset in the Group.

It must, however, be stated precisely, because the preference has a cost and the cost is not evenly distributed.

Nigeria does not impose general data localisation, and this must be said precisely because it is widely assumed. The NDPA permits cross-border transfer under an adequacy decision, an approved cross-border transfer instrument, or another lawful basis under ss.41–43, provided the basis is documented and a transfer impact assessment is performed. But four specific localisation mandates do bite:

  1. Payment transaction data — 1 January 2027 (above).
  2. BVN data must be stored within Nigeria, and BVN use is limited to licensed financial institutions for KYC purposes.
  3. Domestic POS and ATM transactions must route exclusively through local switches — routing abroad is expressly prohibited.
  4. Sovereign data — government-generated or government-controlled data — must be stored exclusively in Nigeria, with cross-border transfer only after local storage and with NITDA's express approval. [This last one rests on law-firm analysis of NITDA's Content Development Guidelines; the primary instrument was not retrievable during preparation — verify it]

And one rule that closes off the easy answer. The GAID expressly states that "profit and personal business/organisational development considerations" do not constitute a lawful basis for cross-border transfer. Convenience is not a basis. Every offshore arrangement in this plan needs a documented legal basis, a transfer impact assessment, and a register of the transfers relying on it.

⚠️ A second deadline that is already in the past, and that affects the Group's storage business rather than its IT. The SEC circular of 11 May 2026 gave operators 90 days — to about 9 August 2026 — to register as collateral management companies, warehouse operators or warehouses, and stated that "current operations do not amount to automatic registration or an exemption." For the Group this is a capital and governance requirement — ₦500m for a warehouse operator, three sponsored individuals, a 20%-of-capital fidelity bond — not an IT one, and it belongs in 51_Aku_Credit.md and 05_Isiome_Storage.md. It is repeated here only because the e-receipt system that must follow it is a build case in §3.

The honest instruction to the family. The preference is affordable for the Group's own controlling data and unaffordable everywhere. Self-hosting the consolidation layer buys real independence at a real price. Self-hosting the ERP of every operating company buys nothing and costs a great deal. The boundary should be drawn at "data that tells the family what it owns", hosted on the Group's own controlled estate, and "data that runs a business", bought wherever the best system lives — with the regulatory mandates above sitting outside that boundary entirely, because they are not a choice.

4.5 Governance

Aku Technology has its own board, including at least two independent directors, and reports to the Akunnia Group CEO with a dotted, non-negotiable line to the Group Audit & Risk Committee for audit trail integrity, access control and the truthfulness of reported data. The person who runs the technology function must not be the person whose compensation depends on the portfolio looking good — which is precisely why the 90-day team in §4.3 reports to the CFO and the Committee, not to the deal team.

5.3 The acquisition route — buying a small Nigerian software or IT services firm

The instruction is to state the acquisition route for every licence. Here it applies not to a licence but to capability, and it is the fastest route to the engineering capacity this plan assumes.

Why buy rather than hire. Recruiting engineering one-by-one in Lagos is slow and uncertain: the competition is fintech (Paystack, Flutterwave, Moniepoint), bank in-house teams, and global remote employers paying in dollars, which sets the ceiling on any naira salary. A twelve-person engineering team recruited individually realistically takes 9–18 months and suffers attrition during the build. Acquiring a 15–30 person Nigerian software or IT services firm delivers the whole team on completion, plus something recruiting cannot buy: existing vendor relationships, an existing enterprise or government reference list, and a delivery process that already functions.

The method, because the number does not exist off the shelf:

  • Build a proprietary comparables set from the two NGX anchors above, apply a documented discount for private illiquidity, customer concentration and key-person dependency, and have the board record the discount it chose and why. No published Nigerian discount factor exists.
  • Commission a valuation from an SEC-registered or NIESV-registered valuer, and require a replacement-cost cross-check as well as a DCF — because Nigerian IT-services revenue is people-driven (₦268m of revenue per employee at the CWG end), replacement cost is unusually meaningful here. The check is: what would it cost to hire this team, acquire these contracts and rebuild this delivery capability?
  • Where the target is loss-making (common), the price is net asset value plus a key-person retention package, not a multiple. Most of the real cost is retention, not consideration: the engineers are the asset and they can leave.
  • Negotiate the terms that move the number, not just the headline: the recurring-versus-project revenue mix is the single largest value driver in services businesses, and customer concentration and churn compress value materially. Structure the consideration as earn-out and deferred payment tied to post-completion revenue and retention, because an unverifiable price is best paid in instalments.
  • Test the economics against the alternative: total acquisition cost ÷ headcount acquired versus 12 months of fully loaded salaries plus recruiter fees plus the delay cost of a 9–18-month build. On most plausible inputs the acquisition wins decisively on time and roughly breaks even on money — and it is the only route that produces a functioning team inside one financial year.

The boundary, stated because it is easy to lose. Aku Technology is not a software business and must not become one by accident. If the acquired firm carries external clients on completion, the plan is to (a) retain and service them under a hard time-box of 36 months, (b) charge the Group's own work at arm's length value, and (c) run the boundary rule: no external client work may delay a Group acquisition, close or reporting cycle. The day external revenue starts driving internal priorities, the acquisition has failed — because an internal infrastructure function which becomes a services business rebuilds exactly the conflict the model correction was meant to remove.

The recommended route, requirement by requirement — and the costed first ninety days. 5.4 The ownership audit, which is not optional

08_Akunnia_Group.md §4 flags that a London or New York investment manager above Nigerian operating companies is a far clearer case of "representing foreign interest" under NBC Act s.9(1), that the licence-by-licence ownership audit is mandatory rather than prudent, and that some licences may need to sit in Nigerian-controlled vehicles entirely separate from the Aku structure. Aku Technology sits underneath that decision, because it will hold the data and run the systems of entities holding NBC, NAFDAC, NUC, NACOC, CBN and NSCDC licences. Any data-sharing or service arrangement across the ownership boundary must be lawful under each licence — and the audit must be complete before the hub company is incorporated.

12. First ninety days

  1. Write the 90-day acquisition playbook before the first acquisition, not after it. The reconciliation checklist, the chart-of-accounts mapping template, the data template and the exception log are the Group's most valuable process assets, and the first deal will move faster than the first plan expects. Appoint the response lead and have the kit ready.
  2. Hire the Group CTO and the Head of Financial Systems first. These two roles decide everything else. The CTO must have run regulated multi-entity financial systems; a consumer-product or infrastructure engineer will build the wrong thing.
  3. Write the requirements from the Group's own close process, not from vendor demos. Ask, in writing: what must each of the five groups report, how often, from which systems, who signs it, and what has failed in the last two closes. A vendor demonstration is a demonstration of the vendor's product, not of the Group's need.
  4. Run the buy-versus-build decision once, formally, for all six systems. Issue an RFP covering consolidation, portfolio monitoring, fund accounting and the deal repository; obtain quotes priced at 90 entities and 10 fund vehicles, not at current size; and record the three build cases and the refusal of everything else as a board resolution. The per-entity pricing model is the single most important term negotiated in this plan.
  5. File the NDPC registration and appoint the DPO in month one, and scope the first CAR. Register as a Data Controller/Processor of Major Importance — remember that the "commercial ICT services" limb captures Aku Technology by category, regardless of data-subject counts; establish the cross-border transfer basis and Transfer Impact Assessment under NDPA ss.41–43 for the Mauritius and offshore fund structure; and assume the first CAR is due 15 months after establishment, not the following March. Grace periods on data protection in Nigeria are over, enforcement is active, and the penalty is up to 2% of gross revenue or ₦10m, whichever is higher.
  6. ⚠️ Obtain the CBN's payment-data localisation circular and test whether it binds the Group — this is a Year-1 deadline, not a Year-5 one. The circular of 15 June 2026 requires payments transaction data generated in Nigeria to be stored and managed in Nigeria by 1 January 2027, and "managed" reaches backups, database administration, access control and encryption-key management even where performed offshore or by offshore personnel. Determine which Group companies are payment participants — Aku Bank and Aku Credit are the obvious candidates — and build local hosting capacity and vendor-contract terms for them now. [The CBN's own PDF was not retrievable during preparation; obtain the primary text before designing the architecture.]
  7. Decide the hosting boundary and write it down, using the rule in §4.4: the data that tells the family what it owns sits on the Group's controlled estate; the data that runs a business is bought wherever the best system lives; and the statutory localisation mandates sit outside the choice entirely. Cost both, and put the numbers to the board — the family's independence preference is affordable at one layer and expensive at another, and it should be a decision rather than a default.
  8. Start the deal pipeline and precedent-transaction archive immediately, even on a spreadsheet. It is the one system with no licence, no vendor and no implementation delay, and Aku Private Equity needs it on the first transaction.
  9. Open a confidential capability-acquisition process in parallel: identify three to five small Nigerian software or IT services firms and commission the valuation and replacement-cost exercise (§5.3). Hiring twelve engineers one by one takes 9–18 months; acquiring them takes one financial year — and this is the plan's answer to the talent constraint, so it should start in the first quarter, not the third year. Budget for re-pricing the acquired team, because the gap between small-firm pay and senior market pay is large.
  10. Complete the licence-by-licence ownership audit required by 08_Akunnia_Group.md §5 before the hub company is incorporated, because Aku Technology will hold the data of entities holding NBC, NAFDAC, NUC, NACOC, CBN and NSCDC licences. In the same exercise, close the Certificate of Capital Importation question — without it the Mauritius chain cannot repatriate, and it is currently the least-researched item in the structure.
  11. Set the stop rule as a board resolution — if the Group's consolidated accounts are not being produced on the system, on a fixed calendar, within 30 days of Year 3's year-end, Aku Technology is frozen at 12 people and portfolio reporting is outsourced. A function whose only indispensable task is the close must be measured on the close.
