12 — AKU MARKETS

Licensed securities dealing, market execution and public-market intelligence

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is the second child's group (Finance & Investment Systems + Governance, Law & Security); her companies take the short form "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Do not compare dollars across plans.

Status: replaces the BlackRock-oriented version of this plan. The index and ETF business — the iShares analogue, benchmark licensing, index-provider revenue, passive products — is deleted entirely and does not return. 08_Akunnia_Group.md §1 recorded Aku Markets as "legacy of the BlackRock model — reduced or closed." This plan states what survives and what it becomes.
GroupAkunnia Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group
HeirAkunnia — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer
EntityAku Markets Ltd (CAMA), a Nigerian company
MandateLicensed dealing, placement, execution and research for the Group, its funds and third-party clients
ModelBlackstone, not BlackRock: control investing at 1.5–2.0% + 20% carry over an 8% hurdle on a platform headed toward ~USD 1.3trn of alternatives AUM — not USD 14trn of passive money at 3–15bps
HorizonYear 1 = 2027; fifteen years

Status of figures: a planning instrument, not legal or investment advice. Items marked [verify] must be confirmed with the regulator, the Exchange or the vendor in writing before money is committed. Naira thresholds in Nigerian capital-markets regulation are moving fast in 2026–27 and this plan says so rather than assuming they hold.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Markets exists because a platform that buys, holds and sells entire companies must be able to execute the securities transactions those decisions create — and paying an outside investment bank for capacity the Group needs every year is both a cost and a surrender of control.

The model correction, stated first because everything else follows from it. The previous version of this plan was built to be the iShares analogue — an African index family, index funds and ETFs, benchmark licensing to third parties, and the argument that "index scale compounds." That business is deleted. Blackstone has no index business. Passive index products at 3–15bps are the model the family has explicitly rejected, and a family that intends to "buy entire companies, reshape industries, and make an astronomical amount of money doing it" does not need a benchmark franchise. Nothing below licenses an index, launches a fund, lists an ETF or sells a methodology.

What a control investor actually needs from a securities business. A buyout platform is not passive — but its transactions are lumpy, and most of them are securities transactions:

Moment in the Blackstone playbookThe securities activity it createsWhat the Group otherwise pays
Exit — sale to a strategic buyerPrivate placement; investor distribution; documentationPlacing agent / financial adviser at 1–3% of deal value
Exit — listing on the NGXA dealing member is required. The Group cannot list a portfolio company without oneInvestment bank underwriting/placing at 2–5%
Exit — secondary sale of a fund interestLicensed intermediary capacity; valuationBroker / adviser
Entry — co-investment syndicationDistributing a share of a deal to third parties is a securities-distribution activityArranger fees
TreasuryFGN securities, T-bills, commercial paper, money-market placement, FX executionDealer spreads, and slow execution
Every underwriting decisionWhat is this company worth, and what would a buyer pay? — research, comparables, transaction evidenceIndependent valuation and fairness advice

Blackstone itself does not own a broker-dealer as a core business. This must be said plainly, because the previous plan's error was dressing a company as a rival to a segment leader. Blackstone executes through external banks; the Group cannot yet, because it is Nigerian, unknown, and will be transacting in sizes no Lagos desk will prioritise. So the honest description of Aku Markets is: a licensed utility the Group owns so that it is not a price-taker in its own transactions. It is not a pillar of the platform, and this plan does not pretend otherwise.

The strategic argument, in four steps.

  1. The licence is a precondition for control exits, not a nice-to-have. A private sale can be done without one. A listing cannot. If any part of the exit strategy is "list the consolidated sector champion on the NGX" — and 08_Akunnia_Group.md §2 names exactly that — the Group must either own dealing capacity or rent it.
  2. Renting is real and cheap, and must be priced against owning. The Exchange licenses Brokers as agents of a Dealing Member, and the published rules require a booth-sharing MOU with another stockbroking firm. SEC registration as a Sub-Broker (Corporate) requires ₦50m of capital — forty times less than a Broker-Dealer at ₦2bn (SEC Revised Minimum Capital, 18 Mar 2026, Annex V). This is the threshold test, and the plan applies it honestly in §7: if the Group does not expect to need capital-markets execution repeatedly, it should buy the sub-broker route and revisit in five years.
  3. Owning converts a fee paid to a bank into an asset the Group can sell. A dealing firm with a clean compliance record, a research product and an institutional client base is a saleable company. A placing fee is gone.
  4. The research capability is the part that pays back first. Every buyout decision needs a defensible view of value. That work exists from Year 1, long before the Group has anything to sell.

What Aku Markets is not. It is not an index provider; it is not a product manufacturer; it does not manage money (that is 10_Aku_Asset_Management); it does not lend (that is 51_Aku_Credit); it does not take deposits (that is 16_Aku_Bank); it does not run the Group's cash (that is 13_Aku_Treasury); and it does not originate deals (that is 15_Aku_Advisory). It executes, places and values.

2. Market

The market is small, and the plan's whole commercial difficulty comes from that. State it before anything else.

Implied annual NGX equity turnoverroughly ₦7–10trn — weekly turnover is volatile; the plan does not assume a trendderived [verify]
NGX ETF turnover, same week₦451.2m — 0.35% of equity turnoveras above
NGX bond turnover, same week₦123.3mas above

The revenue pool, computed honestly. Nigerian equity transaction costs are commonly cited at about 2.19% of consideration, and the components are: the brokerage commission — the dealing member's own revenue — at 0.75%–1.35%; the SEC fee 0.3%; the NGX fee 0.3%; the CSCS fee 0.3% on sales; stamp duty 0.08% on buys; and VAT at 7.5% on commissions and fees (Bamboo fee disclosure; NGX trading market structure). The brokerage band by trade size was taken from a market participant's published disclosure rather than from the rule itself — [verify the commission caps directly with NGX].

At that rate, the entire NGX equity brokerage pool is on the order of ₦70–130bn a year, split across every licensed dealing member. Even the largest Nigerian brokers are, by any global standard, small businesses. Aku Markets will not become significant by winning share of that pool. It becomes significant only if it earns placement, arranging and transaction fees on the Group's own exits — a different business with a different competitive set (investment banks, issuing houses) and a different licence requirement.

Where the money actually is, and who already has it.

SegmentWho competesAku Markets' position
Retail equity brokerageDigital brokers and bank-owned brokers; price-competitive and technology-ledDo not compete. No retail franchise is planned
Institutional equity executionStanbic IBTC, Chapel Hill Denham, Cordros, CardinalStone, Meristem, FBNQuest and similarThird-party desk later, if ever — this is the volume that would justify the cost base

Fixed income and FXFMDQ; banks under CBN dealing licencesVia FMDQ membership, and only where Aku Markets holds the relevant registration

The honest ceiling. A broker-dealer with a handful of Group transactions a year cannot carry its own compliance, technology and research cost. The Nigerian market does not have enough volume to make Aku Markets large. The realistic outcome, stated now: a lean 8–15 person licensed firm whose revenue is lumpy, whose break-even depends on exits that will not begin before Year 5, and whose justification is cost avoidance and control rather than return on capital. §7 quantifies that, and states the condition under which the honest answer is not to build it at all.

3. Product & service lines

Six lines. The first two are the reason the company exists; the last four are why it survives.

Three boundaries drawn deliberately.

  • Aku Markets does not become a fund manager. It does not hold client money in a managed portfolio, does not publish a NAV and does not run a CIS. That is 10_Aku_Asset_Management under SEC fund-management registration.
  • Aku Markets does not become an FX dealer. Dealing in foreign exchange in Nigeria requires CBN authorisation, not an SEC registration. The Group is not buying an FX licence and this plan does not imply one.
  • Secondary interests in Cayman or Delaware fund vehicles are not primarily a Nigerian licensed activity. LP-led and GP-led secondaries in offshore vehicles sit with the hub manager and its Cayman/Delaware counsel. Aku Markets' role is confined to the Nigerian leg — the underlying asset or the naira-side vehicle. Do not build the plan on the assumption that a Lagos dealing licence covers offshore fund secondaries. [verify with counsel in both jurisdictions]

4. Operating model

Two desks, one compliance spine, and a hard wall down the middle.

```

AKU MARKETS LTD

├── GROUP & FUND EXECUTION DESK ← deals for the Group, the funds and Aku Capital

├── THIRD-PARTY EXECUTION DESK ← external institutional clients

├── RESEARCH & VALUATION ← serves both; the Group's underwriting support

├── TREASURY / MONEY MARKETS ← FGN, T-bills, CP, FX via authorised dealers

└── COMPLIANCE, RISK & OPERATIONS ← reports to the Board and the Group Audit & Risk Committee

```

The central conflict, addressed before anything else. Aku Markets is owned by the Group and will deal for the Group. That creates three genuine problems, and each needs a written rule, not a good intention:

  1. Front-running and information asymmetry. Aku Markets will know the Group's intentions before the market does. Rule: the Group's order flow is handled as material non-public information; the proprietary book may not take a position in a security the Group is dealing in, or in a security of any company the deal team is actively examining; pre-clearance for every principal position; a restricted list maintained by Compliance, not by the desk. Nigerian law on insider dealing and market abuse applies to the Group's own staff once it is inside an issuer — and a Group that intends to list companies and buy stakes will be inside issuers constantly.
  2. Best execution for external clients. A third-party client is entitled to execution at least as good as the Group's own orders. Rule: a documented order-handling and best-execution policy, order timestamps, and no priority rule that favours a Group order over a client order on the same terms.
  3. Related-party transactions. Where Aku Markets places a Group company's shares, it is both agent and affiliate. Rule: independent valuation, an independent director's approval, full disclosure to counterparties, and no Aku Markets fee on any transaction where it is the only bidder or the only intermediary.

Governance. Aku Markets has its own board, with a majority of independent directors, its own Compliance Officer registered with the SEC, and a Risk Officer reporting jointly to that board and the Group Audit & Risk Committee. The Chief Compliance Officer can veto a transaction and is not removable by the desk. The entity is set up so a regulator can inspect it without inspecting the whole Group — which is also the structure that makes it saleable.

Technology and settlement. Aku Markets runs a broker back-office and order-management system interfaced to the Exchange's trading engine and to CSCS for clearing, settlement and custody, plus market data. The published Exchange rules name the Horizon trading software for trade execution and require automated trade reconciliation that "negates the need for human intervention" (NGX Rules for Registration as a Dealing Member, §6.1.21). Aku Technology buys and runs this; it does not build it (11_Aku_Technology.md §3). Business continuity, off-site backup and power failover are licence conditions, not choices — in Lagos, with grid instability, that is a real recurring cost, not a checkbox.

Client money and custody. Client funds sit in segregated client accounts, are reconciled daily, and are never used for the firm's own purposes. This is the control that ends careers when it fails, and it is why the CFO and CCO are licence-critical hires rather than support staff. ISA 2025 requires separate accounts and trust accounts, makes unauthorised withdrawal from a trust account an offence, and gives clients a statutory right to inspect contract notes and book entries.

The statutory conduct rules the firm must be built around — because they constrain how the Group is used to doing business. The Investments and Securities Act 2025, Part X is not advisory; it is the operating manual:

ProvisionWhat it requiresConsequence for Aku Markets
s.121Prohibition of cash transactions in securitiesThe Group is a cash-heavy conglomerate. Aku Markets cannot be. Every settlement runs through the banking system
s.122Prohibition of transactions in non-dematerialised securitiesAny Group shareholding in a certificate is untradeable until dematerialised at CSCS. Check every target before planning an exit
s.123Legal entity identifierA LEI is already required by CSCS with a ₦75,000 subscription and ₦30,000 annual renewal

(Investments and Securities Act 2025 — Act No. 2 of 2025, assented 25 March 2025, gazetted 2 May 2025, repealing the ISA 2007 with savings, which is why the older SEC Rules and circulars still bite.)

Capital-markets events are run as projects, not as trading. An exit is a sequence: appoint advisers, prepare the information memorandum or prospectus, run diligence, market to a defined buyer set, price, allocate, settle. The Group should expect to run two to four such projects a decade, not ten a year — and staffing must reflect that lumpiness, which is why the firm is designed lean and uses external counsel and printers per transaction.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Group rule, applied here in full: a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business. For every licence below: (a) who issues it, (b) the capital and process to obtain it directly, and (c) how to acquire it instead — by buying a company that already holds it, roughly what that costs, and the change-of-control process.

5.2 The acquisition route — the recommended one

The published Exchange rules contain an explicit acquisition procedure, which is unusual and useful — and it survived the 2020 SEC-approved rewrite of the Trading Licence Holders Rules. Where a company wishes to acquire 100% of a Dealing Member Firm (Rule 5.1, Acquisition of a Dealing Member Licence, as amended and approved by the SEC on 17 March 2020):

  1. The target Dealing Member Firm shall notify the Exchange of its intention to sell/transfer its licence and seek the Exchange's approval.
  2. The acquiring company must meet all the requirements set forth in the rules to qualify for a dealing membership — so the fit-and-proper test is not avoided, only accelerated.
  3. A sum representing 6% of the consideration for sale/transfer must be paid by bank draft to the Exchange, and is an added condition for obtaining approval.
  4. The acquirer submits the executed Transfer/Sales Agreement, a board resolution approving the acquisition, and evidence of payment of the transfer fee.
  5. An Approval-in-Principle is granted to a successful applicant.
  6. The acquiring company must request a pre-certification inspection within six (6) months of being issued the AIP — the 2020 amendment lengthened this from three months — and must meet all the requirements for commencement of operations.

(NGX Rulebook — Amendments to Dealing Members' Rules, Rule 5.1; NGX Rules for Registration as a Dealing Member, §8–§9. Note that the Exchange has kept the term "Dealing Member" in these rules even as it uses "Trading Licence Holder" elsewhere — confirm which terminology the current application pack uses.)

Acquiring more than 5% rather than 100% follows Rule 5.3 ("Sale/Transfer of a significant shareholding"): the firm must request approval of the change in its shareholding structure, stating the specific number and percentage; submit the acquirer's application or board resolution; file proposed changes in the directorship and management; produce employment and acceptance letters for any new CEO, CFO, CCO or CRO, each with the requisite qualifications; new officers sign undertakings and produce police clearance; and the same 6% transfer sum applies. Rule 6.13(12)(a)(2) additionally requires the Exchange's prior written consent for any change in control or shareholding structure, with a ₦250,000 fine for breach — and Rule 6.9(8) prohibits one person serving as a director of more than one Dealing Member firm at a time.

The constraint that governs the whole acquisition strategy, and it must be stated before anything else: a licence is not an asset you can buy out of a failed firm. Rule 5.2 — "Proprietary Interest of The Exchange over Dealing Membership Licences" — provides that the proprietary interest over every dealing licence "shall remain with The Exchange", and that on the "expulsion, winding up, liquidation or receivership" of a member the licence "shall not form part of the Dealing Member's assets applied towards the settlement of its liabilities but shall immediately be returned to The Exchange." (NGX Rulebook 2015, Rule 5.2) The consequence is decisive for structure: acquire the company by share purchase from a solvent, willing owner. Never plan to pick a licence out of a liquidation, a receivership or an insolvency proceeding — it will not be there. ⚠️ A second trap sits alongside it: Rule 6.5 provides that where a Trading Licence Holder is inactive for six consecutive months, the Exchange "shall revoke the License." A dormant firm cannot be bought and warehoused while the Group raises capital — the acquisition and the recapitalisation must be executable in one sequence.

SEC side — and this is statutory, not merely administrative. ISA 2025 s.349(1)–(2): a capital market operator shall not, without the prior approval in writing of the Commission, change its shareholding or directors, and any such change "shall not be effective without the prior approval in writing of the Commission." s.62(1) separately makes the appointment of the chief executive and other principal officers subject to prior notification and ratification. "Control" is defined in ISA 2025 s.357 — the Part XX Interpretation provision, verified against the Bill text: "control means control of an entity by a Person(s) who — (a) beneficially owns more than one half of the issued share capital or assets of the undertaking; (b) is entitled to vote a majority of the votes…; (c) is able to appoint or veto the appointment of a majority of the directors…" — and includes beneficial ownership of more than half the issued share capital, the ability to appoint or veto a majority of directors, and — in a takeover context — the acquisition of more than 30% of voting rights. Alongside that, the Commission's 2026 capital guidelines expressly contemplate the acquisition route: CMOs may achieve compliance "through mergers, acquisitions, or business combinations," subject to (a) prior notification, (b) compliance with SEC M&A Rules, and (c) the issuance of a formal "No Objection"; and they permit "downgrade of registration", by which an operator scales back its registered functions (SEC Revised Minimum Capital, §§5.2–5.3). ⚠️ No SEC change-of-control application form, fee or published timeline exists — the 2026 SEC Service Level Agreement has no such service line. [Establish the procedure with the SEC directly in the first ninety days.] The Exchange also has its own merger rule (Rule 5.4), consenting to mergers only where the whole undertaking or interest and assets and liabilities transfer and the Exchange is satisfied that clients' obligations are covered.**

The supply argument, restated on verified evidence. The SEC's 2026 regime raises a Broker-Dealer from ₦300m to ₦2bn — a 6.7-fold increase — with a hard deadline of 30 June 2027 (SEC Revised Minimum Capital, Annex V and §1.4). The Commission's own published expectation is that operators may "downscale, merge, or exit" (Nairametrics, 16 Jan 2026); Nigerian financial press reads it as a regime that will "force consolidation, exits and a smaller, more tightly capitalised industry" (BusinessDay, 4 Sept 2026); and the industry association has publicly asked the SEC for "incentives such as reduced fees, low-interest financing, and support for mergers" to ease the process. The consolidation is not a forecast — it has already begun, and one Nigerian fintech has already bought a stockbroker for exactly this reason.

Recommendation: acquire — with the consideration treated as an empirical range, not an assumption. Budget the licence acquisition at "consideration + 6% transfer fee + recapitalisation to ₦2bn + a ₦400m fidelity bond [verify]", and run diligence in the first ninety days against the two active but undercapitalised firms and a shortlist from the named inactive list, remembering that a solvent share purchase is the only lawful route and the six-month inactivity rule sets the clock.

The Exchange rules permit an entity to be licensed as a Broker as an agent of a Dealing Member and to operate "through the Dealing Member Firm," and require an MOU with another stockbroking firm relating to booth sharing (NGX Rules, §6.1.13 and §11). SEC registration as a Sub-Broker (Corporate) carries a minimum capital of ₦50m — one fortieth of the Broker-Dealer requirement.

6. Capital requirement

The most important distinction in this plan: regulatory capital is locked, not spent. ₦2bn of qualifying shareholders' funds sits on the balance sheet and cannot be lent, invested or paid out. The cost of Aku Markets is the operating cost base plus the opportunity cost of that capital — and both must be counted, because for the first five years the capital earns almost nothing. A third category sits between the two: the fidelity bond, which must exist and is at least partly paid away. SEC registration templates require a valid fidelity bond covering at least 20% of the minimum capital requirement, with an end date of 31 December — on a ₦2bn Broker-Dealer, around ₦400m of bonding capacity [derived from two SEC documents, not stated in either — verify]. That is an annual insurance cost on a licence, not an asset the Group gets back.

⚠️ The Rule 7.1 quotation below is CONTESTED — do not rely on it until the amending instrument is read in its original formatting.

This plan quotes Rule 7.1 as providing that a Trading Licence Holder whose capital adequacy falls below the minimum "shall be suspended immediately." Two independent verification passes reached opposite conclusions on whether that sentence is operative:

  • One pass reported it as the amended rule's text, "replacing the old 24-hour cure."
  • A later pass reported it as the text the 6 May 2024 instrument strikes out — "the deleted sentence, presented in quotation marks as operative law."

Both cannot be right, and this library's own rule is that an unresolved statutory question is flagged, not guessed. I verified what is verifiable: the amending instrument — Amendments to Rule 7.1: Minimum Capital Requirements, NGX, 6 May 2024 — is a tracked-changes document whose own legend reads "Additions are underlined and bolded, deletions are Struck through." Sub-rule (4) genuinely contains both formulations in sequence:

"…the Trading License Holder shall be suspended immediately and be required to shore up its capital within twenty-four (24) hours required to immediately notify The Exchange of the reduction in capital and provide a plan to shore up its minimum capital within the allowable time prescribed by SEC."

Which of the two is struck through cannot be determined from text extraction — the distinction lives in the PDF's line formatting, and the file carries 38 thin horizontal rules consistent with the underline/strikethrough legend. It must be read from the document itself.

The instrument is preserved at .research/evidence/ngx_rulebook/rule71_6may2024.pdf — open it and read the formatting of sub-rule (4). This is a five-minute task with the file in hand and it decides whether the two risk-register rows below are built on operative law or on a deleted sentence. Until then, treat Rule 7.1's suspension language as unverified.

And a related numbering finding that should be applied regardless: a separate pass established that the NGX rule numbers this library cites — "6.8(7)", "6.11(10)(d)" and "6.15(14)" — were parsed from an amending instrument's doubled markup, where "6.87", "6.1110" and "6.1514" are printed as single rule numbers rather than rule-plus-subrule. NGX does not use that scheme in enforcement — its own 2024 circular cites Rule 6.4(b) where this library says 6.5. The correct references are 6.6, 6.11(d), 6.14 and 6.4(b). Re-check every NGX rule number cited in this and the other Aku plans against the Rulebook itself rather than against an amendment's rendered text.

A live, immediate-suspension risk that has nothing to do with solvency. Rule 7.1, as amended by instruments the SEC approved on 6 May 2024, provides that where a Trading Licence Holder's capital adequacy falls below the minimum, it "shall be suspended immediately" and must notify the Exchange and provide a plan to shore up capital "within the allowable time prescribed by SEC" — replacing the old 24-hour cure. And Rule 6.11(10)(d) provides that no member may operate for more than six months without a substantive CEO, on pain of immediate suspension and a ₦100,000 fine — a rule the Exchange visibly enforces, since it publishes a list of "Trading Licence Holders Operating without a Managing Director." Together these two rules mean the licence can be suspended for governance failure even when the balance sheet is sound, which is why the MD hire and the daily capital-adequacy report in §8 are control functions, not administration.

The stop rule, written now. If, at the Year 3 gate, Aku Markets has not executed a single Group capital-markets event and has not built third-party revenue above ₦250m, the honest response is not to fund T3 — it is to retain the licence at minimum cost, keep it alive for the Group's own order flow, and stop investing in it as a business. A licence is worth buying early because it is needed. It is not worth funding as a growth business if the growth never arrives. ⚠️ One caveat on "retain at minimum cost": Rule 6.5 revokes the licence of a firm inactive for six consecutive months. A retained licence must still trade.

7. Unit economics

Start with the constraint that decides the whole question. A lean licensed broker-dealer in Lagos — MD, CCO, CFO, two dealers, an operations/settlement pair, research, compliance and client service — costs roughly ₦0.9–1.1bn a year fully loaded (pay, systems, market data, premises, insurance, audit, Exchange and CSCS dues) [verify against Year 1 actuals].

At a blended net commission of ~1.0% of executed value, that cost implies roughly ₦90–110bn of annual executed equity turnover to break even. Against implied NGX annual equity turnover of roughly ₦7–10trn, that is around 1–1.5% of the entire market's turnover — a top-15 broker position in Nigeria. Stated bluntly: commission alone will not carry this firm.

Hard boundaries, written in Year 1 rather than discovered in Year 8.

  • No Group entity is promised a price, an allocation or priority of execution. Every Group order is executed on the same terms as a third-party order of identical size and terms.
  • Aku Markets never manages Group or third-party money. Any arrangement that looks like discretionary portfolio management is a different licence and a different company.
  • Aku Markets may not deal in a security it knows the Group is examining, and Compliance — not the desk — maintains that list.
  • No research is published on a Group company or a company the Group is buying or selling without written disclosure of the relationship in the report itself.
  • The licence is not a Group licence. It belongs to the entity, it is supervised at the entity, and the entity keeps its own board with independent directors so a regulator can inspect it alone. That is also what makes it saleable.

12. First ninety days

  1. Build the target list and open diligence — this is the single most important ninety-day action, and the plan now does it from the Exchange's own register rather than from a guess. The Status of Trading Licence Holders as at 21 September 2026 identifies 187 active, 21 inactive, 7 deregistered and 175 revoked — and, more usefully, it names the nine firms operating with inadequate shareholders' funds, two of which are still classified active: Foresight Securities & Investment Limited and The Brook Securities Limited. Instruct a Nigerian corporate-finance adviser to approach those two first, then work the named inactive list, and to put a defensible range on consideration.
  2. Establish the two legal boundaries before a single approach is made, because they decide whether the strategy is possible at all. First, Rule 5.2: the proprietary interest in the licence remains with the Exchange, and on liquidation or receivership the licence reverts to it — so only a solvent share purchase works. Second, Rule 6.5: six months of inactivity revokes the licence — so a dormant target must be recapitalised and trading inside that window. Neither constraint is negotiable, and both must be written into the deal structure.
  3. Confirm the change-of-control procedure in writing with both regulators. ISA 2025 s.349 makes SEC prior written approval a statutory precondition for any change in shareholding or directors, and s.62(1) makes the CEO's appointment subject to prior notification and ratification — but the SEC publishes no change-of-control form, fee or timeline. Obtain the procedure from the SEC directly, and simultaneously obtain from NGX RegCo the current acquisition procedure, the current fee schedule, and confirmation of whether the Exchange's application pack uses "Dealing Member" or "Trading Licence Holder."
  4. Find the Managing Director before the licence. The office must be supervised by a Director or an Accredited Representative who is a Chartered Stockbroker registered by the SEC, the firm must sponsor at least three individuals including the MD and the Compliance Officer through SEC training, examination and interview, and SEC requires the Dealership Certificate of the authorised dealing clerk it sponsors. This is the scarce input in the entire plan. Appoint first; structure later.
  5. Run the threshold test in §7 as a board decision: does the Group expect two to three capital-markets events a year from Year 5? Record the answer, and the evidence for it, as a board resolution. If the answer is no, adopt the Sub-Broker route at ₦50m plus a booth-sharing MOU and revisit at Year 5.
  6. Draft the conflict, market-abuse and conduct rulebook before the first trade, not after the first incident — and draft it against ISA 2025 Part X, not against good intentions. It must cover: information barriers and a Compliance-controlled restricted list; s.137 insider dealing; s.129 priority to client orders; s.127 dealing as principal and the contract-note disclosure it requires; s.126 disclosure of interests with seven-year record retention; s.121 no cash transactions; s.122 no transactions in non-dematerialised securities; and zero fee where Aku Markets is the only intermediary. The Group will be a price-sensitive insider in its own portfolio companies for years; the rulebook is the licence.
  7. Stand up research and valuation first, because it earns first. Aku Private Equity needs a defensible answer to "what is this company worth and what would a buyer pay?" on the very first transaction. That work needs no licence, no capital and no Exchange approval — and it begins in month one.
  8. Commission the licence-by-licence ownership audit required by 08_Akunnia_Group.md §5. A London or New York investment manager above a Nigerian licensed dealing firm raises the foreign-interest question directly, and a dealing licence may need to sit in a Nigerian-controlled vehicle separate from the Aku structure. Resolve this before the acquisition agreement is signed.
  9. Write the stop rule as a board resolution — Year 3: no Group capital-markets event executed and third-party revenue below ₦250m means the licence is retained at minimum cost and the business is not funded further — with the Rule 6.5 caveat that even a retained licence must keep trading. A company that cannot be stopped is not a plan.

13 — AKU TREASURY

Internal capital allocation, FX, cash pooling and banking

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company. Akunnia Group is her group — the second child's domain, Finance & Governance. Her companies take the short form of her name — "Aku". See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary; dollars are indicative at ₦1,600/USD.

Parent brief: 08_Akunnia_Group.md. Companions: 09_Aku_Capital.md, 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md, 11_Aku_Technology.md.
CompanyAku Treasury — a subsidiary of Akunnia Group, under Ezeme Group
MandateInternal capital allocation · FX management · cash pooling · banking relationships
OwnerAkunnia — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer
StatusNot a deposit-taker; takes no public funds; no CBN licence required as scoped

1. Thesis

Aku Treasury is the Group's internal bank, and it is not a bank. It takes no public deposits and lends to no one outside the Group, so it needs no banking licence. What it does is make the Group's own balance sheet behave like a single balance sheet — allocating capital between the five groups, pricing the naira against the dollar once rather than thirty times, and answering to one set of counterparty limits instead of whichever relationship manager called last.

The structural principle, stated plainly: treasury sits in Akunnia Group and deliberately not in the family office. Treasury is a commercial function serving the enterprise; the family office serves the family. They have different beneficiaries, different duties and different failure modes. A family office optimises the family's wealth across generations; a treasurer optimises the enterprise's liquidity across quarters, under covenants and audit. Mixed, they produce the classic pathology — the family can no longer tell what is theirs from what is the company's, and both sets of accounts become unusable. The Family Treasury receives Aku Treasury's reports. It does not issue Aku Treasury's instructions.

The rules Aku Treasury exists to enforce are Group rules, not treasury preferences: gearing ≤40%; no unhedged USD debt; financing ring-fenced per group with no cross-pledges, so a failure in one group cannot accelerate debt in another; and FX re-based quarterly.

Those rules were written because of a company in the Group's own state. Neimeth, building in Anambra, posted ₦4.5bn of revenue and a ₦1.7bn net loss in 2024, driven by a ₦2bn FX loss on USD debt (BusinessDay). Naira revenue against unhedged dollar debt is how Nigerian manufacturers die — and Neimeth did not fail on operations. It failed on an unmanaged currency position. Aku Treasury is the function that ensures Ezeme Group is never described that way.

One honest framing up front, because it shapes how this company is judged. A treasury's value is overwhelmingly avoided cost, not revenue. Judged as a profit centre it will look like a failure. Judged on the difference between what the Group pays for money and what it would otherwise pay, it is among the highest-return functions in the Group. Section 7 makes that arithmetic explicit.

2. Market

The demand is internal and it is the most certain demand in the Group. Every group uses cash, buys and sells foreign currency, and banks somewhere. No customer acquisition cost, no competitor able to bid for the mandate, no churn.

The Nigerian money-market environment, September 2026:

IndicatorLevelImplication
MPR23%, after a surprise 350bp cut (Nairametrics)Borrowing still expensive; the borrow–deposit spread is the pooling prize
364-day NTB stop rate16.62%, third straight cut (Nairametrics)Surplus cash has a sovereign-risk-free home
Headline inflation~15.9% (May 2026) (WSTC)Idle naira is a slow loss
Bank lending spreadCorporates borrow well above MPRThe gap between a 29% overdraft and an 18% deposit is where pooling earns

A falling rate cycle is a reason to move early. Every cut compresses the pooling spread, so the case must rest on benefits that do not move with rates: one FX policy, one set of counterparty limits, one set of controls.

The regulatory market moved in June 2026 and it constrains the design. The CBN published Draft Guidelines on Ring-Fencing Operations of Closely Linked Entities, proposing to limit loans and guarantees between affiliates and to bar linked financial entities from lending to one another (Nairametrics, Oditah), and issued a new Foreign Exchange Manual, 4th Edition (CBN, Olaniwun Ajayi). Both are design inputs: the pool is built between non-financial operating companies, never inside or across a licensed financial entity. [verify: final form and effective date.]

3. Product & service lines

  1. Cash pooling and liquidity management. Group cash visibility, per-group pooling rings, one Group liquidity forecast. Zero-balancing within a ring; notional offsets between rings.
  2. Intercompany lending and capital allocation. Arm's-length loans priced off a published internal curve, with tenor, security or an express unsecured limit, and no cross-default clauses.
  3. FX exposure management and hedging. Consolidated exposure, a Group hedge policy, execution. Natural offsets first — Uli Freight and Isiome Trading earn the dollars Isiome Foods and Idenze Pharma spend — then forwards and NDFs.
  4. Banking relationship and mandate management. A named-role relationship map, a Group mandate register, and the programme to cut ~20 relationships and ~100 accounts to 6–8 core banks.
  5. Payment and controls architecture. One authority matrix, one payment hub, one sanctions-screening point.
  6. Treasury management system — connectivity, cash visibility, payments, pooling, exposure, hedge accounting — integrated with Aku Technology as the Group's system of record.
  7. Counterparty and bank credit risk. Limits per bank, instrument and tenor; monthly mark-to-market including derivative MTM and undrawn lines.
  8. Investment of surplus cash within policy (tiered IPS, §4), Group funding and structure advisory with a pre-signing compliance check on gearing and ring-fencing, and reporting to the Group Board, the Audit & Risk Committee and the Family Treasury.

4. Operating model

The multiple-approval rule

From the family's own Charter, on the Family Treasury: "multiple approvals — never a single signature — for any major transaction." Aku Treasury encodes this as control doctrine: no single signature authorises any major transaction, at any seniority, including the Group CEO and the Group Treasurer.

ControlRule
Payment authorisationMaker–checker–approver, three distinct people, no delegation chains
Bank mandatesTwo authorised signatories from two different groups above threshold
FX dealsSeparate dealing, confirmation and settlement — never the same person
Intercompany loansTreasury proposes; Group CFO and Group Treasurer sign; Audit & Risk Committee approves
Counterparty limit changesTreasury Risk proposes; Audit & Risk Committee approves
New bank relationshipGroup Treasurer and Group CFO jointly; Group Board notified

Cash pooling under the ring-fence

The ring-fence and the pool pull in opposite directions. Ring-fencing exists so a failure in Isiome cannot accelerate Okodu's debt; a pool that moves cash across group boundaries on a bank's books is, in substance, an implicit cross-group guarantee, and a liquidator can attack it. The design resolves the tension explicitly:

  • Within a ring: physical pooling permitted — zero balancing, one group account, subsidiary ledgers.
  • Between rings: notional offsets and documented intercompany loans only — never a bank-level structure crossing a ring boundary.
  • Across a licensed financial entity: never. When Aku Bank is licensed it sits outside the pool entirely.
  • Every intercompany loan is a real instrument: arm's-length interest, defined tenor, no cross-default.

FX exposure management and hedging policy

Exposure is measured at Group level monthly, by currency and tenor bucket — booked, then committed, then forecast. Hedge ratio 80–100% of committed USD payables within 6 months, 50–80% within 12; forecast-only beyond 12 months is unhedged by policy, and no unhedged USD debt is absolute and admits no discretion. Natural offsets come first and derivatives second — hedging a Group position that nets internally is paying a bank to transfer risk to itself. Hedge accounting applies from Year 2; FX is re-based quarterly as the Group rule requires.

Payment and controls architecture

One payment hub; no direct debits or cheque books outside a controlled register; beneficiary whitelisting with dual change approval; sanctions and PEP screening at the point of payment; a hard block on accounts added within 48 hours. Segregation of duties is enforced in the system, not by convention — creating a beneficiary and approving a payment must never rest with one person.

Investment of surplus cash within policy

T1 — LiquidityCall and overnight placements; ≤91-day NTBs40% of surplusSame day
T2 — Core182–364-day NTBs; FGN bonds ≤3 years45%≤12 months weighted

Counterparty limits: maximum 25% of Group cash with any single bank, and 20% beyond 90 days. D-SIB banks and FGN instruments only. Prohibited without Audit & Risk Committee consent: unrated commercial paper, equities, and anything with a lock-up beyond its tier's horizon.

The treasury management system

Phased, and honest about the binding constraint — Nigerian bank API maturity, not software. Phase 1 (Y1) bank connectivity and cash visibility, likely over MT940/MT101 and SWIFT for offshore accounts. Phase 2 (Y2–3) pooling, FX exposure, hedge accounting, the intercompany loan ledger. Phase 3 (Y3–5) integration with Aku Technology, so treasury feeds the same limits and breach escalations the Audit & Risk Committee reads. Candidates — Kyriba, FIS, ION, SAP TRM — assessed on African bank connectivity first, features second. [verify: bank API and host-to-host capability by institution.]

The acquisition question here, answered honestly

Group policy is that a licence is never a reason to defer a business. In treasury the honest application of that policy is different from everywhere else: the licences that would matter are held by a bank or a dealer, not by a treasury company, and a non-bank cannot apply its way into them. So the route is partnership first, the Group's own licensed entities second, acquisition of a small licensed dealer third — and never a standalone application. The ring-fencing draft settles the last part: a licensed financial entity inside the cash pool is precisely the structure the CBN has proposed to prohibit, so any licence the Group buys for FX or dealing must sit outside the pool, at arm's length, with its own board and its own regulator relationship.

The acquisition question in this plan is therefore answered "no" four times and "later" once. That is not deference to regulation; it is the correct read of where the licences sit. The Group's FX and dealing permissions will be held by Aku Bank (16_Aku_Bank.md) and Aku Markets (12_Aku_Markets.md) — entities with their own capital, boards and regulators — while Treasury keeps its advantage: it needs no licence at all to do the job it exists to do, and the moment it takes third-party money or deals on its own account it has become a different company with a different plan.

First ninety days, named and costed — ₦75m. (1) Instruct counsel and a treasury adviser to obtain the CBN's final ring-fencing guidelines and written confirmation that no Group treasury activity requires a licence (₦30m). (2) Obtain from FMDQ and the SEC, in writing, the current net-liquid-capital requirement, the dues schedule and the registration position, so the perimeter is documented rather than assumed — and reconcile it against the ₦300m/₦200m figures used here (₦25m). (3) Only if FX execution becomes a requirement: price Tier-2 BDC targets and build the CBN change-of-control file (₦20m). The deliverable is a written licence perimeter — what Treasury may do without a licence, what it must never do, and who holds the permission when one is genuinely needed.

Treasury's own P&L, stated honestly: net interest margin on internal lending ~₦45m, FX execution spread at ~₦2/$ ~₦360m, internal arrangement fees ~₦30m — revenue of ~₦435m against a cost base of ₦1,350m: a book loss of roughly ₦915m a year.

That loss is the point of this section. Judged as a profit centre, Aku Treasury is a failing business. Judged on the ₦2.4bn it returns to the Group, it is among the best investments the Group makes — and almost all of it is avoided cost, not revenue. Break-even against the cost base needs roughly ₦4bn of pooled balances; the "three times cost" test is met at roughly ₦8bn. Aku Treasury must therefore be measured on a Group-benefit scorecard signed off by the Audit & Risk Committee, never on its own P&L.

14 — AKU INSURANCE

Risk, credit, guarantees — and eventually a licensed insurer

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is the second child's domain, and her companies take her short form — "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM, Sept 2026). Do not compare dollars across plans.

Horizon: 10–15 years. Year 1 = 2027; NAICOM licence Year 5 (2031).

Status: not legal or investment advice. Figures marked [verify] must be confirmed with NAICOM or Nigerian insurance counsel before capital is committed.
EntitiesAku Insurance Ltd (CAMA) — ring-fenced insurer-in-formation · Aku Insurance Services Ltd — licensed corporate agency and risk-engineering arm
LicenceNAICOM non-life under NIIRA 2025 — not composite, not reinsurance
OwnershipEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Akunnia Group → Aku Insurance

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Insurance exists because the Ezeme Group already pays premium it could retain and cannot reliably buy the cover its own businesses need — so it will take that premium, underwrite it with reinsurance behind it, and hold the float.

Capacity was rebuilt with no demand to absorb it. Nigeria's recapitalisation closed in 2026: 48 insurers and two reinsurers relicensed, six licences cancelled, ₦1.079trn of fresh capital raised (ThisDay). NAICOM's own test is now whether the industry can "translate stronger financial capacity into deeper insurance penetration" (BusinessDay). Aku Insurance must not sell generic capacity; it competes on risks it sees better than anyone because it owns them.

The surety market was opened by law, then restricted by solvency rule. NAICOM and the Bureau of Public Procurement made bid, tender, performance and advance-payment bonds mandatory in public procurement, against savings of over ₦1.1trn in 2025 (BusinessDay) — while requiring issuers to hold a solvency ratio above 100%, pushing weaker insurers into co-insurance. A specialist, well-capitalised surety underwriter is the scarce thing, and it is what Okodu Construction needs to keep bidding.

The law now forces Nigerian risk onshore. NIIRA bars foreign insurers without a physical home presence or consolidated supervision, and deems any Nigerian company arranging or underwriting Nigerian risk abroad to be carrying on business in Nigeria, subject to NAICOM (Tope Adebayo LP). [verify] with counsel.

The counterweight. Aku Capital earns fees with no balance-sheet risk; Aku Insurance must post ₦15bn of equity and lock most of it before writing a policy, and on return on capital it loses for years. It is justified only because it unlocks Group trade, captures premium already leaving the Group, and puts Group risk under one disciplined eye. None of it works until the cap table is institutional and three independent directors sit on the Group Board.

2. Market

Insurers wrote ₦2.30trn of gross premium in 2025, up 47.3%, with life up 54.8% to ₦727.4bn and Oil & Gas up 27.1% to ₦476.6bn. Gross claims were ₦724.70bn (31.5% of premium); the industry net loss ratio was 43.6%; retention rose to 68.1%; assets reached ₦4.79trn (NAICOM Q4 2025 Bulletin, via EnterpriseNGR State of Enterprise Report 2026, pp. 41–48; BusinessDay).

Penetration is the opportunity. Insurance is 0.5% of GDP against an African average of 3.2%; only about 5% of 220 million Nigerians hold cover, and 8% of MSMEs are insured. The sector contributed ₦710.6bn, or 0.32% of output, in 2025, and NAICOM targets 1.5% of GDP by 2028 and 10% by 2031 (NAICOM ISSP proposal; BusinessDay).

Corporate Nigeria is where the premium is. Non-life is 69.5% of premium, concentrated in Oil & Gas 26.0%, Fire 18.9%, General Accident 17.9%, Motor 15.1% and Marine 8.1% (NAICOM Q3 2025 Bulletin). Nine insurers reported net loss ratios at or above 100% in Q3 2025: underwriting is hard and most of the market is not good at it, so the entry argument is not more capacity but better selection. NIIRA also creates seven compulsory classes — group life at 3× emoluments, buildings under construction, public buildings, Federal Government assets and employees, petroleum installations, credit life above ₦10m, and container insurance from port to inland destination — four of which touch the Group directly (Streamsowers & Köhn).

The competition is recapitalised but undifferentiated: generic books, thin construction-surety appetite, and many insurers unable to clear the >100% solvency bar needed to issue bonds alone. NAIC lost its general insurance licence in 2026 after failing recapitalisation, leaving commercial agricultural risk without a specialist.

The gap: nobody underwrites the Group's own risk classes — construction surety, agricultural trade credit, cargo, pharma product liability — with the Group's data, engineers and contracts in hand, while selling that specialty capacity to third parties. Those underwriting files are the asset, and they cannot be bought.

3. Product & service lines

The Group's own risk first, third-party specialty second, retail never.

Underwriting discipline decides whether this works. No line is written without a written underwriting guide with binding authority limits, a rate-adequacy test signed off by the actuary, a named individual accountable for the risk, and a reinsurance treaty in place before the first policy. Authority is tiered — underwriters to ₦50m sum insured, Head of Underwriting to ₦250m, Chief Underwriting Officer to ₦750m, Risk Committee above — and any risk the Group's own engineers will not certify is declined, including Group business.

4. Operating model

Two companies, one discipline. Aku Insurance Services Ltd (Y1) holds a NAICOM corporate insurance agency licence and provides risk engineering, claims advocacy and placement for Group companies. It carries no underwriting risk, and exists to build the loss data, surveys and relationships the insurer will need. Aku Insurance Ltd (Y5) underwrites: ring-fenced, own board, own licence, own capital, non-life only — NIIRA abolished composite licensing for insurers, so life is a separate ₦10bn decision in Year 8+.

Reinsurance for a small balance sheet. On ₦15bn of capital the maximum prudent net retention on any single risk is 2–3% — ₦300m to ₦450m.

Capacity comes from at least three reinsurers of AM Best A− or better through a licensed reinsurance broker. Reinsurance dependence is the plan's central weakness: if terms harden, growth stops. Treaties are negotiated 90 days before renewal and no single reinsurer carries more than 35% of ceded premium.

Claims. Admitted claims must be settled within 60 days, with monthly compound interest on delay. Claims are registered same-day, acknowledged in 48 hours, and a licensed independent loss adjuster appointed within five working days. Reserving follows IBNR and case-basis conventions signed off quarterly by the actuary, with no reserve releases to flatter a result.

Assets. At least 60% of the float sits in FGN bonds and Treasury bills (§11). [verify] related-party limits: NAICOM's MCR guidelines make deposits with related entities and equity or debt of the parent, subsidiaries or co-subsidiaries inadmissible assets — Group paper cannot satisfy ₦1 of the MCR (Olaniwun Ajayi).

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

The MCR figures earlier Group documents flagged as unverified are now confirmed from NAICOM's own circular: NIIRA 2025 prescribes ₦10bn life, ₦15bn non-life, ₦25bn composite and ₦35bn reinsurance, effective 31 July 2025 and compliant by 30 July 2026 with no extension (NAICOM circular; Olaniwun Ajayi). The requirement is the higher of that figure or the risk-based capital NAICOM determines, and a capital adequacy ratio of 100% must be held at all times.

Statutory deposit — reconcile before committing. NIIRA section 16(1) requires a new applicant to deposit "the equivalent of the minimum capital requirement" with the CBN, while NAICOM's January 2026 Guidelines on Licensing and Renewal state 50% of the MCR. This plan assumes ₦7.5bn; [verify], because on the statutory wording the figure is ₦15bn and the gap is ₦7.5bn of liquidity (NAICOM licensing guidelines). Web or electronic insurance business also needs its own NAICOM licence (s.201). NAICOM's own service-level agreement (May 2026) supports the 50% reading — its insurance-company verification stage requires "evidence of statutory deposit with the Central Bank of Nigeria (50% of the Minimum Capital Requirement)" — and it also publishes the fee the plan had left open: a ₦50m non-refundable application fee at Stage 1, against regulator service times of 21 + 35 + 50 + 14 days across the four stages (NAICOM SLA).

The acquisition route, licence by licence — and here it is the recommended one

Group policy, applied here with more force than anywhere else in the library: a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business. NAICOM has just repriced the two routes in opposite directions. The de novo route now costs a ₦50m application fee, a ₦35bn MCR at the top of the ladder and a ₦17.5bn statutory deposit against it, with the licence arriving — if at all — years after the plan needs it. The acquisition route is served by a market that the 30 July 2026 recapitalisation deadline has deliberately manufactured: a large number of licensed Nigerian insurers cannot reach the new MCR and must recapitalise or sell, and NAICOM itself has published a fast, three-stage merger-and-acquisition procedure. Buying a licensed underwriter with an existing book is likely cheaper and far faster than licensing anew.

Two rules govern this route, and the 2026 market has already taught both.

  1. Never buy a licence without confirming it is standing at completion — because it can die between signing and closing. ₦7.128bn was committed for 50.1% of Universal Insurance in a private placement disclosed on 14 August 2026, and NAICOM revoked the licence on 19 August 2026 for failure to meet the MCR (Punch). The lesson is structural, not anecdotal: the recapitalisation deadline means the sellers in this market are, by definition, the firms that could not raise the capital, and a target short of MCR is a target whose licence is at risk until the injection is paid and verified. Make written confirmation of licence standing from NAICOM a condition precedent; escrow the consideration; and never sign before the capital is in hand.
  2. The licence is inert without the people NAICOM has approved. The MD/CEO, the executive directors, the CFO, the CRO, the Head of Internal Audit, the actuary and the technical head are all individually vetted and approved, and their resignations are filed with the Commission. Buying an insurer buys a team or it buys a shell, which is why retention and change-of-control consents are drafted with the SPA, not after it.

First ninety days, named and costed — ₦180m. (1) Mandate insurance-regulatory counsel and a transaction adviser (₦60m). (2) Pull NAICOM's register and the 2026 recapitalisation returns, and score every licensed non-life and microinsurer short of MCR with a clean claims and solvency record — the pool is public, and the deadline is what makes the sellers (₦45m). (3) Obtain from NAICOM, in writing, its acquisition and change-of-control requirements, and written confirmation of the 50%-of-MCR statutory deposit (₦25m). (4) Commission an independent indicative valuation and an actuarial review of reserves on the preferred target (₦50m). The deliverable is a priced target with a cleared route to control — not a licence application. The same ₦180m also buys the Y1–Y3 agency the plan already needs, because the broker registration and the acquisition mandate are run by the same counsel.

6. Capital requirement

Gearing ≤40% is not the binding constraint: regulatory capital must be equity. Subordinated liabilities count toward MCR only if NAICOM approves them, they run at least ten years and are issued for MCR purposes, and they carry interest no higher than the CBN Monetary Policy Rate. Fund this with equity, not debt.

7. Unit economics

A new insurer does not make money underwriting. It makes money on the float, and it loses money on both for years. Illustrative, ₦bn, heavy early cession.

The expense ratio is the killer: a new insurer carries the whole cost base — actuary, engineers, systems, compliance, reinsurance — over a premium base that starts small. The market's own record confirms the caution: a 43.6% net loss ratio for FY2025 but 59.2% in Q3 2025, with nine insurers at 100% or worse. A 53% steady-state loss ratio is a target, not a result.

The float is the business. Technical reserves, plus the equity not locked in the CBN deposit, are invested in admissible assets, at yields modelled falling with the rate cycle — the CBN cut the MPR 350bps to 23% in September 2026 (ThisDay).

So the business is profitable from Year 5 only because of the float — and the float is policyholder money held against promises. Every naira of float income is a loan against future claims, so an insurer that treats it as profit while pricing risk to lose money on underwriting is borrowing from policyholders to pay dividends. The downside is not slow growth, it is a bad year: a 12-point loss-ratio deterioration in every year erases roughly ₦2.8bn of the six-year result, and one catastrophe or surety default does it in a year — which is why the retention limits in §4 are non-negotiable.

The Group's advantage is that its businesses are each other's customers: the risk is created inside the Group before the premium exists.

Related-party discipline is the hard part. Group business is written at arm's-length rates, and related-party transactions are approved only by the independent directors sitting alone. Because NAICOM treats Group equity and related-party deposits as inadmissible assets, the float cannot be recycled into Group paper to satisfy capital — the balance sheet stays genuinely separate, which is the point of the ring-fence.

A Group-internal opportunity found by the Uli Film plan, and it belongs in this plan's product line. A completion bond adds 3–6% to a film's budget and is required by most international financiers and co-producers — so it is a cost the Group's own content business will pay regardless, and no Nigerian insurer offers it at scale.

That makes completion bonding a natural Aku Insurance product line: a fee-earning, capital-light specialty risk that the Group can underwrite for Uli Film, Uli Animation and third-party African producers, with the underwriting discipline learned on its own slate first. It follows the same logic as the rest of this plan — the Group is its own anchor customer, so the product can be proven internally before it is sold externally — and it captures a cost the Group currently exports to foreign insurers.

Action: scope completion bonding as a product line in the insurance plan's second phase, with Uli Film as the first insured. Note it requires underwriting capability in production risk that Nigeria currently lacks, so it may be a partnership before it is a solo product.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — establish the facts.

  1. Appoint a Group Insurance Committee chaired by the Akunnia CIO, mandated to produce the Group's true insurance spend and risk register within 60 days, collecting every policy, schedule, premium invoice, loss run and uninsured exposure across all five groups.
  2. Commission a legal opinion on four questions: the NIIRA perimeter for offshore placement and any Group captive; the corporate-agency route; the statutory-deposit reconciliation; related-party investment limits. [verify] all four. Request NAICOM's Schedule of Fees and the RBC calibration in writing.

Days 31–60 — size the prize.

  1. Quantify the premium leaving the Group, draft the 5-year business plan and feasibility study in NAICOM's Stage 2 format with the underwriting guide and claims manual, test reinsurance appetite with three or more A− reinsurers — written treaty indications are the real diligence — and recruit the Chief Underwriting Officer and Head of Risk Engineering.

Days 61–90 — commit.

  1. Present findings and the capital plan to the Akunnia board, then the Ezeme Group board, for the ₦25.1bn capital call; secure fronting with two licensed insurers so Okodu Construction can bid with insurance-backed bonds in 2027 while the licence is pending.
  2. Do not commit capital to the MCR until NAICOM has confirmed the statutory-deposit treatment, the RBC calibration and the fee schedule in writing. The licence is the foundation; the ₦15bn is the building.
  3. Run the acquisition file in parallel with the application, and decide on evidence. Instruct a transaction adviser to score every licensed non-life and microinsurer short of MCR, price the capital injection each one needs, and bring back a binding recommendation to buy and recapitalise versus applying de novo. Budget ₦180m for Days 1–90 — counsel and adviser ₦60m · register and MCR-status screen ₦45m · NAICOM written confirmations ₦25m · independent valuation and actuarial review ₦50m. A target with a licence in good standing and an existing book beats a four-stage application; a target whose licence is about to be revoked is worse than no licence at all (§5, Universal Insurance).

15 — AKU ADVISORY

M&A, project finance and sovereign advisory — the fee business that buys the pipeline

Naming: Akunnia Group is the second child's domain — First Daughter, Matriarch, the Group's designated Chief Investment Officer — and her companies take her short form, "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Do not compare dollars across plans. Horizon: 15 years, Year 1 = 2027; SEC registration Y1, issuing house Y2–3.

Status: not legal or investment advice. Figures marked [verify] must be confirmed with the SEC, the CBN or Nigerian corporate-finance counsel before capital is committed.
EntityAku Advisory Ltd (CAMA) — ring-fenced, own board, own audit
LicencesSEC capital market operator / corporate investment adviser, Y1 [verify category]; SEC Issuing House ₦2bn, Y2–3
OwnershipEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Akunnia Group → Aku Advisory

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Advisory exists because the Group must be believed before it can be financed — and advice is the only Akunnia business that pays the Group for earning that belief.

Commercially, it is a fee business, and the only one that does not consume the balance sheet. Everything around it does: Aku Capital must post ₦500m for a Tier 3 licence (09_Aku_Capital.md); Aku Asset Management cannot win a mandate without a track record (10_Aku_Asset_Management.md); Aku Insurance must lock ₦15bn of equity (14_Aku_Insurance.md). Aku Advisory earns from a desk, a licence and a reputation.

Strategically, it is the Group's credibility engine and its deal pipeline. Advising infrastructure and energy transactions across West Africa builds the relationships, market intelligence and reputation Aku Capital and Aku Asset Management need before they ask anyone for money — and it means the Group sees transactions before they are auctioned.

The governance point, and it is not negotiable. An advisory arm that advises third parties while the Group invests on its own account is a structural conflict of interest. This plan requires a written conflict policy, enforceable information barriers between Aku Advisory and every investment business, and explicit disclosure standards — under one absolute rule:

Aku Advisory will not advise on a transaction in which any Group entity is a bidder.

It may not act for a seller or target where a Group entity is a competing or actual bidder. Getting this wrong would taint the fund platform's credibility — the most valuable financial asset the Group has. A fee is recoverable; a reputation for conflicted process is not.

2. Market

Three incumbent groups dominate, each beatable in a defined segment. In 2025 Standard Bank led Sub-Saharan African fees at $39.9m (7.9%), just ahead of Afreximbank ($39.4m) and Goldman Sachs ($38.9m) (Ecofin, from LSEG). Global investment banks — Goldman holds 30.5% of M&A advisory — earn it on mega-deals and retreat on the first sign of risk aversion. Pan-African champions — RMB is Euromoney's best African M&A house — have conflict questions of their own. The Big Four are the default lender's and DFI transaction advisers on African infrastructure (Deloitte; KPMG).

Nigeria is the second-largest market in the region and is under-advised at the middle. Nigeria earned $97.9m of fees in 2025 — 19.4% of Sub-Saharan Africa — yet M&A value involving Nigerian entities collapsed 76% to $1.3bn while announced regional M&A reached $37.2bn (Punch/LSEG; BusinessDay). Large-cap M&A is dead and its advisers left with it; the mid-market continues, unserved and unpriced.

The infrastructure pipeline is the addressable market. Africa needs $130–170bn a year for infrastructure alone, and the AfDB's Africa Investment Forum brought 41 projects — 39 investment-ready — to its 2025 boardrooms (AfDB AIF 2025; Business Daily). Nigerian pension assets reached ₦29.52trn at 31 March 2026, only 3.95% in alternatives (PenCom Q1 2026) — a pool that must be structured into infrastructure, and the Group generates the assets.

Sovereign and sub-national advisory is the least contested segment. States must borrow, partner and procure through frameworks most cannot staff — publishing Fiscal Commitment and Contingent Liability frameworks (Oyo State) against structurally weak fiscal capacity (NESG). They need transaction advice and often lack it, and the Group's Anambra relationships are the entry point.

What an entrant can win: infrastructure and project finance, energy, mid-market M&A at ₦5bn–₦150bn EV, sovereign and sub-national advisory, and debt advisory and capital raising.

The first deal flow is internal: Okodu Power's acquisition pipeline (42_Okodu_Power.md), Aku Infrastructure Fund's syndication and the Group's own financing rounds — all priced at arm's length.

4. Operating model

One company, three desks, one wall. Infrastructure & Energy; Corporate & M&A; Sovereign & Public Sector. Compliance and the Conflicts Officer sit outside all three, report to the Aku Advisory board and the Group Audit & Risk Committee, and hold a veto no commercial head can override.

Every mandate clears one gate before it is pitched: written conflict clearance, an engagement letter stating scope, fee and exit, a named engagement partner, and a register entry in the Aku Technology deal system (11_Aku_Technology.md). No engagement letter, no work — including for Group companies. Retainers are billed in advance and no work continues for a client more than 90 days in arrears.

The conflict architecture, board-approved within ninety days:

  1. A written Conflicts of Interest Policy with annual independent review. Refusal is always available; disclosure is not a substitute for it.
  2. Information barriers — access-controlled floors, separate deal folders, and a restricted/watch list held by Compliance. Wall-crossings only in writing, logged, with named approvals.
  3. A Conflicts Committee, majority independent, clearing every matter monthly, and disclosure standards — a standing disclosure of the Group's investment activities, given to every prospective client.
  4. The absolute rule: Aku Advisory will not advise on a transaction in which any Group entity is a bidder.

Compensation must not breach the wall. No incentive may reference a Group investment decision, a Group fund's performance, or a wall-crossed mandate.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

The deadline that shapes entry. The SEC's Guidelines on Revised Minimum Capital, 18 March 2026, set revised thresholds — issuing house ₦2bn and ₦7bn (SEC) — with compliance by 30 June 2027 for existing operators and new applicants complying from day one. [verify] the exact category and threshold with the SEC before filing.

CBN perimeter. Advising on, or raising capital for, a CBN-regulated institution brings the mandate inside CBN supervisory expectations; [verify] with counsel whether a per-mandate approval is required. Professional standards: the SEC Code of Conduct (Schedule IX) (SEC), the CIS Nigeria Code of Ethics (CIS) and the NGX Code of Conduct (NGX). A published Chinese-wall manual is accepted practice here (example).

The acquisition question in advisory — people and mandates, not permissions

Group policy is that a licence is never a reason to defer a business. Applied here it produces the most useful answer in the Akunnia set: advisory broadly requires no licence at all, which means the scarce assets are people, mandates and relationships, and none of those can be conferred by a regulator. Registration becomes necessary only in the narrow band where the advice is a regulated capital-market activity; legal work cannot be sold from a company at any price. So the acquisition route in this business buys capability and mandates, not authorisations — and where a registration genuinely is required, the SEC's March 2026 guidelines make it ₦50m, not ₦2bn.

Two rules, and they are the reason this section is short. First, never buy a boutique whose value leaves through the door — the mandates must be novated with client consent, and the principals locked in for at least three years, because in this business the acquirer is buying names, not a register. Second, never let an unregistered entity hold itself out as offering regulated advisory work: the registration is ₦50m, and the sanction for not having it is the whole franchise.

First ninety days, named and costed — ₦60m. (1) Obtain from the SEC, in writing, a determination of which advisory activities are regulated capital-market activity, the correct category and the applicable capital (₦20m). (2) Instruct a corporate-finance adviser to price three boutique targets on mandate book, revenue quality and principal lock-in, not on a headline multiple (₦25m). (3) Commission counsel's opinion on the Bar boundary and adopt the Chinese-wall manual as a board-approved document (₦15m). The deliverable is a priced target list and a written statement of where advisory ends and regulated or legal work begins — because in this business the licence is not the moat, and the plan should not pretend otherwise.

Advisory is capital-light: the capital is people and regulatory standing, not assets. The largest single item is SEC registration capital, and it is a threshold, not a spend — held, not consumed. Naira first; each tranche released against a licence or mandate gate.

Cost of senior talent is the whole ball game — 50–65% of revenue [verify before hiring]: Managing Director ₦90–150m (~60–70% of global-bank cash), Director ₦55–90m, VP ₦30–50m, Analyst ₦12–22m, Compliance Officer ₦20–32m.

Break-even mandate volume. At Year 3 the fixed cost base is roughly ₦1.9bn (22 staff, office, systems, insurance, audit) — about ₦2.2bn of revenue, or 14–18 closed mandates a year at an average fee of ₦130–160m. Two things kill this business: a hit rate below one closed mandate in three pitched, and a book concentrated in fewer than six clients.

Why advisory is not the scale engine. Advisory revenue scales linearly with headcount — double the bankers, double the fees and the cost, with no operating leverage. Aku Asset Management and Aku Technology scale non-linearly: the same team earns on ₦50bn or ₦500bn of assets, and one platform serves unlimited tenants. Since the whole 2025 Sub-Saharan fee pool was $503.9m (§2), Aku Advisory at ₦16bn in Year 10 is about $10m — a rounding error in that pool and worth multiples of it inside the Group as a pipeline asset.

(3) Pay 60–75% of global-bank cash and say so plainly, then make it up with a long-term incentive on the advisory book vesting over three years on realised fees. Second: where the Group is a bidder, Aku Advisory does not act for the other side and does not run the process. The conflict rule is the price of the pipeline.

12. First ninety days

Governance and licence first — nothing else is safe until they exist.

  1. Incorporate Aku Advisory Ltd — reserved matters, two independent directors, own audit committee, ring-fenced from every other regulated entity.
  2. Take the Conflicts, Information Barrier and Personal Dealing Policy to the board — including the absolute no-bid rule — before the first mandate. Appoint the majority-independent Conflicts Committee.
  3. Hire the Compliance & Conflicts Officer first; open the restricted list, conflicts register and wall-crossing log in Aku Technology.
  4. File the SEC application; confirm the category and minimum capital in writing [verify].
  5. Appoint the Head of Advisory; agree fees and engagement letters; place PI insurance.

Then the pipeline: a new advisory firm with no mandates has no story.

  1. Audit every Group transaction in flight — Okodu Power's screening, Aku Infrastructure Fund I's syndication, the next Group financing round — papering each as an engagement with a fee benchmarked against two external quotes.
  2. Open the mandate register with ≥12 live opportunities: third-party targets in infrastructure, energy and mid-market corporates, plus five state governments and agencies, starting with Anambra's PPP office.
  3. Complete the first ten hires (§8), set the profit share vesting on realised fees, and report monthly to the Akunnia Group CEO and Group Board on mandates, conflicts, utilisation and third-party revenue share.
  4. Answer the acquisition question on evidence, with ₦60m budgeted — SEC written confirmation of which advisory activities are regulated and at what capital (₦20m) · a priced three-target boutique shortlist diligenced on mandate books and principal lock-in (₦25m) · counsel's opinion on the Bar boundary plus the Chinese-wall manual adopted by the board (₦15m). In advisory the scarce assets are people and mandates, so the acquisition plan is a hiring and novation plan, not a licence application (§5).
