plans/16_Aku_Bank.md  ·  3,869 words

AKU BANK — Deposit-Taking & Lending

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is her group; her companies take the short form "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0). Aku Bank is a working name: the legal name awaits CAC availability and CBN approval, and no Aku Bank name may appear on any entity, branch, card or product before a licence is held.

FX note: naira is primary; dollars are indicative at ₦1,600/USD, the library planning rate (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM, Sept 2026).

Entity: Aku Bank Ltd (CAMA) — ring-fenced, own board, own licence · Heir: Akunnia, First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer · Horizon: 15 years, Year 1 = 2027

Status: a planning instrument, not legal, tax or investment advice. Figures marked [verify] must be confirmed with the CBN, the NDIC or counsel before money is committed.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Bank exists because a bank is the cheapest funding base the Ezeme Group can own — deposits mobilised at single-digit cost to fund the Group's credit business instead of wholesale naira borrowed at 22–30% — and the licence to take those deposits is not applied for, it is bought.

StageVehicleTimeline
1Acquire a licensed microfinance bank — due diligence, CBN change-of-control approval, recapitalisationYears 1–2
2Grow the MFB — deposits, loan book, branch network, systemsYears 2–5
3State banking licence — CBN tiered capitalYears 5–8
4National banking licence — full commercial bankingYears 8–12+

Funding cost decides everything. In Nigerian banking the funding cost is the primary determinant of profitability — not lending rate, not branch count, not brand. The MPR was cut 350bps to 23% in September 2026 (Tribune), and the IMF has found Nigerian banks pass on hikes faster than cuts (Nairametrics). Easing compresses asset yields: whoever owns the cheapest liabilities owns the next decade.

The acquisition route is genuinely open. The sector is fragmented and under-capitalised: 962 active MFBs — 8 national, 115 state, 839 unit — after the CBN revoked 46 licences on 1 July 2026, cutting the register from 1,008 (BusinessDay). Most of it is believed dormant, and unused "virgin licences" trade at ₦400m–₦700m (Nairametrics). The licence is a purchasable asset, and buying one is a ninety-day action.

The counterweight, stated first. Licensing is not the constraint; governance is. The Draft Ring-Fencing Guidelines for Closely Linked Entities (June 2026) would bar linked financial entities from lending to one another and cap cross-directorships at 20% (Nairametrics; Oditah). A bank whose board is not independent will be penalised by the CBN and distrusted by depositors.

2. Market

The MFB balance sheet has grown from under ₦300bn to more than ₦6 trillion, with ₦2.4 trillion of loans and about ₦4.3 trillion of deposits at March 2026 (NAMB via TheEconomy). But it is concentrated: Moniepoint alone processed ₦412 trillion in payments in 2025 and lent over ₦1 trillion (Nairametrics). The median unit MFB is a two-branch institution fighting to stay above ₦200m of capital. [verify: register count — Nairametrics cites "about 804" against the CBN's 962.]

Four forces squeeze the small end, and that creates the market. Capital: the 2018 revision raised unit MFBs ₦20m→₦200m, state ₦100m→₦1bn and national ₦2bn→₦5bn, and inflation has eroded all three since. Enforcement: 179 MFBs were revoked in 2023 and 46 more in July 2026 for dormancy, insufficient assets or impaired capital. Deposit competition: OPay, PalmPay and Moniepoint pay wallet rates a community MFB cannot match.

Buyers have already moved. At least seven Nigerian startups bought licences rather than applying — Paystack/Ladder MFB, Flutterwave/Mono, Rank/Zazzau, Payhippo/Maritime, C-One/Bankly (Techmoonshot; Lawyard). For Ezeme the question is price and discipline, not possibility.

Demand. Financial inclusion reached 79%, formal inclusion 73% (EFInA A2F 2026), against a ₦13 trillion SME financing gap. Aku Bank's first market is the Group's own geography and supply chain.

3. Product & service lines

Products follow the licence. An MFB may take deposits, lend, collect payments and remit; it is prohibited from FX, international transfers, international corporate finance, clearing and speculative property (Lawyard).

StageLineMargin logic
MFB (Y1–5)Micro-loans ₦50k–₦2m, weekly or monthly amortising3–4% monthly effective
Savings, target savings, fixed and recurring depositsThe funding base — the reason to own the licence
Agent and POS banking; payments, salary and offtake collectionsFees and deposits at near-zero branch cost
Micro-insurance placed with Aku InsuranceCommission and relationship depth
MFB (Y3–5)SME working capital and supply-chain finance against Group offtake; surplus in FGN bills₦1–2m tickets; risk-free carry
Regional commercial (Y5–8)Current accounts, overdrafts, domestic trade finance, guaranteesLowest-cost CASA; fee-heavy
National commercial (Y8–12+)FX, international trade finance, syndications, custody, cardsThe mature franchise

One line is permanently forbidden: the bank never lends to another Aku financial entity.

4. Operating model

Branch strategy — cluster, then corridor, then country. One dense cluster first: Nkpor and Idemili North, then Onitsha, Nnewi, Awka; a second ring follows the Group's trade geography. Only after the regional licence does the bank enter Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt. No branch opens without a signed deposit anchor.

Digital carries the volume; branches carry trust and cash. Core banking, mobile, USSD and agents run on Aku Technology's stack. Costs differ by an order of magnitude: a staffed branch ₦35–60m a year [verify], an agent outlet ₦1.5–3m, digital near-zero marginal cost.

The deposit engine is the point of the bank. Stage 1 mobilises the Group's own float — payroll, supplier and offtake settlement, freight, clearing and contractor accounts — then extends to the traders and SMEs those flows touch. Group deposits are the seed, never the ceiling: ring-fencing rules cap the Group's share of the balance sheet, and the Year-5 test is the third-party share.

Prudential discipline. An MFB must hold a 10% capital adequacy ratio and a 20%-of-assets liquidity reserve, with T-bills capped at 5–10% of assets (Lawyard).

Deposit insurance. MFBs, PMBs and PSBs are covered by the NDIC to ₦500,000 per depositor, against ₦5m for deposit money banks, mobile money operators and non-interest banks under the 2024 review — now protecting about 99% of depositors (BusinessDay). [verify: current MFB limit.] The commercial upgrade is a deposit-marketing event: coverage per depositor rises tenfold.

5. Acquisition and licensing pathway

Every licence below is obtained by purchase, not petition. If an approval is needed, either apply with capital in hand, or buy the entity that already holds it.

#LicenceIssuerCapital, direct routeDirect process & timelineHow to acquire it instead
1State MFBCBN (FPRD) + NDIC insurance₦1bn paid-up, unimpairedCAC incorporation → CBN portal application → fit-and-proper on directors and management → inspection → licence. 6–18 months, often longerBuy a licensed state MFB. Virgin licences trade at ₦400–700m; a trading MFB prices near 1.0–1.5× adjusted book plus a ₦300–600m licence premium [verify]. Route: SPA → CBN application → CBN approval → NDIC no-objection → CAC filings → board reconstitution, 6–12 months, parallel to recapitalisation
2Unit MFBCBN₦200m (Tier 1 urban) / ₦50m (Tier 2 rural)Same process; one locationSame route, cheaper, no state-wide franchise. Fallback only
3National MFBCBN₦5bn paid-up plus share premium; retained earnings do not countUpgrade; fit-and-proper; prior CBN approval per branch; monthly returns; MFB governance code; compliance officer (Manifield)Only 8 exist, so purchase is rare and dear. Grow the acquired state MFB into it
4Regional commercial ("state banking")CBN₦50bnNew application or conversion; full BOFIA prudential regime; fit-and-proper on significant shareholders; 18–36 monthsBuy a regional commercial or merchant bank — M&A cleared at up to 1.5–2.5× book in the 2024–26 cycle [verify]
5National commercialCBN₦200bn33 of 37 banks met the new thresholds by the September 2026 deadline, no extension (Newswatch)Acquire a national bank, or convert on capital and track record. Stages 4→5 cost ₦150bn
6International commercialCBN₦500bnNot pursued hereUpside option

Naming and structure. The CBN issues regional, national and international commercial licences — there is no licence formally called a "state banking licence." Stage 3 is the regional commercial licence: a bank authorised in a limited number of states at ₦50bn. That is the real step change — where Aku Bank stops being an MFB. [verify: state-count limits; merchant-bank and non-interest variants.]

The change-of-control test. Under BOFIA 2020, no person may acquire 5% or more of a Nigerian bank without the CBN's prior written approval (Leadership). A controlling acquisition triggers fit-and-proper assessment of the new shareholders and of every proposed director and senior officer, and the CBN must approve any later change of shareholding, board, management, name, products, capital or branches (Koriat Law). Expect the CBN to reject at least one nominee director; hold two cleared alternates per seat.

Acquisition plan — costed and dated

WindowActionCost
Days 1–30Mandate regulatory counsel and a transaction adviser; pull the CBN register; score 40 active state MFBs in Anambra and the South-East₦45m
Days 31–90Shortlist 8, then 3; NDAs and offers; verify CBN and NDIC examination reports, returns, related-party loans and licence standing; full diligence; heads of terms; engage the CBN before signing₦205m
Q2–Q3 Y1Sign SPA; file the change-of-control application; commit ₦1bn recapitalisation; constitute a board with a majority of independentsTarget price ₦1.0–2.2bn [verify]
Q4 Y1–Q2 Y2CBN approval and NDIC no-objection; CAC filings; recapitalisation paid; core banking migration; MD and CRO in post₦1bn

Target profile — and the profile to refuse. The right target is an active state MFB with ₦1–3bn of assets, 3–8 branches, ₦400m–₦1bn of paid-up capital, a real third-party deposit base, a clean examination history and no loans to its own directors. Refuse dormant "virgin" licences, FX-arbitrage-era shells, sanctioned entities and platforms whose licence cannot transfer. Sycamore paid for this lesson in July 2026: the Kano MFB licence it had just acquired was among the 46 revoked, days after closing (Nairametrics).

Licence acquisition is a first-ninety-days deliverable, not a caveat: mandate, target list, diligence and the CBN conversation all begin in Q1 of Year 1.

6. Capital requirement

Capital here is regulatory, not economic: the return comes from leverage against deposits, and capital exists to satisfy the CBN and absorb loss. Naira is the build; USD is indicative at ₦1,600.

T1 AcquireT2 Grow the MFBT3 Go commercialT4 National
WindowY1–Y2Y2–Y5Y5–Y8Y8–Y12+
Total₦6.5bn (USD 4.1m)₦14bn (USD 8.8m)₦72bn (USD 45m)₦240bn (USD 150m)
Regulatory capital (incl. acquisition ₦1.8bn in T1)₦1.0bn recapitalisation₦5.0bn national MFB₦50bn regional₦200bn national
Systems, branches, risk & compliance₦1.0bn₦4.5bn₦13bn₦25bn
Banking talent₦0.7bn₦2.4bn₦5bn₦12bn
Operating reserve (24 months)₦2.0bn₦1.2bn₦2bn₦8bn

(Tranche arithmetic — see NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md. T1 reconciles exactly, and needs no correction. The regulatory-capital row is labelled "incl. acquisition ₦1.8bn in T1", so T1 reads ₦1.0bn recapitalisation + ₦1.8bn acquisition + ₦1.0bn systems + ₦0.7bn talent + ₦2.0bn reserve = ₦6.5bn, the stated total; the ₦1.0bn is the CBN state-MFB recapitalisation requirement in §5, and the ₦1.8bn is the acquisition (against §5's ₦1.0–2.2bn target price). Read without that parenthetical the T1 rows appear to total ₦4.7bn, which is how the reported "₦6.5bn against ₦4.7bn" discrepancy arose — it is not a discrepancy. The other three columns do not reconcile, and this plan does not say which side is wrong: T2 sums to ₦13.1bn against a stated ₦14bn, T3 to ₦70bn against ₦72bn, T4 to ₦245bn against ₦240bn. The direction of the gap differs by column (two over, one under), so no single row can be identified as the error and no figure has been changed. All four totals are planning envelopes carried into 08_Akunnia_Group.md:402 as the ₦332.5bn national-tier locked regulatory capital, so they must not be silently restated. [verify] — the plan owner must either re-estimate the component rows or reset the column totals, column by column.)

Two rules. Regulatory capital must be paid-up, unencumbered and free of any Group cross-pledge — the CBN examines source of funds. And no tranche is released until the previous licence gate clears (09_Aku_Capital.md).

7. Unit economics

MetricMFB lendingCommercial lending
Gross loan yield35–48% p.a. (3–4% monthly)24–32% (MPR-linked)
Funding cost — deposits5–9%5–9%
Funding cost — wholesale22–30%22–30%
Net interest margin22–30%6–9%
Cost-to-income75–90% early, 62–70% at scaleIndustry ~55–65%
Provisioning / loss5–12% of book; CBN mandates 100% on classified loans2–4%
Return on equity at scale12–20%18–25%

Indicative ranges; [verify] against the target's audited accounts.

The two funding costs are the entire thesis. Funding ₦10bn of loans with deposits at 7% costs ₦700m a year; at 25%, ₦2.5bn. The ₦1.8bn annual difference exceeds the entire acquisition and recapitalisation cost of the bank, every year.

Branch versus digital. A staffed branch costing ₦35–60m a year needs ₦1.2–1.8bn of deposits to carry itself at a 3% spread; an agent outlet needs ₦50–80m. That is why the branch plan is a cluster, and why acquired branches are valued as deposit machinery, not property.

Fixed cost baseBreak-even loan bookBreak-even deposits
₦900m/yr (Y1–2)₦3.6bn at 25% NIM₦6bn
₦2.2bn/yr (Y3–5)₦8.8bn₦15bn
₦6.5bn/yr (Y6–8, commercial)₦81bn at 8% NIM (corrected — see below)~₦140bn

⚠️ Corrected: this row previously read ₦26bn of break-even book at 8% NIM, which is arithmetically impossible. ₦26bn × 8% = ₦2.08bn of net interest income against a ₦6.5bn fixed cost base — it covers under a third of it. ₦26bn is in fact the break-even at 25% NIM (₦6.5bn ÷ 0.25 = ₦26bn), so the row carried the microfinance-margin calculation under a commercial-margin label. At a genuine 8% NIM the break-even book is ₦6.5bn ÷ 0.08 = ₦81bn, and the deposit base needed to fund it at the table's own ~0.58 loan-to-deposit ratio is ~₦140bn. The corrected figure makes the commercial transition 3.1× harder than the table implied — which is the point the surrounding text already makes ("the commercial licence only on a much larger book at a thinner margin"), and it sharpens the requirement to enter Stage 3 already holding ₦30bn+ of deposits: that is a starting position, not the destination. (Corrected — see ../NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md.)

The honest read: the MFB breaks even on a small book at high margin; the commercial licence only on a much larger book at a thinner margin. Hence the requirement to reach Stage 3 holding ₦30bn+ of deposits and a branch network that cost nothing extra.

8. Organisation

First ten hires, in order. (1) Managing Director — a serving or recent Nigerian bank/MFB CEO with a clean fit-and-proper record; the hire that decides whether the CBN approves the change of control. (2) Chief Risk Officer — to the board risk committee, never the MD. (3) Chief Compliance Officer / MLRO. (4) CFO. (5) Head of Credit — micro-lending methodology and collections. (6) Head of Retail & Branch Operations — the deposit engine. (7) Head of Digital & Agent Banking. (8) Head of Internal Audit. (9) Company Secretary & Head of Legal — CBN filings and the related-party register. (10) Head of Treasury & ALM.

FunctionY1Y3Y5Y10
Executive46812
Lending & credit63090340
Branch operations & retail865190720
Digital, agents, technology51845160
Treasury & ALM261445
Risk, compliance, AML/CFT, audit41642150
Finance, HR, legal, corporate51540130
Total341564291,557

Fit-and-proper is a hard gate. The CBN assesses the MD, executive directors, CFO, CRO, CCO and every non-executive director on integrity, competence, financial soundness and time commitment, and must approve each appointment. The board must have a majority of independent directors and the Group may not control it. Undischarged bankrupts, persons with adverse regulatory findings, and anyone with an unresolved related-party exposure to the Group are disqualified.

Compensation. Bank pay is market pay: an MFB MD ₦60–120m, a commercial MD ₦150–350m [verify], with deferred bonuses subject to malus and clawback. Ownership does not entitle the family to discount management, and the CBN reads any attempt to do so as evidence of control.

9. Milestones

Y1 (2027)Y3 (2029)Y5 (2031)Y10 (2036)Y15 (2041)
LicenceTarget identified, SPA signed, change-of-control filedState MFB acquired and recapitalisedNational MFB (₦5bn)Regional commercial (₦50bn)National commercial (₦200bn)
Branches / agents012 + 180 agents28 + 600 agents90 + 2,500 agents180 + 6,000 agents
Deposits—₦8bn₦35bn₦450bn₦1.2trn

Cost-to-income—82%64%52%46%

Stage gates are capital gates. Deposit growth gates each licence upgrade: 60% of the Year-5 deposit base must be third-party, 75% by Year 10.

10. Risks

#RiskSeverityMitigation
1CBN approval delay or refusalCriticalOpen the CBN conversation before signing; two cleared alternates per board seat; no Aku Bank name pre-licence
2Hidden liabilities or a bad loan bookCriticalBuy only active, trading MFBs; read CBN and NDIC examination reports before price; escrow for undisclosed liabilities
3Recapitalisation cost ahead of planHighCapital released only on licence gates; retained earnings; buying a licence-holder already at the threshold is cheaper
4Related-party lending limitsCriticalTreat Group companies as third parties — market pricing, full collateral, approved by independents sitting alone; report exposure quarterly
5Draft Ring-Fencing Guidelines (June 2026)CriticalBars linked financial entities from lending to or guaranteeing each other without prior approval; caps cross-directorships at 20%; may require a non-operating holding company. Design to the final rule now: bank outside every cash pool, no cross-guarantee, no shared funding with Aku Credit or Aku Insurance. [verify]
6Credit lossesCriticalCap loan officers at 250–300 borrowers, follow-up within seven days (Lawyard); weekly amortisation; board-set concentration caps
7AML/CFT failureCriticalNamed MLRO; monitoring from day one; BVN/NIN KYC at onboarding; independent AML audit
8Management qualityCriticalCBN-approved MD with a real record; 60% of senior management hired externally; no family executive exempt from the same test
9Fintech deposit competition and macro shockHighCompete on cash, traders, farmers and Group supply chains, not app UX; naira-only book; no unhedged FX

11. Integration

CounterpartyWhat the bank givesWhat it receives
Aku Credit / Group creditDeposit funding at a fraction of wholesale costA credit relationship and named borrowers, lent at arm's length, never as an inter-financial loan
Aku TreasuryGroup operating, treasury and settlement accountsThe bank sits outside the cash pool entirely (13_Aku_Treasury.md)
Isiome, Uli, OkoduWorking capital, offtake settlement, freight and contractor paymentsDeposit anchors, transaction volume, a supply chain of borrowers
Aku InsuranceMicro-insurance and credit-life distributionUnderwriting and guarantees for Stage-3 trade finance
Aku TechnologyInternal systems customerCore banking and reporting on the Group's own stack
Idenze GroupInternships and a graduate pipelineBanking and finance graduates; Idenze Learning for CBN-recognised training

The governance firewall is the integration design. The bank has its own board, a majority of independent directors, its own audit and its own regulator relationship. Related-party transactions are benchmarked externally and approved by the independent directors sitting alone. It is not a subsidiary to be instructed but an institution the Group happens to own.

12. First ninety days

  1. Mandate bank-regulatory counsel and a transaction adviser, and pass the licence-acquisition plan as a board resolution with ₦250m budgeted — the action the whole plan depends on.
  2. Pull the CBN's MFB register and score 40 active state MFBs in Anambra and the South-East. Exclude every dormant licence.
  3. Open the CBN conversation before signing anything. Ask what the change-of-control file must contain, and build that file rather than guessing.
  4. Shortlist eight, then three, then one. Read the CBN and NDIC examination reports on each and price the licence separately from the book.
  5. Recruit the Managing Director and the Chief Risk Officer before completing. No credible MD, no CBN approval, and in that order.
  6. Design the independent board now — seven directors, four independent, with two cleared alternates per seat.
  7. Adopt the ring-fence resolution as a Group Board resolution, drafted to the June 2026 draft: no cash-pool participation, no cross-guarantee, no lending to linked financial entities.
  8. Commission the related-party and insider-lending policy — pricing, limits, approval by independents sitting alone, quarterly CBN reporting — before the first loan books.
  9. Build the deposit map — the Group's payroll, supplier, offtake, freight and contractor flows by entity and month. That number is the Year-1 deposit target and the honest test of the acquisition.
  10. Set the price discipline in writing — maximum payable for licence and book, a maximum recapitalisation, and a documented trigger to walk away. The discipline is refusing most licences shown.

Prepared for the Group Board and the Family Holdings Board. Companions: 08_Akunnia_Group.md §3 and §5, 13_Aku_Treasury.md, 09_Aku_Capital.md.

17 — IDENZE GROUP

Education & Human Capital + Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals — the third child's domain

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Idenze Group is her group; every company takes Idenze plus a plain function. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary throughout; dollar figures are indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026).

Position in the programme: third child. Follows 00_Family_Business.md, 01_Isiome_Group.md, 08_Akunnia_Group.md.
GroupIdenze Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group (the mother company)
HeirIdenze — Second Son, Senior Male Heir
SectorsEducation & Human Capital · Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals
CompaniesIdenze Pharma · Therapeutics · Consumer Health · Sterile & Injectables · Distribution · Research · University · Polytechnic · Schools · Learning · Healthcare
GeographyNkpor, Idemili North LGA — the largest land footprint in the Group
Horizon10–15 years, with accreditation and licensing front-loaded

Healthcare added after the domain review. Master Plan §6.3 names three healthcare assets under this domain — "a primary clinic serving all Ezeme staff estates and the Nkpor community, a University Teaching Hospital co-located with the institutional zone, and a pharmaceutical production unit" — and states that "the clinic is a welfare benefit that makes Ezeme estates attractive to skilled workers and their families" while "the teaching hospital is the clinical training ground for health science graduates." The pharmaceutical unit is covered by 18_Idenze_Pharma.md and its siblings; the clinic network and the teaching hospital are covered by 56_Idenze_Healthcare.md. Without the teaching hospital, Idenze University's health sciences programmes have no clinical training ground and cannot be accredited — so this is a precondition of the education half, not an optional addition to the medical half.

1. Thesis

Idenze Group owns the full human capital lifecycle: it builds people, and it keeps them alive and capable.

The Group's own words: "Education builds people; healthcare keeps them alive and capable. A healthy, educated workforce is the foundation of every other division."

Why these two belong together — and this is not a slogan. They are each other's engine in a way no other pairing in the Group is:

  • Education supplies pharma with pharmacists, chemists and lab technicians; with the clinical trial capability that turns a commodity generic into an evidence-backed, defensible brand; and with the research pipeline that makes the difference between a factory and a pharmaceutical company.
  • Pharma supplies education with the money to build and accredit campuses, with the placement and industry training that makes graduates employable, and with a reason for students to enrol — "every faculty produces graduates who enter a living industry."

The single most important structural claim in this plan: the Group's university and teaching hospital can run the pain, arthritis and cannabinoid trials in-house. No competitor in Nigeria can replicate that, because no competitor owns both a pharmaceutical manufacturer and an accredited medical school. It converts a commodity extract into a protected, evidence-backed brand.

And the frame is the Group's own: "education — and childhood itself — is the first investment. Before any expansion, the education and the wellbeing of all five children are funded and protected."

2. Market

Pharmaceuticals

The macro case is the strongest single import-substitution argument in the Group:

FactFigure
Africa's share of global disease burden25%
Africa's share of global population18%
Africa's share of global medicine output~3%
Medicines importedover 70%
Active pharmaceutical ingredients importedover 95%
Nigerian pharma marketUS$2.03bn (2023), 9.1% CAGR (IFC / World Bank)
Nigeria's share of ECOWAS drug manufacturing~60%
Only GMP-compliant Nigerian manufacturers~15%
Sector capacity utilisation40–50%

The interpretation matters more than the numbers. Africa does not have a demand problem — it has a manufacturing problem. Fifteen per cent GMP compliance and half-idle capacity mean the incumbents cannot absorb the demand that already exists, and the policy environment has just turned decisively in the industry's favour.

The policy tailwind — recent and real

  • October 2024 Executive Order removed tariffs, excise and VAT on pharmaceutical machinery, APIs, excipients and packaging for two years — with NGN 6bn+ in waivers to 47 of 115 enrolled manufacturers (Mar–Aug 2025).
  • Nigeria Tax Act 2025 made pharmaceuticals VAT zero-rated from 1 January 2026.
  • NAFDAC retained WHO Maturity Level 3 in June 2025 — the first African regulator to sustain it. Caveat: NAFDAC is not a WHO-Listed Authority, so ML3 confers no automatic international recognition.
  • PVAC's official target is 50% of local demand by 2030 — not the "70%" that circulates in three inconsistent public versions.
  • The counter-risk: 88 pharmaceutical plants were under construction as of March 2026 under the 5+5 policy. Heavy capacity arrives exactly when the Group would be building.

The competitive landscape

  • Emzor — US$23m API plant at Sagamu, first in sub-Saharan Africa. The most serious local competitor in APIs.
  • Fidson — ₦84.1bn revenue (FY2024), and ₦119bn revenue with ₦13.8bn PBT (FY2025). The scale benchmark.
  • May & Baker and Neimeth — both building in Anambra. Neimeth is the cautionary case: ₦4.5bn revenue and a ₦1.7bn net loss in 2024, driven by a ₦2bn FX loss on USD debt. The Group's financing rules exist because of this.
  • Jawa International — Indian-owned beta-lactam plant, Lagos, December 2024.
  • Importers — Indian and Chinese generics exporters. The incumbent to displace.

Education

  • JAMB 2025: 2,007,312 applicants, 1,009,044 admitted across all tertiary institutions — the constraint is not seats, it is credible seats.
  • 159 licensed private universities by July 2025, with the Minister publicly conceding many fail quality standards.
  • Outbound education: US$1.39bn in H1 2025 alone (~US$2.8bn annualised), cited by the CBN Governor as an FX driver. That is the market-share target.
  • Acquisition pipeline: the ~53 under-capitalised new licensees are not only competitors but candidates for acquisition — the same accreditation-arbitrage logic the Group applies elsewhere.

The gap in both halves of this domain is the same: credibility. In pharma it is GMP certification. In education it is accreditation. Idenze Group's moat is holding both.

3. Product & service lines

The pharma platform

Idenze Pharma — generics manufacturing. Full plan at 18_Idenze_Pharma.md. Wave 1 molecules are chosen for BCS Class I/III biowaiver eligibility — paracetamol, metformin, amlodipine, ORS — which avoids US$120k–400k and 12–18 months per molecule in in vivo bioequivalence studies. That single sequencing decision determines whether the plant reaches revenue in year two or year four. Beta-lactams are excluded from Phase 1 because a dedicated ventilated block is separate capex, not a line extension.

Idenze Therapeutics — cannabinoid-derived medicines. Full plan at 19_Idenze_Therapeutics.md. The structure is settled and fully licensed:

  • No cultivation in Nigeria — no licensing pathway exists
  • South Africa holds the first licence of record (SAHPRA GACP + GMP) — acquire, don't build: $2.5–7m rather than $8–15m, 6–12 months rather than 24–36
  • Ghana is the destination licence, held through a qualified family member's Indefinite Residence
  • Nigeria manufactures the finished dose under NAFDAC Narcotics & Controlled Substances import permits
  • CBD-dominant first, anchored on chronic pain, arthritis, spasticity, chemo-induced nausea and refractory epilepsy
  • Ring-fenced in its own vehicle with its own board, so a regulatory problem in one jurisdiction can never reach the university's accreditation or the Group's banking

Idenze Consumer Health — OTC and retail brand. Analgesics, topicals, ORS, vitamins. The consumer-facing brand that generates cash while the institutional business builds, and the volume base that absorbs the plant's fixed cost.

Idenze Sterile & Injectables. Higher-barrier manufacturing — hospital and emergency supply. A separate clean-room capex step, entered only once oral solids are profitable.

Idenze Distribution. Licensed wholesale across ECOWAS. Also the anchor customer for Idenze Pharma: committing a defined share of output to the Group's own distributor from launch guarantees base-load throughput and de-risks the first eighteen months of selling.

Idenze Research. The clinical and analytical arm — bioequivalence studies, stability testing, formulation development, and the investigator-initiated trials that generate the evidence. Runs on the university's and teaching hospital's capability.

The education platform

Idenze University. Full plan at 24_Idenze_University.md. 100 hectares in the institutional zone, NUC-registered, ten faculties mapped to the Group's ten sectors. Capital to first intake ₦253.3bn — ~US$158m at this plan's ₦1,600/USD (the university plan itself states ~US$188m, because it computes its dollar column at ₦1,350/USD; the naira figure is the same and is the one to use). Break-even ~3,000 students, with a funded ₦2.5–4bn/yr deficit across the first four teaching years. NUC requires private universities to be on a permanent site within five years — building on the 100 hectares from day one turns a compliance obligation into a marketing asset.

Idenze Polytechnic. NBTE-accredited, ND and HND, 20 hectares. First intake targets Years 7–9 — earlier than the university, because NBTE requirements are less capital-intensive than NUC. Eleven departments, each tied to a live industry: soft furnishings and textile technology, furniture and wood technology, agricultural technology, electrical and electronic engineering, civil engineering, mechanical engineering, business administration, computer science and IT, mass communication, logistics and transport, plumbing and water engineering.

This is the more immediately valuable education asset. NBTE-accredited programmes can supply machine operators, QC technicians and engineering assistants years before a university exists — which is exactly what Idenze Pharma, Isiome Foods and Okodu Power need in their first three years.

Idenze Schools. Primary and secondary network — launch Years 4–6, and the first revenue-generating assets in the education cluster. Two secondary schools (boys' and girls') feed the polytechnic and university pipelines. The replication engine — the accredited model is what gets licensed into other markets, not the institution.

Idenze Learning. EdTech, curriculum, standards and accreditation-as-a-service. The arm that licenses the accredited model to partner schools across Africa, and the Group's answer to the NUC rule that multi-campus across states is prohibited — the model travels, not the institution.

4. Operating model

The clinical-research loop — the structural advantage

```

Idenze University ──► pharmacists, chemists, lab technicians ──► Idenze Pharma

│ │

│ ▼

└──► Idenze Research ◄── teaching hospital trials ◄── evidence-backed brands

│

└──► funds campus growth + gives graduates somewhere to work

```

One governance caveat, and it is a real one: when the sponsor owns the trial site, regulators and reviewers question the evidence. The hospital's research governance must be visibly independent — separate research ethics committee, documented conflict-of-interest policy, and publication rights that sit with the investigators. Get this wrong and the evidence is not accepted, which destroys the entire advantage.

The licensing and accreditation reality

  • NAFDAC requires an Authority to Manufacture — not a "manufacturing licence"
  • Product registration takes 240 working days from acceptance, and the clock stops on compliance queries
  • API sourcing is a regulatory gate, not a procurement preference: NAFDAC-approved sources, compliance from January 2027
  • GS1 serialisation is mandatory under Traceability 2.0
  • The head of production must be a registered pharmacist in Nigeria, and production and quality heads must be independent of each other
  • QA reports to the board, not the MD — the single control that protects the licence

Manufacturing discipline

Excluded from Phase 1: beta-lactams (separate ventilated block) and sterile injectables (separate clean room). Enter them as capital steps, never as line extensions.

The Group rule for this domain: licence it, or buy the licensee

No licence or accreditation here is a reason to defer or omit a business. The Group either obtains it, or buys the institution that already holds it. In education and health that rule bites harder than anywhere else in the Group, because accreditation — not buildings — is the moat. NUC and NBTE accreditation, MDCN training recognition and NAFDAC product registrations are slow, granted programme-by-programme and molecule-by-molecule, expensive to replicate, and they sit in the entity that holds them — so a share purchase carries them and a de novo application does not. The supply of holders is real: Nigeria carries a long tail of under-enrolled private schools, fragmented private hospitals and dormant NAFDAC registrations. The market that prices them is private and thin, so the Group's own survey sets the price, not a published index. The company plans carry the detail; this is the portfolio view.

Three transactions carry most of the value, and the ninety-day work must price them: a licensed, MDCN-eligible hospital — which is also the clinical site the medical school cannot be accredited without; a licensed pharmaceutical wholesaler — state-by-state coverage takes years to build and weeks to buy; and a portfolio of under-enrolled schools — the replication engine itself. Two instruments resist purchase, and the plans say so plainly rather than pretending otherwise: NCS/NDLEA authorisations, which are earned, and NUC licensing, where what changes hands is control of an existing licensee, not the licence.

First ninety days — commission the domain acquisition register. One mandate to Aku Advisory with one regulatory counsel: a single register of 40–60 named targets across the three cohorts — school groups, private hospitals, licensed manufacturers and wholesalers — each with licence and accreditation holdings, ownership, capacity, published or indicated price, and the change-of-control route. Budget ₦185m: ₦120m advisory and valuation, ₦45m legal opinions, one per regulator, and ₦20m for data rooms and site visits [verify]. It is the cheapest line in the domain, and it converts every "we will license it" in these plans into a priced alternative.

The quantified case for licensing the model rather than building institutions

Idenze Learning delivers the sharpest number in this domain, and it is the economic argument for the whole education strategy. Cost per student reached:

VehicleCost per student place
Idenze Learning (licensed model)₦0.28m (US$178)
Idenze Polytechnic₦6.5m
Idenze Schools₦6.96m
Idenze University₦21.2m

Licensing the accredited model reaches a student for roughly 1/74th of the cost of an owned university place. That single ratio justifies the entire pan-African education ambition — it is why the model travels and the campus does not.

And the moratorium is counter-cyclical for this business. If new institutional licensing is frozen, the value of services to existing licensees rises — because incumbents still need accreditation, management and quality assurance, and there are fewer new entrants to compete with them. So Idenze Learning's revenue is counter-cyclical to new licensing, which is a useful hedge rather than a vulnerability.

Sequencing discipline the plan imposes on itself: curriculum licensing cannot precede proof. In Year 5 the Group has two schools open and no accredited polytechnic — so advisory and teacher training monetise the regulatory learning curve from Year 2, curriculum licensing follows the schools' WASSCE record from Year 6, and tertiary licensing follows NBTE/NUC accreditation. Selling a curriculum before the Group has a track record would be selling an unproven product.

⚠️ A second market-shaping event: the NERDC textbook ranking regime

From September 2026, only NERDC-licensed and nationally ranked titles may be used in Nigerian public schools. The bar is a 70% minimum score, with only 6–10 titles per subject admitted. Fees are ₦1,500 per page plus ₦750,000 per title — about ₦1,050,000 per book before printing, or roughly ₦35.7m for a full curriculum, and non-refundable if the title fails. The Nigerian Publishers Association is litigating it.

Two consequences.

  1. This is an opening for a capitalised entrant, not a barrier. Most Nigerian publishers are small and cannot absorb ₦35.7m of non-refundable application fees across a curriculum. Idenze Group can — and its own schools, polytechnic and university are captive demand that de-risks the first print run. But the plan must carry a fallback that does not depend on the policy surviving, given the litigation.
  2. It connects to the piracy problem directly. Copyright Act 2022 s.23(3) removes the statutory photocopying exception where a licensing scheme exists — so joining Repronig converts an unenforceable right into an enforceable one. That is a concrete Year-1 action, not a legal nicety.

And the Igbo-language case is commercially proven, not sentimental: Kawuriz and Manilas built a business on a single Igbo primary text that still sells ≥500,000 units a year.

⚠️ The education licensing window has moved — this supersedes part of the sequencing above

Two moratoria and a repeal bill now sit over both education institutions, and no earlier version of this plan accounted for them.

  • February 2025: a one-year moratorium on new polytechnic and monotechnic registration.
  • March 2026: a six-year moratorium on the establishment of tertiary institutions. Most coverage frames it around private universities, but several outlets headlined it as covering tertiary institutions generally. Whether it reaches NBTE-registered private polytechnics is genuinely unclear from public reporting.
  • A Senate bill to repeal the NBTE Act is also before the National Assembly, so the regulator's own mandate is in play.

Consequences.

  1. "Polytechnic first, then university" is now conditional, not settled. The sequencing logic still holds — NBTE requirements are far less capital-intensive than NUC's, and the polytechnic costs roughly US$4,040 per student place against the university's US$15,700, about a quarter — but both routes may be closed to new registrations.
  2. The fallback is the accreditation-arbitrage play the Group already applies to universities: acquire or partner an existing accredited institution. That preserves the Years 7–9 timeline instead of losing six years, and it is the same logic the Group uses generally — buy the licence rather than build it.
  3. The Group's own plans contain two NBTE institutions and this has never been reconciled. The Master Plan specifies both Idenze Polytechnic (Years 7–9) and the Akuzo Technical & Vocational College (Year 12). Under a moratorium, only one licence may be obtainable. Recommendation: concentrate the licence, capital and faculty in the polytechnic, and run Akuzo's programmes as satellite cohorts — one accredited institution with two sites, not two institutions competing for one closed window.
  4. The polytechnic's economics depend on a B2B engine, not tuition. A standalone workshop-intensive institution at Anambra fee levels does not break even on tuition alone — break-even is roughly 5,600 students on tuition and boarding, beyond planned capacity, falling to about 3,600 only with an industry-services engine running. That engine — industry training, testing and calibration, apprenticeship assessment, worth on the order of ₦1.4bn a year — is not a side line. It is what makes the institution viable, and the Group's own companies are its anchor customers. Staff cost runs ~51% of revenue at maturity against the university's 34%, because workshop instruction needs more technicians and smaller groups.

Action: written clarification from NBTE and the Federal Ministry of Education on whether the March 2026 moratorium covers private polytechnics, before any T1 capital is committed. Acquire-or-partner is the fallback if the answer is no.

Two blocking unknowns still unresolved, and they gate real spend:

  1. Ghana eligibility — citizens only, or citizens and permanent residents? Press reports conflict. Read it off NACOC's own instrument.
  2. Will NAFDAC NCS accept SAHPRA GMP as the basis for a narcotics import permit?

Do not commit capital against either until answered in writing.

11. Integration

Supplies to:

  • Every Group domain — trained operators, technicians, engineers and administrators. The Group's own talent supply chain.
  • Isiome Group — agricultural research, and a market for its food output through canteens and catering.
  • Okodu Group — clinical and pharmaceutical demand for power, water and construction; and the teaching hospital as a flagship build.
  • Aku Capital — long-life regulated assets with predictable revenue (university, hospital, plant), and the income-share facility for student affordability.
  • Uli Group — content and media training; the media and communication faculty feeds Uli directly.

Buys from:

  • Isiome Group — botanical and herbal inputs for pharmaceutical production. The single most important cross-domain supply line in the Group.
  • Okodu Group — construction, power, water, real estate
  • Uli Group — pharmaceutical and food distribution through Uli Freight; licensed controlled-substance movement through Uli Special Logistics — a genuine moat, since narcotics transit requires authorisations almost no competitor holds
  • Akunnia Group — capital, insurance, treasury, legal
  • Aku Technology — the data, quality and reporting systems the regulated businesses must run on

The internal advantage, stated plainly: Idenze Pharma does not need to find its first customer — Idenze Distribution is contractually committed from launch. Idenze University does not need to find its first students' employers — every faculty feeds a live Group industry. And Idenze Research does not need to buy trial capacity — the teaching hospital is its own.

12. First ninety days

  1. Ask NACOC the two questions in writing — eligibility (citizens vs citizens and permanent residents) and whether the ownership test binds shareholders, directors or both. Nothing in the cannabinoid programme should be spent on until answered.
  2. Ask NAFDAC NCS in writing whether SAHPRA GMP certification supports a narcotics import permit. This determines whether South Africa is mandatory.
  3. Commission the pharma plant tender to at least three vendors, with the Authority to Manufacture pathway documented step by step. Reconcile the ₦21bn lean-plant estimate against competitive tender — it is a benchmark, not a quotation.
  4. Begin the PCN premises process and recruit the registered pharmacist who will head production. This is a statutory precondition, not a hiring preference.
  5. Secure the university land — 100 hectares — before any announcement. Cheapest thing to get right, most expensive to get wrong.
  6. Start the NBTE pathway for the polytechnic in parallel with NUC. NBTE is faster and cheaper, and it supplies the operators the pharma plant needs years earlier.
  7. Design the clinical-research governance now — independent ethics committee, conflict-of-interest policy, investigator publication rights. Retro-fitting independence never convinces a reviewer.
  8. Route the student-affordability facility through Aku Capital — private-university students are excluded from NELFUND, so the deferred-payment and income-share design is a precondition of enrolment, not an afterthought.
  9. Commission the domain acquisition register — one mandate to Aku Advisory plus regulatory counsel: 40–60 named targets across schools, private hospitals and licensed manufacturers or wholesalers, each with its licence and accreditation holdings, ownership, capacity, indicated price and change-of-control route. Budget ₦185m. Every plan in this domain claims it will licence what it needs; this register is what makes those claims costed rather than assumed.

1. Thesis

What it is. A WHO-GMP-standard oral solid dosage plant on the Nkpor campus that formulates, manufactures, packages and registers essential medicines — antimalarials, antibiotics, analgesics, antihypertensives, antidiabetics and oral rehydration salts — for the Nigerian trade, institutional buyers and, later, ECOWAS export.

Why it wins.

  1. Africa imports over 70% of its medicines and over 95% of its active pharmaceutical ingredients, mainly from India and China. It carries 25% of the global disease burden and 18% of the population but produces 3% of the world's medicines (Gavi / The Conversation, 2025).
  2. Incumbent supply is thin. PMG-MAN says its members meet only ~30% of Nigerian consumer demand (Nigeria Health Watch, 2025). NAFDAC put import dependence near 60% in late 2025; the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria argues it exceeds 70% (BusinessDay). GSK and Sanofi exited in 2023, vacating brand and shelf space.
  3. Policy has turned. The October 2024 Executive Order removed tariffs, excise duty and VAT on pharmaceutical machinery, APIs, excipients, reagents and packaging for two years; NGN 6bn+ in waivers reached 47 of 115 enrolled manufacturers between March and August 2025. The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 made pharmaceutical products zero-rated from 1 January 2026, so input VAT on capital is recoverable (BusinessDay).

Why now. NAFDAC retained WHO Maturity Level 3 in June 2025 — the first African regulator to sustain the rating, with 27 of 57 ML4 indicators closed (NAFDAC). A local site under an ML3 regulator is now a credible institutional and regional supplier; five years ago it was not.

Why first. Idenze Pharma builds the three things that cannot be bought — GMP capability, the NAFDAC relationship and a distribution network — which every other Idenze pharma line will then use.

One sentence. Nigeria spends over three billion dollars a year on medicines it largely imports, supplied by an industry meeting under a third of demand, under Africa's first sustained ML3 regulator — and Idenze Pharma is a family-funded manufacturer able to hold the multi-year regulatory and capital clock most Nigerian entrants cannot survive.

2. Market

Continental. The AfDB has estimated ~US$11bn is needed to build Africa's manufacturing base (Gavi; see also the AfDB pharmaceutical industry report) — verify against the primary report before using it in fundraising. The AfCFTA pharmaceutical market is put at US$28.56bn rising to US$63bn by 2030 (Voice of Nigeria).

Nigeria. The most authoritative anchor is the IFC/World Bank country diagnostic: US$2.03bn of pharmaceutical sales in 2023, 14.6% of healthcare spending, growing at a 9.1% seven-year compound rate (2016–2023). Registered manufacturers rose from 115 to 186 between 2018 and 2024 and output more than doubled — but only ~15% of Nigerian manufacturers have GMP-compliant facilities, and sector capacity utilisation is 40–50% (IFC/World Bank CPSD, 2025). Other estimates run higher — Coherent Market Insights puts 2026 at US$3.34bn (9.5% CAGR to 2033), and KPMG cites US$2–4.5bn for 2023–26. Plan on the IFC figure and treat US$2.0–4.5bn as the credible range. Nigeria holds ~60% of ECOWAS drug manufacturing.

Structural read. Finished-dose formulation has localised faster than high-value inputs. Imported finished units reportedly fell from 4.03bn to 1.13bn by 2025 (PMG-MAN), yet local manufacturers still cannot meet demand. That gap — volume demand, weak local supply, value leaking abroad — is the business.

A credible, inspection-grade, locally owned volume manufacturer — not a packer — serving three buyers a packer cannot: the private trade at scale, where brand trust is available after the multinational exits; institutional buyers (NHIA/HMOs, ministries, teaching hospitals) who need a clean inspection record; and ECOWAS public buyers under WAHO harmonisation and AfCFTA. Nkpor sits within a few kilometres of the Onitsha/Ogbo Idenze Pharma medicine market — our greatest distribution advantage and our biggest reputational hazard (§10).

4. Operating model

Plant. A single-storey, purpose-built ~3,500 m² GMP building: production 1,200 m² (dispensing, granulation, compression, coating, capsule filling, packaging, one-way material and personnel flow); warehouse 900 m² with quarantine/released/rejected segregation and a cold room; QC laboratory 450 m²; utilities 500 m²; QA and admin 450 m².

Capacity. Phase 1 nameplate ~500m tablet/capsule units a year on one shift over 300 days; a second shift reaches ~900m without new equipment. Phase 3 reaches ~1.5–2.0bn units.

Technology. Wet granulation (rapid mixer granulator plus fluid bed dryer) and direct compression; two rotary presses, moving to a high-speed unit on expansion; auto-coater; dosing-disc capsule filler; alu-PVC blister packing with a defined upgrade to alu-alu for ACTs; inline vision inspection, checkweighing and metal detection; GS1 DataMatrix serialisation, which NAFDAC's Traceability 2.0 framework makes mandatory — a market-access prerequisite, not an option. ERP, LIMS and eQMS from day one — paper-based quality systems will not survive a modern inspection at this scale.

Power is a design input, not an operating variable. Nigerian manufacturers spent NGN 1.34tn on alternative energy in 2025, up 71.4% in two years (MAN, via Punch). Specify a dedicated transformer and feeder, 400 kWp solar PV with ~1 MWh storage for daytime base load, and two 400 kVA dual-fuel gensets for backup and steam. Add reverse-osmosis purified water with electrodeionisation, Grade C and D HVAC zones with terminal HEPA filtration and documented pressure cascades, oil-free compressed air, chillers and a steam boiler. Voltage instability corrupts pressure cascades and invalidates batches.

APIs. India first, China second, with at least two approved sources per molecule — the best defence against a supplier quality failure or export restriction. Source qualification is now a regulatory gate, not just a procurement preference: NAFDAC requires APIs and excipients to come from NAFDAC-approved listed sources, with compliance required by January 2027, and it applies heightened enforcement to Chinese and Indian origins (Channels TV). Require WHO-GMP certification, a CEP or USDMF where available, an audit and a retained-sample programme. Lead time is 60–90 days door to door including clearing: hold 4–6 months of API cover and 3 months of packaging cover. Cartons, leaflets and labels are locally sourceable; blister film and aluminium are imported and must be dual-sourced.

Quality. ICH Q7/Q10-aligned: quality manual, deviation and CAPA, change control, annual product quality reviews, validated methods, ICH Zone IVb stability programmes, computerised system validation. Quality Assurance reports to the board, not the Managing Director. That reporting line protects the licence.

Distribution. Third-party logistics into the Onitsha coordinated wholesale centre and Lagos for the open trade and chain pharmacy; a direct institutional desk for HMOs, NHIA, state schemes and teaching hospitals; an export desk selling to licensed ECOWAS distributors on WAHO-harmonised dossiers. Selling through the group's own wholesale licence is a Year 4+ goal, not a Year 1 dependency.

The acquisition route — buy the registrations, and buy the manufacturer if the price justifies it.

The 240-day clock, not construction, is this plan's binding constraint. So the Group's rule applies directly: no licence or registration here is a reason to defer the business — the Group obtains it, or buys the entity that already holds it. Registration is slow, molecule-by-molecule and per SKU, the clock stops on every query, and the dossier, artwork and market presence come with the certificate. Nigeria holds a long tail of dormant and under-exploited registrations whose holders cannot fund the launch — and that is the supply the Group wants.

What to diligence, and the strategic choice the acquisition forces. Diligence the licence, not the building. A plant without a current Authority to Manufacture, a current GMP certificate and a closed-out corrective-action record is a shed with pipework: verify the Authority's currency, the last inspection report and any outstanding findings, the GMP certificate's validity, and — the item most often skipped — the actual registered product list, because a manufacturer whose registrations do not overlap the Wave 1 molecules is a real-estate purchase wearing a regulatory story. And the acquisition forces a decision the plan should name rather than discover late: the Authority to Manufacture attaches to the site. Buying a manufacturer gives a licensed site at its own address, not a right to move it to Nkpor. So the choice is explicit — a bridge (launch Wave 1 at the acquired licensed site while Nkpor is built and licensed, de-risking T1 and possibly re-sequencing it) or a substitute (buy, and stop building). Either is defensible; what is not defensible is buying a licensed plant and still spending US$12.6m on a parallel one without re-testing the case — which is why §12's day-90 gate must now include this register's answer.

First ninety days — commission the licensed-manufacturer and registration register. Every NAFDAC-licensed oral-solid manufacturer in the South-East and Lagos: current Authority to Manufacture status, GMP certificate status and last inspection findings, site capacity and dosage forms, the full registered product list, ownership and availability; plus a screened list of dormant or seller-available registrations in the Wave 1 molecules, with the transfer mechanic and NAFDAC's written position on it. Budget ₦95m — ₦45m advisory, valuation and registry search, ₦30m legal and regulatory opinions on change of control and certificate transfer, ₦20m site audits and GMP records review [verify]. This register is the only work in the quarter that can reduce T1's size, and it is cheap beside the ₦21bn lean-plant estimate it is testing.

Cost insight. For low-value solids, packaging — not the API — is the largest single cost line, typically 35–50% of variable cost on a paracetamol tablet. On ACTs the API dominates. Hence Wave 1 buys scale in simple solids, Wave 3 buys margin in fixed-dose combinations, and blister film sourcing is a board-level procurement issue.

Break-even. Year-3 fixed costs (plant overheads, QA/QC, regulatory, engineering and maintenance, insurance, security, depreciation, finance) are estimated at NGN 3.1bn a year. At a portfolio-weighted contribution of NGN 14 per tablet-equivalent unit, break-even is ~220m units — about 44% of Phase 1 nameplate. Achievable, not comfortable, and the reason the mix must weight toward antibiotics, antidiabetics and ACTs rather than paracetamol alone.

Steady state (Y8–10): gross margin 45–55%, EBITDA 18–25%, net 10–15% after FX and finance costs. Revenue: zero in Y1–2 by design; ~US$4m in Y3; ~US$14m by Y5; base case US$42m by Y10, stretch US$70m. Calibration: Fidson — the benchmark listed Nigerian manufacturer — reached NGN 119bn (≈US$85m at ₦1,400) in FY2025 after thirty years in business, so our base case is roughly half its present scale and the stretch case approaches it. Plan on the base case; hold the stretch as ambition.

The sensitivity that dominates. APIs and packaging are 55–65% of cost of goods, roughly 85% of that dollar-denominated, against naira revenue. A 20% naira depreciation with a six-month repricing lag erases the entire gross margin. Mitigations: a monthly FX-linked pricing formula in institutional contracts; 4–6 months of API cover as a natural hedge; naira terms with local packaging suppliers; forward hedging through group treasury from Year 4.

11. Integration

Idenze Pharma will be the group's first operating company with an inspection-grade quality system, making it both a customer and a supplier inside Ezeme Group.

What it buys. From Okodu Group: EPC delivery of the plant, captive power design, ongoing utilities and facilities maintenance — the group builds under its own construction entity for cost visibility and quality control. From Uli Group: primary distribution, warehousing, cold chain and ECOWAS freight, plus brand production for the consumer range. From Isiome Group: cassava-derived starch and, later, standardised botanical inputs for a herbal-medicine registration where NAFDAC permits — modest and not a Phase 1 dependency, because pharmacopoeial-grade excipients are a Year 6+ opportunity, not an agricultural supply contract. From Akunnia Group: treasury and the FX hedging policy, the working-capital facility, insurance and group audit.

What it supplies. the pharma-distribution arm (name pending), Idenze's wholesale arm, is the anchor customer: committing a defined share of output to the group's own licensed distributor from launch guarantees base-load throughput and de-risks the first eighteen months of selling. Idenze University is a genuine, durable moat but a late one — NUC pre-accreditation begins around Year 8 and first intake in Years 12–14, so it can supply neither staff, hospital demand nor clinical trials in the early years. Do not build this plan on it; design the plant for it instead, reserving space for a hospital-formulary packing line and retaining batch documentation to a standard that supports clinical comparators and investigator-initiated trials. That is how commodity products become evidence-backed brands no Nigerian generic competitor can replicate. Idenze Polytechnic is the more immediately valuable education link: NBTE-accredited ND programmes can supply machine operators, QC technicians and engineering assistants years before a university exists, and a structured training scheme from Year 2 is the cheapest answer to risk 7.

One caution. Internal sourcing must never compromise GMP compliance. If the group's construction, logistics or security arm cannot meet the standard, the work goes outside and the decision is documented. The licence outranks the synergy.

12. First ninety days

  1. Incorporate Idenze Pharma Ltd, adopt articles, constitute the board, open the search for two independent directors (Idenze + Akunnia).
  2. Title and ring-fence the Nkpor plot; commission topographic and geotechnical surveys; confirm feeder capacity in writing with EEDC (Okodu Group).
  3. File PCN premises registration (Form B) and begin recruiting the superintendent pharmacist (regulatory lead).
  4. Hold the NAFDAC pre-application meeting, tabling plant classification, licence route, inspection standard, the Wave 1 molecule list and bioequivalence expectations per molecule. This written response is the quarter's most valuable output (MD designate + counsel).
  5. Commission the product-selection study: for twelve candidate molecules, a BCS review against the NAFDAC Bioequivalence Guideline 2025, firm API quotes from three Indian suppliers, a Nigerian price audit, and a biowaiver-versus-BE decision per molecule (regulatory + commercial).
  6. Build the bottom-up bill of materials and cost model for the top six molecules, replacing §7's illustrative table (Finance and Cost Controller).
  7. Issue RFQs to three engineering houses (two Indian, one European) for indicative capex, programme and process-flow proposals (Engineering).
  8. Open the MD and Head of QA searches, and approach two or three senior Indian or South African GMP figures about expatriate advisory contracts (Idenze).
  9. Open the debt conversation with Bank of Industry on the Afreximbank-backed healthcare window, and brief Akunnia on the hedging and gearing policy (Akunnia Group).
  10. Retain Nigerian pharmaceutical regulatory counsel for an opinion on the licence pathway and any Anambra State requirements (counsel).
  11. Commission the environmental and social assessment with NESREA and the Anambra State Ministry of Environment (Okodu Group).
  12. Establish the ring-fencing record: a board minute confirming that this company's board, licence and audit are its own and that no other Idenze Group regulated activity is carried on within it (Idenze + Group Board).
  13. Commission the licensed-manufacturer and registration register (regulatory + Akunnia): every NAFDAC-licensed oral-solid manufacturer in the South-East and Lagos, with Authority to Manufacture and GMP status, capacity, registered product list, ownership and availability; plus dormant or seller-available registrations in the Wave 1 molecules and NAFDAC's written position on transferring them. Budget ₦95m. A registered product, or a licensed site, is cheaper than the 240-day clock and the ₦21bn plant it would otherwise justify — and this register is what tests that trade before T1 is released.

The day-90 gate. Proceed to T1 only if all four hold: (i) written NAFDAC confirmation of the licence and registration pathway; (ii) at least four Wave 1 molecules confirmed biowaiver-eligible, or their BE costed and accepted; (iii) competitive capex proposals within ±20% of the US$12.6m T1 budget; and (iv) the Managing Director and Head of Quality Assurance identified and reachable. If any fails, delay T1 by six months rather than proceed. The cheapest money ever spent in this business is the money not yet committed to a plant.

Prepared for the Ezeme Group Board and Idenze Group. Market, regulatory and pricing figures carry source links; capital and unit-economics figures are planning estimates at NGN 1,400/USD requiring local verification before capital commitment.

Idenze Therapeutics — Cannabinoid-Derived Therapeutics

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary in this plan; it uses ₦1,500/USD. Spot was about ₦1,328/USD (CBN NFEM, Sept 2026). Dollar figures are indicative only and are not comparable across plans — each plan used a different rate. The library planning rate for cross-plan comparison is ₦1,600/USD. See plans/README.md.

Business plan · Ezeme Group

Operating company Idenze Therapeutics Ltd (to be incorporated, Nigeria) · Holdco Idenze Group (Pharma & Education) · Chain Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Mauritius GBC → Ezeme Group Nigeria Ltd → Idenze Group → Idenze Therapeutics · Licensed nodes Nkpor, Idemili North LGA, Anambra State (finished dose) · South Africa (SAHPRA GACP + GMP, licence of record) · Ghana (NACOC, long-term holder).

Standing rule. Every activity here is licensable, licensed and disclosed to the regulator that licenses it. Licences are granted to the named licensee and are non-transferable; holding one for another party's benefit is a licence breach that voids it and exposes individuals to prosecution. NACOC has warned publicly that no entity is authorised to facilitate the acquisition of cannabis licences (NACOC). There are no nominees or fronts anywhere in this chain.

1. Thesis

Nigeria's absence of a cannabis licensing pathway does not remove Nigerian demand for cannabinoid medicines — it hands the licence, the margin and the manufacturing value-added to South Africa. Idenze Therapeutics captures that value instead: the licence of record sits where one is issued (South Africa first, Ghana long-term, Malawi deferred), the finished dosage form is made at Nkpor under NAFDAC's narcotics regime, and the plant, brand, IP and jobs stay in Nigeria.

Why the licence is the asset. Extraction trains, containment suites and tableting lines can be bought by anyone with capital. A SAHPRA GACP and GMP licence, a NACOC licence under Ghana's 11-licence regime, a NAFDAC Narcotics and Controlled Substances (NCS) import permit, or a per-market product registration with its narcotics import permit cannot. They take years, are non-transferable, revocable, and tied to the named licensee's conduct. Idenze Therapeutics's enterprise value is therefore the net present value of a portfolio of licences and registrations, plus the plant those licences make legal to operate. Hence licensing is front-loaded, licence hygiene outranks growth whenever the two conflict, and regulatory affairs is a board-level function.

2. Market

Global. Medical cannabis is commonly sized at $30–40bn today, forecast into the $100–160bn range by the early 2030s (GrowerIQ, Expert Market Research, IMARC). Definitions vary widely, so treat these as directional. Our segment is narrower and far more valuable per kilogram: GMP-certified, standardised, registered cannabinoid medicines for named clinical indications, constrained by licences rather than demand.

Africa. South Africa dominates, with roughly 120 medical cannabis cultivation, manufacturing and export licences issued (dtic/IDC). Ghana has launched a Medicinal Cannabis Regulatory Programme under an 11-licence regime (GNA) and opened applications (NewsGhana). Yet Africa imports over 70% of its medicines (Gavi): the continent sells raw extract and buys back finished medicine.

The gap Nigeria's prohibition creates. Nigeria is Africa's largest population and one of its largest analgesic markets, with no cannabis licensing pathway — the National Assembly is only drafting a reform bill (Pulse, International CBC). Prohibition removes domestic supply, not demand: every Nigerian patient needing a cannabinoid medicine is served by an import, and the licence, margin and employment sit in South Africa or Europe.

Pain and arthritis. Nigerian COPCORD-model community surveys report a heavy rheumatic and musculoskeletal disease burden in adults (PMC), with knee osteoarthritis among the commonest tertiary rheumatology presentations (African Journal of Rheumatology). The addressable market is not "all pain patients" but the subset where NSAIDs, opioids or standard anti-inflammatories are inadequate, contraindicated or poorly tolerated, plus refractory paediatric epilepsy and chemotherapy-induced nausea. Nigerian volume, price and channel data must be commissioned locally — Euromonitor is a starting point, not an answer.

3. Product & service lines

CBD-dominant first, THC-constrained later. CBD is regulated far more liberally across Africa and Ghana's framework is hemp-oriented (≤0.3% THC), so a CBD portfolio needs fewer narcotics authorisations, registers faster and carries less political exposure. THC products come later — not because they are worth less, but because they are less survivable if something goes wrong early.

Anchor indications: chronic pain · arthritis and inflammatory joint disease · spasticity · chemotherapy-induced nausea · refractory epilepsy. Not general wellness — wellness framing destroys pharmaceutical pricing, invites the wrong regulator, and makes the group's exposure political rather than clinical.

Branded and white-label, both. Branded Idenze Therapeutics product where we hold the registration and want the margin; white-label and contract manufacturing at Nkpor where a market is closed to our registration or a partner owns the brand — how the Nkpor suite absorbs fixed cost before our own dossiers mature. No flower, no recreational-adjacent formats, no lifestyle SKUs.

4. Operating model

Three nodes, one licensable chain.

  • Node 1 — South Africa (API; licence of record). Cultivation under GACP, extraction and isolation to pharmaceutical-grade API. SAHPRA issues both the GACP licence (agriculture/collection) and the GMP licence (processing) (SAHPRA application, SAHPRA FAQ, Fasken). Site near Durban or Cape Town. This is the node NAFDAC will most readily accept.
  • Node 2 — Nigeria (Nkpor; finished dosage form). Tableting, encapsulation, liquid fill and topicals under NAFDAC registration and an NCS import permit. Co-located with Idenze Pharma to share utilities, QC lab, warehouse and overhead — but physically segregated and separately licensed as a controlled-substances suite with its own access control, batch records, gram-level reconciliation, security and audit.
  • Node 3 — Distribution. Nigeria and ECOWAS via Idenze Distribution (licensed wholesale); export via Uli Group's Uli Special Logistics, which holds narcotics import/export authorisations, chain-of-custody documentation and transit permits.

Extraction technology. Supercritical CO₂ for pharma-grade material, ethanol for bulk volume, then winterisation, decarboxylation and chromatographic purification to isolate. The technology decision follows the licence decision: acquiring a licensed South African entity means inheriting its extraction train, validated processes and batch history.

Quality systems. ICH Q7 GMP; ICH Q1A stability; Qualified Person release in South Africa and NAFDAC-recognised release in Nigeria; seed-lot-to-patient-pack traceability; ALCOA+ data integrity; serialisation for export. Stability studies must run in Nigerian climatic zone IVb — routinely missed by importers.

Supply chain. Sea freight Durban → Lagos at roughly 4–6 weeks; air for high-value small lots. Every shipment needs an export authorisation from the exporting state and an import authorisation from Nigeria. Hold six months of API buffer stock at Nkpor. CBD API needs no cold chain.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

This is the critical path. If this sequence fails, nothing else matters.

Step 0 — Two answers before any spend. Get NACOC's written confirmation of the eligibility basis and the ownership test (§12).

Step 1 — SAHPRA GACP + GMP (Years 0–2). Recommendation: acquire an already-licensed entity; do not build. Acquisition delivers the licence in roughly 6–12 months including SAHPRA consent to change of control, against 24–36+ months for a de novo build with no guarantee of award; it inherits validated processes, a Qualified Person and an export-authorisation track record, which is far stronger evidence for NAFDAC than a construction plan; and it is cheaper. Because licences are non-transferable, the transaction must be a share purchase of the entity that holds them, with SAHPRA consent to change of control as a condition precedent.

Step 2 — Ghana (Years 1–7; the long pole). A qualifying family member obtains Indefinite Residence from the Ministry of the Interior (Ministry of the Interior, GIS Service Charter) — slow, generally following extended continuous lawful residence, and losable, so it must be maintained deliberately. A Ghanaian company then applies under the 11-licence regime; the Interior Minister has cleared eight companies, so licences appear to attach to corporate entities. Build two qualifying persons into the cap table and board from day one: eligibility cannot be bought or transferred, so one person is a single point of failure.

Step 3 — NAFDAC NCS (Years 1–3). The NCS Directorate publishes guidelines for clearing narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances and drug precursors (permit guidelines) and imported narcotic controlled substances and pharmaceutical raw materials (import-clearing guidelines), plus the Controlled Medicines Regulations 2019 and a risk-categorisation guideline effective 30 July 2024 (NCS Directorate). Sequence: written confirmation that SAHPRA GMP certification supports a permit → facility registration of the Nkpor suite → product registration per SKU.

Step 4 — INCB / 1961 Single Convention (continuous). Each movement needs an export authorisation from the exporting state and an import authorisation from Nigeria, tied to the annual estimates of narcotic requirements filed with INCB (INCB, estimates). With no line in the national estimates for our API quantity, the shipment cannot lawfully move — a calendar constraint managed a year ahead.

Step 5 — Per-market registration. Every export market needs its own product registration plus narcotics import permit; budget on a first wave of five markets. Timeline: SA acquisition and documented NAFDAC pathway by end of Year 2 · first registration and sale Years 2–3 · first in-house clinical data Year 3 · five markets Year 5 · Ghana licence operating Years 5–7.

The acquisition route, stated licence by licence — and the one set that cannot be bought.

This is the hardest licence set in the Group, and the plan should say so plainly rather than assume the Group's general rule solves it. The rule still holds: no licence here is a reason to defer the business. But the rule has two halves — obtain it, or buy the entity that holds it — and around controlled substances the second half largely fails.

The honest conclusion, stated plainly, because the alternative is a plan that assumes a licence can be bought when it cannot: for the South African cultivation and manufacturing leg, buy the licensed entity — that is the acquisition the plan already recommends, and it is worth doing. For the Nigerian controlled-substances leg, this authorisation set cannot realistically be bought and must be earned. Three consequences follow, and none of them closes the plan. First, partner or joint-venture with an existing authorisation holder for the Nigerian manufacture and distribution leg, on a tolling or contract-manufacture basis, with the permit-holder remaining the licensee of record — the Group supplies capital, formulation and demand, and holds no NCS permit. Second, earn it deliberately: the trading history and premises record that NAFDAC and NDLEA require are built in the adjacent regulated lines — which is exactly what 22_Idenze_Distribution.md builds from Year 1, activating its own NCS engagement in Year 3. Third, do not acquire a shell: a dormant company with a lapsed authorisation is worth less than nothing, because the reputational and security scrutiny on change of control is heavier than on a fresh application.

First ninety days — commission the transferability opinion and the holder register. A written opinion from Nigerian counsel, with NAFDAC NCS and NDLEA correspondence attached, on whether any authorisation in the set above survives a change of control; plus a named register of the entities that hold each one, with ownership, capacity and any indication that one could be acquired or partnered. Budget ₦95m — ₦60m counsel and regulator correspondence, ₦25m registry and corporate search work, ₦10m for the Ghana-side equivalent through Ghanaian counsel [verify]. This is the piece of work that converts the paragraph above from an assumption into a decision, and it belongs in the same quarter as the two NACOC questions.

The two blocking unknowns.

  1. Ghana eligibility: citizens only, or citizens and permanent residents? Press reports conflict (Graphic Online versus 3News). If it is citizens only, the residence route fails entirely and the group needs citizenship, a genuine joint venture, or a different jurisdiction. This single sentence determines the Ghana strategy and must be read from NACOC's own licensing instrument, never from news coverage.
  2. Will NAFDAC NCS accept SAHPRA GMP certification as the basis for a narcotics import permit? If not, the South African node may not unlock the Nigerian plant at all and the three-node design must be re-cut. Get this in writing before any acquisition spend.
