Sequencing rule. Lines 2 and 3 carry line 1: a laboratory that cannot validate a method cannot run a bioequivalence study, and stability revenue arrives while the clinical unit is still being commissioned. Line 4 makes line 1 cheap — a molecule engineered into BCS Class I or III never needs the in vivo study at all.

4. Operating model

Physical build. A clinical pharmacology unit of 24–32 beds in two wards with 24-hour nursing, controlled access, a standardized-meal kitchen, dosing bays, −80 °C storage and a defined ICU transfer route into the teaching hospital — co-located with, but physically distinct from, hospital wards. A bioanalytical laboratory built around LC-MS/MS (the single most important instrument), with UPLC/HPLC, GC-headspace, USP I–IV dissolution, UV-Vis, balances, sample prep and a controlled cold chain. A stability facility of walk-in and reach-in ICH Zone IVb chambers, continuously mapped, alarmed and on backup power — a chamber that loses power for six hours does not delay a study, it invalidates a year of it. A formulation laboratory with bench-scale granulation, blending, compression and coating, adjacent to the Pharma pilot plant. Validated EDC, LIMS, eQMS and a controlled-access archive with 15-year retention.

Teaching hospital interface. The hospital is the recruitment engine and the clinical-cover guarantee. As in 24_Idenze_University.md: a clinical services agreement, a joint medical advisory board, and a Chief Medical Director reporting to the hospital board rather than the Vice-Chancellor, so a healthcare mandate and an academic mandate do not cannibalise each other. Idenze Research buys clinical time, bed-days, imaging and pathology at arm's-length tariffs — not at cost, not free. A trial that runs on favours has no verifiable cost base and no defensible indemnity position.

Ethics and governance — the structure that makes the evidence admissible. This is the company's design constraint and must exist before the first study.

RequirementConcrete standard
Research ethics committeeA separate Idenze Research Ethics Committee (IREC) per the NHREC framework and the NAFDAC GCP Guidelines 2025 requirement for independent review. A majority of members are not employed by any Ezeme Group company; external non-executive chair; lay, legal and community members; disclosed fixed sitting fees
Conflict of interestWritten policy covering investigators, sponsor staff, monitors, the statistician and IREC members: annual and per-trial declaration, recusal, and a register held by QA and reported to the board
Publication rightsRights sit with the investigators, in writing. No suppression of unfavourable results, no editorial approval of conclusions, publication within 12 months of database lock. Treasury and Commercial hold no veto
Trial registrationA WHO primary registry before first enrolment, then NCTR and/or PACTR with evidence presented to NAFDAC — both required by the Clinical Trial Regulations. No registration number, no first dose
Data integrityALCOA+; validated systems with non-disableable audit trails; source documents retained 15 years with an independent off-site escrow copy; Trial Master and Investigator Site Files per the GCP Guidelines 2025 retention provisions
Independence of analysisUnblinded statistician for pivotal studies contracted externally; independent DSMB above minimal risk; risk-based central monitoring with a defined on-site plan
Structural separationOwn board with two independent directors, one chairing the IREC appointing panel. QA reports to that board, not the Managing Director

State the sponsor and site relationship, and the governance firewall, in one paragraph in every protocol, dossier and publication, before the methods section. Reviewers do not object to a sponsor running research at its own site. They object to being surprised by it.

Recruitment, data and quality. Recruitment draws on the hospital's rheumatology, neurology, oncology and physiotherapy clinics under the joint advisory board, with no payment to referring clinicians — a COI event under the policy above, not a grey area. Standard practice: pre-screening registers, a consent-to-contact database, a screening-to-randomisation ratio tracked per study and a published stop/go date. Cannabinoid IITs recruit through the same clinics, which is why the Therapeutics plan treats the teaching hospital as its first real-world evidence site. Data management runs validated EDC with a CDISC-aligned model, SDTM/ADaM datasets a foreign regulator can read, and SAS or R with double-programming on primary endpoints. Quality systems follow ICH E6(R3) and ICH M10 — SOPs, training files, CAPA, change control, vendor qualification, self-inspection, annual management review and an annual external mock inspection of both clinical and bioanalytical operations.

A laboratory producing a clean, complete, ICH-format dossier is worth more than a fast one. Regulatory affairs is measured on zero avoidable compliance queries.

The acquisition route — and the one instrument in this domain that money genuinely cannot buy.

No licence in this plan is a reason to defer the work. The Group obtains it or buys the entity that already holds it — and here that rule has a clean edge: accreditation and equipment are acquirable, ethics approval and clinical-trial capability are not. A licensed laboratory is a thing a company owns. An ethics committee's independence, and a principal investigator's willingness to enrol patients, are not.

What to buy, and the two things that decide the price. The acquired laboratory is worth buying for accreditation, qualified equipment and bench staff — the three inputs that make Tranche 1's instrument spend slow to convert into revenue. Two diligence gates: first, equipment qualification records — an instrument without a current IQ/OQ/PQ package and traceable calibration history is a liability, not an asset, and an LC-MS/MS platform cannot be retro-qualified cheaply; second, the accreditation scope, which is far more valuable than the certificate, because a scope that excludes bioanalysis buys the Group nothing. And say the harder thing plainly: no acquisition delivers the clinical half of this business. Trials capability is a partnership with hospitals and named investigators, which is why this plan's leverage is a residency-return programme and a joint medical advisory board, not a balance sheet.

First ninety days — commission the laboratory and CRO register, and open the partnership track. A register of every licensed analytical or medical laboratory and small CRO in the South-East and Lagos: accreditation scope, equipment inventory with qualification status, staff credentials, current utilisation, client base and asking price — then two non-binding approaches; in parallel, a term sheet with one foreign CRO as design-benchmark partner for the CPU sizing study and method transfer. Budget ₦60m — ₦30m advisory, valuation and equipment condition assessment, ₦20m legal and regulatory work on scope transfer, ₦10m partnership scoping and site visits [verify]. Buying a working laboratory compresses Tranche 1's most uncertain line; buying the clinical capability is not possible, and the plan should stop pretending otherwise.

₦55–95m for a full bioequivalence study is the most important number in this plan. Against a foreign CRO at US$120k–400k (₦192m–640m) plus freight, comparator sourcing, import permits and nine to eighteen months of queue time, in-house is a 60–80% saving and a year of calendar. That is the number the Pharma and Therapeutics boards should be deciding on, and it is the price at which third-party manufacturers become customers rather than prospects.

Read the third row carefully — it is the honest constraint on this plan. Pharma and Therapeutics cannot alone fill a bioanalytical laboratory; the Group's own pipeline is roughly a third of break-even volume at Year 5. Third-party contract work is not optional upside; it is the difference between a cost centre and a business. Tranche 2 should not be released until the manufacturer survey evidences 15–20 external studies a year.

Strategic value versus fee income. Fee income produces cash, utilisation and credibility with NAFDAC assessors — ₦4.0–6.5bn of third-party revenue by Year 5. Strategic value produces registrations, brand protection, export dossiers and scientific reputation: roughly ₦4–10bn of avoided outsourced cost, plus the margin on branded rather than commodity products, an order of magnitude larger and never appearing in this company's P&L. Fee income pays for the capability; strategic value is why the capability exists. Reporting must show both: an arm's-length P&L for the company, and a separate Group Board disclosure of avoided cost and brand margin created for sister companies, priced at market rates so the transfer pricing is defensible to FIRS.

Recruiting experienced clinical research staff is the real constraint. There is no deep Nigerian pool of bioanalytical chemists with LC-MS/MS validation experience and none at all of PIs who have run ten GCP trials, because the trials were not run here. Four mechanisms, in order:

  1. Grow from Idenze University and Idenze Polytechnic. Pharmacy, medical laboratory science and chemistry graduates hired in Year 1 and trained under an experienced Head of Bioanalysis are the only route to a bench of 20 by Year 5 — and the Polytechnic supplies technicians in Years 1–3, before the university's first clinical cohort exists.
  2. Recruit the diaspora return from European, Indian and South African CROs — the fastest route to hires 1, 2 and 5. Packages must be contractual and dollar-linked: a promise that erodes with the naira is a resignation letter with a delay.
  3. Buy experienced capacity rather than headcount. A technical services and training agreement with an established CRO, or a fellowship with a WHO collaborating centre, can transfer method validation and audit readiness in 18 months for a fraction of a senior team — provided the agreement names individuals and defines knowledge-transfer deliverables.
  4. Publish and teach. Conference presence, IIT co-authorship with university staff and a formal bioequivalence training programme — which Ncube et al. recommend specifically for African markets — build the reputation that makes recruitment possible. The Group's scientific reputation and its hiring pipeline are the same asset.

Its own growth assumptions say the opposite: §7 puts Year 5 exactly at break-even (24–32 third-party studies are what break-even requires, and that is what the Year-5 column shows), while Year 10 adds multi-site capability, paediatric and oncology IITs, GLP certification, reference-laboratory status in West Africa, registrations in five export markets and partnership in two further African markets, and takes headcount from 91 to 160 (§8). A business the plan places at break-even in Year 5, having roughly doubled its capability and its headcount by Year 10, cannot still be earning the Year-5 band. The correct band is not derivable from this plan — it states no Year-10 study volume, no capacity ceiling and no price escalation — so no figure has been invented here. [verify] — the plan owner must set the Year-10 revenue band, and restate §7's break-even table with it. §2's market limit ("Nigerian BE volume is hundreds of studies a year, not thousands") is the one plateau-shaping constraint the plan names, and it is not invoked in §9.)

10. Risks

Integration is mandatory (library standing constraint 5). This is the clearest case in the Group of a business whose reason to exist is that its sisters exist.

The compounding effect, stated once: the Group's scientific reputation is produced here, and that reputation is what lets an Idenze Pharma molecule price above a commodity, what makes a foreign regulator read Group dossiers as credible, and what makes a diaspora scientist accept a return offer. It is the only asset in the Group that gets stronger every time it is used.

12. First ninety days

  1. Constitute the Idenze Research Ethics Committee — before anything else. Appoint the external chair and external-majority membership; set terms of reference, sitting fees and disclosure requirements; adopt the COI and the publication/no-suppression policies. Nothing in this plan is worth building until this is done. (Group Board + MD designate + external counsel)
  2. Appoint the Managing Director and Head of Bioanalysis. These two hires gate the instrumentation specification — buy the instrument the person you trust can validate, not the one on the brochure.
  3. Hold the NAFDAC pre-application meeting covering laboratory scope, the bioanalytical method list, BE and biowaiver strategy per molecule, and the ethics and registration workflow. The written response is the quarter's most valuable document.
  4. File the IREC registration under the NHREC framework and confirm in writing the current route, the NCTR/PACTR requirement, and the ethics sequence for a sponsor-affiliated site.
  5. Commission the manufacturer pipeline survey: registration calendars of 40–60 Nigerian manufacturers, BE obligations per molecule, where studies are currently sent, what is paid, and what would make a manufacturer switch. This survey is the go/no-go gate for Tranche 2.
  6. Issue firm supplier quotations for the analytical core — two LC-MS/MS vendors minimum, with service contracts, consumables, reference standards, training and in-country engineer coverage priced separately. Re-base Tranche 1 on quotations, not on this plan's ranges.
  7. Commission a CPU sizing study against current NAFDAC BE requirements — bed count, subject throughput, washout scheduling, nursing model — using a foreign CRO as design-benchmark partner.
  8. Agree the teaching hospital interface in writing: clinical services agreement, bed-day and clinical-time tariffs, the recruitment pathway through rheumatology, neurology and oncology clinics, and the joint medical advisory board's terms of reference. Arm's-length, documented, board-approved.
  9. Adopt the five governing documents: Data Integrity Policy (ALCOA+, 15-year retention, audit trails), Conflict of Interest Policy, Publication and Data Sharing Policy, Trial Registration SOP, and Validation Master Plan.
  10. Open the diaspora recruitment search for positions 1, 2, 3 and 5, with dollar-linked contractual packages and named-author publication rights on offer.
  11. Commission the laboratory and CRO register, and open the partnership track. Every licensed analytical or medical laboratory and small CRO in the South-East and Lagos, with accreditation scope, equipment qualification status, staff credentials, utilisation and asking price; two non-binding approaches. In parallel, a design-benchmark term sheet with one foreign CRO for the CPU sizing study and method transfer. Budget ₦60m. A working laboratory can be bought; the clinical-trial capability cannot, and it is partnered hospital by hospital.

Regulatory and market claims are linked inline. Where a figure needs local verification — instrument prices, study pricing, the volume of available third-party work, and the current NHREC registration route — this plan says so rather than inventing precision.

IDENZE UNIVERSITY — University Business Plan

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary in this plan; it uses ₦1,350/USD (the text also cites ₦1,331 and ₦1,395). Spot was about ₦1,328/USD (CBN NFEM, Sept 2026). Dollar figures are indicative only and are not comparable across plans — each plan used a different rate. The library planning rate for cross-plan comparison is ₦1,600/USD. See plans/README.md.

Ezeme Group · Idenze Group (Pharma & Education) · Education Platform — Flagship

Site: 100 hectares, Institutional Zone B, Nkpor, Idemili North LGA, Anambra State

Structure: Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Mauritius GBC → Ezeme Group Nigeria Ltd → Idenze Group → Idenze University (own board, own audit, own regulator)

Horizon: 15 years to first graduating class; 25 years to maturity

FX assumption: ₦1,350 = US$1.00 (NFEM official ~₦1,331/$ in September 2026; parallel ~₦1,395/$ — Newswatch, CBN). ±25% band applied to all USD figures.

The master plan calls this institution "Idenze University". The legal name will be settled with the NUC, which approves proposed university names — see the three-name rule in ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md.

1. Thesis

Idenze University is a ten-faculty, degree-granting university at Nkpor whose every faculty is wired to a live industry inside the Ezeme Group. It is the Group's talent supply chain, its clinical-trial engine, and the asset that makes the Ezeme name mean institution rather than company.

Three advantages no competitor can assemble at once:

  1. Captive graduate demand. 1,850 direct Group roles at maturity plus the polytechnic pipeline. Graduate unemployment is the strongest objection to any Nigerian private university's pitch; we answer it with an owned employer. Industry placement is a curriculum requirement inside Group companies, not a placement-office promise.
  2. Clinical trials as a moat. The teaching hospital lets Idenze run pain, arthritis and cannabinoid trials in-house, converting commodity extracts into evidence-backed, registerable products. No Nigerian competitor university has a pharma group behind it.
  3. The land position. 100 hectares secured before announcement. The Group budgets ₦8.35B (≈US$6.2m) for the parcel; once a licence is announced, adjacent Idemili North land reprices within 12–24 months.

Why accreditation, not buildings, is the moat. Buildings take 36 months to buy; accreditation cannot be bought. The NUC's revised guidelines show the shape of the machine: a non-refundable processing fee of ₦25,000,000, raised from ₦5m in 2025; 90 days after payment to request the first verification visit; 180 days after that for the second; a ₦10m additional fee and a further 180-day window for a confirmation visit if the second is failed — after which the application lapses (NUC, August 2025). The Commission also suspended new private-university licensing for a year from February 2025 (NUC), then reopened with 33 licences in 2026, taking Nigeria to 309 universities (TheCable). Two consequences: the queue is politically administered and can close without notice, so an early, well-documented applicant beats a rich late one; and a licence is a scarce, transferable, heritable asset. The Group's method — replicate the accredited model, absorb or franchise existing schools — is executable only from owned accreditation. Hence: front-load land and regulator work, back-load buildings.

2. Market

Demand is structural. JAMB processed 2,007,312 UTME applicants in 2025; 1,009,044 were admitted across all Nigerian tertiary institutions — a 50% rate (Punch). Roughly one million qualified school-leavers a year go unplaced. Meanwhile licensed private universities reached 159 by July 2025, with the Minister of Education conceding that "too many are failing to meet the quality standards Nigeria demands" (University World News). The gap is not seats; it is credible seats. The mass market is over-supplied with low-trust capacity and under-supplied with institutions an employer will hire from.

Babcock, Afe Babalola, Bowen, LandmarkEstablished second tier₦1.5m–₦2.5mComparable. Placement guarantee is the differentiator.

Federal/state universities (UNIZIK, COOU, FUTO)Cheap, credential-recognised₦150k–₦450kNot a price rival; the rival for faculty.

That last row is the opportunity. Nigerians spent US$1.39bn on foreign education in H1 2025 alone — ~US$2.8bn annualised — with the CBN Governor naming foreign education as a driver of naira weakness (Nairametrics; NISER). We need not beat Covenant; we must make a $9,000 Idenze University place visibly rational against a $30,000 place in Manchester. That needs three launch proofs: placements, a working hospital, and an international accreditation pathway.

Within a 90-minute drive sit Onitsha, Awka, Nnewi, Aba, Owerri and Enugu — Nigeria's densest concentration of trading and manufacturing wealth. Verify locally with Anambra State Bureau of Statistics before fixing programme mix; working target is 900 paid intake in Year 12, 2,400 by Year 15.

3. Product & service lines

Ten faculties, each mapped to a Group domain. NUC accredits per programme, not per faculty, so sequencing is a funding decision.

Postgraduate (from Year 16): PGD/MSc first in the six faculties with functioning laboratories; MPhil/PhD only where research infrastructure and supervisors exist. Professional doctorates (DBA, EdD) from Year 18 — high fee, low capital.

Executive education (from Year 13, before full accreditation): the first revenue line and the reputational bridgehead. Short courses for Group managers, Anambra SMEs and the state civil service — corporate governance (Akunnia), supply chain (Uli), energy systems (Okodu), agro-processing (Isiome). Target ₦1.5–2.5bn/yr by Year 15 at 30–40% margin. Non-award short courses sit outside degree accreditation, but confirm the certificate boundary with the NUC first — the Commission polices award-bearing programmes.

Research and consulting: (a) product development for Isiome and Okodu; (b) clinical trials for Idenze Pharma and third-party sponsors; (c) DFI and government-funded agricultural and policy research. A multi-site Phase III trial with 400 randomised subjects is worth roughly US$1.5–3.0m in site fees over 18 months — to be verified against current CRO benchmarks and NHREC/NAFDAC requirements. That is why the hospital, not the lecture theatre, is the highest-return building on site.

EdTech and licensing (Idenze Learning): a separate company selling what accreditation costs us — curriculum architecture, QA manual, exam moderation and external-examiner system, faculty recruitment packs, LMS, and the accreditation-readiness playbook. Buyers: Group schools (standard-setting), third-party Nigerian schools converting to degree-awarding status, and partner African campuses. Priced at US$40–70 per student per year plus US$150k–500k one-off advisory fees. This is how the Group's standards, not just its capital, leave Nigeria.

4. Operating model

Calendar. Two semesters (September–January; February–June) aligned to JAMB/WAEC and to the polytechnic so hostels and shared services run year-round. A summer term carries executive education and research — idle-asset arbitrage, not an academic term.

Staff model. Permanent academic staff for accreditation (NUC requires qualified full-time staff in discipline ratios, roughly 1:15 science, 1:10 clinical); a visiting/adjunct layer of practising professionals from Group companies and the Onitsha–Nnewi industrial belt at 30–50% of the cost per contact hour; and a funded PhD pipeline sponsoring 6–10 staff into doctoral programmes annually from Year 6. We cannot buy 400 PhDs in Anambra in Year 12; we must grow them from Year 6.

Recruitment. Four channels: Group secondary schools and the polytechnic as guaranteed feeder intake; Anambra, Enugu, Imo, Abia, Delta school-leaver marketing; diaspora and returning-family places at international fees; West African regional intake from Year 14. Cost target ≤5% of tuition revenue at maturity; expect 12–15% for the first three intakes.

Hostels and auxiliaries. Boarding is 20–25% of revenue and the main driver of parent preference. Phase 1: 1,000 beds at ₦1.6m/bed/year, rising to 6,000. Run hostels, catering, bookshop, laundry, transport and medical services in a separate services company so the university's regulated accounts stay clean and the auxiliary business can carry its own debt. Catering contracts to Isiome; hostel construction to Okodu.

Teaching hospital interface. A 200-bed Phase 1 hospital co-owned with Idenze's health platform, governed by a clinical-services agreement, a joint medical advisory board, and a Chief Medical Director reporting to the hospital board rather than the Vice-Chancellor. The university buys clinical teaching time; the hospital bills NHIS, private patients and trial sponsors. This separation keeps a public-healthcare mandate and an academic mandate from cannibalising each other.

Placement inside the Group. Compulsory six-month attachment in Year 3 and a twelve-month supervised placement in Year 4 (five-year programmes in Pharmacy, Law, Engineering). Slots are contracted forward: Isiome (agro-processing, manufacturing), Okodu (energy, construction), Uli (logistics, studio), Akunnia (finance, legal), Idenze (pharma QA, hospital). Group companies get first refusal on graduates. Target: 70% of graduates hold an offer from a Group company or counterparty within six months, measured from the first cohort.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Nigeria (NUC). Sequence: (1) incorporate the university company, perfect land title with a Certificate of Occupancy in the promoter's name, constitute Proprietor and Governing Council; (2) letter of intent to the Executive Secretary; (3) collect the application form and pay the non-refundable processing fee — ₦25,000,000 as of August 2025, up from ₦5m; the fee has moved twice and must be re-verified at payment; (4) submit the feasibility study and needs assessment (academic brief, staff list with qualifications, capital and recurrent funding evidence, land and building drawings, library and laboratory inventory, five-year cash-flow projection, evidence of endowment or liquid reserve); (5) preliminary interview, NUC Management approval, onward transmission to the Minister of Education; (6) first verification visit requested within 90 days of payment or the application lapses; (7) second verification visit within 180 days of the first; (8) if failed, ₦10m additional fee and a confirmation visit request within 180 days; (9) ministerial recommendation and FEC approval; (10) provisional licence (typically 3 years) → full accreditation after resource verification per programme and satisfactory inspection.

Two current rules shape strategy. All licensees must move to a permanent site at the end of the first phase of development (five years) — we build on the 100-hectare permanent site from day one, converting a compliance burden into a marketing asset. Multi-campus designation across states is prohibited and transnational education requires NUC approval — which fixes the replication structure below: each campus abroad is a separate entity under local accreditation.

Timeline. The Group's sequence stands: NUC pre-accreditation begins Year 8; first intake Years 12–14. Treat Year 8 as the filing date, and hold a 24-month regulatory float — the licensing queue has been paused twice since 2025.

Feeder alignment. The polytechnic (20 ha, NBTE, intake Years 7–9) and the two secondary schools plus primary school (Years 4–6) are separate entities with their own plans, but here they matter three ways: first revenue in the education cluster, a documented academic-record and governance history for NUC inspectors, and the first student cohort. Their records should be kept as if they already belonged to a university system.

The acquisition route — and the transferability question that decides it.

NUC approval is not a reason to defer this university. The Group obtains it, or buys the institution that already holds it. But the acquisition route here is materially different from the pharma platform's, and the difference must be stated rather than assumed: what NUC grants is an institutional licence held by a named licensee, not an assignable asset. There is no published NUC regime for change of control, and no Nigerian instrument that says an NUC licence transfers. So the transaction is not a licence purchase at all — it is the purchase of the company that is the licensee, with NUC's consent to the change of control as a condition precedent, or it is nothing. That single question is decisive, it is unresolved in public sources, and it must be answered in writing before any acquisition spend [verify].

Why this route has moved from counter-intuitive to the only route. In February 2026 the NUC suspended action on the establishment of new private universities for one year (The Sun; The Sun, April 2026), on top of the six-year moratorium on new tertiary institutions reported in March 2026 and the NUC's own review of private-university regulations (Leadership). A closed licensing queue does not close this business — it prices the incumbents. The market is already moving: Honoris United Universities acquired Nile University of Nigeria (BusinessDay), and the Honoris group's own holding company is itself in play — in 2025–26 a South African consortium's proposed acquisition of 100% of Honoris Holding Limited was notified to the FCCPC and reviewed by the ECOWAS Regional Competition Authority (FCCPC; ARCC decision) — the template for an education-sector change of control in Nigeria, together with the reminder that promoter sentiment alone can stall one (Guardian).

The valuation test this plan should use, because the Group already contains it. The Group's build benchmark is ₦21.2m of capital per student place (see 17_Idenze_Group.md). An accredited, licensed institution with an existing roll is worth buying whenever the all-in price per student place — enterprise value plus the cost of remedying its accreditation and facility gaps — is below the cost of creating that place. That is the test the first-ninety-days survey must run, and it is the only valuation method available while no transaction values are published.

First ninety days — commission the change-of-control opinion and the accredited-institution register. (1) A written opinion from NUC-experienced counsel — retained on the same mandate as the filing consultant in §12 — on whether an NUC institutional licence and programme accreditations survive a change of control, what NUC requires, and what the change is notified under; this is the gate on the entire acquisition route and must be answered in writing, not assumed [verify]. (2) A register of Nigeria's NUC-licensed private universities: ownership, enrolment, licence status, programme accreditation status, litigation and union history, financial condition, and whether the proprietor is a seller; three approaches, non-binding. Budget ₦150m — ₦60m counsel, ₦65m advisory and valuation, ₦25m data rooms and site visits [verify]. The fee is trivial beside the fee the NUC route now costs in time: a licensing queue that is closed for a year and reported closed for six cannot be waited out, only bought around.

6. Capital requirement

Land is the Group master plan figure (167 plots × ₦50m average). Construction figures are planning estimates from Nigerian institutional build rates and must be tendered competitively, with Okodu Group as one bidder rather than sole source.

Capital cost per student place: US$188m ÷ 12,000 = ~US$15,700 (₦21.2m) per place at full build. The marginal place after Phase 1 costs US$4,000–7,000 — the second hostel block and second faculty tranche need no new power spine, no hospital, no regulator. That falling marginal cost is why campus two is cheaper than campus one, and why replication is the real prize.

Break-even. Phase-1 campus (fixed ~₦9bn/yr, contribution ~₦3.0m/student): ~3,000 students, around Year 16–17 — four to five years after first intake. Full campus (fixed ~₦24bn/yr): ~7,900 students. No Nigerian private university is profitable at first intake; plan for a funded deficit of ₦2.5–4bn a year for the first four teaching years.

Staffing cost ratio: 34% of revenue at maturity, deliberately below the 45–50% norm because of the adjunct layer — but expect 45–55% for the first five teaching years while accredited full-time staff are carried ahead of enrolment. This is the ratio to watch: NUC discipline ratios bind on full-time qualified staff, and no amount of adjunct cheapness substitutes.

8. Organisation

Governance. Two-tier, per Group policy: a Governing Council (Pro-Chancellor/Chair plus four independents — a former Vice-Chancellor of another Nigerian university, a chartered accountant, a medical professor, one international academic) and a Senate owning academic standards. Independent audit committee reporting through Idenze to the Group Board. The Vice-Chancellor is accounting officer; the Council appoints and may dismiss. The university is a separate licensed entity, permanently ring-fenced from pharmaceutical and cannabinoid regulatory risk — no pharma director sits on the University Council.

First ten hires, in order of consequence:

  1. Vice-Chancellor — a Nigerian professor with prior VC/DVC experience and NUC credibility. Appoint by Year 5, not Year 8; this single hire de-risks the licence.
  2. Director, Accreditation & Quality Assurance — owns the NUC relationship, the 90/180-day clocks, every resource-verification file.
  3. Registrar — statutory officer; admissions, Senate records, student register.
  4. Bursar/CFO — must have audited a Nigerian university; owns the funding evidence the NUC tests.
  5. University Librarian — statutory NUC post; holdings and e-resources gate the first visit.
  6. Director, Physical Planning & Campus Development — interfaces with Okodu; controls the ₦150bn+ build.
  7. Provost/Dean, Pharmacy & Health Sciences — sets the clinical curriculum and the hospital interface.
  8. Dean, Agricultural Sciences — fastest faculty to profitable research contracts, tied to Idemmili.
  9. Director, ICT & Digital Learning — LMS and the EdTech product the replication model sells.
  10. Head of Admissions, Corporate Affairs & Marketing (or General Counsel) — build the brand two years before intake.

11. Integration

The internal trade is deliberate and charged at structured rates:

  • People, out to every domain. 1,850 direct roles plus ~70% of graduates entering Group companies. Pharmacy and health into Idenze Pharma and the hospital; engineering into Isiome's plants and Okodu's sites; logistics and media into Uli; finance and law into Akunnia.
  • Construction, in from Okodu. ₦150bn+ of buildings, roads, power spine, water and hostels, competitively tendered against a ten-year pipeline.
  • Power, in from Okodu. 4MW captive generation rising to 8MW; the campus anchors Okodu Power, and the spine later serves surrounding Nkpor.
  • Food, in from Isiome. Catering for 7,200 residents plus staff canteens — a contracted offtake worth ~₦2.4bn a year at maturity, which also lowers Group staff-estate food costs.
  • Media and content, in from Uli. Campus radio and studios double as teaching facilities and as Group production capacity.
  • Evidence, out to Idenze. Hospital plus Pharmacy faculty give Idenze Pharma an in-house trial site, pharmacokinetic capability and a route to evidence-backed cannabinoid and analgesic products — the moat the pharma plan otherwise lacks.
  • Curriculum, reciprocal. The university writes it; Idenze Learning licenses it to Group schools and third parties, turning internal capability into external revenue.
  • Akunnia supplies legal, capital-markets and governance capability for the bond issue and franchise agreements.

The African replication model

The ambition is not one university but control of a private education system across Africa. Nigerian rules prohibit multi-campus designation across states and require NUC approval for transnational education. So the unit of replication is the accredited model, not the institution.

Three structures, ascending in capital intensity:

  1. Owned campus (Ghana, then Kenya). A wholly owned in-country SPV seeks local accreditation — GTEC, then CUE — reusing our academic model, Phase-1 designs, QA manuals and LMS. Capital US$25–40m per campus; campus two should cost 50–60% of campus one because the template is already amortised.
  2. Licensed partner campus — the scale engine. The partner owns and funds the campus and holds local accreditation; Idenze University licenses the curriculum, assessment and moderation system, external-examiner network, LMS, brand and accreditation playbook, and seconds a management team under a 7-year renewable contract. Fee stack: licence fee 3–5% of tuition revenue, management fee 2–3%, platform fee US$40–70 per student per year, plus US$150k–500k accreditation advisory. Zero capital, recurring revenue, and the accreditation stays the partner's legal asset while the standards stay ours.
  3. Accreditation-as-a-service. Sell the readiness playbook and governance pack to schools converting to degree-granting status — including the licensed-but-failing Nigerian private universities the Minister has criticised. Highest margin, no campus at all.

How standards are controlled without owning every campus. A group-level Ezeme Academic Standards Board owns the curriculum, assessment blueprint, external examiner panel and brand licence. Every franchise carries: a 7-year term with revocation on failed inspection; a veto over appointment of the Vice-Chancellor, Registrar and Bursar; mandatory annual inspection by our QA team plus independent external examiners; standardised examinations for core courses in the first two years; and a covenant requiring audited accounts. Standards control, not equity control, is what protects the brand — and the Group's own architecture already names accreditation as the transferable moat.

Sequencing. Phase 1 (Years 12–16): Ghana — English-medium, large Nigerian and West African intake, existing GTEC machinery, and the 2026 liberalisation of chartering. Then Kenya, whose CUE route accommodates branch campuses of recognised institutions. Phase 2 (Years 17–20): Rwanda and Zambia — smaller markets, faster accession, strong DFI support. Phase 3 (Years 20+): francophone West Africa, entered by licence rather than ownership because French-medium delivery changes the cost base.

Recognition is the hidden dependency. A degree not recognised by the target regulator or by employers across ECOWAS and the AU is worthless. Before signing any franchise, secure recognition of Nigerian qualifications in that jurisdiction and align to the AU's continental recognition convention and AfCFTA services commitments. Verify country by country; do not assume mutual recognition.

The acquisition option at home. With 159+ licensed private universities and many unable to fund the permanent-site migration the NUC now requires within five years, there is a buying window. Acquiring a licensed, distressed institution and installing the Ezeme model is faster than filing — the same accreditation arbitrage as franchising, applied first in our own market.

25 — IDENZE POLYTECHNIC

Technical & Vocational Education — NBTE-accredited ND/HND

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Idenze Group is the third child's domain. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0). FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD, not comparable across plans.
GroupIdenze Group — Pharma & Education
StructureEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Idenze Group → Idenze Polytechnic Ltd (own board, own audit, own regulator)
Site20 hectares, Institutional Zone B, Nkpor, Idemili North LGA, Anambra — adjacent to the university parcel
RegulatorNBTE, Kaduna; Anambra State Ministry of Education

1. Thesis

Idenze Polytechnic is the Group's earliest-accreditable education asset and its first internal labour supply, because NBTE accreditation can be reached years before the NUC's and at roughly a quarter of the capital per student place — so the technicians, machine operators, QC staff and engineering assistants that Isiome, Okodu, Uli and Idenze Pharma need in their first three years can be produced by the Group rather than poached or improvised.

Three reasons the polytechnic precedes the university, and they are sequential rather than sentimental.

The regulator is cheaper and faster. The NUC route to a private university now carries a ₦25,000,000 non-refundable fee with 90-day and 180-day verification clocks that lapse the application if missed, and new licensing was suspended for a year from February 2025 (NUC). The NBTE route requires no hospital, no professors and no doctoral faculty ratios — it tests an institution, buildings, workshops, a library, qualified instructors and evidence of funding (NBTE guidelines). First intake lands Years 7–9 rather than Years 12–14, so by Year 10 this institution has graduated a cohort while the university is still a building site.

The demand is internal and dated. The Group's own commissioning schedule needs qualified operators from roughly Year 8. A polytechnic opening in Year 8 supplies them; a university opening in Year 12 does not. This is not a fallback asset — it is the load-bearing one.

Industrial placement is the moat. Nigerian TVET's problem is not enrolment but disconnection from industry (Guardian; World Bank), with roughly 70–80% of curricula assessed as misaligned with industry needs (Semantic Scholar). Every polytechnic promises placement; almost none owns the employer. Ours does, and can contract attachment slots forward because the host companies share the balance sheet. The Group's own master plan states it plainly: the polytechnic "formalises what Igba Odibo produces informally — every technical role across the Group has a qualification pathway."

2. Market

Demand is real and structurally unmet. Nigeria reports thousands of unfilled technical vacancies while graduates go jobless — the gap is skills, not headcount (BusinessDay). Technologists warn an engineering skills crisis risks derailing the country's manufacturing push (BusinessDay) in a nation of 270 universities that still imports toothpicks (Punch).

Industry-linked training demonstrably works here. Nestlé's technical training centres, built on roughly ₦6bn, report a 98% job-placement rate — against a vocational pipeline BusinessDay calls broken (BusinessDay). One manufacturer cannot absorb a national skills gap. That is the opening, and it validates the model: training tied to a guaranteed employer places graduates.

South-East competition is public, price-led and capacity-constrained — Federal Polytechnic Oko and Anambra State Polytechnic Mgbakwu (Anambra); IMT Enugu and Enugu State Polytechnic Iwollo; Federal Polytechnic Nekede (Imo); Akanu Ibiam Federal Polytechnic Unwana (Ebonyi); Abia State Polytechnic Aba. Private polytechnics in the region remain few (Edunigeria).

Competitor tierRead

The specific gap. Nobody in the South-East sells an ND/HND place with a contractual industrial placement inside a live conglomerate that also intends to hire. Public institutions have no owned industry; private ones have no conglomerate. That is the entire marketing proposition, and it holds as long as the Group's other businesses do.

Verify locally before fixing fees and mix: current enrolment and fee levels at Federal Polytechnic Oko and IMT Enugu; Anambra State Ministry of Education registration requirements; Idemili North school-leaver numbers. Group planning target: 1,000+ certified graduates annually at maturity.

Phasing. Six departments at first intake (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) — heaviest Group demand, most standardisable workshops. The other five follow at Year 10–11 as HND comes on stream. NBTE accredits per programme, so sequencing is a capital decision.

Short courses and certificates — CAD/BIM, PLC and automation, solar installation, welding codes, food safety, bookkeeping; ₦80,000–350,000 per participant, delivered in evenings and vacations on otherwise idle workshops. First revenue line; confirm the certificate boundary with NBTE in writing first.

Industry training and certification — contracted operator and technician training for Group companies and third-party Anambra industry, including statutory certification preparation (COREN, professional bodies).

Apprenticeship formalisation — the Group's own intake, and Anambra's informal workshop apprentices, assessed and credentialed through NBTE-recognised assessment. This is the master plan's promise operationalised, and it earns intake and goodwill across the industrial belt.

Consultancy and testing services — materials, soil, concrete, water quality and food testing; calibration; design consultancy. Sold to Okodu Construction, Isiome Manufacturing, SMEs and state agencies. Equipment bought for teaching amortises commercially; this is the highest-margin line and the one that underwrites break-even.

4. Operating model

Campus design (20 ha). Academic core — lecture blocks, library, examinations, administration — at the centre; a workshop and laboratory zone behind it, laid out so heavy equipment, deliveries and noise never cross the academic spine; hostels on the quiet boundary; open ground retained as expansion reserve. Power from Okodu Power as primary with captive backup sized for workshop continuity, because interrupted workshop time is unrecoverable teaching time. Water from the Akuzo spine; sewerage and drainage built by the same Okodu team that designs it.

Workshops and laboratories. Engineering needs machine shops (lathes, milling, welding, foundry), electrical machines and power laboratories, electronics and automation benches, materials and soil mechanics laboratories, hydraulics, surveying and drafting studios. Applied science needs demonstration plots, a processing pilot plant and a water and environmental analysis laboratory. Creative departments need a working TV and radio studio with editing suites. Business and IT need computer laboratories — the cheapest per place, the easiest to fill.

Staffing model. Three layers: permanent academic staff for accreditation (NBTE requires qualified full-time staff in discipline ratios); technicians and instructors, the real constraint, paid above market to be drawn out of industry; and a visiting practitioner layer from Group companies at a fraction of the cost per contact hour. Workshop instruction needs smaller groups than a lecture theatre, so the student:staff ratio is structurally worse than a university's — the single most important cost fact in this plan.

Industrial attachment as a credit-bearing requirement. A three-month supervised attachment at the end of ND I and a six-month attachment in HND I, carrying credit, assessed by a joint industry-academic panel, with signed logbook, a named company supervisor and a written project. No attachment, no award. That is what makes the credential mean something to a third-party employer as well as to us.

The placement pipeline. Slots are contracted forward by company, not sourced reactively: Isiome (farming, machinery, foods, manufacturing), Okodu (power, construction, materials), Uli (freight, warehousing, fleet, studios), Idenze (pharma QA, water utilities), Akunnia (back office, treasury). A standing Industrial Placement Council — Group HR directors plus the placement director — allocates slots annually and reports to the Idenze board. Group companies get first refusal on graduates.

Calendar. Two semesters aligned to the university and schools so hostels and shared services run year-round; a summer term carries short courses, industry training and consultancy.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

NBTE, in sequence. (1) Incorporate Idenze Polytechnic Ltd; perfect land title with a Certificate of Occupancy in the promoter's name; constitute proprietor and governing council. (2) Letter of intent to the Executive Secretary. (3) Pay the prescribed non-refundable processing fee — this figure has moved and must be re-verified at payment. (4) Submit the feasibility study: land and title, site plan and drawings, workshop and laboratory inventories by proposed programme, library holdings, staff list with qualifications, funding evidence. (5) NBTE approval/advisory visit to site. (6) Resource inspection against the NBTE Minimum Guide Curricula and Course Specifications. (7) Approval to run programmes, then programme accreditation — per programme, per level (NBTE guidelines; accreditation standards; new programmes). HND accreditation follows only after the first ND cohort graduates, which fixes the earliest HND intake at Year 11.

⚠️ The critical regulatory unknown — resolve in writing before committing capital. A one-year moratorium on new polytechnic and monotechnic registrations ran from February 2025 (Punch; Vanguard). In March 2026 a six-year moratorium on the establishment of tertiary institutions was reported, framed in most coverage around private universities but headlined by several outlets as covering tertiary institutions generally (Vanguard; Guardian; Leadership). The scope as it applies to NBTE-registered private polytechnics is genuinely unclear from public reporting and must be confirmed directly with NBTE and the Federal Ministry of Education. If polytechnics are excluded, file early and hold a 24-month float. If included, the route is not closed — it converts to the accreditation-arbitrage route the Group already plans for universities: acquire or partner an existing accredited institution and install the Idenze model, preserving the Years 7–9 timeline. Note too that a Senate bill to repeal the NBTE Act is in play (Daily Post).

An internal sequencing decision this forces. The Group's master plan contains two NBTE institutions: this polytechnic (20 ha, first intake Years 7–9) and the Akuzo Technical & Vocational College (first intake Year 12). Under a moratorium only one licence may be obtainable in the window. Recommendation: concentrate licence, capital and faculty on the polytechnic, delivering the Akuzo college's programmes as satellite cohorts and short courses under the polytechnic's accreditation until the moratorium lifts. Do not run two thin applications against one closed queue.

State requirements. Registration and inspection with the Anambra State Ministry of Education; state land-use zoning compliance in the institutional zone; environmental and building approvals through LGA and state ministries; and, for power distribution or water-spine draw-off, the relevant ASERC and state water instruments per 42_Okodu_Power.md.

Difference from the NUC pathway. No professorial or doctoral faculty requirement, no hospital, no research infrastructure or endowment test, no ministerial and FEC step, no multi-campus prohibition of the same severity, and a far smaller fee. NBTE tests workshops, equipment, library and instructors; NUC tests scholarship and institutional depth. That difference is why the workshops — not the lecture halls — are the capex centre of gravity here, and why this institution opens first.

The acquisition route — priced, because the moratorium makes it primary rather than standby.

A closed registration queue is not a reason to defer this polytechnic. The Group obtains the licence or buys the institution that already holds it — and §12 row 9's written dialogues with existing NBTE-accredited institutions are that route. What follows prices it. The honest caveat is the same one that governs 24_Idenze_University.md: NBTE's position on change of control is not published anywhere, so the transferability of accreditation on a sale of the owning company must be confirmed in writing before spend [verify].

And the sequencing consequence, stated plainly. HND is the prize and the clock is the reason to buy. Everything in §5's moratorium analysis now resolves differently if NBTE's written answer is that registration is closed: the acquisition route stops being the standby and becomes the institution's opening plan, and the Akuzo Technical & Vocational College should be delivered as satellite cohorts under the acquired institution's accreditation from the outset rather than deferred as a Year-12 institution. One accredited institution with two sites was already the recommendation under a moratorium; buying the institution makes it the recommendation under every outcome.

First ninety days — convert §12 row 9's dialogues into a costed mandate. A written change-of-control opinion from NBTE-experienced counsel on whether institutional registration and programme accreditations survive a sale of the owning company, and what NBTE requires; plus a named register of NBTE-accredited private polytechnics and monotechnics — programme accreditation lists by department, enrolment, staff credentials, equipment condition, ownership, litigation and seller appetite — with three approaches, non-binding. Budget ₦110m — ₦45m counsel and regulator correspondence, ₦45m advisory and valuation, ₦20m technical inspection of workshops and equipment [verify]. It is the only work in the quarter that can preserve the Years 7–9 intake if registration stays closed.

Cost per student place. ₦32.3bn ÷ 5,000 places = ₦6.5m ≈ US$4,040 at full build; the marginal place after Phase 1 costs ₦2.5–3.5m, since a second hostel block and workshop tranche need no new power connection, regulator or library. Against the university's ~US$15,700 per place, the polytechnic is roughly a quarter of the capital per student — the arithmetic behind the whole sequencing thesis. Expect the first 600 places to cost a multiple of that, because workshops are bought in whole units, not per student.

Break-even enrolment. With the industry-services engine running, ~3,600 students, reached around Year 11–12. On tuition and boarding alone, break-even is ~5,600 students — beyond planned capacity. That is not a flaw to hide but the defining fact of the model: a standalone workshop-intensive polytechnic at Anambra fee levels does not pay for itself from tuition; it pays for itself as a campus plus a B2B industry-services business, and the Group's own companies are the anchor customers for the B2B half.

The staff cost ratio — the number to watch. Workshop instruction cannot be scaled by lecture-hall substitution: small groups, more technicians, more contact hours. Total staff cost runs ~51% of revenue at maturity against 34% for the university in 24_Idenze_University.md, and it is worse before it is better: Year 3 ~68%, Year 5 ~58%, Year 8 ~54%, Year 12 ~51%. The visiting-practitioner layer and the technician ratio are the only real levers, and NBTE's requirement for full-time qualified staff constrains both. Budget the deficit rather than deny it: ₦350–700m a year in each of the first four teaching years, against the university's ₦2.5–4bn.

Affordability. Polytechnic students in private institutions are currently ineligible for NELFUND (Guardian; The Sun), though extension has been signalled (Nigeria Startup Act) against ₦161.9bn already disbursed to 864,000+ students (BusinessDay). Our fees sit at roughly 2.5–3× public rates: affordable only with a deferred-payment and income-share facility routed through Aku Capital, employer sponsorship from Group companies, and workshop work-study. Design it before intake, not after.

8. Organisation

Governance. Two-tier, per Group policy: a Governing Council (Chair plus three independents — an experienced polytechnic Rector, a chartered accountant, an Onitsha–Nnewi industrialist) owning strategy and the Rector's appointment; an Academic Board owning curriculum and standards; an independent audit committee reporting through Idenze to the Group Board. The Rector is accounting officer; Registrar, Bursar and Librarian are statutory posts filled for accreditation, not convention.

First ten hires, in order of consequence: (1) Rector/Provost — NBTE-credible, ideally a serving or former Deputy Rector with resource-inspection experience; appoint by Year 3, not Year 6. (2) Director, Accreditation & Quality Assurance — owns every NBTE file and calendar. (3) Registrar. (4) Bursar — must have audited a Nigerian polytechnic and owns the funding evidence NBTE tests. (5) Polytechnic Librarian — statutory; holdings gate the first inspection. (6) Director, Works & Estates — interfaces Okodu Construction and controls the ₦22.8bn build. (7) Director, Industrial Placement & Industry Partnerships — the moat owner; contracts attachment slots and measures outcomes; hire before intake. (8) Heads of the first six departments, each from industry or an established polytechnic. (9) Director, ICT & Learning Systems. (10) Head, Admissions, Corporate Affairs & Marketing — build the brand two years before intake.

Recruiting and retaining instructors with real industry experience is the hardest problem in this plan and cannot be solved by salary alone. Five mechanisms, used together: pay above the public polytechnic scale, because the alternative employer for a good machinist is a Group factory; offer dual appointment — half-time in a Group company, half-time teaching — which keeps skills current and makes the salary whole; fund industrial sabbaticals every three years; recruit retiring Group technicians and artisans into an instructor cadre with a teaching-qualification pathway; and build a sponsored HND-to-degree pipeline into the university from Year 12, so instructors can be grown rather than only bought. Assume the first six HODs must be bought above market, and that two will leave within three years — plan succession, not surprise.

11. Integration

Integration is not a benefit of this plan; it is the mechanism. Every department serves a named Group business, and the institution's economics depend on it.

  • Supplies Isiome Group — agricultural technicians, machine operators, QC assistants and maintenance staff for Isiome Farms, Machinery, Foods and Manufacturing, plus the wood and soft-furnishings skills behind the Nkpor production clusters.
  • Supplies Okodu Group — civil, electrical, mechanical and plumbing technicians for Okodu Construction, Power, Grid, Materials and the Akuzo water programme, the most skill-intensive infrastructure the Group builds.
  • Supplies Uli Group — logistics and transport operators for Uli Freight, Warehousing and Fleet; media graduates for Uli Film, Broadcast and Studios; and the documented, vetted personnel licensed controlled-substance movement through Uli Special Logistics ultimately requires.
  • Supplies Idenze Pharma and the health platform — QC technicians, oral-solid machine operators, instrumentation and calibration staff, and clean-utility and water-treatment skills. The most time-critical line in the plan: the plant needs qualified operators from roughly Year 8, exactly when this institution first graduates.
  • Feeds Idenze University. The polytechnic becomes the university's guaranteed feeder intake for Years 12–14, the first credible academic-record and governance evidence NUC inspectors will see, and the technician and laboratory-demonstrator base a new university cannot otherwise hire in Anambra.
  • Uses Okodu Construction to build and Okodu Power for electricity — ₦22.8bn of construction competitively tendered against a ten-year pipeline; primary power priced against the customer's real alternative (diesel), with captive backup for continuity.
  • Buys food from Isiome Foods — catering for up to 1,700 residents and ~700 staff: a contracted offtake that lowers Group food-estate costs and gives Isiome a committed institutional customer.
  • Is financed by Akunnia Capital — capital structuring, equipment leases, the affordability facility, treasury discipline on the hard-currency tranche, and campus insurance.
  • Feeds Idenze Learning — curriculum, workshop specifications, QA manual and placement system become a licensable product for other Nigerian technical institutions.

The one internal conflict to manage. The polytechnic is both a training institution and a supplier of labour to businesses under margin pressure; training quality and cheap labour are not the same thing. The Industrial Placement Council must be chaired independently of Group HR, attachment must be assessed educationally as well as productively, and placement data published whether or not it flatters us.

26 — IDENZE SCHOOLS

Primary & Secondary Education — the first revenue in the education cluster

1. Thesis

Idenze Schools are the Group's first revenue in education and its cheapest, fastest test of the only replication model it can export. The Group's ambition is to control private education across Africa. It cannot do that by exporting campuses: Nigerian rules prohibit multi-campus operation across states for universities, and transnational education needs separate approval (NUC). The accredited model is what travels — not the institution. A schools network is the cheapest and fastest way to test it, because school registration is far lighter than NBTE accreditation, and both are trivial beside the NUC's ₦25m fee and 90/180-day verification clocks. Get the school model right and it is licensable in dozens of markets; get it wrong and the Group learns its most expensive lesson cheaply.

Schools launch Years 4–6 because they can — before the polytechnic (Years 7–9), long before the university (Years 12–14). They are also the first visible proof of the commitment to transform the character of Nkpor, and the first feeder into both institutions.

Three claims carry the plan:

  1. Boarding, not the fee level, is what makes the arithmetic work. At Anambra price points a day-only secondary school breaks even at 117% of capacity — impossible. With 33% boarding capture it breaks even at 78%. Boarding is not a premium add-on; it is the load-bearing product line.
  2. The Group starts with demand already in place. Its own staff children are anchor enrolment; Okodu Construction builds, Okodu Power powers, Isiome Foods feeds, and the polytechnic and university are guaranteed onward destinations. No standalone Anambra school starts with a captive customer list, an owned builder, power company and food supplier, and an owned destination for its leavers.
  3. Anambra is the hardest market in Nigeria to enter on quality alone: 944 registered private secondary schools, ~60% of pupils already in private schools, and the best performers charging under ₦800,000 a year (SESP 2026–2030; SchoolRegistry). The moat is the model, the staff package and the integration — never the regulator.

2. Market

Scale. Private schooling is not a niche in Nigeria; it is the majority provider. Non-state primary schools grew 31.56% between 2017 and 2022 against 3.3% for state schools (NPSSN 2024), private schools carry over 60% of the basic-education burden (NAPPS, November 2025), and UBEC puts private enrolment at 7,479,170 learners (UBEC NPA Report). (V) Verify both against current Nigeria Education Statistics before any offering document.

Anambra is the densest and most competitive version of that market:

Demand drivers, honestly stated. The middle class is urbanising into Onitsha–Nnewi–Awka, and Nigeria's outbound education bill reached US$1.39bn in six months — some US$2.8bn annualised (Nairametrics); West African elites spend £30m+ a year on UK boarding schools alone (Carnegie). But the standard "public schools are failing" argument does not hold in Anambra. The state recruited 8,115 qualified teachers since 2022, runs free education from ECCDE to SS3, has reached ~1:31 primary and ~1:26–28 secondary ratios, and wins WAEC merit awards. Public schooling here is a free, improving, credible competitor — so these schools must sell character, languages, boarding and a pathway, never dissatisfaction.

The specific gap. Nobody in the South-East sells a mid-priced place that is also a documented pathway into an owned polytechnic or university, staffed by people the Group houses and schools free, on a campus the Group builds, powers and feeds.

(V) Before fixing fees: survey what families in Idemili North, Onitsha and Nnewi pay today, and current fees at Christ the King College, DMGS, QRC and the leading Nkpor private schools.

3. Product & service lines

Core: three schools on one campus with a shared services spine — which is what makes the primary school viable.

Curriculum. The Nigerian national curriculum is the base — 9-3-4, BECE through the state Examination Development Centre, WASSCE (WAEC) and SSCE (NECO) at the end. Small class sizes (target 1:20) and laboratory science for every pupil.

The Group adds four things the national curriculum does not require, drawn from the family's own Raising Plan:

  • Igbo as a compulsory, examined subject to JSS3 and available at WASSCE, taught in the Idemmili–Onicha dialect, with heritage content — Odinani, ancestral reverence, Igbo proverbs, Ncho — delivered non-doctrinally, alongside comparative religious literacy.
  • The Ezeme Reading Canon, age-banded and assessed by oral defence and reading journal, not examination: Ptahhotep, Igbo folk tales and proverbs, the Great Hymn to the Aten and an epic (8–12); The Trouble with Nigeria, Meditations, Long Walk to Freedom, the Analects, the Kathasaritsagara (13–16); The Republic, Anizoba's Odinani: The Igbo Religion, Ibn Fadlan, and one modern African author (17–20).
  • Language pathways. Core for all: English, Igbo, French. Elective from JSS2: Portuguese (Brazilian), Spanish, Hausa. Two tiers, stated plainly — a school cannot teach six languages well to every pupil, and claiming otherwise is how schools lose credibility. The Raising Plan's full standard applies to the family's own children through protected enrichment; the school teaches what it can honestly deliver to a cohort, plus certificated evening classes.
  • Formation: houses, one instrument and one sport per pupil, public speaking or storytelling, service and leadership. The promise mirrors the family's own rule — enrichment capped, one protected unscheduled day a week, sleep and screen curfews treated as seriously as lessons.

The Idenze Diploma sits alongside the national certificate: the school's own transcript of character, service, leadership and languages — what makes a graduate legible to Idenze University and to a Group employer, at no cost to issue.

Vacation and evening lines are the earliest and highest-margin revenue, delivered when campus would otherwise sit idle: summer school and holiday enrichment, evening language classes, BECE/WASSCE/JAMB preparation, teacher CPD through Idenze Learning, and campus hire through Uli.

Deferred deliberately: an IGCSE/Cambridge pathway and a sixth-form college (Year 8+) — they need separate centre approval, hard-currency textbooks and a teacher pool Anambra lacks; and a diaspora boarding product at premium fees, unsellable before the first WASSCE results exist.

4. Operating model

Campus. Academic spine of classrooms, laboratories, library and assembly at the centre; two secondary compounds with separate gates off the primary's circulation; boarding houses on the quiet boundary with their own access, matron's flats and dining; sports fields retained as the buffer. Power from Okodu Power as primary with captive backup for laboratories and boarding; water from the Akuzo spine with borehole and storage; sewerage and drainage built by the Okodu team that designs it. Built by Okodu Construction — tendered competitively, with Okodu as one bidder rather than sole source, so the transaction stays at arm's length.

One campus, three heads, one spine. Each school has its own Head Teacher and academic identity. A shared-services unit under the Head of Schools runs finance, HR, admissions, examinations, estates, ICT, procurement, transport, catering, security, clinic and communications. The primary school is viable only because it shares that spine — its break-even falls from ~81% to ~62% of capacity once shared costs are properly allocated.

Boarding. Houses of ~60, resident houseparents and matrons, weekend programme, controlled devices, structured prep, visitors' register, clinic cover. A documented child-protection policy with a named safeguarding lead, TRCN verification and police character checks before appointment, and an independent complaints channel — a staff-conduct case is the fastest way to destroy a school's brand, and the Group's brand is the collateral.

Teacher quality is the product. Recruit TRCN-registered teachers only — registration is a legal requirement for all Nigerian teachers, with the Professional Qualifying Examination and Mandatory Continuing Professional Development (TRCN). Pay above the Anambra private-school market, benchmarked against the public scale. Then win on what only this Group offers: staff housing in Okodu estates at preferential rent, free schooling for teachers' children, funded MCPD, a defined promotion ladder, and a Group Teachers' Academy with a "Teach Idenze" residency drawing on the polytechnic and later the university.

Quality assurance. Termly observation; external examiners and moderation through Idenze Learning; published WASSCE and BECE results whether or not they flatter us; and academic records kept from the first pupil to the standard NUC and NBTE inspectors will later expect, because these schools are the first academic history the university will present.

Calendar. Three terms aligned to the state calendar; vacations carry the revenue lines above and teacher CPD.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Anambra State Ministry of Education. The state registers schools, not companies: incorporate Idenze Schools Ltd, then register each school. Per the Ministry's published guidance: letter to the Honourable Commissioner; application form (₦20k nursery / ₦30k primary / ₦50k secondary); registration (₦50k / ₦150k / ₦250k); yearly renewal; sports levy of ₦150 per primary pupil, ₦300 per secondary student. Mandatory documents: perimeter survey plan, evidence of land acquisition, title, evidence of financial capability, a three- or six-year development plan, building plan and site plan (Anambra MoE FAQ; Licensing and Accreditation). Apply before opening — operating without approval attracts penalties and lands the school on the published unapproved-schools list.

The site rules bind the land decision, and one is a genuine risk. A permanent site — never rented premises — not erosion-prone or waterlogged, with a mandatory playground and play equipment, within human habitation, motorable year-round, not near a market or industrial area, and not less than 1 km from an existing school. In built-up Nkpor that 1 km rule can invalidate an otherwise perfect parcel. (V) Map every school within 1 km of each candidate parcel before contracting land.

Inspection and curriculum compliance. Approval is followed by periodic supervision; the Ministry publishes annually approved textbooks and BECE literature, and the SESP commits to an independent accreditation and supervisory body working with the Church, CSOs and DFIs. Seeking that accreditation voluntarily is a differentiator, not a burden — the external validation a new school has no brand to supply.

Examinations. BECE through the state Examination Development Centre; WASSCE as a WAEC-recognised centre and SSCE through NECO (WAEC Nigeria; NECO). Centre approval turns on recognised school status, adequate laboratories, qualified subject teachers and credible records. Hold this sequencing option: present the first cohorts through an established host centre while the school's own application runs, so a centre delay never costs a cohort its certificate. (V) Confirm criteria, timelines and any computer-based-examination facility requirement in writing with the WAEC zonal/branch office and NECO before the first SSS3 cohort.

Teachers. TRCN registration, PQE and MCPD as in §4. (V) Confirm whether the state sets a minimum proportion of TRCN-registered teachers as an approval or retention condition.

Premises, safety and health. Building plan approval; LGA and state environmental and building approvals; fire safety; water, sanitation and hygiene standards; a clinic and first-aid room; food-handler certification for kitchen staff; environmental health inspection. (V) Confirm the current state instrument for school health and safety inspection and who enforces it.

Ring-fencing. Own company, own board, own auditors, own child-protection policy, insurance through Aku Insurance, no cross-guarantees with pharma or the university.

The acquisition route — the strongest in the domain, and this plan's primary growth mechanism beyond the first campus.

No registration here is a reason to defer a school, and in this business the rule is not a fallback but the growth engine. §7 already holds the argument: a new school costs ₦14.2bn and seven years to build, register and fill, while replicating a proven one needs roughly 35–50% of the capital and reaches break-even in two to three years. The plan says that replication runs on "a rented or acquired campus" — this section makes acquired the primary form of it. Nigeria's supply of under-enrolled private schools is large and its proprietors are ageing; each school carries state registration, premises approval, examination-centre status, a pupil roll, a staff and a parent body. The scarce asset in a school is not the buildings. It is the registration, the centre approval and the roll — and all three can be bought.

What an acquired school is worth, and the valuation test this plan should use. No published transaction value exists for a Nigerian school business, and the market prices property rather than the business. The evidence is property listings: a school building on 491 sqm at Aguda, Surulere is marketed at ₦220,000,000 (NigeriaPropertyCentre), and a "well-functioning school on two plots" at Egbeda, Alimosho at ₦340,000,000 (NigeriaPropertyCentre) — Lagos prices, in which land dominates and Anambra's are materially lower. So the plan should not price a school off property at all. Use the plan's own build benchmark instead: ₦6.96m of capital per student place (see 17_Idenze_Group.md). Any acquisition whose all-in price per enrolled pupil — enterprise value plus remediation of registration, staffing and facilities — sits materially below ₦6.96m is accretive, and any that sits above it is a greenfield build wearing a purchase agreement. (V) No published data exists; the register below produces the real numbers.

First ninety days — commission the school acquisition register. Every private nursery, primary and secondary school in the target catchments — Idemili North, Onitsha and Nnewi — with registration and approval status, WAEC/NECO centre status, pupil roll and fee level by class, arrears and collection record, TRCN-registered teacher proportion, land title and encumbrances, ownership and age of proprietor, and willingness to sell; then three non-binding indications of interest. Budget ₦70m — ₦35m brokerage and valuation, ₦20m legal and title diligence, ₦15m academic and compliance review of the shortlist [verify]. At a price per pupil below the cost of creating one, buying is not a shortcut around the Group's registration work — it is the replication engine operating at its intended speed.

6. Capital requirement

Naira first; construction tendered competitively against Okodu Construction's bid. Land at the master-plan Zone B range (~₦83m per hectare) — ₦1.0bn for 12 hectares — plus 5% legal and title diligence per Group policy.

Boarding is not an upsell; it is the difference between a viable school and an unviable one. The primary school breaks even at ~81% of capacity stand-alone and ~62% with shared-campus costs allocated; across the network, the three schools together must run at roughly 85% of capacity to clear the cluster's full cost. Two consequences drive the commercial plan: fill rate matters more than fee level, and every empty place is a permanent loss, because teaching cost is fixed per class, not per pupil.

Replication economics — proven school versus new build. A new school costs ₦14.2bn and seven years to build, register and fill. Replicating a proven one — same curriculum, QA manual, fee-finance product and teacher-training pack, on a rented or acquired campus, licensed through Idenze Learning — needs no land purchase, no regulator learning curve and roughly 35–50% of the capital, reaching break-even in two to three years rather than five to seven. That comparison is the most valuable output of this plan, and why the first three schools must be documented as a franchise system from day one: standard timetables, job descriptions, procurement and inspection files.

8. Organisation

Governance. Two-tier per Group policy: an Idenze Schools board (chair plus three independents — a retired principal of a leading Anambra mission school, a chartered accountant, and a professor of education) owning strategy, the Head of Schools' appointment and safeguarding assurance; the Head of Schools as accounting officer; an independent audit committee reporting through Idenze to the Group Board.

11. Integration

Integration is the mechanism, not a benefit. Remove it and the plan loses its margin, its fill rate and its reason.

  • Feeds Idenze Polytechnic (Years 7–9 intake) and Idenze University (Years 12–14). Guaranteed feeder intake, and the documented academic-record and governance history NUC inspectors will later see. Records are kept from the first pupil as if they already belonged to a university system — by Year 12 they will.
  • Teaches the Group's own staff children at preferential terms as an employment benefit. Guaranteed places, discounted fees, payroll-deducted and arrears-proof, with priority admission for Group drivers and artisans — provided at marginal cost, unmatched by any independent Anambra school, and the Group's strongest non-cash retention tool across all five domains.
  • Buys facilities from Okodu Construction — ₦14.2bn of buildings, competitively tendered against a ten-year Group pipeline, at arm's length.
  • Buys power from Okodu Power — cheap, reliable, and a visible campus proof to every visiting parent.
  • Buys food from Isiome Foods — a contracted standing order for 480 residents and 600 day-pupil meals: exactly the anchor institutional offtake Isiome Foods needs before it commissions its line.
  • Employs Idenze University graduates as teachers and Idenze Polytechnic graduates as laboratory technicians, ICT, catering and maintenance staff, closing the loop this cluster exists to close.
  • Finances fee affordability through Akunnia Capital — deferred-payment and fee-finance facilities, staff payroll deduction, treasury for fee reserves, insurance through Aku Insurance. NELFUND does not cover private basic and secondary education, so affordability must be self-provided.
  • Supplies Idenze Learning with the proven model — curriculum architecture, QA manual, inspection file, teacher-training pack, fee-finance design — the product that carries the Group's standards, rather than its capital, into other African markets.
  • Supplies the community. The bursary pool, community use of sports facilities, local employment and the Akuzo Community Development Fund make these schools the first visible proof of the commitment to transform the character of Nkpor.

The one internal conflict to manage. The schools are simultaneously a business needing 85% fill, an employment benefit needing deep discounts, a community promise needing bursaries, and a talent pipeline needing places for staff children. Those four claims compete for the same 2,040 places. Fix the allocation in writing before the first intake — a board-approved split between fee-paying, staff-benefit, bursary and community places — or the discount will be discovered later as the reason the economics failed.
