27 — IDENZE LEARNING

EdTech, Curriculum, Standards & Accreditation-as-a-Service

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Idenze Group is the third child's domain; every company takes Idenze plus a plain function (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0). FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. 24_Idenze_University.md's working title "Idenze Learning" is settled here as Idenze Learning, fee stack adopted unchanged.
GroupIdenze Group — Pharma & Education
StructureEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Idenze Group → Idenze Learning Ltd (own board, own audit)
BusinessCurriculum licensing · accreditation-as-a-service · teacher training · LMS · assessment · QA and inspection · management contracts
RegulatorCAC; TRCN (teacher certification); NDPC (student data); NUC/NBTE/Anambra MoE via Group institutions
Horizon15 years, Year 1 = 2027; first external partner Year 3. Gearing ≤40%; no unhedged USD debt; integration mandatory

1. Thesis

The Group cannot export campuses. The NUC prohibits multi-campus designation across states and requires separate approval for transnational education (NUC, August 2025). A campus abroad is new land, new capital and a new accreditation clock. The accredited model is what travels, not the institution — and Idenze Learning owns and licenses it.

26_Idenze_Schools.md proves the economics: replicating a proven school needs 35–50% of the capital and 2–3 years to break-even, against ₦14.2bn and seven years greenfield. Registration is lighter still; school registration is trivial beside NBTE accreditation, which is trivial beside the NUC's ₦25m fee and 90/180-day verification clocks. Idenze Learning sells the output of that learning curve.

Demand is not speculative: 309 licensed private universities after 33 new licences in 2026, the Minister conceding many fail quality standards (University World News; TheCable). Accreditation, not capacity, is the scarce good, and the capital here is people, content and systems, not buildings.

The constraint: licensing cannot precede proof. Advisory and training monetise the regulatory learning curve from Year 2; curriculum licensing follows the schools' WASSCE record from Year 6; tertiary licensing follows accreditation.

2. Market

JAMB admitted 1,009,044 of 2,007,312 applicants in 2025 (Punch). The binding complaint is quality, not quantity: Nigerians spent US$1.39bn on foreign education in H1 2025 alone (Nairametrics).

Anambra has 944 private secondary, 2,092 private primary and 2,018 private nursery schools, with ~60% of pupils in private schools (SESP 2026–2030); nationally private schools enrol 7,479,170 learners (UBEC). (V) Re-verify against current education statistics.

Segments: the ~53 under-capitalised licensees need accreditation readiness, management and QA; 159–309 private universities need resource-verification advisory; 3,036 Anambra private schools need curriculum, CPD and assessment; Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda and Zambia need the whole stack (Africa e-learning market). Credibility is purchasable and almost nobody sells it; the brand on our certificate is ours.

3. Product & service lines

1. Accreditation-as-a-service — the flagship. Governance packs, academic briefs, QA manuals, self-study files, mock inspections, and a named officer beside the partner through the regulator's visit. US$150,000–500,000 (₦240m–800m), as 24_Idenze_University.md prices it. No proven campus needed, only proven regulatory competence.

2. Curriculum licensing. The national curriculum plus four Raising Plan additions: Igbo compulsory and examined to JSS3 in the Idemmili–Onicha dialect; the Ezeme Reading Canon, assessed by oral defence; language pathways (English, Igbo, French core; Portuguese, Spanish, Hausa from JSS2); formation — houses, an instrument, a sport, service; and the Idenze Diploma transcript. ₦64,000–112,000 per student per year (US$40–70) in schools; 3–5% of tuition in tertiary partners.

3. Teacher training and certification. TRCN-relevant and a revenue line in itself: PQE preparation, MCPD-creditable CPD, the Teach Idenze residency. ₦180,000–450,000 per teacher per programme, cohorts of 25–40.

4. LMS and digital content. Built with Aku Technology: ₦64,000–96,000 per student per year, or ₦4.5m–15m per institution. The platform is also the enforcement mechanism.

5. Assessment and examination services. Item banking, standardised core examinations, examiner panels and moderation: ₦4,500–9,000 per candidate per series.

6. Quality assurance and inspection. Annual inspection, mystery-student audits, safeguarding review: ₦6m–18m per institution per year.

7. Management contracts. A seconded leadership team on a 7-year renewable contract: retainer ₦180m–360m plus 2–3% of tuition, with veto over the Vice-Chancellor/Rector, Registrar and Bursar.

The acquisition pipeline. The ~53 licensees are the pipeline, not only competitors: permanent-site migration falls due within five years and many cannot fund it. Advise first, manage second, acquire third. The advisory engagement is the diligence; the management contract the observation period. (V) Confirm each licensee's status.

4. Operating model

The product is a specification, not a service: curriculum architecture and scope-and-sequence; assessment blueprints and item banks; a QA manual and inspection instrument; staff-file standards; a child-protection policy; a fee-finance design; a training pack. Idenze Learning owns the specification, not the schools. Delivery is advisory (exits at accreditation), licensed (full stack, annual inspection, revocation), or managed.

Standards at arm's length. A group-level Ezeme Academic Standards Board owns curriculum, assessment blueprint, examiner panel and brand licence. Every franchise carries a 7-year term revocable on failed inspection, a veto over the Vice-Chancellor/Rector, Registrar and Bursar, annual inspection plus independent examiners, standardised core examinations in the first two years, and an audited-accounts covenant. Standards control, not equity control, protects the brand.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

A services company is not an institution, and that is a genuine advantage. Idenze Learning incorporates at CAC and needs no NUC or NBTE institutional licence to sell curriculum, advisory, training, assessment or inspection. It carries none of an institution's burden: no permanent-site rule, no ₦25m fee, no 90/180-day clocks, no discipline-ratio staffing. Licensing a model avoids the entire cost structure of being regulated as a provider — which is why the model, not the campus, travels.

Where the institutional regulators bite. Where a partner or Group institution is licensed, its regulator governs. The NUC polices award-bearing programmes, so the certificate boundary needs written confirmation. TRCN (trcn.gov.ng) owns registration, PQE and MCPD; we deliver preparation and MCPD-creditable CPD and do not certify teachers (V). The NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 (NDPC) require registration, a DPO and a lawful cross-border transfer basis for children's data. Copyright Act 2022 s.23(3) makes Repronig membership a Year-1 action; Anambra MoE registration binds the partner.

⚠️ NERDC ranking. From September 2026 public schools may use only NERDC-licensed and ranked titles: 70% minimum score, 6–10 titles per subject, ₦1,500 per page plus ₦750,000 per title — ~₦35.7m per curriculum, non-refundable if the title fails. The Publishers Association is litigating, so the plan must not depend on the policy surviving.

⚠️ Moratorium. A six-year moratorium on new tertiary institutions was reported in March 2026 (Vanguard; Guardian), after a one-year ban on new polytechnics (Punch). If it covers partner institutions it slows the pipeline and raises the value of lines serving existing licencees: revenue is counter-cyclical to new licensing (V).

The acquisition route — where "build versus buy" applies to this plan.

A services company needs no institutional licence, which is the advantage this plan is built on — but the rule still applies: nothing here waits on a permission, and where the Group needs one it buys the entity that holds it. In this business the acquirable assets are curriculum, accreditation and school relationships, not permits. Two of them are materially faster to buy than to build.

11. Integration

Integration is the product. Idenze Learning licenses what the Group's institutions develop and supplies what they would otherwise import.

  • Licenses the curriculum and standards of Idenze Schools, Idenze Polytechnic and Idenze University. The schools supply Raising Plan content, Igbo and heritage, the Reading Canon and the Idenze Diploma; the polytechnic supplies workshop specifications, the NBTE inspection file, the attachment system and apprenticeship assessment — 25_Idenze_Polytechnic.md names this as its contribution; the university supplies the academic brief, recruitment packs and the accreditation playbook.
  • Supplies the Group's own institutions with the LMS, teacher CPD, examiners and moderation, and the inspection instrument. The internal customer is the pilot, and it pays.
  • Uses Aku Technology for the platform and the telemetry that makes QA possible at arm's length; Uli Group for media content; Akunnia Capital for working capital, receivables and insurance.
  • Employs Idenze University graduates as trainers; until the first class arrives around Year 16, trainers come from the polytechnic and Anambra's mission-school cadre, after which the B.Ed faculty becomes a self-renewing pipeline.
  • Is the vehicle by which the whole education platform becomes pan-African without owning institutions abroad — exporting a curriculum, a platform, a training pack and an accreditation playbook.

The conflict to manage. The Group's institutions are both supplier and customer, and will resist a standard written by a sibling. The Standards Board must sit above both, transfer prices must be published, and Idenze Learning must be free to lose the internal business to a competitor.

28 — ULI GROUP

Media & Information Systems + Transport & Logistics — the fourth child's domain

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Uli Group is her group; every company takes Uli plus a plain function. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary throughout; dollar figures are indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026).

Position in the programme: fourth child. Follows 00_Family_Business.md, 01_Isiome_Group.md, 08_Akunnia_Group.md, 17_Idenze_Group.md.
GroupUli Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group (the mother company)
HeirUli — Second Daughter, Senior Female Heir
SectorsMedia & Information Systems · Transport & Logistics
CompaniesUli Film · Music · Animation · Broadcast · Distribution · Cinemas · Rights · Publishing · Brand · Freight · Warehousing · Fleet · Special Logistics
GeographyNkpor (studios, media HQ in the corporate zone) · expressway-facing plots, Zone A (logistics)

Brand added after the domain review. The Holding Structure lists Uli's sector components as "Media platforms — digital, radio, publishing · Brand and reputation management · Freight, delivery, and warehousing · Supply chain and mobility infrastructure." Brand and reputation management is a named part of her mandate and was the one component of this domain with no company. It is covered by 57_Uli_Brand.md. The strategic case is structural rather than decorative: an agency inside a media group buys airtime and placement at cost from its own group, which no independent Nigerian agency can do — so it can either undercut on price or earn a better margin at the same price, and it can guarantee placement that competitors cannot.

⚠️ But the same integration creates a conflict the Group must govern deliberately. 32_Uli_Broadcast.md's advertising sales house sells the inventory that Uli Brand would buy. If either side is captive, the arrangement is destroyed: a captive buyer cannot be held to market rates, so Broadcast's ad-sales revenue becomes fictional; and a captive seller cannot be held to inventory quality, so Uli Brand cannot prove its prices to a third-party client. The rule should be that Uli Brand buys from Uli Broadcast at a published, board-approved rate card — the same rate card offered to external agencies — and that Uli Broadcast remains free to sell to competitors of Uli Brand's clients. The internal advantage is real, but it must be taken as a documented discount off a published card, not as an unpriceable favour. The plan quantifies the benefit at roughly ₦820m a year retained in Group margin and states honestly that this is a ceiling on what Uli Brand may charge internally, not a guaranteed revenue line — and that break-even requires roughly 33 clients and ₦4.4bn of placed media, which a captive book alone will not deliver.

1. Thesis

Uli Group moves ideas and goods — and in a modern economy those are the same business: both are distribution systems.

The Group's own words: "Uli moves ideas and things. In the modern economy, narrative infrastructure and physical logistics are both distribution systems. Controlling what people hear and how goods reach them gives her enormous combined influence."

This is not a news business, and the distinction matters commercially. Uli's mandate in the family's own documents is "Culture, Press, Broadcasting & Supply Chain", her final degree is Marketing, Distribution & Exhibition at the National Film and Television School, her bachelor's is Global Communication Science (UvA), and the university faculty she owns is "Journalism, digital media, film and broadcasting." This is the creative industries — film, television, music, and the distribution and exhibition of that content — paired with physical supply chain.

Why that distinction is worth stating plainly: a national newsroom makes a conglomerate a political actor, with all the regulatory and fundraising consequences that follow. A film studio and a record label do not. Content and culture build brand rather than political exposure, and they are among the only businesses in the Group that earn hard currency without shipping physical goods.

Two structural advantages, and the plan turns on both:

  1. The catalogue is a financial asset class. Film libraries and music master rights are securitised, financed and traded globally, producing long-tail predictable royalties. They are exactly the asset class Akunnia Capital's funds are built to warehouse — a direct, structural feed from Uli into the finance platform.
  2. Licensed controlled-substance logistics is a moat almost nobody can replicate. The Group's own freight plan calls it "the single most defensible asset in the logistics platform." Almost no Nigerian logistics company holds the authorisations, because the regulatory, security and documentation burden is severe.

2. Market

Creative industries

The thesis anchor, corrected at source and much stronger than the original claim. Nigeria's 2025 box office was ₦15.6bn, up 34.72%, with Nollywood at 49.4% against Hollywood's 48.8% — the first time Nollywood has led. 2.79m admissions at an average ticket of ₦5,596, across 248 new releases of which only 81 were Nollywood titles.

But the number that matters is this: the NFVCB classified 1,185 Nigerian films in 2025, and only 81 reached a cinema screen — under 7%. That ratio, not a market-share claim, is what proves the post-theatrical tail is unmeasured and unmonetised. Which is the whole opportunity: the rights platform exists to capture the other 93%.

And the same gap in music: Nigeria's industry generated ₦901bn (~US$600m) in 2024, but publishing, brand and sync together were only 3% of artist income, against 65.7% live and 30.1% streaming. That 3% is the addressable market.

Two honest constraints to carry into any fund discussion. No disclosed price or multiple exists for any African catalogue transaction, so the 5–8× entry assumption is an assumption, not a citation. And no Africa-focused royalty securitisation vehicle exists — the Atlantic Council found lenders "reluctant to place any collateral value in these IPR." That is simultaneously the first-mover advantage and the reason the fund gate matters: without measurable collection uplift, the asset class cannot be financed at all.

Creative industries — the market case

  • Nollywood is one of the world's largest film industries by output and a genuine African cultural export. Afrobeats is a globally significant music export earning hard currency.
  • Both are under-monetised relative to their reach. Rights are frequently poorly documented, splits are unclear, and content is exploited without payment. African catalogues are being acquired by international rights funds precisely because they are undervalued.
  • Nigeria's creative sector is fragmented and informally financed, with little access to the structured capital that film slates and music catalogues require elsewhere.
  • Streaming and international licensing demand for African content is rising — which is the export window, and it is open now.

Logistics

  • Nigeria's freight and logistics market was US$10.95bn in 2025, forecast ~US$15.97bn by 2031 (6.49% CAGR); manufacturing contributed US$4.24bn.
  • Over 90% of Nigerian freight moves by road. The market is informal — single-truck owner-operators, phone brokers, union-controlled loading points, per-trip negotiation.
  • Diesel is over 35% of trucking expense; roads and insecurity add up to 20% to cost.
  • South-East customs reform is cutting demurrage, and Lekki/Onne expansions add ~4.5m TEU of capacity, raising inland road demand.
  • Union levies are systemic — a reported ₦300bn "shadow state", with port truckers complaining of NURTW/RTEAN extortion.

The gap in both halves is the same: professionalism. In content it is documentation and rights discipline. In logistics it is utilisation, compliance and corridor control. Uli Group's moat is being the professionally run African-owned operator in both.

3. Product & service lines

The creative platform

Uli Film — film and television production: feature, series, documentary. The content engine.

Uli Music — label, publishing, artist management, master rights. Publishing and masters are where the durable money sits, not live performance.

Uli Animation — animation, post-production and visual effects. The highest-margin content category — no location cost, no weather, and it exports universally without dubbing.

Uli Broadcast — broadcasting, streaming carriage and content licensing. Distribution to African audiences and international buyers.

Uli Distribution — the pipes: theatrical, streaming, broadcast licensing and international sales. This is where the margin sits in content, which is precisely why Uli's degrees pair content (UvA) with distribution and exhibition (NFTS) and supply chain (Heriot-Watt). The training says: own the pipes, not just the pictures.

Uli Cinemas — the exhibition chain across anchor markets.

Three findings from the cinemas plan that shape the business.

1. Occupancy is the governing metric, and the bar is high. The industry-average Nigerian screen runs at ~2.7% seat occupancy. Cash break-even is 3.6% — barely above the national average — while full-cost break-even needs ~16.6%, which no Nigerian cinema has sustained. That single fact sets the structure: Tranche 1 is a leased site (₦1.4bn, no land risk), and the ₦3.6bn flagship is gated behind a trading record and held in Aku Infrastructure Fund I rather than on the operating balance sheet.

2. Power can consume the entire exhibitor margin. 462,000 kWh a year costs more than the film share at Okodu Power's tariff — and would exceed total site revenue on diesel. Solar-first is therefore a viability condition, not a sustainability preference.

3. A boundary conflict this plan caught: 50_Akuzo_Development.md zones the Akuzo Residential District exclusively residential — no commercial units. So the cinema sites in Group commercial property or adjacent, never inside Akuzo. Recorded because the earlier assumption was that it would sit in the district.

Market context, sourced: the 2025 box office was ₦15.6bn across 118 cinemas and 2.79m admissions at a ₦5,596 average ticket; Lagos holds 41 of the 118 locations and 15 states have no cinema at all — which is the South-East first-mover case. Named competitors: Filmhouse ₦4.07bn (26%), Genesis ₦3.01bn (19.3%), Silverbird ₦2.93bn. The NFTS "Exhibition" track made operational, and a physical distribution monopoly in the markets where it operates.

Uli Rights — catalogue and royalty management for music masters, publishing and film libraries. Full plan at 33_Uli_Rights.md. The bridge into Akunnia Group.

Uli Publishing — books, formats, adaptation rights. Content IP in its cheapest and most portable form.

The logistics platform

Uli Freight — freight and trade corridors. Full plan at 35_Uli_Freight.md. Corridor control, not fleet size. Cost ₦48/tonne-km against ₦93 revenue; break-even 5.8 loaded legs/month owned versus 8.6 leased, against 10 available — which is why the fleet policy is three-track: own the core, subcontract ≥30% of tonne-km, and lease only for project or peak work. The captive base load must be signed before any truck is ordered.

Uli Warehousing — grade-A warehousing at ports and inland hubs. Storage is a toll business with predictable revenue.

Uli Fleet — owned fleet, cross-border haulage, telematics and the control tower.

Uli Special Logistics — licensed controlled-substance movement. Full plan at 38_Uli_Special_Logistics.md. NAFDAC NCS permits, NDLEA authorisations, INCB-matched quantities and per-shipment authorisation with no standing permit. Ring-fenced in its own company with its own board and audit, because a diversion or licensing failure here must never reach the Group's accreditation, banking or fundraising.

⚠️ One gating question, found by the company plan, qualifies the "moat" claim above. The published NAFDAC NCS instruments address importers and manufacturers — they do not expressly contemplate a third-party custodial carrier holding the movement authorisation in its own name. Whether this company can itself hold the authorisation is not established by the available material. Two possible structures follow, and they are different businesses:

  • If it can hold the licence — a genuine licence monopoly, and the moat stands as described.
  • If it cannot — the carrier operates under the licence holder's authorisation (in practice Idenze Pharma's), and the advantage becomes demonstrated compliance capability rather than an exclusive licence. Still valuable and still hard to replicate, but not a legal monopoly, and it makes the carrier dependent on a Group affiliate's licence.

And the same question repeats one level down, from the Uli Warehousing plan: whether NAFDAC and NDLEA will register a warehousing company as custodian of controlled stock, or require the licence holder to hold it in its own facility. Two separate plans have now hit the same structural uncertainty from different directions, which suggests the Group's controlled-substance architecture depends on a single unanswered regulatory question: can any Group company other than the licence holder hold, store or move controlled material? Ask NAFDAC NCS and NDLEA once, comprehensively, covering carriage and custody together — before either the cage is built or a vehicle is ordered.

Get written confirmation from NAFDAC NCS before ordering a single specialised vehicle. The company plan states this as its gating condition and carries a fallback structure if the answer is no.

4. Operating model

Content: own the pipes, finance the slate

The creative business model is catalogue-building, not project-by-project production. Each title is an asset with a multi-decade royalty tail; the objective is a growing library, not a hit film. That changes investment discipline: slate financing rather than single-project financing, and rights retention rather than outright sale.

Chain-of-title diligence is the hard part and the real expertise. African rights documentation is frequently incomplete, splits are disputed, and unregistered works are common. Disciplined documentation is the competitive advantage — it is what makes a catalogue bankable, and what international buyers pay a premium for.

Logistics: corridor control

The capital-allocation test is explicit: does this spend increase control of the corridor, or merely the count of wheels? Everything follows from that.

Union and levy posture, decided in advance and stated in writing (from the freight plan): a closed, gated private depot with the company's own loading crew and no third-party loading points; drivers on direct payroll; formal written notification to the unions; pay only levies existing in a state law or gazette, by bank transfer with a receipted reference; log every other demand — photograph, amount, location, officer, time — in a corridor obstruction register; escalate through the state internal revenue service, NARTO and, if necessary, litigation. No roadside cash negotiation.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

The Group's rule, stated once here for the whole domain and then applied company by company: a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business. Uli Group either obtains the licence or buys a company that already holds it. In Nigerian markets a licence is frequently cheaper and far faster to buy than to obtain, for three structural reasons — the incumbent is usually undercapitalised and willing to sell, the regulator's de novo process is slow and discretionary, and a licensed entity arrives with the licence, trained staff, equipment and customer contracts that a new applicant must build from nothing.

One honest exception, and it is named here so no company plan invents a market that does not exist. 38_Uli_Special_Logistics.md carries it: NDLEA and NAFDAC NCS controlled-substance authorisations attach to the applicant's own compliance record, are revocable and non-transferable, and no lender will advance against them. They cannot be bought. That plan's route is contract carriage for, or partnership with, an already-authorised operator while the Group builds its own record.

Why this is a Group-level rule rather than a company preference. A licence that must be applied for creates a queue; a licence that can be bought creates a price. The Group's advantage is that it has capital and the incumbents do not — so in every vertical where the licence is transferable, the fastest and usually cheapest path into the business is to buy the entity that already holds it. Where the licence is not transferable — controlled substances, and any authorisation granted on personal or corporate record — the correct answer is the slower one, and the plan should say so rather than assume a market.

29 — ULI FILM

Film & Television Production — the Uli Group's content engine

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026).

Position: company plan under 28_Uli_Group.md; peers 35_Uli_Freight.md, 38_Uli_Special_Logistics.md. Ezeme Group is the mother company; Uli Group is the fourth child's group (EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

In one line: Uli Film is not a production house hoping for a hit — it is a library that happens to make films.

1. Thesis

Catalogue-building, not project-by-project production. Every title is an asset with a multi-decade licensing tail: theatrical in year one, streaming and broadcast in years two to four, then international sales, AVOD, in-flight, educational, format and clip licensing for twenty years after. The objective is a growing library, not a hit film — so the discipline is slate financing rather than single-project financing, and rights retention rather than outright sale.

The trap, named plainly. Most Nigerian producers fund production by selling rights outright — a buy-out, a perpetual all-rights licence, or a distribution advance against 100% of rights — and end up owning nothing. The film circulates for decades; the producer is paid once. Nollywood's under-monetisation is not mainly a box-office or piracy story; it is an ownership story. Rights never documented cannot be licensed twice, valued, securitised or enforced.

Three structural reasons this works inside Ezeme Group:

  1. The catalogue is a financial asset class, and the Group owns the buyer. Uli Film originates the assets; Uli Rights documents them; Akunnia Capital warehouses and syndicates them.
  2. Owning distribution makes production viable. A standalone producer keeps only ~30–40% of theatrical gross after tax, the exhibitor split and the distribution fee (The Nation); inside the Group the exhibitor margin (Uli Cinemas), the distribution fee (Uli Distribution) and the broadcast window (Uli Broadcast) are retained. Section 7: 1.12× in year one integrated against 0.61× standalone — no hit required.
  3. It earns hard currency without shipping anything. Licensing and format deals are dollar-denominated, and Uli's French is a working asset in francophone Africa.

What Uli Film deliberately is not. Not a newsroom: content carries commercial risk, not political-concentration risk.

2. Market

  • Nollywood is one of the world's largest film industries by output and a genuine African cultural export (FMACCE; commonly cited at ~2,500 titles a year — verify).
  • The market is real but badly monetised. Nigeria had 122 cinemas and 369 screens in 2025, a ₦5,959 average ticket and ₦15.6bn of box office against a projected ₦20bn in 2026 (Nairametrics), and only 81 Nigerian titles reached cinemas against roughly 2,000 produced (The Cable). Nigeria's annual box office is smaller than one mid-budget Hollywood release, which is why theatrical cannot be the revenue model.
  • Streaming is growing but consolidating hard. The Nollywood streaming pool is put at US$30–50m a year, with licences of US$10k–90k unproven and US$50k–200k theatrically proven, and Netflix Nigeria at roughly 300k subscribers (BETAR); MultiChoice Nigeria's subscription revenue fell 44% to US$197.7m with 1.4m subscribers lost (BusinessDay), Prime Video left African originals, Netflix now licenses rather than commissions, and Showmax shut down in March 2026 (BETAR).
  • The export window is open, but the commissioning era has cooled. Netflix and Prime Video have carried Nigerian work globally and at Cannes (LA Times), yet filmmakers now publicly discuss commissioning shrinking (Premium Times). A platform that commissions is a customer; one that licenses is a channel.
  • Home-market tailwind. Anambra State is courting the creative economy through an ANAWOOD Film Village MOU (Anambra State Government), and Nkpor sits inside that agenda — confirm the MOU's scope, land status and any state equity.

4. Operating model

Development and green-light. The funnel is 40 : 12 : 8 : 6 per annual cycle — forty concepts, twelve full scripts, eight green-lights, six delivered — on a budgeted development cost of ₦180m a year at scale. All four tests must pass: clean chain of title or a written cure plan (no defective option, unsigned composer or uncleared archive element); a windowing plan naming a buyer or a Uli Distribution commitment for two windows; a funded 10% contingency with the production accountant appointed before principal photography; and ≥70% of cost covered before day one.

Physical production and cost control. Permanent staff are a thin layer of producers, line producers, accountants and post technicians; crew, cast, locations and equipment are procured per production, so over 80% of a title's cost is variable. Uli Studios, Nkpor — two sound stages, standing sets, a post lane and a lighting/grip fleet — is built by Okodu Construction and powered by Okodu Power. Every title carries a production accountant independent of the line producer, weekly cost-versus-budget reporting, and a 5% overspend tolerance with Group CFO sign-off beyond it. The management metric is cost per finished minute.

Rights retention and chain-of-title discipline — the core competency, not a legal chore. Every title carries a title bible: chain-of-title opinion; option and purchase agreements on all underlying works; writer, director and cast grants; composer and sync agreements via Uli Music; releases and clearances; Nigerian Copyright Commission registration evidence; E&O cover; and delivery to an international deliverables schedule — M&E tracks, closed captions, 4K/HDR masters, cue sheets, metadata to a standardised schema. A title a buyer cannot describe in its own format cannot be licensed twice.

Licensing and slate financing. Windows are held, not dumped: theatrical (Uli Cinemas) → paid/SVOD, 3 years non-exclusive → free-to-air and FAST → AVOD and ancillary. Perpetual buy-outs are refused. Finance is a slate facility — a rolling three-year envelope, each drawdown gated by the green-light test — with pre-sales and per-territory minimum guarantees targeted at 25–40% of cost (outside Nigeria the standard stack covers 50–70% through pre-sales).

Co-production. Nigeria's first audiovisual co-production treaty is with Brazil (Deadline). Posture: co-produce for access — territory, finance, craft — never to cheapen the budget; every agreement fixes copyright split, territory allocation and negative control.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

Uli Film's classification, distribution and export route is neither expensive nor slow — the NFVCB fee scale is small against a slate, and the UCC registration is evidentiary and takes days. What is slow is everything around it: standing with the regulator, a permits and compliance habit, a development slate, and a crew that has already delivered. So the Group's rule applies in its commercial form rather than its bare form — the licence is acquired, not waited for, and where the certificate itself is cheap the thing worth buying is the company that already holds it, holds the relationships and holds a slate. The Group does not defer a business for want of a licence; it either obtains it or buys a company that already has it. In Nigerian creative markets the incumbent is usually undercapitalised, the regulator's de novo process is discretionary and slow, and a licensed entity arrives with the licence, trained staff, equipment and customer contracts a new applicant must build from nothing.

What the acquisition actually buys. In a production company the licence is the least valuable thing on the balance sheet. Stated fairly, the alternative. The canonical Nigerian rights sale is a platform paying 100% of the budget plus a 15–30% overhead for all rights in perpetuity (BETAR) — precisely why producers who took it own nothing today. The fee is certain; the rights model is slow and risky, locking cash in a title for 3–5 years. Uli Film accepts that trade because ownership is the only thing that can be valued, rated and sold on to Akunnia's funds: a fee cannot be securitised — and it is why owning distribution makes production viable at all, at 0.61× standalone versus 1.12× integrated in year one.

Catalogue value. At Year 5 the library holds ~40 titles earning roughly ₦450m a year in trailing royalties. International libraries trade at 5–10× net licensing revenue or 4–12× EBITDA (DealStream), though valuers caution that no rule of thumb is reliable — implying ₦1.8–3.2bn of unrealised value. Counterweight to verify: Nigerian catalogues have been valued as low as ~US$10k per title (Entertainment Reporter) — and closing that gap is the entire commercial case for chain-of-title discipline.

8. Organisation

Leadership. Uli is completing the NFTS Marketing, Distribution & Exhibition programme — the discipline this company needs, because the money sits in distribution and rights, not in shooting. Until she takes the chair, a professional Head of Uli Film runs the company, reporting to the Uli Group MD and the Group Board with three independent directors. Uli chairs the green-light committee and owns the slate-financing relationship with Akunnia Capital.

10. Risks

11. Integration

Integration is mandatory, and here it is the business model rather than a courtesy.

Supplies to: Uli Rights — the catalogue: rights, masters, metadata, cue sheets and royalty entitlements, documented so it can be rated and pooled, which is what makes Akunnia Capital's catalogue securitisation possible. Uli Distribution — new titles with clean deliverables and a windowing plan. Uli Cinemas — first-window product and the retained exhibitor margin. Uli Broadcast — series, library content and the broadcast window. Uli Music — sync and score, publishing retained in-Group. Uli Publishing — adaptation rights. Idenze University and Polytechnic — placements and crew training.

Buys from: Okodu Construction — stages, post facility and backlot, fixed-price with liquidated damages. Okodu Power — power for stages, post and the vault. Uli Animation — animation, VFX and finishing. Uli Freight — media, drives and equipment. Isiome Foods — location catering. Akunnia Capital and Aku Insurance — slate facility, catalogue-backed lending, E&O. Aku Technology — the rights and royalty reporting platform.

The two-way loop with Akunnia: Uli Film originates the assets; Uli Rights documents them; Akunnia Capital rates, pools and syndicates them. The Group manufactures the asset class its own funds sell.

12. First ninety days

  1. Hire the Head of Rights and Chain of Title and the Production Accountant before anything is shot — documentation discipline cannot be retrofitted.
  2. Adopt the title-bible standard and metadata schema as written policy, with any missing item a hard stop at green-light, and open the NFVCB pathway — including the 30-day export permit — before the first release.
  3. Answer the incentive and permit questions in writing — the NTA 2025 Tenth Schedule, CEDF eligibility and the Anambra registration position — and model nothing on any of them until answered.
  4. Design the green-light committee and cohort gate with Akunnia Capital — four written tests, Uli chairing; its first recorded decision should be the refusal of one project.
  5. Contract the interim studio at Nkpor and place the first equipment order on lease-to-own terms, and commission the studio demand study with Uli Animation, Broadcast and Music so Stage 1 is sized to contracted demand.
  6. Develop forty concepts to twelve scripts, and open three co-production conversations with a template fixing copyright split, territory allocation and negative control before money moves.

plans/30_Uli_Music.md  ·  5,961 words

Uli Music — Label, Publishing, A&R & Master Rights

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative only at the library rate ₦1,600/USD, held flat nominally. Not comparable across plans.
EntityUli Music Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Uli Group
OwnershipEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group Nigeria Ltd → Uli Group → Uli Music Ltd
ScopeLabel · publishing · A&R and artist development · master rights · sync licensing
SiteStudio and documentation suite, Nkpor; A&R and business affairs, Lagos
Horizon10–15 years · Year 1 = 2027
Ring-fencingOwn contracts, catalogue and audit only. Group-wide rights administration sits in Uli Rights

1. Thesis

Afrobeats is a globally significant Nigerian export earning hard currency, and it is systematically under-monetised at home. The system capturing its value is built abroad: three foreign distributors took 68% of Nigeria's 2025 streaming volume — Empire 32.9%, Universal 21%, Sony 14% (TechCabal, Mar 2026). Harvard's Centre for African Societies and Economies is blunter: Afrobeats earned an estimated US$100m globally in 2023, yet "structurally, the global boom is generating income almost everywhere except Africa", the world's lowest royalty-collecting region (Vanguard, Dec 2025).

The failure is documentation. Compositions go unregistered, splits go unwritten, ISRC and ISWC identifiers are missing, and works reach DSPs without the metadata that lets a society match a recording to a song. The money is not only stolen — it is unclaimed in international pools because nobody can prove ownership (allAfrica, Mar 2026; Downtown Music Africa).

So the thesis is not "sign hits." It is: own the master and the composition, and administer both with industrial discipline. Per 1,000 streams at a ₦4,000 DSP gross (illustrative, blended Nigeria and international): net receipts ₦3,600 after a 10% distribution fee; publishing gross on the composition ≈₦900; a master-only label on a 50/50 split keeps ₦1,800, while Uli Music under co-publishing adds ₦675 of the composition — ₦2,475 total, roughly 38% more per stream on the same play. Across every territory and a 50-year copyright term, that gap is the business.

Second: publishing and masters are where the durable money sits — not live performance. Live is a fee-driven service business, working-capital hungry, dependent on an artist's physical presence. It is 65.7% of Nigerian artist income, against 3% for brand partnerships, publishing and sync combined (Basslines to Billions, NCAC / RegalStone Capital, Nov 2025). Nigeria's music economy was built backwards, on its least durable line. A label building the other 3% is not competing with Nigerian labels; it is competing with the gap.

Third, stated explicitly: the catalogue is a financial asset class. Masters and publishing rights are securitised, financed and traded globally — over US$13bn of catalogue transactions in 2025 (Billboard / Citrin Cooperman), from The Weeknd's reported US$1bn partnership with Lyric Capital (Variety) to retail marketplaces clearing a median 6.1x trailing earnings, a 16.4% entry yield (AltStreet, 2,683 deals). Uli Rights, our sister company, is built to warehouse exactly this; Akunnia Capital's content-catalogue royalty fund — 10–15% target return, 1.0–1.5% management fee — is built to syndicate it. Uli Music is not merely a label; it is the origination engine of an asset class another Group company sells.

One sentence: Afrobeats earns the world hard currency while African rights holders lose it to unregistered works and unwritten splits, and the durable fix is a rights-owning label that treats metadata, chain of title and collection as the product — not the paperwork.

2. Market

Global. Recorded music reached US$31.7bn in 2025, +6.4%, an eleventh consecutive year of growth; streaming passed US$22bn (69.6% of revenue) on 837m paid subscribers (Punch / IFPI Global Music Report 2026; Ripples Nigeria).

Africa. Sub-Saharan Africa recorded US$120m in 2025, +15.2%, joint second-fastest region — but South Africa is 78.1% of it (~US$93.7m), leaving the continent near 0.4% of global recorded revenue. On publishing, CISAC put Africa at €81m (2023) rising to €90m (2024), +14.2%, against a global creators' pool above €13bn.

Nigeria — and the measurement gap that is the opportunity. Government-commissioned research sizes the industry at ₦901.6bn (US$600.7m) in 2024, growing ~7% a year to ~₦1.5tn (US$1.03bn) by 2033 (NCAC / RegalStone Capital). Yet IFPI's ledger tracks under US$26m of Nigerian revenue while Spotify alone paid Nigerian artists over ₦60bn (~US$44m) in 2025 (InterSpace; TechCabal reports ₦58bn / US$41.5m — reconcile (verify)). The formally recorded industry is less than half the real one. Whoever builds the ledger captures the difference.

Competition leaves five things undone. The majors and their African affiliates (UMG/Mavin, Sony/Since '93) have scale and DSP leverage but set catalogue economics abroad and fit mid-tier Nigerian acts and non-anglophone export poorly. Nigerian indies and one-hit imprints have almost no publishing capability, no chain-of-title discipline and no institutional reporting — KPMG notes "a vaguely defined business structure" making local labels hard for traditional investors (via TechCabal). Distributors posing as labels (TuneCore, DistroKid, Boomplay, Audiomack) take a fee, never own, never register a composition and never collect performance. Local publishers and administrators (Downtown Music Africa, small Lagos houses) have the right model but no balance sheet to fund advances. And the collection societies sit on a lane contested since 2018.

The gap: a Nigerian-owned label that funds advances, owns both sides of the copyright, documents chain of title, registers every work, collects internationally through reciprocal agreements, and can show an institution a clean royalty statement. Nobody does all five.

3. Product & service lines

LineWhat is soldPrice basisYr 1Yr 5

Live and touringTours, festivals, ticketing, brand activationsFee; promoter split; ticketing margin10%6%

Live and touring is a supporting line, never the core. It exists to market releases, produce setlist and cue data supporting public-performance claims under s.15 of the Copyright Act 2022, and give artists cash the label need not fund. Capital is not allocated to it; tour working capital is promoter-financed or separately secured through Akunnia.

The roles, stated because conflating them is the commonest failure in Nigerian music. The label owns or exclusively licenses the master and pays the artist a royalty. The publisher owns or administers the composition and collects mechanical, performance and sync income for writers. The distributor moves files and metadata to DSPs for a fee and takes no ownership — a distribution deal is not a record deal. The collection society licenses public performance and broadcast for many rights holders and distributes the pool; in Nigeria it must be NCC-approved.

4. Operating model

The deal ladder. Four tiers. C — development (0–2m streams/title): a royalty deal with no advance, the label funding release and recouping cost first. B — traction (2–20m streams): an advance of ₦40–120m plus a 50/50 net profit split, artist keeping publishing, recouped from 100% of net receipts. A — priority (20m+ streams, export potential): ₦250–600m plus co-publishing, the label taking 75% of the composition, or an assignment of the writer's share where the advance is large. Catalogue: outright acquisition, or an advance against royalties, priced at a multiple of trailing net receipts. Default rule: we buy rights, not loyalty. Advances are priced against documented trailing performance, never projected stardom; each is a loan against an identified revenue stream.

Splits, metadata and chain of title are the core competency — not an administrative function. They are what make a catalogue bankable and what buyers, sub-publishers and lenders price. Five gates, each with a named owner, and no release proceeds until all five close:

  1. Split sheet — signed by every writer and producer before final delivery, percentages adding to exactly 100%, each party's IPI/CAE number recorded. Nigerian practice often leaves splits verbal; that is the source of most disputes.
  2. Chain of title — written assignment or exclusive licence for master and composition. This is statutory: under s.30(3) of the Copyright Act 2022 an assignment of copyright or an exclusive licence "shall have no effect unless it is in writing" (Copyright Act 2022). s.28(1) vests copyright initially in the author, so a label without written assignments owns nothing; s.30(5) makes one co-owner's grant bind the others — an unsigned co-writer is a defect in the whole title.
  3. Identifiers — an ISRC per recording and an ISWC per composition, linked. Platforms report against ISRCs; societies pay against ISWCs; the link is what converts a stream into money — and CISAC's ISWC↔ISRC linking only entered soft launch in 2025, with shared infrastructure renewal targeted for 2027. Catalogues documented now benefit disproportionately; sloppy ones get exposed faster.
  4. Registration — works entered in the NCC Register of Works (s.87). Registration does not confer copyright, but a certified extract is "admissible in evidence in all proceedings without further proof" and the Register is "at first instance, evidence of the work" — an evidentiary moat for the same money.
  5. Territory mapping — which rights, to whom, for how long, where, mirroring what s.30(2) permits an assignment to be limited to. This is what stops a master being licensed twice.

Build a documentation room, not a filing cabinet: one metadata ledger (Aku Technology) as source of truth for every ISRC, ISWC, split, contract and statement, reconciled quarterly against DSP reports and society distributions, with unmatched works tracked as a live list until cleared.

360 deals — and why we will use them narrowly. A 360 takes a share of an artist's entire income in exchange for a larger advance. Three reasons it is a poor default. It taxes the wrong line: live is 65.7% of Nigerian artist income and its least durable part, so taking it converts a service business into our risk. It creates defection pressure: an artist who believes the label is taking money it did not earn leaves at the first offer, and nearly every major catalogue dispute starts in a deal the artist later judged unfair — the Burna Boy / Warner litigation over early masters being the current cautionary case (Channels TV, Mar 2026). And it obstructs the asset, because institutional buyers want clean, separable royalty streams rather than cross-collateralised obligations. Policy: no more than 20% participation in any non-music line, framed as a service fee for services actually rendered, with a written sunset and a right of first refusal rather than an assignment. Never a share of the artist's person.

Advances versus royalty deals. Advances carry the risk and the reward: cash out before a naira returns, but a cleaner and larger ownership position, and they are the only way to sign an act with leverage. Royalty deals shift risk to the artist, recover cost first, and leave the artist's publishing intact — but ownership is thinner and the artist can leave. Both are used deliberately — royalty deals for Tier C, advances for B and A. A label with only advances is a bank; a label with only royalty deals never signs anyone who matters.

Collection runs four parallel channels, because each captures different money: DSP and distributor reporting (recorded), MCSN (domestic public performance and broadcast), sub-publishers and foreign societies through reciprocal agreements (international performance and mechanical), and direct neighbouring-rights registration for masters (SoundExchange in the US, PPL in the UK, and EU and South African equivalents). Most Nigerian labels run only the first. Channels two to four are where the black-box money sits, and running them is a cost advantage rather than a new business.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Accounting standards the catalogue buyer will require. Institutional investors do not accept management accounts. Build to this from the first release; retro-fitting it onto a five-year-old catalogue discounts the asset.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

Uli Music's regulatory position is unusual and the rule must be read carefully here: none of the permissions this company needs is scarce, and none of them is the reason to buy anything. The reason to buy is the master and the composition. But the Group's rule still governs, in its commercial form: a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business — Uli Music either obtains what it needs or buys a company that already holds it, and in Nigerian music the second route is frequently cheaper and far faster, because the incumbent label is undercapitalised, the society and registration processes are slow and discretionary, and a label that already exists arrives with the licence, the registered repertoire, the artists, the equipment and the DSP and sub-publishing contracts a new applicant must build from nothing.

What acquisition actually transfers, and it is more than recordings. A purchased label or catalogue conveys, in one instrument: the masters outright (by assignment), the publishing rights outright (by assignment of the composition copyright, which under s.30(3) has no effect unless in writing), COSON or MCSN membership, because membership attaches to the rights-holding entity and survives a share transfer unchanged; the registered repertoire and its ISRC and ISWC block; the sub-publishing and reciprocal agreements with foreign societies, which are the collection channels most Nigerian labels never open; and the historic royalty statements that make the trailing-earnings multiple provable at all.

Price it on the market, not on the icons. The discipline is already in §7 and it is the discipline that must govern every acquisition: publishing trades at 12–18× NPS, compressed from a 20–25× peak, and the headline deals — The Weeknd at a reported US$1bn (Variety) — describe iconic assets bought by funds. Across 2,683 actual retail royalty transactions the market cleared at a median 6.1× trailing earnings — a 16.4% entry yield (AltStreet). Uli Music buys in the mid-market, so 6× is the reference point and the 8× net-receipts ceiling stands. No African catalogue transaction has a disclosed price or multiple, so any African entry figure is an assumption and not a citation — mark it [verify].

Ninety-day action, costed. Instruct counsel to identify ten Nigerian labels and publishers with a registered repertoire, current MCSN membership and at least three years of royalty statements, and to bring two to indicative price. Budget ₦35m (~US$22,000): ₦15m chain-of-title and s.30(3) diligence on the shortlist, ₦12m royalty-statement normalisation and trailing-NPS rebuild for two targets (one-offs stripped: viral spikes, a single large sync, an artist's death bump), ₦8m MCSN, NCC and ISRC status verification. Report to the Group CFO with a priced recommendation before the first Tier-A advance is approved, because at 6× the acquisition may be the better buy.

6. Capital requirement

Funding mix. Family equity funds Years 1–3, because development spend on unsigned artists cannot be pledged and should not be levered. From Year 4, Akunnia Capital structures catalogue-backed non-recourse lending against contracted royalty streams, so acquisitions are financed by the assets they buy. Gearing ≤40% group-wide; no unhedged USD debt — a rule that bites here, since royalties arrive in dollars and euros while advances and payroll are naira.

Acquisition discipline: nothing is bought on projected upside. Pricing is against a three-to-five-year trailing NPS or net-label-share average, normalised for one-offs (a viral spike, a single large sync, an artist's death bump). Earn-outs tied to realised royalties are the default, with an 8x net receipts ceiling until an internal valuation methodology is audited.

8. Organisation

10. Risks

11. Integration

Supplies to:

  • Uli Rights — the catalogue itself. Uli Music originates masters and compositions; Uli Rights administers registration, collection and statements at an arms-length 8–12% fee. Uli Rights is the Group's copyright-holding and administration vehicle; Uli Music is its largest originator.
  • Akunnia Capital — the catalogue as an investable asset class. Masters and publishing produce long-tail, dollar-denominated, predictable royalties that can be pooled, rated and syndicated. The Aku Capital content-catalogue royalty fund targets 10–15% with a 1.0–1.5% management fee; a catalogue assembled at 6–8x net receipts yields 11–15% net after administration and clears it. This is the single most important line in this plan, and the direct answer to "what will the first fund invest in?"
  • Uli Distribution — masters and metadata to international DSPs; Uli Music is its anchor client and proof of scale.
  • Uli Broadcast — broadcast and streaming carriage, radio and TV promotion, and performance-royalty volume through MCSN.
  • Uli Cinemas — exhibition promotion and pre-show repertoire in the Group's own venues.
  • Uli Film and Uli Animation — sync. Group productions license Uli Music masters and compositions on arms-length terms, giving both sides a first-call counterparty and Uli Music a guaranteed sync floor while international placements build.
  • Uli Publishing — compositions. Uli Music's publishing arm routes composition copyright, print and adaptation rights through Uli Publishing, the Group's copyright-holding vehicle, avoiding duplicate structures.
  • Okodu Real Estate — studio and creative-zone lettings.

Buys from: Okodu Power — power for the studio and documentation suite, so diesel is a fallback rather than a base cost. Okodu Construction — studio, acoustic treatment and creative-zone build-out. Aku Technology — the metadata ledger and royalty-reporting platform that makes the catalogue auditable, and therefore syndicable, from the first release. Akunnia Capital — working capital, catalogue-backed non-recourse lending, acquisition finance and the royalty fund warehouse. Idenze Polytechnic and Idenze University — studio technicians and business-affairs staff. Isiome Foods — location and event catering. Akunnia Group — governance, audit and IFRS reporting standards, and tour and asset insurance.

The loop, plainly: Uli Music originates rights → Uli Rights documents and collects them → Aku Technology makes them auditable → Akunnia Capital warehouses and syndicates them → the proceeds fund the next roster and the next acquisition. Each turn is financed by the one before it, and the catalogue is the asset that never expires.

12. First ninety days

  1. Incorporate Uli Music Ltd and its publishing subsidiary at CAC, with reserved matters, a Family Director, and objects covering copyright ownership, licensing and administration.
  2. Open the MCSN membership and NCC registration pathway before signing a single artist. Confirm current MCSN tariffs, the effect of the COSON appeal, and the exact Register of Works procedure. A catalogue built before registration exists is built on sand.
  3. Write the five gates as policy and make no release proceed without them — split sheet, written assignment under s.30(3), linked ISRC and ISWC, NCC registration, territory map. This is the core competency, and it is cheapest to install now.
  4. Build the metadata ledger with Aku Technology — one source of truth for ISRCs, ISWCs, splits, contracts and quarterly statements, with IFRS 15-compliant recognition and IFRS-ready outputs from day one.
  5. Set the deal ladder and advance policy in writing, signed by the Group CFO — Tier C royalty deals; advances priced on documented trailing streams; a ceiling of 3x trailing annual net receipts; 360 participation capped at 20% with a sunset. Write it before an A&R executive is hired.
  6. Recruit the Managing Director, then the Head of Rights, Metadata and Registrations. Both roles are unusual in Lagos and both are load-bearing; do not hire A&R before the rights function exists.
  7. Commission a Nigerian rights and collection audit — MCSN distribution data, DSP revenue by platform and territory, the realisable publishing share of Nigerian repertoire, and current ISRC manager status. The unit economics here run on figures that must be replaced with measured ones.
  8. Sign eight Tier-C artists on royalty deals and release twelve titles, with the objective not of hits but of twelve fully documented, registered and internationally collectable titles — specimen proof the machine works.
  9. Open sub-publishing conversations in the UK, US and South Africa for Year 2, and register master-side neighbouring rights directly with SoundExchange and PPL. Most Nigerian labels never open this channel, and it is where the black-box money sits.
  10. Agree the Uli Rights interface in writing — administration fee, reporting cadence, data standards and the arms-length certification process — before the first catalogue asset exists. The transfer-pricing posture is the first thing a future investor, lender or tax authority will examine.

31 — ULI ANIMATION

Animation, Post-Production & Visual Effects — the highest-margin line in the creative platform
CompanyUli Animation Ltd (CAMA) under Uli Group Ltd — Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Uli Group Ltd → Uli Animation Ltd
HeirUli — Second Daughter, Senior Female Heir
ActivityAnimation (2D/3D), post-production and VFX. Service-first; original IP later, and only when service work pays for it
LocationNkpor, Idemili North LGA, Anambra State — inside the Uli Studios campus
Horizon15 years · Year 1 = 2027 · gearing ≤40% · no unhedged USD debt · naira primary, dollars at ₦1,600/USD
Mandate"Culture, Press, Broadcasting & Supply Chain"; Marketing, Distribution & Exhibition (NFTS); Global Communication Science (UvA). Content carries commercial risk, not political risk

1. Thesis

Animation is the highest-margin content category in the creative platform. No location cost, no weather, no cast availability, no per-diem, no lost shooting day when it rains in Onitsha. Where live-action Nigerian film is constrained by physical production economics, animation is constrained only by compute and talent. It exports universally without dubbing or cultural translation — a rigged character speaks any language the buyer needs, and a finished minute leaves Nkpor as a file, not a shipment. It is the only content line that can be produced to a foreign buyer's specification from Nigeria without shipping anyone anywhere.

The opening move is outsourcing, not Disney. The addressable market is the animation services trade India, the Philippines and Eastern Europe already run for US and European buyers — US$231.95bn in 2025, US$263.08bn in 2026, 13.4% CAGR (TBRC). Buyers are actively re-siting work: the Animation Guild records DreamWorks moving all future feature animation to Sony Pictures Imageworks (Animation Guild).

Original IP is the long-run prize and not the opening move. African studios take a fee and own nothing (BETAR); inside the Group the exit exists, because IP flows to Uli Rights and is rated by Akunnia Capital. But a studio that has not delivered 400 minutes a year to a foreign spec cannot afford to develop IP: service work builds the bench and the cash; IP spends them.

2. Market

  • Animation is a US$436bn market (2024) heading to ~US$896bn by 2034, ~7.5% a year (BusinessDay). The outsourcing slice is Asia-dominated: India held over 15% of the global animation outsourcing market and exported over US$500m of animation to the US and Canada by 2023, quoting ₹40,000–1,20,000 per finished minute for 2D character animation and ₹40,000–4,00,000 for 3D (Cybertize). These are the competitors to price against — not Disney.
  • Africa is almost absent — ~1.5% of the global creative economy (UNCTAD via BETAR). The ceiling: Triggerfish, Cape Town — 100–250 staff, Disney+ and Netflix credits — is estimated at only ~US$11.7m of revenue, and its Netflix shows animate outside Africa (BETAR). [verify.]
  • Nigeria's landscape is small and mostly self-taught. EVCL's Bino and Fino costs ~US$1,250 per finished minute (BusinessDay). No Nigerian studio has scaled past a few dozen artists, and the industry names the cost lines: software licensing, hardware, power, no unified training.

3. Product & service lines

LineSold toRights

Service work is ≥90% of revenue through Year 5; original IP may not use more than 10% of artist capacity before Year 5, or 15% after, without Board approval.

4. Operating model

Two lanes, one bound. A client lane and an IP lane share the same artists; the client lane always schedules first. Work is won in order of realism: Group demand; African producers who today post to South Africa or India; then foreign outsourcing on a paid 20–60 minute pilot.

Billable utilisation is the whole game — the same principle as Uli Freight's loaded legs. The studio reports billed hours per artist per week through the Aku Technology pipeline, beside cost-per-finished-minute against quote. Target 70% by Year 3 (sector-typical ~55%), 75% at scale. Every project carries a delivery bible (spec, LUTs, naming, metadata).

Render: rent the burst, own the iteration. Workstations and a ~40-node render rack are owned, because iteration cannot wait on an upload; final frames are rented — managed farms at US$0.004/GHz-hour CPU, US$0.003/OctaneBench-hour GPU, or US$0.90–3.50/node-hour (Super Renders Farm) — because GPU capital ages in 3–4 years. Gating question: what is Nkpor's real upstream bandwidth, and what does a 4TB upload cost? [verify before buying compute.]

Software licensing is a rising dollar cost. Maya rose from US$1,875 to US$1,945 a year in 2026, Arnold nodes cost US$105/node/year, a production-ready seat exceeds US$3,000 and there is no perpetual licence (Toolradar). Blender is free and covers 80%+ of Maya workflows, so Maya and Toon Boom for client deliveries — buyers dictate tools — and Blender for original IP and training, holding a 30-seat studio near ₦70–95m a year instead of ₦100–160m. [verify Toon Boom and Adobe pricing.]

Nkpor is a fit-out inside the Uli Studios campus — two animation floors, review theatre, render room, archive and training room — built by Okodu Construction fixed-price, fed by Okodu Power. Power is a production requirement: a farm interrupted mid-frame loses the night.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Every engagement is papered, inward and outward, and s.30(10) bars transferring rights in all future works. Counsel to confirm.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

Uli Animation has no scarce licence to chase, and that is exactly why the Group's rule matters here in its commercial form. A licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business — the Group either obtains it or buys a company that already holds it — and in this company what a target holds is not a certificate worth having. The team is the asset. A studio purchase buys trained artists, a working pipeline, render capacity already commissioned, and — the hardest thing for a new Nigerian studio to win — client contracts with foreign buyers who will only place work with a studio that has delivered before. Nigerian studios are small, mostly self-taught, and almost none has scaled past a few dozen artists, so the sector is a genuine buyers' market where an undercapitalised incumbent will sell; a de novo studio must spend three years building what a purchase delivers in one close.

What the diligence must actually test. Not the certificates. Roster retention, pipeline ownership, and whether the client contracts survive a change of control — an output deal with a foreign buyer commonly terminates on assignment without consent, and if it does, the reason for the acquisition has evaporated. Value [verify]: Nigerian studio transactions are privately priced and thin, and no published multiple exists for a Nigerian animation or post studio. Price on the contracted order book and the replacement cost of the bench, never on certificate count.

Ninety-day action, costed. Instruct counsel to identify six Nigerian animation and post studios with a live foreign or African client base and a bench of eight or more trained artists, and to price two. Budget ₦22m (~US$14,000): ₦10m corporate, staff and pipeline diligence on three targets, ₦7m valuation against contracted order book and bench replacement cost, ₦5m change-of-control review of every client and vendor contract — the test that decides whether the deal is worth doing at all.

The capital-lightest content business in the Group — no stages, cast or locations; the capital is people, seats and compute, at transfer price as Group infrastructure alongside 29_Uli_Film.md. Tranches fund capability; projects fund themselves: only the first IP season is tranche-funded, ring-fenced at ₦120m.

Financing mix: ~70% Group equity through Ezeme Family Holdings; ~20% debt (equipment and receivables finance); ~10% reinvestment. Gearing ≤40%; no unhedged USD debt; no grant or rebate counted as revenue. [verify whether animation is a priority sector under the NTA 2025 Tenth Schedule.]

7. Unit economics

Price and cost per finished minute, Year 3–5, against Indian and Eastern European quotes; blended supervised rate ₦5,000 per billed hour.

Cost per animator-hour, on 1,600 productive hours, a 2.4× loading and 70% billed utilisation. Local bands: ₦150,000–350,000 a month, juniors ₦70,000–150,000, senior 3D/VFX ₦350,000–700,000+ (Profolio).

Loaded cost per billed hour: junior animator ₦3,100–4,600 (US$1.94–2.88); mid ₦6,400–10,300 (US$4.00–6.44); senior animator or VFX artist ₦11,600–18,000 (US$7.25–11.25); director or VFX supervisor ₦20,600–36,000 (US$12.88–22.50).

The arbitrage is measured. A Triggerfish junior earns ~US$9,200 against US$60,000–120,000 for the equivalent US role (BETAR), so a Nkpor senior hour at US$7–11 loaded beats an Indian senior and sits far below North American rates — the buyer's case for placing work here, and a foreign employer's case to our staff.

Render and compute per finished minute. Managed-farm rates — US$0.04–0.09 per frame for broadcast animation, US$0.14–0.30 for character animation, US$0.27–0.67 for heavy 4K VFX comp (Super Renders Farm) — give, at 24 fps, ₦30,000–90,000 per minute of 2D digital work (~2–4% of price), ₦320,000–690,000 for 3D episodic and ₦650,000–1,300,000 for 3D premium (~5–9%). Compute constrains capacity and schedule, not cost.

Utilisation and break-even. Across 55% / 65% / 70% / 75%, cost per billed hour indexes 127 / 108 / 100 / 93 — five points of utilisation is ₦60–80m of annual gross profit at Year-5 scale, with no new client, hire or capital. Year-3 fixed cost is ₦380–420m, so at a 60% contribution margin break-even is ~₦630–700m, or 320–380 finished minutes at a ₦1.9m blended price, against a Year-3 plan of 380–450. The studio is not profitable before Year 3.

Service work versus original IP. Service is certain but capped: 55–60% gross, cash in 30–60 days, revenue limited by utilisation. IP is speculative but uncapped: a 13 × 11-minute season costs ₦120–190m, its certain first revenue is the Group broadcast window at ₦35–60m, and it returns over 3–7 years through a catalogue Uli Rights values at 5–10× net licensing revenue. IP becomes viable at Year 5 — when service revenue covers the fixed cost base and 15% of capacity is genuinely surplus. A fee can be banked; only an owned work can be securitised.

Training juniors versus hiring experienced. An academy junior costs ₦2.4–3.6m to first billable hour; a senior costs nothing to develop but ₦1.0–2.5m to sign and ₦5.4–8.4m a year thereafter, and is gone in 18–24 months when the remote offer arrives. Juniors convert at 60% and stay on a written training-repayment schedule — never a restraint-of-trade covenant, which Nigerian courts view with hostility. Grow our own for volume, buy senior for credibility: 55% junior, 30% mid, 15% senior by Year 5, two juniors per supervisor maximum.

8. Organisation

Leadership. Uli's NFTS training is in marketing, distribution and exhibition — where a studio's margin is won, because animation is sold before it is made. Until she takes the chair a professional Studio Director runs the company under the Uli Group MD and Board; Uli chairs the quarterly capacity and pricing review.

First ten hires, in order: (1) Studio Director; (2) Animation Director (2D); (3) VFX Supervisor; (4) Pipeline TD; (5) Producer, who owns utilisation reporting; (6) CG Supervisor / Senior 3D Animator; (7) Senior Animator (character); (8) Render Wrangler; (9) Business Affairs and Rights Manager; (10) Finance and Utilisation Analyst.

10. Risks

Not a pay war we would win, but a package: a share of export-project revenue paid to the delivery team in the currency the project earned, named IP credits, the academy route into Idenze, hardware allowances, training-repayment schedules. Assume 15–20% attrition.

11. Integration

Integration is mandatory, and here it is the load-bearing wall of the plan.

Supplies to: Uli Film — VFX, inserts, clean-up, titles, finishing; the anchor client whose volume makes the first 200 minutes a year bankable. Uli Broadcast — series, idents, promos, later IP at the broadcast-window transfer price. Uli Distribution — IP titles with clean masters. Uli Cinemas — first-window animated shorts. Uli Rights — the registered IP catalogue, and thence to Akunnia Capital's catalogue fund. Idenze Polytechnic and University — placements and curriculum. Akunnia Capital and Aku Insurance — equipment and receivables finance, render-room cover.

The two-way loop with Akunnia: Uli Animation earns dollars without shipping and originates the IP the Group's funds warehouse.

  1. Hire the Studio Director, the Producer and the Pipeline TD before any software is bought.
  2. Sign the Uli Film anchor agreement — a stated volume of VFX and animation minutes over two years at a transfer price certified arms-length by the Group CFO. No workstation order before it is signed.

32 — ULI BROADCAST

Broadcasting, Streaming Carriage & Content Licensing — the Uli Group's distribution arm

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026).

Position: company plan under 28_Uli_Group.md; peers 29_Uli_Film.md, 30_Uli_Music.md, 33_Uli_Rights.md, 35_Uli_Freight.md. Ezeme Group is the mother company; Uli Group is the fourth child's group (EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

⚠️ Figures marked ⚠️ are indicative and require local verification before any tranche is committed.
CompanyUli Broadcast — subsidiary of Uli Group, itself a subsidiary of Ezeme Group
HeirUli — Second Daughter, Senior Female Heir
ActivityBroadcasting (radio, television), carriage and wholesale, streaming distribution, advertising sales, content licensing
Scope limitEntertainment and cultural content. Not news, not current affairs.
LocationNkpor, Idemili North LGA, Anambra State — studios and play-out; transmission and carriage nationally
Horizon10–15 years
