In one line: Uli Broadcast is not another channel competing for attention — it is the Group's route to the audience, and the audience is the asset every other Uli company needs.

1. Thesis

Distribution, not content, is the scarce position. The Group's own framing: "controlling what people hear and how goods reach them gives her enormous combined influence." Nigeria has an abundance of content and a shortage of owned distribution. A new broadcaster that only makes programmes competes with Nollywood's 1,185 classifications a year (NFVCB, 2025) and loses. One that owns the platform, the carriage agreement and the advertising relationship sets terms for everyone else's content — including its own siblings'.

Four propositions carry this plan:

  1. Radio is the cheapest route to a Nigerian audience, and it is profitable at modest scale. A South-East FM licence costs ₦15m outside Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt (NBC fee schedule) — the same as terrestrial TV in those states — but television's real cost is content and transmission, an order of magnitude above radio's. Radio buys the audience; television monetises it later.
  2. Own the carriage, not just the channel. Wholesale to pay-TV and DTH platforms, free carriage on the national DSO platform, and FAST/AVOD carriage abroad convert one content investment into many revenue relationships. That is the "Marketing, Distribution & Exhibition" training made operational.
  3. The Group is its own advertiser. Isiome, Akunnia, Idenze and Okodu all buy media. A sales house holding the Group's advertising budget and selling third-party inventory starts with revenue no standalone station has.
  4. Entertainment only — a commercial decision, not a cultural one. A national newsroom makes a conglomerate a political actor: it invites antitrust scrutiny, licensing retaliation and caps on international fundraising, because the same family would hold a broadcaster alongside banking, pharmaceutical and university licences. Entertainment, sport, music, film and lifestyle broadcasting carry no such constraint. The plan therefore scopes Uli Broadcast to culture, music, sport, film and lifestyle, and states the prohibition in the company's own charter — see §5 and §10.

The economics that decide everything: broadcast is a fixed-cost business with high operating leverage, and audience must cross a threshold before it is profitable. Below it, every extra naira is swallowed by overheads already incurred; above it, incremental revenue is close to free. §7 quantifies the threshold for one FM station.

2. Market

Radio is still Nigeria's widest medium. More than 127 million Nigerians tune in to terrestrial radio, and rates across a four-tier station market run from ₦8,000 to ₦85,000 for a 60-second peak spot (Soni Baze rate survey); radio is separately described as engaging over 80% of the population (Review of Journalism & Mass Communication). ⚠️ Verify both against NBC returns and the AMS panel.

Television is being rebuilt on satellite, and that helps a new entrant. The NBC replaced the terrestrial Digital Switch Over model — which reached under a quarter of Nigeria after eight states — with a satellite platform carrying more than 73 channels and targeting 100 across 40 million TV households, delivered by NIGCOMSAT (Independent), and has scrapped the annual digital television access fee (Vanguard). National free-to-air carriage without building 160 towers is an opening that did not exist five years ago.

Pay television is contracting. MultiChoice's Rest-of-Africa base fell from 9.3m (2023) to 7.5m (2025), with Nigeria accounting for 77% of the loss (Nairametrics), and StarTimes competes hard at the low end. Carriage revenue from pay TV is a declining-quality asset — negotiate it, do not build on it.

Streaming in Sub-Saharan Africa is an advertising market, not a subscription market. Regional streaming revenue is US$1.8bn in 2026, reaching US$3.1bn by 2031; Nigeria alone is 2.1m SVOD subscriptions rising to 3.2m, with streaming revenue of US$417m rising to US$742m. YouTube's regional AVOD revenue (US$583m in 2026) exceeds any single SVOD platform, and AVOD outgrows SVOD. Showmax was shut in April 2026 after eleven years and US$522m, leaving a commissioning vacuum (3Vision; Showmax data). The lesson is unambiguous: build AVOD and FAST distribution, not a Nigerian SVOD business.

Advertising is shifting away from broadcast faster than broadcast is growing. PwC projects Nigeria's E&M market compounding at 7.2% to 2029 with digital at 84% of total ad spend — above the global average — on 107m internet users (Nairametrics; PwC Nigeria), with total Nigerian E&M revenue at US$5.8bn by 2029 (Guardian). Consequence: the broadcast advertising pool available to a new entrant is a few hundred billion naira shared across hundreds of stations. Uli Broadcast must therefore earn from carriage and licensing as well as spots.

Audience measurement — and its limits. Nigeria had no credible television currency; buying ran on diaries. A new Audience Measurement System — a 60,000-household establishment survey across all 774 LGAs, licensed by the NBC and ARCON to FMEIL-GARB and rolling out from Lagos in 2026 — is intended to create the first automated national currency (BusinessDay; NAN). Limitations priced into this plan: the panel belongs to a third party whose methodology the broadcaster does not control; radio measurement is weaker than television's; the panel is not yet national; and a South-East station will sell against regional research, not national ratings. ⚠️ Build a first-party audience dataset — app logins, SMS and social engagement, ticketing — because the currency will not be handed to you.

The gap Uli Broadcast fills: professional, compliant, entertainment-led regional broadcasting with owned carriage and a captive advertiser base, among fragmented station owners who have neither.

Deliberate exclusions, written into the charter: news bulletins, current-affairs programming, political talk shows, and paid political advertising. If a future board wants any of these, it requires a specific shareholder resolution of Ezeme Family Holdings — not a management decision.

4. Operating model

Sequence: radio → television → carriage → licensing. Capital discipline follows the sequence. A station launched with a ₦1.45bn Year-1 envelope proves audience, sales capability and compliance before any television spend is committed.

Radio operating model. One FM station per market, run lean: a thin permanent core of management, programming, engineering, presentation and sales; content largely music and talk formats rather than drama, with sport and live events as the differentiator. Play-out is automated. Power is the largest controllable cost after staff — the Nkpor site runs on Okodu Power/Grid supply with solar and battery, diesel standby only, targeting under 8% of opex on power ⚠️.

Television operating model. The channel is a scheduler, not a studio. Target schedule mix: ~60% from the Group catalogue and commissioned producers (Uli Film, Uli Animation, Uli Music), ~40% acquired, with heavy repeat windows. Music and lifestyle formats are cheap to originate (₦200k–600k per hour); first-run drama is not (drama hours cost tens of millions to produce) — so drama reaches the channel as a licence from Uli Film at a broadcast-window transfer price, or not at all. This is the single most important cost rule in the company.

Carriage and wholesale model. One posture on every platform: non-exclusive, wholesale, audited. The NBC's anti-competition provisions require premium sports and news channels to be offered to other Pay-TV platforms on non-exclusive, non-discriminatory wholesale terms (Nigeria Broadcasting Code, Addendum s.9.1.1); the same code bars warehousing of sports rights and requires prime foreign sports content to be matched by local sport costing at least 30% of the foreign acquisition. Read that as a licence to compete: premium content cannot be locked away from a new entrant. ⚠️ Verify current wholesale terms with each platform — some independent Nigerian channels pay for carriage rather than receive it.

Advertising sales — including programmatic. Three routes: (a) direct and sponsorship, the highest-yield inventory, sold by a relationship team; (b) the Group's own brands, contracted as anchor inventory at arms-length, audited rates; (c) programmatic — connected-TV, FAST and app inventory through SSP/AdX integrations, where the growth is even though Nigerian yields are thin ⚠️. The rule: programmatic monetises residual inventory; it never sets the price of premium inventory.

Local content compliance is free here. The Code requires Nigerian creative control, 75% of leading cast and crew Nigerian and 75% of programme expenditure paid to Nigerians (Code s.3.15). A Group owning the catalogue, the studio and a university media faculty satisfies this by default — a structural advantage over stations buying foreign filler.

Editorial and compliance discipline. A written Editorial Standards Manual consistent with the Broadcasting Code, an advertiser-content separation rule, and a royalty and copyright reporting function so music payments to COSON/MCSN and registrations are timely. §10 treats any drift toward news as a critical risk — the one risk that ends the business rather than merely damaging it.

The foreign-interest gate — two structures, and they are different businesses.

  • If a Nigerian-incorporated Uli Broadcast with Nigerian-resident control satisfies s.9(1) — the licence sits naturally in the existing chain, and the Group's Mauritius holdco is a financing layer rather than a licensee.
  • If the Commission reads the test as reaching ultimate beneficial ownership — the licence must sit in a Nigerian-controlled licence vehicle (Nigerian-resident directors, Nigerian-resident control, a shareholders' agreement and a management-services contract with Uli Broadcast), with the Group as commercial operator rather than licensee.

Get this answer in writing before the application fee is paid. It determines the corporate structure of the company, and retro-fitting it after a licence is granted is expensive. No tranche in §6 assumes the favourable answer.

The licence is acquired, not waited for — buying a licensed station

The rule that governs this company above all others in the Group: the licence is acquired, not waited for. Uli Broadcast does not wait for the NBC to grant an FM or television licence — it either obtains one or buys a station that already holds one. This is not a shortcut around the regulator; it is the ordinary economics of Nigerian broadcasting. The licence is the scarce asset, and a licence is worth more than the station attached to it. Nigerian broadcasting is full of undercapitalised operating stations — on air, licensed, staffed, with a frequency, a mast and a tower, and no money to convert any of it into profit. The NBC's de novo process is slow, discretionary and contingent on a free frequency (§12, item 2); an existing station has already cleared that constraint. And a purchase brings what no applicant can build cheaply: the licence, a trained staff, transmission plant, a sales book and existing advertiser relationships.

⚠️ The change-of-control gate is NOT statutory — verified, and it changes the acquisition structure

This plan prices and sequences the station acquisition around "NBC approval of change of control" as the critical path. Read against the Act, that gate does not exist. (Corrected 25 September 2026 — the Act has now been read. Two independent verification passes reached this conclusion separately.)

What the Act says. NBC Act, Third Schedule, para 3: "A licence shall not be transferable and the licensed station shall not for such be changed without notifying commission of the intention and the reasons for such change." That is a notification obligation — not a consent, approval or pre-clearance requirement. And the Act contains no change-of-control consent mechanism at all: nothing requires the Commission's prior written approval for a transfer or assignment of a licence, and nothing deems a change of control to be a transfer.

So the sentence this plan previously carried — that "NBC's prior written approval of the transfer or assignment of a licence is a condition of every broadcast licence," and that a change of control is treated as a transfer — is not in Cap N11. It is unpublished practice, and this library has already been caught once treating practice as statute (the "disposal of controlling interest" doctrine on mineral titles, which turned out to be a law-firm gloss).

Three consequences for this acquisition:

  1. The structure is simpler than planned. A share purchase of a licensed broadcaster does not trigger a statutory consent condition, because the licensee is unchanged and the Act bars only transfer of the licence — which a share purchase is not. The licence does not move; the company's shares do.
  2. The critical path is the notification, not an approval. The 3–9 month timeline this plan carries (radio) and 6–12 months (television) is driven by an approval process that the Act does not require. Re-base the timeline against what is actually required — notification, plus the SEC/corporate steps and any NCC interest in the target's other licences.
  3. The real constraint may be a different regulator. NCC operates a prior-approval regime for 10% shareholding changes in communications companies (NCC press release; Olaniwun Ajayi alert), and broadcasters commonly hold NCC licences as well as NBC ones. If the target holds NCC spectrum or carriage authorisations, the binding approval may be the NCC's, not the NBC's — which would make the plan's named critical path the wrong regulator.

And confirm the ownership bar, because it is stricter than this library long stated. s.9(1)(a) requires the applicant to be a body corporate "whose majority shares are owned by citizens of Nigeria." A later verification pass also reports s.9(4)(a) ("the structure of shareholding in the broadcasting organisation" among the matters the Commission shall consider), s.2(1)(r) (a Commission function over "the participation of foreign capital in relation to local capital in broadcasting") and s.9(5) (a prohibition on controlling shares in more than two stations per broadcast sector). Those three could not be independently verified from a writable copy of the Act in this session and are recorded as reported-claims, not confirmed text. They are consistent with s.9(1)(a) and should be read from the Act before the structure is finalised.

Two further checks before any content spend. The Code's enforceability is in issue — the amended 6th Edition Code has been the subject of litigation (a 2022 Channels TV ruling, and reported 2025 nullification proceedings), so the "never pay for exclusivity the Code forbids you to hold" premise at §5 should not be relied on until the current position is confirmed. And the local-content figure this library cites (75%) is the Code's foreign-collaboration rule; the Act's own Third Schedule sets a floor of 60% local content for radio and television (paras 20–21 deal with "proportion of Nigerian content to the foreign content" and increases over the licence period). Cite the Act's figure where the statutory floor is meant.

Two structural reasons the acquisition route is unusually attractive here, and one that makes it unusually delicate.

  • Share purchase preserves the licence; asset purchase does not. Buying the shares of the licensed company leaves the licensee legal person unchanged, so the licence continues — subject to NBC approval of the change of control. Buying the assets means the licence does not come with them and a fresh application is needed, which defeats the purpose. Structure the deal as a share acquisition or not at all.
  • The content entry condition is favourable to a late entrant. As §4 records, the Broadcasting Code requires premium sports and news channels to be wholesaled on non-exclusive, non-discriminatory terms and forbids warehousing of sports rights (Code, Addendum s.9.1.1) — so the premium content that would otherwise be locked up by an incumbent cannot legally be withheld from a new entrant. That changes what a station is worth: never pay for exclusivity the Code forbids you to hold.
  • ⚠️ The change-of-control consent is the critical path, and it re-runs the s.9(1) gate. NBC's prior written approval of the transfer or assignment of a licence is a condition of every broadcast licence, and a change of control of the licensee is treated as a transfer — so the same foreign-interest question above must be answered for the buyer, not only for a new applicant. A deal that closes commercially without that consent can be unwound by the Commission.

Why this does not replace the organic route, and the plan is honest about it. An acquired station is bought with its problems — an ageing transmitter, a unionised staff, an unresolved licence condition, possibly a subsisting sanction or an unpaid renewal. Diligence must test: licence currency and renewal date; any subsisting NBC sanction, query or condition; whether the frequency assignment is still live; the state of the mast and transmitter; union and staff liabilities; and whether any advertiser contract terminates on change of control. A licence acquired inside a broken station is a liability with a good logo.

Ninety-day action, costed. Instruct counsel — with a broadcast-regulatory specialist, not a general practitioner — to identify every licensed radio and television operator in the South-East and South-South (on the working assumption of 15–30 radio and 5–12 television licensees in the target footprint) and screen them for licence currency, ownership willingness and distress. Budget ₦58m (~US$36,000): ₦22m regulatory diligence and licence-status verification with the NBC across up to eight targets; ₦18m indicative valuations and a replacement-cost build-up for two; ₦10m a written NBC opinion on whether a change of control of an existing licensee is available to the Group's ownership chain under s.9(1) — the same question as §12 item 1, and it must be answered for the buyer as well as for an applicant; ₦8m financial and union diligence on the preferred target. Additional to, and not in substitution for, the organic pathway — the two run in parallel, and the first to clear wins.

The threshold, stated plainly. Break-even is ₦14.3m of gross revenue a month — roughly 26 sold 30-second spots a day, or about 13 minutes of sold advertising in a 24-hour broadcast day. The Year-10 test is not audience — it is the revenue mix. A broadcaster still earning 90% of revenue from Nigerian spot advertising will be worth less in Year 10 than in Year 5, because 84% of ad growth is going digital. Carriage and licensing income is the proof the distribution thesis worked.

10. Risks

Two risks are existential and everything else is manageable. The first is scope drift: a broadcaster that adds a news bulletin to win a rating point imports political risk the Group has deliberately avoided, and no amount of audience justifies it. The second is the licence itself — structure and cost. The remaining risks are the ordinary hazards of a fixed-cost business in a fragmented advertising market.

11. Integration

Supplies to:

  • Uli Film, Uli Music, Uli Animation — a guaranteed first broadcast window for Group catalogue. This integration pays twice: Group content gets a national airing without a distributor's margin, and Uli Broadcast fills its schedule at transfer price rather than full production cost.
  • Uli Rights — broadcast performance data, cue sheets and royalty reporting that make catalogue valuations defensible.
  • Akunnia Capital (ultimately) — carriage contracts, licensing receivables and advertising contracts are documented, long-dated cashflows that can be rated, pooled and financed. Broadcast revenue is the proof of demand that makes the content catalogue bankable.
  • Every Group company — media buying, brand campaigns and internal communications.

The internal-customer advantage, stated concretely. Uli Broadcast sells advertising inventory for the Group's own companies — Isiome Foods, Isiome Farms, Aku Insurance, Idenze Pharma, Idenze University, Okodu Power and the rest all buy media. Routing that spend through Uli Ad Sales gives the station contracted anchor revenue from day one, improving break-even timing and lender confidence, booked at arms-length published rates, certified by the Group CFO and minuted by the independent directors — a real requirement, because related-party media buying is exactly where a conglomerate's internal pricing gets challenged. It also makes Uli Broadcast the Group's media agency of record, itself a fee business.

Buys from:

  • Uli Film / Uli Animation — drama, animation and documentary hours at broadcast-window transfer price
  • Uli Music — music programming, live sessions and artist content, with royalties properly reported
  • Uli Freight — movement of event and outside-broadcast equipment (a marginal line: broadcast is digital, so this is events logistics, not content logistics)
  • Idenze University / Idenze Polytechnic — media and communication graduates, a standing internship-to-hire pipeline
  • Okodu Power / Okodu Grid — electricity for studios, play-out and transmission sites
  • Okodu Construction — studio and mast infrastructure
  • Aku Technology — ad server, programmatic stack and audience analytics
  • Akunnia Capital — equipment finance, working capital and insurance

The two-way loop: Uli Broadcast distributes what Uli Film, Music and Animation make; that airing creates the performance data Uli Rights needs; that data lets Akunnia Capital finance the next slate; and the Group's own advertising spend funds the airtime. No standalone Nigerian broadcaster has a captive content supplier, a captive advertiser base and a captive financier at the same time.

12. First ninety days

  1. Answer the foreign-interest question in writing. Commission a formal NBC engagement on s.9(1) and the meaning of "foreign interest" for a Mauritius trust → Mauritius GBC → Nigerian company chain. No licence fee, studio order or transmitter order is committed until the answer arrives. This is the gating item.
  2. Check frequency availability for the target markets — Nkpor/Onitsha first, then Awka. An NBC licence is contingent on a free frequency, and availability determines which markets are possible at all.
  3. Adopt the Editorial Charter and the news prohibition as a board resolution before the licence application, so the scope limit is a constitutional fact of the company rather than a management preference.
  4. Sign the Group advertising commitment — written, arms-length, Group-CFO-certified commitments from the Group's own companies for Year-1 airtime at published rate-card rates, minuted by the independent directors. Target 35% of Year-1 revenue from Group advertisers; this is what makes the §7 break-even credible to a lender.
  5. Commission the Anambra cost study — site and mast approvals, transmitter power and licensing, Okodu's tariff and reliability, and actual achievable local advertising rates. Do not use the national rate survey as a local rate card.
  6. Open carriage conversations before the channel exists — establish in writing with the FreeTV/DSO operator and each pay-TV platform whether carriage is free, paid for, or paid to the channel. The direction of the carriage payment is the largest single uncertainty in this plan.
  7. Register the rights and reporting infrastructure — Copyright Commission registrations for formats and event recordings, COSON/MCSN membership, and a music-use reporting system built before the first record is played.
  8. Recruit the Managing Director and the Finance & Compliance Manager. The Compliance Manager must be in place before the station is on air, not after the first sanction.

Ezeme Group · Uli Group · Entity Uli Rights Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Uli Group Ltd (Uli) · Horizon 15 yrs · Year 1 = 2027.

Companions: 28_Uli_Group.md (domain plan) and 09_Aku_Capital.md (the finance platform this company feeds). The Uli content companies Uli Rights acquires from and licenses through: 29_Uli_Film.md, 30_Uli_Music.md, 32_Uli_Broadcast.md. Logistics interfaces only: 35_Uli_Freight.md, 36_Uli_Warehousing.md. Also in the domain: Uli Animation (31_Uli_Animation.md), Uli Distribution (34_Uli_Distribution.md), Uli Publishing (37_Uli_Publishing.md), Uli Fleet (40_Uli_Fleet.md), Uli Brand (57_Uli_Brand.md).

1. Thesis

Uli Rights exists to make African creative output legible to capital. Nollywood and Afrobeats are among the largest cultural exports in the world and among the worst-documented rights pools in it. Uli Rights buys, remediates, registers, administers and reports on music masters, music publishing and film and television libraries — then hands the resulting cash flows to Akunnia Capital to pool, rate and syndicate.

One sentence: The documented catalogue — not the famous song — is the financial asset, and the African rights market's documentation gap is the only durable source of excess return available to a Nigerian acquirer at scale.

Why a documented catalogue is an asset and not a library. An asset passes three tests. Its cash flow is legally provable — every naira traces to a signed chain of title, not a spreadsheet assertion. It is long-dated and predictable — the weighted-average age of the catalogue in the Canon Music securitisation is about ten years, projected by the rating agency over roughly forty. And it is transferable into a vehicle somebody else will price — Canon Music Issuer Trust raised USD 500m of notes rated A(sf) at a 60.2% advance rate, and Concord issued USD 1.765bn rated A+ / A2 against a catalogue valued above USD 5.1bn (KBRA pre-sale via MBW; Apollo, July 2025). A library that fails those tests is a museum with a playlist.

Why this is the bridge to Akunnia Group. Akunnia Capital's product schedule already carries a content-catalogue royalty line at 1.0–1.5% management and 10–15% carry, flagged in that plan as a novel asset class. A fund cannot launch on a product schedule; it launches on assets that have been diligenced, documented, audited and shown to collect. Uli Rights is the only entity in the Group that manufactures exactly that. Corridors and depots take years to build; a catalogue can be bought, cleaned and reported on inside eighteen months — the fastest route to a real fund track record in the conglomerate.

The arbitrage is documentation, not culture. International funds buy finished catalogues at 12–17× annual net royalty income (Astor via Music Ally, July 2026). African catalogues do not trade at that multiple, because the buyer cannot verify the income or the title — and as §2 shows, no African catalogue transaction has ever disclosed a price or multiple at all. That discount is not a judgment about African music; it is the price of missing paperwork, and it is the whole opportunity. Uli Rights buys at 5–8× semi-documented trailing royalties, spends eighteen to twenty-four months on remediation and registration discipline, and owns a cash flow that then supports a materially higher valuation. The foreign funds decline that work; local players take the easy collection fee and leave the paperwork alone.

Capital rule: every naira must make a royalty stream more provable and more transferable — acquisition capital, diligence, metadata, registrations, collections, audit and reporting pass. Frontline A&R, artist advances without rights, live promotion and anything that buys fame rather than title fail.

2. Market

Global. Recorded music trade revenue reached USD 31.7bn in 2025, up 6.4% — an eleventh consecutive year of growth, with streaming 69.6% of the total and 837m paid subscriptions (IFPI Global Music Report 2026). The rights layer sits inside that number, and it is the layer that trades.

The catalogue market. Multiples settled at 12–17× annual net royalty income for iconic assets, against a 19.4× peak in 2021 — a correction, not a collapse (Astor report via Music Ally, July 2026). The same market saw three transactions within fifty days worth over USD 19bn combined — Sony/Recognition, BMG/Concord (USD 1.16bn cash) and Primary Wave/Kobalt (~USD 1.5bn). The mid-market is being vacated by the giants, and independents with documentation discipline are the natural buyers of what the giants cannot diligence cheaply.

Film libraries price lower, and that suits us. In 2025 Alcon acquired Village Roadshow's 108-title library — The Matrix, Ocean's Eleven, Joker, Mad Max: Fury Road among them — for USD 417.5m against an estimated USD 50m of annual cash flow: roughly 8.4× (Deadline, Nov 2025). Film is a lower-multiple asset than music and it is where Nollywood's unmonetised library sits.

Africa's export markets. IFPI records Sub-Saharan Africa as the world's fastest-growing recorded-music region — USD 120m in 2025, up 15.2%, having passed USD 100m for the first time in 2024 — though South Africa alone is 78.1% of it, which is itself a measure of how little of West Africa's output is captured locally (IFPI, 2026). The crossover is real and measurable: Afrobeats Spotify streams are up 550% over a decade, Rema reached #3 on the Billboard Hot 100, and Shazam logged 200+ African artists on its Global Top 200, with 12 tracks in the global Top 10 and three at No.1 (Spotify SSA MD, via The Exchange; MBW, July 2025). The majors are moving in — Sony Music Publishing opened a Lagos office and UMG launched Def Jam Recordings North Africa — as UMG took a majority stake in Mavin Global and Warner Music acquired Africori. Critically, Uli Rights could find no disclosed price or multiple for any African catalogue transaction — the deals are private, the comparables do not exist, and the plan's entry multiples are therefore assumptions to be tested, not facts to be cited.

Nollywood. Nigeria's cinema market hit a record ₦15.6bn (≈USD 9.8m) in 2025, up 34.72%, and for the first time Nollywood led with 49.4% of gross against Hollywood's 48.8%, on 2.79m admissions at an average ticket of ₦5,596 (Businessday, Jan 2026). The under-monetisation is in the ratio: the NFVCB classified 1,185 Nigerian films in 2025 (The Sun), but only 81 Nollywood titles reached a cinema screen — under 7%. The rest earn whatever they earn where nobody is counting at title level: streaming, broadcast, international sales, online. A library position is a bet on that post-theatrical tail — exactly the part no one has catalogued.

The documentation and collection problem, quantified. Nigeria's music industry generated ₦901bn (~USD 600m) in 2024 — but brand partnerships, publishing and sync licensing together were only 3% of it, against 65.7% from live performance and touring and 30.1% from streaming and social (NCAC/RegalStone, Basslines to Billions, via Tribune, Nov 2025). That 3% is the addressable market this company exists to grow, and the same report names copyright enforcement, publishing efficiency and reform of the collection societies as the industry's critical gaps. The collection evidence is stark: AVRS, the audiovisual society, distributed just over ₦100m to its entire membership in 2024 (AVRS 9th AGM, Oct 2025) — about USD 63,000 for a national film industry. The musical societies are in open conflict, and the sums are the story: MCSN received ₦1,205,956,580.20 — about USD 0.75m — from Nigeria's newly activated Copyright Levy, reported as its first operational use (Mondaq, Mar 2026 — figure as reported; Mondaq blocks automated retrieval, so verify this one against the NCC directly), while COSON approved a ₦409m distribution in November 2025 and then lost a Court of Appeal case holding it lacks a valid collection licence; a ₦1.2bn levy allocation is under a House of Representatives investigation (IPKat, July 2026; Newswatch, Aug 2026). Planning consequence: the country's principal collection vehicles move sums under USD 1m while their legal authority to collect is contested. Nigerian collection infrastructure must therefore be modelled as a cost and a risk — never as an assumed channel. Base-case income is direct DSP delivery, international sub-publishing and sync; CMO income is upside, and is budgeted at zero.

The gap, and its size. The buyer who can diligence a messy African title to an institutional standard, document it, and then report on it monthly does not exist in Nigeria. Foreign capital prices that risk as an unknown; local players cannot document it at all. There is also no Africa-focused royalty securitisation vehicle in existence, and lenders are, in the Atlantic Council's words, "reluctant to place any collateral value in these IPR" — creating what that report calls "an inability to use created assets as collateral for funding", set against African creative industries of roughly USD 1.5tn and a Nigerian entertainment and media market projected at USD 14.82bn in 2025, from USD 4bn in 2013 (Atlantic Council, Dec 2024). A very large asset base carrying effectively zero collateral value is the structuring opportunity — and equally the reason this plan cannot assume an African catalogue will be securitised on Western terms. Documentation, not capital, is the scarce input, and Uli Rights is the buyer that supplies it while the discount is still a documentation discount.

4. Operating model

Acquisition strategy — three tiers, deliberately sequenced.

TierSourceTarget multipleWhy
1 — InternalUli Film, Uli Music and Uli Animation catalogues, transferred at independent valuationAt valuation, arms-lengthFree at the margin, and the diligence laboratory: Uli Rights learns on titles it already controls
2 — RemediationSemi-documented Nigerian catalogues, estates, defunct labels, producers' back catalogues; bilateral, never auctioned5–8× verified trailing net royaltiesThe core trade. Price reflects the paperwork risk Uli Rights removes
3 — CompletedAlready-collected, internationally licensed catalogues where income is documented and audited9–12×Accretive to scale and to fund eligibility; never the first purchase

Chain-of-title diligence — the hard part, and the business. African rights documentation is routinely incomplete: unsigned splits, producer agreements never reduced to writing, deceased writers with no probate, masters held by a defunct label's former employee, films whose screenplay was never cleared. A ten-point file is required for every work before acquisition: writer and composer agreements; assignment or work-for-hire deeds; producer and beat-maker splits; split sheets signed by all contributors; sample, interpolation and re-recording clearances; the master ownership chain; the artist's recording agreement, term and territory; reversion and termination provisions; advances, encumbrances and third-party claims; and for film, NFVCB classification and underlying rights in screenplay, score and performances. Three non-negotiables: no acquisition closes without an unqualified title opinion from external counsel; if more than 15% of expected royalty value sits in defective titles, re-price or walk; and 20% of consideration is held in escrow for twelve months against title defects.

Metadata and registration discipline. Every recording gets an ISRC, every composition an ISWC, every writer an IPI/CAE number, every delivery a DDEX-compliant message. Every work receives a Notification of Copyright filing with the Nigerian Copyright Commission — registration is not a condition of copyright, but it is evidence a court or a rating agency can read (UUBO; Copyright Act 2022). Each asset carries an ID linking to its diligence file, valuations and statement history. Metadata is not an IT project here; it is the difference between an 8× and a 12× exit.

Collections infrastructure and processing. Direct DSP delivery agreements where volume justifies it, otherwise through a distributor; sub-publishing deals with international publishers to reach US, UK and EU mechanical and performance income no Nigerian entity can collect; MCSN membership for the statutory and CISAC reciprocal channels; AVRS for audiovisual; affiliation to claim US mechanicals through the Mechanical Licensing Collective; and YouTube CMS for user-generated claims, consistently material for African catalogue. Monthly ingestion into a single system built with Aku Technology; per-work allocation to writer and performer share; unallocated income tracked separately and never recognised as revenue until claimed; quarterly statements; annual independent valuation under a disclosed DCF; IFRS-audited accounts — so a fund investor or rating agency receives the same pack the board does. Distribution partners are chosen on reporting granularity, not headline rate.

Audit rights. Uli Rights negotiates audit rights in every acquisition and every distribution or sub-publishing agreement, with a look-back period, and grants audit and inspection rights to Akunnia Capital, to fund investors and to administered writers. The right to audit is worth more than the rate negotiated: it is what converts an assertion into a provable number.

The CMO position, stated plainly. This is a live institutional problem, not settled law. COSON's licence has not been renewed since 2019; a 2020 Federal High Court order directed the CAC to strike COSON from the register; the Court of Appeal affirmed in July 2026 that there was no live licence to revoke; MCSN asserts it is the duly approved licensing body; and in June 2026 the House of Representatives directed its Committee on Justice to investigate alleged irregularities, including a disputed ₦1.2bn private-copy-levy allocation (IPKat, July 2026). Uli Rights' response is structural, not political: it takes MCSN membership and pays every statutorily due levy, keeps a documented compliance file for every payment, models zero CMO income in its base case, and builds direct DSP and sub-publishing relationships so that a domestic society's failure cannot remove more than a small fraction of collections. A rights business whose economics depend on a Nigerian CMO is not investable and should not be built.

Accounting and audit standards institutional investors require. Catalogues are intangible assets under IAS 38, carried at cost less amortisation or under the revaluation model with an independent valuer. Amortisation must be matched to the royalty curve, not a straight line — linear amortisation of a decaying catalogue understates early profit and overstates later profit. The market practice a rating agency expects: an independent DCF with a disclosed discount rate and horizon (the Canon Music pool: USD 830m at an 8.00% discount rate over roughly 40 years; Hipgnosis Songs Fund's own disclosed valuation used 8.5%), an advance rate against that value, and overcollateralisation (Canon: 60.2% advance, 39.8% overcollateralised). A Nigerian catalogue fund cannot present an 8% discount rate and be believed — no African catalogue has ever been rated, so there is no comparable; the plan models 14–18% in naira terms and requires the valuer to justify it line by line. Audits are to ISA by a firm acceptable to fund investors; revenue is recognised under IFRS 15; and related-party transfers from Uli Film, Uli Music and Uli Animation are independently valued and approved by the independent directors sitting alone, consistent with the Group rule that no fund holds more than 25% in Group-originated assets, stepping down to 15% by Year 6.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

In this company the rule is the business, not a workaround for one. Uli Rights does not need a licence to buy a catalogue — it needs a diligence file — and the Group's rule that a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business has a direct reading here: no acquisition is deferred because registration, society membership or recordation is imperfect. Uli Rights either obtains the permission or buys the entity that already holds it, and a catalogue purchase is the purest form of the second route — the rights, the society memberships, the identifier blocks, the sub-publishing contracts and the collection history all arrive in one instrument, in place of a queue. Where a licence genuinely is the constraint — securitisation and royalty funds — the discipline is the same one 09_Aku_Capital.md and 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md already apply: buy a registered manager and vary the registration, rather than wait in a de novo queue. ⚠️ But the fund vehicle is not Uli Rights' to hold (see the row above), so the acquisition decision on that licence sits in Akunnia, not here.

The acquisition market in this business is not a licence market at all. There is no regulator to buy past. The scarce thing is documentation, and the price of a Nigerian catalogue is a documentation discount. That is why the acquisition discipline in §4 (the ten-point title file, the 20% escrow, the walk at 15% defective value) and §7 (the multiple) is this section's real content, and why the route matters less than the standard applied on it.

Budget ₦60m (~US$37,500) in total: ₦25m the SEC opinion and manager screen; ₦20m the seller screen across twenty targets; ₦15m preliminary diligence on the three that hold membership and identifiers. This is step 7 of §12 with its cost attached, and it is the cheapest evidence the board can buy: at a mid-market median of 6.1× across 2,683 transactions, the entry price is set by the diligence, not by the seller.

Funding mix. Family equity funds Tranche 1 in full — acquisition capital is released only against a completed diligence file and an independent valuation, never against an announcement. Local-currency debt secured on contracted royalty flows begins in Year 3, with tranche sizing tied to documented trailing collections. No unhedged USD debt: dollar royalty income is a natural match only for dollar-denominated acquisitions, and the mismatch is hedged or avoided. Gearing stays ≤40% at the company level, and the pooled vehicle's leverage is a separate, ring-fenced Akunnia decision.

Distributed across the plan (Tranches 1–3, ₦39.7bn): acquisition capital including the vehicle seed 77%; working capital and reserve 10%; systems and metadata 6%; chain-of-title diligence, legal and valuation 3%; people 3%; registrations and collections 1%. The mix is the thesis: this is a capital-deployment business wrapped around a small, expensive diligence and accounting function — which is exactly why the diligence capacity, not the balance sheet, is the binding constraint.

Verify locally before commitment: Nigerian catalogue pricing at the small end (₦20m–₦300m per deal) — there is no published transaction index and the plan's 5–8× must be tested against at least ten live seller conversations; DSP per-stream and per-catalogue minimum guarantees in Nigeria; sub-publisher advance norms; and current CBN repatriation procedure for royalty remittances.

Where the return actually comes from — and the weakest assumption in this plan. The entry yield alone does not carry a fund equity. In the worked example the net yield is 8.8%; the value is created by closing the collection gap (₦43.8m to ₦56.3m of gross income) and by re-rating the multiple once the same cash flow is documented and auditable. That re-rating is the plan's most optimistic input, and the evidence cuts against taking it for granted. The 12–17× range describes iconic assets bought by funds; across 2,683 actual retail royalty transactions the market cleared at a median 6.1× trailing earnings — a 16.4% entry yield (AltStreet, via 30_Uli_Music.md), and 29_Uli_Film.md puts film libraries at 5–10× net licensing revenue while warning that Nigerian catalogues have been valued as low as ~USD 10,000 per title. The honest reading: the mid-market this company actually buys in trades nearer 6× than 15×, so a 5–8× African entry is far less of a bargain than the icon multiple implies, and re-rating to 11–12× must be justified by the documentation itself — audited, registered, fund-eligible — not assumed from the ceiling. If the mid-market is genuinely ~6×, the value is created by collection uplift and not by multiple expansion, which is exactly why the gate below is the one that matters.

A title-count reality check, which the plan takes seriously. Lionsgate's filings disclose 20,000+ titles producing USD 954m of library revenue — roughly USD 48,000 per title per year — while warning that "a significant portion of Lionsgate's library revenues is derived from a small number of titles" and that "many titles in its library are not actively distributed at any given time and generate little or no revenue." Two consequences. Title count is not a value metric and must never be reported to a fund investor as one — gross titles under management appear in §9 only as an operating statistic. And the concentration cap in §10 (no title above 2% of catalogue value; no artist, writer or estate above 12%) is the control that stops a large, mostly-dormant library from masquerading as a diversified one.

The economics of pooling into a vehicle with Akunnia Capital. Illustrative pool of twelve catalogues, aggregate verified trailing net royalties ₦600m, acquired for ₦5.4bn (9.0× average, blending Tier 2 and Tier 3). Post-remediation the pool grosses ₦750m, and after administration at 18% the net royalty is ₦612m — an 18-point collection uplift and a cost ratio that falls as the pool grows.

8. Organisation

The first ten hires, in order. (1) Managing Director / Head of Rights — a catalogue M&A or publishing professional with a completed deal sheet, ideally trained at an international publisher or rights fund; not a role to learn in. (2) Head of Legal & Business Affairs — a copyright lawyer who owns chain of title and signs the diligence opinion. (3) Head of Royalty Accounting — a qualified accountant who has run royalty statements, not a general ledger. (4) Head of Metadata & Registrations — owns ISRC/ISWC/DDEX discipline and NCC filings. (5) Head of Collections & Society Relations — owns MCSN, AVRS, CISAC and the DSP and sub-publishing relationships. (6) Head of Sync & Licensing — the commercial front door. (7) Senior Rights Executive, Acquisitions (Nigeria) — the deal originator. (8) Rights Executive, Francophone & International — opens Côte d'Ivoire, Senegal and the diaspora market. (9) Data & Systems Lead — seconded jointly with Aku Technology. (10) Finance & Compliance Manager — IFRS, audit, investor reporting, related-party register.

Talent is the binding constraint, not capital. Perhaps a few hundred people in Nigeria can diligence a chain of title to institutional standard; fewer than fifty can run a royalty system that reconciles to an audited valuation. The first two hires therefore carry market-rate packages with a long-dated incentive tied to catalogue performance, and the Head of Rights role may be recruited internationally. Pipeline: an analyst programme with Idenze University's law and media faculties, plus secondments into international sub-publishers, so the second generation is grown rather than poached.

11. Integration

Acquires from — Uli Film, Uli Music, Uli Animation. The Group's own catalogue is Uli Rights' cheapest supply of titles and its legal laboratory: every missing split sheet and unregistered work is found and fixed here, and turned into process, before the first external purchase. Transfers are at independent valuation approved by the independent directors sitting alone, so neither side carries an unearned margin.

Distributes via — Uli Distribution, Uli Broadcast, Uli Cinemas, Uli Publishing. Uli Rights owns the rights; the distribution companies exploit them. Uli Distribution is the primary channel for theatrical, streaming, broadcast and international licensing, paid a market-rate commission never netted invisibly. Uli Broadcast is the licensing counterparty for carriage and the natural first licensee for catalogue never cleared for television. Uli Cinemas generates exhibition data that feeds the royalty engine and gives Uli Rights title-level audience evidence no Nigerian rights holder possesses — an acquisition advantage in itself. Uli Publishing exploits book, format and adaptation rights, and is where underlying literary rights must be cleared before a film library can be licensed freely.

Feeds Akunnia Capital — the strategic purpose of the company. Uli Rights originates the assets; Akunnia Capital pools, rates and syndicates them. Uli Rights holds no fund licence, markets no securities and accepts no third-party capital — those sit inside Akunnia Group, with its SEC and Mauritius FSC permissions. Uli Rights delivers a standard data pack: title files, audited statements, independent valuation, collection history and a servicer's report. Akunnia gets a long-dated, non-construction asset class to seed Fund I while its infrastructure pipeline is still being built, and Uli Rights gets a capital partner that values documentation.

Uses Aku Technology, and Uli Freight for physical media. The royalty and asset-reporting platform is built and run on Aku Technology, so the same system later reports on Aku Capital's other asset classes — marginal cost near zero for the next asset class, and an identical reporting standard for every pension fund and rating agency. Vinyl, CD, boxed sets and cinema DCP prints move on Uli Freight, with Uli Warehousing holding archive masters in humidity-controlled storage. Physical media is a small revenue line; its real value is archival custody, since for older Nigerian recordings the physical master is often the only surviving source.

Boundaries. Uli Rights owns no studio, no A&R function, no broadcast licence and no fund vehicle. Uli Music signs artists; Uli Rights administers what exists.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — build the standard before buying anything. (1) Appoint the Managing Director / Head of Rights and the Head of Legal & Business Affairs; the lawyer's first deliverable is the ten-point title template. (2) Commission counsel opinions on the CMO position after the July 2026 Court of Appeal ruling, the CBN repatriation route for dollar royalties, and NDPA 2023 duties. (3) File the first NCC Copyright Notifications for the Group's existing catalogue. (4) Open MCSN and AVRS membership applications; register for ISRC and ISWC issuance. (5) Design the royalty platform with Aku Technology against Akunnia's investor-reporting requirement, so the first acquisition lands in a system built for a rating agency rather than retro-fitted later.

Days 31–60 — diligence, price discovery and the factory. (6) Audit the Group's own catalogue: sample 500 titles, measure metadata completeness, quantify the collection gap — the first real test of the §7 collection-uplift assumption, free of charge. (7) Hold at least ten seller conversations across legacy labels, estates, producer back catalogues and film producers, to test whether 5–8× is real in Nigeria given that no disclosed comparable exists. (8) Commission an independent valuation of the Group catalogue to fix the arms-length transfer price. (9) Scope and cost the metadata remediation factory before Tranche 1 is drawn. (10) Retain an international sub-publishing partner for UK and US collection, with audit rights.

Days 61–90 — first capital, first asset. (11) Recruit the Heads of Royalty Accounting, Metadata & Registrations and Collections. (12) Complete diligence on the first two Tier-2 targets and put a written offer on one, with escrow, a 12-month title warranty and an earn-out on verified income. (13) Present the fund eligibility pack to the Uli Group board and the Akunnia investment committee — diligence standard, valuation methodology, the 14–18% discount-rate rationale, the collection-uplift gate — so the Year 3 vehicle is designed now, not improvised. (14) Establish the related-party register and annual independent-director review. (15) Day-90 board decision: release Tranche 1 capital only if the Group audit has quantified a collection gap, one external acquisition has cleared diligence, and step 7 supports an entry multiple at or below 8×. If not, run Year 1 as a rights-administration and documentation-services business on the Group catalogue, re-test in twelve months, and buy nothing.

Prepared for the Uli Group board and the Ezeme Group Board. Market, catalogue-multiple, securitisation and copyright-regulatory figures are sourced, including IFPI Global Music Report 2026, the Astor catalogue-multiple report via Music Ally, Hipgnosis Songs Fund's FY2022 valuation disclosures, Canon Music's KBRA pre-sale report, and Nigeria's NCAC/RegalStone music market report. Two limitations are important: no disclosed price or multiple exists for any African catalogue transaction, so every African entry multiple in this plan is an assumption requiring local verification; and no African catalogue has ever been rated or securitised, so the pooled-vehicle advance rate and discount rate are conservative planning judgments rather than comparables. Operating, capital and unit-economics figures are planning estimates at ₦1,600/USD requiring verification — particularly Nigerian catalogue pricing, DSP minimum guarantees and naira cost of funds — before any capital is committed. ULI DISTRIBUTION — Content Distribution

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Uli Group is the fourth child's group; every company takes Uli plus a plain function. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary; dollars are indicative only, at ₦1,600/USD held flat in nominal terms, and are not comparable across the library.

Ezeme Group · Uli Group · Entity Uli Distribution Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Uli Group Ltd (Uli) · Horizon 15 yrs · Year 1 = 2027.

Companions: 28_Uli_Group.md (domain plan); the companies this one is the pipes for: 29_Uli_Film.md, 30_Uli_Music.md, 31_Uli_Animation.md, 32_Uli_Broadcast.md, 33_Uli_Rights.md; the exhibition channel at 39_Uli_Cinemas.md. Aggregation feeds the catalogue at 33_Uli_Rights.md and the fund at 09_Aku_Capital.md.

1. Thesis

Distribution is where the margin sits in content, and Uli's training says so explicitly. Global Communication Science (UvA) supplies the audience reading; Marketing, Distribution & Exhibition at the National Film and Television School supplies the trade itself — windowing, deal structures, the exhibitor relationship; supply chain (Heriot-Watt) supplies the discipline that makes a release repeatable. Own the pipes, not just the pictures.

A producer who sells rights outright to fund production earns once and owns nothing. A distributor earns on every window, in every territory, for the life of the rights. The same title is paid for five or six times; the seller was paid on the first. That is not a margin percentage — it is a count of how many times the asset is paid for.

Uli Distribution is the central pipes business of an integrated content group. The Group owns Uli Cinemas (exhibition), Uli Broadcast, Uli Film, Uli Music, Uli Animation and Uli Rights; this company moves all of it to market. Because the infrastructure and buyer relationships are identical for a title we own and one we do not, it also represents third-party African producers — and aggregation is how a distributor scales without owning content.

Capital rule: every naira buys a window, a territory, or a right to represent.

2. Market

Nigerian theatrical is small, growing, and controlled by one company. West Africa closed 2025 at ₦15.6bn (≈USD 9.8m) on 2.79m admissions across 248 releases in 122 cinemas in Nigeria, Ghana and Liberia; Nollywood took 49.4% against Hollywood's 48.8% (Nairametrics; Businessday).

The concentration is the most important fact in this plan. FilmOne Entertainment distributed ₦11.4bn of that ₦15.6bn — 73% of the market by revenue — as exclusive theatrical licensee for Disney, Warner Bros., Sony, MGM, Angel Studios and Empire across Anglophone West Africa, while also handling most high-profile Nollywood releases. Silverbird ran second at 9%. Holding both slates makes 73% structural, not competitive (Black Film Wire; Businessday).

The release funnel is absurdly narrow. The NFVCB classified 1,185 Nigerian films in 2025, but only 81 reached a screen — under 7%, leaving roughly 1,100 titles a year with no route to market (The Sun).

Streaming terms moved sharply. Licensed titles earn USD 10,000–90,000; commissioned originals were funded at 100% of production plus a 15–30% overhead margin, with all global rights in perpetuity taken. Netflix suspended Nigerian commissioning in November 2024 and moved to revenue share through 2025; Nigerian titles on Netflix fell to five in H1 2025, from ten in 2024 and 19 in 2023, and by March 2026 two of three platforms had exited commissioning (BETAR; SimplVest).

Broadcast has consolidated into one buyer. MultiChoice Nigeria's subscription revenue fell 44% to USD 197.7m, and Canal+ completed its USD 3bn acquisition of MultiChoice — DStv and GOtv across 50+ African countries (BusinessDay; AllAfrica) — one negotiation reaching fifty markets, and a dependency.

International sales is the least contested channel. Trade happens at Cannes' Marché du Film (15,000+ attendees), the American Film Market (over USD 1bn of independent deals a year) and Berlin's EFM (12,000+ buyers) (AFRIFF). African titles reach them through foreign sales agents, or not at all: MAD Solutions (Cairo), via MAD World, is expanding into sub-Saharan Africa, taking worldwide rights to two South African features (African Film Press). A non-African-owned agent is building the position a Nigerian distributor should hold.

4. Operating model

Windowing is a scheduling problem before it is a sales problem. The value chain runs theatrical → premium streaming (SVOD) → broadcast/pay-TV → free-to-air and FAST → library and AVOD. Each window is held for a defined term in a defined territory, and released only once the previous has stopped earning. Licensing everything to one platform at once converts a twenty-year asset into a single cheque. One sale versus many is a calendar decision taken before the first deal is signed. Holding windows costs working capital and nerve: no licence beyond a seven-year term, none in perpetuity, none covering all territories at once.

Commission versus acquired rights — different businesses, different balance sheets, and this company runs both.

Aggregation is the answer to scale. Adding one more title to existing infrastructure costs a fraction of building that infrastructure. The marginal cost of title 200 is far below that of title 2, and revenue per title is not materially lower. Hence the third-party aggregation book, not the internal slate, drives §9.

Entry is cheap. The NFVCB licenses distributors in five tiers under the NFVCB Act Cap N40 LFN 2004 and the Scale of Charges 2025 (NFVCB). Classification is the harder constraint: the Board commits to classifying within 20 working days and issuing the certificate five days after the decision (NFVCB) — a release date is not real until the certificate is in hand (Guardian).

Section 30(3) of the Copyright Act 2022 is the clause the company rests on: an assignment of copyright or an exclusive licence "shall have no effect unless it is in writing" (Copyright Act 2022). Every distribution agreement this company signs is worthless without writing — also a competitive advantage, since most Nigerian deals are still done on handshakes and email. Destination-market rules are where international sales get delayed; the answer is a territory compliance matrix, sub-agents engaged in writing under s.30(3), and audit rights in every agreement.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

Here the rule has to be read precisely, because the licence is the cheap part and buying it alone would be a mistake. The NFVCB National Distributor licence costs ₦5m with ₦5m of minimum share capital — it is obtainable in a month (see §12, item 1) and it is not the barrier. The barrier is the contracts. So the Group's rule that a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business — that Uli Distribution either obtains the permission or buys a company that already holds it — applies in this company to the commercial layer: the output deals and cinema relationships. §2 established that FilmOne holds 73% of Nigerian box office because it holds both the Hollywood studio slates and most premium Nollywood releases — structural, not competitive. A new Nigerian distributor cannot win those two agencies by applying for them. The only route that shortens the queue is to buy a distributor that already holds them, or to buy the agency relationship itself with the incumbent's consent. The contracts are the asset.

Financing rules: gearing ≤40%; no unhedged USD debt; P&A and prints ring-fenced per slate so one failed release cannot consume the next slate's marketing. Prints and marketing are working capital, not capital expenditure — and that governs how this company may be financed.

7. Unit economics

The theatrical waterfall decides whether a release is worth taking. About 10% of gross ticket revenue goes first — federal VAT and state entertainment tax in equal halves. Net box office is then shared on a sliding scale for Nollywood titles: week one 50/50, week two 45% distributor / 55% exhibitor, and 40% / 60% from week three. From the distributor's share come the distribution fee and roughly 10% withholding tax. The producer is left with 30–40% of gross (TVC News) — a co-director of Everybody Loves Jenifa puts the producer's net at 35% (New Telegraph).

Two commission rates apply, and they are not the same number. The observed Nigerian theatrical distribution fee is 10–15% of the distributor's share; a sales agent on an international or acquired-rights deal typically takes 20–35% of gross. Model: 20–25% international, 10–15% domestic [verify].

The arithmetic of failure, stated honestly. Theatrical distribution requires working capital for prints and marketing spent before a single naira is collected, and a failed title is absorbed entirely by the distributor's marketing spend. A ₦12m P&A spend on a title grossing ₦4m is a ₦12m loss, not a loss offset by box office; on an advance or acquired-rights deal Uli Distribution also loses the advance. Hence no title without a recoupment forecast, and aggregation — many titles, low marginal cost, diversified outcomes — is safer than a few expensive bets.

11. Integration

This company connects the Group's content businesses to their markets.

  • Uli Film — the primary supply: theatrical, streaming, broadcast and international release of the slate. Uli Film's plan shows 1.12× in year one integrated against 0.61× standalone — distribution is that difference.
  • Uli Music and Uli Animation — sync, soundtrack and format exploitation; animation is the highest-margin, most exportable category, travelling without dubbing.
  • Uli Cinemas — the release channel. Owned screens remove the largest source of leverage a distributor faces. This integration makes the plan defensible.
  • Uli Broadcast — a captive, arms-length licensee for the post-theatrical broadcast window.
  • Uli Rights — the two-way loop. Distribution aggregates third-party catalogues to scale; the rights it acquires feed Uli Rights' catalogue, documented, valued and reported, and thence sold to Akunnia Capital's fund as an investable asset class. Distribution is the front door through which the Group's catalogue strategy acquires real assets.
  • Uli Freight, Aku Technology, Idenze University — DCPs and physical media; the royalty system, so every statement has one auditable source; and trained media graduates, because a distribution business is a documentation business.

The internal-customer advantage: Uli Film, Uli Music and Uli Animation supply content from Year 1, Uli Cinemas supplies screen access and Uli Broadcast a licensing counterparty — before any third-party deal is signed. That is what makes a Nigerian distribution start-up viable where the incumbent holds 73%.

12. First ninety days

  1. Apply for the NFVCB National Distributor licence in month one — ₦5m fee, ₦5m minimum share capital. No release can be booked without it.
  2. Have the Uli Group board approve the windowing policy — window order, term ceilings, territory rules, the seven-year limit, the P&A gate. The first deal sets the precedent.
  3. Sign the intercompany distribution mandates with Uli Film, Uli Music and Uli Animation at market commission rates, Group CFO-certified as arms-length.
  4. Open the Uli Cinemas release relationship — booking and settlement protocol, screen commitments, data-sharing.
  5. Recruit the Head of Distribution and the Business Affairs and Rights Manager — one negotiates the terms, the other ensures s.30(3) writing exists behind them.
  6. Build the territory compliance matrix for the first fifteen territories — classification, withholding tax, cultural-content rules.
  7. Set the acquisition valuation template — recoupment forecast, advance sizing, MG expectations, escrow and indemnity terms — and sign no advance outside it.
  8. Codify the s.30(3) gate as policy: no agreement signed, no booking made and no third-party title accepted without a written assignment or exclusive licence on file. The cheapest thing the company will ever do, and retro-fitting it is impossible.

ULI FREIGHT — Freight & Trade Corridors

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary in this plan; it uses ₦1,328–1,362/USD, with naira as primary throughout. Spot was about ₦1,328/USD (CBN NFEM, Sept 2026). Dollar figures are indicative only and are not comparable across plans — each plan used a different rate. The library planning rate for cross-plan comparison is ₦1,600/USD. See plans/README.md.

Ezeme Group · Uli Group · Entity Uli Freight Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Uli Group Ltd (Uli) · Horizon 15 yrs · Year 1 = 2027. Naira figures are primary. USD figures are indicative only, converted at ₦1,600/USD held flat in nominal terms; they are not independently sourced USD prices. This plan is built at ₦1,600/USD while the capital plan uses ₦1,500/USD and spot is ~₦1,328/USD — the library requires one harmonising re-base pass, at which point only the USD column changes.

Companions (queued plans): 36_Uli_Warehousing.md, 40_Uli_Fleet.md (Uli Fleet — vehicle, conveyance), 38_Uli_Special_Logistics.md — separate companies and boards; interfaces only here.

1. Thesis

Uli Freight is not a haulage company. It is a corridor operator: it takes control of cargo at a Nigerian seaport or a Nkpor production gate and delivers it, documented and tracked, to a named consignee inland or across an ECOWAS border. Trucks are one input; the depot, the customs capability, the control tower, the customer contract and the licences are the business. The mandate is to control two to three priority African corridors end-to-end — port → warehouse → last mile.

Three advantages no independent haulier can assemble: a captive base load from Isiome's output and Idenze's pharmaceuticals; expressway-facing land in the group's own Nkpor industrial zone at group cost; and group capital plus Akunnia's in-house finance.

One sentence: Onitsha, West Africa's largest inland trading market, sits at the wrong end of a congested 450-kilometre road, and the group already owns the cargo, the land and the capital to fix that — the margin accrues to whoever holds the corridor, not to whoever holds the most trucks.

Why corridor control beats fleet size. Fleet size is a depreciating asset a competitor can match with a bank loan. Corridor control is barriers that compound: a bonded inland depot with a customs presence; the papers and guarantees to clear and move cargo; a chain of custody a regulated manufacturer can put in front of an inspector; a warehouse cargo cannot leave without the operator's release; and multi-year contracts with the manufacturers whose goods fill trucks both ways. Nigeria has thousands of five-to-fifty-truck owners and none controls a corridor, because a corridor needs land, a licence, a bond, a warehouse and the working capital to pay a shipper's duty before invoicing. Dangote's 10,000-truck fleet moves its owner's own product — captive logistics, not a corridor.

Capital rule: every naira is tested by whether it increases control of the corridor or merely count of wheels. Depot, bond, licensing, telematics and working capital pass. Trucks pass only where nothing else can carry the load.

2. Market

Nigeria's freight and logistics market was USD 10.95 bn in 2025 and 11.66 bn in 2026, forecast 15.97 bn by 2031 (6.49% CAGR); manufacturing contributed USD 4.24 bn (Research and Markets via GlobeNewswire, Jan 2026). That spans courier, forwarding and warehousing, so the road-haulage segment must be sized from a shipper survey before the fleet programme is approved. Over 90% of Nigerian freight moves by road (InfraCredit, 2026). The market is informal — single-truck owner-operators, phone brokers, union-controlled loading points, per-trip negotiation. Diesel is >35% of trucking expense; roads and insecurity add up to 20% to cost, so operators price short-term and cannot commit to fixed tariffs. Two shifts favour Uli Freight: South-East customs reform is cutting demurrage (Vanguard, May 2026), and Lekki/Onne expansions add ~4.5 m TEU of capacity, raising inland road demand.

Everyone does one link. Uli Freight sells the chain.

4. Operating model

Depot. The anchor asset is the depot on the expressway-facing Nkpor industrial zone plots. Phase 1 (Year 1): 6,000 m² hardstanding, 6 dock-levelled bays, 1,200 m² transit shed, 600 m² workshop plus control tower, 60-tonne weighbridge, fuel and wash bays, gated perimeter with CCTV, and 150 kWp solar-plus-storage built by Okodu so diesel is a fallback, not the base case — the group's stated "freight depot, warehousing, fleet yard, dispatch," made operational. Phase 2 (Year 2–3): 3,000 m² more shed, 4 bays, a 300 m² validated cold room, second weighbridge. A leased Lagos satellite yard (Apapa/Amuwo) is the highest-value non-Nkpor asset — a secure place to drop, rest and swap trailers rather than queue on port access roads, and the prerequisite for round-trip scheduling. Onne follows by Year 5. Only Nkpor is intended freehold.

Own, lease or subcontract — recommendation. A new artic costs ~₦95 m (≈USD 59,000); leasing one runs ~₦2.4–2.8 m/month, pushing break-even utilisation ~50% higher (§7). Leasing in Nigeria is not cheap — it buys optionality at a real price. Three tracks: (1) own the core — first 19 units on family equity plus long-tenor local-currency debt arranged through Akunnia on contracted order books, not asset collateral; (2) subcontract the tail and peaks — sell the corridor commercially, buy traction from vetted owner-operators under a standard carriage contract with Uli Freight's insurance, Uli Freight-fitted telematics, driver vetting and right of first refusal, targeting ≥30% of tonne-km subcontracted by Year 5; (3) lease only what the market cannot allocate to us — short-cycle lanes, reefers before cold-chain volume is proven, the project fleet.

Drivers. Employed, not contracted: regulated cargo and the insurance programme require an employment relationship with a verifiable record. Correct licence class, annual medical, a defensive-driving module, and fatigue enforced by telematics, not trust — maximum continuous hours, rest logged in the control tower, hard dispatch stop. Pay is fixed salary plus a safety and utilisation bonus, never a per-trip cash incentive that rewards speed. A driver apprentice path feeds from the group's polytechnic, because the driver shortage (IRU, 2025) will bind this business before capital does.

Control tower and maintenance. Every unit reports position, speed, harsh braking, fuel and driver ID to a Nkpor tower staffed 24/7: dispatch against port appointment systems; exception management (breakdown, checkpoint extortion, route deviation, cargo alarm); and the data that makes utilisation real. Nigerian fleets often buy trackers to know when to panic (Daily Trust); Uli Freight buys them to schedule. Preventive maintenance runs at Nkpor on a fixed kilometre schedule, with six months' parts cover on high-turnover items, a per-km tyre contract with casing credit, and fuel reconciled per litre against telematics on every fill — fuel unreconciled is fuel stolen. Target availability 85% by Year 2, 90% by Year 4.

Utilisation anchor. A new carrier cannot win a large external contract, and an idle truck is pure loss. Isiome's processing output, Idenze's pharmaceuticals and Okodu's materials all move by road today on third-party invoices. That volume transfers under a published tariff with no internal discount, giving ~35–45% of Year 1 billable tonne-km, falling to ~20% by Year 5. The tariff is set by the Group CFO and reviewed annually by the independent directors: related-party pricing is the first thing a future investor, lender or tax authority will attack.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Phase 0 — before any truck moves (Months 0–3). Incorporate Uli Freight Ltd at CAC with reserved matters and a Family Director in the Articles. Register with the Anambra State Ministry of Transport and confirm every state levy in writing across Anambra, Enugu, Imo, Abia, Rivers, Lagos and the FCT — a verbal understanding is worth nothing later. Per unit: vehicle licence, roadworthiness, third-party insurance, hackney permit, correct licence class, FRSC Road Transport Safety Standardisation Scheme compliance, plus LASDRI certification for Lagos. Bind insurance before the first load: comprehensive motor, goods-in-transit at declared value, liability, marine open cover.

Phase 1 — customs (Months 3–12). The Nigeria Customs Service licensed customs agent licence, renewal cycle and bank bond. Without it Uli Freight cannot clear its own group cargo and forfeits margin and chain control. CRFFN registration carries live legal uncertainty: courts have stripped CRFFN of regulatory power over licensed customs agents and declared its Practitioners' Operating Fee unlawful, with CRFFN appealing (Vanguard, July 2025; The Sun, June 2026) — counsel opinion before any payment. Then the strategic unlock: a bonded terminal/warehouse licence and customs-controlled area designation for Nkpor, converting a truck park into a lawful inland node and forming the physical basis of corridor control. Add a NAFDAC wholesale premises licence for direct pharmaceutical distribution.

Phase 2 — cross-border (Years 2–4). ECOWAS Inter-State Road Transit under Convention A/P.4/5/82 (ECOWAS; ISRT guidelines): transit declaration, customs seal, transit bond, plus ECOWAS Brown Card insurance, vehicle laissez-passer and driver documentation for every state traversed. Many states still demand a national guarantee on top — confirm per country and budget for it. Cameroon/CEMAC is a separate regime; do not sell Corridor 4 before those permits exist.

Phase 3 — controlled substances: a ring-fenced licensee (Uli Special Logistics), NDLEA permits and NAFDAC Narcotics & Controlled Substances authorisations. See below.

Union and levy posture. NURTW and RTEAN control loading across much of the market and their levies are systemic: a reported ₦300 bn "shadow state" (Nairametrics, Aug 2026), port truckers complaining of NURTW/RTEAN extortion (The Sun, Aug 2026), and the tax reform bill seen as unlikely to curb illegal levies (Businessday, May 2026). Posture, decided in advance and stated in writing: a closed, gated private depot with Uli Freight's own loading crew and no third-party loading points; drivers on direct payroll; formal written notification to the unions; pay only levies existing in a state law or gazette, by bank transfer with a receipted reference; log every other demand — photograph, amount, location, officer, time — in a corridor obstruction register; escalate through the state internal revenue service, NARTO and, if necessary, litigation. No roadside cash negotiation.

Professional standing. The MD and Operations Director should hold CIOTA membership at Chartered or Associate grade (CIOTA Nigeria) — a chartered transport administrator signing the contract differentiates at FMCG and pharma procurement stage. The compliance lead should hold a customs broker qualification and a CILT (UK) logistics qualification.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

Uli Freight's licences are not hard to obtain in principle and they are increasingly expensive in practice — which is precisely the case for buying them. The Group's rule is that a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business: Uli Freight either obtains the licence or buys a company that already holds it. In Nigerian haulage the second route is frequently cheaper and far faster, because the incumbent is undercapitalised, the regulator's de novo queue is discretionary, and an existing operator brings the licence, trained staff, a working fleet and — the thing that cannot be applied for — contracted lanes. Three facts make this concrete. The Nigeria Customs Service reviewed licensed-agent fees upward by a reported 20-fold to ₦10m for licensing and renewal before suspending the increase (BusinessDay; Guardian) — so the direct route is both slow and, on the proposed schedule, expensive; and an entity whose licence is already held and in good standing is not exposed to the same step change. NARTO membership and terminal access are relationship assets, not applications. And a haulage company is bought for its contracted lanes, which take years to assemble and months to lose.

What a mid-size Nigerian haulage company costs. ⚠️ [verify] — this is a privately priced market with no published transaction dataset, so the figure below is derived, not sourced, and must not be used as a valuation. The derivation: a mid-size operator is here defined as 30–80 owned units; §4 puts a new artic at ~₦95m, so new-replacement fleet value alone is ₦2.9bn–₦7.6bn, against which a used fleet in working order is discounted for age and condition; add working capital and a premium for contracted lanes and terminal access, and an indicative consideration of ₦1.5bn–₦6.0bn (~US$0.9m–3.8m) falls out. The only semi-public comparables are listed-sector: ABC Transport Plc trades on the NGX (ABCTRANS) — and a listed passenger-and-parcel carrier is a poor read-across to a heavy corridor hauler. Price on the contracted order book and the fleet's true condition, never on the truck count, and note §10 risk 10: the failure mode in this sector is buying steel against soft demand.

Ninety-day action, costed. Extend §12 item 1: alongside filing the Group's own customs agent application, instruct counsel and a transport broker to identify every licensed customs agent and NARTO-member haulier in the South-East and Lagos with 30–80 owned units, live terminal access and at least one contracted lane, and to price two. Budget ₦75m (~US$47,000): ₦25m regulatory and licence-status diligence on six targets — NCS licence standing, NPA and terminal accounts, per-state permit currency; ₦20m fleet condition survey and independent valuation of two targets' units against §4's ₦95m replacement cost; ₦18m contract and lane diligence, including change-of-control clauses in every shipper contract, since a lane that terminates on assignment is not an asset; ₦12m NARTO, union and litigation diligence. Run this in parallel with the organic Phase 0–2 pathway — the corridors are the prize and either route that secures one is the right route.
