Funding mix. Family equity (Years 1–3) covers depot and licensing — assets that cannot be repossessed into value and so must not be pledged. Akunnia-arranged local-currency debt on 36–60 month tenors matched to contract duration funds truck tranches, so debt service never exceeds contracted revenue. Aku Infrastructure Fund I (Years 3–5) holds the depot and warehousing real estate with Uli Freight as anchor tenant, separating property risk from operating risk. Development finance supports CNG conversion and cold chain.

Recommendation: own the depot and cold chain; own the core fleet on cheap long-tenor debt; subcontract ≥30% of tonne-km and lease only project and peak fleet. Do not fund a 70-truck fleet from equity — that converts a corridor business into a depreciating-asset business with a corridor story attached. Working capital is the most commonly under-funded line in Nigerian haulage; here it is 13% of Tranche 1.

Verify locally before commitment: depot construction rates (Okodu cost survey), new and used unit prices at current FX, per-unit insurance premiums, diesel price at commitment, each state's levy schedule.

At six loaded legs a month an owned unit contributes ~₦0.1 m over fixed cost; at ten it contributes ₦2.13 m a month — ₦25.6 m a year, a 27% pre-tax cash return on the ₦95 m asset. The first ten hires, in order. (1) Managing Director — a working transport operator with a corridor P&L on their CV, not a group executive learning the business. (2) Operations Director. (3) Compliance, Customs & Regulatory Lead — decides whether the corridor is real; on the customs agent licence in week one. (4) Fleet Manager. (5) Control Tower Lead. (6) Commercial Manager. (7) Chief Driver / Driver Trainer — sets the safety culture before twenty bad habits exist. (8) Workshop Foreman. (9) HSE & Security Officer. (10) Finance & Admin Manager (fuel reconciliation, trip costing, credit control).

Drivers — employment, retention, safety. Written contracts, monthly bank payment, pension and NHF/HMO remitted, documented rest and rotation. Pay benchmarked deliberately above the informal market for the same lane, because a driver who can earn more running an unsafe truck at night will do exactly that. Non-negotiables: no night driving on unfamiliar corridors in Years 1–2; no cash handling by drivers; a no-blame incident reporting policy so near-misses surface rather than hide; annual medical including vision; a disciplinary process that never monetises an incident. Retention levers beyond pay: a defined driver-to-chief-driver progression, a trainer role, and priority admission for drivers' children to the group's school network — a benefit the group provides at marginal cost and no independent haulier can match.

11. Integration

Isiome Group. Uli Freight distributes Isiome's processed output — garri, starch, palm oil, flour, canned goods — carries inputs and mechanisation in reverse, and handles exports to port and imports inland, where the customs agent licence pays for itself. Isiome pays the published tariff even though the group owns both sides: that keeps Uli Freight's unit economics honest, makes Isiome's product costing honest, and preserves the arms-length evidence any future lender, investor or tax authority will demand.

Idenze Group. Uli Freight operates the validated cold chain — 2–8 °C and 15–25 °C — for pharmaceuticals and vaccines, with temperature loggers, excursion alarms and lot-level documentation a NAFDAC inspector can audit. It is Uli Freight's highest-margin, highest-barrier line and a capability Idenze cannot buy from the informal market at any price. Controlled-substance movements sit with Uli Special Logistics, not Uli Freight. Uli Freight also covers group staff and student transport.

Okodu Group. Uli Freight buys diesel in bulk, and later depot electric charging, from Okodu; contracts Okodu for depot civil works, sheds and solar-plus-storage; and carries Okodu's construction materials on inbound legs — a heavy, predictable, low-insurance-risk base load ideal for filling backhauls from the north and west. Okodu's build programme supplies Uli Freight's project-cargo pipeline.

Akunnia Group. Akunnia arranges and syndicates asset finance on Uli Freight's trucks and depot — local-currency debt matched to contract tenor, later an infrastructure fund holding depot real estate with Uli Freight as anchor tenant. It also supplies group treasury and the control and audit function that keeps intercompany pricing arms-length. Related-party volumes are large enough that independent directors must review them annually — a feature, not friction.

Uli Group. Uli Freight distributes for the other Uli businesses: equipment and set movements for Uli Film, merchandise and event logistics for Uli Music and Uli Cinemas, and physical media — small in revenue, useful for filling otherwise-empty legs. (corrected — see NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md: the superseded provisional names "Ihe Nkiri", "Egwu" and "Cinema" are replaced by the v5.0 names.)

Boundaries. Uli Freight owns no warehouse (Uli Warehousing), no telematics platform (Uli Fleet) and no controlled-substance licence (Uli Special Logistics) — each a separate company, board, audit and priced intercompany contract.

The controlled-substance capability

This sits in a ring-fenced company — Uli Special Logistics, the group's licensed special-logistics entity — not inside Uli Freight. Uli Freight is the corridor operator and commercial channel; Uli Special Logistics is the licensee. That separation is deliberate and must never be collapsed for administrative convenience.

Why it is a moat. Every manufacturer and importer of narcotics and controlled pharmaceuticals in Nigeria — including Idenze's cannabinoid programme, hospital groups and licensed generics manufacturers — must move those materials, and very few road carriers can lawfully do so. A licensed carrier competes on the ability to exist, not on rate. Once the licence, security infrastructure, documentation system and regulator relationship exist, the barrier to a new entrant is measured in years and inspections, not naira. It is the single most defensible asset in the logistics platform.

Licensing. NAFDAC's Narcotics & Controlled Substances Directorate issues permits to clear imported narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances and drug precursors, with specific guidelines for Schedule 1 narcotic imports and for clearing imported narcotic controlled substances and pharmaceutical raw materials (NAFDAC NCS guidelines; Schedule 1 importation), under the Controlled Medicines Regulations 2019 and the risk-categorisation guideline effective 30 July 2024 (NAFDAC). NDLEA issues possession and movement authorisations and enforces precursor control. Internationally, import and export authorisations are exchanged between national competent authorities with quantities matched to national estimates. Every shipment requires its own authorisation — there is no standing permit.

Security specification — non-negotiable. Dedicated vehicles with a locked, sealed, tamper-evident compartment and a two-lock system with separate keyholders; door and alarm sensors reporting to the 24/7 control tower; dual GPS on independent power; a two-person minimum crew, no individual ever alone with the cargo; no third-party pickup, no ad-hoc stops, no unauthorised passengers; pre-cleared routes with pre-notified arrival times; photograph-and-weight reconciliation at every handover; a documented disposal and returns procedure, because controlled stock cannot simply be written off.

Chain of custody and documentation. Documented at every transfer: serialised consignment note; seal number recorded at load and verified at each seal break; temperature log; driver and escort identification; signature and time at each handover; GPS track archived against the manifest; reconciliation certificate on delivery. Records retained for the regulator's required period — assumed not less than five years, to be confirmed with NAFDAC and NDLEA in writing. Any discrepancy is a reportable incident escalated to the regulator within 24 hours, reported even where the material is later found.

Ring-fencing. Uli Special Logistics has its own board including an independent director, its own audited accounts, its own named responsible person, security staff holding no other duties involving controlled movement, its own insurer and incident register. Its drivers are vetted, referenced and re-screened, and employed by Uli Special Logistics alone. It shares no manifests, staff or vehicle pool with Uli Freight beyond a priced carriage contract for the unlicensed segments of a journey. A regulatory failure there must never reach Uli Freight's contracts, the depot's bonded status, Idenze's NAFDAC registrations or the group's banking relationships. That is why the ring-fence exists, and why the family architecture requires every regulated activity to sit in its own company.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — decide and secure. (1) Appoint the Managing Director and the Compliance, Customs & Regulatory Lead, with the customs agent licence as the compliance lead's first deliverable on a 1 October deadline. (2) Commission counsel opinions on the CRFFN position after the 2025–2026 judgments, the bonded terminal pathway for Nkpor, and ECOWAS ISRT documentation. (3) Obtain written state levy schedules for Anambra, Enugu, Abia, Imo, Rivers, Lagos and the FCT — and, where none exists, a written statement to that effect, which becomes the defence later. (4) Run a Corridor 1 cost survey: measured distances, diesel at three depots, actual levies paid per trip by three independent operators, rates from three shippers, and observed port dwell at Apapa and Tin Can over ten working days — then re-base §7 on real numbers before ordering trucks. (5) Bind the insurance programme and open the Akunnia funding conversation with the contracted-volume model, not an asset list.

Days 31–60 — contract and build. (6) Execute intercompany carriage agreements with Isiome, Idenze and Okodu at published tariffs, Group CFO-certified as arms-length and minuted by the independent directors; target 40 loaded legs a month of committed captive volume. (7) Sign two external anchor contracts — one FMCG manufacturer, one importer or hospital group — on a tariff with a quarterly fuel-surcharge index. (8) Issue the depot Phase 1 works order to Okodu and the solar/storage order in parallel, on fixed-price contracts with liquidated damages. (9) Open Lagos satellite yard negotiations on a 12-month lease with a renewal option — worth more to utilisation than any truck in Tranche 1. (10) Tender 10 artic units on a CNG-capable specification and confirm delivery lead time before committing capital.

Days 61–90 — staff and start. (11) Recruit the control tower team, chief driver/trainer and workshop foreman; stand up telematics with Uli Fleet; run route-reconnaissance pilot runs on Corridor 1 using hired trucks. (12) Hire the first 18 drivers through a referenced, documented process and run the first defensive-driving and fatigue module. (13) Publish the standing levy and union policy to all staff and, in writing, to the transport unions; open the corridor obstruction register on day one. (14) Incorporate Uli Special Logistics and file the NDLEA/NAFDAC preliminary enquiries — the controlled-substance clock starts now, not when the first customer asks. (15) Day-90 board decision: release the fleet order only if captive volume and at least one external anchor contract are signed. If not, run Corridor 1 for a quarter entirely on subcontracted capacity and re-test.

ULI WAREHOUSING — Grade-A Warehousing at Ports and Inland Hubs

Naming: a child's name plus a plain function (v5.0); the entity 35_Uli_Freight.md calls Uli Warehousing is this company. FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD, not comparable across plans.

Ezeme Group · Uli Group · Uli Warehousing Ltd (CAMA) · Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Uli Group → Uli Warehousing · Horizon 15 yrs · Year 1 = 2027. Companions: 35_Uli_Freight.md, 38_Uli_Special_Logistics.md, 05_Isiome_Storage.md, 45_Okodu_Construction.md.

1. Thesis

Warehousing is a toll business with predictable revenue, and it is the least risky asset in the logistics platform. Freight is utilisation-sensitive and margin-thin: a truck earns nothing queuing at Apapa, and its contribution collapses when a rival cuts the rate. Storage earns a fee per pallet position per month whether or not the customer's business is good — no return leg, no diesel, no driver shortage, no uninsured owner-operator to undercut it.

It anchors the freight business. 35_Uli_Freight.md says utilisation is the whole game — six loaded legs a month contributes ~₦0.1 m over fixed cost, ten contributes ₦2.13 m. A grade-A warehouse is the largest single lever on that number: a scheduled destination and reload instead of a broker's phone call, turning a deadhead return into an order. That plan owns no warehouse and buys throughput here.

One sentence: Nigeria has tens of millions of square metres of storage and almost none of it is grade-A; the informal shed cannot be insured, racked, audited, bonded or refrigerated, so this company does not compete with that shed — it sells a different product to the same shipper at a price the shed can never reach.

Capital rule: every naira buys a metre lettable at grade-A rent, or a licence to store what others cannot.

2. Market

Nigeria's warehousing market is USD 1,178 m in 2025–26, rising to USD 1,700 m by 2031 (6.30% CAGR) across roughly 1,450 players (Ken Research), whose outlook expects profit pools to "shift toward temperature-controlled storage, multi-user distribution centres, bonded facilities." Ports handled 103.3 m tons in 2024 including ~1.7 m TEU and over 129 m tons in 2025, concentrating demand at Apapa, Tin Can Island and Lekki.

Supply is bad, not merely short. African warehousing is "dominated by informal and legacy facilities" lacking ceiling height, reinforced floors, docks, fire protection and digital inventory (All Business Africa). Lagos: 25–30 m m² of stock, grade-A only 3–4 m m² (12–15%); demand 1.2–1.5 m m² a year against 700–900 k m² supplied — a 25–40% shortfall; vacancy under 5%; yields 13–16% (N3 Capital, 2026). Rents corroborate at ~$6/m²/month, up nearly 10% since 2020 (Knight Frank via Punch); N3 puts modern space at $8–12 — the market cannot agree on the price of a product it barely has.

Supply is tightening, which helps a 2027 entrant: FX-denominated inputs — steel, cold storage units, bonded fencing, WMS — rose 25–30% year-on-year, and with lending above 30% "warehouse refurbishment and expansion plans are being shelved or downsized" (InfraCredit, 2026).

Where to build: port-adjacent — Apapa, Tin Can, Lekki's 2.5 m TEU deep-sea port — for de-stuffing, CFS and bonded storage; and inland hubs on the corridors Uli Freight already serves: the Nkpor–Onitsha node on Corridor 1, with Onne (WACT/APM Terminals) as the eastern port node. Onitsha, West Africa's largest inland trading market, has no grade-A warehousing at all — that absence, not Lagos, is the seat of the margin.

General warehousing versus specialised storage sets this company apart. General storage is four walls and a floor, priced against the cheapest shed. Specialised storage is a licence with a building attached, priced against the alternative — usually none. Cold chain serves agriculture (against 20–33% post-harvest loss and a national shortfall of ~50,000 tonnes, IIR) and pharmaceuticals, where validated capacity is scarce and the buyer is regulated. Bonded storage lets an importer hold goods without paying duty until removal — a licence, a bond and a customs-controlled area, not a shed. Controlled-substance storage is a separately licensed cage for narcotics and precursors under NAFDAC's Narcotics & Controlled Substances Directorate and the Controlled Medicines Regulations 2019; movement authorisations sit with Uli Special Logistics, storage here.

3PL versus spot. Spot earns more with no certainty — a customer can leave in January. A contract of three to five years with minimum volume and indexation earns less per pallet and converts the asset into an annuity: target ≥70% of ambient positions on terms of twelve months or more by Year 5.

4. Operating model

The grade-A specification is the product, so it is a board-approved build standard: clear internal height 12 m (the biggest driver of yield per m²); floor loading 5–6 t/m² on a sealed slab; dock levellers and sealed bays, about one dock per 600–800 m², plus a drive-in ramp; ESFR sprinkler suppression with a dedicated water reserve, because high-racked stock is unreachable by hose; perimeter security — fencing, a single controlled gate, CCTV, access control, 24/7 guards; power backup — solar-plus-storage first, diesel second, built by Okodu Power, cold rooms on a critical circuit.

The building is sized to the racking plan, not the reverse: unrackable height or a column grid that breaks a pallet module is permanent lost rent on a 25-year asset, so the racking layout is signed off before the foundation is poured. Operations are multi-user by default, and a WMS with barcode location control is mandatory from day one — without it there is no auditable custody, no GDP compliance and no 3PL contract. Custody separation mirrors Isiome Storage: those who handle goods do not count them, and the inventory controller reports to the board.

Cold chain is where the model is won or lost. NAFDAC's Good Storage and Distribution Practice Guidelines (PMS-GDL-019-01, effective 26/11/2024) require temperature mapping across the facility and across dry and rainy seasons, calibrated monitors, alarms tested at least every six months, equipment qualified before use, and records kept for shelf-life plus one year (NAFDAC GSDP). Conditions follow the product: refrigerator 2–8 °C, freezer −25 to −10 °C, cool place 8–15 °C, ambient "store below 25 °C." Redundant refrigeration, an independent logger and a written excursion protocol with a named decision-maker are the price of the line.

Bonded warehousing changes the economics — it lets an importer land, store and de-stuff without paying duty until removal, which a Lagos importer with a cash-flow problem pays a premium for, and it converts the inland hub into a lawful inland node, the asset 35_Uli_Freight.md wants for its corridor. The conditions are the risk: premises to a customs standard, a bond or bank guarantee, records reconciled on demand, and a licence revocable for accounting failures. Counsel opinion on the 2023 Act's conditions and the bond quantum before any application is filed.

Boundaries. This company stores; it does not issue warehouse receipts (Isiome Storage, SEC-registered) and does not hold controlled-substance movement authorisations (Uli Special Logistics). The cage sits here under this company's own NAFDAC/NDLEA registration, on a written custody interface to Special Logistics. Whether NAFDAC and NDLEA will register this company as custodian of controlled stock, or require the licence holder to hold it, must be confirmed in writing before the cage is built.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

Warehousing is the one business in the Group where the licence is genuinely scarce, and where the direct route has just become harder. The Group's rule — a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business; it either obtains the licence or buys a company that already holds it — applies here in its strongest form.

The SEC registration is mandatory, not optional. The Commission's circular of 11 May 2026 on the mandatory registration of collateral management companies, warehouse operators and warehouses requires registration, and states expressly that current operations do not amount to automatic registration or an exemption; it sets ₦500m minimum capital for a warehouse operator and ₦200m–₦500m by tier for a collateral management company, three sponsored individuals including an MD and a Compliance Officer, and a fidelity insurance bond of at least 20% of minimum capital (SEC circular; Pavestones). Under ISA 2025 Part XV (s.246(1)) a warehouse receipt is "first proof of the holder having proprietary rights in the commodities" — the Act's own words, which are evidentiary rather than a conveyance of title, with s.249(1) making it transferable by endorsement and delivery, and the receipt system is a centralised electronic system maintained by an SEC-approved entity (ISA 2025; AO2). Without registration, a receipt is not lawfully issued at all (s.245(1)) and cannot be relied on as proof of proprietary rights — which is why the registration is a capital and governance product, not a filing. ⚠️ The circular's 90-day window closed about 9 August 2026; confirm with the SEC in writing whether a fresh application window is open, because on its own terms operating does not create registration. This company's own boundary is unchanged — receipts sit with Isiome Storage — but a Uli Warehousing that decided to issue receipts could not do so without this registration, and could not buy its way past s.246(1) by issuing them anyway.

Why the scarcity argument holds, stated plainly. §6 already prices a Nkpor hub at ₦5.5bn for 6,000 m² ambient and a 300 m² cold room, and §7 puts cold capex at ₦2.4m/m² against ₦706,000/m² ambient. Building is the Group's default because Okodu builds at cost-plus. But where a bonded, GDP-certified, SEC-registered operator with live contracts exists at asset value, buying it delivers occupancy, licences and clients on day one, while §7 is explicit that a new warehouse takes 24–36 months to reach 75% occupancy. That 24–36-month gap is what the acquisition premium buys back.

Ninety-day action, costed. Instruct counsel to (a) obtain the SEC's written position on whether a registration window is open and what a change of control of a registered operator requires, and (b) screen the acquirable population — bonded warehouse operators, GDP-certified cold-chain operators, NPA-licensed CFS operators and free-zone warehouses in Lagos, Onne and the South-East — for licence currency, title, occupancy and client concentration. Budget ₦48m (~US$30,000): ₦15m SEC and NCS regulatory opinions in writing; ₦18m licence, title and premises diligence on five targets, including fire and planning consents and any outstanding abatement notice; ₦15m occupancy, tariff and client-contract diligence on the two that meet the specification, testing change-of-control clauses in every 3PL contract, since a tenant contract that terminates on assignment removes the reason to buy. Run in parallel with the T1 build: if an operator meeting the grade-A specification and holding the bonded and GDP licences can be bought at or near asset value, §12 item 12's fallback — leasing someone else's building — becomes an acquisition instead.

Warehousing is real-estate-like: land and building dominate capex and the asset is long-lived — 25 years or more, with land and shell unrecoverable if the site is wrong. Planning placeholders, naira first.

Funding mix, and the honest constraint. Family equity funds Tranche 1: land and a purpose-built building cannot be repossessed into value and must not be pledged. Akunnia Capital arranges naira debt on 36–60 month tenors matched to contract duration; racking, MHE and refrigeration — all imported — are bought against naira facilities priced at order, never borrowed in dollars (no unhedged USD debt).

But 40% gearing is a ceiling, not a plan. At a ~13% unlevered yield and naira lending above 30%, debt at 40% of capital consumes essentially the entire net operating income in interest, pushing required occupancy from 44% to 79% (§7). Practical gearing is 15–25%; the rest belongs in Aku Infrastructure Fund I holding the building on a 10–15 year tenor with Uli Warehousing as anchor tenant and operating lessee. This asset is built by a company and owned by a fund; conflating the two is what makes infrastructure expensive in Nigeria.

Verify locally: land values and title at Nkpor, Apapa and Onne; Okodu Construction's warehouse rate (₦280,000–400,000/m², planning basis, not a quotation); racking, MHE and refrigeration prices at current FX; cold-room build and validation cost; power tariff and grid hours per site; the NCS bond quantum.

7. Unit economics

The unit of sale is the occupied pallet position per month; the asset is the square metre that carries it. One ambient grade-A block, Nkpor, Year-3 basis: 6,000 m² GFA, 12 m clear height, 1.2 positions per m² = 7,200 positions; tariff ₦9,600 per position per month (≈$6/m²/month, Knight Frank-anchored); handling and value-added ₦3,500 per occupied position per month. Operating cost ₦4,600/m²/month — power ₦1,400 (ambient; the largest line at an unserved site), security ₦600, labour ₦900, maintenance ₦500, insurance ₦350, WMS/IT ₦250, admin ₦600.

Occupancy is the whole economics — this table is the plan.

Break-even occupancy: 29% on cash opex, 44% full-cost (opex plus capital recovery on ₦706,000/m² over 25 years), 64% levered at 20% debt, 79% at 40% — the last is not financeable at Nigerian rates.

Racking density is the lever nobody prices. Adding a level within the 12 m clear height lifts positions per m² from 0.8 to 1.2 — a 50% revenue increase on an unchanged building, at roughly ₦95,000 per position.

Cold chain — the highest gross margin, and the segment that breaks the company if run casually. A 2,000 m² block at 1,600 positions (0.8/m²), 85% occupied, blended ₦40,400 per position (agri/food ~₦26,000; validated pharma ~₦62,000), earns ₦68.5 m a month — ₦34,250/m²/month (US$21.4) — against power of ₦7,000/m²/month, five times ambient intensity, and other cost of ₦5,200/m²: a 64% contribution margin, about 11 points above ambient, and 2.9× ambient revenue per m². But cold capex is roughly ₦2.4 m/m² against ₦706,000/m² ambient — 3.4× — so on capital employed the lead narrows to modest. Cold chain is the highest-margin and highest-lock-in segment, not automatically the highest-return one, and its risk is asymmetric: one unlogged excursion, one failed alarm test, one night without standby power, and the segment closes at the same moment in the regulator's file and the insurer's.

Year 1 is negative at EBITDA and is meant to be — a new warehouse takes 24–36 months to reach 75%. Verify before releasing capital: achieved rents in Apapa, Lekki and Onitsha; positions per m² actually let by three operators; cold tariffs paid by two pharma distributors; Nkpor power cost per m² over twelve months; cold-room build cost from three contractors.

8. Organisation

The first ten hires, in order. (1) Managing Director — has run a 3PL or multi-user warehouse P&L, not a property. (2) Warehouse Manager. (3) Operations Supervisor, inbound. (4) Operations Supervisor, outbound. (5) Quality & Compliance Manager — the GDP Responsible Person, and a Superintendent Pharmacist once pharmaceutical storage is registered, as NAFDAC requires. (6) Inventory Control & WMS Administrator — reports to the board, not operations. (7) Cold Chain Supervisor / Refrigeration Engineer — owns mapping, calibration and the excursion log. (8) Forklift and reach-truck operators (three) — licenced and certified. (9) Security & Loss Control Supervisor. (10) Maintenance & Facilities Technician — power, dock levellers, sprinklers, MHE. Hire the inventory controller before the first pallet: pilferage, phantom stock, a NAFDAC finding and a rejected insurance claim are all custody failures first.

11. Integration

Isiome Group. Stores Isiome Farms' and Isiome Foods' output — dry ambient positions for bagged and palletised goods, cold for chilled and frozen lines — at a published tariff. Boundary: Isiome Storage owns the bulk silo, the belt cold store and the warehouse receipt; this company owns the palletised racked space and the pharma cold chain.

Idenze Group — the highest-value integration in the plan. Stores Idenze Pharma and Idenze Therapeutics products: finished goods ambient and in validated cold, quarantine/released/rejected segregation as GDP requires, and controlled substances in the segregated alarmed two-key cage, coordinating with Uli Special Logistics, which holds the controlled-substance movement authorisations and is the only group entity permitted to move them. This company stores; Special Logistics moves; the paperwork must never blur the two.

Uli Freight. The warehouse is that business's largest lever on utilisation: it manufactures scheduled inbound and outbound legs on Corridor 1 and turns Lagos → Nkpor → Lagos from one paid leg into two. Uli Freight owns no warehouse and buys throughput here at a published tariff.

Okodu Group. Built by Okodu Construction at open-book cost-plus 6–8% rather than an external contractor's 12–18%, keeping steelwork and materials inside Okodu Materials. Powered by Okodu Power, solar-plus-storage as the base case so diesel is a fallback; the cold rooms are why the power contract matters more here than anywhere else in the Group.

Akunnia Group. Aku Capital arranges naira debt on tenors matched to contract duration, structures the Aku Infrastructure Fund I holding of the real estate with Uli Warehousing as anchor tenant, and supplies Aku Insurance for stock, bailee's liability and business interruption. The independent directors must review the intercompany tariff annually: an unbenchmarked internal rent lets this company look profitable while the freight business subsidises it.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — decide, price and title. (1) Appoint the Managing Director and the Quality & Compliance Manager (GDP Responsible Person). (2) Commission counsel opinions on three gates before any spend: the NCS bonded licensing conditions and bond quantum under the 2023 Act; whether NAFDAC and NDLEA will register this company as custodian of controlled stock or require Uli Special Logistics to hold it; and the Anambra planning and Governor's Consent position at Nkpor. (3) Run a rent and occupancy survey — achieved grade-A rents in Apapa, Lekki and Onitsha, positions per m² actually let by three operators, cold tariffs paid by two pharma distributors, Nkpor power cost per m² over twelve months — and re-base §7 before ordering steel. (4) Open the Akunnia funding conversation with the contracted-volume model, not an asset list.

Days 31–60 — contract and design. (5) Execute intercompany storage agreements with Isiome Foods, Idenze Pharma and Idenze Therapeutics at a published tariff, Group CFO-certified as arms-length and minuted by the independent directors; target 45% of Year-1 positions committed before ground-breaking. (6) Sign one external anchor 3PL contract of three years or more with minimum space and an indexation clause. (7) Freeze the racking plan and column grid, and issue the T1 works order to Okodu Construction on fixed price with liquidated damages, Okodu Power's package in parallel. (8) Tender racking, dock levellers, ESFR and MHE to three vendors each.

Days 61–90 — staff and licence. (9) Recruit the warehouse manager, two operations supervisors, cold chain engineer, WMS administrator, security supervisor and three MHE operators; begin NAFDAC premises registration and the customs bond conversation. (10) Stand up the WMS, custody separation and cycle-count discipline before the first pallet. (11) Publish the grade-A build standard as a board specification and require it of Okodu Construction in writing — a shed built to a shed standard is unrecoverable. (12) Day-90 board decision: release T1 only if the bonded-licence pathway is answered in writing, intercompany volume is contracted and one external anchor is signed. If not, lease 8,000 m² of existing Lagos grade-A space for a year and prove the operating model on someone else's building.

ULI PUBLISHING — Books, Formats & Adaptation Rights

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Uli Group the fourth child's group; companies take Uli plus a plain function (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative only at ₦1,600/USD held flat.

Ezeme Group · Uli Group · Entity Uli Publishing Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Uli Group Ltd · Horizon 15 yrs · Year 1 = 2027.

Companions: 28_Uli_Group.md, 33_Uli_Rights.md, 29_Uli_Film.md, 30_Uli_Music.md, 32_Uli_Broadcast.md, 26_Idenze_Schools.md, 25_Idenze_Polytechnic.md, 24_Idenze_University.md, 35_Uli_Freight.md, 36_Uli_Warehousing.md.

1. Thesis

Publishing is the cheapest and most portable form of intellectual property. A film costs hundreds of millions of naira and sells only where it is dubbed, classified and printed. A book costs a few million and sells in every territory at once at zero incremental cost.

It is the lowest-capital route to a rights catalogue. Copyright in a literary work runs 70 years after the author's death under s.19(1)(a), Copyright Act 2022 — longer than the 50 years for sound recordings or broadcasts (Act). One title is a long-dated, transferable asset bought for the price of a print run.

Adaptation is the prize. A trade title returns roughly ₦7m over its life; an adaptation licence to Uli Film returns ₦8m–₦25m for legal work and no print, and never comes back as stock. Publishing exists to manufacture the underlying right. The catalogue passes to Uli Rights and thence to Akunnia Capital.

Mandate. Pillar "Culture, Press, Broadcasting & Supply Chain"; foundation "storytelling, digital content creation"; bachelor's Global Communication Science (UvA). This is the creative industries — none of the political risk a news operation carries.

2. Market

UNESCO's first mapping put Africa's book industry at a projected US$18.5bn, on a continent holding 5.4% of global publishing revenue, importing US$597m of books and exporting US$81m, where 90% of countries have no book law beyond copyright and legal deposit. Educational publishing is ~70% of the market; religious publishing the other large block; trade the weak limb (UNESCO 2025; Hans Zell 2025). One bookshop serves 116,000 people, so formal retail is not the route to scale.

Education is the realistic entry. Nigeria's market is ₦300bn, with 200+ publishers and 60m+ learners (Guardian; NPA) — and Idenze Schools, Polytechnic and University are captive customers, an advantage no independent publisher has. Trade sells on consignment, bookshops taking 30–40% of cover and remitting only on sale; Cassava Republic was reported owed ₦15m (Black Tower; Publishing Perspectives).

Incumbents are losing money, which is the opening. Learn Africa and University Press together posted a projected Q1 2026 loss of ₦588m on ₦825m revenue. Nigeria spent ₦3.37trn on paper imports in 2021–25, ₦1.1trn in 2025 alone, importing 90–95% of white-grade paper, above US$5bn a year (Businessday). Print is a naira price against a dollar input — short runs, print-on-demand and digital-first are risk management, not fashion.

Igbo is genuinely underserved. Kawuriz and Manilas, an Onitsha house founded 1986, built its business on one primary Igbo text — Mbido Igbo, still selling ≥500,000 units annually (Daily Trust). The family's Ide/Igbo documentation work points at the same specialism: 30m+ speakers, mandatory in South-East schools, almost no modern trade or children's list. No multinational competes here. Audio and digital remain platform-led — a cheap incremental edition, not a market to bet on.

4. Operating model

Three lists, three jobs, one of them pays. Education pays — long runs, institutional demand, annual repeat. Igbo differentiates — the one list no competitor enters credibly. Trade manufactures the adaptation right — trade titles rarely justify their run; they exist because a novel is the raw material for a Uli Film option, and the option is worth more than the book.

Print to contract, never to hope. First runs sized to the captive order plus 30%; offset above 3,000 copies, digital below. Every title carries a written sell-through assumption and reprint trigger; no title is reprinted without a signed adoption or measured sell-through above 55%.

Commissioning is rights-first. No title is signed unless Uli Publishing takes volume, translation, audio and adaptation rights in writing — because s.30(3) is unambiguous: an assignment or exclusive licence "shall have no effect unless it is in writing." Royalties are 10% of net receipts, never cover price.

Returns discipline, decided in advance. No third-party consignment without a signed inventory form, account limit and 12-month sell-through-or-return clause; institutional sales are firm sale; shopworn stock is written off at once.

Production and custody. Every title is produced to EPUB and print-ready PDF at origination, so digital costs nothing later. Stock sits in humidity-controlled space at Uli Warehousing and moves on Uli Freight — books are ~350g, so 10,000 copies is a 3.5-tonne part-load, the cheapest freight in the Group.

The NERDC gate just changed and is now the decisive fact. From September 2026 only titles holding NERDC licensing and passing the new National Textbook Ranking System may be used in public primary and secondary schools; a 70% minimum score applies and only 6–10 titles per subject will be approved. Users of unapproved titles face blacklisting (Punch; Businessday); the NPA is litigating it (Guardian).

Fees are non-refundable even on failure: ₦1,500 per page plus ₦750,000 per title — ₦1,050,000 for a 200-page book before a copy is printed, and roughly ₦35.7m for a 34-subject programme (Bookartville). The NPA warns this "will create a monopoly for only the big 10 publishers." A capitalised, integrated entrant benefits from a policy its smaller competitors are suing over — but the plan must not assume it survives intact.

Photocopying, answered with the statute. s.23 permits educational reprographic copying for instruction but caps it at 5% of a work in three months; s.23(3) removes that exception where a licensing scheme exists, and s.23(4) voids terms restricting copying below the statutory allowance. So join Repronig and require institutional customers to hold a reprographic licence (IFRRO).

The licence is acquired, not waited for

The rule for this company is that the backlist is the asset, and the licence travels with the backlist. A licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business: Uli Publishing either obtains the licence or buys a company that already holds it — and in Nigerian publishing the second route is not merely faster, it is the only way to enter the school market at speed. The NERDC gate is non-refundable, scored, and capped at 6–10 titles per subject from September 2026 (§5), so a new publisher spends ₦1,050,000 a title before a copy is printed and has a 70% minimum score and a ranking committee between it and its first sale. A publisher that already holds ranked titles has already paid that cost, already passed that committee, and already sits on a captive adoption cycle. Buying it transfers the licence, the backlist, the ISBN prefix and the school and trade relationships — the four things that cannot be bought separately, and the reason §10 risk 7 already names "acquire existing Nigerian lists alongside commissioning."

What makes this the best-value acquisition in the creative platform, and what makes it dangerous. A small Nigerian publisher is cheap — the assets are paper, a backlist and relationships, and §2 records that the incumbents themselves are loss-making (Learn Africa and University Press posted a projected ₦588m Q1 2026 loss on ₦825m revenue). But paper is the trap §6 already flags: a publisher's balance sheet is mostly print, and if sell-through misses by twenty points the acquisition buys a warehouse of unsaleable stock that still occupies financed space. So the price must be struck on the ranked and adoption-backed titles plus the reprintable backlist, with inventory valued at realisable value and slow-moving stock written down or excluded, and returns liabilities and consignment obligations assumed only against a defined cap.

Ninety-day action, costed. Instruct counsel to identify ten to fifteen small and mid-size Nigerian educational and trade publishers with an active NERDC-ranking or adoption record, a clean deposit and ISBN history, and a backlist whose grants are in writing — and to put an indicative price on two. Budget ₦42m (~US$26,000): ₦15m NERDC written confirmation on whether ranking survives a change of control, which is the gate on which the whole route turns; ₦12m corporate, deposit, ISBN and rights-grant diligence on four targets, contract by contract under s.30(3); ₦9m inventory valuation — realisable value, slow-moving stock identified for write-down; ₦6m indicative pricing against adoption contracts and ranked titles. Run alongside the organic commissioning plan in §12, not instead of it: the acquisition replaces the approval queue, and the commissioning list replaces the backlist it does not buy.

Returns on unsold stock are publishing's most punishing metric. A trade title at ₦8,000 and 40% distributor margin realises ₦4,320 a copy; printing 3,000 costs ₦2.76m. Break-even is 639 copies — 21% sell-through.

One education adoption win dwarfs a decade of trade publishing. A nationally adopted title selling 40,000 copies over four years returns ₦105.3m against ₦19.7m of cost — ₦85.6m gross from one title. 8. Organisation

First ten hires. (1) Publisher/Managing Director — a commissioning publisher with a ranked textbook list behind them. (2) Commissioning Editor, Education — owns the curriculum programme and the NERDC process. (3) Commissioning Editor, Igbo & Trade. (4) Production Editor — schedules, origination cost, print specification. (5) Rights Manager — s.30(3) compliance, rights register, all licensing. (6) Head of Institutional Sales — Idenze and every other school, polytechnic and university. (7) Head of Trade Sales & Distribution — accounts, consignment discipline, return clauses. (8) Head of Marketing & Adoption Campaigns. (9) Financial Controller — inventory accounting, returns provision, title-level P&L. (10) Systems & Metadata Lead — ISBN/ISSN discipline, seconded with Aku Technology.

11. Integration

Sells to Idenze Schools, Idenze Polytechnic and Idenze University — the advantage no independent publisher has. Group institutions whose textbook needs are known in advance: Idenze Schools reaches ~1,700 pupils by Year 10, the Polytechnic 4,200 students at steady state, the University 2,400 students by Year 14. At roughly five titles per learner per year that is a presold first print run of several thousand units per title, and fixed cost amortised against committed demand. The honest limit: the captive base de-risks the first run and funds the curriculum programme; it is not the market. §10 caps captive volume at 35% of any title.

Licenses adaptation rights to Uli Film, Uli Broadcast and Uli Animation. Uli Film works a funnel of 40 concepts, 12 scripts, 8 green-lights, 6 delivered per cycle and has no in-house source of literary material. Uli Publishing is that source: every trade and Igbo title is commissioned with adaptation rights retained, and Uli Film's rule — clean chain of title, no defective option — is satisfied by the rights register from day one. Terms are option fee plus purchase price plus net-receipt royalty, at independent valuation approved by the independent directors sitting alone.

Licenses audio to Uli Music on advance-and-royalty, so no audio is produced speculatively. Feeds Uli Rights, and thence Akunnia Capital: adaptation contracts, rights register and metadata pass to Uli Rights for registration, valuation and reporting — the same pipeline the rest of the content platform uses, entered at the lowest cost per title.

Uses Uli Freight and Uli Warehousing. Print runs move as high-value part-loads — 3.5 tonnes, ~₦40–50 per copy over the Lagos–Nkpor corridor at the published tariff. Stock is held in humidity-controlled space at Uli Warehousing, which answers the oldest problem in Nigerian publishing: a book that survives storage is a book that can be reprinted. Aku Technology builds the title system; Okodu Power supplies press and warehouse; Idenze University graduates are the editorial and sales pipeline, with a paid editorial internship from Year 2.

Boundaries. Uli Publishing owns no press, newsroom, film production or rights-administration function. Uli Rights administers the catalogue; Uli Film adapts it; Uli Publishing only creates and licenses it.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30. (1) Incorporate Uli Publishing Ltd; constitute the board. (2) Appoint the Publisher and Rights Manager; deliverable one is the rights-grant template covering volume, translation, audio and adaptation, drafted against s.30(3). (3) Counsel opinions on the NERDC policy's status after the NPA litigation, Repronig and s.23(3), CBN routing of translation royalties, and NDPA. (4) Open ISBN issuance and legal deposit with the National Library and Copyright Commission registration. (5) Quote three Nigerian printers at 2,000/5,000/10,000/25,000 — the §7 curve is an assumption until these land.

Days 31–60. (6) Census the captive customer — every required title, class level, enrolment and academic year across Idenze Schools, Polytechnic and University; nobody else can produce this document. (7) Sign intercompany supply agreements at list less standard discount, arms-length certified and minuted by the independent directors. (8) Commission four educational titles against the census and two Igbo titles — a primary text and a children's reader, the proven Kawuriz pattern. (9) Recruit the two commissioning editors and Head of Institutional Sales. (10) Retain an adaptation rights adviser; open the conversation with Uli Film.

Days 61–90. (11) File the first NERDC assessment and ranking submissions at ₦1,050,000 a title, treated as non-refundable. (12) Appoint Uli Freight and Uli Warehousing under written terms. (13) Build the title and rights register with Aku Technology to the reporting standard Uli Rights and Akunnia Capital require. (14) Establish the related-party register, the captive-volume cap and monthly sell-through and returns reporting. (15) Day-90 board gate: release Tranche 1 only if the census supports a presold first run for each of the first four titles, printer quotes confirm the §7 curve within 15%, and the rights template is executed on two author agreements. If not, run Year 1 as a rights-and-co-edition business, buy no inventory, and re-test in twelve months.

ULI SPECIAL LOGISTICS — Licensed Controlled-Substance Logistics

Naming: Uli Special Logistics Ltd — a child's name plus a plain function (v5.0). See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md.

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative only at ₦1,600/USD held flat. Capital plan uses ₦1,500, spot ~₦1,328; the library needs one harmonising re-base pass, changing only the USD column.

Ezeme Group · Uli Group · Uli Special Logistics Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Uli Group Ltd · Horizon 15 yrs · Year 1 = 2027. Companions: 35_Uli_Freight.md, 36_Uli_Warehousing.md, 40_Uli_Fleet.md, 19_Idenze_Therapeutics.md, 18_Idenze_Pharma.md — separate companies and boards; interfaces only.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Nigerian narcotics, psychotropic substances, drug precursors and temperature-sensitive biologics move only under an authorisation issued per shipment to a named licensee — and because almost no Nigerian road carrier holds one, the operator that does, not the one that owns trucks, captures the margin on every consignment that must lawfully move.

The Group's freight plan already concedes this: it is "the single most defensible asset in the logistics platform" (35_Uli_Freight.md).

Why the licence, not the trucks. Trucks are quoted, financed and replaced in ninety days by anyone with a bank facility. An authorisation is non-transferable, revocable, tied to a named licensee and re-tested on every consignment — there is no standing permit. Capital cannot compress the years of premises vetting, personnel screening and documented custody practice that precede an award. The trucks take a quarter; the record takes conduct.

What is sold is not tonne-kilometres but an authorised movement with an unbroken chain of custody — a paper trail that survives inspection and an insurer's claim. Capital rule: every naira must raise the probability of a clean renewal and a clean audit, or it is adding wheels.

2. Market

Nigeria's pharmaceutical market is put at USD 3.34 bn in 2026, rising to USD 5.82 bn (Coherent Market Insights) — Africa's second-largest. Africa imports over 70% of its medicines and over 95% of its APIs (Gavi); NAFDAC put Nigerian import dependence near 60% in late 2025 and the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria above 70% (BusinessDay). Every imported controlled substance, API and biologic lands at a port and must reach an inland plant, wholesale node or hospital. The freight market carrying it was USD 10.95 bn in 2025 and 11.66 bn in 2026 (Research and Markets via GlobeNewswire), over 90% by road (InfraCredit).

Cold chain was forecast at USD ~130 m by 2026, attributed to imports including pharmaceuticals (Ken Research via TMCnet) — but that figure is old, contested and spans agri and pharma, so the pharma sub-segment must be sized from a shipper survey, not from it (§12). The requirement is not in doubt: insulins, oncology products, monoclonal antibodies, most vaccines and a growing share of biosimilars need 2–8 °C, some −20 °C or colder, and Nigeria's only reliable cold chain is the donor-funded public vaccine route.

Who moves these goods today, and how badly. No lawful carrier offers a documented, sealed, temperature-logged, declared-value custody service to a private importer or hospital group. The importer's own pickup has no logger, seal record or documented handover; informal hauliers offer the lowest rate and no lawful basis to move controlled goods at all, so the shipper carries the whole regulatory exposure; foreign 3PLs (DHL, Kuehne+Nagel, Maersk) hold Lagos and air capability but no depot outside Lagos.

Why so few hold the authorisations. The barrier is conduct, not fees. Authorisation is per shipment, so competence is re-examined on every consignment rather than once at application (NAFDAC NCS); NDLEA vets premises and personnel and polices precursor control through its Directorate of Chemical Monitoring and Forensic. One diversion ends the company: the 2018 codeine syrup episode became a regulatory shutdown — three plants closed (BBC, BBC) — and insurers withdraw after a single loss. A rational haulier therefore declines the segment, which is why it is under-supplied and the licence holder prices from strength, not cost.

Market-depth warning, stated plainly. The number of lawful controlled movements available in Nigeria per month is unknown and may not fill a dedicated fleet. §12 validates it rather than assuming it.

4. Operating model

Vehicles — a fixed specification. Purpose-built, never pooled or re-tasked: a locked, sealed tamper-evident compartment with an independent two-lock system whose keys are held by two named individuals who never travel together; door and compartment alarms reporting to the tower; dual GPS on independent power; no cab-side or external access to the compartment. Cold units add redundant refrigeration, an independent logger and an excursion alarm not defeatable from the cab.

Control tower. 24/7, staffed from a room physically separate from operations so monitoring cannot be silenced by commercial pressure. It holds the live route sheet, confirms two-person crew presence at dispatch and each checkpoint, and alarms on geofence deviation, unscheduled stop, seal break, door opening, GPS power loss and temperature excursion. It owns the escalation ladder — supervisor, Head of Operations, Accountable Officer, regulator — and logs every alarm whether or not it is later explained.

Crew vetting. Employed, never contracted, screened on identity verification, criminal and drug-related record checks, two traced guarantors, prior-employer references and a financial-vulnerability assessment — unexplained debt is the strongest known predictor of a crew member accepting money to look away. Crews rotate so no pair becomes fixed, and no driver ever handles cash.

Route planning and pre-clearance. A written route sheet agreed before dispatch: named origin and destination, authorised waypoints only, designated secure rest and fuelling points, pre-notified arrival times to consignee and receiving authority. No ad-hoc stops, no third-party pickup, no unauthorised passengers, no route change without recorded authorisation. An unplanned diversion is treated as a possible diversion of cargo until proven otherwise.

Handover and reconciliation. At every transfer: seal number recorded at loading and re-verified at each seal break; photograph and weight reconciliation against the manifest; receiving officer's identity, signature and timestamp. Any discrepancy — including an overage — is escalated to the regulator within 24 hours, reported even where the material is later found; records are held for the regulator's period, assumed not less than five years and to be confirmed with NAFDAC and NDLEA in writing.

Contingency, disposal and returns. On breakdown: secure the vehicle, transfer cargo to no third party, notify the tower, dispatch the company's own replacement unit and crew. Robbery, suspected diversion, seizure and temperature excursion each carry a written protocol with a named decision-maker — the first hour after an incident is when the licence is protected or lost. Controlled stock cannot simply be written off: returns are quarantined and reconciled, and destruction happens only under witnessed procedure with a destruction certificate.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Every shipment requires its own authorisation. There is no standing permit. Import and export authorisations are exchanged between national competent authorities, quantities matched to the national estimates reported to INCB under the 1961 Single Convention (INCB). That makes the constraint a calendar, not a transaction cost: with no line in the estimate for that material in that quantity, the shipment cannot lawfully move this year and no commercial workaround exists. The company's job is to run a twelve-month estimate calendar and tell a customer in January that their August shipment cannot move. ECOWAS free movement does not waive narcotics control: a controlled consignment crossing a border needs ISRT documents and a transit authorisation from that state.

Realistic sequence. M0–4: incorporate, appoint the Accountable Officer, obtain written regulator guidance on the gating question. M3–9: NAFDAC NCS premises registration. M4–10: NDLEA premises and personnel vetting. M6–12: insurance bound before the first load; crew vetting and custody SOPs complete; first per-shipment authorisation executed on captive volume. Years 2–5: routine operation, first external clients, first inspection closed clean, then ECOWAS transit authorisations.

The gating question — do not proceed past it. The published NAFDAC NCS instruments are framed around permits to clear and to import: they address an importer or manufacturer, not expressly a third-party carrier holding custody between two licensed premises. Whether NAFDAC and NDLEA will authorise this company as the custodial carrier on a controlled movement — as against requiring the importer or licensed manufacturer to hold the authorisation and merely engage a vetted carrier — is not established by the material available to this plan and must be confirmed in writing before any vehicle is ordered. If the answer is no, the lawful role narrows to vetted carriage under the licensee's authorisation and the plan re-cuts around documentation, warehousing and cold chain.

Also requiring confirmation, not assumption: the records-retention period; whether foreign GMP certification supports a Nigerian import authorisation; the risk band of each target material under the 30 July 2024 guideline; the per-shipment documentary set; and fees and timelines for each transit authorisation.

The licence is acquired, not waited for — and here the honest answer is that it cannot be bought

The Group's rule is that a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business: the Group either obtains the licence or buys a company that already holds it. This is the one company in the Group where the second half of that rule does not hold, and the plan states it plainly rather than inventing a market that does not exist.

The NDLEA and NAFDAC NCS authorisations are not an asset that can change hands. Four reasons, each established in this plan already:

  1. There is no standing permit to transfer. Authorisation is per shipment to a named licensee, and §1 puts it exactly right: "non-transferable, revocable, tied to a named licensee and re-tested on every consignment." A vendor has nothing to sell between shipments — its only asset is a permission that must be re-earned by the buyer on the buyer's own next consignment.
  2. The record being tested is a record of conduct, not a certificate. NAFDAC NCS premises registration and NDLEA premises and personnel vetting are granted against these premises and these named people (§5, realistic sequence M3–10). Buying the entity does not buy the vetting of its crew, its keyholders, its Accountable Officer or its cage — and the people who carry that record can resign the week after completion.
  3. The licence is revocable and cannot be collateral. §6 is explicit: "a revocable, non-transferable licence is not collateral and no lender will advance against one." A purchase financed on the strength of the target's licence would be financed on an asset no lender will lend against.
  4. A change of control is the event most likely to trigger re-examination, not the event that evades it — and the 2018 codeine episode shows the regulator's response to a compliance failure is shutdown, not transfer (§2). Worse, this market is adversely selected: a controlled-substance carrier that is for sale is usually one whose compliance record has already weakened, which is precisely when the licence stops being worth buying.

What can legitimately be acquired, and is worth one written question rather than a budget line. Two narrow possibilities exist and neither substitutes for the Group's own record. First, a share purchase of an existing authorised operator would carry the premises registration, the SOP set and the vetting-cleared personnel as a going concern — but whether NAFDAC and NDLEA treat that as a continuation or as a fresh application is unknown, and this plan does not assume it. ⚠️ [verify] in writing, at the same time as the gating question in §5. Second, where the authorisation must sit with the importer or manufacturer — the likely answer to the gating question — the correct acquisition is not of a carrier's licence but of the position that the licence holder be a Group company, and that position already exists: 18_Idenze_Pharma.md and 19_Idenze_Therapeutics.md hold their own NAFDAC registrations. That is the route to build on.

What the Group does instead — three routes, in order.

  1. Build the record on captive volume, and start now. The plan's own M0–4 sequence already opens the licence pathway before any vehicle is discussed, and §12 item 13 is explicit: "run the licence pathway anyway, since the regulatory clock costs legal fees, not capital." The Group's captive Idenze volume is the record on which its own authorisation is earned — that is the asset, and it is built, not bought.
  2. Contract for, or partner with, an existing authorised operator — but only in the shape this plan's rules permit. §3 forbids the company from acting as an unlicensed carrier on a controlled leg, and §11 forbids sharing a vehicle pool, manifests or crew with Uli Freight. So partnership cannot mean the company carrying controlled cargo under someone else's licence. It means supplying what does not require the licence to a licensee that holds it: separately licensed controlled warehousing (§3), the estimate calendar and regulatory documentation service (§3, 8% of revenue), cold chain, control-tower discipline and security. Uli Special Logistics sells the custody capability to an authorised operator while it earns its own authority — revenue in Year 1, and a regulator-visible compliance record at the same time.
  3. Acquire capability, not permissions. Senior Accountable Officer and regulatory documentation staff recruited from existing authorised operators; a GDP-certified storage operator or validated cold-chain facility; pre-underwritten insurance; and staff with corridor-3 transit experience. The trucks, the cage and the tower follow the record — never the reverse, which is the whole of §1.

Ninety-day action, costed. Extend §12 items 3 and 4 rather than adding a parallel workstream. Instruct counsel to put three written questions to the regulators in one filing: (a) the gating question — can a third-party custodial carrier hold the authorisation; (b) the acquisition question — whether a change of control of an existing authorised operator continues or restarts its premises registration and vetting; and (c) the retention period and the per-shipment documentary set. Budget ₦38m (~US$24,000): ₦15m the consolidated regulator filing and counsel opinion; ₦12m a capability survey — the population of authorised operators, their premises registrations and transit experience, and an indicative cost of recruiting an Accountable Officer and a vetted crew from among them; ₦6m pre-underwriting with two insurers; ₦5m GDP-certified storage and validated cold-chain acquisition screen, which is the one acquisition this plan does recommend. No vehicle, cage or strong room is ordered against any of it. A licence in search of trucks is a manageable position; a Group that has bought a licence it cannot lawfully use is not.

6. Capital requirement

Land and the warehouse shell are contributed by the Group at cost and charged in the model. This is capital-light relative to ordinary freight — six highly specified vehicles carry more revenue than twenty ordinary trucks (§7) — and the capital that matters is regulatory, security and cold chain, not wheels.

7. Unit economics

The unit of sale is the authorised movement, not the tonne-kilometre. Ordinary dedicated full-truckload on Lagos → Nkpor (450 km, 25 t) prices at about ₦1.05 m, at ₦48 cost / ₦93 revenue per tonne-km (35_Uli_Freight.md, §7). A controlled movement on the same lane carries perhaps 500 kg — one-fiftieth the payload — and is modelled at ₦4.0 m: a 4× premium on the same vehicle-lane, and over two orders of magnitude per tonne-km. Price is set by the custody obligation, and the tonne-km is the wrong unit to sell in.

Revenue density is the real prize: a controlled unit earns roughly three times an ordinary Group unit on a fraction of the payload, because the licence and the custody record are what is invoiced.

Break-even utilisation. Year 1 fixed and semi-fixed cost is ₦1,095 m — management and compliance 118, 24/7 control tower 78, warehouse and security infrastructure 290, insurance programme 215, regulatory, legal, audit and inspection 165, telematics and software 95, Okodu Power electricity 42, finance, admin and training 92. At a blended contribution of ₦1.51 m per billable movement, break-even is 60 billable movements a month against installed long-haul capacity of 48 from six vehicles.

So Year 1 cannot break even on long-haul work alone, and this plan does not pretend otherwise. It carries a deliberate Year 1 EBITDA loss of roughly ₦50 m and reaches break-even in Year 2 on two routes: short-cycle captive movements — intra-Nkpor plant-to-suite-to-distribution runs and Onitsha/Enugu deliveries cycling several times a week on one vehicle — and warehousing and documentation revenue, which carries near-zero marginal cost. Year 1 revenue is 300 long-haul movements (₦1.20 bn), 900 short-cycle movements (₦0.81 bn), warehousing (₦95 m) and documentation (₦70 m) — ₦2.18 bn. Break-even utilisation of the long-haul fleet is 80%; below it, the company is paying for a licence it is not using.

8. Organisation

The compliance and controlled-substance accountable officer is the most important role in the company and is structurally independent of operations. The Accountable Officer reports to the board, not the Managing Director; owns the licence register (instrument, holder, conditions, expiry, renewal lead time, named owner) and the controlled-substances register (units in, out, waste, variance, escalation); is the named person on the NAFDAC file; holds a direct line to the Group Audit & Risk Committee; and may halt any shipment without commercial approval and cannot be overruled by the Managing Director. It is a pharmacist or lawyer with controlled-substances experience and is never combined with an operations or commercial title — the moment it is, the control it exists to provide is gone. Security follows the same rule.

Two exposures are carried explicitly. Market depth — fewer lawful movements than modelled leaves the fleet under-utilised; mitigated by validating the count in the first ninety days and treating captive Idenze volume as the floor. FX on specialised vehicles — dollar-linked assets against naira revenue; mitigated by naira facilities with FX priced at order and no unhedged USD debt.

11. Integration

Idenze Therapeutics (anchor). Structurally necessary, not merely useful: the South Africa → Nigeria API lane and the Nkpor controlled suite's inbound and outbound movements are the volume that makes the licence worth obtaining. Without them it is uneconomic at Year 1 scale. Uli Special Logistics executes the import handling, transit segments, unit-level custody record and intra-campus movements between the controlled suite and the distribution node.

Idenze Pharma. Moves imported APIs from port to the Nkpor plant with per-shipment documentation and temperature control, and finished goods onward to Idenze Distribution — under an arms-length carriage contract at published tariffs, so both companies' unit costs are honest and the related-party pricing survives independent-director review. Idenze Distribution receives movements at licensed wholesale premises: Uli Special Logistics does the licensed movement, Idenze Distribution the licensed sale, and neither holds the other's authorisation.

Uli Freight and Uli Warehousing. Uli Freight carries ordinary linehaul and may never carry a controlled consignment; the two share no vehicle pool, manifests, control tower or crew, and an unlicensed segment may be subcontracted to Uli Freight but never the reverse. Uli Warehousing provides compliant storage, but the controlled cage and strong room are separately licensed, separately access-controlled and separately alarmed within it, with their own inventory and audit.

Okodu Power and Akunnia Capital. Okodu Power supplies captive power — not a cost decision, since CCTV, alarms, dual GPS and refrigeration cannot depend on an intermittently available grid: a monitoring blackout is an uncontrolled custody gap. Akunnia Capital arranges financing, specialist insurance through Aku Insurance, treasury and the FX policy, and builds the controlled-substance inventory accounting discipline. Aku Advisory may not audit this company.

Boundaries. Uli Special Logistics owns its licences, vehicles, crew and custody record, and buys power, storage, insurance, financing and ordinary linehaul from other Group companies at published, board-approved, arms-length prices. The licence outranks the synergy — where a Group supplier cannot meet the security or documentation standard, the work goes outside and the decision is minuted.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — decide and secure. (1) Incorporate Uli Special Logistics Ltd with reserved matters and a Family Director in the Articles. (2) Appoint the Managing Director and the Compliance and Accountable Officer — before any vehicle is discussed. (3) Commission counsel opinions on the gating question: whether NAFDAC and NDLEA will authorise this company as the custodial carrier, or require the importer or licensed manufacturer to hold the authorisation. (4) Obtain written guidance on the per-shipment documentary set, the retention period, and the risk band of each target material. (5) Open the licence register and the controlled-substances register on day one, empty.

Days 31–60 — validate, do not assume. (6) Validate market depth: estimate lawful controlled movements available per month from importer and manufacturer lists, NAFDAC permit issuance patterns and hospital-group procurement — then re-base §7 before ordering anything. (7) Open pre-underwriting with two insurers on specialist controlled-cargo cover; unwillingness to write it is a stop-ship condition. (8) Sign intercompany carriage agreements with Idenze Therapeutics and Idenze Pharma at published tariffs, certified arms-length by the Group CFO. (9) Design the warehouse and security specification and obtain a fixed-price quotation from Okodu Construction.

Days 61–90 — build controls, then the fleet. (10) File the NAFDAC NCS premises registration; begin NDLEA premises and personnel vetting; open crew screening with traced guarantors. (11) Tender the first six units to controlled specification and stand up control-tower design and telematics with Uli Fleet — the tower physically separate from operations. (12) Table for board approval the custody SOP set: route pre-clearance, handover and reconciliation, alarm escalation, incident response, disposal and returns. (13) Day-90 board gate — release capital only if all three hold: NAFDAC has confirmed in writing that a third-party carrier can hold the authorisation; an insurer will write the cover; and contracted captive volume covers 70% of Year 1 fixed cost. If any fails, do not buy vehicles — run the licence pathway anyway, since the regulatory clock costs legal fees, not capital. A licence in search of trucks is a manageable position. Trucks in search of a licence is not.

Ring-fencing

Uli Special Logistics must sit in its own company with its own board and its own audit. At least two independent directors; its own bank accounts, insurer, licence register, controlled-substances register, incident register and named Accountable Officer. Its audit is a separate engagement reporting to its own board and the Group Audit & Risk Committee — never absorbed into the Group audit, because an auditor reviewing the parent's related-party contracts should not also be the control testing this company's custody records.

There are no cross-guarantees to the university, the hospital, or any other Group entity, in either direction. This company does not guarantee a Group borrowing and no Group company guarantees its obligations. The Group must never present this licence as a Group-wide credential, nor a Group balance sheet as backing for it. It shares no vehicle pool, manifests, control tower, crew or customer data with Uli Freight beyond a priced carriage contract for unlicensed segments.

Why, stated plainly. A licensing failure, a diversion event or a regulatory seizure here must never reach Idenze University's NUC accreditation, the teaching hospital's licence, Idenze Pharma's and Idenze Therapeutics's NAFDAC registrations, the Group's banking covenants or any future fundraising. This is the company where that matters most, because it handles material that cannot be replaced by an insurance cheque and cannot be written off if it goes missing. If the ring-fence is ever relaxed for administrative convenience, the correct response is to restore it, not to explain it.

Prepared for the Uli Group board and the Ezeme Group Board. Regulatory instruments and market figures are sourced and linked; operating, capital and unit-economics figures are planning estimates at ₦1,600/USD requiring local verification before capital is committed. The material regulatory question in §5 — whether a third-party custodial carrier can hold the authorisation — is not resolved by this plan and must be answered in writing by NAFDAC and NDLEA before the fleet gate opens. Ezeme Group · Uli Group · Uli Cinemas Ltd (CAMA) · Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Uli Group → Uli Cinemas · Horizon 15 yrs · Year 1 = 2027. Companions: 29_Uli_Film.md, 36_Uli_Warehousing.md, 42_Okodu_Power.md, 45_Okodu_Construction.md, 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md.

1. Thesis

Exhibition is the physical distribution monopoly of the content value chain. Where a cinema operates it captures the first and highest-margin window of every release — price highest, no substitute, and no distributor reaches the audience without the exhibitor's building. The monopoly is local, temporary, renewed release by release.

It is a property business attached to a content business. Tickets are the traffic; concessions and advertising are where the margin sits. Film rental is a pass-through of roughly half of gross box office at zero margin; concessions carry ~70% gross margin, advertising ~90%. Managing a cinema as a ticket business means managing the wrong half of the revenue.

It also gives the Group what no Nigerian content company has: a guaranteed first window for its own films — 1.12× across a title's life inside the Group against 0.61× standalone (29_Uli_Film.md) — which materially improves the risk profile of Uli Film's slate.

Nigeria has 122 cinemas and 369 screens for over 230 million people, no national chain trades in Anambra, and every naira of the Onitsha first window is unearned.

2. Market

  • Small and growing fast. Anglophone West Africa grossed ₦15.6bn in 2025 on 2.79m admissions, up 34.7% on ₦11.58bn, at a ₦5,596 average ticket; Nigeria's share ₦14.52bn, projected ₦20bn in 2026. Nollywood took 49.4%, ahead of Hollywood's 48.8% (Nairametrics; BusinessDay).
  • Against the population, the story is absence. ₦15.6bn is $9.75m — under one mid-budget Hollywood release. 2.79m admissions among 230m people is one ticket per eighty-five people a year; only 81 Nigerian titles reached a cinema against ~2,000 produced (The Cable). Cinema here is not a distribution channel but a premium boutique at the top of one.
  • Concentration is extreme. Lagos holds 41 of 118 locations and took ₦7.94bn of ₦14.52bn — over half the box office on 45% of tickets, because Lagos prices higher; FCT ₦1.14bn from five sites, Rivers ₦1.03bn from eight. The top ten states are 88.5% of revenue; fifteen states have no modern cinema and the North-East has none (Economy Post). Anambra is among them — six million people on West Africa's largest inland market at Onitsha, and no chain listed there (Nairametrics). First-mover advantage here is not being first; it is being the only.
  • Competition consolidates and mall-anchors. Filmhouse Group (Filmhouse + FilmOne) leads at 12 sites, ₦4.07bn, 26% of revenue; Genesis 12 locations, 47 screens, ₦3.01bn; Silverbird 65 screens in three countries. Viva was built by Persianas, a mall developer, as a traffic driver for retail — the correct way to read this business.
  • Streaming has not taken the occasion. Box office doubled from ₦7.36bn in 2023 to ₦15.6bn in 2025 while Netflix Nigeria sits near 300,000 subscribers and MultiChoice Nigeria's subscription revenue fell 44% to $197.7m (BETAR).

Priced to Anambra incomes, not Lagos. Blended ticket ₦4,200, below the ₦5,596 regional average — the objective is volume and concession attach, not ticket yield. A midweek value day and student pricing on an Idenze ID hold weekday occupancy up.

Concessions are the business. At ₦1,200 per head against a ₦4,200 ticket — a 29% attach against a 45–60% international norm — the line earns ₦105.8m of revenue and ₦74m of gross profit on a mature six-screen site, against the film share's ₦185m at zero incremental margin. Per-capita spend is the metric this company is run on.

Advertising is the highest-margin, most neglected line. Pre-roll reaches a captive seated audience for fifteen minutes before every session; lobby screens and naming rights monetise the dwell around it. 32_Uli_Broadcast.md already owns the salesforce and agency relationships. Alternative content fills what films cannot — weekday mornings are dead under any slate, and no film rental is payable on a hire, so a dry hire carries the highest margin in the building.

Site selection is the investment decision. A mall anchor gives shared footfall and common-area load and fit-out-only capital, at the cost of mall hours, mall rules and escalating rent. Standalone gives control of hours, formats and events and ownership of the asset, but bears 100% of power, land, building, parking and security. Do both, in this order: lease the first site (4 screens, 600 seats, Onitsha retail, ₦1.4bn, no land risk), then purpose-build the flagship on Group land in Tranche 2 once a trading record exists. 4,000 m² of raked-floor auditorium where no cinema has ever traded is not bold; it is unpriced. Parking is not optional: Anambra planning will require it, and a venue without secure parking loses the family audience after dark.

4. Operating model

Format: five standard screens plus one premium. Standard rooms of 150 seats, matching Genesis's proven 130-seat auditorium; the premium screen justifies ₦8,000–9,000 tickets, captures the Lagos premium without Lagos pricing, and is the only format a phone cannot replace.

Power is the second decision after the site, because it can consume the entire exhibitor margin. A six-screen site draws ~110 kW average over a 12-hour day — 462,000 kWh a year. At Okodu Power's indicative C&I tariff of ₦230–280/kWh that is ₦106–129m, above the film share; at the diesel alternative of ₦780/kWh all-in it is ₦360m — the site's entire revenue (42_Okodu_Power.md). Design is solar-first: 200 kWp PV, 300 kWh battery, two 250 kVA gensets on a critical circuit, built by Okodu Power and Okodu Solar, buying from Okodu Power wherever available on an indexed tariff — not sustainability positioning, but the difference between a viable site and an unviable one.

Bookings are centralised from the first site — one manager negotiating release dates, holdovers and week-by-week rental schedules — and sessions are scheduled against historic per-session demand, not habit. A multiplex running four full-price evening shows with dark weekday afternoons gives away the concession revenue that pays its rent.
