NFVCB fees are from the 2025 Scale of Charges, paid only via the RevOP portal; renewals cost 20% of the new fee before expiry, 50% after (NFVCB licensing) — confirm the current scale in writing before filing.

The exhibitor's copyright liability is personal and is this company's sharpest legal exposure. The Copyright Act 2022 gives the owner of an audiovisual work the exclusive right to "cause the audiovisual work… to be seen in public and of sounds to be heard in public", and makes it an infringement to "permit a place of public entertainment or of business to be used for a public performance" that infringes, with a defence only where the person "was not aware and had no reasonable ground to suspect" it (Copyright Act 2022); the Commission has separately advised businesses to licence rather than rely on a supplier's assurance (NCC advisory). Rule: no written exhibition licence, no session — every title carries a signed licence naming territory, term, screens and rental terms, because "the distributor had the rights" is not a defence but the fact pattern of the offence. Lobby music needs COSON/MCSN licences; relayed sport carries its own rights.

Boundaries. This company exhibits; it does not distribute (34_Uli_Distribution) or clear rights (33_Uli_Rights). Uli Film titles are licensed through Uli Distribution at arms-length terms minuted by the independent directors.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

A licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business: Uli Cinemas either obtains the licence or buys a company that already holds it. Here the licence is cheap and the site is the constraint — and because the sector's economics punish a new build, buying an existing cinema is the stronger route for everything except the Anambra first-mover case.

The NFVCB instrument is not the barrier. The National Exhibitor Licence is ₦5,000,000 with ₦5,000,000 minimum capital, premises licences run ₦150,000–₦250,000 per hall per year, and renewals cost 20% of the new fee before expiry and 50% after (NFVCB licensing) — modest against a ₦1.4bn lease fit-out or a ₦3.6bn flagship. What a purchase actually transfers is the trading record, the site, the screens, the projection and sound inventory, the trained staff and the distributor relationships — and in this business the trading record is the gate: §7 shows full-cost break-even needs ~16.6% occupancy and no Nigerian cinema has sustained that, §9 gates the flagship on 6% occupancy at site one, and a new site takes years to earn a booking position with three distributors who allocate screens by track record. An acquisition delivers that record on day one, and a distressed or undercapitalised site can often be bought below the replacement cost of its own fit-out.

Two honest limits, stated before the table.

  • There is no Anambra cinema to buy. §2's finding is that fifteen states have no modern cinema, and Anambra is among them — "first-mover advantage here is not being first; it is being the only." So the first Anambra site must be built or leased, and the acquisition route applies to the chain beyond it: the South-East cluster (T3) and the national chain (T4–T5) where a licensed, trading operator is the faster route to screens than a site-by-site build.
  • The Akuzo finding is a site constraint that no acquisition cures. 50_Akuzo_Development.md makes the Akuzo Residential District exclusively residential, with no commercial activity. No licence, purchase or change of control puts a cinema inside that district — the company sits in Group commercial property or adjacent to Akuzo (§11). Any target site is diligenced against its own zoning, and a purchased premises in an incompatible district is an uninsurable enforcement risk, not an asset.

The pricing discipline, and it is the same one the plan already applies to construction. §6 warns that a 20% building overrun is ₦360m — four years of site EBITDA. An acquisition has the mirror-image risk: paying more than the fit-out's replacement cost for a site whose lease, occupancy or zoning is impaired. So the price is struck on screens and fit-out at depreciated replacement cost, plus the assignable lease at its remaining term, plus the occupancy record — and the licence is not a line in the valuation at all, because it is ₦5m and a month. Where a site is bought cheaply, the correct explanation is that its occupancy, its lease or its location is broken, and the first diligence question is which of the three.

Ninety-day action, costed. Instruct counsel and an exhibition adviser to enumerate the trading cinema estate — 122 cinemas across 118 locations, of which only 41 are in Lagos (§2) — and screen for operators that are undercapitalised, in administration, or holding sites the owner would sell, with current NFVCB exhibitor and premises licences, an assignable lease, and a clean planning and fire record; the priority footprint is the South-East and South-South, where §2 records the absence. Budget ₦55m (~US$34,000): ₦18m corporate, lease and NFVCB licence-status diligence on six targets, including renewal standing and any subsisting sanction; ₦15m a screens, projection, sound and fit-out condition survey on three, valued at depreciated replacement cost against §6's ₦450,000/m² and ₦645m equipment figures; ₦12m occupancy verification — actual admissions by session, day-of-week and screen, not management accounts — because §7's whole model turns on occupancy and the number cannot be taken on trust; ₦10m planning, zoning and fire diligence, confirming that no target site sits in an exclusively residential district of the Akuzo type. Run alongside the T1 lease-first plan: the Onitsha site is still built or leased, but T3 and T4 do not have to be.

Second, 40% gearing is a ceiling, not a plan: at these yields and Nigerian lending rates, debt at 40% of capital consumes most of net operating income in interest. The asset is built by a company and owned by a fund; conflating the two is what makes real estate expensive in Nigeria.

Break-even is 45,190 admissions a year — 3.6% seat occupancy on cash operating cost. That is the good news and the trap: the industry-average screen runs at ~2.7%, so break-even sits only marginally above the national average while everything promised here depends on running two to three times it. At 4% the site loses money, at 5% it returns nothing on capital, at 7% it is a respectable operating business. On a full-cost basis the purpose-built site needs ~16.6% occupancy to clear a 15% unlevered return — 2.4× the base case — and no Nigerian cinema has sustained that. That is why Tranche 1 is lease-first, and why the flagship must be a fund asset funded on property economics rather than an operating asset funded on admission economics. Verify before releasing capital: Onitsha shell rents and service charges; concession spend per head at two Nigerian multiplexes; advertising rates actually paid; the rental schedules above; competitor intentions in Onitsha, Awka and Enugu.

11. Integration

  • Uli Film — the most valuable line here. Inside the Group the exhibitor margin, the distribution fee and the broadcast window are retained: 1.12× across a title's life against 0.61× standalone. The gift is not margin but certainty of release — a green-light decision no longer waits on a distributor's willingness to book a Nigerian title onto a screen it does not control, and that is what materially improves the slate's risk profile. Titles licensed through 34_Uli_Distribution.
  • Uli Animation — the highest-margin content category and the best fit for family and holiday programming, where weekday capacity sits. Uli Broadcast sells on-screen and lobby advertising on the Group's existing rate card, avoiding a cinema-only sales team. Uli Distribution supplies per-session occupancy data by title, daypart, screen and price tier — the Group's proprietary demand dataset, which turns booking from negotiation into calculation and improves 33_Uli_Rights' catalogue valuation.
  • Okodu Construction builds the flagship at open-book cost-plus 6–8% against an external 12–18%, with materials from Okodu Materials: the largest single lever on the payback. Okodu Power and Okodu Solar power it, solar and BESS as base case — on these numbers the shift off diesel is not a saving but the difference between a viable site and an unviable one.
  • Okodu Real Estate and Akunnia Group hold the flagship land and building; Aku Infrastructure Fund I warehouses the asset with Uli Cinemas as anchor tenant and lessee, exactly the long-dated, inflation-linked naira cash flow Aku's mandates are built to hold. Boundary note: 50_Akuzo_Development.md makes the Akuzo Residential District exclusively residential with no commercial activity — this company sits in the Group's commercial property or adjacent to Akuzo, not inside it.
  • Idenze University and Polytechnic supply graduates and interns as ushers, concession staff and projection technicians; auditoriums double as teaching and screening rooms off-peak. Akunnia Group supplies naira debt matched to lease tenor (Aku Capital), liability and equipment cover (Aku Insurance) and ticketing analytics (Aku Technology).

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30. Appoint the Cinema General Manager and Head of Group Exhibition. Commission the Anambra cinema market survey before any spend — Onitsha and Nkpor footfall, mall shells above 2,000 m², land values and title at Nkpor, and written confirmation that no national chain has a committed Anambra site. Open the NFVCB pathway in person: exhibitor and premises licence requirements, and classification lead time for a launch slate. Commission counsel opinions on the Anambra planning, access and fire certificate position, and on Copyright Act 2022 exposure.

Days 31–60. Secure the T1 mall shell on anchor-tenant terms of ten years or more with turnover-rent cap, cinema-use exclusivity and landlord power obligations. Obtain actual film-rental schedules, holdover terms and minimum-screening commitments in writing from three distributors — FilmOne, Genesis Film Distribution, Nile. Freeze the auditorium, concessions and format design. Issue the T1 fit-out works order to Okodu Construction on fixed price with liquidated damages, with the Okodu Power solar and BESS package tendered in parallel.

Days 61–90. Recruit the Chief Projectionist, Concessions Manager, Bookings Manager, Finance and Controls Officer and Facilities Engineer. Stand up the ticketing platform, electronic-payment-only policy and daily reconciliation before the first ticket is sold. Sign the intercompany exhibition licences with Uli Film and Uli Distribution at published arms-length terms, Group CFO-certified and minuted by the independent directors. Day-90 board gate: release T1 only if the lease is executed, the NFVCB licences are on foot, the rental schedules are in writing, and the fixed-price Okodu contract is signed. Otherwise do not build — the Onitsha first window will still be unclaimed in six months, but a cinema built on an unpriced lease is a twenty-year problem.

Prepared for the Uli Group board and the Ezeme Group Board. Market figures are sourced; operating, capital and occupancy figures are planning estimates at ₦1,600/USD requiring local verification against a current Anambra market survey, achieved film-rental schedules and firm construction quotations before capital is committed. 40 — ULI FLEET

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Uli Group is her group; each company takes Uli plus a plain function (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md v5.0). FX: naira primary; dollars indicative only at ₦1,600/USD.

Ezeme Group · Uli Group · Entity Uli Fleet Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Uli Group Ltd · Horizon 15 yrs · Year 1 = 2027.

Companions: 35_Uli_Freight.md, 36_Uli_Warehousing.md, 38_Uli_Special_Logistics.md — separate companies and boards. Numbering note: an earlier revision of this page claimed plan 35's citation of 40_Uli_Fleet.md was wrong. It is correct. Uli Fleet is plan 40 and Uli Publishing is plan 37; the note was the error and has been removed.

1. Thesis

Uli Fleet is not a haulage company and does not sell transport. It owns the vehicles, maintains and instruments them, employs and manages the drivers, and answers for uptime and cost per kilometre.

The boundary: Uli Freight sells and schedules transport; Uli Fleet owns, maintains, and instruments the vehicles and manages the drivers. Where ownership sits on the balance sheet is the line between them.

Capital rule: every naira must raise uptime, utilisation or residual value. The captive base load must be signed before any truck is ordered.

2. Market

  • USD 10.95 bn (2025), 11.66 bn (2026), 15.97 bn by 2031 — 6.49% CAGR (Research and Markets, Jan 2026); over 90% moves by road (InfraCredit, 2026). Sized only by operator survey.
  • Nothing here is priced as an asset; almost no operator knows their own cost per kilometre. Diesel is over 35% of trucking expense: ₦1,361.57/litre (NBS, Jan 2026) → ~₦1,825/litre (Sept 2026), modelled at ₦1,800–1,850 (GlobalPetrolPrices). Union levies are systemic (Nairametrics, 2026).
  • Three markets. Leasing runs ₦2.4–2.8 m per artic per month and telematics costs ₦70,000–200,000 per vehicle in year one, renewing at ₦15,000–45,000, with fuel monitoring ₦250,000–800,000 (Car Tracker Nigeria, 2026; CTN, 2026). Maintenance, fuel control and driver management are priced by nobody — that is the business.

3. Product & service lines

  • Owned fleet leasing (78% of Year 1 revenue) — bare hire to Uli Freight; dedicated units to Uli Special Logistics and Uli Warehousing. Then driver management (8%), telematics and fleet data (5%), workshop and maintenance (6%), fleet engineering (2%) and disposal (1%).
  • Not sold: freight sales, pricing, scheduling or dispatch (Uli Freight); warehousing (Uli Warehousing); controlled-substance carriage (Uli Special Logistics). Fleet never quotes a shipper a rate.
  • Composition. Fleet owns the units Freight schedules — 19 in Year 1 to 380 by Year 10 across artic, rigid, light-van, reefer and project/low-bed classes (35_Uli_Freight.md §4).
  • Controlled-substance units. Plan 38 ring-fences the licence and has Uli Special Logistics owning "its vehicles, crew and custody record", sharing "no vehicle pool" with Uli Freight. Uli Special Logistics is a separate company with its own board. Fleet owns these units and leases them on bare hire only — never loaded with ordinary freight.

4. Operating model

  • Buy versus lease. An artic costs ₦95 m (≈USD 59,000) new against ₦2.4–2.8 m/month leased. A lease lifts fixed cost ₦35.44 m → ₦52.70 m and break-even utilisation from 5.8 loaded legs a month to 8.6 against 10 available — about 50% higher.
  • Plan 35's rule stands: own the core, subcontract ≥30% of tonne-km, lease only project and peak work. Lease a project or a peak, never the base load.
  • Utilisation is worth more than rate. A 10% rate cut on a 450 km, 25 t leg costs ₦105,000 of contribution; four extra loaded legs a month are worth ₦24 m a year (03_Isiome_Machinery.md §7 agrees).
  • Maintenance — own the routine 80% by volume, contract the specialist 20% by value. Nkpor (built by Okodu Construction, powered by Okodu Power) takes preventive work, brakes and diagnostics.
  • Uptime: 78% → 88% → 90% → 92% (Years 1/3/5/10, mechanical availability).
  • Telematics — one device, two views. Freight's control tower takes dispatch and exception data; Fleet's fleet-data platform takes utilisation, fuel, driver behaviour and uptime.
  • Specification: GPS and route replay, driver ID, harsh braking and idling, engine hours, calibrated fuel-level sensing, door and seal sensors on controlled units, temperature probes on reefers. Any fuel variance over 3% is investigated within 24 hours — the sensor typically repays itself inside 60–90 days (CTN, 2026). Per vehicle: ₦470,000 to fit, ₦105,000 a year to run (₦1.14/km).
  • Drivers. Written contracts, direct payroll, pension, NHF and HMO remitted, documented rest and rotation. Pay is benchmarked deliberately above the informal market for the same lane, because a driver who can earn more running an unsafe truck at night will do exactly that. Salary plus a safety-and-utilisation bonus from the telematics scorecard — never a per-trip cash incentive that rewards speed. No cash handling; no night driving on unfamiliar corridors in Years 1–2; a no-blame incident reporting policy; discipline that never monetises an incident.
  • Fuel. No driver ever handles fuel cash. Bulk purchase into the depot tank; metered dispensing against a per-unit tag; litres reconciled monthly against telematics and odometer.
  • Tyres and spares. A per-kilometre tyre contract with casing credit; pressure and tread logged per unit and wheel position — under-inflation kills casings. Six months' cover on high-turnover parts.
  • CNG and alternative fuels. At ₦380/SCM against diesel at ₦1,800–1,850/litre (Businessday, 2026), CNG is the only credible hedge on a line that is 66% of cost per kilometre; Fleet converts only where a station exists at both termini.
  • Disposal and residual value. 7-year life, 15% residual for tractors; trailers depreciated over 15–20 years. The investment case must clear at zero residual — a used-truck price here is a policy variable.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

  • CAC incorporation of Uli Fleet Ltd under Uli Group Ltd, with reserved matters and a Family Director.
  • Papers: licence, roadworthiness, insurance, FRSC safety-standardisation compliance, LASDRI for Lagos; ECOWAS ISRT laissez-passer and Brown Card for Corridors 3–4 (Convention A/P.4/5/82).
  • State haulage levies in Anambra, Enugu, Imo, Abia, Rivers, Lagos and the FCT — a written schedule from each state before the first trip. NURTW/RTEAN registered in writing, treated as not a payment authority.
  • NAFDAC NCS and NDLEA requirements attach to the controlled-specification units, whose custody and authorisation stay with Uli Special Logistics. Insurance through Aku Insurance with external underwriters for Years 1–4 — Aku's motor line is scheduled Year 5–6.
  • Driver licensing and medical certification: correct licence class, annual medical including vision, drug screening for controlled crews.
  • Levy and union posture, from plan 35 and enforced here — Fleet holds the payroll: closed gated private depot with Fleet's own loading crew; drivers on direct payroll; pay only levies existing in a state law or gazette by bank receipted transfer — never roadside cash; log every other demand in a corridor obstruction register.

The licence is acquired, not waited for

A licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business: Uli Fleet either obtains the papers or buys a company that already has them. In this company the papers are individually cheap and collectively expensive — 19 units in Year 1 growing to 380 by Year 10, each needing licence, roadworthiness, insurance and plated compliance across seven states, which is not a licence problem but a months-long administrative load that a purchase skips. The Group's rule reads here as: buying a small haulage or fleet-management operator transfers registered, roadworthy, insured and plated units — together with the two things this plan says will bind it first: workshop capability and employed, vetted drivers. §4 is blunt that pay must be benchmarked above the informal market because the driver shortage binds before capital does; an acquisition that arrives with fifty trained drivers on payroll and a working workshop is buying time this business otherwise spends recruiting.

Why the acquisition case is stronger here than it looks, and where the honest limit sits. This plan's whole thesis is that "almost no operator knows their own cost per kilometre" (§2) — so the characteristic Nigerian haulage company is asset-rich, cash-poor and management-poor, which is why it is available and why the Group's cost-per-km, telematics and fuel-reconciliation discipline is a genuine post-completion uplift rather than a hope. But §7's break-even arithmetic is unforgiving: an owned unit needs 5.8 loaded legs a month to break even and returns ~₦25m a year at ten — a ~26% return on a ₦95m asset (corrected — see NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md: 18% was the ₦17m owning-versus-leasing premium measured against the asset, not the asset's return), in line with plan 35's 27% — so a fleet bought without contracted utilisation is a faster route to the same loss. The 65% volume gate in §10 applies to acquisitions exactly as it applies to orders, and §5's rule stands unchanged: the captive base load must be signed before any truck is bought — including trucks bought inside another company.

Ninety-day action, costed. Extend §12 item 3's cost survey rather than commissioning a separate exercise. Instruct counsel and a fleet valuer to identify haulage and fleet-management operators in the South-East and Lagos with 20–80 units, current papers in all operating states, a working workshop and 30 or more drivers on direct payroll, and to price two. Budget ₦50m (~US$31,000): ₦20m paper and compliance diligence on five targets — registration, roadworthiness, FRSC standing, levy receipt history and every certificate's expiry; ₦15m unit condition and residual-value survey against §7's per-class capex, since §4 requires cases to clear at zero residual; ₦10m open-claim, insurance and liability review, because a subsisting claim transfers with the entity; ₦5m driver retention terms and payroll reconstruction — pension, NHF, HMO and bonus carry-over — the single item on which the deal's asset actually depends. Gate it on §12 item 14: no order, and no acquisition, without signed contracted utilisation covering 65% of the units' fixed cost.

6. Capital requirement

It is the same naira, once. Plan 35's Tranche 1 carries ₦1.39 bn of vehicles, this plan's ₦1.43 bn for the same units — registered to Uli Fleet, so it sits on Fleet's balance sheet as a leasing asset, recognised once.

  • Tranche 1, Year 1 — ₦2.19 bn (≈USD 1.37 m): 19 units 1.43; workshop equipment, tooling and bays 0.18; telematics platform and fitment 0.12; spares float 0.22; working capital 0.15; licensing, legal, insurance 0.09.
  • Tranche 2, Years 2–3 — ₦4.10 bn (≈USD 2.56 m): 51 units to 70; workshop Phase 2; spares warehouse; fleet-wide telematics; CNG pilot on 8 units. Tranche 3, Years 4–6 — ₦6.20 bn (≈USD 3.88 m): 82 units to 152; CNG at scale; Lagos and Onne workshops. Years 7–15 — ₦26–32 bn: to ~380 units; a workshop network; a residual-value desk.
  • Funding. Family equity funds workshop equipment, the telematics platform and licensing. Akunnia Capital arranges naira asset finance on 36–60 month tenors matched to unit life, within gearing ≤40% and no unhedged USD debt; controlled units carry no cross-guarantees.
  • Verify locally: unit prices at current FX; CNG conversion and factory-CNG premium; workshop construction rates (Okodu cost survey); insurance premiums; state levy schedules.

8. Organisation

First ten hires, in order. (1) Fleet Manager — owns uptime and cost per kilometre. (2) Fleet Director — has run a maintenance and utilisation P&L. (3) Workshop Foreman. (9) Spares & Stores Manager. (10) Vehicle Compliance Officer.

10. Risks

1 · Utilisation shortfall — the governing risk. Five legs a month loses ₦5.2 m/yr; 8.5 makes ₦16.0 m. Own only against contracted utilisation; 65% volume gate.

2 · Diesel and CNG conversion cost. Fuel is 66% of cost/km; ₦1,362 → ₦1,825, stress-tested at ₦2,600/L. Bulk purchase; telematics consumption control; CNG only where stations exist at both termini; fuel surcharge.

3 · Driver misconduct and cargo theft. Above-market pay with a safety bonus; no cash in the cab; two-person rule on high-value loads; traced guarantors.

4 · Cargo loss — catastrophic on controlled consignments, risking the Group's licence. Dedicated segregated units, two-lock system, dual GPS, seal sensors, photographic reconciliation.

5 · Accident and liability. Comprehensive motor, goods-in-transit at declared value, liability cover; defensive-driving module.

6 · Maintenance backlog and downtime. A lost day is ₦98,000 standing and up to ₦508,250 of contribution. 95% PM compliance; six months' spares.

7 · Vehicle and parts theft. Gated CCTV depot; geofencing alerts; immobilisation only when stationary and tower-confirmed.

8 · FX on imported spares and units. Naira facilities, FX priced at order, no unhedged USD debt; forward buying and local fabrication.

9 · Residual-value collapse — a policy variable in Nigeria. Cases must clear at zero residual.

10 · Union and levy extraction. Gazetted levies only, by bank receipted transfer; no cash in the cab; corridor obstruction register.

11. Integration

  • Uli Freight. Fleet owns the assets Freight schedules, is its lessor, and manages its drivers; Freight sells and schedules, Fleet owns and instruments. It uses Freight's corridors for recovery.
  • Uli Warehousing and Uli Special Logistics. Fleet maintains Warehousing's shunters and delivery units and the six dedicated controlled-specification units for Special Logistics on bare hire.
  • Cargo. Fleet's units carry Isiome's processed output and inputs, Idenze's pharmaceuticals — the reefer class kept to a GDP standard — and Okodu's construction materials.
  • Okodu Construction builds the workshop, bays and hardstanding; Okodu Power supplies the electricity, maintenance circuits on solar.
  • Akunnia Capital arranges asset finance within gearing ≤40% and no unhedged USD debt, and keeps the intercompany lease arms-length. Aku Insurance covers the fleet from Year 5–6; before that, externally. Idenze Polytechnic supplies technicians.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — decide and price. (1) Incorporate Uli Fleet Ltd at CAC with reserved matters and a Family Director. (2) Appoint the Fleet Manager and Fleet Director. (3) Run the cost survey this plan depends on — unit prices for all five classes at current FX, CNG conversion premium, insurance, the Okodu workshop estimate — then re-base §7. (4) Obtain written levy schedules for the seven states. (5) Settle ownership, crew employer and the intercompany charge in writing.

Days 31–60 — tender and hire. (6) Tender the first 19 units to a CNG- or dual-fuel-capable specification. (7) Issue the workshop equipment order to Okodu Construction, telematics in parallel. (8) Recruit the Workshop Foreman, Chief Driver/Trainer, Telematics Analyst and Fuel Controller. (9) Bind insurance through Aku Insurance with external underwriters for Years 1–4. (10) Open the corridor obstruction register.

Days 61–90 — start, and gate. (11) Commission telematics; start litre-by-litre fuel reconciliation and the monthly driver scorecard on day one. (12) Sign the intercompany lease and service contracts at Group-CFO-certified rates. (13) File the controlled-specification unit specification. (14) Day-90 gate — order the fleet only if the captive base load is signed, one external anchor exists, and the survey confirms ≤₦96 per tonne-km. If not, run a quarter on subcontracted capacity.

Prepared for the Uli Group board and the Ezeme Group Board. Market and pricing figures are sourced and linked; operating, capital and unit-economics figures are estimates at ₦1,600/USD needing local verification before capital is committed. Three items are flagged for board resolution: the empty-return fuel basis in plan 35; ownership of the controlled-specification units against plan 38's ring-fence; and consolidation of headcount and capital between the two companies. Why fuel deserves its own plan rather than a line in the power plan. The Group's power economics are anchored on diesel at ₦1,800/litre as the customer's alternative — which means the Group is itself one of the largest diesel buyers in its own corridor. It buys at retail and, by owning distribution, would buy at wholesale while earning the margin in between. The same logic that puts Okodu Materials inside the construction arm puts fuel inside the energy arm: it converts the Group's largest controllable cost into a Group margin.

1. Thesis

Okodu Group builds and powers the physical world the rest of the Group operates in — and it is the Group's asset factory.

The Group's own words: "You cannot build without power, and power is useless without structures to serve. Okodu is the empire's engineer."

Why this domain matters disproportionately to the Group's finance ambition. Every other domain consumes. Okodu produces tangible, long-lived, cash-generating assets: generation plant, distribution networks, industrial buildings, warehouses, housing, commercial property. Those assets have long-dated, inflation-linked, predictable cash flows — the exact profile African pension funds are structurally under-allocated to and cannot source.

PenCom's own risk register lists R1 as real returns below inflation and R3 as FGN concentration, and prescribes the mitigant as a shift into "alternatives, infrastructure, and inflation-linked instruments." Pension infrastructure allocation sits at roughly ₦262.6bn — about 1% of assets. The regulator is instructing pension funds to buy what Okodu Group builds.

Okodu Group is therefore not merely a construction business. It is the origination engine for Akunnia Capital's funds. Energy and construction are upstream of finance in the value chain, not parallel to it — and the plan is sequenced accordingly.

2. Market

Energy — the headline correction

Electricity regulation is now a state matter, not a federal one. Anambra was among 16 states that completed the transfer of electricity regulation in early 2026, and the Anambra State Electricity Law 2025 created ASERC (the Anambra State Electricity Regulatory Commission), with ASEMA for technical standards.

Two consequences that shape the whole business:

  1. The regulator for Nkpor distribution is ASERC, not NERC — and ASERC must decide an IEDN (independent electricity distribution network) application within a statutory three months, materially faster than the federal route.
  2. One caveat remains open: the transfer order's scope, and whether legacy federal instruments need novation, is unresolved. Do not commit Tranche 2 capital before ASERC answers in writing.

The market is the incumbent's failure

Enugu DisCo, Anambra's franchise holder, runs 41.70% ATC&C losses against a 21.26% MYTO target (NERC Q1 2025). That gap is the opportunity — build where the incumbent has already failed to serve.

Pricing: the anchor is diesel, not the grid

National tariff bands — Band A ₦225/kWh, Bands B–E ₦40–63, with ₦358.32bn of subsidy in Q1 2026 alone — are not a sensible reference price. The customer's real alternative is a generator. At diesel of ₦1,800/litre ÷ ~2.6 kWh/litre + ₦70/kWh O&M, their true cost is ₦780/kWh. A tariff around ₦230/kWh is a 40–50% saving on what they actually pay today, and defensible to ASERC as cost-reflective.

Price against diesel, not against the grid.

Africa's industrial capacity is politically constrained

African governments are imposing local content requirements and export restrictions on raw materials to force domestic value addition. This makes domestic manufacturing and energy independence structurally advantaged — the state wants what this Group builds.

Construction and real estate

  • Nigeria has a severe housing deficit; construction quality is persistently poor and most contractors are informal or under-capitalised.
  • Cement, steel and labour costs have risen sharply with inflation and currency movement — a margin risk that fixed-price contracts must price for.
  • The elevator building is a category that does not currently exist in most of Nkpor — the Group's own plan calls the elevator "the single most visible quality differentiator in Anambra residential property."

3. Product & service lines

The energy platform

Okodu Power — generation and distribution. Full plan at 42_Okodu_Power.md. Solar, gas and hybrid generation with battery storage, transformer stations, and distribution registered with ASERC. Every Group cluster, estate and institution runs on this system, and from a later year it sells to the surrounding neighbourhood.

The avoided-cost case is the strongest number in the library: at diesel of ₦1,800/litre, the Group's own Year-3 energy spend falls from ₦11.16bn to ₦3.17bn a year — ₦7.99bn avoided against ₦52bn of Tranches 1+2 capital, a 6.5-year unlevered payback and ~3.5-year equity payback, holding down to ₦1,200/litre diesel. The first customer is the Group itself, which removes the demand risk entirely.

Okodu Solar — rooftop, commercial and utility-scale solar; and the solar-plus-storage packages that make the Group's facilities resilient.

Okodu Grid — mini-grids, embedded generation, industrial supply and wheeling. The distributed-generation business serving estates, businesses and communities beyond the Group's own footprint.

Note on the MW target: the Nkpor build reaches roughly 31 MW by Year 5. Reaching 500 MW requires acquiring operating portfolios, not building them — so an acquisition pipeline opens from Year 2, with an asset-screening mandate in the first ninety days.

The construction platform

Okodu Construction — building and civil contracting. Full plan at 45_Okodu_Construction.md. The Group's own builder, plus commercial contracting at margin. Built on the direct-labour model the Group's own documents specify: the company is the employer of record, labour is engaged directly on payroll rather than through a labour agency, and a single senior COREN/ARCON-registered engineer is retained full-time as site supervisor at above-market rate. The same supervising structure and crew carry forward between projects, reducing mobilisation cost.

Okodu Materials — cement, blocks, timber, steel fabrication and quarry materials. Internalising inputs is the margin defence — in a market where material costs inflate faster than contract prices, owning the input is the difference between a profitable project and a loss.

Okodu Real Estate — holding, managing and letting the property portfolio. Full plan at 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md.

Okodu Housing — staff housing and estates. Group staff housing lowers the cost of living and makes Group employment more compelling than any competitor can match — a benefit that shows up in retention across all five domains.

Okodu Estate Services — facilities management, metered utilities, security and services to the Group's estates and third-party developments.

Akuzo Development — the urban transformation. Full plan at 50_Akuzo_Development.md.

4. Operating model

Energy: captive first, then third party

The sequence is deliberate and it is what makes the business bankable:

  1. Own generation for Group facilities — the Group is its own anchor customer, so the first tranche has no demand risk
  2. Become the Group's power provider of record — every factory, campus, hospital and estate
  3. Sell to the surrounding neighbourhood from a later year, converting a cost centre into a revenue line
  4. Acquire operating portfolios to reach scale beyond what can be built

Gas is capped at 35% of capacity as firming, not baseload — there is no adjacent pipeline at Nkpor, so the realistic route is trucked CNG/LNG, which constrains its role.

The governing metric for the whole energy platform, from the Okodu Grid plan: collection efficiency. Break-even sits at ~72% collection efficiency — below that, the asset destroys cash at any tariff. So the collection-sensitivity table, not the tariff table, is what determines whether the business survives. Supporting rules now adopted: a 1.00 meter-to-customer ratio enforced on Group facilities too, prepaid STS metering, transformer reconciliation, no cash handling, and the honest treatment of theft — including internal theft.

And a screening rule for network investment: roughly 5.5 GWh of annual sales per ₦1.5bn of network capex, or about 3,700 kWh per connection. Anything below that threshold does not earn its capital.

Two figures still unresolved: the MV/LV line cost is the largest single swing (₦40–70m/km in this plan against US$150,000/km elsewhere in the library), and the state transfer count is reported as 15 or 16. Both need confirmation before Tranche 2.

Construction: the direct-labour model

  • The development and construction company is the employer of record, holder of all site contracts and long-term owner of retained units
  • Labour from the local workforce on direct payroll — masons, iron benders, carpenters, electricians, plumbers — not through a labour agency
  • One senior registered engineer retained full-time at above-market rate for quality control, safety and trade foreman coordination
  • Payroll, welfare and safety administered directly
  • The reusable crew is a competitive asset: the same structure carries from project to project, reducing the learning curve and mobilisation cost

Real estate: the retained-floor strategy

For a commercial residential building, the company retains one full floor under its own name — either as a permanent management office and caretaker presence, or as company-owned rental stock generating recurring income — and sells the remaining floors. Recommended default: retain the ground floor, since upper floors carry a natural price premium for view and privacy, so selling the higher floors captures more revenue. The retained floor is ring-fenced in the building-management by-laws from the outset, so buyers understand the ownership structure before purchase.

And the Year 8 claim does not work the way the Master Plan implies — though it does work. 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md worked it out rather than assuming it:

  • Akuzo premium residential lets at 4–6% gross and 3.5–5% net on new cost — below the cost of naira debt. So speculative residential letting is never levered.
  • The Master Plan's claim still holds, by a different mechanism: sale-plus-retention, not rent. At a 25% development margin, selling the four upper floors repays the entire building and the retained ground floor is free. The sensitivity at 15/25/35% shows the retained floor's effective cost falling from ₦114m to zero.
  • The cap-rate gap is the real constraint. At a 10% naira cap rate, a held building's ₦54m NOI is worth ₦540m against a ₦1.16bn cost — a 53% loss. Speculative letting therefore cannot be sold to a pension fund at any affordable price.
  • The fix is the captive anchor tenant. The same asset leased to Idenze University or Group companies is priced on contracted cash flow, not cap rate — which is precisely why this arm exists beyond its own returns, and why it is the originator of the fund's asset class rather than a landlord.
  • Integration is where the margin is: the ₦420m / 23% gap between Okodu-integrated build cost and open-market turnkey cost is the development margin. Remove it and yield on cost falls below the cost of capital. And because Okodu Power supplies metered power, held buildings need no solar, battery or LPG grid — ₦1.31bn avoided across 16 buildings.

The self-financing property portfolio — and a cost conflict that must be resolved

Rental income from early buildings is intended to fund acquisition of the next plot, with the portfolio self-financing by Year 8 and reaching 27–42 plots, 27 buildings, 216–324 apartments by Year 30.

⚠️ The Year 8 claim rests on a figure the Group's own documents contradict. The Akuzo Urban Transformation Plan costs a storey building at ₦35m–₦50m. The Akuzo Development Programme — a detailed, itemised bill of quantities for the same buildings — totals US$967,000 for Building 1 (14 units, 5 storeys, Akuzo Residence) and US$999,000 for Building 2 (15 units, commercial), roughly ₦1.55–1.60bn each at ₦1,600/USD. That is a factor of 31–44×.

The bill of quantities is the credible figure, because it itemises what it is buying: structural frame US$150,000, passenger elevator US$25,000, 60kW solar array US$68,000, 250kWh battery bank US$38,000, biodigester and generator US$55,000, central LPG grid US$18,000, 100,000-litre cistern with filtration US$55,000, interior fit-out US$110,000 plus US$50,000 for two penthouses. ₦35m — roughly US$22,000 — cannot build any of that. The ₦35–50m figure is not a construction cost; it appears to be the land/plot cost from the land budget, carried across into the real-estate costing by mistake.

Consequences, stated plainly:

  1. The real-estate programme is roughly thirty times more capital-hungry than the Master Plan implies — ₦1.23bn for 27 buildings becomes of the order of ₦40bn+, not ₦1.23bn.
  2. Year 8 self-financing is unsafe as written and must be restated as conditional on: build cost held to ₦650–850m per building by constraining gross area to 1,100–1,400 sqm instead of 2,000 sqm (build fewer square metres, not cheaper ones); occupancy and rent achieved at plan; and construction cost inflation contained. On current figures the slip is to Year 11–13.
  3. The largest single saving available is that a standalone building does not need its own solar, battery, biodigester, cistern and LPG plant where the water spine and Okodu Power already serve the district — worth roughly US$234,000 per building, and it is the reason to build inside Akuzo rather than on isolated plots.

The bill of quantities figure has since been confirmed independently. 45_Okodu_Construction.md, working separately, derived a storey-building rate of ₦750,000/m² by working backwards from the Group's own Akuzo budget envelope — giving roughly ₦1.48bn per five-storey building, within 5% of the BoQ's ₦1.55–1.60bn. It also reached the same conclusion about the ₦1.23bn line: "the family's 'Akuzo storey buildings ×27' line is a land budget, not a build budget." Two independent derivations now agree, which is as settled as this figure will get without a tender.

Action: commission three independent valuations of sale and rental values, and a competitive construction tender, before Building 1 is committed. See 50_Akuzo_Development.md for the full reconciliation.

The Group's rule, and the acquisition posture across the domain

A licence or a clean title is never a reason to defer or omit a business. The Group either obtains it or buys an entity or an asset that already has it. Two facts make the rule unusually valuable here. In Nigerian electricity the licence is the scarce asset — and the position has just changed: Anambra has taken over regulation of its own market, so ASERC, not NERC, is the relevant regulator for Nkpor, deciding an IEDN application within a statutory three months on a complete filing (ASERC). In Nigerian real estate title is the scarce asset, because virgin communal land carries probate, family-claim and consent risk that can take years to clear.

11. Integration

This is the domain that supplies the most and consumes the most. It is the Group's physical fabric.

Supplies to every domain:

  • Power to Isiome's processing and cold storage, Idenze's pharmaceutical plant and campuses, Uli's studios and warehouses, and every Group estate
  • Construction for Idenze University and the teaching hospital, Idenze Pharma's plant, Isiome's processing and storage, Uli's warehouses and studios, and the Akuzo programme
  • Materials to every Group construction project
  • Housing to staff across all five groups — a retention benefit no competitor matches
  • Real estate assets — long-dated inflation-linked rental income — to Akunnia Capital for fund warehousing and syndication

Buys from:

  • Isiome Group — food for worker canteens and site catering
  • Uli Group — freight for materials and equipment; media for project documentation and marketing
  • Idenze Group — polytechnic graduates as electricians, technicians, plant operators and site staff; and clinical services for staff
  • Akunnia Capital — project finance, working capital, insurance, performance bonds
  • Aku Technology — metering, billing, asset and project reporting systems

The critical sequencing point, stated once and applied everywhere: Okodu Group is upstream of Akunnia Capital in the value chain. An asset manager with no investable assets cannot raise third-party capital. Okodu builds the assets; Akunnia warehouses and syndicates them; the fees fund the next tranche of construction. Get the order wrong and the whole finance thesis stalls.

12. First ninety days

  1. Apply to ASERC for the IEDN and get written confirmation on the transfer order's scope and whether legacy federal instruments require novation. This gates Tranche 2 capital.
  2. Open the captive energy design — commission the load study across every Group facility, and have Okodu Power's first tranche sized entirely against Group demand. The first tranche must have no third-party demand risk.
  3. Commission the generation and storage tender against at least three vendors on fixed-price contracts with performance guarantees.
  4. Retain the resident COREN/ARCON-registered engineer before the first project starts, at above-market rate. This is a quality decision and the Group's own documents are explicit that it should not be cost-optimised.
  5. Establish the standing land acquisition mandate in Akuzo and begin title diligence on the first plots. No verbal agreements, no informal purchases, Governor's Consent on every acquisition.
  6. Open the acquisition pipeline for operating generation portfolios — because 500 MW cannot be built on the Nkpor campus, and the screening mandate needs to start before the opportunity appears.
  7. Tender the Akuzo depot Phase 1 and the security system in parallel with the solar and storage order, so that site power and site security land together.
  8. Set the ring-fencing policy — energy, construction and real estate in separate financing rings, with no cross-guarantees, adopted by the Audit & Risk Committee.
  9. Fund the domain's acquisition mandates as one board decision, not seven. Approve a total ₦1.26bn of screening and diligence mandates inside the first ninety days — ₦250m Power (generation and distribution portfolios), ₦200m Grid (licensed networks and mini-grids), ₦150m Solar (mini-grids and NEMSA-certified EPC firms), ₦180m Construction (COREN-registered, state-classified contractors), ₦220m Materials (titled quarries and MANCAP-certified plants), ₦95m Real Estate (title audit and C-of-O plots) and ₦70m Akuzo (scheme-approval audit) — each with a decision by day 90 and counsel instructed once, centrally, on ASERC s.40 consent, Ministerial consent for mineral-title transfer, share-purchase structuring and certification transfer. OKODU POWER — Power Generation & Distribution

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary in this plan; it uses ₦1,600/USD for planning (the text also tests ₦1,200 and ₦1,327). Spot was about ₦1,328/USD (CBN NFEM, Sept 2026). Dollar figures are indicative only and are not comparable across plans — each plan used a different rate. The library planning rate for cross-plan comparison is ₦1,600/USD. See plans/README.md.

Ezeme Group · Okodu Group (Energy, Construction & Real Estate) · Entity: Okodu Power Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Okodu Group Ltd (Okodu). The family's own architecture calls this company "Okodu Power"; Okodu Power is the registered name. Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027 · FX assumption ₦1,600/USD, flat in nominal terms. Spot NFEM was ₦1,327.78/USD on 22 September 2026 (Newswatch); ₦1,600 is a conservative planning rate for equipment that is ~90% imported.

Companions: 43_Okodu_Solar.md and 44_Okodu_Grid.md (Okodu Solar, Okodu Grid) — separate companies, boards and licences, referenced here as interfaces only.

1. Thesis

Okodu Power is a regulated private utility built backwards from a guaranteed customer. It generates and distributes electricity at Nkpor, and its first customer is the Ezeme Group itself: the university, the polytechnic, the teaching hospital, two production clusters, the agro-processing plant and cold store, the logistics depot, the Group HQ, and the Akuzo residential and student estate. Only once that load is served does it sell to the neighbourhood — turning the Group's largest controllable cost line into a revenue line, and eventually into an asset class.

One sentence: Every Ezeme factory, hospital, campus and home already burns diesel at roughly ₦780 per kWh to stay lit, and the Group owns the land, the load, the capital and the regulator relationship to replace that with a ₦150 per kWh asset it will still own in thirty years.

Why captive group demand de-risks the first tranche. Power projects fail for three reasons: no customer, no price, no payment. Captive load removes all three. The customer is a set of companies under one ownership, so demand is contracted before a panel is ordered — no merchant risk, no ramp-up. The price is an intra-group PPA struck at cost-plus, benchmarked against the diesel it displaces — arms-length, board-approved, disclosed to the Family Council, and still 70–75% below what the Group pays today. Payment is a transfer at a parent-guaranteed settlement entity, so captive-tranche collection is effectively 100%, against an industry collection efficiency of 74.39% (NERC Q1 2025). That is why Tranche 1 is financeable on group and development-finance terms rather than merchant-power terms, and why it must be built first.

Why distributed generation beats waiting for the grid. Nigeria has over 13,000 MW of installed generation capacity and less than half of it reliably reaches consumers (Minister of Power Joseph Tegbe, June 2026 — BusinessDay). Average available capacity was 5,366.88 MW at a plant availability factor of 39.39% — roughly 60% of installed capacity unavailable for dispatch. DisCo aggregate technical, commercial and collection losses were 39.61%, and no DisCo met its target: the Anambra franchise holder, Enugu DisCo, ran 41.70% against a 21.26% target (NERC Q1 2025). When an incumbent loses 42 kobo of every naira, the rational response is not to lobby for more grid — it is to build a smaller, better-metered network next door. Okodu Power does not need the national grid to work. It needs it to keep failing.

2. Market

Supply. Twenty-eight grid-connected plants generated 10,304.47 GWh in Q1 2025, while Gencos report over 2,500 MW generated and wasted because the grid cannot absorb it (ThisDay). The grid is not a supplier of last resort; it is a supplier of uncertain resort.

Demand — Okodu Power's real market. Nigerian businesses do not buy grid electricity; they buy uptime, and they pay a generator for it. Diesel reached ₦1,800–1,850/litre in September 2026 (BusinessDay); at realistic partial-load consumption of 0.36–0.40 litres/kWh, self-generation costs ₦700–950/kWh all-in. Simultaneously, Nigerian grid tariffs are among the world's cheapest and largely unusable: Band A ₦225/kWh, Band B ₦63, C ₦50, D ₦43, E ₦40, with the Federal Government absorbing ₦358.32bn of generation cost in Q1 2026 — 51.95% of the ₦689.72bn GenCo invoice (Zawya/Nigerian Tribune).

That subsidy is both the largest structural risk and the most important commercial insight. Do not price against the grid — price against the generator. A Nkpor manufacturer on Band B at ₦63/kWh with 8 hours of supply still runs a diesel set for the other 16; their true blended cost exceeds ₦400/kWh. A ₦230/kWh tariff at 22 hours is a 40–50% saving on their real alternative, and it is defensible before ASERC as cost-reflective on Okodu Power's own cost of supply.

Solar is arriving as distributed generation, not utility-scale. Nigeria added 803 MW of solar in 2025 (+141%), reaching 1.19 GW cumulative — Africa's second-largest market behind South Africa — of which ~96% is off-grid and distributed. Battery storage grew from ~10 MWh to 40.6 MWh (BusinessDay). The market is being won by exactly the model proposed here: distributed assets sized to a known load. The embedded-generation and mini-grid opportunity is the same opportunity — a NERC permit covers mini-grids above 100 kW distribution and up to 1 MW generation, and hundreds of such permits have been issued, but almost all are rural and none is an urban industrial franchise.

Regulation and the successor-company structure. The Electricity Act 2023 moved electricity off the federal exclusive list. The federal market retains its successor structure — GenCos (generation), TCN (transmission), NBET (bulk trading) and the DisCos (distribution) — with NERC regulating the grid and interstate trade but permitted to transfer intrastate oversight to states that legislate (s.230). Anambra is one of sixteen states that have completed the transfer (EnergyWorth). The Anambra State Electricity Law 2025 created the Anambra State Electricity Regulatory Commission (ASERC), with the Anambra State Electricity Management Agency (ASEMA) enforcing technical standards (ASERC). Practically: Okodu Power's licences are Anambra licences. The GenCo/TCN/NBET/DisCo structure is the market Okodu Power interconnects with, not the market it competes in.

Addressable market. Nkpor and the contiguous Idemili North corridor, plus Onitsha's industrial fringe, is a dense, trading, manufacturing-adjacent market with a large self-generating commercial base and no credible private distribution alternative. A customer-density and willingness-to-pay survey is a Tranche 1 deliverable; the connection counts and the "majority of Nkpor" target below must be validated against it, not assumed.

African context for the 5–10 GW mandate. ~600 million Africans lack electricity, ~80% of them in sub-Saharan Africa; Mission 300 has passed 50 million connections, Nigeria's 4.5 million of them delivered mostly through private mini-grids and solar home systems rather than grid extension. Transformer lead times run to four years and prices are up ~75% since 2019 (EnergiTech). The mandate is 5–10 GW installed plus distribution licences in select states — a portfolio of regulated, ring-fenced, locally embedded utilities, each replicating the Nkpor proof.

Discipline rule. Lines 1, 2 and 4 are Okodu Power's core and carry the capital. Mini-grids and grid services (3, 6) are Okodu Grid's business; utility-scale solar farms are Okodu Solar's. Okodu Power is their anchor offtaker and network host, transacting on published, arms-length terms. Okodu Power owns the licence to distribute; the others own the capability to build. That separation keeps a regulated monopoly auditable.

4. Operating model

Siting. Generation, storage and injection equipment sit on the four Zone A energy plots already budgeted at ₦55m each (₦220m). Solar goes first onto Group rooftops and carports (no land cost, no opportunity cost), then ground-mount on the Idemmili belt where land is ₦5–20m per plot. The university's 100 hectares and the Idemmili belt are the two solar land banks; neither competes with Nkpor's highest-value use.

Interconnection vs islanded operation. Nkpor runs islanded-first: an independent 11/33 kV network with a single controlled interconnection point to the EEDC/ASERC market for top-up and later export. Interconnection agreements are the slowest and most politically exposed step in the chain, and islanded operation means Okodu Power's customers never notice a national grid collapse — a marketing asset worth more than the tariff.

Metering and billing. Every customer is metered, group entities included, and group companies are billed monthly in cash, not netted off at year-end. The discipline is the point. Smart prepaid STS-compliant meters (IEC 62055) on every connection; AMI feeding a SCADA/EMS control room at the Nkpor energy compound. Nigeria's national metering rate is 46.98%; Okodu Power targets 100% metered from the first connection, because prepaid metering converts theft into a customer-service issue.

O&M. 24/7 control room on rotated shifts; remote switching and fault detection; string-level PV monitoring; BESS state-of-health tracking; two line crews on a 4-hour urban / 12-hour rural fault SLA; five-year OEM contracts for inverters and engines, with critical spares held at Nkpor, not Lagos. Target 98.5% availability, SAIDI under 8 hours/customer/year.

Power as a group cost-control play. Electricity is the Group's largest controllable operating cost after payroll, it is paid in dollar-linked diesel, and it produces no asset. Under Okodu Power it becomes a naira cost roughly one-fifth the level, an intra-group margin rather than an external loss, and a long-lived balance-sheet asset. Every other plan in this library — the university, the teaching hospital, the kiln-drying furniture lines, the cold store — becomes cheaper to run on the day the first tranche energises. That is why this is the anchor of Okodu.

Three ASERC requirements must be designed in from the start: a lifeline tariff for low-consumption households; the Power Consumer Assistance Fund levy; and local content under s.79 — award line construction and technical services to Anambra-registered firms trained through the Idenze Polytechnic, and say so in the application.

The principle, and the acquisition route it forces

A licence is never a reason to defer or omit the business. The Group either obtains it or buys an entity or an asset that already holds it. That is now Group policy here in the plainest possible terms: this plan's own milestone table concedes that "reaching 500 MW on that timetable requires buying operating portfolios, not building them — an acquisition pipeline must open from Year 2." In Nigerian electricity the licence is the scarce asset, so the acquisition route is the primary route for capacity, not the fallback.

Two consequences for structure. First, because s.40 gates change of control, every generation or distribution acquisition is priced and documented as a share purchase with ASERC consent as a condition precedent — an asset purchase that leaves the licence behind buys nothing. Second, ASERC is demonopolising: its 2026 instruments were signed expressly to "eliminate monopoly in the sector" and it has told operators that "any operator expecting to enjoy monopoly would be making a grave mistake" (BusinessDay). Buy the licence for the head start it gives, not for the protection it used to confer.

A necessary caveat. The NERC-to-ASERC handover is recent. The transfer order's exact scope, and whether legacy federal instruments must be novated, should be confirmed in writing with both regulators in the first ninety days. Do not commit Tranche 2 capital on the assumption that the jurisdictional question is settled. The same answer governs the acquisition route: no generation or distribution acquisition completes, and no deposit becomes non-refundable, before ASERC answers in writing on the transfer order's scope, on the s.40 consent process, and on whether a legacy federal licence held by the target requires novation into a state instrument.

📄 The one unresolved figure in this section — and it is not academic, because by statute this is the only body that can charge it.

The ASERC licence fees are not published anywhere, and that is now a closed inventory rather than an absence of evidence. ASERC's entire media library was enumerated through its own WordPress REST API (X-WP-Total: 41 items, of which 8 are PDFs) and a sweep for naira figures across all seven of its pages returned zero matches; "Public Documents" is login-gated (HTTP 401) and /tariffs/ carries no schedule. The eight PDFs are: the three 2026 regulations

(Application for Licences (Generation, Distribution & Trading), Customer Protection, and Investment in Electricity Market), plus the Anambra State Electricity Law 2025, the Electricity Act 2023, the Anambra State Transfer Order, the EEDC Asset Delineation Order, and the 1999 Constitution Fifth Alteration Act. None is a fees instrument.

And note a correction to an earlier version of this note, which was mine: it said the 59-page scan "holds the Customer Protection and Investment in Electricity Market Regulations." It does not. Those are two separate PDFs published 17 September 2026, at the /2026/09/ paths above. 43_Okodu_Solar.md and 44_Okodu_Grid.md therefore have real sources for their compliance rows rather than a mis-stated one — though both are image-only scans and need reading before those rows are verified.

Why this matters more than a missing number: Electricity Act 2023 s.230(7) makes ASERC the only body that can charge it. Read from the Act — an additional successor company "incorporated and licensed by a State regulator… shall be under the regulatory oversight of the State regulator and shall have no further obligation to pay any form of license fees to the Commission." So Okodu Power's licence fees run to ASERC and to nobody else — and the ASERC schedule does not exist in public form. That is an unpriced item in this plan's own cost base, not a documentation gap.

The likely reason, and it is worth knowing before the Group asks. ASERC's own Clause 6 is near-verbatim boilerplate from NERC Regulation NERC-R-0110A (2010), which points to "Regulations for Licence and Operating Fees 2010" — and ASERC's clauses 13(d), 14(b) and 15(c) are NERC's word for word with the year swapped. A new regulator working from a borrowed template has left a dangling cross-reference to a fee instrument it has not yet made. So the answer to "what are the fees?" may genuinely be "not yet determined" rather than "not published" — which is exactly why the enquiry belongs in the first ninety days, in writing, before any tariff or capital commitment is fixed.

What to request from ASERC in writing: (1) the Regulations for Licence and Operating Fees 2026, or confirmation that none has been made; (2) the licence validity periods, which s.42(10) delegates to the terms set rather than fixing (ASERC's own FAQ Q9 ties them to "the terms set by ASERC under Section 42(10)", corroborated by Electricity Act 2023 s.72(10)); (3) whether captive power registration carries a fee — ASERC's FAQ confirms s.33(3) exempts captive generation for own use below 1 MW, which also confirms a library citation that was previously unverifiable; and (4) the Business Rules signed in June 2026, which are reported by Punch, The Sun and BusinessDay but are absent from ASERC's own /regulations/ page.

A benchmark, labelled as one and not usable as an Anambra figure: NERC's schedule carries a flat ₦1,000,000 administrative fee for a change of shareholding, relevant to the change-of-control analysis below. It is presented as the best available comparator, not as current law — NERC-R-0210A was made under s.96(2)(h) of the Electricity Power Sector Reform Act 2005, a repealed statute, and the Electricity Act 2023 does not itself fix the figures (ss.71(1), 73(2) and 164(a) all defer to a separate schedule). No NERC figure should be used as an Anambra figure. (Fees determined 25 September 2026; the evidence bundle is at .research/evidence/aserc-fees-research/.)

11. Integration

It powers every other group business — as a direct cost saving of ₦7.99bn a year at Year 3, rising as the Group grows, landing on the P&L of every entity. The teaching hospital stops budgeting for diesel. The furniture cluster's kiln-drying line — the most energy-intensive process in the Group — becomes cheap enough to run at full specification. The cold store becomes viable. Every other business plan in this library should be re-underwritten on the post-Okodu Power-Ezeme cost base.

It buys construction from Okodu Group. Substations, control buildings, civil works, trenching, pole erection and the energy compound itself go to Okodu Construction, targeted at 30–40% of programme capex (₦200–270bn over fifteen years at Tranche 3–4 scale). This is a material related-party flow and must be governed as one: competitive tender against at least two external bidders, a benchmarking file per package, independent-director approval, and disclosure to the Family Council. The point is not to route work to the family; it is to build a contractor whose largest customer holds it to institutional standards, so it can win third-party work on merit.

It buys land and infrastructure from Okodu Group. The four Zone A energy plots (₦220m), the injection-substation land, the Idemmili solar land bank, and the Akuzo underground electrical conduit already specified in the Group's street standard. Okodu Real Estate holds and leases; Okodu Power develops. Terms arms-length and documented, because these leases become collateral in the fund structure.

It is the asset class Akunnia Group's infrastructure fund will warehouse and syndicate. Aku Infrastructure Fund I is seeded entirely from Group pipeline, and power is the first and largest seed asset — not logistics, not real estate.

Interface rule. Okodu Power owns the licence and the network. Okodu Solar and Okodu Grid own EPC and O&M capability and bid into Okodu Power's work under the same competitive-tender protocol as Okodu Construction. Okodu Power must remain able to buy from an external EPC, or the Group's cost base is untested and the regulator will notice.

The asset-finance angle

Power is the most financeable asset class the Group will ever own, and Okodu Power is the natural seed portfolio for its first infrastructure fund. The reason is structural, not commercial.

What African pension funds need and cannot source. Nigerian pension assets reached ₦29.52 trillion at 31 March 2026 (PenCom Q1 2026 Industry Report). 58.07% sits in Federal Government securities; alternatives — infrastructure, private equity, REITs, mutual funds and supranationals combined — are 3.95%, and the bulk of that is mutual funds, not infrastructure. PenCom's own risk register names the problem at the top: R1 is real returns falling below inflation, R3 is the FGN concentration, and the prescribed mitigant for both is a shift into "alternatives, infrastructure, and inflation-linked instruments." Pillar 4 of the Commission's programme is to "encourage increased pension fund participation in viable infrastructure... capable of generating sustainable long-term returns." The buyer is not merely willing — the regulator is instructing them to buy, and there is almost nothing qualifying to buy.

The structure. Okodu Power builds, energises and operates Tranches 1–3 to a track record. At Year 5–6 — audited accounts, verified availability and loss statistics, contracted revenue, a live ASERC licence — Akunnia warehouses the operating assets into an SPV and sells 60–70% to Aku Infrastructure Fund I, retaining 30–40% plus the O&M mandate. The Group keeps operational control, releases capital for Tranche 4, and books a development margin. The fund then raises its first third-party close from Nigerian PFAs and DFIs against a portfolio that already exists, already produces cash, and already has audited numbers — the only version of the story that wins a pension mandate.

The inversion this creates. In the Group's architecture, finance is downstream of the asset businesses, and that is correct. It follows that the quality of the finance platform is capped by the quality of the assets it has to warehouse. Okodu Power is therefore not simply Okodu's anchor — it is the proof of concept for whether Akunnia can ever become the leading African asset manager. A fund seeded with a working, licensed, metered Nigerian utility is a fundamentally different proposition from a fund seeded with a plan.

One discipline this requires: the Group must be willing to sell down a performing asset. A family that will not syndicate will never raise third-party capital, and Okodu Power's third and fourth tranches are not fundable on family equity alone.

OKODU SOLAR — Solar & Renewable Energy

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0). FX: naira primary, ₦1,600/USD; dollars indicative, not comparable across plans.

Ezeme Group · Okodu Group (Energy, Construction & Real Estate) · Entity Okodu Solar Ltd (CAMA). Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027. Ownership: Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Okodu Group. Gearing ≤40%; no unhedged USD debt. Companion: 42_Okodu_Power.md — the licensed generation and distribution business. Okodu Solar is the delivery, EPC and O&M arm and holds no distribution licence.

1. Thesis

Nigerian businesses pay the diesel price for electricity, not the grid price. Diesel at ₦1,800/litre ÷ ~2.6 kWh/litre + ₦70/kWh of lubricants, servicing, operator time and genset capital recovery = ₦780/kWh (BusinessDay). Solar plus battery delivers the same kWh at roughly ₦150/kWh. Nothing else in this library has a 5:1 cost gap in front of a customer already paying it.

Grid tariffs are not the reference: Band A ₦225/kWh, Bands B–E ₦40–63/kWh, with government absorbing ₦358.32bn of generation cost in Q1 2026 — 51.95% of the ₦689.72bn GenCo invoice (Zawya/Nigerian Tribune). A subsidised tariff buying eight hours a day is why the generator exists.

One sentence: Okodu Solar sells the meter that replaces the generator — a solar-plus-storage installation priced against ₦780/kWh diesel, earning margin by owning the install, the warranty and the maintenance relationship for twenty-five years.

The Group is its own anchor customer. At ₦1,800/litre Group Year-3 energy spend falls from ₦11.16bn to ₦3.17bn — ₦7.99bn avoided a year against ₦52bn of Tranches 1+2: 6.5-year unlevered payback, ~3.5-year equity payback, holding to 10.2 years at ₦1,200/litre. No external solar business starts with a contracted multi-megawatt pipeline, a balance sheet that can carry a ten-year warranty, and a parent that pays on time.

2. Market

  • Distributed, not utility-scale. Nigeria added 803 MW in 2025 (+141%) to 1.19 GW cumulative — Africa's second-largest market — ~96% off-grid and distributed; battery storage grew ~10 MWh → 40.6 MWh (BusinessDay).
  • The grid does not deliver. Over 13,000 MW installed, less than half reaching consumers (BusinessDay); Gencos waste over 2,500 MW for want of absorption (ThisDay).
  • Our market is the installed base of diesel gensets in Anambra, not the grid's customer list.

Four segments.

  1. Group captive (Yr 1–3). Isiome's plant and cold store; Idenze's plant, university, polytechnic, teaching hospital; Uli's studios and warehouses; HQ and Akuzo. Contracted before a panel is ordered — it funds the capability.
  2. Commercial and industrial (Yr 2–6). Onitsha/Nkpor mills, plastics, packaging, hotels, hospitals, banks, cold chain — creditworthy, daytime-heavy, generator-dependent.
  3. Residential and estate (Yr 3–8). Homes, developers, Group housing — small tickets, highest margin per watt, best referral engine.
  4. Utility-scale and mini-grid (Yr 5–15). Ground-mount on the Idemmili belt and university land — lowest margin per watt, highest capital intensity, only once quality is proven.

3. Product & service lines

  1. Solar-plus-storage package — panels + inverter + LiFePO₄ battery + monitoring, sized to load; ₦/kWp turnkey, 18–25% margin. The core product.
  2. EPC contracting — design, supply, install, commission; fixed-price with liquidated damages, 12–15% margin.
  3. O&M contracts — monitoring, cleaning, inverter service, preventive visits, fault SLA; ₦10–15m per MWp per year, 3–5 year terms, 35–45% margin.
  4. Performance guarantee — contracted irradiance-adjusted yield floor with LDs for shortfall.
  5. Asset management — monitoring, reporting and warranty claims on customer-owned assets; ₦/MWp/year, 50%+ margin.
  6. Retrofit & remediation — repairing other installers' failed systems.
  7. Utility-scale & mini-grid EPC — ground-mount farms and hybrid mini-grids from Yr 5, 10–14% margin.

The product is the package, not the panel. A panel alone produces nothing at 7pm, and Nigerian load peaks after dark. Storage is what makes the system a generator replacement. EPC and O&M are separate contracts: EPC is lumpy and competitive; O&M recurs, compounds and is sold on the asset installed last year. Target: 60% of cumulative MWp under Okodu Solar O&M by Year 5.

The failure mode this business must not have: installation quality. Undersized cables, absent DC protection, no earthing, inverters in direct sun, mismatched strings, batteries without ventilation or BMS commissioning. A bad install delivers 40–60% of modelled yield, fails within two years, voids every warranty and cannot be repaired without redoing the array — destroying the customer's economics and the brand together, and spreading by word of mouth. So installation is the product: a written standard, a photo-documented commissioning checklist per site, QA sign-off by someone who did not build it, and a serialised as-built record.

4. Operating model

The boundary with Okodu Power. Okodu Power owns the ASERC licence, the network, the meters and the tariff. Okodu Solar owns the capability: rooftop, commercial and utility-scale solar plus storage, EPC and O&M. Okodu Solar never distributes, never bills an end user for energy, never holds itself out as a utility. Where a Group facility needs both, Okodu Power is offtaker and network host while Okodu Solar is the contractor — bidding into Okodu Power's work under the same competitive-tender protocol as external EPC firms, so the Group's cost base is tested rather than assumed.

  • Technology. N-type/TOPCon modules, 550–620 W, tier-1 bankable; hybrid string inverters monitored per string; per-string DC and per-inverter AC telemetry to a Nkpor control room — yield is a contractual obligation, so it is measured daily.
  • Battery: lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is the current default, 2–4 hours. Safest chemistry at cell level; tolerates Nigerian ambient temperatures; 6,000 cycles or 10 years to 70% state of health; no cobalt exposure; and where Chinese capacity has concentrated, so it deflates fastest. USD 320/kWh now → USD 280/kWh by Tranche 3: ₦512,000 → ₦448,000 per kWh installed. Decline is a tailwind, but on cost-plus pricing it belongs to the customer — the hedge is the O&M and asset-management annuity, not inventory.
  • Sourcing and the Chinese supply chain. 85–90% of the bill of materials is imported, overwhelmingly Chinese. Two tier-1 manufacturers per component category, never one, seeking authorised-distributor status — that status is what makes a warranty real. Containers move through Uli Freight.
  • Monitoring and performance guarantees. Every system reports to Nkpor; Okodu Solar guarantees an irradiance-adjusted annual yield band per site with LDs for shortfall. Only a company with its own O&M and monitoring can promise that.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Islanded versus grid-connected determines the regulator. The Electricity Act 2023 devolved intrastate electricity to states, but NERC retains jurisdiction where an operation relies on any part of the national grid. Islanded and zero-export sits with the state; grid-connected or exporting sits with NERC. Our default design is islanded/zero-export because it is the cheaper regulatory path.

  • ASERC (Anambra State Electricity Regulatory Commission) — anything touching distribution. Okodu Solar files nothing; it interfaces with Okodu Power's licence.
  • ASEMA — technical standards and per-installation safety sign-off; licensed electrical contractors.
  • NERC — grid-connected or exporting installations: permit, NISO interface, interconnection agreement; 6–18 months.
  • SON — SONCAP conformity per consignment (SON); NIS/IEC 61215, 61730, 62109.
  • NESREA + Anambra Ministry of Environment — EIA for utility-scale ground-mount, and a battery e-waste and end-of-life plan, which is a licence condition, not an afterthought.
  • Import duties and VAT (NCS/FIRS) — ⚠️ VERIFY. Planning range 5–20% duty plus 7.5% VAT.

⚠️ The duty position is a live variable. Effective duty on modules, inverters and lithium cells has moved repeatedly and is applied unevenly across HS codes. CPPE has pressed for a 5% duty with a VAT waiver (Nairametrics); REAN documents the procedural friction (REAN); balance-of-system items have historically been taxed differently from modules (Heinrich Böll Stiftung). Verify with a licensed customs agent in the first ninety days, re-verify every six months, and budget the top of the range — never model a waiver. A ten-point error is ~₦150,000–200,000 per kWp.

The principle, and the acquisition route it forces

A licence is never a reason to defer or omit the business. The Group either obtains it or buys an entity or an asset that already holds it — and in solar the thing worth buying is not the paper but the installed base, the NEMSA-certified technical team and the EPC track record that no amount of filing produces.

Every value above is therefore [verify] and must come from a valuation and a diligence file, not a listing. What is not in doubt is the shape of the trade: a licence, an installed base and a certified technical team are three things the Group cannot manufacture quickly, and can buy in one step.

Named, costed first-ninety-days action: a ₦150m acquisition and diligence mandate (planning figure, Group budget) to shortlist three operating licensed mini-grids and three established Nigerian solar EPC firms holding live NEMSA corporate certification, run technical yield, warranty, as-built and title diligence, and instruct counsel on ASERC s.40 consent, NEMSA certification transfer and share-purchase structuring. 7. Unit economics

The avoided-cost calculation against diesel is the primary return metric — not ROCE, which is secondary. What wins the customer and the board is the naira per kWh the Group stops paying a generator.

Break-even, worked. Year-3 fixed overhead ~₦1.45bn; EPC gross margin ~12% on a blended ₦1.70m/kWp (₦204m per MWp); O&M contribution ~₦105m from a 25 MWp serviced base. Overhead is covered at ~6.6 MWp installed per year; below that, every contract won loses money. Hence the Group captive tranche goes first — it supplies ~3 MWp of Year-1 volume and reaches break-even without a single external sales call.

Payback by segment. Group captive (200 kWp–3 MWp): 3–5 years to the customer, 6.5 years blended to Okodu Solar. C&I (50–500 kWp): immediate on a ₦320–420/kWh PPA against ₦780; 6–8 years to Okodu Solar. Residential and estate (5–50 kWp): 6–9 years cash, or a lease. Utility-scale (5–50 MWp): 8–12 years on a 15–20 year PPA.

Financing structures, and Akunnia's role. Cash sale — no credit risk; Akunnia's role is treasury only. Lease — Okodu Solar owns the asset, the customer pays monthly; Aku Capital funds the receivable and Aku Insurance covers credit and residual value. PPA — the customer buys kWh at ₦320–420 against ₦780, and the contracted 10–15 year cash flow is exactly the long-dated, inflation-linked instrument Aku Infrastructure Fund I exists to hold.

Two floors, and they differ. The running-cost parity floor — where a solar kWh stops beating a diesel kWh — is roughly ₦270/litre at ₦175/kWh rooftop and ₦208/litre at ₦150/kWh ground-mount. The capital-recovery floor — where a commercially-financed solar-only asset no longer repays inside its life — is roughly ₦700/litre. Most of the case is not the diesel price anyway: it is that a customer paying ₦780/kWh today has no alternative. ⚠️ VERIFY — re-base on the 90-day generator audit before committing capital.
