First ten hires, in order. (1) Managing Director — has run a solar EPC or IPP at scale, not a distributor. (2) Technical Director — COREN-registered PV/BESS design; owns the technical standard. (3) Head of QA & Installation Quality — independent of project managers, with authority to refuse commissioning; installation quality is the industry's core failure mode and this is the role that answers it. (4) EPC Project Manager — schedule, subcontractors, LDs, safety. (5) Head of O&M — inverter fleet, string diagnostics, BESS health. (6) Procurement & Supply Chain Manager — Chinese suppliers, SONCAP, LC and FX. (7) Commercial & Finance Controller — PPA and lease modelling. (8) Sales Lead, C&I — sells against the diesel bill. (9) Master Electrician — NEMSA/ASEMA-licensed; protection and earthing. (10) Monitoring & Performance Engineer — telemetry, yield reporting, warranty evidence.

Training, and why the Group's polytechnic makes it cheap. Okodu Solar cannot hire its way to 78 technicians; it must make them. Idenze Polytechnic's Electrical & Electronic Engineering Technology department — 780 students, with a solar rig already in its equipment budget (25_Idenze_Polytechnic.md) — is the supply. Stand up a Okodu Solar Academy there from Year 2: an NBTE-accredited two-year pathway in PV installation and commissioning, BESS integration, DC protection and earthing, and O&M diagnostics, with paid attachment on live sites from semester two. Target 40% of technician hires from the polytechnic by Year 3, 75% by Year 5, 100% by Year 8.

11. Integration

Inside Okodu Group, Okodu Solar installs for every Group facility: Isiome's processing plant and cold storage, Idenze's pharma plant, university, polytechnic and teaching hospital, Uli's studios and warehouses, the Group estates and Akuzo. It does not duplicate Okodu Power — Okodu Power holds the licence, the network and the meter; Okodu Solar builds and services the generation and storage behind it, bidding against external EPC firms under a documented competitive-tender protocol with independent-director approval and Family Council disclosure.

  • Okodu Power — offtake, hosting, metering and control-room integration in; solar/BESS tranche work out. Arms-length terms.
  • Okodu Construction — foundations, roof strengthening, carports, ground-mount civils in; site power out.
  • Uli Freight — container freight, customs clearance and inbound haulage in; depot rooftop solar out.
  • Isiome — the cold store only becomes viable on cheap daytime power; plant and cold-store arrays out.
  • Idenze — technicians via the Polytechnic in; campus and hospital arrays, plus the solar rig and Academy teaching content, out.
  • Akunnia — credit cover, insurance, treasury and PPA/lease structuring in; the contracted cash flows Aku Infrastructure Fund I exists to hold, and installed assets as fund collateral, out.
  • Okodu Real Estate / Estate Services — roof access and the Idemmili and university land bank in; estate packages sold with the unit out.

The finance integration is the strategic one. Okodu Solar originates the asset; Akunnia Capital structures and finances it; once energised and producing audited yield the asset is warehoused into Aku Infrastructure Fund I and syndicated to Nigerian pension funds and DFIs. Nigerian pension assets reached ₦29.52 trillion at 31 March 2026, of which 58.07% sits in Federal Government securities and alternatives are just 3.95% (PenCom Q1 2026). Solar-plus-storage PPAs — long-dated, inflation-linked, collateralised by panels, inverters and batteries — are exactly what PenCom's own risk register instructs pension funds to buy, and there is almost nothing qualifying to buy.

  1. Incorporate Okodu Solar Ltd — ring-fence: own board, two independent directors, own audit. Day 30.
  2. Write the technical standard — install spec, commissioning checklist, as-built register, QA sign-off, refusal authority. This document is the company: before the first order, not after the first failure. Day 45.
  3. Generator audit — litres/hour by load band, hours run, maintenance spend, capex age. The real diesel baseline and the most decision-relevant document in the plan. Day 90.
  4. Load survey by site — hourly profile, criticality, roof condition, shading, switchgear — every Group facility plus the Nkpor/Onitsha C&I target list. Day 90.
  5. Verify customs and duty with a licensed agent: HS codes, duty, VAT, exemption routes; qualify two tier-1 Chinese manufacturers per category. Budget no waiver. Day 75.
  6. Tender Tranche 1 (3 MWp rooftop + 6 MWh BESS) on fixed-price contracts with LDs, mixing international and Anambra-registered bidders. Day 90.
  7. Sign the interface agreement with Okodu Power — offtake, hosting, metering, competitive-tender protocol. Day 60.
  8. Confirm in writing the ASERC/ASEMA standards and the NERC islanded-versus-grid-connected boundary. Day 60.
  9. Scope the Okodu Solar Academy with Idenze Polytechnic — ND curriculum, NBTE route, solar rig, attachment model. Day 90.
  10. Source the first ten hires — MD, Technical Director and Head of QA first. The QA hire is not to be compromised on. Day 90.
  11. Open the Data Room — standards, contracts, as-built register, diesel audit, load surveys, yield data. Day 90.
  12. Fund the acquisition route — approve the ₦150m screening and diligence mandate: three operating licensed mini-grids and three NEMSA-certified solar EPC firms; instruct counsel on ASERC s.40 consent, certification transfer on a share purchase, and warranty and as-built liability. Decision by day 90.

What must not happen: no external installation before the technical standard and QA sign-off exist; no grid-connected or exporting project before the NERC jurisdiction question is answered in writing; no financed sale before credit assessment, security and insurance are in place; and no utility-scale ground-mount commitment before the captive tranche has proven installation quality and measured yield at 3 MWp.

44 — OKODU GRID — Mini-Grids, Embedded Generation, Industrial Supply & Wheeling

Okodu Grid Ltd (CAMA) — ring-fenced Okodu Group subsidiary, own board, licence and audit · Year 1 = 2027 · horizon 15 years · Companions: 42_Okodu_Power.md, 41_Okodu_Group.md, 43_Okodu_Solar.md, 45_Okodu_Construction.md, 46_Okodu_Materials.md, 35_Uli_Freight.md, 25_Idenze_Polytechnic.md.

Decision one — islanded or grid-connected

Every other decision waits on this one.

Section 63(7) of the Electricity Act 2023 makes it "the responsibility of the State Electricity Board or any State authority… to grant licence for mini-grids, IEDN/IEDNOs and IETN/IETNOs" — so ASERC, not NERC, licenses Anambra mini-grids and embedded generation. The proviso decides the regulator: NERC retains power where either (a) the state has no legal and institutional framework, or (b) the operation relies on any part of the national grid.

Anambra closes (a): the Anambra State Electricity Law 2025 created ASERC, with ASEMA for technical standards, and Anambra was among the 16 states that completed the transfer of electricity regulation in early 2026 (EnergyWorth; ThisDay says 15 — verify). Limb (b) is live, and it is a design choice, not geography. Islanded, ASERC licences inside a statutory three-month window; grid-reliant, NERC's residual jurisdiction re-engages for any import, export or wheeling over any part of the national grid.

So Okodu Grid builds islanded by default; a grid connection is a board-approved exception. The s.230(3) window — draft plan in 45 days, completion within 6 months of notification — has closed; Anambra notified in early 2026. The site-level test is the only question left, and it must be answered in writing before capital moves.

1. Thesis

Okodu Grid sells electricity to customers the incumbent cannot reach and the generator cannot beat — islanded, metered, prepaid and dense — because Enugu DisCo loses 41.70% of every unit it handles against a 21.26% target.

Nigerian distribution is a metering and collection problem, not a technology problem: over 13,000 MW installed with less than half reliably reaching consumers (Minister of Power Joseph Tegbe — BusinessDay), on a metering rate of 46.98% (NERC Q1 2025). Estimated billing is where theft hides; a 100%-metered, prepaid, islanded network inherits none of it.

CompanyOwnsRegulator
Okodu PowerLicensed generation and distribution — Nkpor plant, IEDN licence over its own franchiseASERC
Okodu SolarInstallation and EPC — solar, storage, hybrid; no licence, network or customer contractASEMA
Okodu GridDistribution and supply beyond Okodu Power's franchise — mini-grid and IEDN licences, embedded generation, industrial supply, wheelingASERC (islanded)

Okodu Power owns the licence for its own territory, Okodu Grid for everyone else's, Okodu Solar the capability to build for both — and Okodu Grid buys its EPC from Okodu Solar on arms-length terms, which is what tests Okodu Solar's cost base.

2. Market

Enugu DisCo, Anambra's franchise holder, runs 41.70% ATC&C losses against a 21.26% MYTO target; no DisCo met its target, and industry collection efficiency was 74.39% (NERC Q1 2025) — roughly one naira in four billed nationally is never collected. That is the market, and the failure Okodu Grid must not reproduce.

Price against diesel, not the grid. At ₦1,800/litre ÷ ~2.6 kWh/litre plus ₦70/kWh of O&M and capital recovery, the customer's real alternative is ₦780/kWh (BusinessDay). A tariff near ₦230/kWh is a 40–50% saving on what they actually pay, and cost-reflective to ASERC against supply at ₦150–185/kWh. Band A (₦225/kWh) is not the reference: a Band B customer at ₦63/kWh receiving eight hours still runs a generator for the other sixteen.

Four segments, ranked by whether the diesel anchor applies. Group facilities beyond Okodu Power's network (Idemmili farms and cold store, outlying depots, the quarry, rural campuses) and commercial and industrial customers, including industrial supply to manufacturers, both displace diesel at ₦780/kWh — they lead. Estates already running generators come next, on developer-funded reticulation. Communities displace kerosene and dry cells on 500–900 kWh per connection — viable only with grant funding.

Distributed generation is where the market is going: Nigeria added 803 MW of solar in 2025 (+141%), ~96% of it off-grid or distributed (BusinessDay), yet hundreds of mini-grid permits are almost all rural, none an urban industrial franchise. ASERC already licenses private distribution — FirstPower (FPEDC), interim licence, November 2025 (ASERC) — so Okodu Grid will not be first, and the differentiator is density and metering, not territory. The market is the Idemili North corridor: Nkpor, Ogidi, Obosi, Onitsha's industrial fringe — and the customer-density and willingness-to-pay survey is a Tranche 1 deliverable; every connection count here must be validated against it.

3. Product & service lines

Embedded generation is the entry product and the lowest-risk one: one customer, one metering point, a load already logged in the customer's own generator records, no tariff exposure, no community politics — and islanded, so ASERC jurisdiction applies.

Wheeling is last, and complicated. It moves power to an offtaker across somebody else's network — needing a wheeling agreement, a regulator-approved use-of-system charge (Anambra has none) and boundary settlement — and it relies on part of the national grid, triggering the s.63(7)(b) proviso and pulling the transaction toward NERC. Wheel only over networks Okodu Grid owns at both ends; no revenue line here depends on cross-network wheeling.

4. Operating model

Site selection is an engineering screen, not a sales process. A site clears a 15% EBITDA yield only above roughly 5.5 GWh of annual sales per ₦1.5bn of network capex — about 3,700 kWh per connection, or ~690 MWh per km of line per year; community catchments never clear it. Generation is contracted: the core asset is the network, the meter and the customer contract.

Metering, billing and revenue protection — the biggest operational failure mode, stated honestly. Theft and non-payment are the base case in Nigerian distribution and frequently internal: illegal reconnection, meter bypass, unmetered "new" connections created by field staff, cash never banked.

  • Prepaid STS-compliant smart meters (IEC 62055) on every connection, no exceptions. No credit accounts, no estimated billing, no cash collection anywhere.
  • Meter-to-customer ratio of 1.00, enforced, Group facilities included — an unmetered connection is a disciplinary matter — with monthly meter-to-transformer reconciliation; below 78% triggers a name-specific loss audit within seven days.
  • Revenue protection sits separate from field technicians, incentivised on recovery and rotated between zones; vending runs independent of the meter vendor; 2% spares float and a 48-hour meter replacement SLA, because a dead meter is a non-paying customer.

Community relations is where the model changes shape. A captive customer can be metered and invoiced; a community must be negotiated with, because it can physically stop the work. No community is connected without a signed community agreement — tariff and review formula, connection eligibility, lifeline band, local employment, grievance route — with Nkpor-native, Igbo-fluent liaison from Year 1, reporting to the MD.

The principle, and the acquisition route it forces

A licence is never a reason to defer or omit the business. The Group either obtains it or buys an entity or an asset that already holds it — and here that is not a preference but the arithmetic, because a franchise is a bounded thing that can be licensed only once. In Nigerian electricity the licence is the scarce asset, so the most direct route to distribution scale is acquiring an existing licensed distribution asset or a private network operator.

The honest limit. There is no Nigerian market in which licensed distribution networks are routinely traded, so prices are negotiated, not quoted: every valuation figure above is [verify] and must be replaced by a valuation, not a listing. The structural point stands regardless — a franchise licensed once is scarce, ASERC is demonopolising, and the company holding a licence, a tariff order and a connection agreement when competition arrives is worth more than the one still waiting on a decision.

Named, costed first-ninety-days action: a ₦200m acquisition and diligence mandate (planning figure, Group budget) to identify two licensed distribution assets, two private network operators and three licensed mini-grids in Anambra, run regulatory, technical, metering and title diligence on the shortlist, and instruct counsel on s.40 consent and share-purchase structuring.   • Year 5 — first wheeling over Group-owned private lines; 20 MW warehoused into Aku Infrastructure Fund I.
  • Year 10 — majority of the portfolio owned by third-party institutional capital, Okodu Grid as operator; 250 MW is the edge of what can be built, and more requires acquiring operating portfolios, so the screening mandate opens in the first ninety days.

11. Integration

Supplies. Okodu Grid distributes Group-generated power beyond Okodu Power's network and serves Group facilities where that network does not reach — the Idemmili farms and cold store, outlying depots, the quarry, rural campuses. Okodu Power powers the campus; Okodu Grid powers everything the campus is not.

Buys. Okodu Construction for network build — trenching, pole erection, civils, substations — at 30–40% of programme capex, tendered against external bidders; Okodu Materials for poles, concrete structures and steel fabrication; Uli Freight for generation equipment, meters, transformers and switchgear; Idenze Polytechnic for electrical engineering graduates and Aku Technology for metering, vending and billing systems.

Financed by Akunnia Capital — and the network asset is a natural fit for its infrastructure fund. A distribution network is the purest form of what Nigerian pension funds are under-allocated to and cannot source: long-dated, inflation-linked, regulated cash flows with hard, immovable collateral. Pension assets reached ₦29.52 trillion at 31 March 2026, 58.07% in FGN securities and only 3.95% in alternatives combined (PenCom Q1 2026); PenCom's own risk register prescribes a shift into "alternatives, infrastructure, and inflation-linked instruments." Wires and meters cannot be sold on a grey market and are paid for in advance — the closest thing to a bond the Group can build.

12. First ninety days

  1. Obtain the jurisdictional determination in writing — ASERC and NERC, per intended site, on whether each is islanded or grid-reliant under s.63(7). This gates everything. Incorporate Okodu Grid Ltd in parallel with two independent directors (utility regulation; infrastructure finance).
  2. File the mini-grid and IEDN applications with ASERC in person in Awka, diarising the statutory three-month window from a complete filing.
  3. Commission the customer-density and load survey across Nkpor, Ogidi, Obosi and the Onitsha fringe. This validates or kills each segment.
  4. Open the embedded-generation pipeline — twenty C&I targets, their generator logbooks as the load study, one signed PPA before any network capital — and tender the prepaid metering platform (vendor-independent vending, IEC 62055, 48-hour replacement SLA).
  5. Recruit the first five hires — MD, Regulatory & Licensing, Chief Engineer, Metering & Revenue Protection, Community Liaison.
  6. Set the site screen as board policy — the 5.5 GWh/₦1.5bn density gate, the 1.00 meter-to-customer rule, the 72% break-even line, and a ban on unmetered connections.
  7. Sign the intercompany interface terms with Okodu Power, Okodu Solar, Okodu Construction, Okodu Materials, Uli Freight and Idenze Polytechnic, board-approved — and open the Data Room for the fund raise.
  8. Fund and staff the acquisition route — approve the ₦200m screening and diligence mandate: two licensed distribution assets, two private network operators and three licensed mini-grids in Anambra; instruct counsel on ASERC s.40 prior written consent and on structuring as a share purchase; decision by day 90.

What must not happen: no customer connected before prepaid metering is live; no grid-connection application before the islanded design is fixed; no community mini-grid without grant co-funding; no Tranche 2 capital before the ASERC/NERC answer is in writing.

OKODU CONSTRUCTION — Building & Civil Contracting

Naming: companies take a child's name plus a plain function; Ezeme Group is the mother company, Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu its five groups (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

Ezeme Group · Okodu Group (Energy, Construction & Real Estate) · Entity: Okodu Construction Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Okodu Group Ltd. Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027 · ₦1,600/USD flat. Naira primary; dollar figures indicative only (spot NFEM ≈ ₦1,328/USD, Sept 2026).

The builder named in the Group's own documents. The Akuzo Development Programme specifies a newly formed development-and-construction subsidiary as employer of record for the workforce, holder of all site contracts and long-term owner of retained units; holding the build inside the company rather than through a turnkey contractor "gives direct cost visibility and quality control" and creates "a reusable crew and management structure for future developments." Okodu Construction is that company — and the delivery arm of Akuzo Development (#48): the developer owns land and sells units; this company holds the site contracts and the crews.

Companions: 42_Okodu_Power.md, 46_Okodu_Materials.md, 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md, 50_Akuzo_Development.md.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Okodu Construction is the Group's own builder first and a commercial contractor second — internal-only work carries fixed overhead against a lumpy programme, external-only work gives no cost visibility, no quality control and no reusable crew on the Group's own ₦127bn build.

Construction will absorb more Group capital over fifteen years than any other input: university, polytechnic, teaching hospital, pharma plant, processing lines, warehousing, power compounds, staff estates and Akuzo storeys are already decided. The only question is whether that money leaves as a contractor's invoice or stays inside as margin, control and a Year-15 asset.

Why both roles must be held. Internal work alone justifies the structure, but averages only ~8,400 m² a year — below the level that structure needs to be paid for. Together the roles are a load-balancing mechanism: external work fills the valleys and keeps crews and plant utilised, while Group projects supply a backlog no rival has.

The differentiator is deliberately uneconomic. The plan requires one senior COREN- or ARCON-registered engineer or architect retained full-time at an above-market rate — the strongest supervision, not the cheapest. Anambra is short of supervision, not masons: buy supervision at a premium, sell the quality at a premium.

2. Market

Size. Construction was last reported at ₦19.36tn against real estate at ₦58.16tn (Punch); real estate stock is separately valued at $2.60tn (Punch). GDP grew 4.43% year-on-year in Q2 2026, with cement output up 12.75% (Investors King); construction and trade offset weak manufacturing (Trading Economics; The Sun; Guardian).

The housing deficit is badly measured — cited at 17m–28m units by methodology, hence the new national housing data system (Radio Nigeria). The failure is affordability and quality, not demand: a moderate three-bedroom home exceeds ₦20m in materials alone (BizWatch; BusinessDay). This company does not compete for the bottom of that market.

Commercial and institutional work is the Group's own demand: campuses, hospitals, GMP plants, cold storage, warehouses, power compounds, estates. A named, registered, resident supervisor is a tender requirement, not a marketing claim, and public work increasingly demands registration and grading (Vanguard; The Sun).

Material inflation is the defining condition. Cement is up 367% in seven years (The Cable) and building materials roughly 400% (Tribune), with cement at ₦11,000–15,000/bag in 2026 (Daily Trust) amid a building-materials crisis (The Sun). The gap this opens is not price but transparency: when inputs move 20–40% inside a project's life, only contractors who can prove what a change cost survive.

4. Operating model

Direct labour — the core commitment. Every mason, iron bender, carpenter, electrician, plumber, tiler and labourer on site is on the company's own payroll, from Nkpor and the wider Onitsha corridor, not routed through a labour agency. Deliberate and expensive: NSITF/PenCom/ITF compliance, verifiable pension and accident cover, company-accruing training, and supervisory authority a subcontractor's margin cannot mediate. Payroll, welfare and safety are administered direct — weekly payroll, a welfare block, a first-aid post, free PPE. Labour is 22–28% of building cost.

The resident supervisor. One senior COREN-registered civil engineer or ARCON-registered architect, full-time at an above-market ₦30–42m/year against the ₦18–25m an equivalent engineer commands locally. He stamps drawings, approves every pour and reinforcement fixing, may stop work in writing, and reports to the board independently. The first hire.

Crew structure. Each project runs a project manager, site engineer, store officer and trade foremen — masonry/concrete, iron fixing, carpentry, electrical, plumbing, finishing. Foremen are permanent staff, not per-project hires. Ratios hold: 1 foreman to 12–18 tradesmen, 1 site engineer to 2–3 foremen.

Procurement. Direct from manufacturer or accredited distributor, on a three-quote, board-thresholded schedule tracked monthly against the QS budget. Bulk lines sit on framework agreements with volume ceilings and monthly price resets: a monthly reset is the hedge inflation demands. Cement reconciled against concrete produced.

Plant: owned or hired. Own the high-utilisation, low-mobility kit — mixers, vibrators, bar cutters, pumps, scaffolding, formwork, batching plant from Tranche 2. Hire the high-capex, low-utilisation fleet — excavators, tower crane, piling rigs, concrete pumps, tippers — until a 12-month pipeline justifies purchase: an idling owned excavator is fixed cost with no revenue.

The reusable-crew advantage. Because the same supervisor, foremen and tradesmen carry forward building to building, mobilisation cost and learning curve fall with each successive project: a second storey building should mobilise in 40–50% less elapsed time than the first, and cost per m² should fall 6–10% by the third.

The principle, and the acquisition route it forces

A licence is never a reason to defer or omit the business. The Group either obtains it or buys an entity or an asset that already holds it — and construction is the clearest case in the domain, because the things that take longest here are not certificates but the qualifications and the tender record that sit behind them. A firm registration is cheap and quick; five years of supervision history, a classification grade and a prequalification file are not, and are exactly what a purchase buys.

RequirementIssuerDirect route — cost / timeAcquisition route — what to buy, process, timeRecommended
Engineering firm registration — engineering consultancy organisationsCOREN, under s.11 of the Engineers (Registration, etc.) Act, Cap E11 LFN 2004s.11(2): "No firms or partnership shall practice as engineers in Nigeria unless it is registered by the Council." s.11(1): "The Council shall register annually all organisations performing engineering consultancy services." Requirements: the MD or a director must have been a registered engineer for at least five years, and that director must have at least three years in a construction company; plus CVs and current practising licences of the engineers on the board, CAC certificate, C02, C07, Form 1. See the caution below on the 90% rule and on whether this registration is required at all.
Contractor registration — and note whose function this isBPP federally; Anambra State Bureau of Public Procurement under the Anambra State Public Procurement Law 2011 (as amended)COREN does not register contractors and says so in the Act — s.11(3) proviso: "the Council shall not be involved in the registration of contractors." Contractor registration is a procurement function, and the plan's earlier draft conflated the two. BPP registration is entity-attached.

⚠️ Three corrections to this table, all verified against Cap E11 — and one of them may take the registration requirement away entirely.

(i) The 90%-Nigerians rule is NOT in the Act. This table previously attributed to s.11(2) a requirement that "90% of all cadres of registered practitioners must be Nigerians." The figure 90% appears nowhere in Cap E11 — zero occurrences — and the Act's only three uses of the word "Nigerian" concern the Nigerian Society of Engineers and Council membership. The Act in fact points the other way: s.17 provides for the "Provisional registration of persons not citizens of Nigeria." So the 90% rule, if it exists at all, sits in COREN's regulations made under s.11(3) — or in no instrument. It is the only workforce-level citizenship test in the entire library, it sits inside a licence this business depends on, and it must not be relied on until sourced. (The five-year and three-year director requirements are likewise sourced to COREN's registration form rather than the Act and should be confirmed at the same time.)

(ii) It is not established that Okodu Construction needs firm registration at all — and the library never raises the question. s.11(1) is framed around organisations performing engineering consultancy services, and the s.11(3) proviso removes contractors from the Council's remit entirely. Okodu Construction is a building and civil contractor. Whether a contractor is caught by s.11(2)'s general words or excluded by the s.11(3) proviso is a genuine question, and the answer changes which Group companies need the registration and which do not. COREN's own assembly papers cut both ways — "the scope of engineering firms registration limited only to Consulting firms" (2019) supports exclusion, while the consulting page's 55% shareholding test implies a narrower class again. Put it to COREN in writing as the first question, before assuming the registration is required.

(iii) A term correction that does not change this plan's logic. A 2018 Amendment Act — a certified copy of the Bill as passed by both Houses, assented 18 March 2019 and gazetted 25 March 2019 — reportedly makes the renewal term biennial (inserted as s.6(5) by s.7) and deletes s.11(3), whose contractor proviso survives in equivalent form at s.21(c). COREN's own published papers corroborate the biennial rule in the regulator's words: "registered engineering consulting firms shall have their practicing licenses renewed biennially … (meaning once every two years)", and separately confirm that "construction and manufacturing companies are outside the regulation of COREN." So the compliance calendar is two-yearly, and the scope exclusion is the regulator's own stated position.

Two traps for the next reader. A "consolidated" copy of the 2018 Act circulating from a professional body still prints the deleted contractor proviso — verify against the Gazette, not a consolidation. And the contractor words are a proviso attached to a regulation-making power, not a standalone prohibition, which is why the proposition survives either way and only its location is in question.

What this does and does not change here. The acquisition logic is unaffected — a buyer still acquires the completed-works record, the plant, the order book and the classification, because registration follows named engineers whichever way the scope question falls. What changes is whether the registration is needed at all, what it requires, and how often it renews. (Cap E11 LFN 2004 read directly 25 September 2026; all of the above verified against its text except the 2018 Amendment Act and COREN's regulations, which are characterised from the Gazette copy and COREN's own papers and could not be independently confirmed from a writable copy in this session.)

Against Cap E11 LFN 2004, all three citations are correct. Read from the Act: s.11(1) says "register annually"; s.11(2) reads "No firm or partnership shall practice as engineers in Nigeria unless it is registered by the Council"; and s.11(3) carries the contractor proviso in the words this table quotes. The paraphrases are close to verbatim and the section numbers are right.

But a 2018 Amendment Act is in force and changes two of them. The amending instrument is a certified copy of the Bill as passed by both Houses — bearing the Clerk to the National Assembly's certification under s.2(1) of the Acts Authentication Act Cap. A2, passed by the Senate 6 June 2018 and the House of Representatives 16 October 2018, assented 18 March 2019 and gazetted 25 March 2019. It deletes s.11(3) ("by deleting subsection (3)") and provides a biennial term, inserted as s.6(5) by s.7 of the amendment. So the operative renewal cycle is every two years, not annual.

That conclusion is corroborated twice from the regulator's own authorised papers — which matters, because it means this is not a claim resting on a third-party reading:

  • "Engineering Regulation in the Post Covid-19 Era" (COREN-hosted, July 2020), p.21: "registered engineering consulting firms shall have their practicing licenses renewed biennially … (meaning once every two years)" — and at p.23, "construction and manufacturing companies are outside the regulation of COREN."
  • "The Making of the New COREN Act, 2018" (28th COREN Engineering Assembly, August 2019), slide 12: "The scope of engineering firms registration limited only to Consulting firms."

Two traps for the next reader, both real.

  1. A "consolidated" copy of the 2018 Act circulating from a professional body still prints the contractor proviso after s.11(2) — an artefact contradicting the amending Act's own instruction to delete s.11(3). Anyone checking from that copy alone reaches the wrong conclusion. Verify against the Gazette, not a consolidation.
  2. The contractor words are a proviso attached to a regulation-making power, not a standalone prohibition — and a differently-worded but equivalent proviso survives at s.21(c). So the proposition holds either way; only its location is in question. Confirm which with COREN in writing.

What this does and does not change here. The acquisition logic below is unaffected — a buyer still acquires the completed-works record, the plant, the order book and the classification, because registration follows named engineers either way, and COREN's own papers confirm that construction and manufacturing companies sit outside its firm-registration scope. What changes is the compliance calendar (biennial, not annual) and the scope question (consultancy organisations, not firms generally — with a 55%-shareholding test on the consulting page rather than the 90%-Nigerian rule on the contracting page). Put both to COREN in the first ninety days. (Cap E11 LFN 2004 read directly 25 September 2026; the 2018 Amendment Act characterised from the certified scan and corroborated by COREN's own assembly and guidance papers.)

What a mid-size Nigerian contractor costs is not public, and the plan will not pretend otherwise. No disclosed Naira or dollar price for a mid-size Nigerian construction company could be found, and no published EV/EBITDA or turnover multiple specific to Nigerian construction exists — both are explicit negatives, not gaps to be filled with an estimate. What is on the record is the listed leader: Julius Berger turned over ₦567.7bn with ₦29.6bn profit before tax — a PBT margin of about 5.2% — which is the sector's thin-margin reality and the reason a price cannot be anchored to earnings (Julius Berger 2025 Investors Forum). Valuation must therefore be built bottom-up — asset and plant base, WIP and order book, certification and classification, receivables quality — and any seller's quoted multiple treated as unbenchmarked. [verify]

The acquisition logic, stated precisely, because the qualification is the trap. The buyer is acquiring four things that cannot be manufactured quickly: a COREN-registered Engineering Construction Firm with its completed-works record, an Anambra classification grade, a plant and directly employed site workforce, and a clean PenCom/NSITF/ITF file. It is not acquiring the engineering qualification as such — the five-year registered standing and three years in construction attach to named people, can equally be hired, and must be contractually secured either way. The registration is annual and conditional, so the deal documents must keep the qualifying board members in place, and the same applies to ARCON and to the state classification. Where those people will not stay, buy the plant and hire the engineers instead — the registration is not transferable without them.

Named, costed first-ninety-days action: a ₦180m acquisition and diligence mandate (planning figure, Group budget) to shortlist three COREN-registered contractors on the Anambra register and two with federal prequalification, obtain the classification grades and completed-works records in writing, and instruct counsel on change-of-control registration, PenCom/NSITF/ITF and tax indemnities. Decision by day 90.

Working capital is the constraint in contracting, not equipment. Plant is substitutable, deferrable and hireable at a day rate; payroll and materials are neither. Payroll leaves weekly; valuations are certified monthly and paid in 30–60 days privately and 90–180 days publicly, with 5–10% retention split between practical completion and a 6–12 month defects period — so each ₦1bn of annual contract value needs ₦180–260m of permanent working capital. Working capital and bond margins are 47% of the ₦55.4bn requirement against 41% for plant.

Bonds. Performance bonds are typically 10% of contract value, advance-payment guarantees match the advance, and banks require 10–20% cash or counter-indemnity margin — a capital line, not a fee line.

Verification caveat. Own-plant depreciation at 5-year straight line; site establishment ₦60–90m per major site; yard on Group-held Zone A land at no cost. These are planning rates, not quotations, and must be replaced by firm quotes before Tranche 2 approval.

  • Year 10 — commercialise. 130,000 m² built, ₦15bn a year external; teaching hospital and pharmaceutical plant delivered; net margin ≥7%, Group work under 40% of revenue.
  • Year 15 — compound. 230,000 m², 80 projects, ₦34bn annual revenue; regional expansion beyond Anambra; Group work no more than a third of revenue; the Group's built-environment delivery engine.

Ezeme Group · Okodu Group (Energy, Construction & Real Estate) · Entity Okodu Materials Ltd (CAMA). Horizon 10–15 years · Year 1 = 2027. Companions: 42_Okodu_Power.md, 41_Okodu_Group.md, 45_Okodu_Construction.md, 50_Akuzo_Development.md, 35_Uli_Freight.md.

Boundary with Isiome Manufacturing — stated here as well as there, because it is a real overlap. 61_Isiome_Manufacturing.md also manufactures industrial goods, and a second block yard must not be built. The rule, which is reciprocal and should be confirmed by a board minute in the first ninety days:

Okodu Materials manufactures construction materials for the Group's own build programme, at transfer price. Isiome Manufacturing manufactures goods sold to third parties, to other Group domains and to the open market — and takes the products Okodu Materials has deliberately excluded: roofing, pipes and fittings, packaging, solar mounting structures, enclosures, cleanroom fixtures and processing equipment. Where the two lines genuinely overlap — concrete products and light fabrication — Isiome takes the non-structural and non-construction specification (pavers, kerbs, road furniture, light sheet-metal) and supplies only as a second source to Okodu on nominated projects.

Why the split is drawn this way. Okodu Materials exists to internalise the Group's construction input cost — it is a captive supplier to a captive customer, and its economics depend on transfer pricing inside the Group. Isiome Manufacturing exists to convert the Group's own consumption into a margin earned from third parties — it needs external customers to reach utilisation. Merging the two would give one entity a captive customer and an external market with no clear pricing rule, which is how internal suppliers become uncompetitive and invisible. Also note the tariff finding in 01_Isiome_Group.md: agricultural and manufacturing machinery went to 0% import duty on 1 July 2026, so neither company can rest its case on tariff protection — proximity, logistics cost and service responsiveness must carry it.

1. Thesis

In Nigerian construction, material costs inflate faster than contract prices can be adjusted. The contractor who buys at market absorbs the inflation; the contractor who owns the input keeps the margin.

Cement went from about ₦7,500 a 50 kg bag in Q4 2024 to ₦12,000–₦16,000 by August 2026, with a 23% rise in a single week. Over the same window blocks rose from ₦600 to ₦1,100, 30 t of sand from ₦165,000 to ₦250,000, 30 t of granite from ₦530,000 to ₦780,000 and rebar from ₦850,000 to ₦1,150,000 a tonne (BusinessDay); cement is up 367% in seven years (TheCable). A contractor who priced in late 2024 absorbed +35% on steel and +113% on cement with no route to recovery.

One sentence: the Group is already building power plants, a 100-hectare university campus, a teaching hospital, a pharmaceutical plant, warehouses, cinemas and a residential district at Nkpor and Akuzo — committed demand enough to justify owning the blocks, the steel, the timber and the rock, which is the difference between a construction margin and a loss.

Internalising supply also removes a failure mode. Nigerian projects routinely stop for material unavailability, a spike between order and delivery, or a supplier who takes the deposit and delivers late. Schedule certainty is worth more than the transfer-price saving: delay on a hospital costs months of idle payroll.

2. Market

Nigeria has ~62.8m tonnes of installed cement capacity a year and three producers hold over 90% of it — yet prices run near double the African average and the FCCPC has opened an investigation into possible price manipulation (BusinessDay). Surplus capacity with rising prices means the constraint is distribution and logistics, not clinker. Cement sits at ₦11,500–₦15,000 a bag (Bizwatch); poor roads drive the increases (Guardian).

(Cement price — [verify] against the verified market. See NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md. This plan carries two different current ranges, and both sit above the best-verified market. §1 above states ₦12,000–₦16,000 by August 2026 (BusinessDay); this paragraph states ₦11,500–₦15,000 (Bizwatch); and §7 plans on a ₦12,500/bag bulk base. The two ranges are separately sourced and they overlap, so neither is arithmetically wrong, neither can be shown to be the error, and neither has been altered — but a single range should be adopted for a plan whose whole sensitivity is the cement price. An independent 2026 Nigerian cost guide puts a 50 kg bag at ₦8,500–₦12,500 (Rosettee, July 2026), so both of this plan's ranges are above the verified market — conservative, which is the safe direction for a cost base, but it raises the modelled variable cost of a block and brings §7's ₦20,000 stress case closer than it looks. Cement is regional, and the plan may have a local Anambra source that justifies the higher band, so the plan's own figures stand unchanged. 4. Operating model

Manufacture or trade — the sequence, and why

Starting with the plant is the wrong order. Trading first buys the knowledge that sizes every later manufacturing decision, and it ends the Group's failure mode in the first quarter, not the third year.

Capital is risked in that order because capacity is proven before it is built — and the quarry, the largest fixed cost, is filed first and built last: a Quarry Lease runs five years and must survive EIA, royalties and a community agreement.

Siting near Nkpor

The yard belongs on Nkpor's industrial zone, within 5 km of the Akuzo and campus clusters and on a corridor Uli Freight already runs — never inside Akuzo's residential zoning, and always on tipper-grade access, with land reserved for the batching plant and precast beds. The quarry cannot be at Nkpor: it goes where the rock is, which makes it a haulage business with a pit attached.

Blended energy is 15–20% of production cost. At Okodu Power's ₦150/kWh against diesel at ₦780/kWh, each internal kilowatt-hour is worth ₦630: 10 GWh a year by Year 5 avoids roughly ₦6bn a year of diesel cost and lifts Okodu Power's own utilisation.

Quality control and standards

Underspecified blocks are the market norm, because weakening the mix is the fastest way for an informal yard to survive a cement spike. An in-house laboratory from Year 1 supports blocks tested every 5,000 units (failures scrapped, not sold cheap), timber certified at 10–12% moisture, steel with mill certificates and bar-schedule traceability, aggregate graded to a standing sieve specification, and quarterly third-party verification. Certification is the sales proposition to hospitals, universities and schools.

The principle, and the acquisition route it forces

A licence is never a reason to defer or omit the business. The Group either obtains it or buys an entity or an asset that already holds it — and this is the plan where that rule is worth the most money, because the two instruments on the critical path here are a mineral title, which takes 9–24 months, and a MANCAP certificate, which delays revenue while capex depreciates. How a quarry title is actually transferred — read from the Act, and it is materially easier than this plan previously stated. (Corrected 25 September 2026: the previous version of this passage relied on a law-firm gloss and overstated the requirement. The Act has now been read — Nigerian Minerals and Mining Act 2007, s.147 — and it says something different and more favourable.)

What the Act actually says. s.147(1) makes a mineral title transferable "subject to the approval of the transfer by the Minister and registration of the transfer with the Mining Cadastre Office" — not the "prior written consent" this plan previously quoted, which is a practitioner's gloss rather than the statutory words. s.147(3) sends the application to the Mining Cadastre Office, not to the Minister. And three provisions the plan omitted all reduce the risk:

ProvisionWhat it doesWhy it matters here
s.147(5)"The Mining Cadastre Office shall approve a transfer… if the transferee is a qualified applicant, provided that the application for transfer shall be deemed automatically approved if not acted upon by the Mining Cadastre Office within thirty days from official receipt thereof."A 30-day deemed-approval clock. The consent is not open-ended, and refusal by inaction is not available to the regulator. This is the most valuable provision in the section for acquisition timing
s.147(6)"The approval of the Mining Cadastre Office shall not be required for an assignment to an affiliate, where the obligations of the affiliate are guaranteed by the assignor or by a parent company."A structural route this plan does not use. A transfer within the Group — or to an affiliate whose obligations the seller or a parent guarantees — may need no MCO approval at all
s.147(2)Rights may be "wholly and partially assigned, sub-leased, pledged, mortgaged, charged, hypothecated or subject to any security interest."The title is bankable. It can carry security, which matters directly for financing the acquisition

And two provisions that change the mining section for the better

1. There is no ownership, citizenship or foreign-interest test on a corporate mining title — verified from the Act's qualification sections.

s.48(a) makes "a body corporate duly incorporated under the Companies and Allied Matters Act" a qualified applicant for an Exploration Licence, and s.50 makes the same for a Mining Lease ("a body corporate duly incorporated under the Companies and Allied Matters Act or other legal entity that…"). Nothing in ss.47–51 attaches any ownership, citizenship or foreign-interest condition to the holder, whatever its ultimate ownership.

So unlike broadcasting — where s.9(1)(a) requires majority Nigerian share ownership — a mineral title can be held by a company owned through the Mauritius chain. This is the one licence family in the library where the Group's ownership structure raises no question, and the contrast is worth stating because the reverse has been assumed elsewhere in the library.

2. The Act does legislate about controlling shareholders — in s.53, not s.147 — and that contrast is decisive reasoning.

s.53 ("Prohibition of certain persons from obtaining mineral titles") bars the MCO from granting a title where "within a period of five years before the date of the application a shareholder holding a controlling share of the applicant has been convicted of an offence under this Act."

So the Act reaches a controlling shareholder when it wants to — and it says nothing about share transfers in s.147. The silence therefore reads as deliberate rather than an oversight, which is the strongest available support for the view that a share purchase is not itself a transfer requiring approval. Note the limit, though: s.53 is a fit-and-proper conviction bar, not an ownership bar — it disqualifies a criminal controller, not a foreign one.

One internal ambiguity to put in writing, because s.147 does not resolve it. s.147(1) says "the approval of the transfer by the Minister"; s.147(5) says "the Mining Cadastre Office shall approve." Which body in fact issues the approval — and whether the 30-day deemed-approval clock reaches the Minister's limb — must be asked, not assumed. Add it to the three questions already listed at the end of this section.

What the Act does not say — and this corrects the earlier correction. The "disposal of controlling interest" doctrine, that buying the company is itself a transfer requiring consent, appears nowhere in s.147 and nowhere in the NMMA 2007. The source the library relied on introduces it with the words "In practice" — it is practice, not statute, and should be tested rather than assumed.

The corrected position: a share purchase does not straightforwardly sidestep s.147, because s.147(10) bars assignment "to a person to whom that mineral title could not have been granted" and practice reads a change of control as a transfer. But the process is an MCO application carrying a 30-day deemed approval and an affiliate carve-out — not an open-ended Ministerial discretion. The diligence consequence is that the three questions to put in writing are now precise: (1) does the MCO treat a change of control as a transfer; (2) will it confirm the 30-day deemed-approval clock in writing; and (3) does it accept an affiliate structure under s.147(6) for this transaction.

Three diligence items follow from that, and all three are conditions precedent. First, the title's own health: MMSD has revoked thousands of dormant and under-utilised mineral titles for non-payment of annual service fees and failure to develop, so verify at the MCO that the target's service fees, returns and development milestones are current — arrears travel with the title. Second, the transferee test: the Minister's consent turns on whether the buyer is a qualified applicant, so the Group's own financial and technical capacity is part of the filing, not a formality. Third, the 30-day clock: MCO approval is deemed automatic if the office does not act within 30 days of official receipt — which is the one genuinely fast step in this chain, and means a well-prepared application should not sit for months.

What this company deliberately excludes — the reciprocal boundary with 61_Isiome_Manufacturing.md, restated because an acquisition is exactly where it would be broken. Okodu Materials makes what the Group builds with, at transfer price; Isiome Manufacturing makes what the Group and the market buy. Okodu Materials therefore acquires quarries, block yards, cut-and-bend steel lines, timber yards and precast plants for structural and construction specification — and must not acquire, or absorb through any acquisition, roofing and accessories, pipes and fittings, packaging, solar mounting structures, enclosures, cleanroom fixtures, processing equipment, or the non-structural concrete lines (pavers, kerbs, road furniture) and light sheet-metal fabrication that Isiome has taken. No acquisition may create a second block yard. Where a target's product mix straddles the boundary, the boundary rule is applied and board-minuted before the bid, not after completion — and where the straddling is real, Isiome is offered the excluded lines first, as a nominated second source.

Named, costed first-ninety-days action: a ₦220m acquisition and diligence mandate (planning figure, Group budget) to shortlist two titled quarries and two MANCAP-certified block or concrete plants in Anambra and Enugu, run reserve, CDA, title, environmental and certificate diligence, and instruct counsel on Ministerial consent for mineral-title transfer, share-purchase structuring and the boundary rule with Isiome. Decision by day 90.

11. Integration

Okodu Construction is the anchor customer. Transfer at benchmark-minus 5–10% on 30-day terms against an 18-month rolling schedule — targeting 60–70% of Year-1 output and 70% of the Group's construction material spend by Year 6. But every internal package is priced against two external quotations, and Okodu Construction may buy elsewhere if we are not competitive.

Akuzo Development is the second anchor and the Group's best precast customer: its street standard specifies covered precast drains with steel-mesh baskets every 40–50 m, plus kerbs, culverts and structural steel for 27 storey buildings and 216+ apartments — a repeating catalogue, not a project.

Timber serves the furniture and soft-furnishings clusters, the reason the kiln exists: the Group requires kiln-dried timber exclusively, against Anambra timber that warps in three to five years. The apprenticeship cluster's Branch 3 is Materials & Timber Supply — this is that branch, industrialised.

Power comes from Okodu Power — 10 GWh a year by Year 5, its largest industrial customer, avoiding about ₦6bn a year of diesel cost. Uli Freight carries the tonnes, capturing the ₦7,500-to-₦26,000 pit-to-site spread. Idenze Polytechnic supplies the technicians. Akunnia Capital finances and warehouses it: the trading book is a natural inventory and receivables asset, and the quarry is a licence-backed, inflation-linked seed asset for the fund.

The interface rule: Okodu Materials must remain able to buy from third parties and sell to third parties. A supplier that can only sell internally is a cost centre with a letterhead.

What must not happen: no crusher ordered before the QL is granted and the CDA signed; no yard inside Akuzo's residential zoning; no block line sized above contracted Group demand — build to the schedule, not the ambition; no open credit to contractors; no capital for precast or ready-mix before blocks and steel run above 50% utilisation; and never enter cement manufacturing.

Okodu Materials is not a materials company that happens to have a captive customer. It is the Group's margin-defence mechanism, with a merchant arm attached — and the merchant arm is what will prove the business was worth owning.

OKODU REAL ESTATE — Property Holding, Management & Letting

Naming follows ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0). Naira is primary at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM, Sept 2026); dollars are indicative only; figures are constant Year-1 naira.

Entity: Okodu Real Estate Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Okodu Group · Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027. 45_Okodu_Construction.md builds; 46_Okodu_Materials.md supplies; 59_Okodu_Housing.md is the build-and-hold residential business — this company acquires land and develops it, and Housing builds homes and keeps them for rent. Boundary: land bank, development and the commercial/Akuzo portfolio sit here; residential build-to-hold and letting sit in 59_Okodu_Housing.md; management of the finished stock sits in 60_Okodu_Estate_Services.md.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Okodu Real Estate is the Group's property holding, letting and management arm — and it exists beyond its own returns because it converts Nigerian residential and student real estate, which the market prices at 3–6% gross and therefore cannot warehouse, into long-dated, index-linked, contractually committed rental income that Akunnia Capital's funds can place with African pension funds.

Why rental income is the Group's most financeable asset class. Every other Group business sells into a competitive market and is re-underwritten annually. A rented building is not: duration (30–50 years against 3–5 year cycles, matching pension liabilities), contractual escalation (an annual review in the lease — the inflation linkage a fixed-coupon FGN bond does not give), hard collateral (immovable, chargeable, insurable) and size (one transaction can hold ₦5bn).

The honest problem. Anambra residential lets at roughly 4–6% gross on new cost — too thin to lever at naira rates above 20%, far below the entry yield a pension fund needs, so as speculative letting the portfolio is un-financeable. The answer is the captive anchor tenant: Idenze University's 6,000-bed commitment, staff housing demand and the five groups' office requirement convert speculative letting into contracted, index-linked, sponsor-backed income priced as infrastructure — the move Okodu Power makes in contracting captive load before ordering a panel.

Two businesses, run apart. The Master Plan calls the portfolio self-financing by Year Eight — achievable, but not from rent alone: a development-and-sales engine manufactures capital, a rental book manufactures the asset class. Finance sits downstream of the asset businesses, so Akunnia's platform is capped by the quality of the assets it must warehouse.

2. Market

Rents are repricing violently. Anambra self-contained units that let for ₦250,000–300,000 now let for ₦500,000–600,000 (Vanguard); two-bedroom flats now let past ₦1.5m (The Harmattan News); residents have petitioned the Governor (Punch); Nnewi's crisis is deepening (The Sun). The driver is cost: cement reached ₦11,500–15,000 per bag in 2026, roughly a 367% rise (BizWatch, BusinessDay), and security concerns push tenants toward serviced buildings (Guardian).

The quality gap is the product. The Group's own analysis is that the passenger elevator is "the single most visible quality differentiator in Anambra residential property," signalling "a category of building that does not currently exist in most of Nkpor." The official housing deficit was pegged at 15 million units in July 2026 (EnviroNews) — contested, so read as direction, not precision.

Yields by category. Purpose-built student hostels are reported at 16–24%, the highest-yielding residential format nationally, because pricing is per bed (Nigerian Real Estate Blog) — against Lagos luxury residential in the mid single digits (Northcourt H1 2025). A peer-reviewed study finds secondary-city residential property often lags inflation (IIARD, 2026) — why leases here are short and annually reviewed.

Student demand is contractual; diaspora demand builds badly. Idenze University's Phase 1 provides 1,000 beds at ₦1.6m per bed per year, rising to 6,000, maturity 12,000 students at ~60% resident (24_Idenze_University.md); the polytechnic follows at years 7–9 — the only residential format with a single creditworthy tenant that has published its bed requirement, so it is built first. Igbo diaspora capital flows home into land and houses (NaijaOnPoint) — overwhelmingly self-built, unmanaged, unlet.

Competitors and the specific gap. There is no institutional landlord in Nkpor or Onitsha: the market is fragmented individual landlords and developers who build to sell, with no South-East-focused institutional developer of consequence. The gap is not supply but custody — nobody holds, manages and lets residential property at institutional standard, or originates rental income as an investable asset.

Flagged for local verification: rents and sale prices by unit type; commercial rent per square metre; the tenancy statute in force; title status per plot; comparable student bed pricing. None should be assumed from national averages.

4. Operating model

Acquisition. The Group's standing-interest method: every Akuzo property that comes up for sale is acquired at fair market price — no pressure, no manipulation — so sellers approach the Group first. Zone D plots are budgeted at ₦25m–₦100m; the land budget allocates 27–42 Akuzo plots at an average ₦60m.

Development via Okodu Construction. Fixed-price, open-book contracts with a benchmarking file per package and at least two external bidders, priced against real cost rather than transfer price.

Letting. One standard agreement, one to two year terms — never longer, because the short term is the inflation linkage. Rent annually in advance; agency and legal fees capped at one month.

Collection and arrears. Billing and receipts run on Aku Technology — no cash. Because rent is taken in advance, arrears surface at renewal, not in collection. Ladder: day 7 reminder, day 14 notice, day 30 statutory notice of intention to recover possession, day 60 instruction to counsel. Self-help eviction is prohibited in every circumstance.

Facilities and service charge. A planned-preventive schedule for lift, pumps, water treatment, generator, roof and drainage, with a per-building sinking fund. The lift OEM contract is non-negotiable — the elevator is the differentiator, the largest safety exposure and the most visible failure. Service charge runs through a designated account per building on published budgets, audited accounts and a 95% recovery target; where recovery fails the deficit falls on rent (NIESV Journal).

Retained-floor and by-law structure. Each commercial building retains one full floor — three units plus its share of common circulation — under the company name; the other four floors, twelve units, are sold on the open market. Default: retain the ground floor, because upper floors carry a natural price premium for view and privacy, so selling higher floors captures more revenue, and ground-floor units give the company the management office and caretaker presence it needs. The retained floor is ring-fenced in the building-management by-laws from the outset, so buyers understand the ownership structure before purchase and the by-laws — not a private arrangement — carry the management mandate over the twelve third-party units, the service-charge administration right and the ground-floor use.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Title and structure. Every acquisition is perfected by Deed of Assignment plus Governor's Consent, registered at the Anambra State Land Registry, Awka (three to nine months — verify the queue); physical planning approval runs three to six months per building. The company is ring-fenced with its own board, two independent directors (property valuation; tenancy law), its own audit and a related-party protocol.

Tenancy law is moving. Anambra's Assembly moved to enact a rent control law in 2026 (Vanguard; Anambra State Government), and the Governor has declared war on illegal agent fees, the 10% commission and youth development levies (BusinessDay). The first ninety days must establish the statute in force — whether the Rent Control and Recovery of Residential Premises Act (Cap R4 LFN 2004) or a new state instrument applies to Nkpor — and the recovery procedure. Read the reform as opportunity: it harms the small landlord extracting cash from a captive tenant, not one whose buildings are the reason the rent is payable.

By-laws and tax. Management by-laws are registered and incorporated by reference into every sale deed and tenancy agreement, carrying the service-charge covenant. The company pays CIT on rental profits and VAT where applicable (residential letting is generally outside VAT — verify), remits withholding tax on rent paid to third-party landlords under management and pays CGT on disposals; Land Use Charge and LGA tenement rates fall on the buildings, while buyers of the twelve sold units carry their own personal income tax. Indicative only — confirm every rate with FIRS and the Anambra IRS before the first filing.

The principle, and the acquisition route it forces

A licence is never a reason to defer or omit the business — and in Nigerian real estate it is not a licence that is scarce but title. The Group either perfects it or buys land that is already perfected. Virgin communal land carries probate, family-claim and consent risk that can take years to clear; buying land already covered by a Certificate of Occupancy costs more but removes the single largest risk this company carries.

What perfection actually costs in Anambra, from the state's own published schedule. The Ministry of Lands guideline sets C of O charges at a ₦2,000 form, a ₦50,000 non-refundable application fee (state land), and a premium per square metre by layout — at Unity Layout, Nkpor, ₦1,000/m² residential and ₦2,500/m² commercial; non-state land runs on bands from ₦250,000–₦300,000 (1–1,000 m², urban residential) to ₦850,000 (2,501–5,000 m²), with direct tax of ₦250,000 per individual — ₦500,000 where the applicant is a company, two directors each — stamp duty at 0.03% of premium, and CGT of ₦50,000–₦160,000 by area. The Ministry commits to 60 working days after all fees are paid (Anambra Ministry of Lands). Separately, the state's April 2025 fee review raised the consent fee for perfection of title documents from 1% to 7% of value, with stamp duty at 2%, registration ₦10,000, computer ₦20,000, recertification ₦25,000 and ground rent of ₦15/m² residential and ₦30/m² commercial (Allen & Marylebone).

So the honest arithmetic, on this plan's own ₦60m plot: the fee stack lands at roughly ₦6m–₦8m — about 10–13% of value — plus three to twelve months, before legal fees and before the risk that the title still fails. The 20–40% premium is larger than the fee stack. The Group pays it anyway, and the reason must be stated precisely rather than glossed: it is buying certainty, speed and a saleable title, not a cheaper transaction. Where the discount on virgin land is under roughly 15%, the premium is not justified on fees alone. Where it exceeds that — and in Nkpor it does — buying perfected land is cheaper than the discount is worth. The consent-fee rate applicable to an assignment (as opposed to a mortgage) must be confirmed in writing with the Ministry in the first ninety days. [verify]

What to demand before a naira is paid — and it is a checklist, not a negotiation: root of title and the vendor's own acquisition documents; a survey plan signed by a registered surveyor with evidence of its deposition; the Certificate of Occupancy or the instrument actually relied on; the executed Deed of Assignment; probate — letters of administration or the will — where the vendor is an estate; kindred and family resolutions with every necessary party executing and witnessed; excision and gazette evidence for the layout; receipts for ground rent, Land Use Charge and tenement rates; the vendor's tax clearance; and a Land Registry search at Awka against the survey coordinates, plus physical inspection of the land against the survey (Ministry of Lands). Any one of these missing is a reason to renegotiate the price, not to proceed on a promise.

Named, costed first-ninety-days action: a ₦95m title audit and acquisition mandate (planning figure, Group budget) — ₦25m to audit every Akuzo and Zone B/C/D plot and search each title at Awka, ₦40m for Governor's Consent filings on two already-perfected plots, and ₦30m to shortlist five plots already under a Certificate of Occupancy, with counsel instructed to obtain the Ministry's assignment-consent rate in writing. Yield on cost exceeds yield on market value in every line, and that gap is the development margin — it exists only because Okodu integrates construction and materials. Akuzo premium residential lets at 4–6% gross, and 3.5–5% net of voids and operating costs — below the cost of naira debt. So speculative letting is never levered, and the formats that work have captive tenants: student beds at 9–12%, commercial above 20%.

The cap-rate gap, and how contracted income closes it. At a 10% naira capitalisation rate, a held building's ₦54m net operating income is worth ₦540m against a ₦1.16bn cost basis — a 53% loss; at 6% it is worth ₦900m, still a loss. Speculative residential letting cannot be sold to a Nigerian pension fund at any price the Group can afford. The same building on a 15-year index-linked nomination agreement to Idenze University, or leased to Group companies for staff housing with a parent covenant, is priced on contracted cash flow, not cap rate, as the market prices a regulated utility. The Group is its own anchor tenant.

At a 25% development margin the sale of four floors repays the entire building and the retained floor costs nothing — the arithmetic behind the Group's self-financing claim, which works by sale-plus-retention, not by rent. Across this programme's 24 buildings (16 held, 8 for sale) it delivers 24 owned units at zero net cost, worth ₦2.86bn, plus the management mandate over 96 third-party units at a 7.5% fee on service charge and 5% of rent collected.

Assumptions. Annual rent escalation of 12–15% against assumed CPI of ~15–18%, anything better being upside. Occupancy: 90% in year one of lease-up, 93% by Year 5, 95% at stabilisation; student beds contracted at 80% minimum occupancy; Group commercial at 100% for the term. Operating ratios: management 8–10% of collected rent, maintenance 10–12%, insurance and security 6.5–8.5%, service-charge recovery 95% — a blended 25–30%, giving a 6–7.5% net-on-cost portfolio yield at stabilisation.

(3) Head of Facilities & Maintenance — lift contracts, preventive schedule, sinking fund. (4) Head of Tenancy Enforcement & Compliance — a lawyer: statutory notices, lawful recovery, no self-help eviction. (5) CFO — property accounting, service-charge segregation. (6) Property Accountant. (7) Head of Sales — the development margin belongs to whoever owns the price list. (8) Development Manager — Okodu Construction interface. (9) Community Relations Lead — Nkpor-native. (10) Data & Systems Lead — Aku Technology billing. 40% of technical hires from Group institutions by Year 3, 75% by Year 5.

Sales revenue is the Akuzo programme — a one-off funding engine, not the asset class. Year 3 adds 400 student beds let under the Idenze University nomination agreement; Year 5 adds a net yield on cost ≥6% and the first warehousing transactions into SPVs offered to Aku Capital; Year 10 reaches 3,237 units under management at 94% occupancy on ₦5.8bn of rental and fee revenue and places the rental-income sleeve into an Aku Capital vehicle with a first third-party close; Year 15 operates the second-city portfolio without consuming Group equity.

10. Risks

1. Tenant default and arrears (High). Rent annually in advance; payroll-linked staff rent; a 7/14/30/60-day ladder; Aku Technology arrears analytics.

2. Void periods (High). Twelve months' operating cost held per building in lease-up; annual-review leases; student beds at 80% minimum occupancy.

3. Maintenance cost inflation (High). ~367% cement inflation; a sinking fund from service charge reviewed annually; rolling vendor contracts; Okodu Materials and Construction insulate where outsiders cannot.

4. Title defects (Very high). Governor's Consent on every acquisition; Land Registry verification; 5% due diligence; per-SPV clean-up before any fund transaction — a defect found after a sale to a pension fund is unrecoverable.

5. Rent control or tenancy regulation (Very high). Anambra is drafting a tenancy law now. Comply before it passes; hold revenue in the contracted formats rent control least reaches and prepare for statutory renewal rights.

6. Over-supply in the local market (Medium). Sized to the Group's land budget, not market ambition. Build against sales, never ahead of them; if a competitor matches the elevator, compete on management quality.

7. Currency exposure on imported fittings (Medium). Order price fixed, not delivery price; localise through Okodu Materials and the Group's furnishing clusters; no unhedged USD debt.

8. Reputational risk of aggressive enforcement (Very high). The strategy is framed as development, never acquisition — destroyed by one televised eviction. Self-help eviction prohibited absolutely; lawful process under a published policy; a hardship protocol applied; the Akuzo Development Council consulted before any recovery reaches a household.

9. The asset class does not price (Very high). If Nigerian cap rates never fall, the fund exit fails. Validate with Aku Capital and two PFAs in the first ninety days, before Tranche 2.

11. Integration

Built by Okodu Construction, supplied by Okodu Materials. Every building goes to 45_Okodu_Construction.md on fixed-price, open-book contracts with structure, blockwork, joinery and external works localised — 70–75% of programme construction value, ≈₦95bn over fifteen years. It is the plan's largest related-party flow and is governed as one: competitive tender against two external bidders minimum, a benchmarking file per package, independent-director approval, disclosure to the Family Council. This is not patronage: the 23% cost advantage in Section 6 is the margin that makes the model work.

Powered by Okodu Power, metered. 42_Okodu_Power.md supplies metered electricity to every unit, and metering is what makes the saving real — each tenant pays for their own consumption, so the landlord does not carry an uncapped utility cost through inflation, historically the commonest cause of residential landlord failure in Nigeria. It is also why held rental buildings need no solar array, battery bank or LPG grid — roughly ₦1.31bn avoided across the 16 held buildings, and why held-spec cost is ₦77m per unit against ₦95m for the sale spec.

Houses staff from all five groups and students from Idenze University and Idenze Polytechnic. Staff housing is the portfolio's highest-quality tenancy: payroll-linked, indexed, collected at source, so collection is effectively 100%, and the Group converts a cash housing allowance it would otherwise pay to anonymous landlords into a fixed asset it owns — which "lowers the cost of living and makes Group employment a more compelling proposition than any competitor in the area." Student beds are let under a nomination agreement with a minimum-occupancy floor, built to the University's Phase-1 1,000-bed requirement and scaled to 6,000. Commercial space for the Group HQ, Akunnia's finance and legal office, Uli's media premises and Isiome's Agro-Processing HQ is let at arms-length, board-approved rents benchmarked against external comparables, because these leases become the contracted revenue a fund coordinates.

Supplies the rental-income asset class to Akunnia's funds for syndication. Okodu Real Estate builds to a track record, not a valuation: audited service-charge accounts, verified occupancy, contracted escalations, independent valuations. From Year 5, stabilised assets move into SPVs and are offered to 09_Aku_Capital.md's Aku Infrastructure Fund, with Okodu Real Estate retaining the property-management and facilities mandate. Note the boundary: the fund owns the asset, Okodu operates it. The Group keeps operational control, releases capital, books a development margin and creates audited track record — subject to Aku Capital's own constraint that no fund be more than 25% Group-originated, stepping to 15% by Year 6. 11_Aku_Technology.md carries billing, arrears ageing, service-charge apportionment and per-building cost reporting — the platform that later supplies a pension fund's investor reporting. Property data is the product that makes the assets auditable.

Why this asset class matters to the Group's finance platform

Long-dated, inflation-linked rental income is precisely what African pension funds are under-allocated to and cannot source. Nigerian pension assets reached ₦29.52 trillion at 31 March 2026, of which 58.07% sits in Federal Government securities while alternatives — infrastructure, private equity, REITs, mutual funds and supranationals combined — are 3.95% (PenCom Q1 2026 Industry Report). PenCom's own risk register names real returns falling below inflation as risk R1 and FGN concentration as R3, prescribing a shift into "alternatives, infrastructure, and inflation-linked instruments." The regulator is instructing pension funds to buy what they cannot find.

Nigeria has no deep market in inflation-linked bonds: a fund can buy a fixed-coupon FGN bond and watch inflation eat it, or take equity risk it is not mandated for. A rented building with a contractual annual review is the most practical inflation-linked, long-dated, naira-denominated instrument available in this market — with hard, immovable, insurable collateral and no technology obsolescence risk.

This is why Okodu Real Estate is not merely a landlord but the originator of assets for the Group's funds. Nigeria's listed REIT market is small and illiquid: investors wanting residential and student rental exposure have almost no instrument to buy, and Okodu Real Estate manufactures them.

The one discipline this requires. The Group must accept that the buyer's entry yield — not its own development margin — sets the price, and must be willing to sell down a performing asset; Tranche 4 is not fundable on family equity alone. The retained-floor portfolio, carried at or near zero net cost, is what lets the Group sell into a fund at an entry yield the fund can underwrite without a loss on the way in. That is why the ground floor is retained.
