plans/50_Akuzo_Development.md  ·  7,158 words

AKUZO DEVELOPMENT — The Akuzo Urban Transformation

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. Akuzo Development is Okodu Group's urban transformation vehicle. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX note: naira is primary; this plan uses ₦1,600/USD. The Group's own Akuzo document used ₦1,360/USD (June 2025) — dollar figures here are re-based and are not comparable with that document's dollar column. Spot NFEM was about ₦1,328/USD in September 2026. See plans/README.md.

Ezeme Group · Okodu Group (Energy, Construction & Real Estate) · Entity: Akuzo Development Ltd (CAMA), with Okodu Real Estate holding the building SPVs. Horizon 10–15 years for the milestones, inside a documented 30-year (2025–2055) Akuzo plan. This is the Group's flagship urban programme.

Companions: 42_Okodu_Power.md, 35_Uli_Freight.md, 09_Aku_Capital.md. Sources: ../text/Akuzo Urban Transformation Plan v3.txt, ../text/Akuzo Development Programme-1.txt.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Akuzo's infrastructure — security, water, roads, schools, civic space — is the same capital expenditure that re-rates every property standing on it, so Akuzo Development buys early, builds to a standard Nkpor has never had, and owns 216–324 apartments by Year 30 in the district it transformed.

The Group's own framing is the operating instruction, and this plan is built on it:

"The Akuzo transformation is not philanthropy. It is one of the most deliberate long-term real estate accumulation strategies in Anambra… As Akuzo's infrastructure improves — security, water, roads, schools, civic spaces — property values rise. Every building Ezeme Group acquires early is worth significantly more by Year 10, and dramatically more by Year 30. The community transformation and the real estate portfolio are the same project."

Why they are the same project, mechanically. A residential district is worth what its services are worth. Nkpor buyers pay for three things they cannot get today: reliable water, reliable power, and a street a child can walk at night. Those are a trench programme, a distribution network and a CCTV system — capital spent once on the community's account, which every apartment the company already owns then collects on forever. The community gets the asset; the company gets the yield on it; neither happens without the other. That is not a metaphor. It is the same trench, the same poles, the same perimeter.

The thesis only pays if the arithmetic survives contact. The Group costs a building at ₦35–50m; its own detailed bill of quantities for the same building comes to about ₦1.6bn — a factor of thirty. That gap decides whether this programme compounds or stalls, and reconciling it before any building is committed is the board's first duty. The thesis is right; the cost basis has to be made true.

2. Market

Nigeria's housing gap is a quality gap, not only a volume gap. The Federal Ministry of Housing puts inadequate stock at 15.2 million units (FMINO). In the South-East the binding constraint is not demand or land; it is that almost nothing is built to a standard a middle-class household will pay a premium for.

Anambra is repricing on infrastructure. Prime residential values have risen across Nigerian cities on an infrastructure-led thesis (Nigerian Residential Market Review 2026; Prime Residential Price Index 2025). In Anambra the state is itself a developer — the government unveiled Seaview Estate in Awka, and private schemes followed (Tribune, Raphmaths/Seaview Amansea). Rents have followed, with two-bedroom flats reported past ₦1.5m a year in parts of the state (Punch, Harmattan News).

Nkpor's gap is specific. Nkpor sits in Idemili North, inside the Onitsha conurbation that UN-Habitat treats as one urban system whose weakness is unplanned densification without a service spine (UN-Habitat). The quality gap shows in four ways: broken internal roads and open gutters; water bought by the jerrycan; two- and three-storey buildings with no lift and no parking; and no street lighting, which turns dusk into curfew for anyone not driving.

The elevator building is a category that does not exist here. Four to six floors, one passenger lift, metered water from a district spine, mains power with backup, tiled stairwells, covered parking, a garden — a product Nkpor has never had at any price. That creates the premium and the risk: there is no local comparable to price against, so the first two buildings are price discovery and the sale assumptions must be validated by three independent agent valuations before Building 1 is committed. Two observations bracket the range: older stock trades cheaply — a four-storey block of flats in Onitsha is advertised at ₦250m (Nigeria Property Centre) — while new-build Awka flats command a clear premium over that (Awka 2-bed average). Nkpor cannot yet charge Awka prices. That is the gap the transformation closes.

Competitors are three: state-led and state-partnered estate schemes (Seaview, Amansea) selling titled, serviced plots and shells in Awka, not Nkpor; regional developers such as Pineleaf Estates selling to civil servants and the diaspora (ThisDay); and the real incumbent — the informal self-builder, who adds a floor at a time to no common standard and no services. Akuzo competes with the self-builder, not with Awka, and its advantage is the one the self-builder structurally cannot copy: a district spine paid for once and shared across every building.

The diaspora is the buyer who pays for quality. Nigeria received about $21.8bn in remittances in 2025 (Vanguard), and Anambra's investment agency is courting it directly (ANSIPPA). That buyer is loss-averse and evidence-driven rather than sentimental (AFRES 2026): they buy clean title, a managed building, a visible street, and someone accountable in Nigeria. Akuzo Development can meet that specification. The self-builder cannot.

3. Product & service lines

Discipline rule. Lines 1–3 carry the capital and are the core. Line 5 is delivered by Okodu Estate Services on a management contract — billing residents is an operating business, not a development business. Line 6 is Akuzo Development as developer and landlord; the trading businesses inside the townships belong to the Group's manufacturing companies. Line 4 earns nothing and is not measured as a business, only as a cost against the future value of lines 1–3.

The townships, and the retired equity model. The original model settled each apprentice into 50% equity of a new production unit. That model is retired. It is incompatible with an institutional-grade cap table: an equity register that grows by a branch per settled apprentice cannot be diligenced, consolidated cleanly, or offered to a pension fund or a listing. The production township — open streets, ground-floor workshop, apartment above, no perimeter wall — remains exactly as specified. Only the entry mechanism changes.

RetiredReplacementEffect

Community participation does not depend on equity. Residents and apprentices get construction and refurbishment wages, workshop leases, Technical College training, and a share of net rental income paid into the Akuzo Community Development Trust. That is a cleaner route to a genuine stake than a slice of an equity register nobody can audit.

4. Operating model

The three zones.

ZoneCharacterPermitted use
Akuzo Residential DistrictQuiet, clean, walkable, greenExclusively residential — no production, commercial or industrial activity
Soft Furnishings & Upholstery ClusterOpen production townshipGround-floor workshops and showrooms, apartments above, open streets, no perimeter wall
Furniture ClusterOpen production townshipKiln-dried timber fabrication; drying yards at cluster edges; apartments above

The residential district is served by the clusters and stays clean because production is next door, not inside. Cluster residents may live in Akuzo and commute, or live above the workshop. Both are valid.

The street standard, on every road in Akuzo. Tarmac carriageway minimum 6 m, two-way · concrete kerbed footpath minimum 1.2 m each side · covered drainage with trash-filter catch basins both sides · solar lighting poles every 25 m with CCTV at every intersection · verge trees (neem, mango, African mahogany) every 10 m · underground electrical and water conduits beneath the footpath zone · building setback minimum 3 m enforced, no encroachments. This standard is a covenant in every sale contract and lease; it is what protects the value of stock the company retains.

The underground water spine. One trench beneath the main road carrying clean water, a sewage collector, a stormwater drain and the electrical conduit — "dug once, maintained permanently." Drainage, water and road paving are sequenced into the same ground opening, so the street is dug once, not three times. That single sequencing decision saves more than any procurement negotiation in the programme.

Acquisition through standing interest, never pressure. Every Akuzo property offered for sale is acquired at fair market price through a consistently expressed standing interest, so sellers approach Ezeme Group first. The policy, in writing and published to the Council: (1) two independent registered valuations before any offer; (2) the approach is always the seller's — no door-to-door canvassing, no repeat unsolicited visits, no offer timed to a family's difficulty, every inbound approach logged; (3) a community right of first refusal on kindred and family land; (4) a thirty-day cooling-off before execution; (5) inherited property requires probate — a diaspora seller without letters of administration is the commonest defective title in the market, and the answer is to help them get probate, not to buy a problem; (6) nothing verbal, ever.

The refurbishment model — Otu Ulo applied to a town. One street or cluster per year decides together to plaster, paint, repair gutters and fix roofs. Residents provide labour; the Group supplies bulk materials at cost through Okodu Materials. Nobody sells anything. This is the Igbo tradition of communal self-help applied to urban improvement, and the before-and-after record does triple duty: community pride, a diaspora sales story, and paid on-site training for apprentices.

The framing rule is a management instruction, not public relations.

"How to frame it to residents: 'Akuzo should become the cleanest, safest, and most prosperous community in Nkpor.' Not: 'I want to develop Akuzo.' The first includes everyone. The second centres you. The real estate strategy must never be framed as acquisition. It is framed as development… This is true. Let that truth do the persuasion."

It has teeth or it means nothing. The company therefore reports one non-financial KPI to its board every year: the ratio of Akuzo households that refurbished their homes to the number that sold to the company. If sales outnumber refurbishments in a street, the framing has failed there and the acquisition mandate pauses in that street until refurbishment catches up. A programme seen to acquire will be stopped — by kindred disputes, by a planning authority, or by the next administration.

Construction. Built by Okodu Construction's direct-labour model: the workforce is on the company's payroll — masons, iron benders, carpenters, electricians, plumbers from Nkpor and the Onitsha corridor as employer of record, not through a labour agency. One senior COREN/ARCON-registered engineer or architect is retained full-time above market rate with authority over quality, safety and every trade foreman, and the same crew and supervision roll from Building 1 into Building 2, cutting mobilisation cost on every subsequent building. Related-party flows to Okodu Construction and Okodu Materials are governed as such: competitive tender against at least two external bidders, a benchmarking file per package, independent-director approval.

Governance — the Akuzo Development Council. The Council is a community institution; the company does not chair, staff or control it. Akuzo Development funds a Community Development Trust receiving a fixed share of net rental income from retained floors, governed by the Council and independently audited; the company publishes its accounts and attends as Real Estate Liaison. The Council's authority is civic, the company's is contractual, and minutes are public to residents. That separation is what lets the Council say no to the company and survive the answer.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Land is the risk. 5% of every land transaction budget is spent on legal due diligence — not a fee to negotiate down, but the cheapest insurance in the programme. No verbal agreements. No informal purchases. At any stage.

Sequencing. Consent, probate and EIA are the long poles, so they start first and run in parallel with everything else. Do not buy on an unconsented deed and fix the title later: Anambra's recertification regime and the planning board's enforcement record show the state tightening, not loosening, and an unperfected title is unsaleable to exactly the diaspora buyer this plan depends on. Current fees, timelines and the status of the recertification programme must be confirmed in writing with the Land Registry and the Physical Planning Board in the first ninety days; the timelines above are planning estimates, not quotations.

The principle, and the acquisition route it forces

A licence, an approval or a clean title is never a reason to defer or omit a business. The Group either obtains it or buys an asset that already has it — and a township is the purest case in the library, because here the approvals are not paperwork about the asset; they are most of the asset's value. A layout approval, an EIA envelope and a formalised residential zoning are the three things a scheme cannot proceed without, and all three take longer than the buildings.

What a scheme with existing approvals is worth relative to raw land. No Nigerian price series isolates that premium, so it must be priced, not quoted: benchmark it as the avoided fee stack plus the avoided carry. The fee stack is published — layout and planning consent, per-structure permits, the C of O premium, direct tax, stamp duty, registration and recertification. The carry is the 6–12 months of EIA, 3–12 months of Governor's Consent and 2–6 months of layout consent that an unapproved parcel costs in delay, priced at the Group's cost of capital. On a scheme of this size that gap dominates the land price, and it is the whole argument for buying approved rather than assembling raw. [verify] against an actual target's books.

Named, costed first-ninety-days action: a ₦70m scheme-approval audit (planning figure, Group budget) to identify every parcel inside the Akuzo envelope that already carries a layout approval, an EIA envelope, a C of O or a formalised residential zoning, register the approval and consent position for each at the Planning Board and Land Registry, and instruct counsel on the state's change-of-developer and assignment-of-development-rights consent process. Report to the board by day 90.

6. Capital requirement

Community infrastructure and real estate are not the same kind of money. Real estate is capital investment generating sale, rental and appreciation returns. Community infrastructure is an investment with no direct return — its return is realised through the value of the real estate portfolio, and it must be funded on that understanding or it will be cut the first time cash is tight.

A. Community infrastructure — no direct return. Group plan, 2025 prices, dollars re-based at ₦1,600.

What the retained floor is actually for. It is not a yield asset: ₦4.2–6.0m a year against a ₦130–170m floor is a low single-digit return, and a plan that pretends otherwise will be disappointed. It is an operating asset — the building manager's office and caretaker presence in every building, a hard appreciating asset, and through the Community Development Trust the funding source that makes the Council independent of the company. The return in this programme is capital appreciation and land, not rent. Anyone underwriting Akuzo on rental yield will conclude it does not work; anyone underwriting a thirty-year hold of titled, serviced, self-managed property in a transformed district will conclude the opposite.

Community infrastructure as the value driver. The mechanisms are specific: the water spine moves a household from purchased jerrycans to a metered tap; the street standard moves a street from open gutter and darkness to drainage, lighting and CCTV; the colleges create a tenant pool with a reason to live within walking distance; the park, sports complex and fisheries make the district a place people choose rather than tolerate. Each of those is a rent and a price. The programme spends ₦549.88m of community money to raise the value of a portfolio it expects to be worth multiples of that. The ordering matters: infrastructure first, acquisition early, construction after.

It holds, conditionally. Self-financing at Year 8 requires all three of: build cost per building landing at ₦650–850m; absorption of 3–6 units a year, with proceeds recycled 100% into the next building rather than distributed; and land banked early, because land is the one cost that rises with the programme's own success. If build cost stays at the bill-of-quantities basis, or absorption runs at 2 units a year, self-financing slips to Year 11–13 and the shortfall is family equity, not debt. 51 — AKU CREDIT

Private credit and direct lending to the African mid-market

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is the second child's group; her companies take the short form "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira is primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Do not compare dollars across plans.

Status: new plan under the Blackstone model in 08_Akunnia_Group.md, not the superseded BlackRock version.
GroupAkunnia Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group
HeirAkunnia — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer
Yield25–35% naira loans; USD-linked where possible
EconomicsMargin and fees on the book; 1.5–2.0% fee + 20% carry over 8% in funds
HorizonYear 1 = 2027; fifteen years

1. Thesis

Blackstone's largest and fastest-growing business is credit, not private equity. Credit & Insurance manages about USD 443bn of the firm's USD 1.35trn (Blackstone 2026 10-K; Investing.com, Q2 2026). Private credit became a multi-trillion-dollar asset class because after 2008 banks retreated from mid-market lending, leaving sound businesses that did not fit a bank's collateral template. Aku Credit is that lender, in Nigeria.

Nigeria's version of the gap is wider. Private-sector credit is roughly 17% of GDP (The Sun); the CPPE puts the real-sector financing gap at ₦50trn (Guardian). With the MPR at 23% (Nairametrics), corporates borrow at 29%+ while deposits earn about 18%. That spread is the business.

Why banks do not serve the middle. Deposits are shorter than a three-year amortising loan; security over chattels and receivables is slow to perfect and slower to enforce; single-obligor limits cap exposure to any one name; workout capability is scarce. Microfinance banks are too small; DFIs are concessional, slow and sized far above the middle. Nobody lends ₦200m–₦2bn for three to five years against cash flow.

The advantage Blackstone does not have. Aku Bank's deposits are the cheapest funding base in the structure (08_Akunnia_Group.md §3). Two caveats are stated now, not discovered later: the CBN Draft Ring-Fencing Guidelines for Closely Linked Entities (June 2026) would bar linked financial entities from lending to one another, and related-party limits bind the bank regardless. §5 names the compliant alternative, and the plan does not depend on the deposit link surviving.

What it is not. Not asset-gathering. A private lender's return comes from loss avoidance, not origination volume.

Warehouse receipts are a real legal asset. Under the Investments and Securities Act 2025, Part XV (s.246(1)) a receipt is "first proof of the holder having proprietary rights in the commodities" (s.246(1)), and transferable by endorsement and delivery (s.249(1)) — security over stored commodities, not a promise. The SEC has made registration of collateral management companies, warehouse operators and warehouses mandatory (SEC circular). Isiome Storage's warehouses and the collateral manager must therefore be SEC-registered first — a Year 1 action.

4. Operating model

Origination → credit committee → documentation → disbursement → monitoring → recovery. Sourcing is Group-internal, from partner banks that have declined but will introduce, and by direct sector outreach.

Underwriting rules.

  1. Cash flow first — minimum DSCR 1.5×, stress-tested at −30% revenue.
  2. Two ways out — repayment from operations and a realisable secondary source.
  3. Enforceable security — debenture, perfection where lawful, guarantees, share pledges; covenants on leverage, interest cover and capex; quarterly field visit by a credit officer, not the relationship manager.
  4. Concentration caps — no obligor above 10% of book, no sector above 25%, Group-related obligors 25% falling to 15% by Year 6.

Funding, in sequence.

The fund structure is the core, not an afterthought. Balance-sheet lending earns spread; lending other people's money earns fees and carry on capital the family did not provide. Aku Credit Management Company (Lagos, SEC-registered) manages Aku Credit Fund I LP (Cayman or Delaware) — third-party LPs plus a Group anchor of ≤25% — lending through Nigerian feeder and co-investment SPVs.

  • Offshore master, Nigerian feeder. A Cayman or Delaware LP is what institutional LPs expect and holds USD capital; a naira feeder registered with the SEC lets pension funds and insurers hold what they are permitted to hold.
  • The Nigerian regime. SEC fund-manager minimum capital runs ₦500m to ₦10bn, new applicants complying from day one, existing operators by 30 June 2027 (SEC guidelines; Aluko & Oyebode). As a new applicant Aku Credit meets the full threshold immediately — a barrier to competitors worth welcoming.
  • Foreign manager. With the manager at the London or New York hub, Nigerian activity may need local registration as a foreign fund manager: build both managers in parallel; [verify] current SEC treatment.
  • Governance. Independent administrator and custodian (never an Aku entity), ILPA reporting, Big-4 audit, an independent chair on each credit committee.

Exits. Amortisation (primary), refinancing once bankable, secondary-market sale, eventually securitisation.

The ring-fencing problem, addressed head-on. The Aku Bank → Aku Credit deposit link is the plan's most attractive feature and the most likely to be prohibited. Compliant alternatives, in order:

  2. Fund from the parent, not a sibling. Equity from Akunnia Group / Aku Capital is not lending between linked financial entities.
  3. Third-party capital first — DFI lines, a rated note programme, fund LP capital — or an arm's-length syndication with the bank, independently approved, never a disguised affiliate facility.

Stage 1 reconciles exactly; Stages 2–4 leave ₦5bn, ₦15bn and ₦30bn of lending capacity unfunded. The likely and legitimate explanation is retained earnings — a lending book at these spreads should retain a growing capital base each year, and the equity column is labelled "retained" from Stage 3. But the plan does not say so, and it must. Retained earnings on a book earning a ~10.8% risk-adjusted margin, against a 3.0–3.75× debt/equity constraint, is the difference between this business being fundable and being a promise — and Stage 3's own equity is already labelled "retained," so retained earnings cannot be counted twice.

A second gap, larger and separate: "Total credit AUM" exceeds fund capital plus book at Stages 3 and 4. Stage 3 states ₦240bn against ₦120bn of fund capital plus a ₦100bn book = ₦220bn; Stage 4 states ₦1.6–3.2trn against ₦480bn plus ₦220bn = ₦700bn. AUM legitimately includes committed but undeployed capital and the Group's platform fees on third-party books, so an AUM figure above deployed capital is not wrong in principle — but a 2.3–4.6× multiple at Stage 4 needs stating, not implying. As written, a reader cannot tell whether the Stage 4 target is deployed capital, committed capital, or a gross-fee metric.

What to fix, and it is a task for the plan owner, not an edit to make here: add a funding column to the table showing, for each stage, equity · debt · retained earnings · fund capital, with the four summing to the book; and define what "Total credit AUM" measures — deployed, committed, or gross. Flagged in ../NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md; the leverage arithmetic error in Stage 4 (3.0× → 3.75×) has been corrected above, but the funding gaps have not been closed.

⚠️ Two corrections and one policy question the Group must settle, because this table breaches the Group's own gearing rule from Stage 2 onwards.

Correction 1 — the arithmetic. Stage 4 previously showed 3.0× against ₦150bn of debt and ₦40bn of equity. ₦150bn ÷ ₦40bn = 3.75×. The row has been corrected. Stages 1–3 were internally consistent and are unchanged.

Correction 2 — the denominator was not stated. The Group's rule is gearing = debt ÷ (debt + equity) ≤ 40%. On that convention this business sits at 71% in Stage 2, 71% in Stage 3 and 79% in Stage 4 — well past the ceiling, from the moment it takes a lending licence. The second row above now states both conventions so the breach is visible rather than hidden by an undefined ratio.

The policy question, stated plainly: a licensed lender cannot operate inside a 40% gearing rule, and the Group needs to decide this deliberately rather than discover it at a credit committee. A private credit book funded 40% debt and 60% equity earns an ROE close to its asset yield — which for a lender is roughly the coupon minus losses, before any of the leverage that makes lending a business. Leverage is not a risk appetite here; it is the product. The correct treatment is therefore not to force Aku Credit under a rule designed for asset-backed operating companies, but to replace it with the controls that actually govern a lender: a hard debt/equity cap set by the board for this company alone (the audit's finding implies something in the 2.5–3.75× range is intended), regulatory capital headroom monitored monthly, wholesale funding maturity matched to loan tenor so the book cannot be called, no cross-guarantees into the bank or the insurer, and — the real constraint — a portfolio loss-rate gate, since a 2-point miss on losses costs roughly 30% of ROE while leverage merely magnifies whatever the loss rate turns out to be. ../NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md §5 flags this as one of two outright breaches in the library; the other is Okodu Power's 60% debt.

52 — AKU PRIVATE EQUITY

Control investing — the business that makes the Group resemble Blackstone

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is the second child's group; her companies take the short form "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira is primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Do not compare dollars across plans.

Status: new plan under the Blackstone model in 08_Akunnia_Group.md — the business the family's founding ambition describes.
GroupAkunnia Group — subsidiary of Ezeme Group
HeirAkunnia — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer
HorizonYear 1 = 2027; fifteen years

1. Thesis

The family's stated ambition is a buyout mandate, not a holding-company strategy. "Orchestrating the structural, private development of African industry from a global hub… buying entire companies, reshaping industries." That is Blackstone's original business: raise capital, buy control, improve the company, sell it, and keep a share of the profit.

The distinction that must stay crisp: the Group builds; Aku Private Equity buys. Isiome, Idenze, Uli and Okodu own plant, employ thousands and make things. Aku PE is a manager: it employs deal professionals, raises capital, buys companies, sets strategy and boards, and exits. Operating companies earn margin; Aku PE earns a fee on committed capital and a share of profits. Confusing the two is how conglomerates end up with an investment arm that is really a treasury function.

Two mandates, deliberately separated.

  1. The Group's own acquisition engine. Bolt-ons for Isiome, Idenze, Uli and Okodu, funded from the Group's balance sheet. This is where "buy rather than build" lives, and it includes buying companies because they hold licences the Group needs — a licensed microfinance bank, a NAICOM insurer, an SEC-registered fund manager. Year 1 activity; no fund required.
  2. A third-party fund. Outside capital earning the Group fees and carry. This cannot launch first — Years 1–5 build the record with the Group's own money.

Why carry does not dilute the dynasty. The family rule is that no equity is issued above subsidiary level, and carry is not equity: it sits at fund level, shares in fund profits, and never confers ownership of Ezeme Group, Akunnia Group or any operating company (08_Akunnia_Group.md §7). Blackstone-grade incentives, with no share leaving the family.

2. Market

African private capital is shifting to larger deals and fewer, more focused sectors, with exits increasing but capital still trapped in older vintages (BusinessDay; AVCA). The defining feature is illiquidity, which is why GP-led secondaries and continuation funds have appeared (betar.africa; secondaries). For an entrant that is good news: a buyer of control in a market where others cannot exit has pricing power.

Sectors: manufacturing, healthcare, food processing, logistics, financial services — each a Group domain.

How Aku PE wins. Pan-African buyout funds and DFI-backed managers have capital and process. None has an operating conglomerate behind it — five domains supplying customers, executives who can be seconded as operating partners, construction at cost, and credit and insurance in-house. Deal flow and operating capability are the edge.

The licence-acquisition line is the fastest route to regulated businesses the Group needs. Aku Bank's microfinance licence, Aku Insurance's NAICOM licence, Aku Credit's finance company licence and Aku Asset Management's SEC registration are all acquisitions of licensed entities, not applications — executed by Aku PE, with diligence focused on licence conditions, regulatory history and change-of-control approval.

4. Operating model

The buyout model.

Thesis-led, not opportunistic. Aku PE invests against four named theses, and declines anything outside them:

  1. Import substitution in manufacturing — producing in Nigeria what is imported today, where the Group already owns distribution (Isiome Trading, Okodu Materials).
  2. Healthcare consolidation — fragmented pharmaceutical distribution, diagnostics and clinics, alongside Idenze Pharma.
  3. Logistics and cold chain — corridors, warehousing and fleets, alongside Uli Freight and Isiome Storage.
  4. Food processing and packaging — aggregation and processing alongside Isiome Foods.

Value creation levers, in order of reliability.

  1. Professionalise management — the finance function first, then operations; formalise accounts; monthly management reporting.
  2. Pricing discipline — the largest and least-used lever in Nigerian mid-market businesses.
  3. Procurement — consolidate suppliers and renegotiate terms; the Group's own domains are often the best suppliers.
  4. Systems and data — one ERP, one chart of accounts, one board pack, on Aku Technology.
  5. Growth capital and distribution — connect the company to Group demand.

Governance of value creation. Using the Group as a supplier or customer of a portfolio company is a genuine advantage and a genuine conflict. Every such arrangement is benchmark-priced, documented as arm's length, and approved by the independent directors sitting alone — portfolio companies must be able to show Group business was won on third-party terms.

Acquiring bolt-ons without a fund. Three tools, in preference order: (i) the holding company balance sheet (Aku Capital), buying small companies outright without fund formalities; (ii) earn-outs, so the seller is paid for performance the Group has not proved; and (iii) staged acquisitions, buying 51–70% now with a path to 100% on agreed metrics. Every deal above the board threshold still needs independent valuation and independent approval, fund or no fund.

The discipline to say no. A fund that overpays destroys value however well it operates. The rule: model the deal at the entry multiple with no multiple expansion — if it does not clear the hurdle on operational improvement alone, pass.

The platform point. Aku Credit and Aku PE are the two halves of the alternatives platform: credit funds the deals for a margin, equity buys them for the upside. Both sit under Akunnia and are managed as one franchise — what Blackstone does, and what no Nigerian competitor is structured to do.

12. First ninety days

  1. Hire the Managing Partner first. The first senior hire is the strategy; without a credible deal originator the fund cannot be raised.
  2. Buy the Nigerian fund-manager licence rather than applying — diligence dormant SEC-registered managers at ₦150m–₦600m over net assets [verify], with counsel engaged on 30 June 2027 tier compliance.
  3. Write the four theses and the no-list, and register the licence-acquisition pipeline — microfinance bank, insurer, fund manager: Aku PE's first transactions, needing no fund.
  4. Close the first bolt-on from the Group balance sheet, integrated and reporting within 100 days. The track record begins here.
  5. Stand up the related-party protocol before the first Group-adjacent deal — independent valuation, approval by directors sitting alone, benchmark pricing, and the 25%→15% Group-originated cap as a board resolution.
  6. Appoint an independent administrator, Big-4 auditor and LPAC, open the track-record file, and open the merger-control playbook with counsel (FCCPC thresholds, SEC takeover rules, sector consents) — [verify] every threshold before signing a term sheet.

53 — AKU LEGAL

The Group's legal function, run as a business — title, contract and compliance

Naming: Akunnia Group is the second child's domain — First Daughter, Matriarch, the Group's designated Chief Investment Officer; her companies take her short form "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md). FX: naira primary, dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Horizon: 15 years, Year 1 = 2027.

Status: not legal advice. Figures marked [verify] need confirmation with the NBA, the CAC, the Anambra State Ministry of Lands and Nigerian conveyancing counsel.
VehiclesAku Legal LP — the practice of law, held by Nigerian legal practitioners personally · Aku Legal Services Ltd — non-practising work only
MandateMaster Plan §6.2 — "all land title conveyancing, Igba Odibo equity documentation, Group contract law, and arbitration"; Holding Structure — "legal structure and compliance"
OwnershipEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Akunnia Group → Aku Legal Services. The practice: Nigerian lawyers only, never the offshore chain
Capital₦240m (~USD 150k) to Year 3. No regulatory capital — there is no licence to buy

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Legal exists because the Group cannot buy land it cannot prove it owns — and proof of ownership is a legal product, manufactured one file at a time.

Anambra land is largely held under family or communal title with no registered instrument, and is routinely sold twice, sold by a branch of a family without authority, or caught by outstanding probate (59_Okodu_Housing.md §5). The Group's rule is already absolute: a Deed of Assignment and the Governor's Consent on every acquisition, 5% of every land transaction for due diligence, "no verbal agreements."

Three claims. (1) Risk control — an unperfected title is a latent dispute that surfaces when the asset is worth most, after construction. (2) Bankability — perfected title makes land collateral, and a Group buying ~₦590m of land a year must be able to charge what it buys: title perfection is a financing function, not a filing function. (3) It is a business — every landowner and developer in Anambra has the same problem, and no in-house answer.

The constraint, stated first. The practice of law is reserved to legal practitioners; a non-lawyer-owned company may neither practise law nor share a practitioner's fees (RPC 2023; Legal Practitioners Act). This is the one Aku company from which the Group may not take a profit. §5 resolves it. Fees are regulated floors: the gain is certainty and speed, not cheap law.

2. Market

The profession is fragmented and thin. Over 80% of Nigerian law firms are small partnerships or sole proprietorships (UNIZIK JHRL, 2025); the capable top is Lagos-centric (Chambers Nigeria) and thin in the South-East for volume title work.

Fees are set by statute, the plan's most useful fact. The Legal Practitioners (Remuneration for Business, Legal Services and Representation) Order 2023 fixes minimum scales — Scale 1 consultation, Scale 2 incorporation, Scale 3 litigation, Scale 4 property, Scale 5 commercial (Order text; overview):

Scale 4 — purchaser's lawyerMinimum fee
Value below ₦50m10% of value
₦50m–₦100m₦5m on the first ₦50m + 5% thereafter
Above ₦100m₦7.5m on the first ₦100m + 3% thereafter

Three consequences. A ₦300m acquisition carries a purchaser-side floor of ~₦13.5m — so the 5% due-diligence rule and the statutory scale are the same order of magnitude, which is why insourcing pays. Fees may not be cut below scale, so this business cannot win on price; and disbursements sit outside the scale — consent fees, searches, stamp duty — with interest at 10% a year (Order, paras 3, 6).

Anambra's stack is published: a ₦50,000 application deposit, CGT from ₦50,000 to ₦5,000,000 by parcel band, stamp duty at 0.03% of premium, and a 60-working-day processing period (Anambra Ministry of Lands); confirm the consent fee percentage before modelling [verify]. Land work is heavily intermediated by non-lawyers (AJLR, 2025), and compliance is permanent — every Group licence needs a calendar, not a per-matter engagement.

3. Product & service lines

2Corporate & commercial law; employmentIncorporation, share transfers, shareholders' agreements, board governance; guard and site-worker contracts, union recognition, disciplineScale 2 / 5; retainerY1

7Third-party title & complianceDiaspora buyers, estates, cooperatives, developers, lendersScale floors, realised below scaleY3

Out of scope by design: administering arbitrations (Aku Arbitration), advocacy for third parties, and any conflicted matter.

4. Operating model

Three desks, one standard: Title & Conveyancing; Corporate, Contract & Compliance; Disputes & Litigation Management. The perfection gate is a Group rule — no capital beyond the option price until search, probate and family-resolution work is complete and the consent is signed and registered.

The title file is the product, and a lender must be able to read it: registry and probate searches, survey overlaid on the deed plan, vendor authority and warranty, kindred resolution, tax clearance, executed deed, consent application and registration particulars — one file, one owner, one deliverable, mirrored digitally in 11_Aku_Technology.md.

The contract factory. Twelve standard forms; deviations require sign-off; related-party contracts are priced arm's length against two external bids. Above a stated value, disputes go to independent institutions — never to Aku Arbitration. Litigation runs through three panel firms per state on capped fees, each matter carrying a case assessment and a reserve recommendation to Aku Insurance. Consent fees, stamp duty and registration fees are third-party money: client account, two signatories, monthly reconciliation, annual audit.

5. Licensing and structure

The constraint, head-on. A lawyer may not practise through, or share fees with, a non-lawyer-owned entity; the RPC governs aiding unauthorised practice, division of fees and salaried employment. There is no practice licence to buy — the asset is people, files and standing. The Mauritius/London chain creates the same foreign-interest problem here as elsewhere in Akunnia: the practice must be owned by Nigerian practitioners, and every registered activity must sit in a Nigerian-controlled vehicle outside the offshore chain.

Practice of lawBody of Benchers / NBAEnrol; Bar Practising Fee and dues [verify]Lift out a practice: recruit a partner-level lawyer and team, take over files with client consent. A 3–8-lawyer Anambra practice: ₦40–150m [verify], ~0.5–1.5× annual revenue

Agency and appointmentsTrademarks, Patents & Designs Registry; Chief Justice of NigeriaRegister as an IP agent; a notary is appointed to an individual [verify]Hire a registered agent, or buy a small IP agency: ₦15–50m [verify]. A notary cannot be bought

The structure adopted: two vehicles, one boundary, no offshore profit from law. Aku Legal LP is owned and managed by Nigerian legal practitioners personally; a law-firm LLP under CAMA 2020 is possible in principle, but the profession's position on it and on non-lawyer participation is unsettled — confirm in writing [verify]. Aku Legal Services Ltd, which may sit under the Group chain, does only non-reserved work — registry agency, records, compliance calendar, contract lifecycle, IP docketing, training — charging arm's-length, cost-plus fees for services actually rendered, with nothing amounting to fee-sharing. Fallback: if the profession forbids even that, the practice is wholly lawyer-owned and contracts with the Group as a client; the Group gets certainty either way and never consolidates the practice's surplus. An independent legal-ethics opinion is the first spend, refreshed annually.

Associates at 3–6 years' PQE are paid at the 75th–90th percentile of the South-East market — indicatively ₦350,000–650,000 a month [verify] — and the offer is: title volume no Lagos firm can match, Group housing through Okodu Housing, autonomy over a portfolio, and a stated partnership track with a fee share inside the practice.

54 — AKU SECURITY

Security coordination for every Group zone, operated as a business

Naming: Akunnia Group is the second child's domain — First Daughter, Matriarch, the Group's Chief Investment Officer; her companies take her short form "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md). FX: naira primary, dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD. Horizon: 15 years, Year 1 = 2027.

Status: not legal advice. Figures marked [verify] must be confirmed with the NSCDC, the Ministry of Interior, the Anambra State Government and Nigerian security-sector counsel.
EntityAku Security Ltd — a Nigerian-controlled company holding the private guard company licence
MandateMaster Plan §6.2 — "Security coordination for all Nkpor zones is also under her domain, ensuring that the Group's legal framework and physical protection operate as a single integrated function"
LicencePrivate guard company licence — Minister of Interior through the NSCDC; plus Anambra State registration under the Homeland Security Law 2025. Acquire a licensed company; do not wait for a new licence
Capital₦1.05bn (~USD 660k) in Year 1, of which ~₦340m is guard payroll working capital

1. Thesis

One sentence: Aku Security exists because the Group's own plan says security is achieved through community integration, not walls — and that is a company, not a purchase order.

The Group's position is explicit: "people protect what they own." The Akuzo plan specifies a community gateway, a 16-camera CCTV network, solar streetlights with CCTV mounts, night patrols in two shifts, and a youth neighbourhood watch (50_Akuzo_Development.md). Bought from several vendors who never speak to each other, those elements are a cost. Aku Security runs them as one system — one standard, one control room, one incident log.

Three claims. (1) The Group is its own first line of defence — campuses, pharmaceutical plants under NAFDAC conditions, warehouses holding other people's goods, a residential portfolio, and a controlled-substance fleet whose diversion would end a licence. (2) Security is a cost the Group already pays, to several vendors with no Group standard: consolidating it is the saving, and the standard is the risk control. (3) It is a business — Anambra's estates and institutions are served by small manpower firms.

The constraint, stated first. Private guarding here is licensed, nationality-restricted and actively enforced, and the Group's Mauritius trust and London hub create a genuine foreign-interest problem for this licence — §5 gives the Nigerian-controlled vehicle that solves it. Acquiring a licensed company is the route; applying for a new licence is the fallback.

2. Market

Large, growing, and favourable to an entrant with a method. Nigeria's private security industry runs over 250,000 personnel across more than 2,000 licensed companies, and the report that measures it concludes the moat has "moved from muscle to method" — technology, third-party validation and regulatory maturity, not headcount (Nigeria Private Security Report 2026). Another count puts it at 1,745 licensed companies and over four million guards (New Telegraph), with 893 firms awaiting licences (Newsexpress).

The demand shock is recent and specific. In early 2026 the Nigeria Police Force began withdrawing personnel from private and VIP guard duties, moving thousands of contracts to licensed firms — "the post-police-withdrawal gap" (Nigeria Private Security Report 2026). Security is now an operating cost and a compliance requirement at once (BusinessDay).

Incumbents are strong in Lagos and thin here — and the report names two openings this plan takes. Kings Guards, Halogen and Terrahaptix lead the ranked field, seven of the top ten are Lagos-headquartered, and the South-East is served by small firms with no control room, no accreditation and no reporting standard. The openings are the professionalisation gap — accredited training is "a scalable, asset-light business hiding in plain sight" — and tech-enablement. The internal market is the anchor: Nkpor zones A–D, the Idemmili belt, Akuzo, campuses, estates, depots and the controlled-substance fleet. No third-party vendor is accountable for a narcotics diversion. Aku Security would be.

3. Product & service lines

#LineScopeChargeLaunch
1Manned guardingClusters, estates, campuses, industrial sites, depots, offices — trained, vetted, supervised, insured₦ per guard per month; per site packageY1
2Community-integrated surveillanceCommunity gateway, CCTV at intersections and on solar streetlight mounts, two-shift night patrols, youth neighbourhood watch run with the town security committeeCommunity contract + Group service chargeY1
3Control room and monitoring24/7 monitoring of cameras, alarms, access control and lone-worker check-ins; incident log and escalation ladder; staffed apart from operations₦ per monitored point per monthY1
4Event, executive and in-transit protectionBoard and family movements, diaspora delegations, events; bank runs, payroll, high-value stockPer event/per movementY2
5Risk assessment and security designSite surveys, threat and vulnerability assessment, security drawings, insurance-grade reportsFixed fee per siteY1
6Controlled-substance and high-value logistics securityTwo-lock sealed compartments, separate keyholders, dual GPS, two-person crews, pre-cleared routes, escort crews, control-tower staffingPremium per authorised movementY1–2
7Guard training and certificationNSCDC-approved syllabus and qualifying examination; third-party courses from Y3Per recruit/per courseY3

Not offered, deliberately: armed private operatives (no lawful framework today), investigations and debt recovery (the Act prohibits debt collection), and any role in a labour dispute.

4. Operating model

One Group standard: a single security manual, approved post orders per site, one incident-reporting format. No site manager buys on price alone; a site wanting a cheaper vendor must show the Board what standard it is giving up. Vetting and welfare are the control, not the uniform: every guard is vetted before deployment — police clearance, guarantors, biometrics, references, NSCDC employee approval — and paid above the national minimum wage with pension, NSITF and group life, because a guard paid below subsistence is a guard for sale. Guard complicity, not the perimeter, is how Nigerian sites lose goods.

Command runs post → shift supervisor → zonal supervisor → 24/7 control room → Head of Operations → Managing Director. The control room sits physically separate from operations and alarms on missed checkpoints, gate failures, camera loss, panic activations and vehicle deviation — logging every alarm whether or not it is later explained (38_Uli_Special_Logistics.md control-tower rule). Community integration is a discipline: a named community liaison officer works with the Akuzo Development Council's Security Coordinator and the town security committee, the youth watch is organised through that statutory channel, and incidents are reported to the Council monthly. In transit: two-person crews, sealed compartments, dual GPS on independent power, pre-cleared routes, checkpoint call-ins. No arms, and no arrest powers beyond citizen's arrest.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

The law, and why it is restrictive. Private guarding is governed by the Private Guard Companies Act, Cap P30, LFN 2004: a licence is granted by the Minister of Interior through the licensing authority (NSCDC); an unlicensed operator cannot recover its fees in court and is closed in enforcement sweeps (Act text; NSCDC sealing unlicensed firms).

Statutory requirementEffect on Aku Security
Licence from the Minister, valid two years, specifying offices and branches (s.4); revocable where ownership or control passes to a company unsuitable to hold it (s.4(4))Change of control is a regulatory event — pre-cleared, not notified afterwards
Every employee requires approval (Forms C and D) with an identity card (s.7)Per-guard approval makes recruitment a compliance process with lead time
Authority shall not grant a licence where a director is not a citizen of Nigeria, or has a firearms, fraud, theft or breach-of-trust conviction, or was dismissed from the Police, Armed Forces, Customs or Prisons (s.13)The foreign-interest problem in one line: the board must be Nigerian citizens with clean records
Uniforms, badges and the training syllabus need ministerial approval (ss.24–25); a licence cannot be sold, let or rented (s.26), with an annual return each January (s.14)Uniform and curriculum are regulatory submissions; the licence is not what changes hands — the company is

Licensing costs are modest; the queue is not. NSCDC practice requires ₦10m minimum share capital and three directors, one a retired senior military or senior police officer, a ₦100,000 Personal History Statement per director, a ₦500,000 processing fee and a ₦2.5–3.0m Category B licence fee (₦3.0m Category A), plus CAC fees, tax clearance, NSITF, police clearances, insurance and NSCDC qualifying examinations for guards — ₦4–6m in total [verify] (schedule). Against that, 893 applications are reported as waiting and only 50 licences were issued in 2025 (NSCDC). Budget 9–18 months [verify] — so buy, do not apply.

Acquisition stepWhat happensIndicative cost
Target and diligenceA Category B holder (up to 3,000 guards is sufficient) with 50–150 deployed guards and a clean, current licence, in Anambra, Enugu or Delta. Check employee approvals against the guard list, uniform and syllabus approvals, pending sanctions, injury claims, wage arrears, unremitted pension, PAYE/NSITF and contract novation₦80–400m trading [verify]; ₦25–80m small or dormant [verify]; fees ₦15–40m [verify]
Structure and regulatoryShare purchase — the licence cannot be transferred (s.26), so the company changes hands. Then written NSCDC/Ministry pre-clearance of the change of control (s.4(4)), a fit-and-proper review of every director (s.13), recapitalisation to ₦10m and renewal — 3–6 months, against 9–18 for a new licenceRenewal ₦2.5–3.0m

The foreign-interest problem, and the Nigerian-controlled vehicle that solves it. Section 13(1)(e) bars a director who is not a Nigerian citizen, and s.4(4) permits revocation where control passes to an unsuitable company. The chain — Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Akunnia Group — cannot sit above this licence. Instead, Aku Security Ltd is held by a Nigerian-controlled vehicle outside the offshore chain, with an all-citizen board of at least three directors, one a retired senior military or police officer. The Group's economic interest is delivered by documented arm's-length management, secondment and systems contracts and by dividends to the Nigerian holder — never by offshore equity or a non-citizen director. Written NSCDC confirmation of acceptability is a condition precedent to any purchase.

Anambra State registration is a second, separate requirement. The Homeland Security Law 2025, s.7(1) requires any person operating a private security outfit or company in the State to register with the State Government, giving particulars of the company and of all armed operatives deployed; s.7(2) empowers the Governor to regulate private outfits to ensure synergy and avoid security conflicts with Agunechemba (Law). That law repeals the Anambra State Group Vigilante Law 2014 and rebuilds community security under Agunechemba at state, local-government and community level, with a Town Security Management and Finance Committee — chaired by the Traditional Ruler — that recruits and pays community operatives (Agunechemba; AVG disbandment). That is the channel the Group's neighbourhood-watch plan needs: the Akuzo youth watch is organised through that committee and the Agunechemba unit, not as a private force, while Aku Security supplies cameras, streetlight mounts, patrol equipment, monitoring and training — registered and sequenced they reinforce each other; unregistered they collide, which is what s.7(2) exists to prevent. The police interface is separate: a memorandum with the Divisional Police Officer on incident handover, arms-free response and joint patrol protocol — a security company has no police powers and must not appear to have them.

It is a working-capital business wearing a security uniform: guards are paid weekly or monthly and clients pay on 30–60 day terms, so two months of payroll must be funded permanently — that line, not the licence, is the real capital requirement. And do not double-count the Akuzo kit: the community's gateway, CCTV and solar streetlight mounts sit in the Akuzo programme's phase-one security line of ₦23.1m (50_Akuzo_Development.md), bought by the community company; Aku Security supplies the guarding, monitoring and training that operate it.

55 — AKU ARBITRATION

Dispute resolution, arbitration and mediation — the mandate with no company

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Akunnia Group is the second child's domain — First Daughter, Matriarch, designated Chief Investment Officer — and her companies take her short form, "Aku" (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM, Sept 2026).

Horizon: Year 1 = 2027. Institution incorporated Y1; first case Y1–Y2; self-sustaining ~Y10–Y12, if ever.

Status: not legal advice. [verify] marks figures and legal positions to confirm with counsel.
Mandate sourceHolding Structure, Akunnia: "Legal structure and compliance · Internal security · Arbitration and conflict resolution." Master Plan §6.2: "…land title conveyancing, Group contract law, and arbitration."
EntitiesAku Arbitration Ltd — institution, company limited by guarantee, non-profit, majority-independent board · Aku Arbitration Services Ltd — for-profit neutrals, training, dispute boards
LicenceNone exists. There is no arbitration-institution licence in Nigeria — that is the plan's problem, not its convenience.
OwnershipEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Akunnia Group → Aku Arbitration

1. Thesis

One sentence: the Group will be a party to construction, land, offtake, insurance, joint-venture and estate disputes for fifteen years, and the capability that manages them internally becomes a saleable institution the moment it exists — provided the Group is never seen to hold the gavel.

It is a volume case. Okodu Construction contracts, Isiome offtake and supplier agreements, land and title matters, Aku Insurance claims, Akuzo joint ventures and family/estate questions will generate disputes at a rate no small company does. A dispute is not an event; it is a schedule item, and the Group will carry dozens at any time.

Why a company and not a department. Two reasons, the second contestable. (1) The capability is saleable — a registrar, a ruleset, case management, a hearing centre and a panel are a going concern third parties can hire; a department cannot be hired by outsiders, sold, or trusted with client funds. (2) Neutrality must be visible, and visibility is expensive — a Group party to disputes needs a forum it trusts, and the honest way to get one is to build an institution genuinely independent of it. That is the only version worth anything, and it means funding a forum the Group may not use for its own large matters.

The counterweight. Nigerian courts are why this is viable: a commercial case sits 4 years 2 months in the High Court, 3 years 4 months on appeal, 6 years 6 months at the Supreme Court — nearly 13 years from filing to final judgment (Justice Research Institute, cited by Prof. Yemi Osinbajo, BusinessDay). But a new institution has no credibility until parties choose it, and it may take a decade to become self-sustaining. This plan admits and prices both.

2. Market

The law was modernised in 2023; the market has not moved. The Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (26 May 2023) replaced the 1988 Act, adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law, and carries the New York Convention in its Second Schedule with no reservations (Keating Chambers; Legal 500).

FeatureProvisionWhy an institution cares
Emergency arbitrator reliefs.16A time-critical product courts cannot match
Third-party funding permitteds.61 — maintenance and champerty abolished; disclosure requiredA funding market needs administering
Costss.50 — includes institutional and appointing-authority costsThe fee is recoverable by statute
Expedition · enforcements.1(4) binds arbitrators, arbitral institutions, appointing authorities and the court; s.34(4) six years, excluding time in arbitrationA statutory service standard

Nigeria's institutions are few: CIArb UK Nigeria Branch, LACIAC, the Lagos Court of Arbitration, NICArb and RCICAL — rules dated 2015, 2016, 2018, 2018 and 2019, none under amendment. There is no specialist arbitration court in Nigeria. RCICAL is an AALCO-established, non-profit regional centre, the only one here with a treaty-derived mandate (Legal 500; AALCO).

The loss is the opportunity. Africa hosts over 90 arbitral institutions, yet most African-related disputes are resolved outside the continent — investors and lenders insist on English law and a London seat, and FIDIC construction forms default to an ICC clause seated in Paris (SOAS survey, via Anjarwalla & Khanna). The same source records "a lack of trust in African arbitral institutions, many of which are newly established compared to seasoned entities like the ICC and LCIA." That sentence is this plan's risk register in one line.

What the Group brings is demand, not reputation — construction, land and title, supply and offtake, insurance, family and estate: the classes Nigerian institutions underserve. Build on Group and small third-party matters; then sell.

3. Product & service lines

Two activities, never one P&L. (A) Dispute resolution services — administering cases: appointing neutrals, managing exchanges, holding deposits, scrutinising awards. (B) Advisory and neutrals — the Group's experts sitting as arbitrator, mediator or dispute-board member in other people's disputes; revenue is professional fees, not administration.

Discipline rule: no line launches before the preceding one has run 25 concluded cases and a published, anonymised case note. An institution's asset is its award history, not its rulebook.

4. Operating model

Aku Arbitration Ltd — the institution. A company limited by guarantee: no share capital, no dividends. The board has three Group directors of seven; the Appointments Committee that selects tribunals for third-party cases is entirely non-Group, on fixed five-year terms. Rules are UNCITRAL-based with expedited, small-claims and mediation tracks, and a published fee schedule. Client funds sit in segregated, separately audited accounts, never netted against Group cash. No Group employee may sit on a tribunal in an administered case.

Aku Arbitration Services Ltd — the practice. For-profit, wholly Group-owned. This is where the Group may legitimately earn. It may not administer an arbitration.

The governance rule, and it is not negotiable:

Any Group dispute above ₦250m — and any Group dispute where the counterparty has not consented in writing to Aku Arbitration — is referred to an independent institution: LCA, LACIAC, RCICAL, ICC, or ad hoc under UNCITRAL Rules with an independent appointing authority. Aku Arbitration does not administer Group disputes above that threshold, and the Group does not draft contracts directing them there.

An institution owned by a party is not neutral. Where the Group looks like it is building a forum for its own matters, it loses every third-party case it needs — and the business case goes with them. The Group's Nigerian public-procurement and construction contracts are the most likely way this company is destroyed, and the rule above is the whole mitigation. It binds in reverse too: Aku Arbitration must decline a Group-referred case, and the refusal must be minuted.

The bootstrapping problem. Nobody chooses a new institution. Four routes out, run at once: (1) Named people, hired not bought — a Registrar who has sat on Nigerian commercial references (retired appellate Justice, or senior SAN with an arbitration practice); the registrar is the product for three years. (2) Partner, don't compete — a cooperation arrangement with RCICAL; membership and training delivery with CIArb Nigeria and NICArb. (3) Small matters at scale — MSME and small-claims tracks conclude fast; volume of low-value conclusion is the only credibility currency a new institution can mint. (4) Recognition earned — panel membership requires CIArb or NICArb accreditation, and institutional standing follows concluded cases, published statistics and unpaid independent review.

Administration standard. Registration same-day, acknowledgement in 48 hours, tribunal constituted within 30 days (14 expedited). Deposits called in one tranche; awards scrutinised for form before issue. Statistics published annually, including duration and cost medians — the most credible thing a new institution can do.

The honest conclusion: this business cannot be bought, because there is no licence to acquire.

A. Institution — no institutional licence exists. The AMA recognises arbitral institutions and imposes on them a duty of expedition (s.1(4)), but creates no registration, approval or licensing regime, and no regulator administers them (Legal 500; FUNAILAW). Incorporation is ordinary CAC registration under CAMA. [verify] whether any state instrument — such as the Lagos State law behind the Lagos Court of Arbitration — bears on how an institution may describe itself.

7. Unit economics

Arbitrator and mediator fees are not institutional revenue — they pass through to the tribunal. The institution earns administrative fees and hearing services.

Benchmark scales. The LCA runs to ₦100,000/hour and ₦800,000/day standard (₦60,000 / ₦500,000 expedited), with a ₦945,000 minimum per appointment for disputes up to ₦17.5m, rising to up to 16.22% of the sum in dispute; its small-claims procedure is a flat ₦80,000 below ₦500,000. RCICAL prices in dollars: US$3,000 minimum rising to 7% to US$150,000, then 1–4% to US$300,000, and US$750 as appointing authority. JICAM charges US$2,000/day sole arbitrator; the ICC requires a US$5,000 filing fee, capped at US$180,000 administrative costs above US$515m; the LCIA bills administrative time at GBP 190–300/hour (Profolio; LCIA).

Aku's scale — priced to be chosen, not maximised (indicative, [verify] against the Group's own cost base): registration fee ₦500,000, then an ad valorem administrative fee of 1.50% on ₦25m–₦100m, 1.00% on ₦100m–₦500m, 0.60% on ₦500m–₦2bn and 0.30% above ₦2bn, capped at ₦25m; a flat ₦350,000 below ₦25m.

Profit comes from volume, and only from volume. Cost per case is high fixed and low marginal: the registrar, systems, premises, compliance and audit cost the same at five cases as at 100. At a fixed base of ₦520m (Y3) break-even is 64 cases a year; at ₦850m (Y5), 104; at ₦1,450m (Y10), 178 — each assuming an average ₦1.5bn dispute.

That assumption is generous. At a realistic average dispute of ₦400m — where Nigerian domestic commercial arbitration actually sits — institution revenue falls to ~₦4.5m and contribution to ~₦2.3m a case, so Year-5 break-even needs roughly 370 administered cases a year. No Nigerian institution is close. The modelled ramp is 8 cases Y1, 35 by Y3, 90 by Y5, 220 by Y10, putting institutional break-even in the early 2030s at the earliest. Said plainly: this company may never be self-sustaining, and its justification is Group risk management plus a call option on African dispute resolution, not a return on capital.

The small-claims track loses money by design — a ₦80,000 flat fee against ~₦400,000 of case-management time is a ₦320,000 loss per case, budgeted and reported separately, because it buys the credibility.

The first ten hires, in order — and the first is the whole business. (4) Counsel — rules, challenges, award scrutiny. (5) Head of Panel and Appointments — manages 300 neutrals who are not employees. (6) Finance and Client Accounts Manager — segregated deposits; a trust-account failure ends the institution. (7) Hearing Centre Manager — venue, AV, transcription. 12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — establish the facts and the bound. (1) Build a Group Dispute Register: every live and contingent dispute across all five groups, with amounts, counterparties, governing law, seat and status. The register is the demand study — without it, the case volumes in §7 are invented. (2) Commission a legal opinion on four questions: whether any registration or approval applies to an arbitral institution; the treatment of an institution owned by a party under AMA ss.1(4), 8 and 50; client-money and trust-account requirements; and whether public-procurement arbitration clauses may lawfully name a Group-affiliated institution. [verify] all four. (3) Draft and minute the §4 governance rule — the ₦250m threshold, independent-institution routing, and the duty to decline a Group case — before incorporation, so the rule precedes the temptation.

Days 31–60 — build the credibility plan. (4) Approach RCICAL on a cooperation arrangement; CIArb Nigeria and NICArb on corporate membership and training partnership; and two retired appellate Justices and two senior SANs with sitting experience on the Registrarship. The registrar conversation is the diligence — if the plan cannot recruit one, it should not proceed. (5) Draft the rulebook and fee schedule against the LCA, LACIAC and UNCITRAL scales, and build the per-case cost model from the Group's own salaries and premises rather than the benchmarks in §7.

Days 61–90 — commit. (6) Present the register, the §7 model and the ten-year subsidy to the Akunnia board, then the Ezeme Group board, for the ₦3.25bn tranched call (corrected — see NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md); incorporate Aku Arbitration Ltd with the non-Group-majority board seated in the same resolutions. (7) Do not sign a single Group contract clause directing disputes to Aku Arbitration. Publish the fee schedule, open the small-claims scheme, and let the first case be someone else's.

plans/56_Idenze_Healthcare.md  ·  7,014 words

IDENZE HEALTHCARE — Clinics, Teaching Hospital & Public Health

Naming: companies take the children's names plus a plain function — Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome · Akunnia · Idenze · Uli · Okodu Group are its five groups. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0).

FX: naira primary; ₦1,600/USD library rate (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM, Sept 2026). Dollars indicative, not comparable across plans. See README.md.

Ezeme Group · Idenze Group (Education & Human Capital + Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals)

Entity: Idenze Healthcare Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Idenze Group Ltd — own board, own audit, own clinical governance

Structure: Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Idenze Group → Idenze Healthcare

Sites: Nkpor, Idemili North LGA — estate clinics, a flagship clinic, and a 200-bed teaching hospital co-located with Idenze University's institutional zone

Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027 · Companions: 17_Idenze_Group.md · 24_Idenze_University.md · 23_Idenze_Research.md · 42_Okodu_Power.md · 45_Okodu_Construction.md

1. Thesis

One sentence: Idenze Healthcare builds two assets with two economics — a clinic network whose return is partly a staff-retention benefit the Group books as a cost, and one University Teaching Hospital whose return is capital, reputation, and the licence Idenze University's medical programmes cannot exist without.

The mandate is Master Plan §6.3 — "The healthcare arm includes a primary clinic serving all Ezeme staff estates and the Nkpor community, a University Teaching Hospital co-located with the institutional zone, and a pharmaceutical production unit. The clinic is a welfare benefit that makes Ezeme estates attractive to skilled workers and their families. The teaching hospital is the clinical training ground for health science graduates." This plan executes that sentence and refuses to blur its two halves.

Three claims, one uncomfortable.

  1. The licence is cheap; accreditation is not. Anambra registers a hospital above twenty beds for ₦31,250 (₦48,000 specialist), renewing at ₦11,250 (ASHEFAMU). What costs years is MDCN housemanship accreditation, NHIA and HMO contracting, and the consultant cadre. Plan around the licence fee and you have planned around the wrong number.
  2. The teaching hospital cannot be deferred. "The setting up of medical schools is not an emergency exercise… prospective proprietors must own and have in place (prior to a request for a Resource Verification), a fully functional and well run tertiary type hospital" — or, on the affiliation route, an institution "fully functional with a minimum of 150 beds and a rural health medical unit" (NUC, July 2016). That sets the floor for our 200-bed Phase 1.
  3. Buy the first hospital; build the second. A licensed, accredited, staffed Anambra hospital can be bought and trading in one to three months; building and licensing takes thirty-six to forty-eight. The acquisition is the bridge clinical site that clears NUC's precondition years before Nkpor exists.

The honest problem. A 200-bed hospital at Nigerian tariffs does not return its capital: cash break-even is ~61% occupancy and full-cost break-even needs 330–350 beds (§7). So the plan is staged — clinics, an acquired bridge hospital, the teaching hospital, then scale.

2. Market

The shortage is structural. Nigeria runs 0.25 hospital beds per 1,000 people, against an African average of 1.0 and a global 2.7 (BusinessDay). The widely cited 0.5 per 1,000 is a 2004 data point that overstates present capacity (Our World in Data / WHO). Anambra's registry: 1,151 registered private hospitals and maternities, 382 maternity homes, 30 nursing homes and 260 laboratories and diagnostic centres — against two government tertiary hospitals and 617 primary health centres (ASHEFAMU, Jan 2024).

Fragmentation is the opportunity. Parsing the Ministry's registered-hospital list by bed count: median facility 18 beds; 64% at 30 beds or fewer; 92% at 100 or fewer; only 27 statewide exceed 100 beds (registered hospitals). Anambra has a thousand hospitals and almost no large one. St Charles Borromeo Specialist Hospital, Onitsha — 270 beds, Catholic Archdiocese, five dialysis machines — is the benchmark private facility in the state (hospital), and NAUTH Nnewi runs 1,500 functional beds with a stated plan to reach 5,000 (Per Second News). Supply is moving: Enugu International Hospital opened 300 beds in 2026 (The Sun), Graceland International opened in Awka in August 2026, and Anambra has flagged off its first private kidney hospital and a ₦3bn AI-assisted diagnostic centre. A 200-bed teaching hospital would still rank among the state's largest — and remain the only one attached to a university.

Workforce is the binding constraint. Nigeria is the world's leading exporter of medical cadres: Nigeria has ~55,000 licensed doctors for over 200 million people and a nurse/midwife density of 15.64 per 10,000 against a WHO-recommended 83 (UK Home Office CPIN); rich countries absorb 20,000 Nigerian health workers (Punch Healthwise) with 10,494 in the UK health sector alone (Premium Times). One signal cuts the other way: new UK nurse registrants educated in Nigeria fell 25.5% year on year to 2,363 in the year to March 2025 (NMC) — an assumption to re-test annually, not a reason to relax the retention package.

Medical tourism is the reachable revenue, though the headline figure is wrong. The much-quoted "US$550m a year" is in fact US$549.29m for the first nine months of 2025 (Q1 $151.53m, Q2 $189.41m, Q3 $208.35m), rounded up by a headline; the full year was US$684.72m, up 6.5% (NILDS issue brief, March 2026; ATQ). These are CBN official-channel flows only; the true figure, including cash and parallel channels, is higher but unmeasured. Africa loses US$7bn a year (Afreximbank via Nairametrics). Phase 1 does not chase oncology and cardiac surgery. The honest target is the middle of the market — obstetrics, general and orthopaedic surgery, dialysis, diagnostics, intensive care — where an Onitsha or Nnewi family currently travels to Lagos, Enugu or India for want of a bed and a scanner.

Payment: insurance grows from a low base. NHIA enrolment reached 22 million of roughly 240 million Nigerians (NHIA via BusinessDay), reform widening coverage while still missing the poor (BusinessDay). Insurance is mandatory in principle under the NHIA Act 2022 — the mechanism exists, is expanding, and pays slowly and below cost. Payer mix is a management decision, not a market outcome (§7).

3. Product & service lines

Asset 1 — the clinic network. Primary care, occupational health and emergency stabilisation for Group staff estates and the Nkpor community. Group employment is a health scheme, not a cash allowance — the logic the Group already applies to housing and food, which "lowers the cost of living and makes Group employment a more compelling proposition than any competitor in the area" (47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md).

Asset 3 — public health. Immunisation, maternal and child health, chronic-disease screening, and a school-health programme through Idenze Schools: the licence to operate, and the community denominators a teaching hospital needs.

4. Operating model

Two companies, one governance spine. Clinics and hospital sit in Idenze Healthcare Ltd but are separately costed and reported — the clinic network as a Group staff-benefit centre whose subsidy is budgeted and visible, the hospital as a clinical business with its own P&L, board sub-committee and capital charge. Blurring them hides the subsidy and destroys the discipline.

Clinical governance before revenue. A Medical Advisory Committee; fortnightly Mortality and Morbidity review to the board; a credentialing file per clinician with MDCN licence expiry tracked daily; an infection-control committee; consent in Igbo and English. Aku Insurance carries professional indemnity and clinical liability from the first patient, not the first claim.

The academic–clinical interface. The hospital is the clinical training ground for Idenze University's pharmacy and health sciences graduates and the site that makes its medical programmes credible. The separation is structural: the Chief Medical Director reports to the hospital board, not the Vice-Chancellor; the university buys clinical teaching time; the hospital bills patients, HMOs and sponsors (24_Idenze_University.md).

The governance point that decides whether any of it is believed. Idenze Research needs this hospital as its trial site — and because the sponsor would own the site, the hospital's research and ethics governance must be visibly independent or its clinical evidence will be discounted. Concretely: a Research Ethics Committee with an external majority, external chair, and lay, legal and community members; a conflict-of-interest register covering investigators, sponsor staff, monitors, statisticians and committee members; publication rights resting with investigators; an externally contracted unblinded statistician; an independent DSMB above minimal risk; QA reporting to the board rather than the Medical Director; and the sponsor–site relationship disclosed before the methods section in every protocol (23_Idenze_Research.md). Reviewers do not object to a sponsor running research at its own site; they object to being surprised by it.

Equipment is a liability from the day it is unboxed. OEM service contracts are negotiated inside the purchase order, 8–12% of equipment value is budgeted annually, and critical spares for CT, MRI and dialysis are held on site. Power is a clinical safety system: Okodu Power supplies N+1 on the life-safety load with BESS firming and diesel at true standby only, replacing self-generation at ₦700–950/kWh with ~₦150/kWh (42_Okodu_Power.md).

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

No licence is a blocker. Each is a named, costed first-ninety-days action — and where one is slow, we buy the entity that holds it.

Speed is not the main reason to buy. The acquired hospital is the licensed, accredited, staffed clinical site that clears NUC's precondition for the medical school while Nkpor is still on the drawing board. Without it, the university's clinical programmes wait for Years 9–11.

What actually transfers on an acquisition — the distinction that decides what the Group can pay.

No licence or accreditation in this plan is a reason to defer a clinic or a hospital. The Group obtains it, or buys the facility that already holds it — and in Anambra, buying is not merely faster: the state is fragmented, owner-operated and under-equipped, which is the condition in which licences trade cheaply and buildings do not. But the acquisition prices correctly only if the Group knows which instruments move and which do not. The "acquisition shortcut" column above compresses four different legal positions into one word. They are not the same, and confusing them is how a buyer overpays:

CategoryInstrumentsWhat happens on a share purchase of the licensed hospital
