The registration number remains with the company; the new owner files the change-of-directors and shareholding notification and updates the Medical Director and superintendent pharmacist of record. Does buying beat building and licensing here? Yes — and the market is now proven rather than theoretical. The sequence above already gives buying a two-to-three-year advantage and first revenue in 1–3 months against 36–48; the decisive argument remains the NUC precondition. What has changed is that this is no longer an untested structure. Iwosan acquired Paelon Memorial Hospital, merger-notified to the FCCPC in November 2025, and then Euracare Multi-Specialist Hospital (TheCable; BusinessDay); R-Jolad acquired 100% of Princess Medical Centre in Port Harcourt, entering a greenfield market entirely by acquisition (Nairametrics; BusinessDay). Three private-hospital acquisitions in twelve months is a functioning market — the Group is adopting a structure others are already using, not inventing one.

The honest qualification, and it matters more than the precedents. None of those transactions disclosed a value. FCCPC notifications publish the parties, not the price, and Nigerian private healthcare does not report deal values. So the price indications above remain planning estimates and must be replaced by the §12 survey — never by analogy to these deals. The only published figure in the market is a Lagos property listing: a hospital in Victoria Island marketed at ₦16bn (NigeriaPropertyCentre) — which prices land and buildings rather than a licensed business, and is useful only as a ceiling on a Lagos asset, not as a hospital valuation. Anambra has no public transaction data at all. A purchase agreement signed on a number inferred from a Lagos property advert would be the most expensive mistake available in this plan.

First ninety days — one written opinion, ring-fenced inside an existing line. Of the ₦45m licence and professional fee line in §12, ring-fence ₦18m for a single written health-regulatory change-of-control opinion covering every instrument classified above: whether the Anambra facility registration issues to the entity or the premises; whether MDCN training accreditation attaches to the facility or the company and survives a change of control; whether NMCN, PCN, MLSCN and RRBN registrations re-issue to new office-holders or to the establishment; and whether NHIA and HMO provider numbers and tariffs assign or require re-application. Commission it from Aku Legal or an Onitsha health-regulatory practice, delivered within 45 days, and make completion of any acquisition conditional on it. At ₦18m it is under 1.5% of the ninety-day budget, and it is the document that decides whether the Group prices a licence or a building — the difference between the ranges above is measured in billions.

6. Capital requirement

Hospital capex is dominated by buildings, medical equipment and imaging — and imaging is the single largest equipment line. Planning estimates at 2027 Nkpor rates; replace with firm tenders and FX-fixed quotations before each tranche release.

Financing rules. 7. Unit economics

Hospital economics turn on occupancy and payer mix, and nothing here deserves more management attention.

Staff cost is the dominant operating line — 75–85% of revenue in the first two operating years. The public anchor agrees: personnel is ~48% of Nigeria's 2026 federal health budget (BudgIT). Full-cost break-even at 330–350 beds is unreachable at 200 beds — which is why Phase 2 exists.

The benchmark that should worry the board. Across six years, South-East public teaching hospitals averaged 42.14% occupancy and 8.15 days ALOS, with only 10–20% of hospital-years near the efficient zone (Aloh et al., 2020). Our 65% and 3.8 days are private-sector assumptions that must be earned — and the whole model turns on them.

Imaging is the largest capital line and close to the weakest-yielding. A 1.5T MRI is the biggest single purchase, yet a regional scan retails at ₦50,000–80,000 — so the ₦6.2bn block earns on volume, not price, and every idle scan-hour is unrecoverable cost. Memfys Hospital, Enugu has been described as the only MRI in the whole South-East — the clearest gap this hospital closes. Two brakes: CT and MRI carry a 50% patient co-pay under insurance, and a new MRI costs US$2–3m (Cedarcrest CEO, 2025). The case therefore rests on the orthopaedic, neurosurgical and oncology referral volume the South-East sends to Lagos and abroad — not on scan price.

Payer mix is the deliberate part, and the evidence is now explicit. NHIA raised capitation 93% and fee-for-service rates 378%, and hospitals still say the money falls short; some now refuse certain HMOs outright (Nairametrics, 2025). The spread is quantified: insurers pay ₦55,000 for a caesarean against ₦300,000–1.5m private cash — a 5–27× gap on the same procedure. State schemes have overtaken NHIA-managed enrolment (9.74m vs 7.07m, Q4 2025), so Anambra's scheme matters as much as the national one — ASHIA covers 230,000+ and targets 90% of the state by 2030 (Anambra State Government). Out-of-pocket payment is ~70% of health expenditure, higher in Anambra and Imo (BudgIT) — hence self-pay stays the largest line and must be priced and collected with discipline.

HMO and NHIA are 42% of volume but only 32% of revenue. Hence: HMO revenue capped at 35%; no HMO contract signed below measured cost; NHIA contracted for volume and credibility, not margin; monthly claims-ageing to the board with a named owner per payer; and ~₦0.93bn of receivables (42% of revenue × ~95 days) pre-funded as working capital rather than discovered as a cash crisis. The Group carries that cheaper than any Anambra competitor, so working capital is itself a weapon.

Clinic network economics — the honest version. One estate clinic: fixed cash cost ₦70.4m a year (staff ₦56.4m, power ₦6m, other ₦8m), variable cost 22% of clinical revenue, so cash break-even at ₦90.3m — about 1,735 enrolled lives at a blended ₦52,000. An estate clinic carrying 1,200 staff and 2,000 dependants clears that comfortably; a standalone community clinic does not. Full-cost break-even, adding ~₦59m of capital charge on the ₦240m fit-out, needs ~3,200 lives — reached only by the estate clinics. So the estate clinics pay their way and return a modest surplus; the community clinic is a welfare subsidy and is budgeted as one. The return the Group buys is retention and productivity — visible in payroll and turnover, not the clinic's P&L. A financial hurdle rate would kill it; treating it as free would hide its cost.

Tariff card (2027 planning, naira). Specialist consultation ₦15,000–35,000; general ward bed-day ₦45,000–65,000; private room bed-day ₦110,000–160,000; ICU bed-day ₦220,000–320,000; normal delivery ₦150,000–500,000; caesarean section ₦300,000–1.5m; major surgery ₦1.2m–2.5m; ultrasound ₦25,000–45,000; MRI regional scan ₦50,000–80,000 (full-body ₦200,000–800,000); dialysis per session ₦45,000–120,000, against ₦12,000 subsidised in the public sector. 8. Organisation

First ten hires. (1) Managing Director — has run a tertiary hospital P&L, not a clinic. (2) Medical Director — the statutory officer: Anambra requires a named doctor with five or more years' experience where the hospital is not doctor-owned, usable once, for one year, renewable (ASHEFAMU) — a permanent post, not a nominee. (3) Chief Matron / Director of Nursing — NMCN-registered RN/RM with accreditation experience. (4) Head of Clinical Services (Consultant Surgeon) — with MDCN housemanship-training experience, because that accreditation is the gate. (5) Head of Obstetrics & Gynaecology — the volume and cash engine. (6) Head of Internal Medicine. (7) Head of Paediatrics. (8) Head of Diagnostics & Imaging — RRBN-registered radiographer. (9) Hospital Administrator / COO — owns HMO and NHIA contracting and the revenue cycle. (10) Chief Finance Officer — healthcare revenue cycle, claims ageing, payer-mix reporting. An immediate eleventh, non-negotiable: Head of Quality, Clinical Governance & Infection Control.

Recruitment is the binding constraint, and money plus pipeline is the only answer. Consultants and specialist nurses are the scarcest and most mobile inputs in Nigerian healthcare. Four responses: pay 120–140% of the Anambra market on a documented review cycle; sessional consultant contracts so a Lagos or Nnewi specialist can hold two appointments; grow our own through Idenze University's pharmacy and health sciences graduates and Idenze Polytechnic's technician and health-records cohorts, with housemanship slots and bonded training places as the retention mechanism; and recruit returners and diaspora with relocation, spousal-support and school-place packages the Group already owns. Target: 40% of technical hires from Group institutions by Year 5, 75% by Year 10. Every clinician's MDCN/NMCN licence expiry is tracked centrally and reported monthly — an expired licence is a closure risk, not an HR lapse.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — decide, register, start buying. (1) Incorporate Idenze Healthcare Ltd (CAMA); adopt the ring-fence; a board with two independent directors — one clinician, one healthcare financier. (2) Appoint the Managing Director and the Medical Director (the statutory Anambra requirement for a non-doctor-owned hospital). (3) File Anambra facility registration for the first two estate clinics with ASHEFAMU — building plan with room dimensions and uses, three years' tax clearance, three nurses' letters of acceptance with current practising licences, NMA and AGPMPN membership, state NMA clearance letter, CAC certificate. Budget ₦8m of fees and professional costs — the state's own fee is under ₦100,000. (4) Instruct counsel on three gates before any spend: whether Anambra registration transfers on acquisition; whether MDCN accreditation attaches to the facility or the company; whether NHIA/HMO provider contracts assign. (5) Commission the acquisition survey — every Anambra facility above 60 beds, with bed count, occupancy, payer mix, accreditation history and asking price.

Days 31–60 — open the files, price the market. (6) Write to MDCN for housemanship accreditation requirements and fee schedule — not published; obtain in writing — and open the Medical Director's credential file. (7) Open NMCN, PCN, MLSCN and RRBN files; hire the superintendent pharmacist (a PCN precondition); confirm the PCN inspection clock. (8) Sign the Group staff health scheme mandate with all five groups — capitation, dependant enrolment, occupational-health service level. (9) Shortlist three acquisition targets; open due diligence on title, licence, accreditation history, staff contracts, equipment condition, receivables and litigation.

Days 61–90 — commit, and constitute governance. (10) Make a conditional offer on the preferred target, priced on the licence and accreditation history, completion contingent on written MDCN and Anambra confirmations. (11) Award the two clinic fit-out contracts to Okodu Construction. (12) File the NHIA provider application and open HMO discussions. (13) Constitute the Research Ethics Committee with an external majority, and the Clinical Governance Committee — before any trial is discussed, because retro-fitted independence convinces nobody. (14) Commission the health-regulatory change-of-control opinion set out in §5 — whether the Anambra registration issues to the entity or the premises, whether MDCN accreditation attaches to the facility or the company, and whether NMCN, PCN, MLSCN, RRBN and NHIA/HMO registrations and contracts transfer or must be re-earned. ₦18m, ring-fenced inside the licence and professional fee line, from Aku Legal or an Onitsha health-regulatory practice, delivered within 45 days and made a condition precedent in every offer — because the difference between a licence that transfers and a building that does not is measured in billions.

Ninety-day committed spend: ₦1.35bn — clinic fit-outs ₦480m; acquisition due diligence and deposit ₦600m; licence and professional fees ₦45m; Medical Director, Matron and eight staff ₦120m; HIS and equipment deposits ₦105m. The licence and accreditation workstream is ₦45m — under 3.5% of that budget. That ratio is the point: the licences are cheap, the accreditation and the staff are not, and only one of the three can be bought with a cheque.

Figures requiring local verification before capital release: CT, bed-day and ICU tariffs, and all occupancy, ALOS and payer-mix assumptions in §7; equipment prices and the 43% imaging share; the Anambra fee schedule (published rates date from 2020–2021); MDCN accreditation fees and timelines, and PCN/MLSCN/RRBN fee schedules (all unpublished — obtain at the Awka offices); the NHIA provider registration fee (NHIS-era, pre-dating the NHIA Act 2022); ASHIA tariff rates; the HMO payment-terms ranges in §7; all acquisition prices, which have no public Anambra transaction data and depend entirely on the §12 survey; the South-East bed counts that are unpublished for COOUTH, ESUT Parklane and FMC Umuahia; Group staff and dependant counts; and the ₦850,000/m² build rate, which must be replaced by firm tenders.

Prepared for the Idenze Group board and the Ezeme Group Board. Market and regulatory figures are sourced; operating, capital and clinical volume figures are planning estimates at ₦1,600/USD requiring local verification against an Anambra tariff and acquisition survey, firm construction and equipment quotations, and written regulator fee schedules before capital is committed. ULI BRAND — Brand, Marketing, Advertising & Reputation Management

Naming: the children's names plus a plain function — see ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0). FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026), not comparable across plans. Verification: costs and prices are planning estimates, not quotations; (V) marks figures needing local checks.

Ezeme Group · Uli Group (Media & Information Systems · Transport & Logistics) · Entity Uli Brand Ltd (CAMA). Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027. Companions: 28_Uli_Group.md, 32_Uli_Broadcast.md, 29_Uli_Film.md, 31_Uli_Animation.md, 39_Uli_Cinemas.md.

1. Thesis

Uli's mandate names "Brand and reputation management" as one of four components of Media & Information Systems — and it has no company. The Holding Structure lists "Media platforms — digital, radio, publishing · Brand and reputation management · Freight, delivery, and warehousing · Supply chain and mobility infrastructure." Three of those four have plans. This fills the gap.

The argument is structural: a brand agency inside a media group buys media at cost from its own group rather than from a third party with a commission. That produces three things no independent agency can match. A price advantage — Uli Brand can undercut independents and still earn a normal margin, because it captures the 10–15% media commission instead of paying it away. A guarantee of placement — the Group owns the airtime, the cinema screens, the carriage and the pages; no independent can promise a client that a campaign will clear. And a production cost base no agency can rent — Uli Film, Uli Animation and Uli Music produce at internal cost-plus, against an external agency paying a 20–30% market mark-up.

One sentence: the Group already spends money on brand, marketing and reputation work that leaves the building as somebody else's margin, and it owns the media, the studios and the audience data to bring that work inside at cost while selling the same service to third parties who want it.

Why reputation management is a business and not a service line. Nigerian corporates face recurring, expensive, reputation-shaped events: regulatory sanctions, product recalls, fraud allegations, licence suspensions, industrial disputes and coordinated online attack. ARCON, NAFDAC, SEC, CBN and the FCCPC all publish sanctions, and each is a communications event. Almost no Nigerian company retains a crisis capability before it needs one — and when it needs one it buys at any price. That is the highest-margin retainer in the portfolio and the least contested by Lagos creative shops.

2. Market

Size. PwC, commissioned by ARCON and funded jointly by the AAAN, EXMAN, OAAN, MIPAN and BON, put total Nigerian marketing communications expenditure at ₦605.2bn in 2023, grown at an 18.7% CAGR from ₦216bn in 2018, projected ₦893bn by 2028, lifting the sector's GDP contribution from 0.7% in 2023 to 1.08% by 2028 (BusinessDay; TheCable; Nairametrics). The AAAN separately describes a ₦500bn industry (AAAN/LAIF). The two measure different things — commissioned expenditure versus agency billings — so the PwC figure is the better anchor because it is the regulator's own commissioned study.

Shape matters more than size.

FeatureConsequence
Media buying dominates creative — most agency revenue is commission on placed mediaEnter as a media-led agency, because owned inventory is the advantage
Agency commission is conventionally 10–15% of gross media (Uli Broadcast nets 15% off a ₦14,000 spot)Commission income is thin and volume-driven; creative and reputation fees are not
Digital absorbs the market — PwC projects digital at 84% of Nigerian ad spend by 2029, above the global average (Nairametrics; PwC)Performance and digital capability is a Year-1 requirement, not a Year-3 ambition
Lagos concentration — AAAN, MIPAN, EXMAN and OAAN sit overwhelmingly in LagosSouth-East brands, including most of the Group's own, are served remotely
ARCON now regulates all of it, including digital, under the ARCON Act 2022Compliance is a barrier to entry, and therefore a moat — if we are on the right side of it

Two customer types, and the plan needs both. (a) The Group's own businesses, which would otherwise buy externally — every domain needs brand work: Idenze Pharma and Consumer Health's consumer products, Isiome Foods, Uli's own content and platforms, Okodu Real Estate and Akuzo Development, and Akunnia's institutional brand. That is the anchor revenue that makes break-even credible to a lender. (b) Third-party African companies wanting media buying, brand strategy and reputation management — the test of whether this is a business rather than a cost centre with a logo.

Lines 3 and 4 carry the volume; lines 1 and 6 carry the margin. An agency that is mostly media buying is a low-margin, working-capital-hungry business — which is why line 6 exists from Year 2 and why the external book must outgrow the internal one. No political advertising, and no work for candidates or parties, consistent with the Uli Broadcast editorial charter.

4. Operating model

Agency, in-house studio, or both — the answer is both, legally separated

Register Uli Brand as a licensed agency that holds clients, charges fees and can be fired. An in-house studio can do none of those, cannot be benchmarked, and becomes a cost centre the Group cannot price — the failure Okodu Materials names when it insists a supplier that can only sell internally "is a cost centre with a letterhead." So Uli Brand Ltd is the client-facing agency with an ARCON corporate licence, while creative capacity stays where it already is — in Uli Film, Uli Animation and Uli Music — sold to Uli Brand at cost-plus like any other supplier.

The conflict of interest, named and controlled

Uli Broadcast's Ad Sales house sells inventory; Uli Brand buys it. Inside one group that is a real related-party conflict, and an external client, auditor or regulator will challenge it. The controls are not negotiable: the agency may buy from any media owner and the media owner may sell to any agency — neither is captive; internal media is priced off the published rate card, arms-length, Group-CFO certified and minuted by the independent directors, the protocol 32_Uli_Broadcast.md already sets; Uli Brand receives the standard agency commission from Group media owners, identically to any third party, with no special terms; and every internal package is priced against two external quotations, with the Group client free to buy elsewhere.

The honest framing: ₦820m is the ceiling on what Uli Brand may charge internally, not an entitlement. If it cannot deliver the same work for less than the external margin it replaces, the Group should keep buying outside.

Fee mechanics: retainers (strategy, PR, reputation — predictable, margin-rich), commission on placed media (volume, thin, working-capital-hungry) and project fees (identity, campaigns — spiky, high-margin). Media is bought on 30-day Group terms and sold on 30–60 day client terms, so the agency funds the gap: a 60–75 day billings runway is the working-capital floor.

5. Licensing and structure

The regulator is ARCON — the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria — under the ARCON Act No. 23 of 2022, which repealed the APCON Act. The history matters: the Court of Appeal in MIC Royal Limited v. APCON had held that the APCON Act reached only registered practitioners, letting unregistered ad businesses escape federal scrutiny. The ARCON Act closed that gap and now reaches all forms of advertising, online or otherwise, targeting the Nigerian market (Templars).

The pre-exposure penalty is the trap and it bites three parties at once. A media house, an agency that creates or places, and an advertiser who authorises exposure are each liable to a minimum ₦500,000 for publishing without a Certificate of Approval. This is the most important operational discipline in the company, and it is why a registered ARPA sits in compliance, not in the creative department.

Acquisition route — buying a licensed agency is faster than registering anew

  • What to buy: a small-to-mid Nigerian agency holding a live ARCON Corporate Licence (Full Service or Media Buyer) — with an ARPA-registered practitioner on staff, an ASP filing history, MIPAN or AAAN membership, and two to four staff willing to stay. Or a media independent with a MIPAN seat and standing credit lines with media owners.
  • Why it is better: the practitioner register and the corporate-licence rollout have been phased, not instantaneous. A licence-holding entity arrives de-risked, with the ASP history and, critically, media credit terms that take years to build. Time to first campaign falls from 6–9 months to weeks.
  • What it costs: no Nigerian agency transaction price is publicly disclosed. Build the range from international precedent — creative and marketing-services agencies clear at roughly 0.8–1.5× revenue or 4–8× EBITDA, with small, client-concentrated independents at the bottom (Robert Glazer; DealStream; Aviaan, Nigerian agency valuation). On a target with ₦300–800m revenue: ₦250m–₦1.0bn purchase price plus ₦50–150m of legal, valuation, FDD and assignment costs. (V) — a framework, not a quotation; verify against audited accounts of three named targets.
  • The cheap alternative, and its limit: hiring an ARPA practitioner and buying a dormant licensed shell looks cheaper. Ask ARCON in writing whether a corporate licence survives a change of control and whether it is entity-bound or practitioner-bound. (V) A shell with no registered practitioner confers no practice rights.
  • Named and costed: a ₦75m acquisition mandate with a decision by day 90 (§12).

Structure. Uli Brand Ltd (CAMA), a subsidiary of Uli Group, ring-fenced with no cross-guarantees. Board with two independent directors — one a senior ARCON-registered practitioner, one a chartered accountant. The related-party media protocol and the internal agency-of-record terms are board-approved, Group-CFO certified, minuted and disclosed to the Family Council.

Idenze University's media and communication faculty is the recruitment channel — paid internships from Year 1, targeting 50% of junior creative and media hires by Year 5 from Group institutions. Senior hires come from Lagos; the pitch is the Group's client list and ownership of the media, which no independent agency can offer.

11. Integration

Uli Brand buys media at cost from Uli Broadcast, Uli Cinemas and Uli Distribution. That single line is the whole argument: the Group's own inventory is available without an external commission leaving the building, and Uli Brand can guarantee placement no independent agency can. Uli Publishing adds print and formats.

It produces content with Uli Film, Uli Animation and Uli Music at cost-plus, so the Group keeps the production mark-up instead of exporting 20–30% to a third-party producer. Uli Animation matters disproportionately — the highest-margin content category, and the natural supplier of the branded content, explainer and social assets now at the centre of Nigerian campaigns.

It brands every Group company across all five domains — the internal revenue floor that makes break-even credible: Idenze Pharma, Idenze Consumer Health and Idenze University; Isiome Foods and Isiome Farms; Aku Insurance, Aku Capital and Aku Technology; Uli's own platforms, content and cinemas; Okodu Power, Okodu Real Estate and Akuzo Development. No Lagos independent has a contracted client list of that breadth at launch.

It uses Aku Technology for campaign analytics and first-party audience data. Uli Broadcast's plan is explicit that "the currency will not be handed to you" — the national Audience Measurement System belongs to a third party and is not yet national. Uli Brand and Aku Technology should build the Group's own campaign-performance dataset, as both a client deliverable and an asset that improves media pricing over time.

It employs Idenze University media and communication graduates, closing the education-to-media loop as Okodu Materials does with Idenze Polytechnic. Akunnia Capital finances the working capital — and there is a deeper fit, because media receivables and retainer contracts are documented, long-dated cashflows of exactly the kind the Broadcast plan identifies as rateable and financeable. Aku Insurance writes professional indemnity and media liability cover, a real exposure given the ₦500,000-per-party pre-exposure penalty and the defamation risk in reputation work.

The interface rule: Uli Brand must remain able to buy from third-party media owners and sell to third-party clients. An agency that can only serve its own family is a marketing department with an invoice book.

What must not happen: no advertising exposed without an ASP Certificate of Approval; no media placement funded beyond a 60-day working-capital runway; no internal package awarded without two external quotations; no single Group client above 25% of revenue; no growth of the Group book faster than the external book; no political advertising, ever; and no related-party media rate a third party would not recognise.

Uli Brand is not a marketing department that charges fees. It is the mechanism by which the Group stops exporting the margin on its own brand spend — and the test of whether it was worth building is the external client list, not the family one.

OKODU FUEL — Fuel & Energy Distribution: the Downstream Petroleum and Gas Business

Naming: the children's names plus a plain function — see ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0). FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026), not comparable across plans. Verification: costs, fees and margins are planning estimates, not quotations; (V) marks figures needing local checks.

Ezeme Group · Okodu Group (Energy & Utilities · Construction & Real Estate) · Entity Okodu Fuel Ltd (CAMA). Horizon 15 years · Year 1 = 2027. Companions: 41_Okodu_Group.md, 42_Okodu_Power.md, 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md, 40_Uli_Fleet.md, 35_Uli_Freight.md.

1. Thesis

Okodu's mandate names "Fuel and energy distribution" as one of four components of Energy & Utilities — and it has no company. The Holding Structure lists "Electricity generation — solar, grid, hybrid · Fuel and energy distribution · Land acquisition and development · Housing, commercial buildings, and infrastructure." The existing Okodu plans cover electricity generation and distribution only. This one covers the fuel.

The argument mirrors Okodu Materials. The Group's power plan anchors its customer economics on diesel at ₦1,800/litre as the alternative a customer already pays (42_Okodu_Power.md; BusinessDay). That anchor is also a fact about us: Ezeme Group is itself a very large diesel buyer — power, haulage, construction plant, generators and facilities all burn AGO, every litre carrying a marketer's margin. Owning fuel distribution converts a major Group cost into a Group margin, exactly as Okodu Materials does for construction.

One sentence: the Group already buys diesel by the litre and pays a marketer's margin on every one of them, and it has the fleet, the land, the balance sheet and the internal demand to own that margin instead — then sell the same capability to the South-East's industrial and haulage customers.

The honest caveat, stated first. Downstream petroleum is a thin-margin, working-capital-hungry, price-exposed commodity business with no licence monopoly. A distributor's EBITDA margin on turnover is 2–4%, and its return depends on how fast working capital turns, not on how much fuel it sells. The internal conversion is what makes this worth doing. The entry model is therefore chosen for the opposite of ambition: bulk supply to the Group's own fleet and generators.

2. Market

Deregulation is complete in structure, even where politics pushes back. The Petroleum Industry Act 2021 created the NMDPRA as successor to the Department of Petroleum Resources, subsidy removal ended the assumption of a regulated margin, and NNPC Ltd is now a competitor, not a supplier of last resort.

The Dangote refinery changed the supply map — and imported a currency risk.

FactConsequence for Okodu Fuel
Dangote's 650,000 bpd refinery is the dominant domestic supply source; it lifted petrol to ₦1,275/litre and diesel to ₦1,950/litre in September 2026 (BusinessDay)Domestic supply exists at scale; the gantry, not an import terminal, is the marginal source
It began pricing local sales in dollars in July 2026 (AllAfrica)FX risk is now embedded in a naira business — a genuine structural exposure, not a passing one
Prices fell then rose through 2026; PETROAN's members explain that "old stock must be sold first" (The Sun)Inventory is a price position. Falling prices create real losses on stock already bought
The Federal Government ordered marketers to reduce prices, and marketers threatened shutdown over ₦15bn of losses (News Central; Naija News)Retail margins are politically contestable. Do not underwrite them
LPG prices moved violently — a 12.5 kg refill above ₦22,000 in mid-2026, then a crash to ₦1,100–1,550/kg on a surge of imports (The Real Media)LPG is the growth line and the most volatile
CNG is the policy-backed substitute — the FG is pushing conversion, and cooking gas and CNG are often confused by consumers (Business Times)CNG follows Uli Fleet's own conversion — an internal anchor demand before an external one

Structure. NMDPRA regulates; NNPC Retail and the major marketers (Oando, TotalEnergies, Ardova, Conoil, MRS) hold the branded retail chains; DAPPMAN depot owners and PETROAN and IPMAN members hold the distribution and retail tail — fragmented, informally financed and unevenly compliant. The commercial gap is not price; it is reliability, metering honesty and product quality. Adulteration is endemic and is the most damaging thing a fuel brand can be accused of.

The Group's real market is the corridor, not the country. The Onitsha–Nkpor–Nnewi–Awka–Enugu axis is one of Nigeria's densest industrial and haulage markets, and the Group's own demand is a contracted base load no independent marketer holds — the power plan's captive-demand advantage, applied to a commodity.

3. Product & service lines

Discipline, written into the charter: Okodu Fuel never refines and never imports crude. It buys from the refinery, from NNPC and from the depots, and competes on proximity, metering honesty, quality assurance and delivery reliability — the four things the informal tail cannot offer. Line 1 is the anchor and lines 7 and 8 the destination; building retail before proving the cost book is the classic way to lose money in this sector.

4. Operating model

Three possible models — and the sequence is not a preference, it is arithmetic

ModelCapitalWorking capitalMargin/LRiskTime to revenueVerdict
Bulk supply to the Group and industrial customersLowHigh₦60–100Low — contracted60–90 daysStart here, Year 1
Wholesale distribution to retailersMediumVery high₦40–80Medium — credit and diversion3–6 monthsYear 2
Retail stationsHighMedium₦125–200Medium–high — site, licence, theft9–18 monthsYear 3–5

Bulk supply to the Group's own fleet and generators is the lowest-risk entry and needs no retail footprint. It requires a licence, two trucks or a haulier, offtake from a primary source, metered storage at Nkpor and a written internal supply agreement — turning revenue on inside a quarter instead of a year and proving the cost book before any site is bought.

Storage and depot — lease before you build

An inland depot at Nkpor or Onitsha serves the corridor. Two routes: lease 200,000–500,000 litres of tank capacity at an existing licensed depot (fast — no EIA, no construction licence) or build 2–5m litres (capital, EIA or ESIA, NMDPRA licences to establish and construct, land, fire certification, 18–36 months). Recommendation: lease for the first three to five years; revisit a built depot only when throughput exceeds 60% of leased capacity, and treat it then as a 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md project.

Transport — a dedicated sub-fleet, not the general fleet

Fuel moves in baffled tankers with calibrated meters under NMDPRA transporter compliance — not general haulage, and not to be absorbed into Uli Fleet's general operations. Recommendation: a dedicated Okodu Fuel sub-fleet of two to four units in Year 1, run under a service agreement with Uli Fleet on published day rates — with Uli Fleet free to carry other people's fuel and Okodu Fuel free to use third-party hauliers.

Quality control, which is the real licence to operate

Product adulteration and quality liability is the risk that ends the brand, not the balance sheet. Mandatory from the first load: primary sources only — no depot blending, no "wet" stock, no unexplained discounts; a retained sealed sample per load, the seal number recorded against the invoice; independent laboratory testing on a rolling sample, not only on complaint; NMDPRA product certification and accounting compliance; and a Quality Assurance Manager with written authority to reject a load or stop a sale, reporting to the MD and never to the trading desk.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

The regulator is the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA), created by the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 as the successor to the Department of Petroleum Resources. Two instruments govern: the Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Operations Regulations, listing the activities requiring a licence, and the Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Fees Regulations 2024, setting the fees — which revoked and replaced the fee schedules previously prescribed under several regulations, including the MDPO Regulations 2023 (Aluko & Oyebode; Advocaat Law). The fee figures below are the published schedule entries (V).

Two facts matter more than any individual fee. First, the levies are the real cost, not the licences. Against a bulk diesel margin of ₦60–100 a litre, a 1% statutory levy is ₦18 — 18–30% of gross margin — and non-compliance attracts a 10% monthly penalty on the unpaid levy and possible licence suspension; the Federal High Court in IHS (Nigeria) Ltd & Anor v NMDPRA upheld the Authority's power to collect. Second, fees are non-refundable and non-transferable, but the Sixth Schedule of the Fees Regulations 2024 separately prescribes fees for the assignment or transfer of licences and permits — transfer is contemplated and priced. (V) — confirm the current schedule and assignment mechanism with NMDPRA before pricing any licence in.

Acquisition route — stated explicitly

Do not assume Okodu Fuel must build and licence from scratch. Buying a licensed operator is faster and cheaper on the critical path.

  • What to buy. Either (a) a licensed retail station with a live NMDPRA retail licence and an established, titled forecourt on the Onitsha–Nnewi–Awka corridor; or (b) cheaper, faster and better first — a bulk distribution company holding a wholesale supply licence, with depot relationships, meter and tanker assets and 20–60 industrial accounts.- What it costs.
  • Licensed filling station: from ₦250m for a small site (listing evidence) up to ₦2.5bn for a six-pump urban station in Lagos with PMS, DPK and AGO pumps, a lubricant blender and registered title (Golden Sgrove; PropertyPro). A South-East corridor station of two to four pumps is more likely ₦150–450m. (V) — verify against three live transactions, not listings.
  • Bulk distributor with a wholesale licence: ₦300m–₦1.2bn, depending on depot relationships, receivables quality and working capital carried. (V)
  • What the licence itself is worth — the honest answer. NMDPRA instrument fees run to tens or hundreds of thousands of naira, so almost all of an acquisition's value is the site, the title, the environmental and fire certificates, the tank integrity and the trading history — not the paper. But that paper lets a site trade on day one, and a licence transferred with a going concern removes six to twelve months of NMDPRA, state and fire process from the critical path. That is the whole argument for buying rather than building.
  • What buying does not transfer. Neither the land problem nor the environmental liability. Title verification, tank integrity testing and soil and groundwater testing for historic contamination are conditions precedent — a used forecourt's tanks may need replacement, and remediating a leaking tank is the buyer's cost. Model tank replacement and remediation into every acquisition.
  • Settle in writing: whether the buyer must independently satisfy the "competent persons" requirement — the licensee must appoint competent persons for construction, operations, maintenance, storage, retailing and HSE and report every appointment or change to the Authority within 72 hours. (V) A licence without the people who satisfy it is a liability, not an asset.
  • This is a named, costed first-ninety-days action: a ₦120m acquisition mandate with a decision by day 90 (§12).

Structure. Okodu Fuel Ltd (CAMA), a subsidiary of Okodu Group, ring-fenced from Okodu Power with no cross-guarantees — the power plan's ASERC position must never be exposed to a downstream compliance event. Board with two independent directors — one with downstream petroleum operations experience, one an HSE specialist — and an HSE and Compliance Director holding a written veto over any load, site or operation.

⚠️ This plan prices diesel two ways, and the number it disagrees with itself on is the one the whole Group energy case rests on. The line above uses ₦1,750/litre — the plan's own landed bulk buy — while 58:13 and 58:132 anchor the customer's alternative at ₦1,800/litre, as do 41_Okodu_Group and 42_Okodu_Power. And the anchor itself is now stale in the Group's favour, which is the more useful half of the finding: verified September 2026 depot prices are ₦1,830–₦2,120/litre (Ibachem Lagos ₦2,000, Ibeto ₦1,970, Matrix Warri ₦2,120) with retail up to ₦2,300 — so ₦1,800 now understates the avoided-cost case rather than overstating it. Two things follow, and neither is a one-cell edit. First, the Group should adopt one measured diesel price from actual depot invoices and use it in 41, 42 and here — 58:150 already instructs that "nothing be built on these numbers until they are replaced with NMDPRA weekly price bulletins and actual depot invoices", and the two figures in this plan show why. Second, and more consequentially: if Okodu Fuel buys wholesale, the Group's own captive avoided-cost case falls even though the external case holds — because the ₦1,800 the Group prices against is the retail price it would no longer be paying once it supplies itself at cost. That interaction is flagged in ../NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md §8.2 and thirteen plans depend on the derivation, so it must be re-based in one pass rather than patched here.

First eight hires, in order: (1) Managing Director — has run a Nigerian downstream P&L and knows depots and the NMDPRA; (2) HSE and Compliance Director, with veto power — fuel is a safety business before it is a trading business; (3) Head of Supply and Trading — owns the cost book and the price desk; (4) Depot and Storage Manager — dip discipline, tank integrity, calibration; (5) Head of Transport — driver accountability and loss control; (6) Quality Assurance Manager with authority to reject a load, reporting to the MD and not to trading; (7) Credit Controller — industrial accounts are where the bad debt lives; (8) Financial Controller — margin per litre by product, by truck and by station.

Employment. Idenze Polytechnic supplies technicians, drivers and HSE officers — target 40% of technical hires by Year 3 and 70% by Year 5, with paid attachment. Drivers are employed directly on payroll, not through intermediaries, because fuel diversion happens fastest where nobody is accountable to the company that owns the product.

Read the revenue column with suspicion and the margin column with respect. Downstream fuel is a 2–4% EBITDA-margin business on turnover; ₦777bn of revenue producing ₦22.8bn of EBITDA is not a triumph, it is arithmetic. The return comes from working capital turning 15–20 times a year, which is why treasury discipline, not sales ambition, is the core competence. Year 15 volume of 420m litres is under 1% of the national product market and a meaningful share of the South-East corridor (V).

  • Year 1 — bulk supply licence in hand; Group consumption metered and under a written internal supply agreement; two tankers running; leased storage at Nkpor; first external industrial accounts.
  • Year 3 — two retail stations operating or acquired; LPG plant commissioned; external revenue above 50%; loss control under 0.5% of volume.
  • Year 5 — six stations; 130m litres; lubricants and LPG above 20% of gross profit; a built-depot decision made on throughput evidence.
  • Year 10 — 16 stations; CNG dispensing at four sites serving the converted Group fleet; depot in operation.
  • Year 15 — the test is not volume but mix: a fuel business earning most of its gross profit outside its own family, on loss control that stands up to audit.

10. Risks

11. Integration

Okodu Fuel supplies the Group's own fleet, generators and facilities — a major internal cost converted to internal margin. At Group consumption of 10–20m litres a year (V) across Okodu Power's displaced diesel, Uli Fleet's trucks, Okodu Construction and Materials' plant and every facility's generators, the marketer's margin previously exported to a third party is ₦0.8–2.4bn a year returned to the Group. Okodu Power is the anchor internal customer and the reason the business exists — the ₦1,800/litre figure anchoring the whole power plan is Okodu Fuel's revenue line — and Group demand is the utilisation floor that makes the first tranche financeable.

Uli Freight and Uli Fleet move the product, under a service agreement on published day rates — but with a deliberate specialisation: a dedicated sub-fleet of baffled, meter-calibrated tankers under NMDPRA transporter compliance, not general haulage. Uli Fleet may carry other people's fuel; Okodu Fuel may use third-party hauliers.

Sites may be developed with Okodu Real Estate — forecourt sites on the Onitsha–Nnewi–Awka corridor, acquired or developed on commercial terms. Never inside Akuzo's residential zoning, already caught as an exclusive-residential boundary; a fuel station is the least compatible neighbour a residential district can have, and the rule is absolute.

It buys power for depots from Okodu Power. A depot, an LPG plant and a CNG compressor are all substantial electric loads, and running them on diesel would be absurd — the depot is a natural Okodu Power anchor customer, alongside Okodu Materials.

It employs Idenze Polytechnic graduates — technicians, drivers, HSE officers and depot operators — with paid attachment and certification.

Akunnia Capital finances it, and the asset suits it: fuel inventory and receivables are short-dated, high-turnover, commodity-backed — the classic working-capital profile. The caveat is price exposure, so the advance rate must be struck against a weekly mark-to-market, not the purchase price, with margin-call mechanics if the market falls beyond an agreed threshold. Aku Insurance covers the inventory risk — fire at the depot and, specifically, stock throughput and marine cargo cover for product in transit.

The interface rule: Okodu Fuel must be able to buy from third parties and sell to third parties. A fuel business that exists only to serve its parent is a procurement department with a licence, and it will never develop the cost discipline the merchant business needs.

12. First ninety days

#ActionOwnerBy day

2Meter and audit the Group's actual fuel consumption — every generator, truck, item of plant and facility, by litres and by month. It sizes the licence, the fleet, the storage and the whole first tranche.MD45
3Lodge the NMDPRA bulk-consumer / industrial storage application and open the wholesale supply licence file — a named, costed action, not a downstream formalityMD / Compliance30 / 60
4Fund the ₦120m acquisition mandate: identify three licensed retail stations and two bulk distributors on the corridor; complete technical, environmental (tank integrity, soil and groundwater) and title due diligence; decision by day 90MD / CFO90
5Build the real cost book from written depot quotations and the NMDPRA weekly price bulletin, including the 1% statutory levy at ₦18 a litre on diesel — replace every margin in §7Head of Supply60
6Secure Nkpor storage — lease 200,000–500,000 L of tank capacity at an existing licensed depot; confirm Okodu Power supply in writing; file the fire certificate applicationOperations Director60 / 90
7Sign the internal supply agreement — arms-length, benchmarked against two external quotations, Group-CFO certified, with a written annual volume schedule per Group companyMD / Group CFO75
8Commit the Akunnia working-capital facility at 60 days of inventory and receivables, and commission Aku Insurance stock-throughput cover for product in transit and in storeCFO90
9Recruit the first eight hires — HSE and Compliance Director first, with the written veto in the appointment letterMD / HR90

What must not happen: no retail site acquired before tank integrity, soil and groundwater testing and title verification; no product bought other than from a primary refinery, NNPC or a licensed depot; no stock above 10 days held as a price position; no credit to a new industrial customer; no site inside Akuzo's residential zoning; no site, depot or vehicle operating without a current fire certificate; and no greenfield retail station before bulk supply has proved the cost book and the loss controls.

Okodu Fuel is not a petroleum marketer that happens to have a captive customer. It is the mechanism by which the Group stops paying a marketer's margin on its own diesel — and the merchant book is what will prove it was a business rather than a discount.

OKODU HOUSING — Residential Development & Letting

Naming follows ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0). Naira primary at ₦1,600/USD; dollars indicative; figures constant Year-1 naira.
EntityOkodu Housing Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Okodu Group Ltd
OwnershipEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings GBC → Ezeme Group → Okodu Group → Okodu Housing
BusinessResidential development and letting — build homes, keep them, collect rent
GeographyNkpor, Idemili North LGA, and the Akuzo residential district, Anambra State · 15 years, Year 1 = 2027

Boundary with Okodu Real Estate

47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md is the land bank and development business — acquiring land, perfecting title, master-planning, selling or developing plots; it earns land appreciation and development margin. Okodu Housing is the build-and-hold business — it builds homes and keeps them, earning rent and long-run appreciation. Different businesses: different capital, time horizons and risks. The family's Master Plan separates them — "his real estate arm manages all staff apartments, student housing, commercial letting, and the Akuzo storey building portfolio." Three rules: (1) Housing buys land from Real Estate at arm's-length, board-approved prices; (2) Housing never sells plots; (3) build-to-sell is a capped funding engine, never the reason the company exists.

1. Thesis

One sentence: Okodu Housing builds homes for a tenant the Group already employs and students the Group already teaches, then holds them — because where mortgage finance is below 1% of GDP and developers can therefore only build for cash buyers, the only residential business that scales without a mortgage market rents to a captive tenant the sponsor controls.

The captive demand is the Group's own. The Group hires teachers, nurses, factory workers, farm staff and administrators across five domains and must house them to attract them from outside Nkpor; housing through a Group-owned asset converts a cash allowance paid to anonymous landlords into an asset the Group owns. 24_Idenze_University.md publishes its requirement: 1,000 beds at Phase 1 at ₦1.6m per bed per year, rising to 6,000, with 12,000 students at maturity, ~60% resident. 25_Idenze_Polytechnic.md follows, and 50_Akuzo_Development.md already carries a residential cluster with staff apartments.

The honest problem, first. Nigerian residential lets at roughly 5–9% gross on new cost — below naira debt and far below a pension fund's entry yield. So the return is not rent alone. It is rent, appreciation, and a cost base no competitor can match, because this company is built by Okodu Construction, supplied by Okodu Materials and Isiome Manufacturing, and powered by metered Okodu Power. A sold house produces a margin once; a held house produces the instrument 09_Aku_Capital.md exists to warehouse.

2. Market

The deficit is real; the number is contested. Government pegged it at 15 million units in July 2026 (EnviroNews); other methodologies run 17–28m (Radio Nigeria). Direction, not precision.

The binding constraint is finance, not construction. Mortgage penetration is below 1% of GDP (Daily Trust) against double digits in comparable markets (BusinessDay). With no long-tenor buyer finance, the only viable developer customer is one with cash in hand — so developers build to sell, rental stock is left to individuals, and the rental market is starved of institutional supply (BusinessDay).

Rents are repricing because cost is. Anambra self-contained units that let at ₦250,000–300,000 now let at ₦500,000–600,000 (Vanguard); two-bedroom flats let past ₦1.5m (Harmattan News), on cement up roughly 367% in seven years (The Cable).

Rental models that work: employer housing (rent deducted at source, ~100% collection, 5–7%); purpose-built student hostels (priced per bed to one creditworthy tenant — 16–24%, per Nigeria RE Blog); managed market-rate rental with per-unit metering and an enforced service charge (5–9%). The unmanaged single landlord fails — no metering, no enforcement, no reserve.

The gap is custody and collection, not supply — there is no institutional residential landlord in Nkpor or Onitsha. ⚠️ Flagged for local verification: rents by unit type; voids; student bed pricing; build rate per m²; land price per plot.

3. Product & service lines

1. Staff apartments — all five domains; payroll-linked, indexed; Year 1. 2. Student hostels — Idenze University and Polytechnic, per bed per session under a nomination agreement; Year 2. 3. Market-rate rental apartments — professional and diaspora tenants, annual rent in advance, reviewed yearly; Year 4. 4. Serviced apartments — corporate, diaspora and medical visitors, nightly and monthly; Year 6. 5. Build-to-sell — the funding engine, outright sale to cash and diaspora buyers, capped at 25% of programme; Year 3.

The sequence is the strategy: 1 and 2 first, then 3. Lines 1 and 2 have a named tenant the Group controls, so demand is contracted before the first block is poured — removing lease-up risk, the largest risk in residential development. Line 3 is entered only once a collection record and a cost book exist, and is never levered. Line 5 runs to a development-margin target: at 25% it manufactures the equity for line 3.

4. Operating model

Build fewer square metres, not cheaper ones. A low-rise block of 90 m² gross per unit at ₦250,000–450,000/m² is a different asset from the 2,000 m² five-storey Akuzo building costed in the Akuzo Development Programme at ₦750,000/m² — roughly ₦1.5bn, because it carries an elevator, solar array, battery bank, biodigester, cistern and LPG grid. Staff and student housing needs none of those where Okodu Power serves the district. The specification, not the price per m², is the cost lever.

Rent collection is the core competence, not an administrative task.

  1. No cash, ever — billing, arrears ageing and service-charge apportionment run on 11_Aku_Technology.md; staff rent is deducted at source.
  2. Rent is taken annually in advance, leases one to two years and never longer — the short term is the inflation linkage, so arrears surface at renewal rather than in collection.
  3. The arrears ladder is published and applied without exception: day 7 reminder, day 14 notice, day 30 statutory notice of intention to recover possession, day 60 instruction to counsel. Self-help eviction is prohibited in every circumstance.

Service charge and metering. Every unit is individually metered: an unmetered landlord carries an uncapped utility cost through inflation, the commonest cause of residential landlord failure in Nigeria. Service charge runs through a designated account per estate on a published budget, with a 95% recovery target and a per-estate sinking fund. Student hostels carry a minimum 80% occupancy floor.

5. Licensing, title and acquisition pathway

Nothing here is a blocker. Each item is a named, costed first-ninety-days action with the route to acquisition stated.

#RequirementIssuerProcess and costHow to acquire it

Paying 20–40% more for perfected land buys back the Group's largest risk.
2Certificate of OccupancyGovernor, via Ministry of Lands12 months to years on virgin landDo not apply for one. Take an assignment of a titled plot with consent.
3Survey + perimeter surveySurveyor-General, Anambra4–12 weeks; ₦250,000–₦1.5m per plot (verify)One registered surveyor on retainer, so every plot is surveyed to one standard.
4Building plan approvalAnambra State Physical Planning Board; LGA permit3–6 months; fees by floor areaPre-application consultation in Awka; one standard house type approved once.
5Environmental impact assessmentNESREA; State Ministry of EnvironmentLarger schemes, sewage, borehole, drainage; 3–9 monthsCommission once for the whole district.
6Land Use Charge + tenement ratesAnambra IRS (APLUC); Idemili North LGAAnnual on assessed value; non-payment attracts sealing (Anambra State)Budget as a recoverable service-charge line.

Title risk is the dominant risk in Nigerian real estate. Most Anambra land is held under family or communal title with no registered instrument, and is routinely sold twice or caught by outstanding probate. The Group's rule is absolute: perfection before construction — no foundation, and no capital beyond the option price, until consent is registered. 5% of every land transaction is budgeted for due diligence: registry and probate search, inspection against the survey, and an opinion from Aku Legal.

Only T1 and the student-bed core of T2 need family equity, because those assets cannot be pledged before they exist. Thereafter naira debt within the 40% gearing ceiling funds only contracted income — staff housing and student beds under nomination — ring-fenced per estate, never unhedged USD. Speculative market-rate letting is never levered: at 5–9% gross against naira debt above 20% it cannot cover its own interest.

Worked example — one 90 m² two-bedroom unit, low-rise, Group-built and Group-powered.

Rent ₦2.4m a year → 5.1% gross on cost; net of 8% void and 10% operating cost, ₦1.99m → 4.2% net — below the cost of naira debt. At a ₦2.4m rent and the same non-build costs:

Break-even: to clear a 5% net yield the unit must cost no more than ₦39.8m — roughly ₦280,000/m². Below that the business works on rent; above it, only on appreciation. ⚠️ Replace the ₦250,000–450,000/m² band with a firm Okodu Construction tender before T1 is committed (cost evidence).

What works on its own numbers: a student bed at ₦12m against the Phase-1 price of ₦1.6m yields 13.3% on cost — the first thing to build. Build-to-sell carries a 25–30% margin, once. The rest is appreciation and the integrated cost base: 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md puts the gap between Okodu-integrated build cost and open-market turnkey cost at ₦420m per building — 23%, and that gap is the entire margin.

Cap-rate warning. At a 10% naira cap rate, ₦1.99m of net rent is worth ₦19.9m against a ₦47.4m cost, so this book cannot be sold at cost on rent alone. The exit is a contracted-income vehicle under 09_Aku_Capital.md, priced on cash flow rather than cap rate.

(2) Head of Rent and Collections — a credit-control background. (3) Head of Estate Management. (4) Development Manager — COREN-registered. (5) Head of Land and Title. (6) Property Accountant. Constant Year-1 naira. Year 1: first staff housing across all five domains. Year 2: first student hostel under the Idenze nomination agreement. Year 4: first market-rate block, only after a 24-month collection record. Year 10: 6,400 units at 94% occupancy, with a stabilised rental sleeve placed into an Aku Capital vehicle. Year 15: a second-city portfolio without further Group equity.

10. Risks

1. Title risk (Very high — dominant). Communal and family land, double sales, defective probate. Mitigated by perfection before construction, Governor's Consent on every acquisition, the 5% due diligence budget, and preferring already-perfected land.

2. Construction cost inflation (High). Mitigated by Okodu Materials internalisation, price-adjustment clauses, and building fewer square metres rather than cheaper ones.

3. Rent arrears and eviction difficulty (Very high). Recovery is slow; self-help eviction is unlawful (Tribune). Mitigated by payroll deduction, annual rent in advance, the published ladder, and a credit screen.

4. Void periods and occupancy shortfall (High). Mitigated by building staff and student housing first, and holding twelve months of operating cost per estate.

5. Interest rates on development debt (High). Rates above 20% destroy a 5% yield. Mitigated by never levering speculative letting; gearing stays under 40%.

6. The deficit may be a financing problem, not a construction problem (Very high). If absent mortgages cap prices, building more cannot solve it and prices cannot rise to meet cost. Hence the anchor on contracted tenants, and hence Section 7 must be tested against a firm tender before capital is committed.

7. Building for employees is not building for profit (High). Unpriced, subsidised staff housing makes the company a welfare cost centre. Mitigated by an arm's-length, board-approved, externally benchmarked internal rent.

8. Tenancy and rent-control regulation (High). Anambra moved to enact a rent law in 2026 (Vanguard). Mitigated by complying before it passes.

11. Integration

This company exists inside the Group, and its margin is the integration. Tenants are Group staff across all five domains and students of Idenze University and Idenze Polytechnic under nomination agreements. Stock is built by 45_Okodu_Construction.md on fixed-price open-book contracts with two external bidders, supplied by 46_Okodu_Materials.md (cement, blocks, steel, joinery) and by Isiome Manufacturing (fittings, furniture). It is powered and metered by 42_Okodu_Power.md — the largest cost advantage, since where Okodu Power serves the estate a held building needs no solar array, battery bank, biodigester, cistern or LPG grid (₦1.31bn avoided across 16 buildings), and metering removes the uncapped utility exposure that fails Nigerian landlords. Land comes from 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md; finished stock is managed by 60_Okodu_Estate_Services.md — Housing builds, Estate Services operates. 09_Aku_Capital.md finances it, with stabilised sleeves moved into SPVs subject to its rule that no fund be more than 25% Group-originated; billing runs on 11_Aku_Technology.md; the book is insured by 14_Aku_Insurance.md and documented by Aku Legal.

12. First ninety days

Licence and title acquisition is a named, costed action — not a gate that defers the business.

  1. Incorporate the company — CAC, TIN, VAT, two independent directors. ₦2.5m · day 30
  2. Confirm the tenancy statute in force for Nkpor. Aku Legal · ₦6m · day 30
  3. Title audit of every plot; prefer plots already under a C of O. ₦18m · day 60
  4. File Governor's Consent applications on two perfected plots. ₦45m · day 90
  5. Okodu Construction tender — one measured cost book. ₦12m · day 60
  6. Sign Idenze nomination heads of terms — 400 beds, ₦1.6m each. ₦5m · day 60
  7. Agree the Okodu Power metering and tariff interface. ₦4m · day 60
  8. Register the first service-charge budget and sinking fund. ₦3m · day 75
  9. License the Aku Technology rent module. ₦25m · day 90
  10. Pre-application consultation with the Physical Planning Board. ₦8m · day 90
  11. Register the standing-interest land programme with the Akuzo Council. day 45
  12. First ten hires, MD and Head of Rent and Collections first. ₦120m · day 90

What must not happen: no foundation before Governor's Consent is registered; no acquisition without the 5% due diligence spend; no cash rent collection; no self-help eviction; no lease over two years; no leveraged market-rate letting; and no T1 capital before a measured cost per square metre exists.

Prepared for the Okodu Group board and the Ezeme Group Board. plans/60_Okodu_Estate_Services.md  ·  3,104 words

OKODU ESTATE SERVICES — Facilities, Estate & Property Management

Naming follows ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md (v5.0). Naira primary at ₦1,600/USD; dollars indicative; figures constant Year-1 naira.
EntityOkodu Estate Services Ltd (CAMA), subsidiary of Okodu Group Ltd
OwnershipEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings GBC → Ezeme Group → Okodu Group → Okodu Estate Services
BusinessFacilities management, estate operations, letting and property services
ClientsThe Group's own portfolio first, then third-party landlords and estates
GeographyNkpor, Idemili North LGA, Onitsha and the Akuzo district, Anambra State · 15 years, Year 1 = 2027

1. Thesis

One sentence: The Group's Master Plan states that its real estate arm "manages all staff apartments, student housing, commercial letting, and the Akuzo storey building portfolio" — and managing a portfolio is a different business from building one, so it should be run as a company earning fees, not as a cost centre absorbing them.

The portfolio the Group will accumulate is large and unusually varied. Staff apartments across five domains. University and polytechnic hostels and campus buildings. The Akuzo storey building portfolio. Commercial and retail letting. Industrial sheds and warehouses. Uli's cinemas. No Nigerian facilities business starts with a book like that — and 50_Akuzo_Development.md says so directly: billing residents "is an operating business, not a development business."

Facilities management at that scale is a real service business, not an overhead. Several thousand units and hundreds of thousands of square metres of commercial and industrial space need preventive maintenance, metering, security coordination, cleaning, waste, landscaping, lift and pump contracts, sinking funds and audited service-charge accounts. Every one of those is a line item a third party would happily bill for — and Nigerian estates are chronically badly managed, which is the market.

The professionalisation argument is also the value-creation argument. A managed estate with a funded reserve and audited service-charge accounts is worth more than an unmanaged one with the same bricks: recovery, occupancy and rent all improve when residents can see where the money goes. So this company raises the capital value of the Group's own stock — the reason to run it inside the Group rather than tender it out.

2. Market

The facilities management market is real but immature. Nigeria's integrated FM market is put by commercial research houses in the hundreds of millions of dollars, growing at low double digits, and dominated by multinational providers serving banks, telcos and oil majors (Mordor; 6WResearch). ⚠️ Verify locally before use in any lender model.

Two structural facts define the opportunity. Nobody is competing for residential estates — the multinationals serve head offices, while the residential market is served by individual caretakers and informal contractors with no standard and no accountability. And the client base, not the capability, is the scarce asset: barriers to entry are low and barriers to retention are high.

Why Nigerian estates fail, consistently. No sinking fund, so roofs, pumps and roads are never replaced and the estate decays. No reserve, so one failure becomes a special levy nobody pays. No transparent accounts, so residents cannot see what their service charge bought and stop paying. No enforcement, so the diligent subsidise the defaulters. And no professional management, so the association, the caretaker and the landlord each hold a fragment of authority and nothing is decided — service-charge recovery being the core operational problem of Nigerian multi-occupancy property (NIESV Journal Vol 43).

Rents are repricing, which makes arrears the live issue. Anambra self-contained units that let at ₦250,000–300,000 now let at ₦500,000–600,000 (Vanguard); two-bedroom flats let past ₦1.5m (Harmattan News) — while the Assembly moved to enact a rent law and the Governor attacked illegal agent fees (Vanguard). Rising rent raises the fee pool and the arrears risk together.

Competitors. Multinational IFM firms will not take a 200-unit estate; informal caretakers have no accounting, insurance or enforcement power; residents' associations are unpaid volunteers without standing to recover. The gap is a professionally managed, transparently accounted estate manager with the legal machinery to enforce.

3. Product & service lines

#LinePrice basisCore
1Facilities management — hard and soft FMper unit or per m²/year
2Estate management — the governing mandate% of rent collectedcore
3Letting and sales agencyone month's rent per tenancy
4Rent collection and arrears managementwithin the management feecore
5Service-charge administration and reserve planning% of service chargecore
6Maintenance contracting — routine and reactiveschedule of rates
7Security coordination — guarding, access, CCTVdelivered by Aku Security
8Cleaning, landscaping, wastescheduled services
9Utility management including powermetering, billing, recharging

Lines 2, 4 and 5 are the core — they carry the mandate.

4. Operating model

Two mandates, one standard. Group-owned stock is managed under an arm's-length agreement priced on the same schedule as third-party stock. The Group's own stock is never favoured, never subsidised and never used to underwrite a third-party bid — that rule makes the third-party business credible, and it is audited annually by an independent director.

Contract structures. Estate management runs on a three-to-five-year renewable mandate as a percentage of rent collected plus a percentage of service charge administered, against a published scope. Facilities management runs per unit or per m² per year against a service-level schedule with liquidated damages. Letting runs on a standard agency fee within whatever the state tenancy instrument permits. Every contract is terminable for non-payment.

Collection is the operating system. Billing, receipting, arrears ageing and apportionment run on 11_Aku_Technology.md, and no cash is handled anywhere in the business. Service charge is held in a designated account per estate, never commingled with fees or Group funds, reported quarterly to residents and audited annually.

Enforcement. The arrears ladder is published at the outset and applied without exception: day 7 reminder, day 14 notice, day 30 statutory notice of intention to recover possession, day 60 instruction to counsel. Self-help eviction is prohibited in absolutely every circumstance; lawful process only, with arbitration through Aku Arbitration preferred to litigation where permitted (Tribune). Fidelity guarantees cover every collection role, four-eyes approval governs every waiver, and reconciliation is done independently of the collection team.

5. Licensing, title and acquisition pathway

Facilities management broadly requires no licence — which is precisely why the client base, not the licence, is the scarce asset here.

#RequirementIssuerProcess and costHow to acquire it
1Company registrationCAC2–4 weeks; ₦2.5mIncorporate; TIN, VAT, PAYE follow
2Estate surveying firm registrationNIESV (institution); ESVARBON (statutory regulator)Firm registration plus a registered principal; ₦1–3m plus annual dues (NIESV; ESVARBON)Buy or hire a registered estate surveyor as principal. Qualification takes years; acquisition takes months
3Valuation workESVARBON onlyOnly registered estate surveyors may value property for lending, probate and taxDo not attempt valuation unregistered. Partner or refer, and charge referral fees
4Property agency and lettingLightly regulated; NIESV/ESVARBON disciplineNo state licence in Anambra; agent fees now politically constrainedRegister with NIESV; comply with whatever fee cap the tenancy instrument sets
5Facilities managementNo statutory licenceVoluntary good practice onlyThe absence of a licence is the opportunity — differentiate on audited accounts, funded reserves and service levels
6Private security deliveryNSCDC private guard licensingRequired only if the company guards directlyDo not license in-house: contract Aku Security, which holds the capability
7Tax and labour complianceFIRS, Anambra IRS, PenCom, NSITFPAYE, pension and employee compensation leviesRegister before the first hire — the largest legal exposure for a people business

The acquisition route, and why it comes first. A small Nigerian property or estate management firm of 500–1,500 units, with a registered estate surveyor, a supervision layer and an existing client book, is indicatively valued at ₦250m–₦600m — roughly 2–4× recurring fee revenue, or ₦200,000–₦400,000 per unit managed (⚠️ planning estimate; commission two valuations and a fee-revenue quality check first). Buying brings the contracts, the staff, the systems and the registration in one transaction — faster and less risky than building a client base from scratch. Command of a portfolio is the asset; everything else can be hired.

6. Capital requirement

TrancheYearsScope₦bnUS$m
T1 — Prove1Mobilisation, systems, first mandate staff, working capital0.90.6
T2 — Acquire and scale2–3One management-firm acquisition (₦250–600m); FM equipment; two more mandate teams1.61.0
T3 — Regional base4–7Third-party mobilisation; plant, vehicles, tools; supervisory layer3.42.1
T4 — Beyond Nkpor8–15Awka and Enugu offices; maintenance depot; further acquisitions5.63.5
Total11.57.2

This is a low-capital, high-working-capital business. There is almost no fixed asset: the spend is payroll, tools, vehicles, systems and one acquisition. The binding constraint is collection working capital — fees are earned on collection, so 60–90 days of operating cost must be funded per mandate during mobilisation. No unhedged USD debt; gearing under 40%; each mandate self-funding within twelve months or terminated.

7. Unit economics

The fee schedule. Estate management at 7.5% of rent collected (market range 5–10%); service-charge administration at 8% of service charge administered (5–10%); letting agency at one month's rent per new tenancy; facilities management at ₦1,500–2,500 per m² per year for soft FM (⚠️ verify locally).

Revenue componentBasis₦ per unit/year
Letting and tenancy management7.5% of ₦2.4m rent180,000
Service-charge administration8% of ₦720,000 charge57,600
Facilities management (where contracted)blended45,000
Gross, market-rate unit≈282,600
Blended across the book (staff units carry a lower fee)≈165,000

This is labour-intensive and margin-thin, so profit comes from scale and from the number of units under management, not from the fee rate — and fees are earned on collection, not on billing. Staffing ratios govern cost: one estate manager per 300–500 units; one maintenance technician per 120–180 units; one rent accountant per 600–900 units.

The collection-rate problem is the whole business. Because fees are a percentage of collected rent, a fall in collection is not a revenue haircut — it is a margin loss against fixed payroll. At a 95% collection rate on 1,000 units the company earns ₦157m; at 70% it earns ₦116m — a 26% revenue fall with almost no cost reduction. Collection capability, not fee negotiation, is the competence and the KPI the board should hold management to.

ScaleUnitsRevenueNet margin
Year 1900₦0.15bnnegative
Year 32,400₦0.40bn~10%
Year 54,200₦0.69bn~11%
Year 1011,000₦1.82bn~12%

Break-even. Year-1 fixed cost is ₦190m; at ₦165,000 blended revenue per unit, break-even is roughly 1,150 units under management, reached in Year 2. Year 1 at 900 units is a planned loss of about ₦40m — the cost of proving the model on the Group's own stock.

8. Organisation

FunctionYr 1Yr 3Yr 5Yr 10
Executive (MD, CFO, Operations Director)2346

First ten hires. (1) Managing Director — a Nigerian estate or facilities management operator with a managed-portfolio record. (2) Head of Estate Management — service-charge budgets, reserves, by-laws, resident relations. (3) Head of Rent and Service-Charge Collection — a credit-control background; the core competence. (4) Facilities Manager — preventive maintenance, lift and pump contracts. (5) Estate Surveyor — NIESV/ESVARBON-registered. (6) Letting Manager. (7) Rent Accountant. (8) Maintenance Supervisor. (9) Data and Systems Lead — 11_Aku_Technology.md billing and arrears. (10) Compliance and Integrity Officer — reconciliations, spot audits, fidelity control. Target: 60% of facilities trades hires from Idenze Polytechnic by Year 5.

9. Milestones

YearUnits (Group)Units (third party)Total unitsThird-party contractsCollection rateRevenue
1900—900—88%₦0.15bn
