Constant Year-1 naira. Year 1 takes the mandate over the Group's existing stock only. Year 2 completes the acquisition of one management firm. Year 3 wins the first third-party estate and reaches break-even. Year 5 reaches 95% collection with a funded sinking fund on every estate. Year 10 crosses 50% third-party revenue — the test that the business stands without the Group.

10. Risks

1. Rent and service-charge arrears (Very high). The dominant risk, because fees are earned on collection. Mitigated by payroll deduction on staff stock, monthly rather than annual service charge, the published 7/14/30/60 ladder, and a credit screen on every tenant.

2. The difficulty of eviction in Nigeria (Very high). Recovery is slow and self-help eviction is unlawful (Tribune). Mitigated by lawful process only, arbitration through Aku Arbitration where permitted, and a hardship protocol before any recovery reaches a household.

3. Tenant disputes (Medium). Mitigated by published by-laws, a written complaints procedure with response times, and quarterly resident accounts.

4. Conflict of interest between Group and third-party stock (High). Mitigated by identical arm's-length contracts and fee schedules, a separate client account per property, an independent director, and an annual audit of staff-time allocation across mandates.

5. Thin margins and wage inflation (High). Mitigated by scale, staff ratios held per unit, and index-linked contract escalation.

6. Staff integrity — rent collection is a fraud risk (Very high). Mitigated by no cash handling anywhere, fidelity guarantees via 14_Aku_Insurance.md, four-eyes approval on every waiver, independent monthly reconciliation, and spot audits.

7. Maintenance cost escalation on ageing stock (High). Materials have risen roughly 367% in seven years (The Cable). Mitigated by a funded sinking fund from day one, preventive rather than reactive maintenance, and annually benchmarked vendor contracts.

8. Utilities cost pass-through (High). An unmetered estate leaves the manager with an uncapped cost. Mitigated by per-unit metering on every mandate and a written refusal to accept an unmetered property.

11. Integration

This company is the Group's operating layer over its own property, and it earns fees for doing it. It manages 59_Okodu_Housing.md's residential stock and 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md's commercial and retail lettings, and takes the mandate over the 50_Akuzo_Development.md portfolio — where a dense, metered, billable estate is the easiest customer base an estate-services business will ever get. It coordinates estate security through Aku Security, which holds the NSCDC private guard licence so this company need not, and estate utilities through 42_Okodu_Power.md, whose per-unit metering makes utility pass-through safe. Tenancy documentation runs through Aku Legal and disputes through Aku Arbitration. It employs Idenze Polytechnic graduates in facilities trades. And billing, arrears ageing and apportionment run on 11_Aku_Technology.md, producing the audited per-estate reporting that residents and, later, 09_Aku_Capital.md's investors require.

12. First ninety days

Licence, registration and acquisition is a named, costed action — not a gate that defers the business.

  1. Incorporate the company — CAC, TIN, VAT, PAYE, PenCom, NSITF. ₦3m · day 30
  2. Register with NIESV and ESVARBON; engage a registered estate surveyor as principal. ₦4m · day 60
  3. Take the mandate over the Group's existing stock on arm's-length terms. day 90
  4. Shortlist acquisition targets — 500–1,500 units, registered surveyor, clean fee revenue — and commission two valuations. ₦12m · day 75
  5. Publish the standard documents — management agreement, fee schedule, service-charge budget, by-laws, arrears ladder. ₦6m · day 60
  6. Open a designated client account per property and confirm no-commingling controls. day 60
  7. License the Aku Technology collection and service-charge module. ₦22m · day 90
  8. Place fidelity guarantees and four-eyes controls on all collection roles. ₦5m · day 75
  9. Audit every meter on Group stock and issue a remediation list. ₦8m · day 90
  10. Sign the Aku Security and Okodu Power interface agreements. ₦4m · day 90
  11. Source the first ten hires, MD and Head of Collection first. ₦150m · day 90
  12. Register the compulsory sinking-fund policy for every estate under mandate. day 90

What must not happen: no mandate accepted on an unmetered property; no cash collection anywhere; no self-help eviction; no commingling of service charge with management fees or Group funds; no Group property given a lower fee or a faster response than a third-party one; and no acquisition completed before two independent valuations and a fee-revenue quality check.

Prepared for the Okodu Group board and the Ezeme Group Board. Market and regulatory claims are sourced; fee rates, market size, acquisition multiples and headcount are planning estimates in constant Year-1 naira at ₦1,600/USD requiring a local market survey, two valuations and a legal opinion before capital is committed. Companions: 59_Okodu_Housing.md, 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md, 50_Akuzo_Development.md, 11_Aku_Technology.md.

plans/61_Isiome_Manufacturing.md  ·  5,823 words

61 — ISIOME MANUFACTURING

General industrial manufacturing — the factory layer of the Group

Naming: Ezeme Group is the mother company; Isiome Group is the first child's domain — Agriculture & Food Systems · Manufacturing & Industrial Production — and his companies carry his name (../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md, v5.0).

FX: naira primary; dollars indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM, Sept 2026).

Horizon: Year 1 = 2027; first line Y1; MANCAP Y2; packaging and fabrication Y2–Y3; complex goods Y7+.

Status: costs are planning estimates, not quotations. [verify] marks figures needing local confirmation before capital is released.
Mandate sourceHolding Structure, Isiome's sector: "Agriculture & Food Systems · Manufacturing & Industrial Production." Master Plan §6.1: "…agricultural machinery design and manufacturing, agro-processing, food packaging and distribution, and general manufacturing."
EntitiesIsiome Manufacturing Ltd (CAMA) — the plant · Isiome Manufacturing Services Ltd — installation, after-sales and spares
SitingZone A, Nkpor, on the Okodu Power captive network; second site or an acquired plant in the Onitsha–Nnewi–Aba corridor
OwnershipEzeme Family Trust (Mauritius) → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd → Ezeme Group → Isiome Group → Isiome Manufacturing
Call on capital₦6.7bn (~USD 4.2m) to first production; ₦38.2bn (~USD 23.9m) to Year 11

1. Thesis

One sentence: the Group already buys, every year, the exact goods this company would make — blocks, roofing, steel, pipes, crates, packaging, mounting structures and enclosures — from third parties and importers, so Isiome Manufacturing converts that demand into internal margin and import substitution, which is the same logic as Okodu Materials and Okodu Fuel.

The internal demand is large, dated and already committed. Okodu Construction and Housing need blocks, roofing, steel and pipes. Isiome Farms and Foods need crates, packaging and processing equipment. Okodu Power needs solar mounting structures, cables and enclosures. Idenze needs cleanroom fixtures and pharmaceutical packaging. Every one of those is today imported or bought from a third party — none of it is speculative.

The structural advantage is power, and it is measurable. Nigerian manufacturers spent ₦1.4 trillion generating their own electricity in 2025, and energy is 30–40% of production cost for cement, steel and food processing (BusinessDay). Self-generation costs ₦700–950/kWh all-in; Okodu Power's captive tranche is modelled at ₦150/kWh. On a concrete block, that is the difference between ₦963 and ₦743 of variable cost — a ₦220 swing on a ₦1,100 product, or 20% of the selling price. A Group factory on its own power is not a marginally cheaper factory. It is a differently viable one, and it is the only reason this plan clears.

The sequence problem, stated first. Starting with complex goods is the standard Nigerian industrial mistake: a factory is built to make a product nobody has ordered, at a specification nobody has certified, financed in dollars and priced in naira. This plan starts with the highest-volume, lowest-complexity, highest-internal-demand goods — concrete products, roofing sheets, packaging, light steel and sheet-metal fabrication — and moves to pipes, enclosures, cleanroom fixtures and processing equipment only after the first lines are above 70% utilisation and MANCAP-certified.

The honest counterweight. Nigerian manufacturing is not a growth story: its share of real GDP fell from 8.24% in 2024 to 8.05% in 2025, growth was 1.6% in Q2 2025, capital is scarce and credit has run at 32–35%, and imports undercut domestic output on cost. This company is justified by captive demand and cheap power, not by the sector's macroeconomics — and where those two advantages do not apply, it should not manufacture.

2. Market

A large sector that has been shrinking relative to the economy. Manufacturing contributed 8.05% of real GDP in 2025, down from 8.24% in 2024, recovering to 9.57% in Q1 2026 on 3.29% real year-on-year growth; it paid ₦1.17trn in VAT in 2025, up from ₦803.53bn (Nairametrics/NBS). MAN projects 3.1% output growth in 2026 against 1.6% in Q2 2025, a 10.2% GDP contribution, and a naira at ₦1,300–1,400/USD (BizWatch). Capacity utilisation, MAN's own measure, was 61.3% in H1 2025, up from 57.6% in H2 2024 — the single most important number in this plan, because it is where the whole industry's profitability is lost.

The three constraints are known and ranked. The PAMA survey of over 100 manufacturers ranks power outages, costly credit and poor logistics as the primary barriers to competitiveness — ahead of exchange rates and policy (BusinessDay). This plan is designed against all three: power from Okodu Power, materials moved by Uli Freight and Uli Warehousing, and financing through Akunnia Capital with equipment finance from Aku Credit.

Nigeria's building-material prices show what import dependence costs. Cement went from about ₦7,500 a 50 kg bag in Q4 2024 to ₦11,500–₦16,000 by 2026; blocks from ₦600 to ₦1,100; rebar to ₦1,150,000 a tonne (BusinessDay). Every one of those increases is margin transferred out of the Group and into a supplier or an importer, and every manufactured input the Group makes for itself stops the transfer.

The overlap with Okodu Materials must be settled, not ignored. Okodu Materials already makes structural blocks, aggregates, cut-and-bend rebar, timber and precast for the construction programme. Isiome Manufacturing must not build a second block yard. The boundary rule:

Okodu Materials manufactures construction materials for the Group's own build programme, at transfer price. Isiome Manufacturing manufactures goods sold to third parties, to other Group domains and to the open market — and takes the products Okodu Materials has deliberately excluded: roofing, pipes and fittings, packaging, solar mounting structures, enclosures, cleanroom fixtures and processing equipment. Where the two lines genuinely overlap — concrete products and light fabrication — Isiome takes the non-structural and non-construction specification (pavers, kerbs, road furniture, light sheet-metal) and supplies only as a second source to Okodu on nominated projects.

The export question, answered realistically. Onitsha Main Market is West Africa's largest distribution node, with estimated annual trade above US$5bn across more than forty markets (Pulse) — which makes the South-East the right place to sell into ECOWAS, and MANCAP-certified products may be exported to any West African country. AfCFTA lowers tariffs but not border friction: exporters still spend ₦10.84m to move one ₦100m truckload to Ghana — 10.8% of cargo value, dominated by a 7.23% statistics levy in Benin (Shipping Position). Export is a Year 5+ margin opportunity for high-value, low-weight goods — never the business case.

3. Product & service lines

The sequence is the strategy: volume and simplicity first, complexity later.

#LinePrimary customerLaunchWhy this position in the sequence
1Concrete products — interlocking pavers, kerbs, culverts, road furnitureOkodu Construction, Akuzo, estates, externalY1Lowest capex, immediate demand, simplest process
2Roofing sheets — roll-formed galvanised, aluminium-zinc and pre-painted, plus accessoriesOkodu Construction and Housing; Onitsha marketY1High volume, one machine, universal and undifferentiated demand
3Packaging — woven PP bags, injection-moulded crates, pallets, corrugated cartons, sachet filmIsiome Foods, Isiome Storage, Isiome Farms, IdenzeY2The Group is the anchor customer for all of it
4Light steel and sheet-metal fabrication — purlins, trusses, doors, tanks, guardsOkodu Construction, Uli set construction, Group plantsY2–Y3Uses the same shop as roofing; low marginal capex
5Pipes, fittings and water infrastructure — uPVC and HDPEEstates, Akuzo, government WASH, agricultureY4More complex tooling; requires the fabrication discipline first
6Solar mounting structures, cable trays, enclosures and panelsOkodu Solar and Okodu Power, then externalY4–Y5Highest-value internal demand in the Group's fastest-growing domain
7Cleanroom fixtures, pharma packaging and consumablesIdenze Pharma, Sterile & Injectables, DistributionY5–Y7High margin, high specification; demands a proven quality system
8Agro-processing and irrigation equipment — with Isiome MachineryIsiome Farms, Storage, Foods; externalY7–Y10The import-substitution prize; needs CNC and engineering depth

Discipline rule: no new line opens until the previous line is above 70% utilisation and MANCAP-certified. Adding a line at 40% utilisation converts a marginal factory into a loss-making one, and is the most common way Nigerian manufacturers die.

4. Operating model

Power first, then the machine. Site, buildings, layout and load schedule are designed around the Okodu Power captive connection from day one, with the plant on one 11 kV incombustible feed, one 33 kV ring for the second plant, sub-metering on every line, and power cost charged to each product as a direct cost, at the actual intra-group PPA rate, monthly. A factory that does not see its power cost per unit cannot manage it — so power appears on every line's cost sheet, not in overhead.

Build or acquire — the plan's answer is mostly build, with targeted acquisition. Build the first two lines, because nothing on the market makes exactly what the Group needs at the specification it needs. Then acquire, because a distressed or idle Nigerian plant brings equipment, staff, certification and a customer list that would otherwise take two to three years to assemble (§5).

Utilisation is the operating religion. Weekly production meeting against plan; monthly review of output per machine hour, scrap rate, and delivered cost per unit; no overtime authorised to chase a volume the order book does not have. Capacity is added in modules sized to the next committed customer, not to ambition.

Quality control. An in-house laboratory from Y1 — cube crushing and block dimensional testing, coil thickness and coating-mass checks, bag tensile and drop tests — with results filed so that MANCAP is a formality rather than a discovery. Every batch is traceable to raw-material lot and machine shift. Rejected batches are scrapped, not downgraded and sold into the market, because the Group's institutional customers are the ones who test.

Raw materials and spares. Cement and coil are the largest inputs and both are price-volatile in naira. Two suppliers per input, no speculative stockpiling, and a written FX policy: imported coil is bought against a 60-day LC at the rate on the day of order with a 5% FX buffer, gains retained against the next order rather than released to margin. A critical-spares register — every bearing, belt, roller and die on the critical path — held at two months' cover, because the spares lead time, not the machine, sets uptime.

Distribution. Internal transfers on 30-day terms at benchmark-minus 5–10%, re-benchmarked quarterly against two independent quotations and disclosed to the Family Council; external sales cash or 14 days. Uli Freight carries everything above a light-vehicle load; Uli Warehousing holds finished goods at Onitsha and Lagos.

Export discipline. No export until the product is MANCAP-certified, the pack and label comply with destination rules, and an ECOWAS or AfCFTA origin certificate is in hand.

5. Licensing and acquisition pathway

Licensing is a filing sequence, not a barrier — the barrier is time and inspection, and both can be bought.

The insight this plan is built on. MANCAP from scratch costs ₦42,500–₦325,000 in SON charges — trivial money. What is not trivial is 60 days of clock, two quarterly inspections, a laboratory failure, a deficiency report and a re-inspection, all of which delay revenue while capex depreciates. A factory that already holds MANCAP has already paid that price, and paying 3–6× EBITDA for it is usually cheaper than building and certifying from scratch. Distressed Nigerian factories are frequently available at or near asset value, because the constraint on them was never the plant — it was power, working capital and a customer. The Group supplies all three, which makes this arbitrage specifically available to it and to few others.

Rule: acquire before build wherever the acquired asset makes a product the Group already intends to make, and hold MANCAP as the test of value. Never acquire a plant without a live certificate or a clear route to one within 90 days.

Two questions the table above does not settle, and both move the price.

Does MANCAP travel with the asset? A SON certificate attaches to a product and a production site, not to a shareholder — which suggests a share purchase preserves the certificate while an asset purchase out of receivership may require it reissued in the new owner's name. The plan found no published SON rule on the point and therefore assumes nothing: counsel is instructed to obtain the answer in writing from SON before any bid, and every offer is priced on the assumption that recertification is payable — the same ₦42,500–₦325,000 of SON charges, 60 days of clock and two quarterly inspections per product tier that this plan exists to avoid. Where the certificate does transfer, that saving is the premium the Group is paying.

The same question applies to NAFDAC, and it is answered per target. Product registrations are granted to a named applicant against a named premises; whether they survive a share sale, an asset sale, or a change of production address must be confirmed in writing for the specific target rather than in general. A food-contact or consumable line acquired without live registrations is a factory with no revenue, which is the whole failure mode this plan is written against.

And the strategic point, stated explicitly because it governs the sequencing of this plan: across Isiome Group, this is the single highest-value acquisition route in the domain. Storage's SEC receipt licence is the scarcest (05_Isiome_Storage.md); Manufacturing's distressed factory is the largest — no other transaction in the domain buys plant, buildings, trained staff, SON certification and a customer list in one step, and none is available at or near asset value, because the binding constraint on these factories was never the plant. It was power, working capital and a customer, and the Group supplies all three from inside itself (42_Okodu_Power.md; 09_Aku_Capital.md; Isiome's own captive demand). That is an arbitrage available to this Group and to few others — so where a live MANCAP-certified plant making a product in §3 can be bought for less than building and certifying it, this plan builds nothing.

Working capital is 18–22% of revenue — 45–60 days of raw material including the 60-day coil LC, 30–45 days of receivables, 30 days of finished goods. Working capital, not capex, is what kills Nigerian factories — so it is funded at the start of each tranche, never from operations.

8. Organisation

The first ten hires, in order. (1) Plant Manager — has run a Nigerian factory at scale; not a family appointment. (2) Production Supervisor for concrete and roofing. (3) Quality Control and Laboratory Officer — owns MANCAP, NIS testing and the SON relationship. (4) Maintenance Engineer — preventive maintenance, critical-spares register, uptime; in Nigeria the spares lead time, not the machine, sets output. (5) Electrical and Instrumentation Technician — power quality and the Okodu Power interface. (6) Sales Manager — external and third-party, distinct from internal transfer demand. (7) Procurement and Imports Officer — LCs, FX, cement and coil supply, spares. (8) Financial Controller — product costing, FX policy, working capital. (9) HSE Officer — NESREA, fire safety, factory safety, with veto power. (10) Warehouse and Logistics Coordinator — Uli Freight and Uli Warehousing interface, dispatch and stock accuracy.

Boundary rule restated: Okodu Materials makes what the Group builds with; Isiome Manufacturing makes what the Group and the market buy. The two companies share no product line except as nominated second sources, and internal prices are struck at benchmark-minus 5–10% on 30-day terms, re-benchmarked quarterly and disclosed to the Family Council.

12. First ninety days

Days 1–30 — establish the demand and the boundary. (1) Commission a Group Manufacturing Demand Register: every manufactured good the five groups bought in the last twenty-four months, with volumes, specifications, prices, suppliers, lead times and country of origin. This register is the order book, and without it the sequence in §3 is a guess. (2) Agree and board-minute the boundary rule with Okodu Materials — which products belong to which company, and how second-sourcing works — before either factory is designed, because two Group block yards is the failure mode this plan exists to prevent.

Days 31–60 — price the inputs and hunt the assets. (3) Run a local materials and power survey: cement, sand, coil and resin prices delivered to Nkpor with supplier quotations; the Okodu Power captive PPA rate in writing; achievable machine throughput and waste rates from at least three equipment vendors; and the actual grid supply hours at Zone A. Re-underwrite §7 on the survey, not on the plan. (4) Open an acquisition file: approach AMCON and Anambra, Abia and Enugu state asset-holding agencies for idle and distressed plants in the corridor, and instruct counsel on AMCON asset purchase, title, staff transfer and whether MANCAP and NAFDAC certificates transfer with the asset. [verify] Budget ₦35m for this file: ₦5m per target for legal, financial and regulatory-file diligence across up to five candidates, a valuation on each live MANCAP plant, and one written SON view on certificate transferability. The output is a priced alternative to T1 build — and T1 is only committed if the build is cheaper than the buy.

Days 61–90 — commit the first tranche only. (5) Present the register, the survey, the §7 model and the acquisition file to the Isiome board, then the Ezeme Group board, for the ₦6.70bn T1 call — concrete and roofing only, with MANCAP and the Power connection named as conditions precedent to commissioning. (6) File MANCAP applications for concrete products in the same quarter the plant is ordered. (7) Do not order the packaging, pipes or enclosure lines, and do not commit T3 or T4 capital, until utilisation on T1 lines exceeds 70% and MANCAP is in hand.

EZEME GROUP — BUSINESS PLAN LIBRARY

60 plans: the mother company, five group plans, and 54 company plans — complete.

Ezeme Group is the mother company. Every other company is named for one of the five children plus a plain function — the Dangote pattern. Akunnia's companies take the short form "Aku." Naming is settled at v5.0; all Igbo word registers are dropped. See ../EZEME_NAMING_ARCHITECTURE.md.

Ownership chain: Ezeme Family Trust (Mauritius, Trusts Act 2001) → trustee Ezeme Family Holdings PTC Ltd → Ezeme Family Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd (GBC) → Ezeme Group Nigeria Ltd → the five groups → operating companies.

Horizon: 15 years, Year 1 = 2027, with licensing and land front-loaded.

FX convention: naira is primary in every plan; dollars are indicative at ₦1,600/USD (spot ~₦1,328, CBN NFEM Sept 2026). Do not compare dollars across plans — each states its own rate.

Numbering note. Plan numbers are authoring order, not a ranking, and the original blocks were kept stable so that the 250+ cross-references inside the existing plans remain valid. Plans written after the domain review take the free slot 16 and then continue from 51. This table is the authoritative index.

"Licensing and acquisition pathway" replaced "Regulatory pathway" across the library, deliberately. The Group's rule is that a licence is never a reason to defer or omit a business. The model: Blackstone, not BlackRock

The library was first built toward the wrong model. BlackRock gathers passive money at 3–15 basis points; Blackstone buys control at 1.5–2.0% plus 20% carried interest. The family's own words describe the second: "orchestrating the structural, private development of African industry from a global hub — like London or New York… I want to buy entire companies, reshape industries, and make an astronomical amount of money doing it."

Four plans were rewritten because of it: 09_Aku_Capital (now the principal-investment and GP holding company), 10_Aku_Asset_Management (now fund management and capital formation), 11_Aku_Technology (now internal infrastructure, not a product to sell), and 12_Aku_Markets (now securities dealing, not an index platform).

Two rules make it work inside a family structure:

  • Carried interest is not equity. Carry sits at fund level and shares in fund profits; it never touches ownership of Ezeme Group, the five groups, or any operating company. The family keeps 100% of the operating conglomerate; partners share in the returns their own funds generate.
  • No fund above 25% Group-originated assets, stepping to 15% by Year 6, with related-party transactions approved by independent directors sitting alone.

One unresolved consequence worth the family's attention. The rule that no equity is issued above subsidiary level also means Ezeme Group, Akunnia and Aku Capital cannot issue shares to a seller — so listed equity cannot be used as acquisition currency at holdco level. Consideration must be cash, hedged debt, or rollover equity inside the target. Acquisition pace is therefore capped by Aku Capital's own cash generation and borrowing capacity, which makes Aku Bank's deposit base strategically important rather than merely convenient. This should be decided deliberately rather than discovered in a negotiation.

The Group's three structural advantages

1. Its businesses are each other's customers. Isiome feeds every estate and canteen. Okodu powers and builds for everyone. Uli moves everyone's goods and holds the Group's only licensed controlled-substance capability. Idenze trains every operator and supplies the clinical evidence. Akunnia finances, insures, defends and perfects title for the whole thing. No standalone competitor starts with demand already contracted — and none can match the internal margin.

2. It originates the assets its own funds will buy. Okodu builds generation and property; Uli builds freight corridors and a content catalogue producing long-tail royalties. These are exactly the long-dated, inflation-linked cash flows African pension funds are under-allocated to and cannot source. PenCom's Q1 2026 data shows Nigerian pension assets at ₦29.52tn, with 58.07% in FGN securities and only 3.95% in alternatives — and PenCom's own risk register lists R1 as real returns below inflation and R3 as FGN concentration, prescribing the mitigant as a shift into "alternatives, infrastructure, and inflation-linked instruments." The regulator is instructing pension funds to buy what this Group builds.

3. It owns both halves of two rare pairings. A pharmaceutical manufacturer and an accredited teaching hospital and medical school — so it can generate its own clinical evidence in-house. And freight and licensed controlled-substance logistics — so it can move what almost no competitor legally can.

Standing constraints applied to every plan

  1. No apprentice-equity model. An institutional-grade cap table is the precondition for third-party capital, listing and pension mandates.
  2. Ring-fence every regulated business in its own company with its own board, licence and audit — especially Idenze Therapeutics, Uli Special Logistics, Aku Bank and Aku Security.
  3. Two-tier governance. Family institutions hold shareholder decisions; a Group Board with three independent directors runs the business.
  4. Licensing is acquired, not waited for. A business intending to be large in Year 12 starts its licence acquisition in Year 1.
  5. Integration is mandatory. Each plan states what it supplies to and buys from the other domains.
  6. Gearing ≤40%, practically 15–25% for asset-backed businesses; no unhedged USD debt; financing ring-fenced per group.

Open items

These are the seven things standing between this library and a document a lender can act on. The first two are the ones that matter most.

  1. One consolidated capital plan per group, netting the known double-counts. No group plan in the library has a stated total that equals the sum of its company plans — every group table is a first-phase build programme that is read as a total, and each understates its own group by 7×–10×. The worst cases are self-flagged: Okodu ₦196bn against Okodu Power alone at ₦684bn, and Isiome ₦35bn against four of its own seven companies (Trading ₦83.1bn, Storage ₦75.0bn, Seed ₦66.9bn, Manufacturing ₦38.2bn). Akunnia's capital section now exists (08_Akunnia_Group.md §6) but deliberately states no single figure — it explains that this domain's money is three different kinds (deployable Group equity, locked regulatory capital, and third-party LP capital that is not the Group's at all), that the ₦120bn GP commitment reserve is double-counted between 09_Aku_Capital.md and 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md, and that Fund I's target is stated four different ways across the library (USD 100m in one plan against an explicit floor of USD 250m in another and USD 300–500m in two more). Any Akunnia total is an artefact until those two are fixed. Known double-counts to net: the ₦120bn GP commitment reserve carried in both 09_Aku_Capital.md and 10_Aku_Asset_Management.md; Okodu Power, Solar and Grid all building solar and battery storage; the Uli fleet in both 35_Uli_Freight.md and 40_Uli_Fleet.md; and 47_Okodu_Real_Estate.md and 50_Akuzo_Development.md counting the same Akuzo buildings and the same land. Until this is done the Group's capital requirement is not determinable. See ../EXECUTIVE_SUMMARY.md §5 and ../NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md §3.
  2. The Akuzo construction-cost basis — commission one measured cost book. But read the good news first. 50_Akuzo_Development.md costs a five-storey, 2,000 m² building at ₦35–50m (≈₦17,500/m²) while its own bill of quantities totals ₦1.55–1.60bn each — a 31–44× error, on a figure the plan itself declares unusable. The ₦35–50m figure is the per-plot land rate mis-carried into the build column: the land budget allocates 27–42 Akuzo plots at an average ₦60m (47:56), consistent with the ₦45.6m/plot implied by the ₦1.23bn land line. This is a mis-carried rate, not an unviable programme — and the family's own plans already contain a specification that works. 41:138 prescribes holding build cost to ₦650–850m per building by constraining gross area to 1,100–1,400 m² rather than 2,000 — "build fewer square metres, not cheaper ones" — and 50:164 reaches the same figure by stripping five redundant items (standalone solar, battery, biodigester, cistern, LPG grid) because Okodu Power serves the district anyway. ₦650–850m ÷ 1,100–1,400 m² = ₦464,000–773,000/m², which lands inside the independently verified ₦500,000–800,000/m² higher-spec band. So the target is defensible and the ₦35–50m line is the outlier. What is still missing is the tender. 59_Okodu_Housing.md already budgets ₦12m · day 60 for exactly this, and the Akuzo plan makes reconciling it "the board's first duty." The change cascades into five capital stacks, which is why it is a board decision and not an edit. See ../NUMBER_RECONCILIATION.md §8.4.
  3. A consolidated financial model — no Group-level P&L, balance sheet or cash-flow statement exists. The Group cannot be tested on consolidated leverage, interest cover, currency exposure, or the cash profile of a programme in which much of the working capital is revolving.
  4. Define gearing, then decide whether it applies to a lender at all. "Gearing ≤40%" was stated in six plans and defined in none, with three different denominators in use. The library now defines it as debt ÷ (debt + equity) (../EZEME_GROUP_OPERATING_ARCHITECTURE.md §10). On that basis Okodu Power's assumed 60% debt is a genuine breach — a power company is an asset-backed business and the ceiling applies to it. Aku Credit is a different case and needs a deliberate carve-out rather than a waiver by accident: it is funded 71% debt in Stages 2–3 and 79% in Stage 4, because in lending leverage is the product, not the risk appetite. A credit book at 40% debt earns an ROE close to its asset yield. The right control is a board-set debt/equity cap for that company alone plus a portfolio loss-rate gate — a 2-point miss on losses costs ~30% of ROE, while leverage only magnifies whatever the loss rate turns out to be. The arithmetic error the audit found here is now corrected: Stage 4 leverage is 3.75×, not the 3.0× the plan previously showed.
  5. Licence-by-licence ownership audit — mandatory. A London or New York manager above Nigerian operating companies is squarely "foreign interest" under NBC Act s.9(1) and possibly under other licence regimes; the broadcast licence and the private-guard-company licence may need Nigerian-controlled vehicles held separately from Aku (54_Aku_Security.md already assumes this and structures for it). Complete this before the hub is incorporated — it gates the whole finance platform.
  6. One price book and one tariff, and the grain error is not the one it looks like. Maize is carried at ₦650,000/t in three plans, not two — 04_Isiome_Farms.md is the origin, and 05_Isiome_Storage.md and 07_Isiome_Trading.md disagree with it. The reconciliation found the figure ~1.9× the Federal Government's own floor and unsupported; the defensible band is ₦350,000–470,000/t. Two consequences, and the second is the one that was missed: Storage's Year-5 working capital roughly halves, from ₦22–26bn to ₦12–16bn — and 04's per-hectare crop economics are built on the same number, so its main rain-fed maize row falls from ₦2.3–3.3m/ha to ₦1.48–2.12m/ha, a ~35% revenue cut. So the error is not uniformly conservative — it flatters the farm while penalising the store, and 04 already concludes the farm earns "low-to-mid single digits… below the cost of naira debt." Adopting the reconciled price therefore makes the farm's case harder, not easier. Both are financing decisions, not transcription fixes, which is why neither was applied. Electricity: the Group charges itself ₦150, ₦160 or ₦250/kWh depending on the plan, worth ₦60–129m a year at Uli Cinemas alone against ₦95.3m of EBITDA.
  7. The remaining decisive unknowns — ASERC's answer on the Anambra transfer order's scope and whether legacy federal instruments require novation (do not commit Okodu Power Tranche 2 before this); Ghana/NACOC eligibility (citizens only or citizens and permanent residents, and whether the test binds shareholders, directors or both); NAFDAC NCS on whether SAHPRA GMP supports a narcotics import permit; NUC's change-of-control position and whether NCS/NDLEA authorisations are transferable at all; and whether the six-year tertiary moratorium reaches NBTE-registered private polytechnics.

Two of these now decide strategy rather than tactics, and each has a costed ninety-day action whose only purpose is to establish the answer in writing. NUC change-of-control (24_Idenze_University.md) — the university's route is acquisition, because NUC suspended action on new private-university applications in February 2026 and imposed a six-year moratorium in March 2026, so there is no de novo path left open. But no published NUC guideline on change of control exists, which means the whole transaction structure rests on an unpublished position. ₦150m opinion, three approaches. And NCS/NDLEA transferability (19_Idenze_Therapeutics.md) — the controlled-substances set is the one licence family in the Group that the acquisition strategy probably cannot reach, and the plan says so plainly rather than inventing a market; the alternatives are a partner/JV on a tolling basis, or earning the record through 22_Idenze_Distribution's own trading history. ₦95m opinion, register of authorisation holders. Until these are answered in writing, Idenze University and Idenze Therapeutics are both planned but not underwritable — and both are among the largest capital commitments in the Group.

programme/akuzo-buildings.html.html:
WRITTEN

Akuzo Residence and Akuzo Court

The first two buildings — and a repeatable commercial model, not a one-off house.

Two buildings on the Akuzo compound in Nkpor, costed phase by phase. Building 1, Akuzo Residence, is the family's own home. Building 2, Akuzo Court, is the same envelope built commercially and sold unit by unit.

A newly formed development and construction company — an Ezeme Group subsidiary — is the direct employer of record for the workforce, the holder of all site contracts, and the long-term owner of any retained units. Labour is engaged directly on the company's own payroll rather than through a labour agency.

The commercial logic: retain one full floor, sell the other twelve units, and apply the proceeds to fund a third replication.

The numbers

Building 1 — Akuzo ResidenceUS$967,000 · five storeys · fourteen units · two 4-bed penthouses on floor 5
Building 2 — Akuzo CourtUS$999,000 · five storeys · fifteen units · a uniform maximum of three bedrooms anywhere in the building
Land2–3 Akuzo plots, US$40,000
FoundationReinforced raft — no piling required on inland soil, US$45,000
Structure and envelopeStructural frame, slabs, blockwork, roofing at about 2,000 m², US$150,000
ElevatorOne VVVF passenger lift, five stops, US$25,000 — “the single most visible quality differentiator in Anambra residential property”
Solar60 kW array with three-phase hybrid inverter bank, ~45 kW continuous / 65–70 kW surge — US$68,000
Battery250 kWh LiFePO4, one day of autonomy at 85% depth of discharge — US$38,000
Biodigester and generatorUnderground biodigester with H₂S scrubber plus a 10–15 kVA dual-fuel generator — US$55,000
Water100,000-litre underground cistern with sand, carbon and UV filtration — US$55,000
GasCentral LPG grid with smart meters to every kitchen — US$18,000
In-building fibreGPON head-end with an ONT per unit — US$25,000 / US$27,000
Daily load, per building~213 kWh/day: ~10 kWh per standard unit, ~16 per penthouse, ~55–60 for building systems
SupervisionOne COREN/ARCON-registered engineer or architect, full-time, above-market retainer — US$45,000

The sequence

  1. Phases 1–3 — Land, soil testing, access road, perimeter, raft foundation; drawings and Anambra State Physical Planning approvals; structural frame, blockwork and roofing — with the fibre conduit and riser shaft embedded in the structure, sharing the elevator and service core path.
  2. Phases 4–5 — Elevator, then the full off-grid services package: solar, battery, biodigester, generator, cistern and LPG.
  3. Phase 6 — Fit-out of twelve standard units and two penthouses, courtyard landscaping, and the active GPON fibre.
  4. Phase 7 — Full-time site supervision, company formation and payroll, and load testing of solar, gas and elevator systems.
  5. Then — Complete Building 1 first. Apply the proceeds of Building 2's unit sales to fund a third replication.

Open items

  • Sizing basis is stated but two inputs remain unconfirmed: the elevator vendor's actual motor rated power and starting current, and the expected air-conditioning and appliance load per unit. The elevator's starting surge, not the battery, is what drives inverter sizing.
  • The arithmetic does not reconcile. The document's closing paragraph cites “the full combined $1.85M exposure”, but its own line items sum to US$1,966,000. Resolve before budgeting.
  • The 30-year Akuzo plan prices a storey building at ₦35–50m for 27 buildings — ₦1.23bn in total — while these two buildings alone cost about US$1.97m, roughly ₦2.67bn at that plan's own ₦1,360 rate. And the 30-year cost model has no line at all for the US$234,000 per building of standalone solar, battery, biodigester, cistern and LPG added here. The two documents must be reconciled before either is used for pricing.

Source: Akuzo Development Programme-1.txt — the original document, unedited.

programme/akuzo-servers.html.html:
WRITTEN

Akuzo Dual Server Programme

Two independent server facilities. Not in the library at all — and it must be designed into the foundation.

Two physically and logically independent server facilities on the Akuzo compound, within the same fenced perimeter but separated by network, power and access control. Zero shared cabling, switches or credentials.

The Ezeme Family Server sits underground beneath Building 1 and serves the household and nothing else, in five VLAN-isolated tiers. The Akuzo Building Management Server is a ground-level room between the two buildings and is a revenue-generating business asset — it runs the estate's solar, water, biodigester, elevator and common-area CCTV, and bills the extended-family and cousin households resident across Akuzo.

The numbers

Family Server — coreDell R760xd2, 2× Xeon Gold 6448Y, 512 GB ECC (expandable to 1 TB)
Family Server — storage24 × 20 TB in ZFS RAID-Z2 across four vdevs → ~380 TB usable
Family Server — computeSupermicro 4U, 2× EPYC 9354, 512 GB, 2× RTX 5090 32 GB
Family Server — vaultFanless i7 with TPM 2.0 on its own default-deny VLAN
Family Server — backup60-bay Storinator, 1.2 PB raw → ~900–960 TB usable
Family Server — off-siteVault backups only, to rsync.net or Backblaze B2
Building Management — compute3× Dell R660 in Proxmox HA, 1.5 TB RAM cluster, Ceph-backed NVMe
Building Management — storage2× 60-bay Storinator, 2.4 PB raw → ~1.15–1.2 PB usable
Building Management — softwareOdoo for billing on mobile money and bank transfer; Authentik in a separate realm
Building Management — CCTVLobby, courtyard and elevator lobby only. Never unit interiors.
Combined~3.65 TB RAM · ~3.4–3.6 PB storage
Growth allowanceTier 1 and Tier 4 bays left unpopulated, reserved for the five children's data growth over the next decade

The sequence

  1. Before groundbreaking — This specification must reach the COREN/ARCON-registered site supervisor so that the family server room's floor loading, tanking and dual power and fibre entries are designed into Building 1's foundation rather than retrofitted.
  2. Months 1–6 — Firewall and switching, the household core, compute, vault and backup tiers; then the estate platform.
  3. Later — Local AI on the household compute tier.
  4. Per additional building — +512 GB RAM and roughly +900 TB–1.2 PB, being one more 60-bay chassis.

Open items

  • The document ends with an instruction that is easy to miss and expensive to ignore — it is listed first under sequencing above for that reason.
  • The programme notes that an NCC-licensed ISP subsidiary is “not warranted at the scale of one or two buildings”, while the building management server already bills 100+ households and is specified to serve every future Ezeme Group building. That is a scale argument closer to the licensing question than one or two buildings suggests.
  • No plan in the 60-plan library describes this facility. Only two plans mention servers at all, and neither describes this.

Source: Akuzo Dual Server Specification-1.txt — the original document, unedited.

Ezeme Hardware Platform

Five generations of devices, beginning with a pilot of ten media frames.

A hardware roadmap that grows out of the household's own technology stack. Generation 1 is an Ezeme Family Media Frame: an IPS display in a CNC walnut or oak and aluminium enclosure with a custom PCB and a secure element.

Manufacturing is specified as PCB fabrication in Nigeria or internationally, CNC machining and cabinet making within Nigeria, laser cutting by Nigerian manufacturers, with possible local final assembly.

Underneath sits Ezeme OS — secure boot, verified boot, signed over-the-air updates, offline-first — and the Ezeme Home companion apps for Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, Linux and the web.

The numbers

Gen 1Ezeme Family Media Frame. Pilot: assembly of ten units, then production batches of 50–100, with injection moulding considered later
Gen 2Smart mirror, kitchen display, voice assistant, information display
Gen 3Family tablet, children's learning tablet, notice board, portable dashboard, meeting-room and office displays
Gen 4Network gateway, backup appliance, storage expansion, smart power monitor, solar monitoring controller, farm monitoring gateway
Gen 5AI devices, elder care, vehicle displays
Household infrastructure firstFour-box server stack: OPNsense firewall · MS-01 application server · failover with off-site backup · Threadripper Pro with 256 GB ECC and an RTX 5090
Self-hosted servicesTailscale, Authentik, Nextcloud, Immich, Vaultwarden, Home Assistant, Jellyfin, Paperless, Ollama, AdGuard
Drone programme“Built as an aviation department, not a gadget purchase” — Pixhawk-class flight controller, RTK to 1–2 cm, Jetson Orin Nano, OpenDroneMap
Voice assistantWhisper, Piper and Ollama, with a staged Igbo plan tied to the dialect dictionary already under way
Commercial extensions sketchedEzeme Cloud, and an Ezeme Enterprise Server for schools, churches, hotels, hospitals, museums and government

The sequence

  1. Now — The household stack, so the family runs on its own infrastructure.
  2. Then — The media frame pilot of ten, then batches of 50–100.
  3. Later — Each generation reusing the same OS, supply chain and enclosure capability.

Open items

  • Commercial intent is stated in the future tense throughout — “a commercially hosted deployment operated by Ezeme”. No entity, price or channel exists for Ezeme Cloud or the Enterprise Server yet.
  • The São Paulo course map is written as a companion to “The Founder's Hardware & AI Curriculum” and cites “the Reference Unit”. Neither document is in the Drive corpus — they are the two referenced but missing files.

programme/jewellery-bank.html.title: Ezeme Jewellery Bank
programme/jewellery-bank.html.html:
WRITTEN

Ezeme Jewellery Bank

A lending business whose collateral is the family's own watches. Pledge, never sell.

A business owned and operated within the Ezeme Group. An heir who holds one of the charter watches may pledge it as collateral for a loan rather than ever selling it.

The watch is deposited in the bank's vault against a Receipt of Custody recording the reference, serial, condition rating and loan amount, with photographs. The heir receives cash — and the decisive rule is what must happen to it.

The watch is not being sold. It is being put to work. No heir of this House should ever feel compelled to sell what their parent left them.

The numbers

Loan to valueMaximum 65% of the independently appraised secondary market value
Minimum loanOrdinarily not below US$65,000
InterestNot to exceed a ceiling approved annually by the Patriarch and Matriarch; competitive with private banking
The fourteen-day ruleThe entire loan must be placed into income-generating fixed-interest instruments within 14 days — FGN bonds, Treasury bills, savings bonds or sovereign Eurobonds. No part of the principal may be spent on consumption, business, property or anything else
ReportingQuarterly bond statements are required. Failure to provide them constitutes default
RedemptionWithin five business days of repayment; serviced at the bank's expense if custody exceeded twelve months
DefaultAdjudicated internally by the Patriarch and Matriarch. Under no circumstances may the watch pass to an external creditor, recovery agency or court appointee
ServicingManufacturer service every five years without exception, at House treasury cost

The sequence

  1. The charter first — The Horological Succession Charter binds five named watches to offices rather than persons — a Patek Philippe Nautilus for the Patriarch, an Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Jumbo for the Matriarch, an A. Lange & Söhne Datograph for the Senior Male Heir, a Vacheron Constantin Overseas for the Senior Female Heir, and a Patek Philippe 5270G for the Third Son. Each above US$100,000.
  2. The prohibition — No charter watch may be sold, gifted outside the bloodline, donated, auctioned or pawned commercially. The prohibition is absolute and permanent, and no will or court order may direct one outside the bloodline.
  3. The one permitted transaction — The pledge above — the only route by which a watch may be encumbered.

Open items

  • This is functionally a pawnbroking and private-credit operation with a written credit policy, vault custody and receipts, and it touches Nigerian moneylending licensing questions. It should be reviewed as a lending business, not as a family rule, before any loan is made.

programme/nkpor-furniture-cluster.html.html:
WRITTEN

Nkpor Furniture & Soft Furnishings Cluster

The business being started: one workshop, two crafts, in Nkpor.

One workshop in Nkpor with a woodworking floor and a soft furnishings floor side by side, run as one business. Furniture builds the frame; soft furnishings finish it. Run together so an institutional buyer can order a complete fit-out — framed and finished — from a single contract.

Most competitors sell furniture or furnishings. The group sells a finished room.

The two crafts belong together because each is incomplete without the other, and because they share a supply chain, a delivery fleet and a quality standard. An institution furnishing a dormitory or a hotel does not want to buy frames from one supplier and covers from another.

The numbers

LocationNkpor, Idemili North, Anambra State
Anchor productsSchool, office, hospital and hotel furniture with the soft furnishings that complete each
Quality standardKiln-dried timber exclusively, with verified foam and fabric
Cycle One (Years 1–6)400–600 pieces per month · 2–3 institutional clients on repeat
Cycle Two (Years 7–12)20–30 units · 3,000–5,000 employees · first exports to Ghana and Cameroon
Cycle Three (Years 13–18)65–90 units · 16,000–26,000 employees · 6–8 training subsidiaries
Cycle Four (Years 19–25)150+ workshops · 35,000–65,000 direct and 40,000–80,000 indirect jobs · exports across five ECOWAS markets
SourcingTimber via Onitsha merchants from Niger Delta hardwoods and Cross River and Ondo plantations · MDF and plywood through Apapa · foam, fabric and thread through Onitsha

The sequence

  1. Year Zero — Secure the workshop space in Nkpor. Equip both floors. Solve power independently first — woodworking is the heavier load and must be solved once, for both crafts. Win the anchor contract. Set quality standards from day one.
  2. Cycle One — Establish the anchor workshop and the supporting functions the later units depend on: materials and timber supply, logistics and delivery, and training and quality. Getting the supply chain standing early is what lets every later workshop start working.
  3. Cycle Two — The cluster expands from the anchor into further units, each sharing the group's supply, logistics and standards, and the first exports go out to Ghana and Cameroon through the Onitsha network.
  4. Cycle Three onwards — Training becomes an export in its own right, and the cluster exports furniture and furnishings to Ghana, Cameroon, Togo and Côte d'Ivoire.

Open items

  • The apprenticeship equity model has been scrapped. The Nkpor model document is built entirely on Igba Odibo — settling apprentices into 50% ownership of new branches and compounding equity through the settling cycle. That is no longer the plan, so the document's growth mechanism no longer describes how this business expands. The workshop, the two crafts, the products, the quality standard and the cycle targets above stand; the equity mechanics do not. How the cluster expands in their place — hired management, direct-owned branches, franchising, or something else — is not yet written down anywhere, and needs to be before Year Zero.
  • The four pillars that survive the change: power solved independently · material quality (kiln-dried timber, verified foam and fabric) · institutional contracts before retail · export orientation.
  • Anchor contracts to win first: school furniture paired with classroom and dormitory soft furnishings; office furniture with upholstered seating and window treatments; hospital and clinic furniture with bedding, curtains and screens; hotel and hospitality fit-outs.

programme/ozi-ikoro-museum.html.title: Ozi Ikoro — Museum, Gallery and Research Hub
programme/ozi-ikoro-museum.html.html:
WRITTEN

Ozi Ikoro — Museum, Gallery and Research Hub

The only venture with a plan of its own, and the one with a registered company behind it.

A hybrid museum, art gallery and anthropological research hub in a converted warehouse in Awka, Anambra State. The name is the purpose: Ozi Ikoro — “Message of the Drum”. The museum speaks, communicating history and identity through objects, images and scholarship.

The concept is deliberately two-sided: the intellectual depth of a museum with the commercial energy of a gallery, so that preservation funds itself. Three wings carry the visitor — The Artefacts (“Footprints in Red Earth”), The Art (“The Future of Form”, a commercial contemporary gallery), and The Mixed (“Drawing and Object”, pairing 19th-century sketches with the tools they depict).

Around them sit an anthropology library and archive, a digital theatre, a glass-walled conservation laboratory the public can watch, and a store and café. The building is treated as a narrative rather than a container: spaces are divided by suspended Akwete and indigo textiles, mobile partitions on industrial tracks and lighting zones — not by permanent walls.

The numbers

LocationAwka, Anambra State — a converted warehouse
AdmissionsAdults ₦1,500 · students ₦500 · under-12s free · family ₦3,500 · groups ₦1,200 per person
MembershipFriend ₦15,000 · Patron ₦75,000 · Benefactor ₦250,000 · Corporate ₦200,000 a year
Gallery commission40% to the gallery, 60% to the artist
Price tiersMantlepiece ₦50,000–250,000 · Statement ₦250,000–1,000,000 · Monument ₦1,000,000–10,000,000+
Gala nightsTickets ₦50,000–100,000 · corporate tables ₦500,000–1,000,000 · net target ₦10–20m a year
Digital theatre8 × 10 m: a 12-screen decoder wall in a 3 × 4 grid, plus 3–5 individual viewing stations
Conservation labAbout 6 × 8 m, glass-enclosed and visible from the main path, with wet preservation in 70% ethanol
Digitisation rate5 objects a week, 260 a year, in English and Igbo
Year-3 revenue mixArt sales 40% · admissions 15% · store and café 15% · membership 10% · events and rentals 10% · consultancy 5% · grants 5%
Core teamDirector/Curator, Assistant Curator/Registrar, Gallery Manager and Conservation Assistant full-time; librarian, marketing and docents part-time
University partnersChukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University · Paul University Awka · Godfrey Okoye University · Madonna University · ESUT
Target marketsOnitsha business elite · Lagos collectors · the Abuja diplomatic community · diaspora Igbo in the UK, US and Canada · corporate collections

The sequence

  1. Year 1 — Infrastructure — Convert the warehouse, install the systems, begin the collection, launch the digital archive, establish the university partnerships, soft opening.
  2. Year 2 — Market presence — Six exhibitions mounted, the annual gala launched, the first catalogue published, 100 members.
  3. Year 3 — Institutional authority — Transition to foundation status, host a regional conference, secure international grants, 200+ members.

Open items

  • The plan contains no capital budget at all. It specifies a warehouse conversion down to the fume hood and the eyewash station, and asserts “lower capital costs” as an advantage — but it never states what the conversion, fit-out, initial collection or working capital actually cost, and it gives no break-even. This is the single largest gap: everything else in the plan is costed, and the building is not.
  • The location conflicts with the rest of the group. This plan is for Awka. The family base, the furniture clusters, both Akuzo buildings and the 30-year master plan all sit at Nkpor and Akuzo in Idemili North — a different city, roughly 40 km away. Either the museum is deliberately separate from the group's base, or one of the two locations is wrong.
  • The legal form is inconsistent. The plan's own draft letter of intent is signed “Director, Ozi Ikoro Foundation” and Year 3 proposes “transition to foundation status” — while the entity that exists is Ozi Ikoro Limited, RC 8955047, a company. A foundation and a limited company are different instruments with different rules; the plan should say which one this is.
  • The revenue model leans on admissions and membership, but the plan never estimates visitor numbers — so the 15% admissions and 10% membership lines cannot be checked against anything.
  • The wet specimen collection (roadkill collected under permit, natural deaths, zoo donations) requires permits and a documented ethical-sourcing policy. The plan states the policy but names no permit pathway or regulator.
  • The gala is benchmarked to “Agoziem Art's calendar”, which is an external comparator worth verifying before the ₦10–20m net target is relied on.

programme/sao-paulo.html.html:
WRITTEN

São Paulo — a separate company

Not the Nkpor group. One founder, one city, one product that works.

A different plan in the same corpus, and it should be held apart from the Nigerian group. It is a single-founder company in São Paulo, built between the ages of 29 and 40, selling a smart salon mirror with installation, software and after-care.

You have 11 years, not unlimited time and money. Your goal should not be ‘launch across Latin America, the USA, and EU.’ Your goal is to build one company that works in one city, then one country, then one additional market.

As in Nigeria, the discipline is explicit: Do not count an unproven business valuation as wealth. Real wealth is cash flow, investments, assets you control.

The numbers

ProductMirror 700 × 500 × 80 mm with a 10″ display; Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4; LED at CRI ≥90
Prototype budgetR$25,000–40,000 over about six months
Bill of materialsR$5,400 per station
Target priceR$8,500–12,000 per station
Gross margin35–45% on pilots, rising to 43–55% by year three
Break-even1.5 premium units a month against R$4,800 monthly overhead
ServicesEzeme Home app · Ezeme Space turnkey fit-out · Ezeme Care after-sales at R$150–250 a month
CertificationANATEL, INMETRO, LGPD
ExpansionBrazil, then one Latin American city, then one US city — and only on real demand

The sequence

  1. Phase 0 — Three to six months of preparation.
  2. Phase 1 — Learn and prototype in Brazil.
  3. Phase 2 — Close three to five paid pilot installations.
  4. Phases 3–4 — One product line profitable; then a repeatable premium-interiors company.
  5. Phases 5–7 — Latin America, then the United States, then scale value rather than complexity.

  • This is a personal founder roadmap, not a family holding company activity, and its product is unrelated to furniture. The corpus does not reconcile it with the 30-year Nkpor plan, and both use the name Ezeme.
  • The enrolment route into it is real and costed separately: free Fab Lab Livre SP for CNC, laser and PCB work; the 80-hour SENAI Brás fitted-kitchen cabinetry course and CTT Escola de Marcenaria; four SENAI-SP técnicos of roughly 1,200 hours each; and SENAC alternatives — sequenced across months 1–12.

programme/secure-hotspot.html.html:
UNDER WAY

Secure Personal Hotspot Programme

The one thing here that is genuinely under way: twenty units from a Shenzhen ODM.

A keychain-fob personal hotspot, designed for the family and specified for manufacture in Shenzhen. Twenty units: seven family members × two engraved units each, plus six spares branded “Ezeme”.

It is a deliberate privacy design. GPS and Bluetooth are excluded. UWB, NFC, an e-ink display and dual active eSIM are added. No custom moulds, to avoid over US$15,000 in upfront tooling costs.

The numbers

Quantity20 units, into one ODM in the Shenzhen area
FormKeychain fob, ~62 × 42 × 20–22 mm, IP68, gasket-sealed USB-C, Qi
Radio5G RedCap footprint, Wi-Fi 6 dual-band, UWB (10–30 m), NFC, LDS antenna
Excluded by designGPS / GNSS and Bluetooth
ComputeARM, 512 MB RAM, 2–4 GB eMMC, secure element
Battery2,200–2,500 mAh, 30+ hours
SoftwareOpenWrt or embedded Linux; WireGuard, WPA3, DNS-over-HTTPS
eSIMRemote switching via SM-DP+; Holafly named, and its plan must permit tethering
CertificationCE for EU travel, NCC for Nigeria
TimelineSourcing 4–8 weeks · sampling 3–4 · revision 2–3 weeks each · production 3–4 · deployment

The sequence

  1. Sourcing — ODM selection and quotation.
  2. Sampling — First articles, then revision rounds.
  3. Production — Twenty units, engraved and allocated.
  4. Deployment — Two units each to seven family members; six spares held branded.

Open items

  • The specification contradicts its own RFQ, and this must be settled before the RFQ is sent. The specification says one USB-C port, no SIM tray, and 2–3 simultaneous client devices. The ready-to-send RFQ asks for two USB-C ports on opposite sides, a dual physical nano-SIM tray supporting up to four carrier profiles, and 10–15 simultaneous client devices. The document itself flags the thickness conflict this creates.

Akuzo Development Programme 1

AKUZO DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME
A Home, and a Repeatable Commercial Model — Nkpor, Anambra State
Corporate Build Structure & Two-Project Budget Plan
1. Corporate & Labour Structure
Both projects are built under a newly formed development and construction company (an Ezeme Group subsidiary), which becomes the direct employer of record for the workforce, the holder of all site contracts, and the long-term owner of any retained units. Building under the company, rather than through a third-party turnkey contractor, gives Idenze direct cost visibility and quality control across both projects, and creates a reusable crew and management structure for future developments.
Labour is drawn from the local workforce on the ground in Nkpor and the wider Onitsha corridor — masons, iron benders, carpenters, electricians, and plumbers — engaged directly on the company's payroll rather than through a labour agency.
A single senior, registered civil engineer or architect (COREN/ARCON-registered) is retained full-time as site supervisor, at an above-market rate, to secure the strongest available oversight rather than the cheapest. This person carries responsibility for quality control, safety, and coordination of all trade foremen across the site.
The company handles payroll, welfare, and safety administration directly for the workforce — this replaces any reliance on foreign or agency labour.
The same supervising structure and crew can carry forward from Building 1 into Building 2, reducing the learning curve and mobilisation cost on the second project.
2. Off-Grid Load & Sizing Basis
Solar array and battery capacity are sized from an estimated daily energy load for each building, rather than assumed round numbers. The table below shows the basis for a typical building of this footprint; both Building 1 and Building 2 land within a similar range despite their different unit mixes.
Unit loads: ~10 kWh/day for a standard 1-3 bed unit (lighting, refrigerator, fans, one AC unit, general sockets); ~16 kWh/day for a larger 4-bed penthouse unit.
Elevator: 11kW motor, estimated ~30 minutes of cumulative daily runtime across all trips — roughly 5.5 kWh/day in energy terms, but its VFD starting surge (~1.5-2x rated load) is what drives inverter sizing, not battery capacity.
Building systems: water pumps, common-area lighting, security, telecom equipment, and biodigester scrubber together add roughly 55-60 kWh/day.
Total estimated demand: ~213 kWh/day for Building 1 (14 units incl. 2 penthouses) and ~212 kWh/day for Building 2 (15 uniform units) — close enough that both buildings use the same solar/battery specification below.
Solar array: 60kW panels, sized against ~4-4.5 peak sun hours in Anambra with an 80% system-loss allowance, is enough to cover average daily demand — but the inverter bank behind it must be rated for the elevator's starting surge, not just the array's wattage, hence the 3-phase hybrid inverter bank rated near 45kW continuous / 65-70kW surge.
Battery bank: 250kWh LiFePO4, sized for the full daily load at 85% usable depth-of-discharge with roughly one day of autonomy — deliberately not sized for multi-day full autonomy, since the dual-fuel backup generator already budgeted covers extended low-sun stretches.
This is a preliminary sizing based on estimated appliance and occupancy assumptions. Two things should be confirmed before finalizing the electrical design: the actual elevator motor's rated power and starting current from the chosen vendor's datasheet, and the expected AC/appliance load per unit once tenant or family usage patterns are known — both materially affect the final inverter and battery specification.
3. Building 1 — Akuzo Residence (Personal Home)
Five storeys, fourteen units, retaining the original layout: a 1-bedroom unit at the central core, a 2-bedroom unit in the left wing, and a 3-bedroom unit in the right wing on each of Floors 1-4, with two 4-bedroom penthouse suites on Floor 5. This building is intended as Idenze's personal residence and is not for sale. The budget now includes a private in-building fiber network, designed into the structure from Phase 2 rather than retrofitted after completion.

commissioning | $15,000 | Phase 7 | Contingency reserve | $114,500 | BUILDING 2 TOTAL | $999,000 | 5. Ownership & Sales Structure — Building 2
The company retains one full floor (three units, plus its share of common circulation) under the company name for long-term building management: either as a permanent management office and caretaker presence for the building, or held as company-owned rental stock generating recurring income. The remaining four floors — twelve units — are sold on the open market.
Recommended default: retain the ground floor. Ground-floor units are typically the easiest for the company to access and manage day-to-day, while upper floors carry a natural price premium from buyers for view and privacy — selling the higher floors captures more revenue than selling the ground floor would.
Alternative: retain the top floor instead, if the priority is long-term capital appreciation on the company's own holding rather than maximising immediate sale revenue. This is a judgement call best made once the sales pricing per floor is tested with local agents.
Either way, the retained floor should be ring-fenced in the company's building-management by-laws from the outset, so buyers of the other floors understand the ownership structure before they purchase.
6. Connectivity Strategy
Both buildings own their internal fiber network outright (private build), rather than leasing that infrastructure from an ISP. The telecom conduit and riser shaft are designed into the MEP drawings at Phase 2 and physically embedded into the structure at Phase 3, sharing a path with the elevator/service core, so no walls are chased or re-opened after finishing. The active equipment — GPON head-end and per-unit terminals — is installed during interior fit-out at Phase 6, in the same sequence as electrical wiring.
Bandwidth is sourced initially as a bulk wholesale agreement with a local Anambra-area ISP (e.g. PHSWEB), distributed internally over the company-owned network and billed to residents as part of rent or service charge.
Because the physical network is fully company-owned, it can later be leased to open-access fiber/infrastructure operators (e.g. GICL, ipNX, Spectranet, MainOne) as an additional passive-infrastructure income stream, independent of who supplies the bandwidth.
Forming a dedicated, NCC-licensed ISP subsidiary is not warranted at the scale of one or two buildings; it becomes worth revisiting once the Akuzo development grows into a multi-building estate with enough aggregate subscriber lines to justify buying wholesale transit directly.
7. Sequencing Note
Building 1 (home) and Building 2 (commercial) do not need to be funded simultaneously. A common approach is to complete Building 1 first, using the same land-banking, direct-labour, and supervising-engineer structure to prove out the model and refine real costs on the ground, then apply the proceeds of Building 2's unit sales to fund a third replication — rather than carrying the full combined $1.85M exposure across both projects at once.

Akuzo Dual Server Specification 1

EZEME GROUP — PRIVATE INFRASTRUCTURE
Akuzo Dual-Server Programme
Full Hardware & Systems Specification — Ezeme Family Server and Akuzo Building Management Server
Nkpor, Idemili North, Anambra State
1. Programme Overview
This document specifies two physically and logically independent server facilities on the Akuzo compound, both sited within the same fenced perimeter but separated by network, power, and access control.
Ezeme Family Server — underground, beneath Building 1 (Akuzo Residence), serving the Ezeme household (five children plus household systems) and nothing else. Business-grade capacity, private-trust tier.
Akuzo Building Management Server (BMS) — ground-level dedicated server room, centrally sited between Building 1 and Building 2, run as a standalone business platform: building operations (solar, water, biodigester, elevator, common-area CCTV) plus a capped, view-only Jellyfin library billed to the 100+ extended-family and cousin households resident across Akuzo, sized larger than the Family Server since it serves far more people today and every future Ezeme Group building added to the compound.
No cable, VLAN, credential, or shared switch connects the two facilities. Where the family wishes to view BMS status data (e.g. solar output) on a home dashboard, this is a single read-only feed through the family firewall — never a path back the other way.

Akuzo Urban Transformation Plan v3

THE AKUZO URBANTRANSFORMATION PLAN

A 30-Year Vision | Premium Residential District & Production Township

Ezeme Group  —  Akuzo Development Initiative

Nkpor, Idemili North LGA, Anambra State, Nigeria

2025 — 2055

PART ONE: THE VISION
1.1  What Akuzo Becomes
By 2055, Akuzo is a premium residential district — the place people in Nkpor want to live. Its streets are clean, shaded, and walkable. Its homes are a mix of community-refurbished traditional buildings and Ezeme Group storey buildings with elevators. Its civic infrastructure — the park, the civic centre, the football fields, the underground water network — is maintained by the residents who own it. It feeds two adjacent production townships and two colleges that together define the economic identity of Nkpor.
The reference is a Dutch residential neighbourhood: not a gated estate, not a compound, not a controlled development — but an open, walkable community where the quality of the streets, buildings, and civic spaces does the work that walls and fences do elsewhere.
1.2  The Three-Zone Structure
The broader Nkpor plan operates across three distinct zones, each with its own character:
Zone | Character | Primary Function | Akuzo Residential District | Quiet, clean, walkable, green | Premium housing — community-refurbished homes + Ezeme storey buildings | Apprenticeship Soft Furnishings & Upholstery Cluster | Open production township — Xingchen model | Soft furnishings & upholstery manufacturing — workers live and produce in integrated streets | Apprenticeship Furniture Cluster | Open production township — Xingchen model | Furniture manufacturing — kiln-dried timber, school tenders as anchor | These three zones are distinct but connected. The residential district is served by the two clusters; the clusters are supplied by the broader Nkpor agricultural and logistics infrastructure.
1.3  Real Estate as the Underlying Strategy
The Akuzo transformation is not philanthropy. It is one of the most deliberate long-term real estate accumulation strategies in Anambra. As Akuzo's infrastructure improves — security, water, roads, schools, civic spaces — property values rise. Every building Ezeme Group acquires early is worth significantly more by Year 10, and dramatically more by Year 30. The community transformation and the real estate portfolio are the same project.

PART TWO: AKUZO RESIDENTIAL DISTRICT — MASTER PLAN
2.1  Zoning Principle: Residential Only
Akuzo is zoned exclusively for residential use. No production workshops, no commercial units, no industrial activity. The civic centre, park, football fields, fisheries, and colleges are community and institutional uses — they serve the residential population but do not generate industrial activity within the residential streets.
The commercial and production activity of the community happens in the two apprenticeship cluster townships adjacent to Akuzo. Residents of those clusters may also choose to live in Akuzo and commute to their workshops — or live above their workshops in the cluster. Both are valid. Akuzo itself stays clean, quiet, and residential.

PART THREE: EZEME GROUP REAL ESTATE STRATEGY
3.1  The Core Principle
Every community improvement made in Akuzo increases the value of every property in Akuzo. The strategy is to own as much of that property as possible before the improvements are complete. This is not speculation — it is building the community and capturing the value that the community creates, which is then reinvested back into further improvements.
Over 30 years, Ezeme Group targets ownership of a significant and growing share of Akuzo's residential real estate — through acquisition of properties that come up for sale, strategic redevelopment, and building new structures on acquired land. The portfolio compounds as the neighbourhood improves.
3.2  Two Tracks Running Simultaneously
Track 1 — Community-Led Refurbishment of Existing Homes
Homes already owned by residents are refurbished through collective community effort. This is the Igbo tradition of communal self-help (Otu Ulo) applied to urban improvement. The Akuzo Development Council coordinates refurbishment campaigns: a street or cluster decides together to paint, plaster, repair gutters, and fix roofs. Ezeme Group provides materials at cost or subsidised, residents provide labour. The result is a neighbourhood that looks upgraded without requiring anyone to sell their home.
Annual refurbishment campaign — one street or cluster per year
Ezeme Group supplies bulk materials (cement, paint, roofing sheets) at reduced cost
Labour from residents, youth groups, and Skills Hub apprentices as on-site training
Before-and-after documentation reinforces community pride and attracts diaspora investment
Track 2 — Ezeme Group Property Acquisition and Development
When a property comes up for sale anywhere in Akuzo, Ezeme Group has a standing mandate to acquire it at fair market price. No pressure, no manipulation — but a consistently expressed interest so that sellers approach Ezeme Group first. Over 30 years, through natural turnover (families leaving for Abuja, diaspora selling inherited land, owners unable to maintain properties), this produces a significant portfolio.
Each acquired plot is developed into a storey building designed to the Akuzo residential standard — 4 to 6 floors, concrete frame construction, elevator, tiled stairwells, backup generator, metered utilities. The elevator is the single most visible quality differentiator in Anambra residential property. It signals a category of building that does not exist in most of Nkpor — and creates a premium rental and sale market.
3.3  The Storey Building Standard
Every Ezeme Group building constructed in Akuzo meets the following specification:

Each Ezeme Group building in Akuzo generates revenue through three streams:
Rental income — apartments rented to residents, professionals, and students from the colleges
Unit sales — some apartments sold outright, recycling capital for further acquisitions
Property value appreciation — the portfolio value compounds as Akuzo's infrastructure improves
Rental income from early buildings funds acquisition of the next plot. The portfolio is self-financing by Year 8, meaning no further external capital injection is required for real estate expansion — the portfolio grows from its own cash flow.
