PART FOUR: APPRENTICESHIP PRODUCTION TOWNSHIPS — THE XINGCHEN MODEL
4.1  The Reference: Xingchen Production Cluster
The Xingchen Underwear Production Cluster in China is one of the most studied examples of an organic production township — an entire district built around a single trade, where production, residence, supply chain, wholesale, and retail are all integrated into open, walkable streets. There are no compound walls, no security fences, no separation between where people work and where people live. The cluster is a neighbourhood.
Every building in a Xingchen-style cluster follows the same basic logic: ground floor is a workshop or showroom; upper floors are the owner's or workers' living quarters. Suppliers of raw materials occupy neighbouring streets. Buyers walk in and out freely. The whole district hums with visible, open production. This openness is not a security weakness — it is a commercial strength, because buyers can see exactly what is being made and place orders on the spot.
This is the model for both apprenticeship clusters in Nkpor. No compound. No fence. Open production streets where apprentices own their units, families live above workshops, and the district identity is built around the craft.
4.2  How the Apprenticeship Equity Model Fits the Xingchen Structure
The Ezeme Apprenticeship Model — where a settled apprentice receives 50% equity in a new production unit, with the parent company retaining 50% — maps perfectly onto the Xingchen physical structure. Each settled apprentice’s new unit is not just a business: it is a building. Ground floor workshop, upper floor apartment. The apprentice owns 50% of that building. The Ezeme Group retains 50%. Both benefit from the property value appreciation as the cluster grows.
Over time, as each Odibo settles more of their own apprentices, the cluster grows organically. New units are added to adjacent streets. The supply chain fills in around them. The cluster becomes a self-replicating economic organism that Ezeme Group anchors but does not have to manage centrally.
4.3  Apprenticeship Soft Furnishings & Upholstery Cluster
Location and Character
A distinct street or district adjacent to Akuzo, dedicated to soft furnishings and upholstery production. Streets are open and walkable. Ground floor of each building: a sewing and upholstery workshop, cutting room, or fabric and materials showroom. Upper floors: apartment for the owner-apprentice and their household. Foam suppliers, fabric and thread merchants, and hardware fittings traders all occupy ground-floor units in the same streets — the full supply chain in walking distance.
Anchor Product Strategy

Export target by Year 20: West African hotel and institutional market via AfCFTA logistics corridor

4.4  Apprenticeship Furniture Cluster
Location and Character
A separate district from the Soft Furnishings & Upholstery Cluster, dedicated to furniture production. The same Xingchen open-street model applies. Ground floor workshops for carpentry, finishing, and upholstery; upper floor apartments for owner-apprentices. Timber yards and kiln-drying facilities are located at the edges of the cluster where vehicle access and drying space allow.
Quality Differentiator: Kiln-Dried Timber
The vast majority of furniture made in Anambra uses air-dried or green timber, which warps, cracks, and degrades within 3-5 years. The Apprenticeship Furniture Cluster uses kiln-dried timber exclusively — timber that has been dried in a controlled kiln to the correct moisture content before cutting. This produces furniture that maintains its shape, resists cracking, and lasts decades. In the Anambra market, this is a significant and clearly communicable quality advantage.
Anchor Contract Strategy
School furniture tenders — the largest and most consistent furniture contract in any state
University and polytechnic furniture for the Nkpor higher institution cluster (internal tender)
Office furniture for government and corporate clients in Onitsha and Awka
Residential furniture for Ezeme Group storey buildings — internal supply chain, guaranteed volume
Export target by Year 20: West African institutional market via AfCFTA logistics corridor

PART FIVE: SECURITY MODEL
The security model covers three distinct zones: the Akuzo Residential District, the Soft Furnishings & Upholstery Cluster, and the Furniture Cluster. Each has a different character and different security needs. The unifying principle is community-integrated security — CCTV, lighting, and neighbourhood watch — not walls, compounds, or private armies.
5.1  Akuzo Residential District Security
Community gateway: single main entrance point with guard kiosk, barrier arm, and CCTV
16-camera CCTV network: entrance, all main road intersections, park, civic centre, fisheries, football fields
Solar streetlights with integrated CCTV mounts on all roads — lighting and surveillance on the same pole
Night patrol team (3 men, 2 shifts): covers fisheries, residential streets, and sports area
Youth age-grade neighbourhood watch: daytime coverage, incident reporting, community deterrence
Formal MOU with nearest police divisional station: emergency response protocol
Anambra State Neighbourhood Watch registration: institutional cover and government cooperation
5.2  Apprenticeship Cluster Security
The clusters are open — no compound walls. Security is achieved through visibility, lighting, and community stake. People protect what they own. Every workshop owner in the cluster has an equity stake in their building. They are the most motivated security actors in the district.
CCTV at all cluster road entrances and the cluster square — not fences
Solar floodlights throughout cluster streets — active all night
Night watchman shared across cluster residents — funded from a cluster maintenance levy
Cluster residents' association — monthly meeting, incident log, rapid response coordination
Fire safety: extinguishers at every workshop unit, shared sand buckets, clear egress paths
No barrier or gate — open access is a commercial advantage for buyer traffic during day hours

6.1  Underground Water Spine
One central underground corridor runs beneath the main Akuzo road from the gateway to the agricultural zone. A single trench carries four systems at different depths: clean water supply pipe, sewage collector, stormwater drain, and electrical conduit. Dug once, maintained permanently, extended phase by phase.
A Mexican tunneling engineer residency in Year 1 trains local Akuzo youth — enrolled in the Skills Hub water engineering track — in microtunneling and pipe-jacking techniques. After Year 6, the community is fully self-sufficient in maintaining and extending the network.
6.2  Covered Drainage with Trash Filters
Precast concrete covered drains on both sides of every road, with removable steel mesh trash-filter baskets every 40-50 metres. Covered gutters give nobody anything to dump into. All drainage work is done in the same ground-opening as road paving and pipe installation — one disruption, not three separate ones.

7.1  Purpose and Species
The Akuzo Community Fisheries is a permanent non-profit community infrastructure. Its sole purpose is to make fresh fish affordable and consistently available to residents of Akuzo and the surrounding Nkpor community. It is not an Ezeme Group revenue line. The apprenticeship equity model does not apply here. Fish sale prices are set below open market by the Fisheries Committee annually.
Two species are farmed, chosen for complementary reasons:
Species | Why This Species | Market Positioning | Grey Mullet (Asa/Titus) | Thrives in freshwater ponds with minimal intervention; excellent eating quality; high demand in Anambra and Onitsha market; less common in farmed supply = premium positioning | Premium fresh fish at subsidised community price — a clear differentiator from tilapia-dominated market | Catfish (Clarias) | The dominant farmed fish in Southeast Nigeria; proven in earthen ponds; fast growth; strong local demand year-round; easily smokeable for preservation | Everyday staple supply at consistently below-market price — food security anchor for the community | 7.2  Self-Sustaining Mechanism
Initial capital is a one-time community investment. After that, fish sales cover all recurring costs — fingerlings, feed, labour, cold storage power, and maintenance. Surplus above operating costs is reinvested in pond expansion, not distributed. Staggered harvest cycles ensure at least one pond is always near harvest readiness, eliminating supply gaps. Four ponds at full capacity produce a continuous rotation.

The Honest Starting Point
You have 11 years, not unlimited time and money.
Your goal should not be “launch across Latin America, the USA, and EU.” Your goal is to build one company that works in one city, then one country, then one additional market.
Ezeme OS is not a separate digital product. It is part of the Ezeme system. Customers buy a physical smart-living experience: furniture, installation, design, functionality, support, and the embedded Ezeme OS.
The first five years are for proving that Ezeme can make money. The next six years are for scaling what works.
FOUNDATIONAL DEFINITIONS
Before you build anything, you must know exactly what each part of Ezeme means in practical, technical, and commercial terms.
Ezeme OS — What It Actually Is
Ezeme OS is the embedded software layer that runs on a small, cost-effective computing board (initially a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 or equivalent industrial-grade board) installed inside each smart mirror or vanity unit. Version 1 does not include voice control, AI, or cloud-heavy features.
Version 1.0 feature set (must-have):
Touch display interface – a 10-inch or 15-inch screen behind the mirror glass that shows:
Time, date, and local weather
A simple salon-specific widget (e.g., client queue, appointment reminders – syncs with Google Calendar via API)
Lighting colour-temperature and brightness controls (presets: “Daylight”, “Warm”, “Cool”, “Evening”)
Bluetooth pairing – allows the salon owner to stream audio (playlist) through built-in speakers (optional)
USB-C charging port – integrated into the vanity for client devices
Over-the-air (OTA) update capability – the OS can receive security and feature patches via Wi-Fi
Local-only operation – all core functions work without internet; cloud sync is optional and only used for updates and non-critical analytics
Admin panel (web-based) – for the salon owner to adjust settings, view usage, and request support
What Version 1 does NOT do (saved for later):
Facial recognition
Inventory tracking
Voice assistants (Alexa/Google)
Autonomous scheduling
Development plan: You will not build this alone. Contract a Brazilian or remote embedded-systems freelancer (upwork.com / local via SENAI networks) during Phase 1 to port an open-source touch-UI framework (e.g., Flutter or Qt) to the Raspberry Pi. Budget ~6 months and R$ 25,000–40,000 for the first working prototype.
Ezeme Home — The Companion Application & Management Platform
Ezeme Home is the official companion application and management platform for the Ezeme ecosystem. It is the web/app layer that sits above each individual Ezeme OS unit, giving an owner one consistent place to configure, monitor, and manage every Ezeme device they own, whether that is a single salon mirror or a multi-station studio.
Ezeme Home will be available on Android, iPhone, iPad, Windows, macOS, Linux, and modern web browsers, so an owner can manage their devices from whichever platform they already use.
Through Ezeme Home, users will be able to:
Add and configure Ezeme devices.
Connect photo, music, video, calendar, and weather sources.
Customise Smart Mirror layouts and widgets using a live preview.
Monitor device health and security.
Receive notifications and alerts.
Ezeme Home is the natural counterpart to the local, on-device admin panel described under Ezeme OS above: the on-device panel handles day-to-day operation at a single station, while Ezeme Home is the cross-device layer for an owner managing one or many installations remotely. Treat it as part of the same Ezeme OS development track in Phase 1, not a separate product — it shares the same freelancer/contractor budget and timeline discussed above.

Sales Process for Pilots
Lead generation: Direct outreach to 50 São Paulo salons via Instagram DM, email, and in-person visits. Use your blog content as a conversation starter.
Discovery call (15 min): Understand their current setup, pain points, budget, and decision-making timeline.
Proposal: Send a one-page PDF with product image/render, what's included, price with early-adopter discount, installation timeline, and a testimonial from beta testers once available.
Site visit: Measure the salon space, discuss customisation, take photos.
Contract & deposit: 50% upfront, 50% on completion.
Installation: You lead the first 5 installations personally to learn every pain point.
Follow-up: 7-day check-in; request a video testimonial; ask for a referral.
Pilot pricing guide:
Cost of materials + labour (Brazilian rates): ~R$ 4,500–6,000 per station
Your price to salon: R$ 8,500–10,000 (early-adopter discount)
Gross margin per station: ~35–45%
Minimum viable pilot: 3 stations at R$ 9,000 each = R$ 27,000 revenue
End-of-year test:
At least three paying customers
At least two strong video case studies
Clear project margin data
At least one referral
A repeatable installation checklist
If pilots only work because you underprice yourself, the business is not ready.

EZEME CARE — EXPANDED
Ezeme Care is not a digital product. It is a service agreement covering maintenance, repairs, inspections, support, and upgrades.
What it includes (Standard plan — R$ 150/month per station):
Annual on-site inspection (cleaning, firmware update, calibration)
Priority support via WhatsApp (response within 4 business hours)
Software updates (security patches, new features)
Hardware warranty extension (covers parts, labour for repairs — excludes accidental damage)
Premium plan (R$ 250/month):
All of the above + quarterly inspections + 24-hour response time + a 10% discount on future upgrades
Terms:
Minimum 12-month contract
Automatic renewal unless cancelled
Client pays a small call-out fee (R$ 200) for non-warranty issues
Why it matters:
Generates recurring revenue (highly valuable for valuation)
Keeps you in touch with clients (upsell opportunities)
Builds long-term relationships
Legal and Privacy Requirements
Because Ezeme includes software and connected hardware, take privacy and compliance seriously from the start.
Brazil has the LGPD data-protection law.
EU privacy obligations can apply to non-EU companies targeting people in the EU.
Do not collect personal data that Ezeme does not need.
Build clear consent, account deletion, secure access, and software-update processes.
Use specialist legal and technical advice before selling connected hardware internationally.
EXIT STRATEGY
By age 40, you may want to sell or step back. Here is a realistic path:
Exit Type | What It Looks Like | Likely Buyer | Approx. Timing | Minority investment | Sell 20–30% equity to a strategic partner or angel to fund growth while you retain control | High-net-worth individuals, family offices, or design-sector VCs | Year 7–9 | Trade sale | Sell the whole company to a larger interiors/hospitality group | Furniture manufacturers (e.g., Tok&Stok, local brands), smart-home conglomerates | Year 10–11 | Licensing model | Instead of selling, license Ezeme OS and design standards to third-party manufacturers; collect royalties | Multiple licensees across countries | Year 8 onward | Management buyout | Hand over day-to-day operations to a trusted team while you retain ownership and receive dividends | Internal team | Year 11+ | Valuation guide for a premium-interiors company:
Typical multiple: 3–5× annual net profit (for small businesses) or 6–8× EBITDA (if well-established with recurring Care revenue)
Example: If Year 10 net profit = R$ 1.2M, valuation could be R$ 3.6M–6M (US$ 700k–1.2M). Your 60% equity = US$ 420k–720k.
To reach the multimillionaire case, you need net profit > R$ 2.5M/year or a strong brand premium.
Preparation for any exit:
Clean financial records (audited if possible)
Documented processes (so the business runs without you)
Strong recurring revenue (Ezeme Care contracts)
Owned IP (trademarks, designs, software)
Your Next 30 Days
Audit what already exists in Ezeme: hardware, software, designs, suppliers, money, team, and intellectual property.
Decide exactly what Mirror One does and does not do (now defined above).
Talk to 20 target buyers; do not ask whether they “like” the idea — ask what they currently spend, what frustrates them, and what would make them change.
Contact the São Paulo and Bento Gonçalves schools.
Start Portuguese lessons.
Build a 12-month relocation and living budget.
Start the Ezeme website and publish the first founder article.
Speak with a Brazilian immigration lawyer and accountant.
Create a one-page pilot offer for a premium salon.
Do not expand product scope until the first paid pilot works.
APPENDICES — TOOLS & TEMPLATES
Appendix A: Pilot Contract — Key Clauses
Clause | What to Include | Scope | “Ezeme Salon Mirror V1 – supply, installation, training” | Price | Fixed price + payment schedule (50/50) | Timeline | Deposit to installation in ≤ 30 days | Warranty | 12 months parts/labour, excludes misuse | Ezeme Care | Optional add-on (price and terms) | Liability | Limited to the contract value; no consequential damages | IP | Ezeme retains all design and software rights | Confidentiality | Client cannot share pricing or design details | Appendix B: Monthly Cash-Flow Template (Year 1–2)
Month | Starting Cash | Revenue | Direct Costs | Overhead | Net Cash Flow | Ending Cash | Jan | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | Overhead categories: Rent, utilities, accounting, legal, marketing, insurance, software hosting, transport, meals/incidentals.
Appendix C: Quality-Control Checklist (Pre-Delivery)
Item | Pass/Fail | Mirror glass: no scratches, chips, or distortion | ☐ | LEDs: all pixels working, colour temperature adjust smoothly | ☐ | Touchscreen: responsive, no dead zones | ☐ | Cabinetry: all drawers close flush, soft-close works | ☐ | Cable management: all wires concealed, secure | ☐ | OS: boots, Wi-Fi connects, all widgets display | ☐ | USB ports: charge devices | ☐ | Installation kit: complete (brackets, screws, template) | ☐ | Appendix D: First 5 Pilot Customer Feedback Form
Ask each pilot client:
On a scale of 1–10, how satisfied are you with the product?
What is the #1 thing you would change?
How much time does it save you daily?
Would you buy again? Would you refer?
What price do you think is fair?
Any technical issues? Please describe.
The One-Sentence Plan
Move to Brazil to gain real furniture-making and supplier knowledge; prove one premium Ezeme mirror-and-vanity system in São Paulo; use media to create demand; build profitable Brazilian installations; repeat through local partners in one Latin American market; then enter the U.S. with a proven, compliant, high-value system.
This amended plan gives you every operational definition, cost estimate, checklist, and contingency you need to start. Now go execute — one workshop, one salon owner, one prototype at a time.

Ezeme Family Governance Charter

THE HOUSE OF EZEME
Family Governance Charter
Assembly · Council · Court · Business Board · Treasury · Secretariat

“Onye aghala nwanne ya.” — Let no one abandon their kin.
This Charter establishes the governing institutions of the House of Ezeme — the immediate family and lineage founded by Somtoo and Ifeoma Ezeme, and carried forward by their children Isiome, Akunnia, Idenze, Uli, and Okodu, and their descendants. It draws its spirit from Ụmụnna — the wider Igbo kindred's tradition of collective deliberation, mutual accountability, and elder-guided consensus — but is deliberately scoped to this household and its bloodline, rather than the extended kindred of Akuzo.
Where Ụmụnna governs a community bound by common ancestry across many households, this Charter governs one household's internal order: how it settles disputes, how it decides its future, how it stewards what it builds, and how it remembers itself. It is offered as a living document — amendable as the family grows — not a fixed law. In effect, this Charter is the Ezeme Family Constitution: every institution described below draws its authority from it.
I. Structure of Governance
The House of Ezeme is governed through five institutions, each with a distinct mandate, all standing under this Charter.
THE EZEME FAMILY
↓
FAMILY ASSEMBLY
( the sovereign gathering — monthly, with a larger annual sitting )
↓
FAMILY COUNCIL
( day-to-day governance )
↓                                    ↓
FAMILY COURT                FAMILY BUSINESS BOARD
( justice & disputes )        ( business & wealth )
↓
FAMILY TREASURY
( collective financial resources )
FAMILY SECRETARIAT & ARCHIVE
( records and institutional memory — serves all five bodies )
The Family Assembly is sovereign: it is where the whole family — including children as observers — hears reports, celebrates, and approves the matters that shape the household's direction. The Family Council conducts the day-to-day governance that Assembly does not have time for, and prepares matters for Assembly's attention. The Court and the Business Board are peers beneath the Council — deliberately separated so that a dispute in one never becomes leverage in the other. The Treasury and the Secretariat are standing support institutions: the Treasury guards what the family owns collectively, and the Secretariat guards what the family remembers.
Guiding principle — the firewall
A disagreement between siblings who also work together in an Ezeme Group business is a family matter, not a business matter, unless and until the Business Board formally determines that it has business consequences requiring its own separate process. The Court does not decide business questions. The Board does not adjudicate personal grievances. Membership on one body does not grant standing on another.
II. The Family Assembly
The Family Assembly is the highest and most inclusive gathering of the House of Ezeme. It brings together all family members — regardless of voting status — for the matters that concern the whole household.
Purpose
Hear reports from the Family Council and the Family Business Board
Discuss major family matters affecting the household as a whole
Approve major changes to family rules or to this Charter
Discuss the education and welfare of children
Discuss family traditions, heritage, and the Odinani cultural anchor
Celebrate achievements
Elect or confirm Family Officers
Review the state of the family each year
Frequency
The Assembly convenes monthly, distinct from the informal weekly family gathering described in Section IX. A larger Annual Family Assembly is held each December to review the year in full: what the family accomplished, how the businesses performed, how the Treasury stands, how the children progressed, what went wrong, what was learned, and what the objectives are for the year ahead.
III. The Family Council
The Family Council is the House of Ezeme's day-to-day governing body — a cabinet rather than a court — and the institution closest in spirit to Ụmụnna, restricted here to the immediate family rather than the wider kindred.
Jurisdiction
Family values, traditions, and the Odinani cultural anchor of the household
Children's development, education, and the Family Education Structure
Family welfare, health, and general wellbeing
Relationships, roles, and responsibilities among family members
Household responsibilities and family property
Family projects, including the Akuzo Residence and Akuzo Court developments
Major purchases and family travel
Family reputation
Long-term dynastic planning, including the Family Holding Structure and Raising Plan
The Council prepares matters that require full family input for the Family Assembly, and refers matters requiring adjudication to the Family Court.
Composition
Somtoo and Ifeoma sit as founding co-chairs for the life of the Council's first generation. Each of the five children — Isiome, Akunnia, Idenze, Uli, and Okodu — holds a seat, with voting rights activating on admission to full membership as set out in Section IX.
Meeting rhythm
The Family Council convenes weekly, on Saturday evening, following the Family Court where applicable. It may also convene in emergency session for urgent matters at the request of any two members with voting rights.
IV. The Family Court
The Family Court exists to resolve internal disputes fairly — not to punish, but to teach justice, responsibility, evidence, listening, and reconciliation, consistent with Odinani's emphasis on balance and repair over retribution.
Jurisdiction
Serious disagreements between family members
Breaking a family agreement or breach of this Charter
Repeated failure to fulfil responsibilities
Property or financial disputes
Accusations of dishonesty or serious disrespect
Damage to another member's property
Disputes concerning family projects
Complaints, grievances, and requests for apology or reconciliation
Procedure
1. Petition — a member brings a complaint before the Court.
2. Notice — the person complained about is informed of the matter.
3. Hearing — both sides explain what happened, in full, before anyone responds.
4. Evidence — where appropriate, evidence is presented.
5. Questions — the Court asks questions to establish what actually occurred.
6. Defence — the person complained about is given a full opportunity to respond.
7. Deliberation — the presiding elders or panel discuss the matter privately.
8. Judgment — a decision is issued.
9. Restoration — wherever possible, the outcome repairs the relationship rather than simply punishing someone.
Possible outcomes
No wrongdoing established
Warning or apology
Restitution or replacement of damaged property
Temporary loss of a privilege, or additional responsibility
Mediation, reconciliation, or a behavioural agreement
Referral to the Family Council where the matter touches family policy
For children, consequences are age-appropriate and educational — never humiliating, and never abusive.
Two governing principles
No person may be simultaneously judge, prosecutor, and accused in the same matter. If a dispute is between a parent and a child, that parent does not personally decide the case — another elder or panel member presides instead.
The Family Court is not for ordinary disagreements that a conversation could resolve. It exists for serious or genuinely unresolved matters; using it for every small argument would put the whole family on trial for nothing.
Any party may appeal a Court decision to the full Family Council at its next sitting. No matter heard by the Court may be raised in, or influence, a Business Board proceeding, and vice versa.
Composition
The Court is convened by Somtoo and Ifeoma as presiding elders during the founding generation, joined by a rotating panel of members not directly party to the matter at hand. As the second generation matures, presidency of the Court may rotate among senior members by Council decision — and always excludes anyone with a personal stake in the matter being heard.
Meeting rhythm
The Family Court convenes on Saturday morning, ahead of the Family Council, and only when a matter has genuinely been raised requiring it. It does not meet as a matter of routine.
V. The Family Business Board
The Family Business Board is deliberately separated from the Family Court. It functions as a family office and board of directors for the House of Ezeme's commercial interests — chiefly the Ezeme Group and its ten sectors across the five domains, together with family-owned ventures such as Ozikoro and Ozituma, which remain administratively distinct from the Group but fall within the Board's oversight as family-owned assets.
Jurisdiction
Business strategy across the Ezeme Group's domains
Investments, assets, and property, including the Akuzo developments and private infrastructure
Budgets, financial performance, and risk management
New ventures, including Ezeme (smart interiors) and future domain projects
Hiring senior employees and placing family members into business roles
Succession planning and ownership
Dividends, reinvestment, and business ethics
Membership is not the same as employment
Being a family member does not automatically make someone a business director, and family membership does not by itself entitle anyone to a role, a title, or a share of profit. Any family member who takes on work within an Ezeme Group business does so in a proper role, with responsibilities matched to that role — and is paid for that work like any other position would be paid, according to what the work is worth and what it delivers. Family membership and family employment are two separate things, held to two separate standards.
Composition
Somtoo chairs the Business Board as founding principal until succession. Each domain heir — Isiome, Akunnia, Idenze, Uli, and Okodu — holds a seat corresponding to their paired sectors (Agriculture & Manufacturing; Finance & Governance; Education & Healthcare; Media & Logistics, including Brazil operations; and Energy & Construction respectively), with voting rights activating on admission to full membership as set out in Section IX. Akunnia, as designated Chief Investment Officer, holds standing responsibility for consolidated financial reporting to the Board and the Treasury.
Meeting rhythm
The Family Business Board convenes on the first Saturday of each month, reviewing performance, budgets, and pending decisions across all five domains. Matters requiring more urgent attention may be escalated to an extraordinary session by the chair or any two domain heirs holding voting rights.
VI. The Family Treasury
As the family's collective wealth grows, the Family Treasury manages resources held in common — distinct from any individual member's earnings or any single business's accounts.
Scope
The family's collective investment portfolio
An emergency reserve for the household
Family property held in common
Education funds for the children and future generations
The family's ownership interests in Ezeme Group businesses and other ventures
Philanthropic funds
Intergenerational wealth intended to outlast any one generation
The Treasury keeps proper records and requires multiple approvals — never a single signature — for any major transaction. It reports to the Family Business Board on a monthly basis and to the Family Assembly at least annually.
VII. The Family Secretariat & Archive
Someone must be responsible for the family's records, or its history and decisions will be lost to memory alone. The Secretariat maintains:
This Charter and any amendments to it
Minutes of the Council, Court, Business Board, and Assembly
Family agreements and Court decisions
The family tree, birth records, and marriage records
Property and business records
Family photographs, achievements, and historical documents
Annual reports presented to the Family Assembly
Over time, the Secretariat's holdings are intended to grow into a proper Ezeme Family Archive, alongside the cultural documentation already underway through Ozikoro.
VIII. Family Officers
As the family grows, formal offices give each institution a clear person to answer to, rather than leaving responsibility diffuse. These positions are filled by Council appointment during the founding generation and are intended to become elected or confirmed by the Family Assembly as the household enters its second generation.
Family Head — overall leadership and external representation of the family (Somtoo, founding)
Family Chairperson — chairs Family Council meetings
Family Judge / Justice Chair — presides over Family Court proceedings, excluded from any matter in which they have a personal stake
Family Secretary — maintains records and minutes for the Secretariat
Family Treasurer — oversees the Family Treasury
Business Board Chair — leads the Family Business Board (Somtoo, founding; Akunnia holding standing financial-reporting responsibility)
Family Archivist — preserves family history and documents
Children's Representative — gives the younger generation a formal voice in Council and Assembly proceedings before they reach full voting membership
IX. Membership & Voting Rights
Children move through stages of participation as they grow, aligned with the age tiers already established in the Family Education Structure and Family Library. But the House of Ezeme follows Igbo kindred custom on the question of the vote itself: once a person is admitted to sit in the meetings as a full member, their voice carries equal weight to any other member's, regardless of age, seniority, or how recently they were admitted. There is no partial or graduated vote — a member either has not yet been admitted, or is admitted and equal.
Observer (ages 8–12)
Present at the weekly family gathering and, where age-appropriate, the Family Assembly. May speak when invited. Not yet a member; no vote.
Participant (ages 13–17)
May raise matters directly, and speaks in Court, Council, and Assembly proceedings that concern them. Their account and preferences are formally recorded and weighed by the Secretariat. Not yet a member; no vote.
Member (from age 18, on admission by the Council)
Full and equal voting rights in the Family Assembly, the Family Council, the Family Court, and the Family Business Board simultaneously, from the moment of admission — consistent with the kindred custom that the right to sit in the meeting is the right to vote in it. Domain-heir responsibilities on the Business Board formalise separately, according to the Family Holding Structure, but do not gate the underlying vote.
Spouses admitted into the family in later generations join as full members upon marriage, at the Council's discretion.
X. Foundational Principles
Family before personal interest — members consider the long-term wellbeing of the family in major decisions
Equality before family rules — rules apply regardless of age, wealth, or status, while recognising appropriate parental authority over young children
The right to be heard — no serious accusation results in a decision without the accused being given the chance to respond
Respect — family disagreements must not become personal attacks
Responsibility — every member has responsibilities appropriate to their age and position
Transparency — family money and family businesses are properly accounted for through the Treasury and Business Board
Pay for work — everyone who works, whether inside or outside the family businesses, is paid for that work; membership in the family is not itself a form of compensation
Education — every child is prepared to understand the family's history, responsibilities, and resources
Independence — children are encouraged to develop their own careers and identities rather than being forced into the family businesses
Stewardship — family wealth is preserved and developed for future generations, not simply spent by the present one
Reconciliation — the objective of family justice is ultimately the restoration of relationships
The firewall — the Court, the Council, and the Business Board are never combined in a single sitting or a single dispute
XI. Rhythm of Governance
Weekly — Saturday
Morning: Family Court, convened only where a matter genuinely requires it
Evening: Family Council
Following Council: informal family time — meal, conversation, and education
Monthly
First Saturday: Family Business Board
A separate Saturday: Family Assembly, hearing reports and taking decisions that require the whole family
Annually — December or January
Annual Family Assembly: a full review of the year — achievements, business performance, the state of the Treasury, the children's progress, and objectives for the year ahead
XII. Amendment
This Charter may be amended by the Family Council at any regular sitting, provided the proposed amendment has been circulated to all members at least one week in advance, and ratified by the Family Assembly at its next sitting. Amendments to the founding co-chairs' reserve veto, to the equal-vote principle in Section IX, or to the separation of powers between the Court and the Business Board, require unanimous consent of all voting members.

Ezeme Family Holding Structure

EZEME FAMILY
Holding Structure
Five Children. Ten Sectors. One Empire.
Building a great intelligence network around Nigeria and Africa.
Part One · The Holding Structure
All sectors are owned under a single entity: the Ezeme Family Holding Company. Each of the five children owns and operates two naturally-paired sectors, creating deep vertical mastery rather than shallow breadth. No child works in isolation — the structure is designed for permanent interdependence.
1. Isiome · Agriculture & Food Systems · Manufacturing & Industrial Production
Domain: Raw production → value creation pipeline
Farming operations — crops, livestock, fisheries
Agricultural machinery design and manufacturing — tractors, tillers, harvesters, irrigation systems, and agro-processing equipment
Agro-processing and food packaging
Food distribution networks
Factories and processing plants
Industrial goods and exports
Why this merge works: Isiome grows it, builds the machines that work the land, and then processes what comes off it. His edge is owning the equipment layer that every farm and factory in the empire depends on.
2. Akunnia · Finance & Investment Systems · Governance, Law & Security
Domain: Capital control + institutional stability
Family investment fund and banking relationships
Credit, insurance, and capital allocation
Legal structure and compliance
Internal security and risk management
Arbitration and conflict resolution
Why this merge works: Akunnia controls what gets funded and ensures it is protected legally. She is the structural backbone of the entire holding company.
3. Idenze · Education & Human Capital · Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals
Domain: Human development — from formation to preservation
Schools, training institutions, and scholarships
Research and innovation pipelines
Clinics, hospitals, and public health
Herbal and pharmaceutical production
Why this merge works: Education builds people; healthcare keeps them alive and capable. A healthy, educated workforce is the foundation of every other division.
4. Uli · Media & Information Systems · Transport & Logistics
Domain: Movement of ideas and movement of goods
Media platforms — digital, radio, publishing
Brand and reputation management
Freight, delivery, and warehousing
Supply chain and mobility infrastructure
Why this merge works: narrative infrastructure and physical logistics are both distribution systems. Controlling what people hear and how goods reach them gives Uli enormous soft and hard power.
5. Okodu · Energy & Utilities · Construction & Real Estate
Domain: Physical infrastructure — power and built environment
Electricity generation — solar, grid, hybrid
Fuel and energy distribution
Land acquisition and development
Housing, commercial buildings, and infrastructure
Why this merge works: you cannot build without power, and power is useless without structures to serve. Okodu is the empire's engineer.
How the System Works
One Ownership Structure
All sectors sit under the Ezeme Family Holding Company. There is one roof, one ledger, one name.
The Family Council
The Council is led jointly by senior family founders or elders. Akunnia holds dual authority over finance and legal matters as the structural backbone. Isiome serves as strategic voice as first son. Every major decision passes through this body before it moves.
Interdependence Rule
No division is self-sufficient and none is meant to be. Isiome feeds the system; Akunnia funds and protects it; Idenze builds and sustains the workforce; Uli moves information and goods; Okodu powers and builds the physical world. Remove any one of them and the structure weakens — that vulnerability is intentional.
Part Two · Education Strategy
Core principle: foundation at home, then regional specialisation, then professional mastery — built without dependence on any single country's system. Each child works in at least two regions between ages 18 and 30, and spends structured time inside a sibling's sector.
All five children share the same language baseline before any domain-specific study begins: Igbo, English, French, Portuguese, and Spanish, as set out in the House of Ezeme Raising Plan. Below, each child's domain-specific sixth language — where one is needed — is listed alongside their academic track.
1. Isiome — Agriculture & Manufacturing
Age | Stage | Details | 0–10 | Home Foundation | Practical farming and mechanical fabrication at home | 10–15/16 | Secondary | DMGS, Onitsha · Industrial training at Geo-Lind Nigeria Limited, Rivers State | 16/17–19/20 | Bachelor's | Industrial Engineering — Tsinghua University, China | 21–23 | Master's 1 | Biosystems Engineering — Wageningen University & Research, Netherlands | 23–25 | Master's 2 | MSc Smart Manufacturing — Nanyang Technological University, Singapore | 25–28 | PhD | Agro-industrial Systems — University of São Paulo (USP), Brazil | Domain sixth language: Mandarin, for the China-facing industrial and supply track.
2. Akunnia — Finance, Law & Governance
Age | Stage | Details | 0–10 | Home Foundation | Mathematics, ethics, governance, and conflict resolution | 10–15/16 | Secondary | Queen of the Rosary College (QRC), Onitsha · Diplomatic academy courses | 16/17–19/20 | Bachelor's | Finance & Economics — National University of Singapore | 19/20–20/21 | LLB | Buckingham University, UK | 20/21–21/22 | Law School | Nigerian Law School, Abuja | 21/22–23/24 | Master's | Investment & Capital Systems — London Business School | 23/24–25/26 | PhD | Sovereign Wealth & Private Equity — Booth School of Business, University of Chicago | In Nigeria, entry to the Nigerian Law School requires an LLB. Akunnia completes her law degree first and earns her Call to Bar before building her finance credentials abroad. Domain sixth language: added only if a specific European posting requires it.
3. Idenze — Education & Healthcare / Pharmaceuticals
Age | Stage | Details | 0–10 | Home Foundation | Language, history, biology, and herbal medicine knowledge | 10–15/16 | Secondary | DMGS, Onitsha | 16/17–19/20 | Bachelor's | BSc Education + Biochemistry / Biological Sciences — University of Hong Kong | 21–23 | Master's 1 | MSc Education (Child Development & Education) — University of Oxford | 23–25 | Master's 2 | Master's in Pharmaceutics — NIPER, Mohali, India | 25–28 | PhD | Biotechnology & Pharmaceutical Sciences — University of Colorado Anschutz, USA | The BSc science component at the University of Hong Kong must be structured around Biochemistry or Biological Sciences from year one — a general education degree alone would not qualify. Domain sixth language: added only if a specific posting requires it.
4. Uli — Media & Transport / Logistics
Age | Stage | Details | 0–10 | Home Foundation | Storytelling, digital content creation, geography, trade systems | 10–15/16 | Secondary | Queen of the Rosary College (QRC), Onitsha · Logistics training at Zabeel Institute, UAE | 16/17–19/20 | Bachelor's | Global Communication Science — University of Amsterdam (UvA), Netherlands | 21–23 | Master's | MSc Logistics & Supply Chain Management — Heriot-Watt University, Dubai | Domain sixth language: Arabic, added only if her Middle East logistics posting requires it.
5. Okodu — Energy & Construction / Real Estate
Age | Stage | Details | 0–10 | Home Foundation | Physics, practical engineering, design, and spatial reasoning | 10–15/16 | Secondary | Ide Technical College, Nkpor · BOSIET certification | 16/17–19/20 | Bachelor's | Energy and Power Engineering — Tsinghua University, China | 21–23 | Master's 1 | Energy Systems Engineering — University College Dublin, Ireland | 23–25 | Master's 2 | Architecture & Urban Infrastructure — Architectural Association (AA), UK | Domain sixth language: Mandarin or German, for his China and European engineering partners.
Part Three · Key Decisions & Timelines
Language Strategy
Every child shares the same five-language foundation — Igbo, English, French, Portuguese, and Spanish — built through the House of Ezeme Raising Plan before any domain-specific study begins. A sixth language is added only where a child's specific university track or business region requires it: Mandarin for Isiome and Okodu, and Arabic or German where a specific posting for Akunnia, Idenze, or Uli calls for it. No child carries a language they do not have active use for.
Education Timeline
Academic Milestones
Home foundation: ages 0–10
Secondary school: ages 10–15/16
Bachelor's degree (3 years): ages 16/17–19/20
First master's: ages 21–23
Second master's: ages 23–25
PhD where applicable (Isiome, Akunnia, Idenze): ages 25–28
Best age to complete all formal education: 24–25 for master's-only tracks; 27–28 where a PhD is pursued. This keeps academic performance strong and avoids rushing postgraduate work.
Family Milestones
Marriage: ages 22–24
First child: ages 23–25
Second child: ages 25–27
Third child: ages 27–29
Fourth child: ages 29–32
Done having children: by ages 30–32 (ideal target: 31–32)
Rotation System
Between ages 18 and 30, each child works in at least two regions and spends structured time inside a sibling's sector. This is mandatory, not optional. The goal is to build cross-sector intelligence, prevent institutional blindness, and ensure every child understands the full system — not only their own division.
EZEME FAMILY HOLDING COMPANY
Five children. Ten sectors. One empire.

Ezeme Family Secure Hotspot Device

EZEME FAMILY
SECURE PERSONAL HOTSPOT PROGRAM
Revised Specification, Family Allocation & China ODM Sourcing Plan
Prepared for the Ezeme Group
July 2026

1. Executive Summary
This document defines the revised specification for the Ezeme Family Secure Hotspot: a custom, keychain-sized personal cellular gateway carried by each member of the family, sourced and manufactured through a China-based ODM (original design manufacturer) partner rather than built from a scratch PCB. The device gives each family member their own cellular identity, separate entirely from their phone's IMEI, while remaining centrally manageable by the family's own infrastructure.
The production run covers 20 units: two identical, name-engraved units for each of the seven family members (14 units), plus six additional units branded simply “Ezeme” held as a shared spare pool for guests, staff, or replacement stock.
Relative to the first prototype concept, this revision excludes GPS/GNSS and Bluetooth, and adds ultra-wideband (UWB) for short-range device-finding, NFC, an e-ink display, IP68 sealing, one USB-C charging port alongside retained Qi wireless charging, and dual active eSIM for two total carrier profiles. The unit also retains and reinforces the keyring/carabiner attachment shown in the original reference photo, so it continues to double as a physical keyholder.

2. Family Members & Device Allocation
The seven household members and their device allocation:
Family Member | Role in Household | Units Assigned | Engraving | Somtoo Ezeme | Principal / Father | 2 | “Somtoo” | Ifeoma Ezeme | Mother | 2 | “Ifeoma” | Isiome Ezeme | First Son | 2 | “Isiome” | Akunnia Ezeme | First Daughter | 2 | “Akunnia” | Idenze Ezeme | Second Son | 2 | “Idenze” | Uli Ezeme | Second Daughter | 2 | “Uli” | Okodu Ezeme | Third Son | 2 | “Okodu” | Shared / Spare Pool | Replacements | 6 | “Ezeme” | Total: 20 units. Personal units share identical hardware and firmware; only the laser engraving and the pre-loaded eSIM/WireGuard identity differ per unit.
3. Hardware & Firmware Specification
3.1 Form Factor
Keychain fob, approximately 62 × 42 × 20–22 mm
Use a structural plastic mid-frame with an integrated LDS (Laser Direct Structuring) antenna, and limit the aluminum to purely aesthetic side plates or a reinforced top loop for the carabiner
Fully sealed enclosure featuring a single gasket-sealed USB-C port at the base
IP68 rated (upgraded from IP67): sustained submersion resistance, not just splash resistance
3.2 Excluded By Design
GPS / GNSS receiver — not present. Location is not tracked by the device itself.
Bluetooth radio — not present. This shrinks the wireless attack surface; NFC and Wi-Fi cover pairing and connectivity without it.
3.3 Ultra-Wideband (UWB) — Safety Note
UWB is a distinct radio technology from GPS and does not compromise the no-satellite-tracking goal. It works by measuring the time-of-flight of radio pulses between two UWB chips (the same principle behind Apple's precision Find My and AirTag locating) — there is no satellite link, and typical usable range is roughly 10–30 metres. It supports the family's “find a misplaced unit” use case at short range, without any persistent location logging or third-party location reporting.
3.4 Charging & Data Connectivity
A single gasket-sealed USB-C port located at the base of the unit handles both wired charging and secure diagnostics
Have the ODM use a custom, smaller-diameter wearable-grade charging coil (similar to those found in smartwatches)
IP68 sealing is maintained using gasket-sealed USB-C connectors, standard on many rugged/marine-grade devices
3.5 Cellular Connectivity
Dual active eSIM (eUICC) — two eSIM profiles resident simultaneously with automatic failover
Firmware-level priority and failover logic across all two (2 eSIM) profiles, configurable per family member from the home management server
3.6 Added Capabilities
Ultra-wideband (UWB) — short-range precision device-finding (see 3.3)
NFC — tap-to-connect pairing between the fob and a phone or PC, and tap-to-authenticate for the management app
E-ink display — replaces OLED; shows signal, battery %, active eSIM profile. Near-zero idle power draw, always legible, readable in direct sunlight
Reinforced keyring clip / carabiner-style loop — the unit doubles as a keyholder, which is why the original reference photo showed a keyring attachment; this is retained and reinforced in the revised design
3.7 Retained From Original Concept
Automotive or Wearable-Grade LGA (Land Grid Array) 5G RedCap footprint (e.g., platforms based on Qualcomm X35). Meigsmart.com
Wi-Fi 6 (Dual-Band 2.4 GHz / 5 GHz only), optimized strictly for 2–3 simultaneous client devices to maximize standby battery efficiency for browsing/tethering only — no other pairing method is exposed
ARM processor, 512MB RAM and 2GB to 4GB eMMC Flash (anyone one that fits in and works better)
Secure element for cryptographic key storage
2,200 - 2,500 mAh battery (30+ hours target use)
Embedded Linux / OpenWrt firmware base
WireGuard VPN, WPA3, DNS-over-HTTPS, local firewall
LDS (Laser Direct Structuring) 2x2 MIMO Antennas
4. Security & Remote Management
Each unit is provisioned with a unique serial number, unique encryption keypair, and its own eSIM profile(s) at manufacturing time. Management runs from a home server under your own infrastructure, communicating with each unit over an authenticated WireGuard tunnel — not through the factory's or a third party's cloud.
4.1 Remote eSIM / Carrier Switching
To change a unit's active network carrier without physical access to the device, the management path is:
Phone app or PC utility → authenticated session (NFC tap or password manager + authenticator) → encrypted command channel over WireGuard → device's secure element validates the command → eSIM profile switch or download via SM-DP+ (the standard eSIM remote provisioning protocol) executes on-device
Both control paths (phone app and PC utility) authenticate against the same home management server; neither talks to the device directly over an unsecured local link
A lost or compromised unit can be remotely revoked from the home server, disabling its VPN and eSIM access without needing to recover the physical device
4.2 Key & Identity Management
Per-device encryption keys, rotated on a defined schedule from the home server
Family identity system: each person's two units share one logical identity in the management system, so usage policy and profile follow the person, not the individual fob
Firmware updates signed and pushed from the home server only — no direct-to-internet auto-update from the ODM's servers
4.3 USB-C Data Port Handling
The data-capable USB-C port stays in charge-only mode by default; data mode is enabled only after an NFC-tap authentication or an authenticated session from the phone app
Even when enabled, the port exposes only the signed management protocol — not generic mass storage, ADB, or a general-purpose data channel — so a malicious host computer cannot pull files off the device or push unsigned code to it
5. Prototype Concept
The physical layout of the device utilizes a pre-existing, ultra-compact factory shell instead of a custom-stamped metal ring. The front panel features the static E-ink display framed by a ruggedized rubber border, with a clear laser-engraved nameplate space near the base. A single gasketed USB-C port resides flush at the bottom rim, completely eliminating the bulky opposite-side dual ports and the physical SIM card tray openings. The integrated carabiner loop forms the dominant top anchor point of the chassis. Internally, the double-sided PCB sits flat against the E-ink display assembly, with the 2,500mAh LiHV battery pouch and the smartwatch-grade Qi wireless charging coil stacked directly beneath it along the back chassis plate.

6. China ODM Sourcing Plan
Custom hotspot hardware at this small scale (20 units) is best sourced through a Shenzhen-area ODM that already manufactures MiFi/hotspot devices, rather than a from-scratch hardware or custom PCB design. These factories can take an existing, mass-produced internal circuit board (PCBA), place it directly into a rugged, pre-existing factory enclosure from their current catalogue, apply custom per-unit laser engraving, and flash custom OpenWrt firmware images at low minimum order quantities (MOQs). This method completely eliminates upfront injection molding tooling fees and guarantees that the device keeps its certified IP68 water sealing out of the box.
6.1 Target Factory Profile
Existing Product Line: Factory must have active production lines for 4G/5G MiFi or pocket hotspot devices with native eSIM (eUICC) support
Willing to Support Low MOQs: Capable of supporting a 20-unit batch by using off-the-shelf internal boards (PCBA) and existing plastic housing parts
Sealing Experience: Experienced with assembling IP68 or rugged wearable enclosures using internal silicone gaskets and ultrasonic plastic welding
Firmware Access: Familiar with OpenWrt or provides a complete Linux SDK/API that allows the family's engineers to load custom security configurations
Personalization & Provisioning: Capable of laser-engraving custom names on the shell and flashing unique cryptographic keypairs onto each unit before shipping
6.2 Tooling and Enclosure Strategy (Zero Custom Molds)
To keep this 20-unit production run economically viable and avoid over $15,000 in upfront tooling costs, no custom injection molds will be created
Enclosure Selection: The ODM must select a pre-existing, rugged plastic or composite keychain/pocket enclosure from their current catalogue that closely fits the target dimensions.
Internal Modifications: Any adjustments needed to secure the single USB-C port, the E-ink display screen, or the smartwatch-grade Qi wireless charging coil must be done using custom internal 3D-printed or CNC-milled plastic brackets, leaving the outer factory shell completely unmodified to preserve its original IP68 seal
Antenna Optimization: Because an off-the-shelf plastic enclosure is used, the ODM can easily apply internal LDS (Laser Direct Structuring) or flexible adhesive PCB (FPC) antennas inside the shell without needing to cut custom external windows.
6.3 Certification
Even for private family use, request that the factory's base board retain its existing CE certification for EU travel, and confirm NCC type-approval status for use within Nigeria. Re-skinning a certified board is far simpler to certify than a ground-up design.
7. Outreach Message to ODM Factories (Ready to Send)
The following can be sent as-is via Alibaba/Global Sources messaging or email to shortlisted MiFi/hotspot ODM factories:
Subject: RFQ — Custom Personal 4G/5G eSIM Hotspot, 20-Unit Semi-Custom Run
Hello,We are requesting a quote for a small, semi-custom production run of 20 personal cellular hotspot units for a private family deployment (not for resale). We are looking for a factory with an existing MiFi/hotspot product line that can accommodate the following modifications:
Form factor: keychain fob, approx. 62 × 42 × 20–22 mm, aluminium frame with rubberised edge, reinforced keyring/carabiner clip (unit doubles as a keyholder)
Connectivity: industrial 4G/5G modem, dual active eSIM (eUICC) with automatic failover, plus a dual physical nano-SIM tray (up to 4 total carrier profiles)
Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi 6 or 6E access point, 10–15 simultaneous client devices, hotspot/tethering only
Display: e-ink (not OLED), showing signal strength, battery percentage, active eSIM/SIM profile
Charging: two USB-C ports on opposite sides, plus Qi wireless charging — all three charging paths present simultaneously
Data: one USB-C port additionally supports a restricted, authenticated PC data/management link (no generic mass storage or ADB exposure)
Additional radios: NFC (tap-to-connect) and UWB (short-range precision device-finding; not GPS-based)
Radios to exclude: no Bluetooth, no GPS/GNSS module
Sealing: IP68 rating, including gasket-sealed USB-C connectors
Firmware: OpenWrt or embedded Linux with WireGuard VPN, WPA3, and secure-element-backed key storage; please confirm SDK availability for custom firmware
Per-unit customization: 14 units require individual laser engraving with a name we will supply per serial number; remaining 6 units require uniform “Ezeme” branding
Per-unit provisioning: each unit requires a unique device serial, unique encryption keypair, and a distinct pre-loaded eSIM profile at time of manufacture
Could you please advise: (1) whether an existing mold can be adapted or a new mold is required, (2) unit cost and mold/tooling cost at this quantity, (3) lead time for a first sample unit, (4) your firmware customization process and SDK documentation, and (5) current certification status (CE / NCC) of your base board.Thank you — we look forward to your quotation.
8. Phased Timeline
Phase | Activity | Sourcing | Shortlist ODM factories, send RFQ, evaluate mold options — 4–8 weeks | Sampling | First sample unit built and shipped for testing — 3–4 weeks | Revision | Battery, heat, Wi-Fi range, Holafly/roaming, VPN reliability testing; 1–2 revision rounds — 2–3 weeks each | Production | Full run of 20 units, individually provisioned and engraved — 3–4 weeks | Deployment | Home management server setup, per-person onboarding, travel workflow testing | 9. Open Risks & Considerations
Two USB-C ports plus a Qi coil in a 62×42×20–22mm shell is tight; expect the ODM to push back toward the upper end of that thickness range, or to request a slightly larger shell, once dual SIM tray and dual charging ports are added to the e-ink display and antenna array
Even with firmware restricted to a signed management protocol, a USB-C data port is inherently a larger attack surface than none at all; the mitigation (charge-only by default, NFC/app-authenticated to enable data mode) should be treated as a requirement in the RFQ, not an afterthought during firmware development
Confirm with Holafly (or chosen eSIM provider) that the specific plan purchased explicitly permits hotspot/tethering use before relying on it as the primary connectivity path
Dual eSIM plus dual physical SIM adds RF design complexity (four possible active profiles sharing the antenna array); confirm with the ODM how many can be simultaneously active versus standby, since this affects real-world failover speed
UWB and NFC add bill-of-materials cost and require the ODM to confirm chipset availability at this order volume — verify during RFQ stage rather than assuming standard MiFi platforms include them
