Ezeme Family Tech Independence Guide

Ezeme Family Tech Independence Guide
FEDORA LINUX · LINUX MINT · GREPHENEOS · LINEAGEOS
A practical, buy-and-build guide: desktop OS, phones, laptops, and a gaming/editing PC.
1. Desktop Operating Systems
No Linux distro perfectly clones macOS or Windows, but two get close enough for real daily use — especially paired with the right ecosystem tools.
Closest to macOS — Fedora Workstation (GNOME)
Clean top bar, hidden app dock, smooth multi-finger trackpad gestures
KDE Connect / GSConnect — shared clipboard, wireless file transfer, phone notifications on desktop
Software Center works like the Mac App Store — click “Install,” no terminal needed
Closest to Windows — Linux Mint (Cinnamon)
Traditional taskbar, organised start menu, familiar shortcuts (Win+E = file explorer)
Built-in Driver Manager auto-detects printers, drawing tablets, GPUs
Downloads .deb files straight from the browser, plus a full software manager
Ecosystem replacements
Apple / Windows feature | Open-source replacement | How it works | iCloud / OneDrive | Nextcloud | Free cloud storage for photos, contacts, calendar sync | AirDrop / Nearby Share | LocalSend or KDE Connect | Instant file sharing over Wi-Fi between PCs and phones | MS Office / iWork | LibreOffice | Reads/writes native .docx and .xlsx | Find My Phone | OwnTracks | Self-hosted, private location tracking | The recommendation
Install Fedora Workstation on the family’s laptops/desktops and link them to GrapheneOS phones (see below) with KDE Connect. You get macOS-level polish on the desktop with none of the vendor lock-in, and a private, auditable phone ecosystem to match.
Reality check: some proprietary software (Adobe Creative Cloud, certain corporate VPN clients, kernel-anti-cheat games) still won’t run natively on Linux. Keep a dual-boot or VM option for these edge cases.
2. Phones — GrapheneOS on Pixel
GrapheneOS is a fully open-source, hardened Android build with Google’s tracking layer stripped out.
Free to install — your only cost is the phone itself
Officially supported only on Google Pixel hardware (its security model depends on Pixel-specific chips)
Which Pixel to buy
Budget: Pixel 9a or Pixel 10a
Best balance: Pixel 9 / 9 Pro or Pixel 10 / 10 Pro — 8th-gen+ Pixels get a 7-year update guarantee plus hardware memory tagging
Buy new and carrier-unlocked — locked phones can block the bootloader unlock GrapheneOS installation needs
Skip the Pixel 6 series for a fresh purchase now — nearing end-of-life for security patches
App ecosystem — GrapheneOS
GrapheneOS ships deliberately bare-bones. The Fossify suite (formerly Simple Mobile Tools) is the most-used community pick to fill it out — open-source, ad-free, and each app only requests permissions it actually needs.
Fossify Contacts and Fossify Messages — clean replacements for Google’s contacts and SMS/MMS apps, with no Google account or RCS backend required.
GrapheneOS Files stays as the system file picker — it’s what other apps call for “choose a file” and share-sheet actions, and GrapheneOS integrates it tightly, so there’s no need to replace it at that level.
Fossify File Manager becomes the everyday file manager — the app you actually open to browse, move, zip, and search files day to day, sitting alongside (not instead of) GrapheneOS Files.
Aves Libre — everyday photo and video gallery for quick viewing and browsing on-device.
Immich (app) — handles automatic backup, syncing every new photo and video to Immich running on the MS-01 for long-term storage on your own server, replacing Google Photos.
GrapheneOS Camera — Default camera for everyday use.
Google Camera — Installed with network access disabled, used only when you want its superior computational photography.
GeoShare — Its primary purpose is to translate map links between different mapping services, allowing you to open a location from one map app in another.
Fossify Calendar – A calendar app for managing events, reminders, birthdays, and recurring appointments. It supports local calendars and CalDAV synchronisation if you use a compatible server.
Fossify Clock – Provides alarms, timers, stopwatch, and world clock features. It works entirely offline.
Standard Notes – A lightweight encrypted note-taking app for creating and organising text notes.
Pocket Paint — An open-source image editor for drawing, painting and basic photo editing with layer support.
Translate You — A privacy-friendly translator supporting multiple translation engines, including LibreTranslate, DeepL and Lingva.
Cheogram — An XMPP messaging app with support for bridging to SMS and other messaging networks through compatible servers.
CalcYou — A modern open-source calculator with scientific functions, history and unit conversions.
HeliBoard — A privacy-focused open-source keyboard with multilingual support and gesture typing.
FUTO Keyboard — An offline keyboard with local voice typing and predictive text powered by on-device AI.
Proton VPN — An encrypted VPN app designed to protect your internet traffic and privacy.
Ente Auth — An end-to-end encrypted authenticator app for securely storing and syncing 2FA codes.
LibreTorrent — An open-source BitTorrent client supporting magnet links, encryption and sequential downloading.
Tuta Mail — An end-to-end encrypted email app focused on privacy and security.
Vaultwarden — A Bitwarden-compatible password manager client for connecting to your self-hosted Vaultwarden server.
Nextcloud Calendar — A CalDAV calendar app for synchronising events with your self-hosted Nextcloud server.
Tuta Calendar — An end-to-end encrypted calendar integrated with Tuta Mail.
MySudo — A privacy service providing additional phone numbers, email addresses and virtual identities.
Metro — An open-source YouTube Music client with a clean, privacy-friendly interface.
MPV — A lightweight open-source media player supporting virtually every audio and video format.
Jellyfin — A client app for streaming media from your self-hosted Jellyfin server.
Fossify Voice Recorder — An open-source voice recorder that stores recordings locally.
Brave Browser — A Chromium-based browser with built-in ad, tracker and fingerprinting protection.
Cromite — A privacy-focused Chromium browser with enhanced security and anti-tracking features.
Collabora Office — An office suite for viewing and editing Microsoft Office and OpenDocument files.
Aurora Store — An anonymous client for downloading apps from Google Play without a Google account.
SearXNG Search (Searxist) — A privacy-respecting search app for querying your own or public SearXNG instances without tracking.
KeePassDX — An offline password manager compatible with KeePass databases.
Aegis — An open-source authenticator app with encrypted backups and offline 2FA support.
Obtainium — An app manager that installs and updates apps directly from developers’ official releases.
LibreTorrent — An open-source BitTorrent client supporting magnet links, torrent encryption, sequential downloading and background downloads.
Jitsi Meet — An open-source, end-to-end encrypted (where supported) video conferencing app that lets you host or join secure meetings without requiring an account.
Worth rounding out the same way: Fossify Calendar, Fossify Clock, and Standard Notes cover Google Calendar/Clock/Keep, and DAVx5 syncs Fossify Contacts and Calendar to Nextcloud (CalDAV/CardDAV) so phone data lands on the MS-01 automatically — closing the loop with the Section 6 stack. For the handful of apps only on the Play Store, Aurora Store gives anonymous, account-free access to that catalog, and Obtainium auto-updates anything installed directly from GitHub or F-Droid outside an app store.
Smartwatches — Gadgetbridge
Most smartwatches and fitness trackers only work through the manufacturer’s own app and cloud account — Gadgetbridge replaces that. It’s an open-source Android app that pairs directly with the watch over Bluetooth and keeps all step, sleep, and heart-rate data on the phone itself, with no vendor account, no cloud sync, and no internet permission required at all.
Supports a wide range of budget-friendly hardware — Mi Band, Amazfit, and Pebble are among the best-supported, with partial support for many Fossil, Garmin, and other watch families
Installs from F-Droid or Aurora Store, same as the rest of the app stack — no Google Play account needed
Can export activity data locally, or sync it into Home Assistant for anyone who wants their step count or sleep pattern to show up alongside the rest of the home dashboard
What’s lost vs. retained moving from stock Pixel to GrapheneOS
Honest breakdown of Google’s AI camera, calling, and hardware features — what’s gone, what has a private alternative, and where the original genuinely wins.
Feature | On GrapheneOS | Alternative | Magic Editor / Magic Eraser | Lost — needs Google Photos + cloud processing | IOPaint | Camera Coach, Add Me, Auto Best Take | Lost — Google Camera app proprietary | Open Camera | Video Boost | Lost — uploads video to Google to process | None, but also nothing of yours leaves the house | Pixel Studio / Gemini image generation | Lost | Self-hosted Stable Diffusion/Flux via ComfyUI on Box 4 — arguably better once built, loses in-camera convenience | Gemini video generation | Lost | Open video models exist but meaningfully behind Google’s quality; original wins here | Live Translate (calls), Call Screen, Hold for Me | Lost — Assistant/server-dependent | None off-the-shelf; original wins | Call Notes | Lost — needs Gemini Nano/Private Compute Core | Manual recording (where legal) plus your own Whisper/Ollama transcription after the fact | Spam/Scam Detection, Direct My Call, Wait Times | Lost — tied to Google’s carrier spam database | Third-party apps (Truecaller etc.) harvest contacts to their own cloud — not recommended for a privacy-focused family; genuine gap | Pixel Feature Drops | GrapheneOS follows its own release cadence, tracking Android security patches only | Different update model, not a single lost feature | Wireless charging (Qi2/Pixelsnap) | Retained — hardware standard, unrelated to Google software | No loss at all | RCS messaging | Partially retained via optional Sandboxed Google Play running Google Messages | Fossify Messages alone drops RCS entirely, falling back to SMS/MMS with non-family contacts | For kids
Google Family Link doesn’t work reliably on GrapheneOS. Use TimeLimit (F-Droid, open-source) for screen-time limits, plus GrapheneOS’s built-in per-app network/permission controls and separate restricted user profiles.
3. Laptops That Rival the Latest MacBooks
Laptop | Why it competes | Razer Blade 16 (2026) | Thin aluminum chassis, OLED display, MacBook Pro-level build quality with far more raw GPU power | Dell XPS 14 (2026) | Intel Lunar Lake efficiency, adaptive-refresh display, 20+ hours of real-world battery | Lenovo ThinkPad T14s Gen 6 | Best durability and keyboard, 21+ hours battery in testing | For full tech independence: modular and Linux-native options
If you want laptops built around the same philosophy as the rest of this guide — repairable, auditable, no forced OS — these two are the premium picks:
Framework Laptop 13 or 16 (DIY Edition): The ultimate premium option for a tech-independent family. These high-performance laptops are completely modular — you can upgrade, repair, or swap every single part yourself. Buying the DIY Edition means it ships with no operating system installed, so you pay zero Windows licensing fees.
System76 Laptops (Oryx Pro or Lemur Pro): A premium US-based company that designs high-end laptops specifically for Linux. Their computers feature open-source firmware (Coreboot), meaning corporate spyware cannot hide at the motherboard level.
4. Gaming Laptops
Laptop | Best for | ASUS ROG Zephyrus G16 (RTX 5080) | Best balance of portability (under 4.5 lbs) and power, 240Hz OLED | Razer Blade 16 (2026) (RTX 5090) | Thinnest chassis in its power class, dual-mode 4K/240Hz or 1080p/440Hz display | Lenovo Legion Pro 7i / Pro 9i (RTX 5090) | Desktop-class cooling (liquid metal, triple fans) for sustained heavy loads | HP Omen Max 16 (RTX 5090) | Near-flagship performance at a more competitive price than Razer/Alienware | Razer Blade 18 / MSI Titan (RTX 5090) | 18-inch 4K panels — closest a laptop gets to full desktop performance | Rule of thumb: portability-first -> Zephyrus G16 or Blade 16. Laptop-replacing-a-desktop -> Blade 18 or Legion Pro 9i class.
5. Gaming + Editing PC — Full Build Guide
Since you’re building rather than buying, here are three complete, ready-to-buy parts lists. Desktop still gives the best performance per dollar and is the easiest to upgrade over time.
Tier 1 — Mid-range (~$1,700–1,900): 1440p/4K gaming, light editing
Part | Pick | CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D | Motherboard | MSI MAG B850 Tomahawk MAX WiFi | GPU | RTX 5070 (12GB) | RAM | 32GB DDR5-6000 CL30 | Storage | 2TB Gen4 NVMe SSD | Cooler | Noctua NH-D15 (air) or 280mm AIO | PSU | Corsair RM850x — 850W, 80+ Gold, fully modular | Case | Lian Li Lancool III | Tier 2 — High-end (~$2,600–2,900): native 4K gaming, serious video editing/rendering
Part | Pick | CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 9900X | Motherboard | ASUS ROG Strix X870E-E WiFi | GPU | RTX 5080 (16GB GDDR7) | RAM | 64GB DDR5-6000 CL30 | Storage | 4TB Gen5 NVMe SSD | Cooler | 360mm AIO (e.g., Corsair Titan 360 RX ARGB) | PSU | Corsair RM1000x — 1000W, 80+ Gold, fully modular | Case | Lian Li O11D EVO | This tier is genuinely dual-purpose: handles 4K/240Hz gaming, streaming, and heavy Premiere/DaVinci Resolve timelines without hesitation.
Tier 3 — Flagship (~$4,500+): no-compromise 4K, AI-assisted editing/rendering
Part | Pick | CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D | Motherboard | ASUS ROG Strix X870E-E WiFi (or E-ATX equivalent) | GPU | RTX 5090 (32GB GDDR7) | RAM | 64–128GB DDR5-6000+ | Storage | 4TB+ Gen5 NVMe SSD | Cooler | Custom water loop or 420mm AIO (essential at this power draw) | PSU | Corsair AX1500i — 1500W, Titanium efficiency | Case | Corsair 1000D Airflow (E-ATX, supports dual 360mm radiators) | Overkill for gaming alone, but the RTX 5090’s 32GB VRAM is what actually matters for AI-assisted rendering, local AI model use, and future-proofing against 2027–2028 titles.
Build notes
Building takes 3–4 hours your first time; budget an evening, not an afternoon
Confirm PSU has enough dedicated 12V-2x6 (or 8-pin) connectors for your GPU — the 5080/5090 draw significant transient power spikes
For Tier 2/3, use PCIe Gen5-native motherboards to get full bandwidth from Gen5 SSDs and future GPU upgrades
6. Private Family Digital Infrastructure — The MS-01 Blueprint
This is the design document for a fully family-controlled digital ecosystem, replacing dependence on Google, Microsoft, Dropbox, rented RDPs, and scattered cloud subscriptions with one private, self-hosted stack.
Core philosophy
Your family owns its own: data, identity, photos, documents, communication, passwords, knowledge, remote computers, and smart-home systems. The system is built around privacy, security, redundancy, long-term ownership, and family archive preservation.
Hardware foundation
Rather than one box running everything, the infrastructure splits across four machines (the fourth optional but recommended for AI workloads). This removes the single point of failure a lone server creates and keeps the firewall on its own hardware — best practice regardless of scale, since a service crash or update should never be able to take the firewall down with it.
Box 1 — Dedicated firewall appliance: a Protectli Vault or fanless Intel N100 mini PC (~$150–250) running OPNsense only. Nothing else runs on this box, so the firewall stays up regardless of what happens on the other two.
Box 2 — Minisforum MS-01 Mini Workstation (core services): the main machine: private family server, workstation, and cloud platform in one, running Nextcloud, Immich, Vaultwarden, Authentik, Home Assistant, and Frigate day to day. It replaces rented RDP servers, several cloud subscriptions, and external storage dependency. CPU: Intel Core i9-13900H (14 cores / 20 threads), dual 10GbE SFP+ and dual 2.5GbE ports. RAM ceiling: 96GB DDR5 — plenty for the full container + VM stack. Storage: 3x M.2 NVMe slots plus a PCIe x16 (x8 speed) slot for a U.2/SATA expansion card — reaching ~24TB realistically means either 3x large NVMe drives or adding a HBA/expansion card for extra SSDs, not a single drive. Worth knowing: Minisforum’s newer MS-02 Ultra (launching 2026) supports up to 256GB RAM and 32TB storage across four M.2 slots — worth comparing if you want more headroom than the MS-01 offers before committing.
Box 3 — Secondary mini-PC (backup + failover): a second, smaller machine — a used mini PC or a second Minisforum unit — that does two jobs. First, it’s the local-backup leg of the 3-2-1 rule: it receives nightly BorgBackup snapshots from the MS-01. Second, it runs its own dormant copies of Vaultwarden and Nextcloud, stopped by default, that start up and point at the latest snapshot if the MS-01 goes offline — so family password access and file sync survive a hardware failure instead of going dark until it’s repaired. Tailscale keeps the same hostnames reachable no matter which box is actually serving a given app, so nothing changes on the family’s phones or laptops during a failover. Box 3 also pushes an encrypted copy of its backups to off-site storage (rsync.net or Backblaze B2) — completing the 3-2-1 rule end to end: production on Box 2, local backup and failover on Box 3, off-site copy in the cloud.
Box 4 — AI Acceleration Server (Optional, but Recommended for the Full Stack) While Box 2 runs the family’s daily services, the AI capabilities described throughout this guide — local LLMs (Ollama), image/video generation (Stable Diffusion/Flux), advanced speech-to-text (Whisper), high-quality text-to-speech (Coqui TTS), and heavy Jellyfin transcoding — perform best when they have dedicated, GPU-optimised hardware.
The recommended “Sensible Starter” AI Server configuration:
Component | Specification | Platform | AMD Threadripper Pro workstation (enterprise-class board) | RAM | 256 GB ECC DDR5 (error-correcting, critical for long AI jobs) | GPU | 1 x NVIDIA RTX 5090 (32 GB GDDR7 VRAM) | Storage (System) | 2 TB NVMe SSD (Fedora/KVM host OS and containers) | Storage (AI Models) | 4 TB NVMe SSD (dedicated to Ollama models, ComfyUI checkpoints, and Whisper pipelines) | Storage (Data/Cache) | 16 TB HDD (local dataset cache, temporary rendering output, or an additional backup mirror) | Networking | 10 GbE (fits seamlessly with the MS-01’s dual SFP+ ports) | Power Protection | 2 kVA online UPS (dedicated, matching the UPS strategy for Boxes 1-3) | Why this build works for Box 4:
Threadripper Pro’s PCIe lanes let the RTX 5090 run at full x16 bandwidth while simultaneously driving 10 GbE and both NVMe drives.
32 GB VRAM comfortably runs quantized 70B-parameter models (Llama 3.1 70B) entirely in memory, and makes Flux image generation, 4K video upscaling, and real-time Frigate object detection effortless.
The 4 TB AI model drive means the family can keep multiple foundation models loaded without shuffling files.
10 GbE matches Box 2’s port speed, so Box 4 can pull 4K video files for transcoding or feed raw Frigate clips into a vision model at wire speed.
The 16 TB HDD gives Box 4 local scratch space for rendered AI outputs, large dataset caches, or an extra backup destination.
Box 4 connects to the same Tailscale network, mounts the MS-01’s shares, and exposes its services only to the internal VLAN via Caddy, keeping the four machines isolated by purpose:
Box 1 — Gateway (OPNsense)
Box 2 — Family data & daily logic
Box 3 — Resilience & off-site backups
Box 4 — Heavy computation & AI

6.1 Hardware Philosophy
The Ezeme family’s long-term objective extends beyond self-hosting software and data. It is to progressively own and control the hardware that delivers those services wherever doing so provides meaningful advantages in privacy, security, repairability, longevity, and integration.
The Ezeme family develops custom software only when it delivers capabilities that existing open-source software cannot reasonably provide. Wherever mature, secure, and well-maintained open-source solutions already meet the family’s requirements, they are adopted instead of being unnecessarily recreated.
The family follows a pragmatic engineering philosophy rather than attempting to reinvent every device. Mature, enterprise-grade hardware such as servers, networking equipment, storage systems, and laptops will continue to be purchased from trusted manufacturers when they already meet the family’s security and reliability requirements. Custom hardware is developed only where it provides clear value that commercial products cannot.
Every dedicated Ezeme hardware product follows the same design principles:
Family ownership rather than vendor dependence.
Privacy by design, with no mandatory third-party cloud services.
Security-first architecture using modern cryptographic standards.
Offline-first operation, allowing core functions to continue without Internet access.
Repairability through modular construction and replaceable components.
Long-term software support with family-controlled firmware updates.
Open standards wherever practical to avoid vendor lock-in.
Integration with the Ezeme Backend as the trusted source of identity, storage, automation, and management.
Rather than viewing each device as an isolated product, the family treats every hardware device as part of one integrated ecosystem. Phones, laptops, media frames, smart mirrors, voice assistants, home dashboards, and future appliances communicate securely with the family’s infrastructure using the same authentication, update, and management framework.
Hardware development follows an incremental approach. New devices begin as prototypes using commercially available modules and development boards to validate functionality and user experience. Once the design has stabilised, custom printed circuit boards (PCBs) are developed to improve reliability, reduce wiring complexity, optimise power consumption, simplify assembly, and provide dedicated security hardware. This staged approach reduces development risk while ensuring that only mature designs progress into custom manufacturing.
This philosophy allows the Ezeme family to balance innovation with practicality. Commodity hardware is adopted where it already satisfies the family’s requirements, while custom hardware is reserved for products that become long-term family assets and contribute directly to the family’s digital independence.
The Ezeme Hardware Platform
The Ezeme Hardware Platform is the standard hardware architecture developed for dedicated devices within the Ezeme Family ecosystem. It establishes common engineering, security, software, and manufacturing standards to ensure that all family-owned devices operate as a unified platform rather than as isolated products.
Every device built under the Ezeme Hardware Platform is designed according to the same core principles:

Privacy by design with no mandatory third-party cloud services.
Security-first architecture using hardware-backed cryptography and encrypted communications.
Long-term software support through Ezeme OS.
Modular and repairable construction using replaceable components wherever practical.
Offline-first operation for essential functions.
Seamless integration with the Ezeme Backend and Ezeme Portal.
Standardised authentication, firmware updates, and device management.

6.3 Hardware Security Architecture
The Ezeme Family ecosystem is designed according to a Zero Trust security model. No device is automatically trusted simply because it is connected to the family network. Every device must prove its identity before it is granted access to family services. Security is implemented as multiple independent layers that work together to protect the family’s data, infrastructure, and hardware throughout the device lifecycle.
Rather than relying on a single security mechanism, every Ezeme device incorporates hardware-backed security, encrypted communications, secure software updates, strong authentication, and continuous integrity verification.
Security Design Principles
Every Ezeme hardware device follows these principles:
Security by design rather than as an afterthought.
Hardware-backed trust wherever practical.
Defence in depth using multiple independent security layers.
Least-privilege access for every application and service.
Zero Trust authentication between devices.
Privacy by default.
Offline-first operation.
Family ownership of encryption keys.
Secure recovery without exposing sensitive data.
Hardware Root of Trust
Each Ezeme device establishes a hardware root of trust during manufacturing. This hardware identity forms the basis of all future authentication, encryption, firmware verification, and secure communication.
Where supported by the hardware platform, cryptographic keys are generated within a dedicated secure element or Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and cannot be extracted by software.
The hardware root of trust enables:
Secure device identity.
Secure Boot verification.
Firmware validation.
Device authentication.
Encryption key protection.
Secure certificate storage.
Secure Boot
Every Ezeme device should support Secure Boot.
Secure Boot ensures that only firmware digitally signed by the Ezeme Family can be executed during startup. If firmware has been modified or replaced by unauthorised software, the device refuses to continue the boot process and enters recovery mode.
This prevents malicious firmware from compromising the device before the operating system has loaded.
Verified Boot
Following Secure Boot, Verified Boot validates every stage of the operating system startup process.
This includes verification of:
Bootloader.
Operating system kernel.
System partitions.
Recovery partitions.
Security configuration.
If any component has been altered unexpectedly, the device prevents normal startup until the integrity of the software has been restored.
Device Identity
Every Ezeme device receives a permanent identity during provisioning.
Each device is assigned:
Universally Unique Identifier (UUID).
Hardware serial number.
Device model.
Hardware revision.
Firmware version.
Manufacturing date.
Owner assignment.
Cryptographic device certificate.
These identities allow the Ezeme Backend to distinguish trusted devices from unknown hardware.
Encrypted Storage
Sensitive information stored on each device is encrypted.
Protected information includes:
Operating system configuration.
Device certificates.
Authentication tokens.
Local media cache.
Family data.
User preferences.
If a device is lost or stolen, encrypted storage significantly reduces the likelihood of sensitive data being recovered.
Communication Security
All communication between Ezeme devices and family infrastructure is encrypted.
Communication security includes:
Mutual TLS authentication.
Device certificate verification.
Modern TLS encryption.
Certificate rotation.
Certificate revocation.
Replay attack protection.
Secure API authentication.
Devices communicate only with trusted services within the Ezeme Family ecosystem unless explicitly authorised.

Every update is:

Cryptographically verified before installation.
Installed through secure update channels.
Automatically rolled back if verification fails.
Recorded in the device audit history.

7. Extra Privacy Layers — Without Cutting Yourself Off
A few additions round out the household’s privacy without forcing an all-or-nothing break from mainstream services.
Network-level
VLANs on OPNsense to segment IoT devices, guest Wi-Fi, and family devices from each other — a compromised smart plug shouldn’t be able to reach your server
DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS on top of AdGuard Home so even your ISP can’t see plaintext DNS queries
SearXNG (self-hosted, can run on the same MS-01) as a private search proxy — keeps search queries off Google without giving up search results
WiFi hardening checklist
Four steps do essentially all the real work; two commonly-recommended steps add daily friction without meaningfully stopping anyone determined, so they’re left off.
Strong, random password — 12+ random characters, changed from any router default, set under the router/AP’s Wireless -> Security page
WPA3-Personal (or WPA2/WPA3 mixed) — set the Security Mode on the same page; mixed mode keeps older devices connecting while still using WPA3 where supported
WPS disabled — the WPS PIN can be brute-forced in hours; turn it off in the same wireless settings
Guest network on its own VLAN — already covered above; visitor devices never reach the family network or the MS-01 boxes
Skip MAC address filtering and SSID hiding — MAC addresses are trivially spoofed by anyone already on the network, and a hidden SSID is still broadcast in device probe requests. Both add daily hassle (re-adding every new device, breaking guest auto-connect) without stopping a motivated attacker.
Messaging and browsing
Signal for day-to-day family messaging — end-to-end encrypted, minimal metadata, easy for non-technical family members
Molly (a hardened Signal fork) as an optional upgrade — adds a database passphrase and extra lock-screen hardening on top of Signal for anyone who wants it
Matrix/Element self-hosted (optional, more advanced) if you want messaging fully under the family’s own server
A hardened browser (Librewolf or Brave) with uBlock Origin across all family devices
OrganicMaps or a self-hosted OSM-based maps app in place of Google Maps for routine navigation
NewPipe or LibreTube for YouTube without an account, ads, or Google Play Services
Physical and camera privacy
Frigate NVR + enterprise PoE IP cameras instead of Ring/Nest — footage stays on the MS-01, not a vendor’s cloud. PoE (Power over Ethernet) cameras take both power and network over a single Ethernet cable and stream over RTSP/ONVIF, which Frigate connects to directly with no vendor app or cloud account in the loop.
Axis PoE IP cameras — the best-regarded option for this setup: enterprise build quality, streams over RTSP/ONVIF, and Axis’s own VMS software is entirely optional — connect straight to Frigate and ignore it.
Managed PoE switch on a dedicated camera VLAN — isolates cameras from the rest of the family network, the same VLAN principle already used for IoT devices above.
OPNsense firewall rule: cameras can reach the MS-01, nothing else — no internet access at all for the camera VLAN, so even a compromised or vulnerable camera has nowhere to phone home to.
Google Coral TPU for on-device AI detection — plugs into the MS-01 and gives Frigate fast, local person/vehicle/animal detection, so nothing about what the cameras see ever leaves the house.
Tailscale for remote viewing — open the Frigate or Home Assistant app on a GrapheneOS phone from anywhere — Bansko, Dubai, Sao Paulo — and watch live or recorded footage over an encrypted tunnel, using the same Tailscale connection already set up for the rest of the MS-01 stack. No separate coordination server to run, no vendor sees the traffic.
Label one guest-network SSID clearly for visitors’ phones so their devices never touch the family VLAN
Resilience and continuity
Follow the 3-2-1 backup rule: production data + local backup + one encrypted off-site copy (e.g., rsync.net or Backblaze B2, encrypted client-side by BorgBackup before upload)
Store Nitrokey backup and Vaultwarden emergency-access details somewhere a trusted family member or lawyer can reach if you’re unavailable — private infrastructure still needs a succession plan
Keep one conventional email/cloud account alive (used for nothing sensitive) for services that flatly require Google/Microsoft login — banking portals, government sites, school systems — so the family isn’t blocked out of anything essential
8. Ezeme Smart Mirror Platform
8.10.1 Overview
The Ezeme Smart Mirror is designed to operate as a trusted device within the Ezeme Digital Platform rather than as an isolated appliance. Every Ezeme device communicates securely with an Ezeme Backend, which provides identity management, synchronisation, application distribution, policy enforcement, device management, media services, and shared platform services.
The Ezeme Backend is deployment-independent and may be implemented in several ways depending on the user's requirements:
Ezeme Family Server – the self-hosted deployment recommended throughout this guide for families who want complete ownership of their data and infrastructure.
Ezeme Cloud – a commercially hosted deployment operated by Ezeme for users who prefer managed services.
Ezeme Enterprise Server – a self-hosted deployment for businesses, schools, churches, hotels, hospitals, museums, government organisations, and other institutions.
Hybrid Deployment – a combination of local infrastructure and cloud-hosted services, allowing organisations or families to choose where individual services operate.
Regardless of the deployment model, every Ezeme device communicates using the same secure APIs, authentication mechanisms, application framework, and security architecture provided by Ezeme OS. This allows devices to move between deployment models without requiring changes to their firmware or applications.
The Smart Mirror is one member of the Ezeme Display Platform, a common hardware and software architecture that also powers the Ezeme Family Media Frame, future Kitchen Display, Home Dashboard, and other display-based family devices. All of these products share the same operating system, security architecture, module framework, update mechanism, and device management platform while delivering user experiences tailored to their individual roles.
Rather than functioning as a general-purpose computer, the Ezeme Smart Mirror is designed to provide only the information appropriate for a mirror. Information should be immediately understandable within a few seconds while standing in front of the mirror. More detailed management tasks are performed through dedicated Ezeme applications and dashboards elsewhere within the family ecosystem.
The Smart Mirror therefore serves as a trusted, secure, and permanent household appliance that contributes to the family’s long-term vision of building an entirely family-owned digital infrastructure.
8.2 Objectives
The Ezeme Smart Mirror is designed with a clear purpose: to provide useful daily information without compromising privacy, security, or simplicity. Every design decision should support the wider objectives of the Ezeme Family Digital Infrastructure.
The objectives of the Smart Mirror are to:
Provide glanceable information that can be understood within a few seconds.
Preserve the appearance and primary function of a traditional household mirror.
Integrate securely with the Ezeme Backend.

Present relevant information automatically without requiring users to unlock a phone or launch applications.
Support multiple family members through personalised user profiles where appropriate.
Protect family privacy through secure authentication, encrypted communications, and hardware-based security features.
Receive secure operating system, firmware, and application updates throughout its service life.
Share a common hardware and software platform with other Ezeme display devices to simplify development, maintenance, and manufacturing.
Remain modular, repairable, and upgradeable to maximise its useful lifespan.
Support future expansion through the Ezeme Module Framework without requiring fundamental hardware redesign.
The Smart Mirror is not intended to replace the Ezeme Home Dashboard, Farm Dashboard, Kitchen Display, or Family Media Frame. Instead, it provides a focused, distraction-free interface for essential daily information while specialised devices handle more advanced monitoring, administration, and interactive tasks.

8.7 Ezeme OS
8.7.1 Overview
Ezeme OS is the trusted operating system powering every hardware device within the Ezeme Family Digital Infrastructure. Rather than functioning as a traditional desktop operating system, Ezeme OS is purpose-built for dedicated family appliances where privacy, security, reliability, and long-term maintainability take precedence over general-purpose computing.
The operating system provides a common software foundation for all Ezeme hardware products, ensuring consistent behaviour, security policies, update mechanisms, and hardware management across the ecosystem. Whether running on the Smart Mirror, Family Media Frame, Kitchen Display, or future devices, every Ezeme device shares the same operating system while delivering experiences tailored to its intended role.
Ezeme OS separates the operating system from user-facing applications. Device-specific functionality is provided through dedicated applications such as Ezeme Mirror, Ezeme Frame, and Ezeme Kitchen, allowing new hardware products to be introduced without creating separate operating systems.
8.7.2 Core Responsibilities
Ezeme OS is responsible for managing all core system functionality, including:
System boot and hardware initialisation.
Processor, memory, and storage management.
Hardware abstraction.
Device drivers.
Display management.
Audio management.
Networking.
Secure communications.
User authentication.
Device identity.
Hardware security.
Secure storage.
Background services.
Application lifecycle management.
Software updates.
Device diagnostics.
System logging.
Communication with the Ezeme Backend.
Applications should rely on these shared services rather than implementing duplicate functionality.

8.7.4 Secure Boot Process
Every Ezeme device should follow an authenticated startup sequence.
Power is applied.
Boot ROM executes.
Secure Boot verifies the bootloader.
Verified Boot validates the operating system.
Security hardware is initialised.
Ezeme OS loads.
The Ezeme Runtime starts.
The appropriate Ezeme application launches.
The device authenticates with the Ezeme Backend.
Normal operation begins.
If any verification stage fails, the device should refuse to boot untrusted software and instead enter a secure recovery mode.

Secure recovery environment.

Unified Platform Architecture

Ezeme Applications.

This separation between device software and backend infrastructure ensures that Ezeme remains scalable, maintainable, and adaptable to future family, commercial, and enterprise deployments while preserving a consistent user experience and security model.
8.7.11 Design Philosophy
Ezeme OS is designed to remain the long-term software foundation of the Ezeme Family Digital Infrastructure. It prioritises family ownership, privacy, security, and interoperability over dependence on proprietary cloud ecosystems.
The operating system should be modular, hardware-independent where practical, and capable of supporting multiple generations of hardware without requiring significant architectural changes. 9. Local Voice Assistant — Voice and Text, Fully Offline
A single assistant, built on Home Assistant Assist, handles both spoken and typed requests for the whole family, running entirely on the MS-01 stack with no cloud service in the loop. Every stage — hearing, understanding, thinking, and replying — runs locally.
Future generations will migrate to dedicated Ezeme hardware featuring a custom PCB, secure hardware architecture, and Ezeme OS while remaining compatible with the family’s self-hosted infrastructure.
The stack
Stage | Tool | Role | Wake word | Home Assistant Voice satellite (openWakeWord) | Listens locally for the trigger phrase before sending anything onward | Speech-to-text | Whisper (faster-whisper) on the MS-01 | Converts speech to text without sending audio anywhere off the house | Intent handling | Home Assistant Assist | Matches known phrases straight to actions (lights, locks, sensors) without needing the AI model at all | Open-ended AI | Ollama | Handles anything that isn’t a defined smart-home command — questions, conversation, help with homework | Text-to-speech | Piper | Converts the reply back to natural-sounding speech, fully offline, and is the best foundation if an Igbo voice gets trained later | Text interface | Home Assistant app’s Assist chat, or a custom family chat page | Lets anyone type instead of speak and still reach the same pipeline | Future generations will migrate to dedicated Ezeme hardware featuring a custom PCB, secure hardware architecture, and Ezeme OS while remaining compatible with the family’s self-hosted infrastructure.
One assistant, voice or text
Rather than separate systems for speaking and typing, both paths feed the same backend: a wake word or a typed message both land in Home Assistant Assist, which checks known intents first and falls through to Ollama for anything open-ended, then replies in writing, out loud through Piper, or both. Every family member can speak to it, type to it, and get either kind of reply back, from a phone, tablet, or a speaker in the room.
Building toward Igbo language support
Out of the box, neither Whisper nor Piper understand or speak Igbo — this is the honest starting point. But the architecture is built to accept custom language models rather than being locked to what ships by default, and there’s a practical path forward in stages:
Available today — hand-defined Igbo intents: Home Assistant Assist (and Rhasspy’s approach, which can be borrowed the same way) lets you map specific Igbo phrases straight to actions without needing a full Igbo speech model at all — e.g. “Gbanwuo oku ulo” -> turn on the living room lights, or “Gosi m akuko Anambra” -> show Anambra news. This works immediately with a handwritten phrase list.
Medium term — fine-tuning Whisper for Igbo speech recognition: requires an Igbo speech corpus (recorded audio paired with text) to fine-tune Whisper or faster-whisper, so the assistant can understand open-ended Igbo speech rather than only fixed phrases.
Medium term — training a Piper voice for Igbo: Piper can be trained on new languages given enough recorded voice data, giving the assistant a natural-sounding Igbo speaking voice rather than falling back to text only.
This connects directly to the Ide Igbo dialect dictionary project already underway — the pronunciation data, phrase entries, and phonological rules being built for the dictionary are the same kind of resource an Igbo Whisper or Piper model would need, so the two efforts can share groundwork rather than duplicate it.
Coqui TTS as an alternative worth knowing about — higher voice quality and voice-cloning support than Piper, at the cost of being heavier and more GPU-intensive — realistic once Box 4’s AI hardware is in place, if a distinctive family voice matters more than raw efficiency.

10. Drone Program — Agriculture and Family Business
Built as an aviation department, not a gadget purchase: the airframe is one part of a stack that spans flight hardware, autopilot software, AI, and the same self-hosted infrastructure already running the rest of the family’s systems.
Airframe and flight hardware
Airframe — chosen by purpose: quadcopter for general use, hexacopter for heavy lifting, octocopter for professional camera work and redundancy, fixed-wing for long-distance mapping, VTOL for vertical takeoff plus long range. Holybro, Tarot, T-Motor, and Foxtech are the established manufacturers.
Flight controller — Pixhawk 6X or Cube Orange+ as the top picks; Cube Red, Pixhawk 5X, and Holybro Durandal as alternatives.
Autopilot software — PX4 (best for research, AI, autonomous work, future expansion) or ArduPilot (best for agriculture, heavy lifting, the more mature ecosystem). Both are free and open source.
Companion computer — NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano is the top pick for on-board AI (computer vision, object detection, obstacle avoidance, live inference); Raspberry Pi 5, Jetson AGX Orin, Intel NUC, and UP Squared are the alternatives depending on how much AI horsepower is needed on the airframe itself.
GPS — Here4, HerePro, Holybro H-RTK F9P, or Cube RTK — skip cheap GPS modules. RTK GPS specifically is needed for surveying, agriculture, and mapping, and gets accuracy down to roughly 1-2 cm.
Telemetry radio — Holybro SiK Radio, RFD900, or Microhard for drone-to-ground-station communication.
Radio controller — RadioMaster TX16S running EdgeTX (open source firmware) as the top pick; FrSky Tandem and Jumper T20 as alternatives.
FPV system — OpenHD for open-source, high-definition digital video; the ExpressLRS ecosystem for analogue.
Camera and gimbal — Sony cameras or Raspberry Pi Camera HQ for video, Sony global shutter cameras for mapping, FLIR for thermal; Gremsy or Tarot gimbals for stabilization, with Storm32 as the open-source option.
Motors, ESCs, propellers — T-Motor, KDE Direct, BrotherHobby, or Sunnysky for motors; Hobbywing, T-Motor, or Holybro for ESCs; APC, Gemfan, Master Airscrew, or T-Motor for propellers.
Batteries — LiPo or Li-ion with smart chargers (ISDT, HOTA, ToolkitRC) and fire-safe storage; a battery tester to monitor health and internal resistance over time.
Software — ground station, mapping, and AI
Purpose | Tool | Ground station | QGroundControl (top pick), Mission Planner, or MAVProxy | Flight logging | OpenDroneLog, self-hosted | Mapping | OpenDroneMap + WebODM — produces orthophotos, 3D models, point clouds, digital elevation models, fully self-hosted | On-board AI | YOLO, OpenCV, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime — runs locally on the Jetson | Where it plugs into the existing MS-01 stack
File storage — Nextcloud holds videos, maps, flight logs, manuals, and firmware, same as the rest of the family archive.
Photo management — Immich for imagery captured on missions.
Documentation — Wiki.js for maintenance procedures, training manuals, repair guides, and checklists.
Source code and firmware — Forgejo (see Section 14) stores firmware, AI models, scripts, and CAD files under version control.
Monitoring — Grafana and Prometheus (see Section 13) track battery cycles, storage, telemetry service uptime, and server health.

Bulk imagery storage — MinIO (see Section 14) is genuinely useful here specifically, since OpenDroneMap/WebODM output (orthophotos, point clouds) is large binary data that some tooling expects to reach through an S3-compatible API rather than a plain filesystem.

11. Media Library — Jellyfin Ecosystem
Jellyfin (already in the Section 6 stack) is the streaming server; everything below builds around it — tracking what’s been watched, getting purchased discs into the library, letting the family request titles, and keeping everything organized automatically.
Watch tracking
Ryot — self-hosted tracker covering movies, TV, books, and games in one place, with automatic scrobbling from Jellyfin so watched status updates without manual entry.
Movary and MediaTracker are the other options in this space — Movary is movie-only (TV support planned), and MediaTracker has reported slowdowns in recent versions that are worth testing on your own hardware before relying on it. Ryot is the pick going in here.
Getting owned Blu-rays into the library
For the best long-term experience, use a dedicated Media Ingestion Station connected to your home server. Rather than ripping discs from the playback device, this separate appliance handles the entire process automatically while Jellyfin clients focus solely on watching content.
Dedicated Media Ingestion Station — a small Linux-based appliance (Mini PC or server with one or more Blu-ray drives) that acts as the family’s disc archive. Simply insert a Blu-ray or DVD, close the tray, and the system performs the entire workflow automatically without requiring a keyboard or monitor.
ARM (Automatic Ripping Machine) — monitors the optical drive, automatically detects an inserted Blu-ray or DVD, launches the ripping process, and manages the complete workflow without user intervention.
MakeMKV — the decryption and archival engine used by ARM to create a full-quality MKV copy of the disc while preserving video, audio, subtitles and chapters. It can also be used manually for one-off discs.
HandBrake (or FFmpeg) — optionally creates smaller, streaming-friendly versions for phones, tablets and slower network connections while keeping the original archival-quality rip.
Metadata automation — tools such as Tiny Media Manager automatically identify the title, download posters, artwork, cast information and descriptions, and organise the files into the correct Jellyfin folder structure.
Jellyfin — automatically detects the newly added media, updates the library, downloads any remaining metadata if required, and makes the film or series available across authorised family devices without any manual importing.
The complete workflow becomes:
Insert disc → ARM detects it → MakeMKV creates an archival-quality copy → HandBrake optionally creates additional streaming versions → Metadata is downloaded and organised → Jellyfin scans the library automatically → Eject disc → The title is immediately available throughout the home.
Real limitation worth planning around: not every film or television series receives a physical DVD or Blu-ray release. Most major theatrical films eventually do, but many streaming-exclusive Originals from services such as Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, Apple TV+ and others are never released on physical media. As a result, a library built entirely from owned discs will inevitably have gaps—not because of any technical limitation, but because no physical edition exists to archive.
Requests and library organization
Jellyseerr — the Jellyfin-compatible fork of Overseerr (Overseerr itself is built for Plex). Gives family members a clean interface to browse and request titles, with an optional approval step for what the kids can request.
Radarr and Sonarr — automatically organize, rename, and file new movies (Radarr) and TV episodes (Sonarr) into the library once they arrive, and notify Jellyfin to refresh. Scoped here to the family’s own ripped Blu-ray collection and other legally-acquired files.
Streaming vs. downloading
Streaming directly from the MS-01 without downloading anything is Jellyfin’s default behavior on every device — the kids just press play, same as Netflix, pointed at the family server instead. Downloading for offline viewing is a separate, optional button in the Jellyfin apps. On a weaker connection, Jellyfin also does real-time server-side transcoding, adjusting bitrate/resolution on the fly — worth factoring into Box 4’s compute headroom, since transcoding several simultaneous streams is real load.
Automating StreamFab
Can StreamFab Be Automated?
Officially, no. StreamFab does not provide a public API that the Ezeme Family Dashboard, Jellyfin, Jellyseerr, Radarr, or Sonarr can communicate with directly.
Although StreamFab is only available for Windows, macOS, and Android, it can still be integrated into the family’s Linux-first infrastructure by running it inside a dedicated Windows virtual machine hosted on the family server using KVM/QEMU (or Proxmox VE, where applicable). The remainder of the family’s self-hosted ecosystem—including Jellyfin, the ARR stack, and the Ezeme Family Dashboard—continues to run natively on Linux.
A custom StreamFab Automation Agent runs inside the Windows virtual machine and acts as the bridge between the Linux-based Dashboard and StreamFab. Rather than communicating through an API, the agent automates StreamFab’s graphical interface in the same way a user would by using desktop automation tools such as AutoHotkey or Python.
Automatic Acquisition Workflow
The Ezeme Family Dashboard orchestrates media acquisition automatically while allowing family members to continue using Jellyfin as their primary interface for discovering, watching, and requesting films and television series.
 A family member searches for a film or television series in Jellyfin.
If the title already exists in the library, playback begins immediately.
If the title is unavailable, the user selects Request, which sends the request to the Ezeme Family Dashboard.
The Dashboard verifies the user’s permissions, applies AI moderation and parental-control policies, and forwards the request to Jellyseerr.
 Jellyseerr coordinates Radarr or Sonarr to search the configured indexers and download clients.
If a suitable release is found, the media is downloaded, imported into Jellyfin, and the requester is notified automatically.
If Radarr or Sonarr reports “No release found”, “Failed”, or cannot successfully acquire the media within the configured timeout, the Dashboard automatically triggers the StreamFab Automation Agent.
The automation agent launches StreamFab inside the Windows virtual machine, opens the configured streaming provider (such as Netflix or Amazon Prime Video), searches for the requested title, and starts the download automatically.
After the download completes, the media is copied into the family’s shared Linux media library.
Jellyfin automatically detects the new media, or the Dashboard refreshes the library, and the requester receives a notification that the content is available.
If the requested title cannot be acquired through either the ARR stack or the configured streaming services, only the family administrator is notified for manual review.

This workflow provides a seamless experience for the family. Members continue to use Jellyfin as their media application, while the Ezeme Family Dashboard transparently coordinates requests, parental approvals, automation, notifications, and fallback acquisition without exposing the underlying infrastructure. The Windows virtual machine exists solely to host StreamFab, ensuring the remainder of the family’s self-hosted ecosystem remains Linux-native.

As the stack has grown well past a dozen services, grouping them this way keeps the whole system understandable rather than a flat list of app names.
Group | Services | Administration | OPNsense, AdGuard Home, Authentik, Caddy, Cockpit, Ntfy | Personal | Nextcloud, Immich, Vaultwarden, Paperless-ngx, Wiki.js, Home Assistant, Syncthing, Tuta, TriliumNext/BookStack, Firefly III | Monitoring | Uptime Kuma, Grafana, Prometheus, Scrutiny, Beszel/Netdata, Speedtest Tracker | Development | Forgejo, It-Tools, Ollama/Open WebUI, Perplexica | Media | Jellyfin, Ryot, Jellyseerr, Radarr, Sonarr, Bazarr, Prowlarr, Jellyfin Intro Skipper, Jellystat, Wizarr, Recyclarr, Maintainerr, Decluttarr, Unpackerr, Tdarr, FileFlows, Notifiarr, Frigate, Immich, Kavita, Calibre-Web | Drone & Workshop | QGroundControl, OpenDroneLog, OpenDroneMap/WebODM, MinIO, OctoPrint | Knowledge & News | MuckScraper, Ollama, SearXNG | The Ezeme Family Dashboard, built on Homepage or Homarr, is the central control centre for the family’s technology ecosystem. Beyond providing a unified homepage, it coordinates authentication, API integrations, notifications, automation, AI moderation, parental controls, request management, and system monitoring. All specialised services—such as Jellyfin, Audiobookshelf, Immich, Nextcloud, Calibre-Web, and Home Assistant—integrate with the Dashboard, which orchestrates communication between them while leaving each service focused on its core function.
Future Direction: Homepage serves as the family dashboard during the initial phases of the project. As the Ezeme ecosystem matures, it will gradually be replaced by Ezeme Home, the official companion application and management platform for the Ezeme ecosystem. Ezeme Home will be available on Android, iPhone, iPad, Windows, macOS, Linux, and modern web browsers, providing a consistent interface for configuring, monitoring, and managing every Ezeme device.
Through Ezeme Home, users will be able to:
Add and configure Ezeme devices.
Connect photo, music, video, calendar, weather, and AI providers.
Customise Smart Mirror layouts and widgets using a live preview.
Manage family members and permissions.
Install software, firmware, and approved modules.
Monitor device health and security.
Receive notifications and alerts.
Access devices remotely where permitted.
Ezeme Home becomes the central management platform for the entire Ezeme ecosystem while specialised services such as Jellyfin, Immich, Nextcloud, Home Assistant, and Audiobookshelf continue performing their own dedicated functions.
Universal Request Workflow
The Ezeme Family Dashboard uses a consistent workflow for all requests across the family’s self-hosted ecosystem. Whether a family member requests a movie, audiobook, eBook, music album, software package, or other digital content, the Dashboard follows the same process while delegating service-specific tasks to the appropriate application.
Each integrated service then performs its specialised role. For example:
Movies & TV → Overseerr → Radarr/Sonarr → Jellyfin
Audiobooks → Audible → Libation → Audiobookshelf
eBooks → Calibre-Web or Kavita
Music → Navidrome
Photos → Immich

Ezeme Family Vibe coding Structure

EZEME FAMILY
Holding Structure — Part Four
Vibe Coding & Technology Literacy
Every child codes. Each child codes differently.
The Principle
The future does not belong to those who can write code. It belongs to those who can direct machines precisely — who know what to build, how to describe it, and how to evaluate what comes back. This is vibe coding: the discipline of building software through natural language, intelligent prompting, and iterative refinement using AI tools.
All five Ezeme children will master vibe coding as a baseline life skill, the same way they will all master the family's core languages. It is not optional, and it is not technical — it is literate.
Beyond this universal baseline, each child develops a second layer of technology fluency specific to their two domains. The baseline is the same; the depth is their own.
Part A · Universal Vibe Coding Baseline
1. Prompting Discipline
The ability to describe what you want to a machine with precision and intent — a writing skill, a thinking skill, and a communication skill, which is why it begins in the home foundation years alongside language and storytelling.
Describing problems before describing solutions
Iterating on outputs — knowing what is wrong and why
Providing context, constraints, tone, and format in a single instruction
Chain-prompting: breaking complex builds into logical sequences
2. Core AI Tool Fluency
Hands-on use of the leading vibe coding and AI-assisted build tools. Children begin with the simplest tools at age 10 and graduate to the full professional stack by age 16.
Claude · ChatGPT · Gemini — language model fluency
Lovable · Bolt · v0 — UI and product vibe coding
Cursor · GitHub Copilot — code-adjacent AI editing
Notion AI · Perplexity — research and document intelligence
Midjourney · Runway · ElevenLabs — multimodal generation
3. Product Thinking
Knowing what to build is more valuable than knowing how to build it.
User problem framing: who is this for, and what pain does it solve?
Feature scoping: what is the minimum version that delivers value?
Flow mapping: what does a user actually do inside this product?
Feedback loops: how do you know if something is working?
4. Data Literacy
Every division of the Ezeme Group runs on data. Every child learns to read it, question it, and act on it before they reach university.
Reading dashboards and interpreting KPIs
Understanding the difference between correlation and causation
Building simple models and projections in AI-assisted spreadsheet tools
Querying data with natural language (asking Claude to analyse a dataset)
5. Basic Systems Understanding
Not coding — systems. Understanding that the digital world is made of databases, APIs, front ends, and servers makes every child a better director of machines and a better manager of technical teams.
What a database is and why structure matters
What an API is and how services talk to each other
What a front end is and how users interact with systems
Hosting, deployment, and the difference between a prototype and a live product
Part B · Universal Delivery Timeline
Phase | Ages | What is taught | Home Foundation | 0 – 10 | Storytelling, logic games, and age-appropriate AI exploration. Children learn to describe what they imagine before they can type it. | Secondary School | 10 – 16 | Formal vibe coding curriculum begins: tool fluency, product thinking workshops, one personal AI-built project per year, and introduction to domain-relevant technology. | Pre-University | 16 – 18 | Each child completes one personal vibe-coded project in their primary domain before leaving for university, reviewed by the Family Council. | University & Beyond | 18+ | Domain-specific tech fluency deepens through field exposure. The universal baseline is already complete. | Part C · Domain-Specific Technology Fluency
Each child's vibe coding baseline is identical. What differs is the technology landscape they learn to command as a director, not an operator, of the systems that run their industry.
1. Isiome — Agriculture & Food Systems · Manufacturing & Industrial Production
Farm Management Systems (Granular, Trimble), IoT soil/climate sensors, drone and satellite imagery, commodity pricing platforms, cold chain logistics
MES and ERP systems (SAP, Odoo), quality control and defect tracking, supply chain visibility, industrial automation interfaces
Pre-university project: an AI-powered farm-to-factory dashboard tracking one crop from field to packaged product.
2. Akunnia — Finance & Investment Systems · Governance, Law & Security
Bloomberg Terminal literacy, AI-assisted financial modelling, FactSet/Refinitiv, capital markets data, deal tracking tools
Contract analysis AI (Harvey, Clio), compliance systems, risk dashboards, legal document management, governance reporting
Pre-university project: a live investment dashboard for the Ezeme Family Holding Company, with a governance log of major family decisions and their financial impact.
3. Idenze — Education & Human Capital · Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals
LMS platforms (Canvas, Moodle), adaptive learning AI, student performance dashboards, curriculum design tools, credentialling platforms
EHR systems, clinical trial management, drug discovery databases (PubChem, ChEMBL), telemedicine infrastructure, pharma supply chain monitoring
Pre-university project: an AI-powered student health and learning tracker surfacing patterns that suggest intervention needs.
4. Uli — Media & Information Systems · Transport & Logistics
CMS platforms, audience analytics (GA4, Chartbeat), programmatic advertising, podcast/video distribution, SEO and AI writing tools
TMS and WMS systems, last-mile delivery tracking, freight forwarding and customs documentation, fleet telematics
Pre-university project: a dual-dashboard platform pairing media audience engagement with a logistics shipment corridor on one screen.
5. Okodu — Energy & Utilities · Construction & Real Estate
Microgrid modelling (HOMER Pro), SCADA systems, solar and grid monitoring, smart meter analytics, carbon accounting tools
BIM (Revit, ArchiCAD), GIS and spatial planning (QGIS, ArcGIS), construction project management (Procore), real estate data platforms, digital twins
Pre-university project: a GIS-based development tracker for Akuzo, connected to a financial model showing cost per unit of built infrastructure.
Part D · Implementation Summary
Vibe coding literacy is threaded through the existing education structure. The additions are minimal and targeted.
What changes | How it is implemented | Home Foundation (0–10) | Structured AI play alongside existing language and storytelling practice: describe-and-build games, logic puzzles, age-appropriate tool exposure. | Secondary School (10–16) | A dedicated technology literacy block — 2 to 3 hours per week — covering universal tool fluency and beginning domain-specific exposure. One personal project per year. | Pre-University Project (16–18) | Each child completes and presents one domain-specific vibe-coded product to the Family Council before departure for university — a rite of passage, not an exam. | University (18+) | Domain-specific tools deepen through coursework and fieldwork. No formal curriculum needed — the baseline and the habit are already established. | Family-wide practice | Annual family review: each child demos one AI-built tool or insight from their domain, keeping all siblings literate in each other's technology landscape. | No child of this family will be managed by a technical team they cannot direct. No child will sign off on a digital product they cannot evaluate. And no child will leave secondary school without having built something that works, something that solves a real problem, something they made with the power of language alone.
EZEME FAMILY HOLDING COMPANY · Part Four · Vibe Coding & Technology Literacy
